This is an odd one that I almost didn't pick up, but I'm glad I did.
Graphics:  Republique is a pretty game.  The level design and the lighting are very well done, and the art direction is very interesting. Sometimes the only way to see a guard is the looming shadow he's casting from around the corner, and Hope's (main character) face is remarkably detailed.  The only gripe for me is the character models themselves, what they're wearing, are not very detailed.  But this game was originally released for the iPad so I think that may be part of the problem.
Gameplay:  I was initially put off by this being a point and click stealth game, but having played if for myself now I can say the controls work very well.  The player switches between security cameras in the level to gain a vantage point and direct Hope through the levels.  It's a little akward at first, but once you get used to I think you have even better situational awareness this way than you would with a traditional third person camera.  The stealth is very reminiscent of the first two Metal Gear Solid games where stealth is completely based on line of sight, so the gameplay is all about hiding behind objects (or inside lockers), determining guard patrol paths, and waiting for an opening.
I tend to think of stealth games as a kind of puzzle game.  Where the puzzle is figuring out how to get form A to B without being seen.  Most games like Splinter Cell or Metal Gear Solid have combat systems which allow you to, if you get frustrated, throw the puzzle out the window and then pick the next one up from the pile.  Republique has no combat system aside from using items like tazers or pepper spray, so you cannot brute force your way through the tougher sections of the game.  Having said that, after I got firmly aquinted with the game sometime early in the second episode I would say that while some areas are tougher I haven't yet found a section I deemed unfair.
Story:  In my opinion, as interesting as the game is, the narrative is the real high point of this game.  Set in a fictional cult society isolated from the rest of the world, you live in a surveilence state where everyone is both a name and a number.  We aren't told what it is Hope did to get in trouble but the system has had it out for you when the game begins and it's up to you to help her escape.
But what is truely impressive is not the main story itself, but the world that the writers create around you.  Throughout the game you have ample opportunities to scan objects in the environment that reveal tid bits about the mysterious city you are trying to escape, or conversations between people that are very telling of the live they have to live in this place.  I would say that the depth of the universe here rivals the work done by 2k's writers in Bioshock and Bioshock Infinite.  And similarly to those games it is through audio logs, email exchanges, and hacking people's voicemails that you find out little bits and pieces of this world you are in that make it so believable.
Overall:  It's a very interesting concept that really works.  It will take some getting used to, but it's a solid stealth game.  And if you are into losing yourself in a virtual world, there are few games that create as convincing a universe as Republique.
Final Note: This game is episodic.  At the time of this review, only episodes 1-3 of the 5 episode story are available.  This should not, however, discourage you from buying the game, as you do not pay by the episode as other episodics do.  When you buy the game, you are paying for all five episodes, it's just that not all five episodes are ready right now.

The Thinking with Time Machine Mod for Portal 2 has a nice idea, but it's a kinda boring in my opinion.
So I saw that mod and was kinda excited about it, because I love the Portal games and mods for it have to be good. Too bad this mod proved that I was wrong ...
At first the idea behind this mod is that you use a clone of you to help you completing testchambers.
First you record actions you would do to get progress and after that you play the recordings. These will create a clone, who will go through the actions you recorded in before, and while that clone does the actions, you recorded, you can do other actions and that's key to success in a testchamber.
Sounds great doesn't it?
Yeah sure, but the problem is some of the few testchamber, this mod has, are  that confusing, so you will take quite some time to understand what to do and where to use your clone. Unlike the portal 1 and portal 2 games, which had nearly none of such testchamber, so you mostly got into a testchamber and knew what to do, the only problem there was the execution.
So back to the mod, besides the problem with confusing testchamber another problem the mod has is that is none real story,  so this mod not more than a level pack with a new mechanic.
Also that new mechanic was kinda boring in my opinion, because after the first 2 or 3 testchamber I was kinda bored from the mechanic, because it was always the same in the few testchambers of the mod:
1. Figuring out how to finish the chamber
2. Record the action for the clone
3. Stand in a specific place
4. Wait for the clone to finish the action
5. Press the last button
Yeah I know portal in general was also always the same somehow, but every few levels there was something new and also you advanced in the story of the game, but in this mod there isn't much a story as I said in before.
So all in all I have to say I wouldn't recommend this mod, because it gets boring pretty fast and without a story there isn't a real motivation to finish it. You can try it out on your own, but don't expect much from that mod, because it isn't much more than a level pack with a new mechanic for portal 2.

I'm done playing this game. I enjoyed the lore and was interested in pursuing the story, but I wanted to play on Permadeath mode to force myself to manage resources and not get drawn too far into the sandbox aspect to finish quests.
My most recent problem was the last straw of many similar problems: a singleplayer latency/lag bug caused me to fall into the lava at the core of the planet while I was building a path over it in a way that should not have caused me any problems. The game then lagged too much for me to hop back out onto the adjacent platform before damage, stacked through the lag spike, annihilated me. I lost several hours of gameplay on permadeath mode, along with my first diamond.
Permadeath is a nice challenge mode in concept, but if an engine flaw is what kills you instead of actual game design, then it really only leads to frustration; it's not anything the player can improve upon other than "well, that part of the game's broken- avoid it completely." This stinks if you're trying to explore the progressive difficulty of the game's levels and planets.
It's a fun enough sandbox on the surface if you're bored, and it's got a quirky sense of humor in its flavor text; as far as challenge, it's difficult to measure until/if single player lag spike / memory leak issues are managed. I'm disappointed that I won't see it through because of its strong concept and style, but the game flow is constantly interrupted by issues on the software backend, so the tradeoff in frustration sadly wasn't worth it to me.

Enjoying this game so far. I have made it about 52% of the way through the story mode and tried out the Bright Lord and Master of the Hunt modes, both of which have very similar gamplay to the story mode.  Cut scenes with background information on the characters are included when you start and complete major quests relevent to the story line, all are short and sweet so you don't feel impatent waiting for them to finish. One thing I most definitely love are the characters. I never thought I would appreciate an orc but there's at least one with interesting personality traits that makes him a good comedic sidekick for a good chunk of story. The dwarf also has some funny back and forth with Talion once you get to the second stage. Throughout the game you get smaller quests to boost your experience such as revenge, assasination, aid the rebels, rescue the slaves, look for sigils, look for relics, etc quests. For the first three you generally have to kill a minor captain and his goons, which will leave a position open for a new captain so these quests recycle themselves so there's always something to do.
Very few graphical problems, on occasion it will spontaneously stop working and shut down but in all instances it has never happened while I was in the middle of a quest so I'm not too bothered by it. Also on rare occasions the window will shrink down and I have to go open it up again, sometime during battle sometimes not, but it hasn't gotten me killed yet so again not too much of a bother for me.The only thing that took me by surprise midway through my gameplay was a specific revenge side quest. Not the quest itself, it was very basic, but the title of the quest threw me for one. I don't know how these quests names are generated or who inculded this one in the list of possible quest titles but "Revenge for the Boiled Jew" struck me as ... dark, is the best word I can come up with. Yes, I know this is a game that involves killing in gruesome often bloody ways but these are all fantastical/science fiction creatures and in keeping with that fantasy theme there should not include any mention of a real group of people who were the victims of a real life genocidal maniac. JRR Tolkien, the creator of the world this game is based off of, fought and lost friends fighting against the Nazis in WWII and for the game creators to include this is disrespectful to him and all those who lost their lives. While this on its own will not prevent me from continuing gameplay it has lessened my enjoyment.

Hello, this is my review of Stranded Deep. I will list the pros and cons, also my personal thoughts of this game down below.
Cons:
Can get boring after a while
Some glitches they still need to work out

Island hopping can be a bit annoying
Pros:
Very visually appealing, especially people who are attracted to the tropical feel
Castaway simulator

Personal thoughts of this game, and what could be done to have a more positive affect:
The team who made this game NEEDS to hire some more staff if they want to get this game done while it is relevant, as of right now they make an update about once a month. They really need to add more content other than gameplay changes and graphical changes, not to say those are bad, the new primitive fire system makes this game feel a lot more realistic and gives a warm feeling. Graphical changes are nice but not needed, the game looks fine. They just need to add new materials and creatures, also some items would be nice. Overall I'd give this game an 8/10. The game is very nice but can get really boring after you complete the little amount there is to do in this game. As stated above, getting more staff and releasing updates more often would be very good for this game. Also, hunting sharks in the water is equally terrifying as it is fun. Would recommend waiting for some updates before buying, but still a very good game with a lot of potential.

I am recommending this game (the Complete Edition is best) with some serious caveats. First, the good bits... it is an entertaining, light-hearted, turn-based, fantasy 4x strategy game that is quite good at evoking that infamous "one more turn" feeling. The unit voices and descriptions are hilarious and there are a lot of fun units and spells. The skills your units acquire as they gain levels are also a lot of fun. It should be noted that the game puts you into conflict with other mages really quickly, so expect to be battling right away. If you like subtle victory conditions in your 4x games (diplomacy, intrigue, culture, research, etc.) then this is not your game. This sucker is all about stomping your rivals to goo with the biggest, baddest units you can muster. While that's not terribly deep, it's strangely gratifying to just bash the hell out of everybody.
Now for the bad bits. The game is horribly unoptimized (every spell effect in the game causes the graphics to stutter), quite buggy (there are even some game crashing bugs here along with the little stuff), and there are gameplay aspects that REALLY need improvement. The game is particularly bad at providing information you need to make good strategic decisions, such as telling you the prerequisites for buildings and units or telling you what a skill will do if you select it when upgrading a unit. Want to recruit an Elder Vampire unit? The only way to get one is to randomly build stuff in your city until you accidentally bump into the ones required. You can look up all that stuff on a wiki, but unfortunately, you can't do that while playing because alt-tabbing out introduces graphics refresh problems on the overland map. The final issue is the developer simply stopped supporting Warlock to release Warlock II, which appears to be just a badly patched version of Warlock. It feels a bit like Warlock was a scam to get people to buy something that was never going to be finished so they could charge us again for patches. If Ino-Co Plus showed ANY inclination to support this game and fix the issues, I would whole-heartedly recommend it, but they have not released a patch since December 2012, so it is obvious they intend to let it rot. I hold Paradox Interactive (the publisher) to be somewhat at fault here too for not insisting that Ino-Co Plus provide proper support for Warlock before agreeing to publish a sequel. I'll be very leary about purchasing anything published by them in the future.
If the game still sounds interesting to you, I recommend you only buy Warlock if it is heavily discounted. It's just sad when a developer has so little pride and sense of responsibility that they would leave their product in such an 'almost done' state. I'll certainly never buy anything developed by Ino-Co Plus again. There really are some good things here and ultimately it manages to be quite enjoyable in spite of itself. I've certainly gotten my money's worth out of it, though I'm glad it cost me less than $10.

If you like other turn-based strategy games, you will like this one as well.
Things it has in common with other turn-based strategy games:
This this game does differently, compared to other turn-based strategy games:
At first, some people will feel weird with each unit taking up on hex, but you get used to it and actually learn to like it. As your troops and heroes level up, get more upgrades, and become stronger, you learn to value each unit and want to keep them alive.
You research spells and harvest mana to cast them. Each spell has a mana cost, but there is also a limit on how much you can use per tern. Spells will use up a small part of what you can use per turn, a big part, all of it, or even take several turns to charge.
You don't really get moments like that in other games. In Total War, you have something similar during the RTS, but it's a lot more fun with spells blowing things up everywhere and randomly appearing armies.
The game is not very well optimized and there are a few bugs. The game may crash and may even freeze your computer.
There are typos and it's clear that development was abandoned, but it's a fun experience. I got the game from a pack for 1$, but it may be worth buying when it is on sale.

So it's about a year until Street Fighter V comes out and people who haven't really took Street Fighter seriously are wondering if it's worth the purchase.
The answer is yes.
I've been a complete casual Street Fighter player for years. But gradually over the years I always saw the pros and wonder if I can compete at their same level. Quite honestly anything is possible.. Except in a fighting game you don't rely on what level you are, or what kind of stats and skills determine the outcome of your character. It all boils down to memorization, muscle memory, adaptation. Honestly, the entire point of Street Fighter is the interesting aspect of the mind games between 2 players. It has the ruggedness of not a multiplayer game but some odd form of chess/board game appeal. As I played dozens of hours of this game I seem to realize it really does have a chess-like learning curve to all of these characters. As long as you put forth the effort into learning patterns and the characters mechanics (strength/weakness) and overcome all the mistakes you've been making as a casual player, this is a very rewarding game. Anyways, All I'm saying is if you're looking for a worthwhile fighting game I suggest you pick this up strictly to learn the fundamentals until Street Fighter V comes out. Also, Online play is very habitable. Pick it up before V comes out I promise you.. You won't regret it.

This is the game where you realise David Hayter plays a very convincing (and mildly entertaining) crazy person.
Also the game is pretty good. The story is at this point still ongoing but is pretty solid, if rather predictable even at this early stage; while some details of the overarching plot are pretty easy to suss out, there are plenty of things that remain pretty opaque, and the ends of the chapters especially all tend to have some sudden unexpected little revelation or twist to hook you in for the next episode. If you're paying attention, you should be able to see a lot of the big plot points coming - but some of the smaller ones will still probably blindside you. Beyond a few minor plotholes (which might be resolved later anyway), it's pretty well crafted storytelling, to be honest with you.
You play a mysteriously omnipotent 'computer hacker' who is contacted by a young teenage girl in the hopes that you can help her escape confinement in a strange facility. Without going into full spoilers, however, there are numerous little things in the game which cast serious doubt on whether or not the player truly
who and what she thinks they are.
Gameplay-wise, you leap between a series of fixed cameras to observe the environment ahead of Hope, the protagonist, giving her signals about when and where to move, hide, attempt to steal from a guard, etcetera. As your inroad into the facility comes from Hope's phone, you can't access cameras that are too far away from her due to signal degradation, meaning you have to keep her on the move to fully explore the facility. As you progress, you can unlock new abilities (such as being able to temporarily jam doors, trapping guards or stopping them from catching up to Hope) by trading the information you've discovered with an anonymous 'broker'. Using these abilities becomes especially important later on as the game ramps up the difficulty pretty steadily; by the end of the third chapter, there can be as many as four or five guards in any given room, any number of whom could be wearing tear-gas resistant masks or tazer-proof vests - nullifying the only direct way Hope has to escape when cornered.
The tone of the game is pretty mature; for example, it raises some questions about what does and doesn't count as censorship, but does so without being patronizing. There appear to be branching paths, based on whether you do or don't choose to share certain information with Hope, but it's not as simple as a binary 'do you want to tell her the truth or lie to her?' choice. On at least one occasion, Hope basically
you that she
something, leaving you with a choice: Do you show her the footage anyway, because it's something she needs to know? Or do you just view it alone, shielding her from the unpleasant images - but potentially blocking her from something she'd want to see, if she knew about it?
It's a much more mature take on the subject and I really hope that the rest of the episodes continue in the same vein, without just suddenly shouting 'ANY AND ALL CENSORSHIP IS WRONG' at the end. I'm fairly hopeful that won't happen though; the devs of this game seem to be pretty well-read or at least have easy access to a bunch of crib notes on a lot of famous literature (some of the collectibles are banned books, all of which have notes attached from the facility's administrator explaining exactly what about them and the themes they represent is so repulsive to his new order), so with a bit of luck the ending will be more complex than that.
Basically, it's pretty good! If the third-person no-direct-control aspect doesn't turn you off, give it a try.

This is a good transportation tycoon simulator, with refreshingly nice graphics and a solid engine to work with. It features modding support, allowing for additional game features, and to me is well worth the purchase price. It's a shame it doesn't have multiplayer though.

It's not Transport Tycoon. Yet. And look at the differences between OTTD and the original Transport Tycoon Deluxe. These things come over time. These guys know that community development is key, and mod support strengthens the game immensely.
Whilst not perfect, the game fares really well overall and is the first game to do free (non-tiled) track building really nicely. And it's quite hard to master, even for a TTD-veteran. There's some more room for features and content, but that's always good, and they're continously working on the game, still. Also the music's spot-on, and really nicely following the TTD/Locomotion/RRT-style of smokey and jazzy bluegrass-esque mixtures.
If you're into trains, or at least into transport sims, you're not gonna regret this. There's a nice community behind it, and there's tons of mods already around. But the vanilla game - plus the free DLC, not to forget - are good enough to have a great deal of fun with. These games are rare enough in itself.

This game is rad. It's been on my backlog for a while, but I'm really glad I played it. I haven't finished the story yet (I'm about 2 story missions away), but I feel that I've seen enough of the game to review it.
First off, this game is all about the gameplay. The story and characters are, frankly, uninteresting to me. I'm not a big LOTR fan in general. But, all that aside, it's still not intersting. In fact, my biggest gripe about the game is that the characters and story are so generic, rushed, and flat that it's pretty uninteresting. I don't care about Talion, his mission, or any of the characters. The dude is your typical edgy, gritty, humorless, clichéd LOTR-human stereotype. On a quest for revenge because bad guys murdered his family and blah blah blah yawn… You've heard this story a hundred times before. Unfortunately, many of the awesome game mechanics are unlocked by story missions. So, the game only starts feeling really awesome pretty late into the story.
You might think that I think the game sucks because of that, but you're wrong! The gameplay is amazing. Some of the best 3rd person action fighting mechanics I've played. The dynamic orc hierarchy and nemesis system is great. So great that you start building your own stories around these characters. The orc captains and warchiefs themselves are extremely varied. Some are pretty weak and others are practically demigods. Knowing the strengths and weaknesses between the orcs is usually essential before fighting them until late-game. That often requires you gather intelligence on your targets, either by gathering documents or interrogating orcs.
Eventually you get the ability to insert your own agents into the orc hierarchy and “assist” them to becoming warchiefs, which is a really awesome mechanic (but, I felt like it could have been expanded to be even more cool, like if you could recruit bodyguards that followed you). There are some hickups. I've gotten stuck on multiple occasions and knowing what you can and can't climb isn't always clear. The game is often easy because of how OP Talion becomes, as others have said, but don't let that fool you: the orcs can and will easily make up for that with sheer numbers. And, the random immunities and buffs the captains or warchiefs have can make battles challenging.
This is one of those games where you just want to keep poking the sandbox to see what happens next. It's one of the few games where I've wanted to play as many side quests as possible, even though they're largely generic, because of how the world was affected and how the orc hierarchy changed. It's not a masterpiece, but it's still a ton of fun. For people who enjoy the Assassin's Creed or Arkam Asylum kind of games.

I've survived for 45 days now. My cheap digital watch/health monitor records the days.It seems like yesterday when my Private Jet sank deep in the Pacific Ocean. In my haste to escape all i managed to grab was a battered yellow life raft. I reached this medium sized Island and quickly scavenged all the resources i could find around the Island, Including 2 buckets!
I made a campfire and small shelter and dined on coconuts before falling fast asleep. I awoke early the next morning and decided to scout out a wreck near the island. I located a roll of duck tape and carb for a boat motor. As i left to wreck i heard a strange sound. I stood and looked around and to my horror not one but two tiger sharks were swimming around and under my little life raft! I quickly paddled back to my campsite and ate some more coconuts while crafting spears, both crude and fishing types.
My only companion during this time was Squeeler, a wild boar who always kept his distance but squeeled like mad when startled. He quickly started to look like a walking feast! I took my spears and stalked him all over the island and after 4 broken or lost spears, darkness was setting in and squeeler was running around with a single speak sticking out of him and i returned to camp hungry. The Spears require practice!
More coconuts for dinner and by now my supply was shrinking and all the islands palms were picked clean. I went to bed vowing to explore the nearby islands for resources the next day. I awaken to a rain storm that cancels my trip, i can hardly even see the closest island, too risky to raft out into the open ocean so i spend the day spear fishing in the shallows and watching for squeeler, i only scored two small fish but it was a nice change from coconuts!
With the resources i had found i managed to craft a crude axe and solar still to collect water. The fish were tasty and i slept the rest of the night. The next day the weather cleared and i was able to scavenge two islands and drag the loot back to my home. While dropping a pile of rocks i had brought back i notice squeeler and switch to my spears. He still has the spear hanging from his side where i wounded him before! I stalk him and finally corner him between some rocks, two more spears out of four thrown stab into squeeler and he drops! Looks like ham and bacon is back on the menu!
Since that time i have explored the nearby islands and wrecks,built a smoker, 2 more solar stills, a small raft and a little 2 sectioned house with a bed inside. Built up a decent supply of resources and items including a flare gun from wrecks. Still no compass, so long range rafting trips are not happening yet and i managed to get bitten by a snake and kill and eat a tiger shark!
All in All, Its a great survival game with a lot of potential! I'm really enjoying it and look forward to future updates! The graphics are great and the water is amazing! You have to learn how things work, but once you do the game becomes a lot of fun and lets you write your own survival story! Well worth buying, especially if its on sale!

It's hard not to start a review for this game with "Civilization V in a fantasy setting" so I decided I won't.
Won't not, that is.
Because this is very, very much like Civilization V except in a fantasy setting, and that is by no means a bad thing.
In case you've never played a Civilization or more generally a 4X game, you're tasking with the survival of a faction and will need to manage cities, armies, diplomacy and the discovery of the world around you.
There were barely any features truly unique to this game, in fact the only thing that appears to be without a direct Civ V parallel would be the magic system.
I would definitely recommend this to people that want to play long campaigns guiding a civilization as it develops in a fantasy setting. The game did exactly what I hoped it would and I had no technical problems or concerns about design choices at all.
Whether you'll ever prefer this to Civ depends on what you want, this being slightly more focussed on combat and less on development, but it's definitely a fun game to play.
Really good game once you give it a chance. Fans of the Civilization series will feel at home.

Don't be fooled by me having less than an hour on this game here on Steam. I first played Dark Souls 1 some years ago on my ps3 and it's still one of my favourite games of all times! The fact that I bought it on Steam too serves only as further proof that this game is incredible. I got the Steam version in order to play with some friends who don't own a ps3 looking forward to the day (which is drawing near) I will have a decent pc to play this gem on.
Now, to review the game. The feel you get playing it is impossible to describe unless you've played it yourself, and I can only try to suggest it vaguely: you are alone in a world that apparently wants to kill you to death. In reality, to most enemies you are no more than an annoying fly snooping around and, as such, deserve a good swat. You must somehow progress through the nightmarish land that is Lordran by taking a journey that will change forever the way you look at videogames (I hope this sounds more passionate than fanboyish hahaha).
I'm entirely serious when I say that the Souls series has ruined videogames for me (in a good way): it spoiled the crap out of me and now, for example, I'm annoyed when the reason why you die and respawn isn't part of the in-game lore.
Speaking of which, lore and gameplay are majestically intertwined. Almost every single gameplay mechanic also has an in-game explaination and this game makes a great job preserving the immersion it creates.
Dark Souls as a whole has incredible mechanics, a breathtaking environment, awesome bosses and fantastic NPCs.
There is only one complaint I can make, and that is the fact that, at least on ps3, it was extremely hard to play with your friends (they fixed this in later games, for example by adding the engraved ring in DS2 and passwords in Bloodborne and DS3). I don't know wether the Steam version is any better on that regard, so I will not count it as a complete flaw here.
Finally, I will also give you a piece of advice: it's perfectly normal to get stuck on a boss. It's perfectly normal to rage. It's perfectly normal to even hate the game at first. But, whatever happens, never, ever get discouraged. Every boss can be defeated. Every area can be bested. Every weapon can be mastered. I believe in you.
I hope this little review will convince new players to try out the game and experience its beauty. I know there are tons of other reviews and that Dark Souls is universally known by now, but if I helped even one person to make up their mind and pick up the game, then I'm happy. Praise the sun, make the flames guide thee and may you all find your worth in the waking world.

Night in the Woods is a perfect example of an adventure game. You play as Mae Borowski, a 20-year-old (she will stress this a lot) catperson (?) who drops out of college and returns to her hometown of Possum Springs -  a stagnating small mining town which would be located somewhere in the real American north-east.
What Mae does after that is entirely up to you. This game, and, in turn, the player dedicates a lot of attention towards building up a routine. Chat with mom in the morning or play a cult roguelike game. Feed rats or listen in on fishermen poets. Annoy the townsfolk by walking on hanging cables, hang with the coolest people in Possum Springs, and then go to band practice. Almost everything in this game leads to a small narrative or storyline of sorts, adding more to the rich tapestry of Night in the Woods.
Since all you do in terms of gameplay is run around and jump (something this game's characters like to mention), the developers had to compensate with the writing. Oh, and what an amazing script they wrote. Mae's monologue and dialogue are hilarious. Bea is an incredibly multi-layered person with plenty of emotional baggage. Gregg just rules, ok? I'm not here to list all the characters, so I'll just say that this game masterfully juggles plenty of emotions (the ending had me going from choked up to laughing in a few seconds), explores a library of themes, and, in general, creates a very believable world and characters that you can resonate or identify with. Also, this is probably the only game so far to get millenials so right. It didn't feel like a caricature, didn't feel like condescending - it was an all-around truthful portrait of the modern generation.
And sweet Judas, that soundtrack! It's absolutely incredible. There's happy and spooky ambient, almost orchestral music, garage band post-punk... What I'm trying to say is that it's very versatile. The soundtrack is a joy to listen to, and, thanks to the routine you've set up, you'll be able to enjoy it a lot. Legitimately consider getting the soundtrack DLCs for this, since the music in this game isn't just the cherry on top that you can toss away if you feel like it.
However, no amount of reading about Night in the Woods will give you an idea about this game. Go into it without knowing anything, probably even stop reading this review? Night in the Woods is one of those incredible experiences that reaches out to you. This game spoke to me, it really did. And, I feel like it spoke FOR me, too. It's not just a 12-hour long Twin Peaks reference, it's a biographical, historical, economical statement. This game says a lot and doesn't shy away from any of it. Its bluntness, variety, and charm carried this game into my list of favorites. Maybe it'll do the same for you, too?

A 1080p60 video review of Republique Remastered:
Republique Remastered is a newly released PC version of a game that first appeared on iOS devices more than a year ago. It turns out that taking a year to create a well-crafted PC version is actually worth it, because this game looks, feels, and plays as if it were made for PC from scratch. As for the game itself - the Stealth Adventure mix works surprisingly well and its story is quite engrossing, but please see the video review above for more details.
If you enjoy any of the following, you'll have a good time with Republique Remastered:
Conversely if none of those concepts sound appealing, this is probably not the game you're looking for.
120Hz - Yes!
Borderless Window - No
Graphics Options - Solid (missing anti-aliasing)
Texture Quality - Good
Key Rebinding - No
It uses Unity 5 and physically based shading, so you can expect great lighting, reflections and shadows throughout!

Republique is a brilliant stealth game from a small development team with an
story. If you don't cry a little at the end of Chapter 3, well, you may not have a soul. The story is just that good.
The simple "point-and-click" controls are reminiscent of later Kings Quest games which means that your grandmother could play this. But don't think that means Republique will be a walk in the park! The guards are smart, the puzzles are intriguing, and there are several places off the beaten path to explore. BRILLIANT voice acting by Rena Strober, Jennifer Hale, David Hayter, Khary Payton, and Dwight Schultz make this a must buy for me. (I'm a sucker for good voice acting, what can I say?)
I played this on my Android, and I had a blast, but I want you to understand: This is no mere phone port. The graphics have been upgraded to take full advantage of the Unity 5 engine, and it shows. The new cinematics are amazing, and the environments really benefit from the new lighting and textures. I was happy to see that this came to PC, but wasn't sure about the price. But I took a risk, and I'm glad I did. It was totally worth it. I can't wait for chapters 4 and 5 to come out so I can see what happens next.
5/5 stars. A+++ would recommend.

When I bought Republique I wasn’t really sure what to expect from the game, what I knew came from the description of the game on the page. That it was a topical point-and-click stealth game made by people that had separately on Halo, Metal Gear Solid and F.E.A.R which means we have people from Bungie, Kojima Productions and Monolith Studios. These are all good games in their own way but I wasn’t sure what this game would be.
The first episode began with a minor interrogation of a Pre-Cal known as 390-H or as we came to know her Hope (H-093) after which her cell phone is delivered to her via a security guard simply called Cooper who will help you and give you advice via messages as well as comment on indie game cartridges of his that Hope with your help finds throughout the episode (and presumably in future episodes as well).
You however don’t play as Hope, you merely guide her, you know how in some games there are invisible people who help you and guide you but you don't know who they are, well in this game that is who you play as. You are an unknown person who via Hope’s phone has infiltrated a facility, this république, for some reason. You hack yourself into the cameras that are all over the facility and look around after guards and scout head to learn the patrols of guards and with this information you guide Hope from hiding  spot to hiding spot.
There are certain cyber-abilities that you can purchase with information you find throughout the very large level to use to your advantage, I purchased 4 out the 5 available but only ever used 2 of those, 2 of those was the abilities which allowed me to get more information just because I wanted to read all the emails and listen to the audio messages. One of the other abilities I had I forgot I had and the other I never risked to use. Hope can also find pepper-spray, tasers and screwdrivers to help her, screwdrivers to get into air-vents, pepper-spray to temporarily disable guards and tasers to permanently disable them. As for them all of them are useful and help but I didn't have to use more than 2 of both pepper-spray and tasers and I believe 3 screwdrivers.
The stealth is quite easy, apparently if you get apprehended you get escorted back to a cell but that never happened to me so I can’t say that is the case for certain that is only what I’ve been told, but it felt tense and I was constantly afraid of failure which kept me on the edge of my mind for the 4 hours it took me to complete the first episode. The story and atmosphere are both exceptional and interesting and it is a very good start and I look forward to the rest of the episodes, I will not say more on the story than I already have since I don’t wish to spoil it to anyone who think this is enough to buy the game already.
* Each review for each episode are written shortly after their completion.

Marcus. Oh Marcus. How did I let you die?
Okay, the thing you should know about State of Decay is that once your player character dies, they're dead for good within the game. There are no reloading previous saves. You can't revive a player character. I didn't know that before doing a mission where numerous zombies and a tank looking one attack a house. My Marcus, he died.
The reason this upset me was Marcus is the starting character. So that makes him important in various ways. He has a great skillset. Great leadership skills. Is able to maintain trust. If I had known about this feature before diving into State of Decay, my gameplay style would have been more cautious. Unfortanately, I hadn't known about it.
For that reason, I will hold off playing State of Decay any further. Well, that and the fact that the game lags like every f***ing thirty seconds. No, really. You could be playing along at 60 fps and bam! it'll drop down to like 8 fps. What's the first thing you do? Check drivers are up to date. Okay. Lower resolution. Okay. Lower graphics settings. Okay. Same problem. This game has serious lagging. Which is why I'm going to hold off until I'm able to have a better PC.
A bit about the game's story and gameplay before I set off: You start as Marcus (who died in my game, god darnit) a young man on a fishing trip with his buddy Ed. The game gets right into the action. Ed is being attacked by zombies and you have to help him. Right off the bat, you meet others at a ranger station. Some stuff happens. And you decide to escape the mountain and head into town. This is where the bulk of the game will be centered. Your home base is a church occupied by some townfolk trying to help survivors.
Your role, as any of the player characters that you meet, is to gather supplies, reinforce the churches defense, help others, dive into multiple storylines involving the army, judge, some locals, and stuff. You scavenge homes, radio in for supply runs. Fight zombies. Scavenge warehouses, radio in for supply runs. Fight hordes. Scavenge....okay, you get the point, there's a bit of scavenging involved which is great as it reinforces that this game is an ARPG, not a horror game.
So far, I'd give SoD a 7.9/10. (I detracted points because Marcus died and it's laggy as fu.) Otherwise, good game. Good graphics too. I realize I hadn't mentioned that. It runs on one of the Crytek engines, so it has an over abundance of lighting and high res textures.

Terrible game. And not because the game itself is awful - I wouldn't know. I only got a few hours of actual game time, because this game is a terrible port from console.
Yes, these are the days where games are developed for consoles and then ported to PC; no longer are the days where games are made specifically for PC. This would be fine if the company would invest some time porting the codebase over. i read somewhere that this is the result of the drivers required to run this on the 360, and they never changed it when they ported it. Basically, a bunch of people have issues where their graphics cards massively overheat. About half of those people end up with a kernel deadlock. About half of those people, can't get a fix that works.
This is the kind of thing I would expect from an alpha, or beta, or even a fresh released game. This game has been out since Nov of 2013 though...this is pathetic. To make matters worse, their support consists of one lady, who can't help you because she has no support from the devs. I went through the usual channels, of me sending them the dxdiag to make sure all my system was in a good state, then she recommmended all the things I can easily google for myself that I already know for a fact didn't work, then she went silent for about a month. The only reason I ever talked to her again, is because I had to send a reminder, asking if she had any progress from the devs. These people had the audacity to have the dev send me a single sentence, telling me to enable vsync...something that I can easily find on how to make ANY game run easier.
Pros:
- you can cook eggs on your graphics card
Cons:
- support is near non-existent, and pathetic
- the game is in the state of an alpha or beta, even still a year after its actual full release
- the overheating issue I described applies to a wide variety of cards, by my research. If you buy this game you run a big risk
I have a i7930, but the big thing here is graphics cards, which is a HD RADEON 5870 which I ran with the latest drivers, and the drivers prior to the latest drivers to be sure. This is certainly not a card that I would expect to struggle with a mediocre graphics game like State of Decay.
I got my refund through Steam after explaining the support conversation and showing them how pathetic the company and game was.

Of course, those of you who do not like VN's or roleplay games, will not enjoy this game. Those of you who do, on the other hand, will find this to be one of the more entertaining VN's you could lay eyes on. For most people, the fact that you can decide your fate based on skillfully selecting classes on which your survival rests, is a thrilling ability.
Most players of VN platforms are used to a mono-dimensional structure in which the game has preset goals or things that are always going to happen. Now I am not saying that these kind of things cannot occur in Long Live The Queen, yet it is almost impossible to play through a certain amount of events in one runthrough. The game is complex in the sense that you will have to keep playing it multiple times in which to finish everything.
Some of the other VN's that have touched the surface on steam also deserve notification, but I, at heart, feel like Long Live The Queen deserves first place.
Now onto the main point:
The gameplay is exceptionally commendable in the sense that you get drawn into being Elodie. Of course, when saying gameplay, I mean the strategy in which you have to decide on what certain events are going to take place. Some examples of this, would be to overall decide the endings of the said game. In one playthrough, you will have to have a powerful singing voice in which to woo the King Consort, Togami. If you had not built up such ability, and tried to face him this way, you would have died. There are also many other facts in which could prevent this from happening, but playing through multiple times and save scumming are things that are going to happen with almost every player of this VN. Sometimes you will forget to save and die before the coronation, in which you will have to restart.
This frustrating occurrence, though, is what makes the game evermore challenging, in which playing it becomes even more fun than before.
The character designs and animation (Of course just meaning the artwork) are also something to be noted. The backdrops for certain scenes and events changes based on what kind of event is taking place at the time. There are many different types of event that will take place during the course, but you will remember some by the illustrious music and the change in scenery.
The characters are also something to be seen in a aristocratic society drawn up by the Japanese. Every single girl and boy has a colorful sort of passion about them, and the emotions portrayed through the text seems somewhat real. The way the characters are drawn is in the traditional manga-type style, but it is enjoyable in the sense that they are characters that are very easy to connect with after a playthrough or two.

There are few games with such beautiful piano skits and numbers within them, that it is a rarity when one comes across one. The matching of the certain tones of music with the drama in certain scenes makes this even more believable. You will come to be humming the tunes of certain scenes, no matter where you are during the day, if you play this game a couple of times.
That is all! Thank you for reading!

Do you love Zombie survival but hate getting greefed in multiplayer?
Then this is the perfect game for you!
PRO:
1. Freedom:
As one would expect from a survival game, the player has to roam an open world in order to gather supplies and weapons. But this game has so much more. Instead of just being by yourself, you have a base with a lot of allies. There are many different resources to collect, and any item you find in in the wild can be used by you or your friends. You can go anywhere on the map, and every area has renewing items and resources that respawn. You can move your base to any suitable place and make outposts where ever you think they best serve the survival of your team. The size of your team is only limited by your ability to support them.
2. Building a "Family":
If you are trying to survive the zombie apocalypse, you are going to need help, and this game's devs know that. Across the map there are many people you can befriend by helping them out, and if you are kind enough to them they will join your team. While you start with a single character, you can freely choose between anyone you have befriended. They all level seperately, can master different skills and combat styles, and each have their own personality. All that makes this the most interesting single-player team game I have ever played. But having a lot of friends also has it's downsides. The bigger the crew, the more problems arise, and you have to help your pals overcome things like fear, anger, and hopelessness.
3. The Tools:
Crowbars, Katanas, Frying pans, Revolvers, Machine guns, and much much more. All these things can be used to combat the never-ending hordes of the undead. Along side your weapons you can use traps, silencers, egg timers and many other utilities to give yourself an edge in the fight. But it doesn't have to be just you. Once you help out enough in your neighborhood, you can ask for favours in return to help you out of a tight spot.
CON:
1. Too Easy:
Not sure if this is a bad thing, as zombies are after all brain dead, but it's incredibly easy to outsmart the dead. Once you know their responses to certain things, you can easily navigate even big towns without much worry. Since you can see them from a long way away on your mini map, avoiding zombie mobs is a piece of cake. Also, even when 5 zombies are eating you at once, you can get them off you without too much effort.
2. CPU Intensive:
My CPU is pretty old, and it has a huge problem handling all the different zombies. If I drive around town and load enough undead NPCs into memory, my CPU gives out. This is a big problem since it fulfills the minimum requirements. Basically you will need a decent quad-core in order to really play this game over a prolonged period of time, despite what the sys reqs say.
3. Small World:
At this point I should mention that I haven't beaten the game, mostly because of point 2. So it's possible that I can unlock more of the world. But at the time it consists of only a small village and a town, as well as a lot of open country. The core game seems to be pretty small so far, but there are 2 DLCs which hopefully will add more to the world.
4. No Multiplayer:
This is only a single-player game. Doesn't bother me, as I play console or MMOs when I want other players in my games, but it should be mentioned in the review.
I would definately recommend this game. Most of the negative points are down to my aging hardware, so if you have a decent gaming PC, you should really pick it up if you love zombie survival!

How to make chocolate cake
-----------------------------------------
Ingredients
1 cup white sugar
1 1/8 cups all-purpose flour
1/2 cup unsweetened cocoa powder
1 teaspoon baking soda
1 teaspoon salt
1/2 cup butter
1 egg
1 teaspoon vanilla extract
1 cup cold, strong, brewed coffee
Directions
Preheat oven to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C). Grease and flour an 8 inch pan. Sift together flour, cocoa, baking soda and salt. Set aside.
In a medium bowl, cream butter and sugar until light and fluffy. Add egg and vanilla and beat well. Add flour mixture, alternating with coffee. Beat until just incorporated.
Bake at 350 degrees F (175 degrees C) for 35 to 45 minutes, or until a toothpick inserted into the cake comes out clean.

If you're like me, you've played OpenTTD and always wished for a similar game without the grid. This is sort-of that game. I probably would not have bought this at full price; as many other reviewers have noted, it feels incomplete. Track-building needs to be refined, more industry chains need to be added with more variation between them. There's no texture for transitions between the two main road types, which has no consequence on gameplay but agitates me to no end. The random maps all feel the same, and the game badly needs a map editor and Workshop support.
The UI is surprisingly good, with a couple exceptions. The developers clearly have learned from OpenTTD and tried to minimize needless clicking as much as possible. The graphics are technically great but artistically just OK, though the smoke from steam trains always looks beautiful. Most importantly, it scratches the itch for a modern 3D transportation game, and at sale prices, it's worth the cost for me.
People who are into transportation games to make rediculously complex networks *might* not find this worth it. Players who aren't familiar with the genre will probably end up bored or find it takes too long to learn. People who like transportation games because YAY TRAINS!!! should probably get this, just don't set your expectations too high.
I get the feeling the developers have the design part down pretty well, and hopefully their next game will give them more resources to execute that vision. I look forward to it.

A Good game all round but left me wanting more! - 6.5/10
-------------------------------------------------------------
A nice fun game that draws you in, it’s very easy to pick up and play with simple controls that never have you wondering what key to hit. It is a little too hack and slash for me but after a while you kill the enemy’s so fast the combo/hit streak system seems almost pointless.
The graphics are nice but there was no Wow or awful moments, so nothing really to note. I played it all the way through the game glitch fee.
Shadow of Mordor has a few RPG elements but it was wrong on so many levels - I love XP and levelling up systems in games, but normally the point is that you level up, get stronger and pick where to spend your next skill point carefully.
In Shadow of Mordor you do not get any stronger for levelling up, you gain skill points but you can have every skill/perk in the game.
This lack of hard choices in the skill tree makes it feel more annoying the rewarding.  XP is given way to fast I had 75% of the skills before I reached the second half (2nd area).
Too Easy - The game is easy so frustration free, when you die, the punishment is light enough that you don't feel like you need to start a fresh game but it did make the game feel repetitive.
I found myself jumping in to huge crowds of enemy’s just to find something challenging. Once you have taken on a few “boss’s” you will know how to defeat them and with no new challenges or change in attack style as the game progresses, killing enemy’s just felt unrewarding.
All of this is worsened by the XP, as you level up so fast, you end up with the last ¼ of the game with nothing to buy, so no point killing anything that’s not for the mission.
Skill wise there is a good range, you will be attacking from afar with the “ranger” mode, sneaking up to slit a few throats then hacking and slashing in close combat while throwing in a few “wrath” skills in.
The combat in Shadow of Mordor is its redeeming feature. Due to its flexibility you do end up trying to kill bigger and bigger groups in one go. The number of times I ran round getting as many Orks to follow me to a possible, just to blow them all up with a “fire” or “grog barrel”.
Collectables – throughout Mordor there is lots of bits you can pick up, me being a must get 100% kind of guy, I was left feeling disappointed once again. You receive nothing when you have got them all. The job of collecting them was not fun as they are all marked on your map so no finding, the two zones are so repetitive in there textures and feel that there’s nothing to even call a “interesting area”.
The Story line is nothing special and very predictable almost not worth a mention.
---------------------------------------------------------
Overall its worth playing, but it has “0” replay factor. I found the game to “let me down” in so many areas that despite it being nice smooth gameplay and fun fights skills, the lack of variety with enemy’s or reward form any aspect in the game its only just in the worth playing category.

I'm done playing this game. I enjoyed the lore and was interested in pursuing the story, but I wanted to play on Permadeath mode to force myself to manage resources and not get drawn too far into the sandbox aspect to finish quests.
My most recent problem was the last straw of many similar problems: a singleplayer latency/lag bug caused me to fall into the lava at the core of the planet while I was building a path over it in a way that should not have caused me any problems. The game then lagged too much for me to hop back out onto the adjacent platform before damage, stacked through the lag spike, annihilated me. I lost several hours of gameplay on permadeath mode, along with my first diamond.
Permadeath is a nice challenge mode in concept, but if an engine flaw is what kills you instead of actual game design, then it really only leads to frustration; it's not anything the player can improve upon other than "well, that part of the game's broken- avoid it completely." This stinks if you're trying to explore the progressive difficulty of the game's levels and planets.
It's a fun enough sandbox on the surface if you're bored, and it's got a quirky sense of humor in its flavor text; as far as challenge, it's difficult to measure until/if single player lag spike / memory leak issues are managed. I'm disappointed that I won't see it through because of its strong concept and style, but the game flow is constantly interrupted by issues on the software backend, so the tradeoff in frustration sadly wasn't worth it to me.

Okay, this review will be a bit long, sorry for that, but I try to be profound. So, I'm one of those guys who actually like these survival style games, like Stranded Deep.
The idea is, in itself, not original but it's okay, playing the 'role of Robinson Crusoe' is cool. You have to make decisions by yourself, no help, no tips, no nothing (except from browsing the net and wiki), so the consequences might be even lethal - just like that kind of gameplay a survivor game needs!
The game's graphic is cool as well, the dinamic waves and stuff on the ocean is realistic, landscape is nice, you can check this by browsing the screenshots. The fact that you can see your character's body parts is also good I think - I actually liked that. Okey, sometimes the game might crash, but I'm actually not annoyed by that: remember that it's still an early access game, this might occur.
And yes. That's for the pros, now let's see the cons. I think the in-game crafting system really needs a major improvement. But let's start from the beginning. I'm okey with the way you have to gather resources. It is true that you will not find enough of them for your long (or mid) term purposes on one island but that's still fine, as you can still build bigger island(s) in the map builder menu option, so, yes, you have to solve this on your own and is a bit tricky and might be time-consuming but okey, I can still accept this.
Let's get back to where I've started - the crafting system. The crafting system which I think is the biggest drawback in this game :( It works via a menu system, you have to have the required resources either in your inventory, or somewhere around you (e.g. on the ground, which, I think, is a cool idea). But! When you click on the craft button, the item's silhouette appears on the screen and it drops on the ground after you click again - that's how the crafting is done. It's really annoying even in itself, but especially it's true considering the fact that you have to do this multiple times if you want to craft more pieces of something.
Yet, you can still get used to it, but having some kind of a function where you could craft more of an item with one step would be more convenient. But what really makes me sad, is the amount of craftables available. Yes, there are many tools craftable, some of them even with a primitive and upgraded version; yes, you can make a hut from driftwood, wood, steel etc.; but actually I could simply not figure out why you even need a hut! You can store everything safety on the ground, and for survival, it's enough to craft a little shelter (for saving the game and for sleeping) and several cooking pots and campfires with water distiller. And if they're done, without any other purposes, you'll soon lose your motivation to play this game, as there's nowhere to evolve. You might want to craft a better raft from something so you can move faster on water, but as soon as you have the tools to make your food and drinkable water, well - that's it. You just play to keep yourself alive via food and water gathering. And this happens because of the lack of bigger and more wide-spread crafting possibilities.
So after playing about 15-20 hours at maximum or so (even calculating the time of island building via map editor), you reach a point from where you cannot move forward, and become bored. And that's sad. :( And that's why I do not really recommend this game, yet I see a great potential in this!
Okay, I'm literally no one, but my idea or advice would be the development of a more user-friendly crafting system with much more crafting possibilities, or even an experience-point-based system, which would mean you have to 'fight' yourself through - maybe even - life threathening events, leading you to a point where better tools and stuff become available. I'd also really love to see, for example, events or something which would make hut building reasonable, for example heavy storms (which could, by chance, destroy your on-ground stuff), or terrestrial organisms (NPC-s like, well, I don't know, bears or wolfes or whatever creatures might habit these islands, which should also be a bit bigger I think). These, just as sharks on ocean, would mean a threat on the ground. Okey, there are these tiny snakes, but... that's all.
Thanks for reading, that's just an opinion of a guy who bought this game with great hopes, yet, had to feel a bit disappointed. I'll not uninstall this, as I'll check regularly for major updates, but, until that point, well - you can read my thoughts above.

This is a fantasy themed modification of Civilization V. Some of the same core mechanics are here; research, city building, army building, war and combat, leader traits and multiple paths to victory. Resource management, commerce, trade and diplomacy are also here, but are heavily simplified and limited compared to Civ V's mechanics; land management and building management have been combined for example. This game is geared much more towards war and combat.
Wonders have been replaced by Gods who grant rewards based on your favor with them. Technology is replaced by magic spells, but magic spells do not operate like technologies do in Civ V. Magic spells require mana and time to cast and do not provide civilization wide changes like technologies do. Most magic spells provide only small changes to the game such as damage to all units in a small area, the summoning of a unit or the raising or lowering of land and are not as important to the game as technologies are to Civ V.
The Civ V religion system is gone, there are no great people and many other mechanics of Civ 5 are gone as well. Some of the unique additions to the game are quests that randomly appear and grant rewards upon completion, 'Heroes' which are powerful units that can be purchased or found and Temple units which are powerful units granted by Gods. As said earlier, this game is geared towards war and combat and most of the additions to gameplay reflect that.
It's built on Civ 5, a solid and widely enjoyed game. In turn, it is a solid albeit simplied game that many would enjoy especially if war and combat is what you enjoy most in Civ 5.

What at first seems like a brutally hard and unfair generic medieval hack-and-slash gradually turns into a difficult-but-fair game, with you knowing why you die and learning from it. It will shove you into the ground and grind your face into the dirt, but as long as you keep getting up you have a chance.
Which, through a story told solely through scarce bits of easily-missed NPC dialogue, enemy and item placements, and item descriptions, is the one of the themes of the game. Puzzling your way through the narrative and lore is the best part of the game and the series in general, and as you play, the puzzle pieces slowly fall into place as names and concepts start to come into cohesion.
The mechanics have aged a bit. If you can figure out humanity and kindling bonfires without a guide, you deserve an achevement. When it came out, mapping the controller (and that's the way to play) to use R1 and R2 for attacks was a bizzare choice that made me and several other people I know using items when they meant to attack because of muscle memory. That's not the game's fault, though, and more recent games are using that control scheme in an attempt to emulate the Souls series (and failing).
This version is a legendary bad port unless you use DSFix, which lets you unlock the resolution and framerate from 720x30, even though there are in-game menu options for resolution that literally do nothing. Check out the guides section of the community hub if you don't want your experience ruined.

Edit: when I first wrote this review I didn't have any real knowledge of the game, but 240 hours in I feel as though I have some more understanding of it. This game is great. It really is. One of the most satisfying survival games I've come across. However the spawns are down right terrible along with base building. Those are some of the most unsatisfactory aspects of the game it's self. To the point I can see where some people would not enjoy it. There should be sleeping bags as I mentioned when I first started playing. At least being able to put one down in the base that you made and after respawing having to wait a good 10-15 minutes before being able to craft and place another.  I believe that's the best route to fixing the spawn issue. Now with base building it is really janky. The peices do not snap together making the whole experience of building a fortress a "wanting to bang your head on a brick wall experience". Adding to that thought, floating bases is a huge problem(in my eyes anyways) it just ruins the real ness of the game completely. Along with some of the positions of the bases being near check points where people camp in their bases and shoot you while you're trying to loot or worse, where I've just spawned. Last and not least storage. People are hoarding cars for the storage space( myself included ) there just isn't enough. We should be able to craft a fair amount of boxes to store items and we should be able to craft the crafted weapons. That would be great. I love this game and fully support this game. I'm 240 hours in and I will be here for another 2,000+ hours. Shout out to the developers for this masterpiece. It's not easy getting a foothold in the survival genre but in my eyes they have wiped the table clear of titles such as Just Survive, DayZ, and Next Day. This game is beautiful. I recommend x10. Triple thumbs up!!!!

NOTE: This game was given to me by the developer for review purposes. This did not influence my review in any way.
Note: Into the Belly of the Beast is currently in Early Access. The version reviewed was released on 20160204.
Into the Belly of the Beast is a fairly slow-paced two-dimensional action/puzzle game with a unique premise: you play a strange skeletal worm-like sea creature who must rescue its children from a giant monster of the deep that has swallowed them -- and you.
The game was created in Unity using what I assume to be completely original assets and has very high production values. Although still in Early Access it has obviously been well planned out. This is not just another "grab some free assets from the Unity store and bundle them together for sale as a game on Steam" game. No, Into the Belly of the Beast is a real, playable Early Access title with planned development and impressive originality.
Graphics - The graphics in Into the Belly of the Beast are very pretty indeed. The game begins with a brief introduction in the sea, but after only a few moments you'll find yourself in eerie internal tunnels and cavities within the sea monster's body. So far these each have different graphical themes for the different parts of the creature's body and each is well done, if a bit gruesome in places. As you control a sea creature inside another much larger sea creature, each level unsurprisingly is under water, but with different lights and colouring, and different levels of murkiness prevalent in the different areas, it all looks great. Water effects are nice and the 'waviness' of movement of some of the objects and creatures in the game convincingly portrays a gently undulating environment. There are no boring still backgrounds here; everything pulses and wiggles and sways in the current. Still screenshots just don't do it justice.
Even though the game is played in the 2D plane of the screen, the graphics are three dimensional. Models are well made and mostly extremely well animated, with your swallowed children in particular oozing cute personality; I found myself going 'awwww' when I rescued any of them. And the creature that you control as the player is well made and animated, too, although rather strange looking!
Graphics settings are fairly limited and, strangely, don't include the nearly ubiquitous Unity "Fastest" to "Beautiful" presets. Instead all we have are resolution, quality (low, medium, and high), and two on/off toggles for effects: bloom and vignette. ALT-ENTER also seems to work to toggle between full screen and window.
Sound - The game's title music could have come straight out of a Tim Burton film. It's fun and quirky and sets the scene well. It seems to only be the one track playing through the standard game levels as well, at least so far, but it has a number of different aspects to it. Sometimes it's strong enough to be almost orchestral, pushing you along as you play, and at other times it's only a distantly heard note or two scattered every few seconds, leaving you to listen to the gentle bubbling and gurgling of the giant beast's body around you. There's also a more dark, foreboding, and panic-laden music track that plays during the end-of-level boss stages. This is also good, but not as fun as the main track.
Sound effects are nice, with thematic burbles and gurgles throughout, as well as booming and crunching when various objects move about or shake. The creature sound effects are also good, with the high-pitched mews of your children being particularly endearing.
Gameplay - The first level of the game is an easy tutorial stage that introduces you to the game's simple controls and concepts. You can move around freely, open your jaws and bite objects or other creatures, pick up or drop something (e.g. an electrical charge, which can be used to stun enemies or open 'doors'), and use one of the available special abilities, and that's it. Biting can harm other creatures or open up areas of the environment, as well as allow you to heal or consume DNA cells of certain colours. consume enough DNA and you'll mimic other creatures of that colour, who will then allow you to pass without attacking you. So far i've found only one 'set' of special abilities, but it changes depending on the colour of DNA you have picked up: green DNA speeds you up when you activate the ability, or purple DNA scares off other creatures. Activating the ability also uses up some of the DNA you've eaten, thereby limiting use of the abilities.
After you've completed the tutorial you find yourself in the Heart, which functions as the hub for the game. From here you can select other levels to go to, and find different coloured DNA cells to alter your affinity with other creatures, as well as heal from blood cells floating about, to prepare for the next level. You select a level by swimming through the fleshy tunnel leading to it from the heart.
At the moment there are already plenty of levels, each with multiple stages and a 'boss', but there are also a number of 'under construction' signs humorously placed around the heart showing where development will occur as the game moves through Early Access. There's also a bestiary where you can presumably see the different creatures you've encountered while playing the game, but at the moment that is also under construction and thus inaccessible.
Pros:
+ Fun and cheerful music, great sound effects
+ Good graphics, particularly water and DoF effects; great creature and 'water' type animations
+ Main character and its children are given a lot of personality through their models, animations, and sounds
+ It's fun!
Cons:
- Not very intuitive or usable default keyboard controls and no way to change them through the settings menu
- It's not always obvious when you're at the end of a level, so you may end up leaving unintentionally
- many of the stages within each level are sort of samey; I was getting a bit bored of the first level's theme by the time I reached the last stage of it
- no trading cards, and no achievements to promote replayability; at the moment the only real goal in each of the intermediate (non-boss) stages is to get to the end (although you can find some secret caches of upgrade DNA to improve your creature's abilities if you look around a bit)
Into the Belly of the Beast is a very creative and highly original casual action / puzzle game. It's slow pacing and unique setting won't appeal to every gamer, but I am already very impressed with it, and I think it's only going to get better.

I wasn't expecting too much of Assault Horizon, but I was very pleasantly surprised. It shakes up the conventions of arcade jet shooters in ways I didn't expect - mostly for the good.  The dog fighting mode is brilliant; yes it briefly turns the game into a rail shooter, but these games have always just been about lining up a crosshair over a target with only the most fragile connection to actually piloting a plane.  In exchange for a superficial loss of freedom you get the coolest looking player controlled action sequences ever seen in any sort of flight game.
The game has it's faults, the story isn't particularly engaging and the helicopter and gunship bits are more tedious than fun, but the jet missions that comprise the bulk of the game never ceased to be entertaining despite the inherent repetition.  Worth picking up if you want jet porn without any semblance of realism to make things more boring.

So many tiny things that are messed up that could have made this game great.
1. Units have no auto explore. This has been a part of 4x games since Civ 3 I think. It is absurdly frustrating and time consuming to have to literally click on every unit every turn.
2. Clicking: WHY did you not use both the right and left mouse buttons? It's insane. The clicking over a unit to then do all actions with the same button is very frustrating and often leads to multiple clicks to get one action done. Also click zones are very tiny and leave you inching your mouse to get the right thing.
3. Minimal control of your economy and tech tree. Basicly you have no input onto what is happening. Should I build more gold or more mana collectors, who knows. Oh I'm suddenly bankrupt, but wait, it has no effect because the next turn I'm fine. WIthout some kind of feedback into your economy/techtree the user is very disconnected from the guidance of their own civ.
4. On that same note, you elminated so much of the users investment in their character by nutering the character design. I know this is just a reskinning of Master of Magic so I'm not expecting anything groundbreaking, but by removing the faction aliance to life/death/fire/air/etc you took away the special feeling of a character growing and learning a certain type of magic for a certain philosophy. Now all characters are bland and seem to take magic from all schools.
5. Never ending enemy spawn. Now I get that this is a core part of the game but it's also unnecessarily frustrating. As a builder I want the sence that I'm taking over this land and making it safer/better for my people. What's the point of me having magic walls around my cities if skeletons, vampires, and cheap humans just suddenly appear. On the same note they really don't do anything to you except attack your cities again and again and very rarely can they beat your cities ability to heal, essentially making them just a nusiance.
6. Oh last but not least, Users CAN'T SKIP ACTIONS! I don't care if some random village was built and I don't care if a sea monster is swimming past my capital. I should not have to bomb every enemy that walks by. I should have the choice.
Overall I cannot recomend this game. The reskinning of MOM is long awaited and the graphics for the most part are great, though many buildings are difficult to distinguish adding another minor frustration. This game was almost good but overall I say skip it.

This game is rad. It's been on my backlog for a while, but I'm really glad I played it. I haven't finished the story yet (I'm about 2 story missions away), but I feel that I've seen enough of the game to review it.
First off, this game is all about the gameplay. The story and characters are, frankly, uninteresting to me. I'm not a big LOTR fan in general. But, all that aside, it's still not intersting. In fact, my biggest gripe about the game is that the characters and story are so generic, rushed, and flat that it's pretty uninteresting. I don't care about Talion, his mission, or any of the characters. The dude is your typical edgy, gritty, humorless, clichéd LOTR-human stereotype. On a quest for revenge because bad guys murdered his family and blah blah blah yawn… You've heard this story a hundred times before. Unfortunately, many of the awesome game mechanics are unlocked by story missions. So, the game only starts feeling really awesome pretty late into the story.
You might think that I think the game sucks because of that, but you're wrong! The gameplay is amazing. Some of the best 3rd person action fighting mechanics I've played. The dynamic orc hierarchy and nemesis system is great. So great that you start building your own stories around these characters. The orc captains and warchiefs themselves are extremely varied. Some are pretty weak and others are practically demigods. Knowing the strengths and weaknesses between the orcs is usually essential before fighting them until late-game. That often requires you gather intelligence on your targets, either by gathering documents or interrogating orcs.
Eventually you get the ability to insert your own agents into the orc hierarchy and “assist” them to becoming warchiefs, which is a really awesome mechanic (but, I felt like it could have been expanded to be even more cool, like if you could recruit bodyguards that followed you). There are some hickups. I've gotten stuck on multiple occasions and knowing what you can and can't climb isn't always clear. The game is often easy because of how OP Talion becomes, as others have said, but don't let that fool you: the orcs can and will easily make up for that with sheer numbers. And, the random immunities and buffs the captains or warchiefs have can make battles challenging.
This is one of those games where you just want to keep poking the sandbox to see what happens next. It's one of the few games where I've wanted to play as many side quests as possible, even though they're largely generic, because of how the world was affected and how the orc hierarchy changed. It's not a masterpiece, but it's still a ton of fun. For people who enjoy the Assassin's Creed or Arkam Asylum kind of games.

So final verdict. I like this VN and i have enjoyed reading it despite bad translation.
