A Good game all round but left me wanting more! - 6.5/10
-------------------------------------------------------------
A nice fun game that draws you in, it’s very easy to pick up and play with simple controls that never have you wondering what key to hit. It is a little too hack and slash for me but after a while you kill the enemy’s so fast the combo/hit streak system seems almost pointless.
The graphics are nice but there was no Wow or awful moments, so nothing really to note. I played it all the way through the game glitch fee.
Shadow of Mordor has a few RPG elements but it was wrong on so many levels - I love XP and levelling up systems in games, but normally the point is that you level up, get stronger and pick where to spend your next skill point carefully.
In Shadow of Mordor you do not get any stronger for levelling up, you gain skill points but you can have every skill/perk in the game.
This lack of hard choices in the skill tree makes it feel more annoying the rewarding.  XP is given way to fast I had 75% of the skills before I reached the second half (2nd area).
Too Easy - The game is easy so frustration free, when you die, the punishment is light enough that you don't feel like you need to start a fresh game but it did make the game feel repetitive.
I found myself jumping in to huge crowds of enemy’s just to find something challenging. Once you have taken on a few “boss’s” you will know how to defeat them and with no new challenges or change in attack style as the game progresses, killing enemy’s just felt unrewarding.
All of this is worsened by the XP, as you level up so fast, you end up with the last ¼ of the game with nothing to buy, so no point killing anything that’s not for the mission.
Skill wise there is a good range, you will be attacking from afar with the “ranger” mode, sneaking up to slit a few throats then hacking and slashing in close combat while throwing in a few “wrath” skills in.
The combat in Shadow of Mordor is its redeeming feature. Due to its flexibility you do end up trying to kill bigger and bigger groups in one go. The number of times I ran round getting as many Orks to follow me to a possible, just to blow them all up with a “fire” or “grog barrel”.
Collectables – throughout Mordor there is lots of bits you can pick up, me being a must get 100% kind of guy, I was left feeling disappointed once again. You receive nothing when you have got them all. The job of collecting them was not fun as they are all marked on your map so no finding, the two zones are so repetitive in there textures and feel that there’s nothing to even call a “interesting area”.
The Story line is nothing special and very predictable almost not worth a mention.
---------------------------------------------------------
Overall its worth playing, but it has “0” replay factor. I found the game to “let me down” in so many areas that despite it being nice smooth gameplay and fun fights skills, the lack of variety with enemy’s or reward form any aspect in the game its only just in the worth playing category.

Not really a game, at least not as far as I have seen so far.  more like a click-through story which is incredibly sweet and touching.   I have spent 8 hours digging through the story line so far, and definitely look forward to finishing up what's left.... no matter how long it takes.
The anime artwork is top notch --- some of the better stuff I have seen so far --- though I have to be up front.... if you are looking for Japan-a-ponn, you're not gonna find it here.
So.... just what is here?   A high school story of rebellion and friendship.   Of betrayal and loss.   All seen through the eyes of an Asian perspective.   It is not all that common (as it is in America) for teens to openly defy their parents.   So the very beginning of the story sets you up for a shock... and then gives you the foundation for what is to follow.  I don't want to say to much... because it really is worth reading through.
The English is a bit off.... there are words that even I had to look up (Sequelae ?????)  but for the most part it's understandable.   I would say that the English really does need to be re-worked overall though, if they really want to reach the American market.  A bit more explanation of the Asian school system, some better word choices, clearer indication of when Ashley is thinking.... or talking.... that sort of thing.   But for the price, it's still worth getting.
On a 10 star rating system, I would give this a 6 star rating for sure (above average).  The artwork is a 7 (Greatly above average).  and if I do find that later on in the game there are interactive portions to the story... I will definitely raise my ratings.
For the price of $2.... it's worth it.

A pretty fun tower defense, not too easy and not too hard, but lots of focus on coop can make the game not-so-fun if you don't have someone to play with. Once you do though, highly recommended.
Upsides
-well balanced game that requires skill to complete, but not unfair
-great coop play
-satisfying trap mechanics
-good comedy
Downsides
-bad netcode (any lag or port problems will disconnect your partner or you, which can be a problem if you're trying to get to wave 50+ on endless). this could have been easily fixed with a "wait for partner to reconnect" function but it's absent
-requires coop to be truly fun
-some achievements require buying the orginal game (orcs must die 1), and one of them is viral
-the comedy gets old after your character makes the same joke for the thousandth time ("looks like he turned into orc salsa!"), and you can't disable voice acting really because it includes warnings for harder enemies like sappers and gnoll hunters.

Getting all of the achievements is really satisfying, as is learning to play as the different characters and figuring out the best strategies for each. All in all, it's alright.

Night in the Woods is about a girl with a sordid past, a sordid present and a increasingly more hazadous and sordid future.
It pulls of it's story very well despite the use of cliches, however, in spite of the presence of these the charm, style, and sincerncity of the characters in their interactions is enough to carry them through. It's a good example that execution can turn something that should be tired around.
The game revolves strongly around story and you should be prepared to take it as a story before a game but it dosen't forget what medium it is and retains a strong sense interactivity. I mean, it's definitely more interactive and gives you at least the feeling-be it true or not- that your input is important to the world and the character than games like the walking dead.
It utilizes simple but effective visuals to deliver a sense of atmosphere straight from the get go and the soundtrack is consistently enjoyable. I have not heard a song from Night in the Woods that I didn't  like, nor did I neccesarily have a scene I didn't like even if sometimes old character tropes did blunt the stab of the emotion of the scene a bit.
A big thing about this game is that it isn't scared to reference politics, and while it does not reference real world events. It does reference political movements consistently, especially with one character. While this isn't good or bad, in today world politics is everywhere and games are a casual way of escaping the snark and righteous tutting of moral stances and  national cynicism.
It is feasible that someone suffering with a bit of fatigue and aggrevation from any of that may find their enjoyment of the story a bit dampened if they are already riled up or feel ambushed by this stuff a lot.

This is a great* (casual) game. The mingames are fun, the characters were enjoyable, the scenarios were interesting. This is something like an open letter to the devs.
I'll start with the bad.
- I couldn't stand the dream sequences. Every time I went to sleep I audibly said "please god NO. NO PLEASE," and was happy to wake up the next day or upset to find myself baby platforming/backtracking to the same four instruments of the same song, seemingly disconnected from the 'important' dreams and the story at large. We get two 'important' ones, and five of the unconnected time-padders.
- A few of the characters felt unrealistic at times, saying things that (ab)normal people wouldn't say. Like, the main character went to college for two years, you telling me she can't form sentences? "Still putting it all together" will be on her tombstone. What's with the croc, she's apparently smart but can't rationalize her own behaviour? What's with the ghost stuff being taken seriously, aren't these people in their twenties? It's made out to 'seem' like Mae has physical brain problems, but it turns out she's really not. (She's having cosmic problems, to be vague for spoiler-free.) Jebaited. This would have been understandable behaviour from teens.
- Running through town each day just to get to Gregg was not fun. I didn't mind it the first few days, but once the light is fixed I feel some 'shortcut' should have opened. How are you going to skip forced-walking sections understanding it isn't fun to walk for ages but not think about doing that in the town/earlier in the game?
- While I'm on the town, the waterway under the church was unused. It wasn't a shortcut, and it skipped the croc's place. Maybe put Beatrice and the Gregg's workplaces nearer next time, so when you tell one "I'll get back to you" you don't have to trek through a loading screen and close to a minute of running. Twice. It was more of a chore to continually go through the WHOLE town looking, most of the time in vain, for someone to be somewhere. Especially the waterway. The church/cliff is fine, but the waterway, Food Donkey, and town entrance were upsetting all but one time.
- Verbal choices didn't matter. I knew they wouldn't for the most part, but some dialogue sounded like what I said could have made SOME sort of impact. I get that we're playing Mae, not us in the game, but can't the illusion of choice be a little more... illusory?
- People play games to escape politics. Just couldn't help yourselves, huh? That could be removed from the game and no character would be destroyed. Not even Bea.
- Spelling and grammar. C'mon guys, it isn't hard to proofread your seven-hour game. It'll take... seven total man hours to double check, and 14 to triple check.
The big one:
- THE GAME ABRUPTLY ENDS. Thanks for baiting me with the promise of a fun minigame, the thought of adventure in such bizarre times, then ambushin' me with the Credits. The game JUST got interesting. The mystery had JUST been expanded. There was even a hint in the last day to what might come ahead, but no. NO. Ya slam us with the dev names and let us take a final look at what we'd discovered. I really wanted to see how the characters reacted to such a... revelation. "Let's just take the day off," but it turned out to be taking forever off. The game needs an extension, because if the point— the artistic expression— was to explain nihilistic optimism, it failed. It just left us high & dry, and empty, like we fell into the event horizon of that hole. This is ultimately the reason for the negative (Not Recommended) review.
Like, let me play the last song while the credits roll by at least.
I guess I can move onto the good(+)/neutral(~) now.
+ The characters. It's hard to make me care about video game characters, especially characters like Angus. Congratz on passing this ambiguous bar of mine.
~ Gregg is effing amazing. It's a bad meme, but it's true: gregg rulz. Wasn't too keen on his deviousness and what seemed like cavalierness, especially towards Mae at times— like, I get he's supposed to be aloof, but isn't Mae, like, one of his best friends he'd die (and kill) for? So why is he ultimately unconcerned about her nearly dying each time (the minor times. The major times he responds correctly). Otherwise, a fun character I wish I knew in real life.
~ Angus was distant. I enjoyed his character finally being revealed five minutes before the game ended. Maybe don't do that: wait until the end to expand a main character. The game felt like it was three main cast members, plus two side characters: Angus and Germ. (Though he is definitely not like Germ since you can actually hang out with him. Once. Hint: open the 'whirly things' before you do so to maximize exposition.)
+ Bea was very realistic, aside from her irrational breakdown on the [dinner] night considering her otherwise intelligent and demure manner. The party was good, and she's ultimately the best character written.
+ You let us skip chunks of the walking scenes. Thank god. I enjoy the somberness of mandatory walking scenes, but most devs seem to think we like playing that stuff for extended periods of time. The most recent offender I've played was Destiny 2 after the intro. Ho-ly crap. So, thanks for teleporting us ahead.
~ The dungeon-crawler minigame would have been p good, but the dodging was wonky. Try dodging in one direction, then 'back dodging' in the other multiple times, then let go. You swing back. What. Also, check my screenshot of the final boss' bloodstain blocking the final door, resulting in a soft-lock. Cool. The best boss was the guy plus adds who dodged around and threw knives, that was a lot of fun, and I wish I could play a 'boss-rush' after I beat it. Pretty please?
~ I get trying to go for replayability, but I'm not big on the only difference being whose finale you see and therefore who you talk with at the end of the game. I'd've liked it to be able to hang out with everyone, like real people do in real life. Guess I WILL be playing it again, since I can't stand watching LPs or something like it, but I won't be all too happy about it. At least I get to play the rhythm minigame again.
~ The puzzles were simple and insulting to the age group this game targets (anyone older than 15). Thankfully there weren't many.
+ The songs. I love the songs. I love rhythm games, so naturally I aced them, but I wished there were (a few) more [at least one^]. The first one is especially good, "Die anywhere else." Add the game's soundtrack to this. I won't buy it, because it's definitely BGM for this atmospheric gem, but it's still very good. I'd buy the Dead Possums' albums, though!
I ultimately can't see the game being worth a Jackson— a solid 15 base price would be good— because of the length and how hard it drops you at the end of it. Maybe I'll flip the thumb if it goes down or if a 'FreeLC' extension is added to give... a couple of days in the game (maybe just two). If you made it this far in and haven't purchased the game yet, see about getting it on sale. Like right now. Now woud be worth it.
Well, I'm gonna obsess over this game a little now (it was great, after all). Thanks for making it.

You play as Elodie, a wide-eyed and innocent princess with pink hair (I told you to ignore the graphics for a reason) whose mother has just died leaving her in line to the throne. Needless to say there are plenty of people who don't think she is up for the job and will to their best to remove her over the next 40-odd weeks. Your task is to make her study a variety of subjects - from public speaking to falconry, intrigue to magic, dancing, flower arranging, sword fighting, you get the idea - and hopefully have her survive till her coronation. Of course, you could simply kill her off in dozens of different ways while searching out as many different plotlines as possible....
Whatever your take on becoming a royal, you are sure to have fun with this game. Highly recommended.

TLDR: while it looks great and has a wide variety of trains to choose from, especially thanks to mods, it is just not a great game and the DEV's are moving on to another game. I mostly played this game earlier, before the US update, but I reinstalled it some time afterwards and gave it another shot. Not that much appears to have changed, which is disappointing, as there are still quite a few things that could be improved. They promise they will keep supporting this one at least for a while, but major updates probably won't be forthcoming. I'm expecting only some bugfixes, not added content or changed mechanics. Such a shame. It is, in many ways, a decent game. There are also various mods which improve the game even further. But it is certainly not a great game. It really showed a lot of promise and might have ended up as a much better game than even Railroad Tycoon or any of its successors, never mind Transport Tycoon. Now my hope for that is fading fast. So not recommended, unless you're a hardcore train fanatic, eager to play anything to do with trains.
Long version: there are many good things about this game. It looks pretty great. It allows you to play with trains and road transport alike. It allows you to build a transport network across a map, connecting various cities and industries, which evolve and grow as you play. New trains and vehicles are unlocked with time. You can play with European or US buildings. It can be a lot of fun to lay out a track and watch your trains, even high speed TGVs, race across them. Unfortunately, the flaws of the game are very distracting.
Track laying is often anything but intuitive. There are a few guides on how to create overpasses and the like, but that kind of thing should be easy to do and it isn't. It often feels as if you're wrestling the game, to try and trick it and get it to do what you want it to do. I've had episodes where the game kept telling me something couldn't be done, or where tunnels ended up coming out just wrong so I had to relay track that then didn't match up, costing me literally millions or whatever coin is used in game, bankrupting my company so I had to restart from a save game. Sometimes I was just trying to lay track alongside of existing track, or turn a single track bridge into a two track bridge and the game just wouldn't cooperate. Why is there no option to lay out track, check if it is the right way, THEN confirm to actually lay the track? How about an undo option? Sometimes you try to lay track and the game things it is easier to carve down a hill, costing you millions, instead of just building a tunnel. Although there is something to be said for the feeling of being victorious when I managed to do something that the game had absolutely refused to cooperate with, even told me repeatedly that it couldn't be done, I highly doubt that any game should be made that way and that people would want to play a game that worked like that.
I also ran into trouble trying to get my trains to pass each other at a crossing. They ended up stopped, again costing me millions before I was able to fix it or forcing me to go back to an earlier save. Just when you think you've laid it out properly, a train stops, for no apparent reason and just turns back, headed the wrong way, all the way to the other side of the map, only losing money in the process. This game really should be able to use signals in a proper and realistic way. But even trying to create proper switches or points (intersections) is next to impossible. When I think I've managed to do exactly what I wanted, they end up confusing my trains so much they just stop altogether or start running on the wrong track. This is a game that tries to appeal to train enthusiasts, the trams and road vehicles seem to be thrown in as an extra, but it doesn't even get the train thing right. All in all, it feels unfinished.
Some things are really still pretty basic. You can't create a map from scratch or adjust the random map in any way. So no placing industries, creating or deleting villages, nothing. Adjusting the settings un such a manner as to make it as flat as possible still results in a map with significant hills, so I can forget playing on a map that even remotely resembles my native country, never mind create an exact replica of an existing area, no matter how small, as the maps are also still pretty small even at the largest settings. The game inclused road vehicles in addition to rail vehicles, but don't include either water or air transport at all. This makes no sense and further limits the opportunities in the game.
Improving or deleting streets is also quite difficult. Some options, like highways, don't even exist. Other options don't work very well, as you quickly end up having to destroy entire buildings, at great expense. In the end, you still end up with gridlock, with no clear way of getting people to get out of their cars, to take public transport. I have a sneaking suspicion that the AI that governs where people want to go is very, very basic and very, very flawed. That makes a game like this pretty much pointless, as instead of a realistic and challenging transport network, you end up having to play along with some obscure rules.
When I played earlier, there were several serious issues, that should not have been allowed to exist in a released game. At one point, I ended up with several corrupted savegames, at another I was completely unable to remove sections of road as they were deemed to be an essential connection, despite them not leading anywhere. I haven't played the current release of the game long enough to be sure, but I haven't encountered them again and am willing to give them the benefit of the doubt and assume both are fixed now. However, it says something about the state the game was in when I bought it and the level of Quality Control that these flaws were in a released game in the first place. So what hope do I have that their next game will be released in a better state? Why would I preorder that one, or buy it at full price, or even at all, based on this experience?
This game comes pretty close to being great however, which makes it all the more sad. With the Developers moving onto another game, there won't be as much support as there was, so all hope of this game being improved to be all that it could ever be, seems lost. It is not terrible, but it is certainly not great. It has something for enthusiasts, but mostly because of how little competition there has been in this field in the past few years. It leaves me feeling disappointed and sad, eager for more. And yet it could have been so much more and seemingly without too much effort. I've seen some interesting suggestions on the community hub and if the publisher changed its mind and came out with a solid update, that would fix the remaining flaws of the game and expand on its possibilities, I might even be persuaded to buy it. Something that I would do with reluctance, as it is still rewarding a company for releasing an unfinished game, but if it was good enough, I'd be willing to set that aside. They have people to feed too and moreover, I really want a game like this, only better. Just a bit better. I get the impression the developers were disappointed too, that they were too ambitious and now want to wash their hands of this game and move onto the real thing. But that would be wrong. Not only because they risk losing the trust of their customers forever, but also because they pass up the opportunity of making something really impressive out of this. They should invest in this game and really build it into a flagship product, show us what they really can do. Then keep releasing expansions. Then move onto the next engine and improve the game even further. They could milk us for years. How is that for a marketing strategy?

Now and then available at 75% off standard price -- keep an eye on this title and buy it then, not at full price, which it really isn't worth.  As sims go its basic, circa Windows 98 quality, despite a new recent release.  The colour palette is limited and this immediately makes it look retro and dated.  In use, its incredibly simple once you've grasped the basics, and so long as you just need to tootle softly along and not achieve anything great, it's a pleasing little game.  It's all too easy to lose money quickly so start small and only build once profits start going up; bus stops, train stops and stuff like that all cost money to maintain, used or not, and that's one area where the sim is very life-like.  Otherwise it can be rigid and mathematical, when it really ought to be organic and auto-adjusting.  The "achievements" are mostly stuff you'd do in the game anyway so don't start patting yourself on the back when you get an award for building two bus stops...zzz.
Some anti-virus programs (AVG is the one i use, and it's top of the list) won't allow this game to run so they need to be temporarily disabled, you do wonder what kind of "information gathering" bugs are sniffing through your computer while the game is operating....

12.8 hours in and I am already growing weary. Sure it is a free game, sure it is amusing, but there is a lot that leaves me wondering how long this title will maintain servers.

The progression is very slow. You level up by gathering forces from the various crates you get from winning games. Opening crates takes time, the longer the time the better the loot. You can spend gold bars to unlock the crates instantly or wait for the timer to expire. Only one crate can be on the timer at a time and you can have 4 crates stored. I used up the little bit of free gold I had and have made it to level 4 and I have some decent units. This is a very blatant pay to win structure but goes beyond many other pay to win structured games. In order to progress at a rate that would actually offer some enjoyment you will need to pay. You can get gold bars in the crates but I have only seen stacks of truly insignificant size.
I can't see this game lasting very long unless the developers/publishers give their heads a shake and come to realize that a happy customer is a return customer. That being said, it is a fun little game with some great potential. There is so much room for additional content in the form of game types, visuals, map variations and much more. I do hope the people calling the shots can figure out how to reach that potential.
I will recommend this game but I wont recommend falling into the pay to win trap. For the love of games, lets put that business model to an end. What would you rather do, pay to win or win with skill and pay to look cool doing it?

Normally I don't like Free-2-Play-Games and the likes because they often feel like the most commercial games of all. However, I guess as long as it's not "pay to win" or "pay or else you'll have to grind for a thousand years" it's ok.
I'm glad I checked this game out. I was intrigued by the art design and still am.
I have only had 7 matches or so, so this is not a "complete" review, but thought I'd let you guys know this seems to be worth checking out (being free2play).
In the beginning I had the feeling the mechanics were rather slim and every match would be pretty much the same, but I quickly realized that I knew only half of the strategic possibilities (and maybe tomorrow I'll say I knew only a quarter ;) ).
It doesn't take you more than an hour to get through the little tutorial, watch the two further tutorial videos (click on the banner in the upper right of the town screen to get there) and look at the special abilities of your warriors in the proving halls. Then you pretty much know all you need; the rest you'll learn on the battle field and when upgrading to other warrior types with different abilities.
The game has an atmospheric presentation and sound, is rather "quiet" but the tension in the matches can get your blood boiling.
For now, the game is in a rather early state (so a full review wouldn't even be fair). Everything seems to work (except for battling friends for now) but sometimes you cannot get into the game because of server load or maintenance. Also the game feels a little sluggish and laggy at times, but that's not much of a problem because of the turn-based nature of the game.
The in-game purchases don't seem to be necessary to enjoy the game (otherwise I would immediately stop playing it). Other than other colors for your warriors' clothes you can buy "renown" which is kinda like the currency in this game. You need it to upgrade your warriors and expanding your barracks. But you also earn renown for playing matches (even more when winning them) and it doesn't take forever for you to earn enough to upgrade your team from time to time. And since matches are put together via match-making, you won't have to fight an utterly overpowered team.
So if you're really impatient, you can spend money (and I'm sure there will be plenty people who will), but you'll have just as much a good gaming experience without; so that's a fair system in my book.
If you like chess-like games and/or nordic flair, try this game - it's not like it costs ya ;)
See y'all on the battlefield (when friend matches are back on) :]

Having gone through 3 episodes out of 5, I say with certainty - this is my kind of story. And if you're into immersive worldbuilding, exploration of hot topic issues of the modern world and story over action - this is your game as well.
[the review will be updated as the last episodes become available]
"I am not a Number, I am a free man!"
Republique is set in a compound called Metamorphosis, ruled by charismatic and tyrannical Overseer/Headmaster. The setup resembles, frankly speaking, a totalitarian sect; everyone is prisoner in this Orwellian surveillance microcountry: from the Pre-Cal children raised within to security enforcers called Prizrak (Russian for 'ghost') and even their higher-ups.
Big Brother can watch through every camera, and there are plenty of them. Fortunately, so can you. But is this truly a blessing? Just who is the player, the nameless silent hacker who guides the protagonist to escape?
While you certainly can rush from one plot point to another, Republique encourages to and rewards you for poking your nose in nooks and crannies, exploring its world and gathering evidence.
The gameplay is simple. Stealth is not the point, it's a vehicle that carries the plot and the setting. The point is exploration: of totalitarism, social engineering, propaganda, influence of mass media and fiction; and surveillance. Always surveillance. "Control is a lie", dead revolutionary Zager asserts, and the events inside the compound seem to prove him right. But there are Overseer's mysterious allies on the outside to contend with. Someone, someone powerful out there is, if not supportive, then at the very least tolerant of his insular, oppressive vision of ideal state and yes-men citizens.
A separate word needs to be said for the soundtrack. Immersive thrillers, be it a game or movie, always benefit greatly from quality auditory component, and Republique has its music right where and how it needs to be.
All in all. I give the game 8/10 so far, while I await anxiously episodes 4 and 5. Good going, Camouflaj. We'll be waiting with bated breath to see where you'll be taking us next.

So, with 10 hours into this game, and 300 in DayZ, I can firmly say that I do recommend this game to others. To sumarize, the game looks good, and plays well My extended thoughts are below.
Starting with the visuals,
.
prettier than my beloved DayZ. In this game, grass and trees are green, and vibrant, there are different plans and flora, and it all looks good. Where as DayZ has everything washed in grey, and it looks... dull... this is not the case with Miscreated. The game feels much more 'Alive' for it. There are many several story buildings, and the atmosphere fits the game's 'lore'. Yet, it was less intensive on my computer, which is strange, but not unwelcome. My one complaint was that the characters all look pretty generic, but the clothing helps.
Playing the game after playing DayZ, I will say the controls are a bit more complex. This isn't bad, though, but it takes a while to actually get the hang of it. I think it feels smoother than DayZ's clunky controls, but they still aren't perfect, and some things feel better, while some feel worse. Shooting feels good, and melee combat is a bit strange but you can adjust. There is a good variety of clothing, foods, weapons, and vehicles, and the crafting element makes the game feel like there is more to do. Crafting can be a bit buggy, but it overall adds to a good survival experience.
Miscreated is an unfinished game, but feels like more care has gone into than some of the other survival  sandbox games out there. It's far from perfect, and does have flaws, but if you like the whole 'Survival Sandbox Zombies' genre, then I would highly recommend it for you.

It pulls of it's story very well despite the use of cliches, however, in spite of the presence of these the charm, style, and sincerncity of the characters in their interactions is enough to carry them through. It's a good example that execution can turn something that should be tired around.
The game revolves strongly around story and you should be prepared to take it as a story before a game but it dosen't forget what medium it is and retains a strong sense interactivity. I mean, it's definitely more interactive and gives you at least the feeling-be it true or not- that your input is important to the world and the character than games like the walking dead.
It utilizes simple but effective visuals to deliver a sense of atmosphere straight from the get go and the soundtrack is consistently enjoyable. I have not heard a song from Night in the Woods that I didn't  like, nor did I neccesarily have a scene I didn't like even if sometimes old character tropes did blunt the stab of the emotion of the scene a bit.
A big thing about this game is that it isn't scared to reference politics, and while it does not reference real world events. It does reference political movements consistently, especially with one character. While this isn't good or bad, in today world politics is everywhere and games are a casual way of escaping the snark and righteous tutting of moral stances and  national cynicism.
It is feasible that someone suffering with a bit of fatigue and aggrevation from any of that may find their enjoyment of the story a bit dampened if they are already riled up or feel ambushed by this stuff a lot.
It is however, only passingly referencial and most of the time despite one characters frame work you can attest most of the actual opinions to the personalities of characters and not the characters to the opinions of the author themselves. If you have to hear one more "oh my god, you're a conservative" or something to snap, you might want to take a break before you play this.
If you don't give a rat♥♥♥♥♥ then you might be able to enjoy that from a perspective of character and not politics.

This is a great* (casual) game. The mingames are fun, the characters were enjoyable, the scenarios were interesting. This is something like an open letter to the devs.
I'll start with the bad.
- I couldn't stand the dream sequences. Every time I went to sleep I audibly said "please god NO. NO PLEASE," and was happy to wake up the next day or upset to find myself baby platforming/backtracking to the same four instruments of the same song, seemingly disconnected from the 'important' dreams and the story at large. We get two 'important' ones, and five of the unconnected time-padders.
- A few of the characters felt unrealistic at times, saying things that (ab)normal people wouldn't say. Like, the main character went to college for two years, you telling me she can't form sentences? "Still putting it all together" will be on her tombstone. What's with the croc, she's apparently smart but can't rationalize her own behaviour? What's with the ghost stuff being taken seriously, aren't these people in their twenties? It's made out to 'seem' like Mae has physical brain problems, but it turns out she's really not. (She's having cosmic problems, to be vague for spoiler-free.) Jebaited. This would have been understandable behaviour from teens.
- Running through town each day just to get to Gregg was not fun. I didn't mind it the first few days, but once the light is fixed I feel some 'shortcut' should have opened. How are you going to skip forced-walking sections understanding it isn't fun to walk for ages but not think about doing that in the town/earlier in the game?
- While I'm on the town, the waterway under the church was unused. It wasn't a shortcut, and it skipped the croc's place. Maybe put Beatrice and the Gregg's workplaces nearer next time, so when you tell one "I'll get back to you" you don't have to trek through a loading screen and close to a minute of running. Twice. It was more of a chore to continually go through the WHOLE town looking, most of the time in vain, for someone to be somewhere. Especially the waterway. The church/cliff is fine, but the waterway, Food Donkey, and town entrance were upsetting all but one time.
- Verbal choices didn't matter. I knew they wouldn't for the most part, but some dialogue sounded like what I said could have made SOME sort of impact. I get that we're playing Mae, not us in the game, but can't the illusion of choice be a little more... illusory?
- People play games to escape politics. Just couldn't help yourselves, huh? That could be removed from the game and no character would be destroyed. Not even Bea.
- Spelling and grammar. C'mon guys, it isn't hard to proofread your seven-hour game. It'll take... seven total man hours to double check, and 14 to triple check.
The big one:
- THE GAME ABRUPTLY ENDS. Thanks for baiting me with the promise of a fun minigame, the thought of adventure in such bizarre times, then ambushin' me with the Credits. The game JUST got interesting. The mystery had JUST been expanded. There was even a hint in the last day to what might come ahead, but no. NO. Ya slam us with the dev names and let us take a final look at what we'd discovered. I really wanted to see how the characters reacted to such a... revelation. "Let's just take the day off," but it turned out to be taking forever off. The game needs an extension, because if the point— the artistic expression— was to explain nihilistic optimism, it failed. It just left us high & dry, and empty, like we fell into the event horizon of that hole. This is ultimately the reason for the negative (Not Recommended) review.
Like, let me play the last song while the credits roll by at least.
I guess I can move onto the good(+)/neutral(~) now.
+ The characters. It's hard to make me care about video game characters, especially characters like Angus. Congratz on passing this ambiguous bar of mine.
~ Gregg is effing amazing. It's a bad meme, but it's true: gregg rulz. Wasn't too keen on his deviousness and what seemed like cavalierness, especially towards Mae at times— like, I get he's supposed to be aloof, but isn't Mae, like, one of his best friends he'd die (and kill) for? So why is he ultimately unconcerned about her nearly dying each time (the minor times. The major times he responds correctly). Otherwise, a fun character I wish I knew in real life.
~ Angus was distant. I enjoyed his character finally being revealed five minutes before the game ended. Maybe don't do that: wait until the end to expand a main character. The game felt like it was three main cast members, plus two side characters: Angus and Germ. (Though he is definitely not like Germ since you can actually hang out with him. Once. Hint: open the 'whirly things' before you do so to maximize exposition.)
+ Bea was very realistic, aside from her irrational breakdown on the [dinner] night considering her otherwise intelligent and demure manner. The party was good, and she's ultimately the best character written.
+ You let us skip chunks of the walking scenes. Thank god. I enjoy the somberness of mandatory walking scenes, but most devs seem to think we like playing that stuff for extended periods of time. The most recent offender I've played was Destiny 2 after the intro. Ho-ly crap. So, thanks for teleporting us ahead.
~ The dungeon-crawler minigame would have been p good, but the dodging was wonky. Try dodging in one direction, then 'back dodging' in the other multiple times, then let go. You swing back. What. Also, check my screenshot of the final boss' bloodstain blocking the final door, resulting in a soft-lock. Cool. The best boss was the guy plus adds who dodged around and threw knives, that was a lot of fun, and I wish I could play a 'boss-rush' after I beat it. Pretty please?
~ I get trying to go for replayability, but I'm not big on the only difference being whose finale you see and therefore who you talk with at the end of the game. I'd've liked it to be able to hang out with everyone, like real people do in real life. Guess I WILL be playing it again, since I can't stand watching LPs or something like it, but I won't be all too happy about it. At least I get to play the rhythm minigame again.
~ The puzzles were simple and insulting to the age group this game targets (anyone older than 15). Thankfully there weren't many.
+ The songs. I love the songs. I love rhythm games, so naturally I aced them, but I wished there were (a few) more [at least one^]. The first one is especially good, "Die anywhere else." Add the game's soundtrack to this. I won't buy it, because it's definitely BGM for this atmospheric gem, but it's still very good. I'd buy the Dead Possums' albums, though!
I ultimately can't see the game being worth a Jackson— a solid 15 base price would be good— because of the length and how hard it drops you at the end of it. Maybe I'll flip the thumb if it goes down or if a 'FreeLC' extension is added to give... a couple of days in the game (maybe just two). If you made it this far in and haven't purchased the game yet, see about getting it on sale. Like right now. Now woud be worth it.
Well, I'm gonna obsess over this game a little now (it was great, after all). Thanks for making it.

It's a survival game that may or may not survive. And, if it doesn't, I may not miss it.
I've been playing Stranded Deep since March of 2015. It is still in early access, and I haven't heard of an expected release date. I currently have 62 hours in the game, and honestly that is the only reason I keep coming back to check on the progress. I maintain this crazy hope that the game will improve. My year and a half playing this game tells me it may not, even though a lot more people have bought the game in the past year. But, the game continues to have so many flaws, despite the updates.

Castaway, the movie, with Tom Hanks. Ok, so the story is not original. But, it really doesn't have to be. The movie was great... a classic that I've watched multiple times, which I rarely do with movies. So, the game has a great premise and a classic movie to build upon. Who could go wrong with that? You wander around a desert island, building makeshift hut homes, collect flotsam from the sea, and salvage from sea wrecks; besides seeing all the sea life. Not much could improve on this setting. So, where did the game take such a sad nosedive?
The interface for the game is sad. It must be the worst crafting system I have yet to experience in gaming. Seriously! Whose idea was this? And, over the course of updates, this has gone from bad to worse. Chop a tree 13 times, then chop the individual logs 13 times, then drag it around, all in a stilted way that resembles real life in no way.
Originally they had you piling everything in a pile and hovering over it to craft something from mid air. In the latest updates, they've removed that mechanic, and you just hit c for a menu of craftable items you have on you. But, is that any more realistic? No. Is it simpler? Simply silly if you are on a deserted island. And, they've removed the hotbar and the item in your hand does not show as being in your inventory when you press tab. All in all, they've made changes that are just as ridiculous as the original interface. It takes away from my enjoyment of the atmosphere.
I mentioned the stilted character above. Well, he now is more visible, because you can see his legs when you look down, as if seeing his arm swinging wildly before the camera as you walk & wobble with the arm bounce around the island weren't enough. It makes me more nauseous than eating the raw crabs did. And, now they've changed it so that even the potatoes make you sick in the game. I suppose they must be cooked. But, what is the rationale behind that? Raw potatoes do not make a person sick. Only in Stranded Deep do raw potatoes make a person sick.
The art is beautiful and certainly draws me back hoping for something more from this game. But, the graphics are substandard. The character barely moves across the screen, the lag is insufferable, and the framerate struggles. Then there are the numerous surface distortions in the graphics. And, I haven’t seen any of this improve in the past year and a half. I see no hope for this game to ever come out of early access.
When I first started playing, I put over 50 hours into the game, trying to make a go of it. I quickly realized there just weren't enough resources on one tiny island to build a hut of much more than one little cube. This presented the problem of obtaining resources from other islands, which were far enough away that you would have to set up a new base there. Moving resources from one island to another is unwieldy, considering the limit to items you could carry in your inventory. And, there is no way to carry items on a raft that will most likely capsize when hit by a shark in the ocean. So, I lost interest in playing a game where I could not build very much. SInce then, I have only come back to check to see if this is being improved, despite the fact that I can't play for more than 30 minutes at a time because of the swinging camera and swinging arm, without getting nauseous. There really aren't enough resources on these tiny islands. I would suggest making a bigger island for the spawn island, perhaps with caves like in Robinson Crusoe, or the movie.
* Great story
* Island atmosphere
* Island survival
* Horribly clunky interface
* Camera swings make you nauseous
* Lack of substantial resources
* Game improvements few & far between, with scant effect
* The graphics are poor quality

For all of you looking for a true zombie survival game, you've come to the right place.  You're going to spend a ridiculous amount of time having stories to share with your friends unfold before your eyes.
The base game has an enjoyable story, though it's the sandboxy feel that goes along with it that makes this game an excellent one.  You are continually capable of working toward your next story goal at your own pace, though if you're like me you'll find the majority of the game is spent exploring, collecting supplies, building up your base, dealing with other survivor groups, gaining skills for you survivors, etc.  Every character has a unique backstory and there are -a lot- of survivors out there that you might run into and have join you.
The base building is simple, yet very enjoyable as well.  Depending on what skills your survivors have, different options are available and you have plenty of options available to you.  Do you want to be able to support more survivors?  Build a bunkhouse and a garden so that they have a comfortable place to sleep and food to eat if your scavenged supplies run low.  Looking to cut back on the sneaking around and really take the fight to the zombies?  An infirmary will keep your survivors healthy and a munitions shop will keep them well armed.  Just remember, even healthy, well armed survivors might run into a challenge when facing off against the 'freaks' or special zombies.
The Breakdown DLC removes the deep story aspect of the the vanilla campaign, though it adds a brand new achievement system that unlocks 'hero' survivors that, more often than not, are more capable than your average survivor.  This mode also has 'Breakdown Levels', each time you complete one you move on to the next, more challenging phase, with new survivor achievements to unlock.
I highly recommend this game to anyone who enjoys the zombie survival genre.  I'd been looking for a game like this for a very long time and was extremely happy when I installed it and truly learned what it was all about.  Enjoy and I'd love to hear your stories!

As you may gather from the amount of time that I have spent playing this game I do love it. This game has great replay value. It captures you. It is a lot like when you are playing GTA and you find yourself just simply going on a rampage and killing everything in sight for hours on end. The reason I compare this game to GTA mass killing sprees is that for some reason you can find yourself doing the same things over and over for hours without being bothered by how repetetive it is.
This game gives you full control over most of your group and allows you to build and customize the skills of each character. You can find survivors, relocate your base, rebuild your base, and last but not least kill tons of zombies. The survival aspect of the game is something to be reckoned with. The game is well balanced though at times a bit frustrating. There are frame rate issues but easily ignored. If anything the frame rate issues only destroy the beauty potential of this game.
All of that being said there are a few things that could be improved and added to the upcoming games or add-ons in this soon to be great franchise. First and foremost is character depth and personality. I feel that this game could use a lot more of a personal touch with characters that we could love, hate, or connect with. I currently find myself choosing my favorite survivors based on how they look from behind than any other reason. The game could also use more story depth and cut scenes. I love cut scenes and feel that they can make or break games and in this case it could only help. Of course there are minor tweaks here and there that would make this game perfect.
We should all be looking for this in the future!

This sequel has some significant improvements over the original.
The basic gameplay is still the same. You're still fighting a defensive battle against a horde of orcs and other baddies. But now there's a lot more spells, traps, monsters, and levels to play with.
In Story Mode the War Mage has been joined by a new playable character, which (in a nice plot twist) turns out to be the main villain from the previous game. The War Mage and Sorceress each have different stats and abilities, with the War Mage being more trap-focused, and the Sorceress being more spell-focused. So now you can play co-op with your friends, which is good because this is definitely the sort of game that works for co-op.
The bad news is the story isn't that great. In the first game it was cool that you were the last war mage fighting an impossible battle against an endless horde...But in the sequel they basically say, "Sorry, due to some rather careless actions taken in the first game your victory didn't actually mean anything. So here's some more orcs for you to fight." Blah! There are many reasons they could have come up with to justify defending fortresses from orcs; denigrating your victory in the previous game was not a good idea I don't think.
But even though the story was rather lackluster, the gameplay is as fun as ever! And now Story Mode is now just one of many modes that you can play. Now you can try Endless Mode, where you try to see how long you can survive on a particular map. There's also Classic Mode, which brings back some fun maps from the first game. And there's even a Weekly Challenge and some fun DLC.
With even more traps and options there are tons of ways to play this game. Many times I found myself re-evaluating my strategy, thinking things such as, "Well spring traps didn't work for this level. Hmmm! Maybe if I place some archers here in this bottleneck..."
It's easy and fun to get lost in planning how many ways you can kill orcs. Slice them, dice them, toss them into lava, blow them up with gunpowder barrels, crush them under boulders, drop vats of acid on them, turn them into chickens...
If you liked the original game or you like defense-centered tactical games you'll like Orcs Must Die 2!

For the most part, this is a great train game. The graphics are nice, laying track is well done, i like the map generator. And you can build some reasonably complex rail networks.
However, this game badly needs some code optimization. Once you build up your rail network a little bit.. enough that you're covering 4 or 5 cities, the performance takes a serious nose-dive and the game becomes unplayable. Every in-game month the game has to calculate & apply the expenses for all your vehicles. Once youve got more than 30 or 40 vehicles, this process locks the game up for a good minute or more, if you grind through that enough to get up to 60 or 70 vehicles, the game will lock up for over 2 minutes while it calculates your monthly expenses. Couple this with the fact that it does this every game month, which is about 5 minutes IRL, you'll spend approx 30 to 40% of your playtime looking at a frozen mouse pointer. Ugh..
And thats not necessarily a huge rail network. Maps have about a dozen cities in them, but you wont get to more than 1/3rd of them before the game becomes unplayable.
And from the looks of it, there are no plans to develop this game further. So it's likely to stay broken.

I really liked Sid Meier's Railroads. When I discovered Train Fever and decided to buy it, I really hoped it would be a worthy successor, as Sid Meier's Railroads is pretty much an antique by today's standards. I've been editing this review quite a few times as I've been playing and learning the game, and after playing for around 25 hours, I believe I finally have a good enough perspective to give a thorough and fair review.
The positive points:
1) The game is, or at least *should be*, fun to play, if and when it works properly. Needless to say, I wouldn't have wasted 25 hours playing a game I didn't enjoy playing, so that fact speaks for itself.
2) The vehicles look good, graphically. I can't judge for myself how accurate and realistic they look, but by reading other reviews and comments, I got the impression the developers did quite a good job about that.
3) The soundtrack is nice and fun to listen to while playing.
The negative points:
1) The performance is *really* bad. I have a decent PC. Nothing too fancy or cutting-edge, but enough to run most modern games smoothly on medium-high settings (Cities: Skylines, for one). Train Fever, on the other hand, barely works. It starts out okay, but as soon as the cities get a little larger than their starting size and there are over 30-40 vehicles moving, the game stutters constantly. I read somewhere that the main reason for that is that the game only uses one CPU core, as it doesn't support multi-core. All in all, the game seems not to use the hardware resources it has, which implies poor programming.
2) The interface is very uncomfortable, there are no tutorials or in-game beginner-friendly guides to help understand how the game works. The information screens are vague and confusing. You pretty much need to learn the basics by trial and error, which is quite frustrating, considering you also have to struggle with the lousy performance while at it. I work as an accountant and I deal with companies' financial reports on a daily basis, but even I have been having troubles figuring out the financial data the game gives me about my company. Totally counter-intuitive. Needless to say, I know practically nothing about engineering or anything related to trains, which seems like a serious disadvantage when playing such a game. I've managed to improve a bit in my track building skills, but I'm still pretty clueless about how the cargo industries work, and the little I do know - I had to learn from a guide I read online. The little information the game gives about that is so cryptic, that it made me wonder what the developers had in mind when they released the game in such a state.
3) Not enough content. There are no AI competitors, no random events, no side-quests, missions or anything else to make the game more interesting. While the game could be interesting enough without all those things (if it worked properly), they would sure be an important addition.
All in all, I only recommend this game to hard-core fans of the genre, and even then - I'd suggest waiting for it to go on sale. For anyone else, I'd suggest to pass on this game. Not worth it.
===========
While I stand by my analysis of the game, I decided I've been enjoying the game so much (as evident by my play-time counter, that has already passed the 100 hours mark), that it would be unfair on my part to leave the negative rating as it is, so I'm about to flip it to positive.

I have played many games of this genre before, including Locomotion, all of the Transport Tycoons, Railroads!, all of the Railroad Tycoon games and a few others, and never before have I encountered a product as well balanced and easy to use as this. Granted, the economy works differently than most other games in this genre. For example, in most transport games, trains only run when they are full of goods in order to make a profit, however, in Train Fever, running trains without them needing to be full is essential to make a profit, because, much like in real life, a train on a siding is burning fuel and going nowhere, while its load decays in value. The game is well priced and has a strong user interface that is easy to use and a refeshingly easy approach to replacing and re-routing vehicles. I higly recomend this game to anyone that wants to think while playing a game, and or is interested in logistics and transportation.

The game puts you in the shoes of Mae Borowski. You explore your hometown at your own pace, visiting familiar faces and hanging out with friends each day. The overall art style, animation, and music gives the game a comforting feel and...
wait, what's that in the woods?

First off I'd like to start with the style of the game. The color schemes are spectacular and serve to convey feelings very well. The animations are smooth and expressive. The design of the characters is so well done after a while they stop looking like animals.
The music is one of my favorite things, especially the songs in the dreams. It has a sort of feeling to it, something that tells you you'll become nostalgic when you hear it in the future.
Gameplay is pretty fun, with sort of an open world you can explore while progressing. Tons of hidden stuff and tons of choices to make.
There's some pretty deep and serious things in this game as well, but they're neither too serious nor too light hearted. The pacing is great and development of the characters makes you feel emotions for them you rarely feel with rushed or overdramatic characters like in some other stories.
What really astonished me about this game was that so many of the characters were EXACTLY like people I know. Not like they just share tiny bits of personality, but so close to the point where you start imagining the video game characters talking with the real life counterpart's voices.
The game's setting and characters first came off to me as very depressing and sad, but over time the feeling of the game starts getting hopeful and warm. This game is definitely the type of thing I'll remember forever, I am very glad I bought this.
If I had to complain about anything I'd say the minigames are tough as hell, but other than that, I have no criticisms.

Update: Previously I described a game breaking bug in here, which is still not fixed, but it is possible to workaround for now  (See comments)- So this review focuses on the game without bugs..
To the game itself:
I really like the concept behind this game! It is totally fresh and different to other games. The story is very believable, especially when you look at the raise in surveillance in our everyday world. I played from chapter 1-3 and took around 6 hours, however I did not collect every book or audio file.
Story
As described above, the story is very believable. The voice actors are amazing. There are no ground breaking plot twists or such, but I'd say the story is better than most AAA games (as they often have none).
Gameplay
The gameplay feels fresh because the camera is controlled by (mostly) you. Its quite cool to have Hope wait at some spot, while you scout the place through the cameras, reaveal patrol routes, hack into computers, gather information and so on. Especially the later bigger levels are great!
The planning process that is possible due to the many different perspectives (through each camera) is enlightening. In near every level there is a multitude of routes to succeed. The develpers also included the right amount of backtracking - not too much.
However the game itself is a little to easy towards the end, as you have a stuffed inventory and full batteries, so basically in episode 3 I was not once caught by a guard. Also it seems there is no punishment for being caught in episode 1/2 - i dont know about episode 3, except the setback to a certain location in the level.
Another minor bad thing about the gameplay is the automatic camera switching - it's quite annoying, as I like to have full control over the camera. Maybe there will be a setting in the future to turn this off?
Graphics:
Most of the time the graphics is spot on. I did not play the mobile version so I can't compare. But I'd say the graphics suits the game very well. Sometimes the colors are a little washed out, and in some parts you can see recyled posters, newspapers, textures and even level parts. But it always seems kind of realistic, and does not disturb the gameplay. I like Hope's animations a lot - she feels very believable in general. There are some cool effects during camera/room switches, however they tend to stutter a little.
Sound:
As stated previously, the voice acting is phenomenal. Every piece of content and be it so little got a voice. Ok I have to admit for some posters etc. they used a little trick by not using a voice actor but a text to speech solution. But it is quite rare, and it fits the game world, and is also explained storywise so I have to give credit for this. Oh and the eerie music of the game really improves the overall immersion - really cool.
I guess that was a quite long review lets get to the summary.
Summary:
All in all the game is great! I would even say one of my favorite stealth action games. Ok it could be a little harder, but maybe that happens in the next episodes anyway. The voice acting is great, the story and characters are believable, the graphics and music make you feel a part of this futuristic world. I only fear that there will be some backtracking in future episodes as there were a lot of doors in the complex undiscovered (omni v5), however I'm looking forward to the final? 2 episodes.
Hope this review helps some of you with your decision. I know it's a little long.
PS: I reported the bug via email, hope it get's resolved soon. Seems the crashes are due to the engine (Unity 5) which is still in beta state. However they are rare and there is a workaround (see comments)
It's still a BETA version so it's hard to make review about that but it's going in good way. Developers needs to add a lot of thing and improvement - we will see.

Little girls dream of being queens—but ruling a kingdom is harder than you would think. Long Live the Queen is a cute visual novel that combines elements from tabletop strategy games with in-depth stat building to create a choose-your-own-adventure journey to queendom. The road to rulership is never easy, though, and players of Long Live the Queen will find themselves dazzled by a vast array of possible death scenarios and addicted to the thrill of finding new strategies to overcome obstacles.
As Crown Princess Elodie, you spend the majority of Long Live the Queen choosing how to spend your valuable time in weekly classes that boost Elodie's various stats. Each week allows you to choose two classes to take, some of which will boost Elodie's softer skills (like conversation, royal demeanor, history, and medicine) while others will add points to more aggressive skills (such as weapons, intrigue, and military knowledge). The broad scope of skills and abilities allows for many styles of play: perhaps you'll choose to be a fierce warlord who is skilled with a sword or maybe you'll choose to be a radiant debutant with the manners of a young socialite. Both strategies are viable options in Long Live the Queen, and the endless amount of weekly options makes for varied strategies and approaches.
In between times spent studying, Elodie will be given the option to attend various events, pass judgment on people of her kingdom, and pass laws and taxes. Players can start wars, behead criminals, break betrothals, and challenge opponents to duels. The player is frequently presented with skill checks and decisions that, depending on Elodie's ability to pass or fail these checks and your choices of actions and dialogue, can change the course of Elodie's story and, yes, even lead to her untimely death!
In sum, Long Live the Queen is a wonderful little casual game meant for those who are attracted to visual novels with strong elements of strategy to them. Its large number of choices lends itself well to several playthroughs, especially for those seeking to collect Long Live the Queen's achievement for discovering all eleven ways to die. Unlocking the tragic story of the death of Elodie's mother (and getting revenge for her demise!) is an experience that demands recommendation.

This is a letter for the devs, I
, but should also be here.
Dear BI:C Devs,
I've been playing BI:C daily since introduced by the E3 humble bundle. I'm really enjoying playing it in the background while watching YouTube etc.
The only complaint I have, is how the crate system works. It's become evident with the limited "Special offer", to open crates instantly. Here are the problems with current crate system (when not during instant unlock event).
Long unlock times - The amount of time needed to unlock crates is far too long; it would be fine if this were a mobile game. However, this is a desktop game so I can't just close the game put it in my pocket to play later, I want to be able to unlock crates within my play session, or for rarer crates, within a few play sessions. I understand this is to attract more microtransactions, though you need to draw a line in the sand to where microtransactions affect the games enjoyment too much. You must remember this is a desktop game now; it's fine to have this sort of mechanic on the mobile version, though it kind of ruins the desktop experience.
Very small inventory to store crates - Due to the long unlock times, in a play session you accumulate all four slots for crates very quickly. Now, I understand this is again to attract more microtransactions, though the same dilemma as point 1 is encountered. The real problem here is, once I've filled out my four slots, it feels pointless to keep playing as I won't get crates for winning.
This is how you could fix these issues:
Decrease unlock times - As described above, it takes way to long to unlock crates for it to be enjoyable, sure the times are fine for a mobile app, though play sessions are longer on desktop, so you fill up for crates slots to quickly.
Increase # of crate slots - The number of crates you can have should be either larger or expandable (through leveling, not microtransaction), this way we can play for longer and still obtain crates on wins. Seems silly to limit slots unless you're hungry for microtransactions, which doesn't work for desktop games, just ruins the experience.

No successful desktop game run on mobile style microtransactions, if you want more money, change microtransactions to match other desktop games, CS:GO, TF2 are examples where it's been done right and have profited because of it, even if you don't like the games, you can see how successful their microtransaction systems work. Because, in the end, removing these limitations will affect the amount of gold bought with $, but will give you better reviews, more players which in turn and the long run will get you far more $. is an amazing take on a tower defense/3rd-person action combo. Attributes of both genres are blended together perfectly to form an addictive and entertaining little game. This is a game that is very easy to enjoy.
does a great job taking 3rd-person action elements and blending them with some tower defense to establish a good basis. Then they sprinkle in the lighthearted atmosphere and charming characters with the simplistic-yet-captivating mechanics of the game… and it shapes up to be a really fun, delightful experience. It’s definitely the kind of game you can dive right into and get hooked for hours.
There is a relatively large amount of different towers and abilities in the game when compared to many other games in the tower defense genre. You have plenty of options and can have fun experimenting with different strategies. The level designs also vary enough that they call for different approaches to beat them, so you will have to try out different tactics in order to succeed. And there is a fair amount of different enemies which keeps things fresh as you progress through the game.
There is also a scoring system and leaderboards to add replay value.
is a step forward from the already amazing first game.  All the good aspects return, with some new ideas sprinkled in. There are many more traps and abilities, and a more extensive upgrade system.  There are many new enemies.  There’s a new extensive campaign, new game modes (like endless mode), and with the Steam Workshop there are now limitless possibilities for maps.
Also the addition of cooperative mode makes the experience exponentially more fun if you have a friend to play with.
I would say practically everyone should enjoy the

Gamedesign is very solid and it makes much fun building the traffic lines and earn money with them.
The vehicles are designed well and with the USA DLC theres even more diversity. However i still think vehicle running costs could be balanced a little better.
Building train tracks(double+) is also a little frustrating sometimes when you can see no logic reason why the terrain can't be aligned and will drive you nearly nuts when trying to connect two stations through a tunnel or when the station istelf has to be in hilly terrain.However after some time practicing one is able to mostly avoid such situations.
Well considering only Gameplay/Design i would give the game a 8/10
BUT
There is the technical side that is pretty much a gamebreaker. In the Endgame or roughly after 1950 when the Cities start expanding the frame rate Drops significantly (for me from 60FPS frame cap to 8-15 FPS depending on camera view)
and the autosave at the end of the year tends to stop the game for several seconds) Having the line overview open or a train window (the one where the train is viewed in the frame of the window) will drop the frames even more.
All in all it can be called a slideshow.
All you can do against it is play on small maps then the performance drops are kept at bay, but with a middle to large map (which are much more fun) you are pretty much doomed.
The perfomance issues seem to be caused by poor programming since cpu Utilization never rises above 20-25% and the graphic card is only utilized to a third of its potential.So even having a pretty high end system won't help much, since only 1or 2 Threads seem to be used by the game.
In my case its an FX8320(overclocked to 4.5ghz) paired with gtx 980 ti.
my final Rating would be a 2/10 considering perfomance drops in the endgame nullify the fun of the work you invested in the Previous 100-150 simulated years.

This is what happens when you have 3 cooks in the kitchen and take too long to get a game out. Compared to Half-Life 2 and Counter-Strike: Source, which both came out in the same year as this game (2004), Condition Zero offers practically nothing. The game was so bad during development that Valve even reverted its "gold" status and changed developers on the project 3 times. The result is that very few ideas feel consistent and connected.
Single-Player experience? You just get a bunch of bot matches with arbitrary and unimaginative restrictions and goals to complete missions that are not connected in any way (there isn't even any pretend story). The nicest word I can use for the sense of progression is "limited". Also, when you finish the game, there's just... nothing.
Multi-player experience? This game plays exactly like Counter-Strike 1.6, but partitions the players instead of just offering the campaign as an expansion (similar to Diablo II and Diablo II: LoD, which also came out around the same time). There are some exclusive maps, but I failed to see how any of them were an improvement to their CS 1.6 counterparts. Even if the maps were enough of an incentive, it was a pretty low effort endeavor for someone to copy-paste them into the CS 1.6 workshop. This means that you essentially had 2 versions of CS going on at one time, except one of them costed extra so people just stuck with 1.6 instead lol.
Graphics? They look like hot garbage compared to the other games from Valve that came out at the same time (Half-Life 2 and CS: Source). The game looks like it was made in 1998.
I got this as part of the Counter-Strike complete package during a Steam Sale, and it felt like an incredible chore to finish. There is a video from a recent CS:GO major talking about the history of Counter-Strike, and they mention how "
". Funny how they comment on that while actually omitting CS:CZ from CS history. Honestly, this game is an embarassment.

It doesn't matter if you good or bad at fighting games. I am not good-at-all at it but Ultra Street Fighter IV (USFIV) is clearly the only fighting game that make me want to be better at it. This game is awesome. Really, it is. It's also a great game if you're really strong at fighting games of course don't worry.
Let's make a list.
Pros ;
+ Controls ; You have a couple of choice, arcade controller (the best), the XBOX or basic controller (the good) and the keyboard (the not-so-good). I am playing on keyboard and Capcom show us that it's possible to play with a keyboard at Street Fighter.
+ Ambiance ; One of the most intense and greatest ambiance I ever saw in a videogame.
+ Sound ; With quality voice acting and sounds, it won't hurt your ears and it keep the great ambiance.
+ Music ; I am not into Techno music but this game have clearly great musics that fit every situations.
+ Graphism ; Colorful and awesome. The characters animations were really polished and all the extra effects look perfect.
+ Storyline ; Yes, there is a storyline for EVERY SINGLE CHARACTER in the Arcade mode. Every character have their own theme, rivals, boss and cutscene (let's not forget about the animation that starts at the begining of a fight too.)
+ Character choice ; There is a lot of playable characters which made the Street Fighter Universe so great. Make your choice. Play only with your special someone or try'em all.
+ Character customization ; You can change the color of your character clothes and even changing them if you have the correct DLC of course.
+ Difficulty ; There not only Easy Medium and Hard there is like 10 differents difficulties. You just need to pick-up the one that fits you which make this game perfect for Not-good players or Super strong players.
+ 2 Players party ; Of course, why in the world would you not being able to play with your (real-life) friend at a Street Fighter game?
+ Training and Challenge Mode ; Those are great and can really help you to figure out some new tricks for your favorite character.
Cons ;
- Online ; No much people and most of them are smurfs and people that is playing fighting games from the time they're 5. No actual rookie, initiated, causual or even intermediate players. Only brainless phycos that absolutely need to play with a stick.
- Online lag ; Like the online matchmaking isn't already that hard. There is a serious problem about the lags in this game.
- Team Match ; It looks interesting, but I was never able to find a single server.
- DLCs ; It bring great customization possibilities but it's expensive. Like 5€ for 4~5 outfits.
- Difficulty at the end of the Arcade Mode ; When you're going for the boss it will be really, really, really harder that the other folks you just met ealier. It can be really frustrating sometimes.
- Achievements difficulty ; Why Capcom, why ? These achivements are super hard, really.
TL;DR
Overall, this is great. Really. But don't bet on the Online mode, it's not nice. However the Arcade and Versus Mode are awesome. You will really have fun by playing this game. It worth the price, definitly

It hurts me to say this, but as much as I enjoyed my time with Night in the Woods' charming world and characters, I find myself wishing that this really wasn't a game at all.
Let me explain that a bit.
Night in the Woods has charm to go round; from its adorable character designs and lovingly crafted soundtrack to the utterly stellar writing and cosy little town it takes place in, NITW absolutely nails the atmosphere and sank me deep into its story instantly.
That story is also suitably nuanced, being a strange comedy/drama combo (until a certain point) depending on which characters you decide to hang out with, letting you choose between, say, going on a walk with Mae's mother, or engaging in adorably petty crimes with Gregg.
As mentioned earlier, that dialogue is also a masterpiece; not only are the characters all written so intricately, but their dialogue also comes accross as totally natural and also carries a real understanding of "millennial" culture found so rarely elsewhere.
In fact, in just about every artistic element, Night in the Woods is a wonderful game and I SO NEARLY gave it a pass on that alone.
But unfortunately this is a game, and as such it asks you to interact with it.
And I rather wish it didn't.
Unfortunately, while the story, world, dialogue, characters - the whole a kit-n-kaboodle - is a treasure, the gameplay is utterly dreadful in just about every facet, and I wonder if it might not be if it just focused on one or two things and did them well.
As it stands, NIght in the Woods features an ungodly mix of thoroughly underwhelming platforming throughout, unskippable sections where the game suddenly decides to be a terrible ripoff of guitar hero and mindless button-mashing, all of which serves to break up a core gameplay loop which boils down to absolutely nothing more than "press X to cutscene".
Absolutely none of the many gameplay elements present in the game are any fun, or offer any meaningful complexity, and often serve to drag the story down.
There is even a whole dungeon-crawler in the game, and even that fails to operate properly and qhickly becomes just another of NITW's infuriating minigames.
All of this brings me to the conclusion that Night in the Woods would be best served in literally any other medium. I would read a Night in the Woods comic, I would watch a NITW tv show or film, I would even probably listen to a NITW podcast, but the last thing I want to do is to play it.
But as it stands, the best thing to do is to find its soundtrack on Spotify or such, then put on a lets play and mute the video as it plays.
And at that point it's not a game anymore, it's a kind of tv show.
