When you get Counter-Strike: Condition Zero, you are actually buying two separate games, Condition Zero, which is the final product and is essentially a bunch of bots matches, and the Deleted Scenes, which is a series of unconnected singleplayer level and is essentially the remains of an older version of the game before it was completely redone. The irony is that the final product seems to have less content and not be of as high quality as the Deleted Scenes.
Condition Zero itself is simply an ordered series of bot matches across many counter-strike maps. You can recruit bots using points won by winning matches which is pretty nice as it allows you to have some level of control over team management.
Within each match you have individual goals you must complete like 'kill a certain numbers of enemies with a particular weapon' or 'rescue a certain number of hostages'. These are presumably to try and force the player to vary their gameplay, but most of them end up just being frustrating and annoying to complete.
Another frustrating feature is that if you die, there's no 'control bot' option like in CS:GO, you are instead forced to watch the bots play out the rest of the round. As I'm sure you can imagine, watching this can be very painful indeed, and it is also very frustrating and time-consuming.
There is also a multiplayer component to Condition Zero, which is simply the same as in the original CS. There are surprisingly a significant number of populated servers, and it is very easy to simply jump onto a server and start playing. However if the multiplayer is the main component you’re after, it would be wiser to look into .6 as its playerbase is a lot, lot bigger.
Despite its flaws, Condition Zero is overall still a pretty fun game though.
Deleted Scenes however is a very different game entirely. It is a group of many call of duty style singleplayer missions. Although they are in the style of newer games call of duty, they still retain all the elements of classic counter-strike games, such as hitscan weapons with no aiming down sights and a fixed health percentage with no regeneration, as well as that classic GoldSrc ‘feel’. This in my opinion means that the game has a really interesting and unique feel to it.
The missions can be played in a pre-set order, however they aren't related in terms of context or story at all, each is its own separate unrelated 'episode' if you like. This might sound like a flaw to the game, but personally I believe it is a benefit as it means that each level can go in a different direction and is unique from the others.
The gameplay mostly consists of call of duty style missions. Although the main overall gameplay is the same in all missions, the individual nature of each mission means that are all varied in terms of settings, plots and structure. For example, some missions contain lots of stealth sections, some require you to use various tools and gadgets like snake cameras, radios and explosives to progress whereas others contain boss fights against enemy leaders or vehicles.
The levels are all of a perfect length too. You can easily complete a mission in one sitting, yet it'll still take you a reasonable amount of time to do so, allowing them to have a structure.
In conclusion, if you're looking for the classic counter-strike multiplayer experience or the opportunity to play bot matches, while Condition Zero will allow you to do those, it would be wiser to look towards 1.6 or GO respectively. However if you are a fan of games like Call of Duty, Half-Life or just GoldSrc games in general, then Deleted Scenes is an underrated fun experience.

I recommend this game. It is cheap and I have spent a lot of time playing it. I've had a lot of fun, especially with mods.
PROS:
- The goal is always the same, but the floors and their contents are different through every run, which gives this game a lot of replay value to me.
- There's a lot of items that do many different things, so 2 runs are never the same (you can download new ones from the community pages too)
- You won't get overwhelmed by the number of items because you unlock them little by little as you play, so you can learn about them little by little.
- The game is fun in general. You will unlock better and better items, and the ennemies will be stronger and stronger, but in the end they all have their patterns. This game is all about learning.
- I don't think the Afterbirth DLC is that great in itself, but being able to access the steam community is awesome. A lot of people have great ideas that could be added to the game, and from time to time, some workshop items ARE added into the game (so you could say it is still evolving).
- The music is good. I especially like the cathedral's music.
- It's a 2D game. I love 2D games, they feel
to me, since I'm looking at a flat screen (that's just my opinion).
CONS:
- I don't like the way sprites are pixelated. I prefer how it looked in the first game, but you can enable a weird filter to make things smoother (and you stop noticing it after a while anyway).
- The story is really sad. If you use the informations you get from endings, loading screens and items, you can find what happened to Isaac and his family. And it's really sad. There are days when I just like the mechanics, and there are days when I feel overwhelmed by the sadness of this game. I think the worst part is Magdalene, since her name is close to mine, I feel even more connected to her story.
All in all, I wouldn't say this game is hard, or easy. You can change anything with mods, which makes the difficulty very variable. Change it up to your liking.

Shadow of Mordor is medium fun.
Taking control of a quasi-dead Gondor guard, you wreak havoc among the Mordor camps hunting down the orc/ urakai leaders and, really, its mostly just killing things.
For those who aren't familiar with Lord of the Rings, you are a ghostly human who fights human looking monsters in a desolate wastland.
The central gameplay is combat, and the combat is ripped straight from the Arkham franchise.  It is a fast paced flow system that involves quick hack and slash with counters and extra moves to respond to the enemies and thier unique units and abilities.  There have been some slight changes from Arkham in that the fighting is slower and has more weight.  The overall difficulty is much higher as well.  Both to scale and given the fact that the number of enemies can easily swell and leave you at an insane disadvantage.
The overall quality is much lower however.  Arkham had color coded enemies with obvious designs.  Large, ranged, etc enemies were easy to identify and react to.  The Shadow of Mordor Urakai look exactly the same.  Having played somethign better, it's more than little frustrating to be smacked down by one unit hiding in a group of one hundred that I could have easily dealt with if I had realized he was there.
Outside of combat, the world map is very small.   You can explore everything within the first hour of play if you are intent on just looking around and don't get caught up in missions.
Missions are. . . pretty much combat.  They try and flavor them with different objectives, challenges using a bow, stealth.  But they all come back to combat.  Stealth is a missed oppurtunity.  Half the map is open fields, and even in the sections wtih cover, the player isn't given any tools to utilize stealth like in normal stealth gameplay. It's mostly just waiting for patrols to clear out so you can sneak behind and knife someone.
The player character has the ability to level up.  This section is fleshed out.  The level up system has meaningful upgrades that can add flavor to the different core abilities.  There is also a second skill tree that allows bulk upgrade to stats such as health.
A big problem I ran into, however, is that most of the abilities are locked behind a secondary experience system called power.  Power is recieved by killing bosses that roam the map.  We'll get into them in a second, but the ammount of power you need to advance tiers and unlock abilties was absurd.  I had to straight farm bosses for no other reason than to be allowed to use the level ups I earned.
Finally the boss system that the game calls Nemesis.  This is a fantastic inovation and the real saving grace to the game.  A score of perhaps 20 enemies with unique personalities, traits, and abilities roam the map.  They will fight eachother, become stronger and level up themselves.  They will try and live, running away when in danger, and they remember when they lose to you.  This is the one area the game truely shines.
At the end of the day, being a Lord of the Rings fan is probably not that important.  There isn't a lot of lore, sights to see, or characters to recognize.  The narrative and world are bare bones.  At least this means that people coming into the series won't be lost.
I would recommend playing one of the Batman Arkham games over this.  That game has slightly better combat with a much richer, diverse world that you can play with.  However, if you want that style of game with a more sword and sorcery feel and don't mind a challenge, then Shadow of Mordor is perfectly adequate.

Excellent worldbuilding and alien cultures, but difficult game mechanics. For starters, there is no pause feature, even when opening the menu. Crafting and other mechanics are not intuitive or simple to use, and advancement in the game can require a good deal of outside research since much of the necessary information is either gained through lots and lots of experience or is not given at all.
The good news is that Starbound is very multiplayer-friendly. Even in single player, you can gain crew members and a pet in your party. But don't buy this game just because you enjoyed playing Terraria. They're very different.
Starbound has a building system with more options, a greater variety of enemies, more diverse biomes, and the ability to find new places without the need to exit to the main menu repeatedly; but Terraria has developed an easier-to-use crafting system plus an immensely useful item-and-storage sorting system, and there's no need to put bookmarks at all points of interest so that you won't lose them.
Starbound can be fun to play, too, but it's important to be prepared and informed before diving in.

Miscreated is one of those games that’ll keep you on your toes. I can honestly say that I enjoyed this game more while playing with friends. After stalking, being stalked, killing, and being killed by other players; I can honestly say I’ve never been so paranoid playing a game. I was constantly looking over my shoulder to make sure no one was waiting for me to slip up and kill me. The sound effects are ok; you can tell if another player was having a gun fight in my vicinity or a great deal away, another player was trampling around the area or sneaking around the bushes. This can work to your benefit or your downfall, as your character is a klutz and makes the most noise possible e.g. changing weapons, dropping items, and walking around a house in what seems to be tap shoes.
The base building needs work! The developers seem hell bent on not allowing a snap together option for those who choose to or not. The perfectionist in me would spend hours trying to get wall sections on straight, as this game will see to it to offset sections that show they’re aligned on your screen, which over time can become very frustrating. Not to mention the threat of other players aiming to kill you when you’re more focused on building your base as opposed to being on the look out for them. And when your base gets raided, which it will to almost every new player (hopefully not as often with the durability update), you’ll spend another dozen hours trying to modify and refortify your base under constant fear of being shot in the back with access to all your storage. Next is storage, starting off you can store a total of 10 items, increasing to another 20 slots if you’re able to locate the blueprints. In addition to that, vehicles hold another 10 slots if you’re able to locate one and successfully return it to your base, randomly generated tents will hold anywhere between 10 – 30 slots, that is, if you can return it to your base. Now here’s the catch, tents and vehicles you find will just randomly disappear. No warning, no decay meter, no nothing just poof! gone with everything you had stashed.
Glitches. Yes, I know it’s an early access game and to be prepared to encounter many glitches. There are some, if not many that is just completely unacceptable at this point in the game. For instance, getting killed by a random “phantom” mutant that cannot be avoided resulting in a very frustrating death or the perhaps glitching through another player’s base. Those are just a few of the many frustrating glitches in this game. Again, I can understand there are going to be glitches in a "early access" game, but come on, 3 years this game has been out, please resolve the issue.
Overall, Miscreated isn’t a bad game, it just needs some major improvements in order to be able stand up to the many competitors our there in the same genre.

Warlock - Master of the Arcane is a turn-based strategy game, like many strategy games, the longer you play, the more elaborate the tactics get, and the longer your turn gets as your control over the world increases!
...or you get constantly bombarded by random world events and you can't expand because you're fighting off hoards of giants, dragons, undead, and random quest heroes.


Welcome to Adrania, maybe you've been here before, maybe this is your first visit, regardless welcome, welcome. This land has appeared in numerous games, the first game I played in the series was "Majesty Gold Edition".
In this game, you are one of (X) amount of Mages/Warlocks, depending on the world size you may have more or less mages/AI/NPC's in the game. The more AI the more competition in the game. (But on the flip side, the more people fighting back the wild landscape... and trust me, it's wild)

Starting with the most basic explanation about the game play, you have Hex's which represent segments of the land, very similar other strategy games, some hex's increase gold, food, or magic... while others are just taking up space, or even reduce values.
I compare this game to one of the Civilization games except that you're fighting with magic instead of science, and the "Rock, Paper, Scissors" game of Land, Air, and Water units. It is now more like "Rock, Paper, Scissors, TNT, Chuck Norris, God"; There's magic that you can cast, there's magic units, heroes which can be equipped with better armor and weapons, you can upgrade them with gold, in addition to the typical "ship, flying, and land" units.
I need to point out I haven't played the multiplayer yet. However, after looking it up, the game doesn't have "simultaneous turns", so the multiplayer will be at an even slower pace. You probably don't want to get into a very large game, smaller skirmishes so you can play the game for a day... ...instead of spanning over several weeks.

Water units are also lacking, with very little varity or ways to upgrade compared to land. I found games becoming a hassle and the AI stopping being a threat late on, and had the shrink down the worlds and factions generated to make things quicker.
Despite that nitpicking it is an engrossing 4x, managing the one-more-turn compulsion. I've already played a lot and enjoyed it, without even touching multiplayer or the apocalypse mode.

There is a picture of a cute little anime princess on the menu splash screen. The game, though, is not cute - it's actually rather heavy and full of political intrigue and tough decisions, and it is surprisingly difficult. You have a year or so to prepare to be crowned queen, but you have to survive assassination plots and foreign military invasions as well as navigate the treacherous waters of court etiquette.  But what do you focus on? Where do you need to succeed, and where is it "safe" to fail?
I don't know.  I can't seem to keep myself alive long enough to see myself crowned queen.
But I like this game - or, rather, "visual novel" - enough to keep trying. There is lots of replayability because there are umpteen little decisions to be made which can influence the outcome significantly.  I haven't played through a visual novel of this sort before, so this has been an impressive introduction, and definitely (for me at least) worth the money.

Fun zombie survival simulator.
However, you will do basically the same thing every time. Kill zombies, loot, protect ai survivors, and defend against hordes. There's a variety of loot including medical stuff and guns; ammo is scarce so choose your actions wisely. DLC is also worth picking up to further extend your survivor experience. Single player is short and basic. Trying to survive for months is the real challenge because you must manage your resources. You, your group, and your base must be strong with plenty of resources to survive. Exploration is the main highlight of the game. You must explore inorder to find materials to help you survive with your group. If you die, you will play as another playable character. 1. Frustrating. Non-existent tutorial makes this a tough game to jump into straight away. After spending an evening watching YouTube videos, I was finally able to get a business up and running and breaking even. Raw materials are scattered across the map, as expected, but the factories are also stuck out in the middle of nowhere, instead of congregating in the industrial sectors of your towns. Not having the ability to build new factories, where you really need them, is also extremely irritating.
2. Fun. Not nearly as playable as Sid Meiers' Railroads and with no real goals or opponents it boils down to a straight builder. If you like SimCity or Banished, this is for you.
3. UI. Horrible. To track performance and profitibility you need to have several windows open which cover most of the play area. With no ability to push these windows over to a second monitor you have to pause often to review your status. When new trains become available there is no accompanying information to let you know if they are passenger or freight trains.
I really was expecting more. Hopefully there are expansions, updates or mods out there to make this a better, more satisfying gaming experience.

Bought this game because everyone says it is like Sid Meiers Railroads, a game I love but can not play since switching to Linux.
Now the only similar thing is the building of train networks between cities and resources but that is where it ends.  The game actually is more complex.  Laying of tracks and setting up trains requires more work than Railroads.
In Railroads you simply lay your track then pick your train and train cars for that section of track.  In Train Fever you must do more, like create a train depot which MUST be connected to the track you want to train to be on.  I could not figure out how to delete a train nor have I figured out yet how to properly connect resources.  BTW, every station MUST be connected to a road which makes placing your tracks even harder.
On top of creating train routes, you also need to create bus routes to move people around each city to your train station.
Unlike Railroads though, there doesn't appear to be any computer players to compete against.  For some people like myself, this can result in a not as fun game but if you are a huge fan of sim city type games where there is no one to compete against then you should enjoy this game.

Train Fever is a delightfully enthralling management game that you can plunge hours into. I found myself staying up all night in a 'Just One More Turn' sort of way, either because I was desperately trying to keep my fledgling Rail company above water or because I wanted to see if new technology's or expanding profits would allow me to splash out on a new project or to reinvigorate an old one. In terms of management, I've found that learning the basics isn't overly hard, but mastering it is the real challenge. In other management games, I have often found that once you plug the main problem, you have nothing more to do; it's too easy to find the perfect equilibrium and once you've played it once there's little reason to go back and play it again and you rarely had to restart for lack of skill in the first place. In Train Fever, you'll solve a short term problem only to later discover that there's a much bigger long term problem built upon more short term problems. There's lots to manage and lots to do (although not so much as to overwhelm you), and as technology advances new avenues for profit and loss will open up and you'll have to adapt to changing circumstances. Things that are in 1850 unprofitable and infeasible may in 1900 be profitable and very doable.
In short, Train Fever is a game of adaption, of chasing profits and avoiding losses, which can be tough, but very rewarding. You may have to play a failed game or two before you learn all of it's secrets, but a management game in which you instantly have the cure to any ailment is a short lived and unrewarding one.

I liked it but I knew when I was going in that it was a one-dimensional railroad SIM. The mods really flesh out the options available otherwise the gameplay is simple: start with closed bus loops -> fund your rail lines -> wait for next epoch to unlock new trains.
Graphically, the game looks fantastic, but unless you are running a top of the line vid card, you will experience stuttering and slowness when the game has to start tracking more vehicles and lines.
All that being said, if you like an open ended train SIM with lots of options for reskinning then go ahead and pick this up but if you are looking for an in-depth, modern Transport Tycoon give this one a pass.

Conclusion: awesome track laying game that poorly explains itself (aka has a learning curve)
I am thoroughly enjoying this game but many, many feature only become apparent after looking through guides on steam and after trial and error.
For example I thought there was a cargo staying on the platform bug.. I had 1 route designed like this: pickup cargo, drop off at station 1, pickup cargo again, drop off at station 2. Turns out.. the demand for goods in station 1 is low, so the goods stream in slowly, so the train keeps waiting to fill it up - and never getting to station 2 which is building up. The easy solution: create 2 separate lines and all is good.
So after learning how to lay bus tracks efficiently, place signals effectively, build bridges, ... you end up with a game that's a bit like it suggests in title.. first a fever to overcome it, then a fever because it will suck you back in. Because you can borrow enough money and making it profitable at easy level isn't all that hard, it's more a game about making a beautiful operating railroad than a tough challenge. And that's fine to me.
It's the best game in laying out an efficient routed railway - in any game. I really can't remember that that part was executed that well, and looked this good. I personally love setting the landscape to hilly and create a great flowing double track railroad running through with tight blocks so accommodate all the goods & passenger traffic.
The game runs very well on my GTX 970 at 2560x1024 with everything maxed out.
There are some quirks which I'll hope they fix soon, and I do want to mention that it's good to see the devs have just released another update and support the product:
(1) Keys only work after clicking on the landscape
(2) No mention when trains get stuck (especially after breaking up a section to expand)
(3) The 'two steps'  required is tedious and doesn't belong in games.. figure it out guys
(4) Upgrade a street won't fit while staying a 2 lane road.. really?
(5) Bigger stations please
(6) Allow alternative platforms through alternative waypoints
So all in all it's a very enjoyable game, if you can deal with it's learning curve - and especially when on offer for a special price, it's great value. If you liked transport tycoon, or similar games from Chris Sawyer or Sid Meier ... you'll enjoy this one. I think it's beaten their latest efforts for sure.

[This review contains spoilers]
This game was a severe letdown. I've heard such good news about it and came in with anticipation for something great.
To start, the gameplay isn't much of anything: hop around, press "e", that's it outside of a few minigames that are somehow worse in playability/even more boring. Though the gameplay isn't supposed to be the highlight of the entire game, it would've been nice to have a bit more freedom in your abilities. The morality of the characters are also a bit questionable, with petty theft, vandalism, and grave robbing being common occurrence between the main characters. The worst being Mae outright murdering someone with a bat because of something happening in a game. I would be a bit more empathetic about it if they were early teens instead of being in their early 20's. This game also sports the replayability factor, but in the wrong senses. The paths aren't interesting enough to completely redo about 3-4 times and will completely tire someone out if they tried. The characters' personalities, the lack of freedom in your choices, and the overall lack of emotion portrayed by the characters are the three main the reasons why most won't replay. Take the scene in the club across town for example, where Bea is becoming anxious because of what you're saying is embarrasing her. You have no ability to save the conversation or fix what you've said before, you're supposed to sit through this knowing you can't do anything about it. The story is bent on moving in a linear fashion with almost no freedom or variety other than a few "quirky" dialog options that have zero impact on the story. Left-sided politics are also pretty common in this game but not in a manner that respects those who don't share the same political beliefs. The enemies near the end of the game are literally conservative rednecks in clan clothing who hunt people down as well as wanting to "make the town great again". Speaking of, the ending wasn't much of anything. It just stopped at the garage, leaving the player confused at what just happened.
However, there were positive features of this game that stood out. I absolutely loved the atmosphere, illuminated with fall colors and beautiful scenery in a simplistic artstyle that gave off the fall feeling rather well. The designs of the main characters are distinguishable, expressing who that character is solely by looks alone. This game also has an amazing OST when grouped together with the scenery, sets the perfect mood needed for that scene. Mallard's tomb for example, where you rob a grave to find a ghost. The soundtrack starts right as you open the grave, combined with the fog and cool color scheme, which has actually sent me chills the first time I played it.
In short, Night in the Woods fails as a story-telling game but it surpasses artistically, which can be a mixed bag to most.
I personally would not recommend this game to my friends unless they were interested in the art since the bad vastly outweighs the good.

There is a lot of potential to this game, and it is, of course, in early access, so who knows what it will become. I am unsure, since the start of the "early access" program, how much it is used as a way to help indie developers create games vs. how much it is used to fart out a skeleton of a game and ocassionally add a "hotfix" but I am aware I should forgive games that aren't complete yet - even if I'm not sure they ever will be.
I start to lose my patience with Early Access games when I play them for a while, then come back to them a year later, and none of the issues have been fixed. It's like...you've had time. And that's why I feel compelled to write this.
Stranded Deep sufffers from two major problems.
1. Dreadful monotony.
2. Lack of purpose.
The lack of purpose isn't the worst thing ever; there are a lot of startup survival games that haven't yet figured out what exactly they want the POINT to be. I'm sure they realize that "staying alive" is only fun as long as it is challenging, and in most survival games it doesn't take more than a few in-game days to be able to survive any troubles. In this game as long as you've got the will to create a spear and the fortune to find a bucket, you'll never die. And because there's no greater point - you're not trying to get rescued, you're not trying to make it to civilization - one could argue that after your character has done these two things (which takes upward of 30 minutes of game time) you've beat the game. You can build a little hut, but it appears to be entirely cosmetic.
Despite being a survival game, the exploration aspect seems to be what they are more concerned with in developing this game. There are places to find lockers, trunks, etc. that contain a loot item, and for an hour or two, discovering all these things is fun. But the life drains out of that real fast, when you realize that a) there are, ultimately, like 12 items you can find, and b) there are like 5 places to find them (in the cabin of sunken boats, in the ruins of old row boats, ocassionally on the deck of ruined boats...okay, so maybe not even five).
I have heard games like DayZ referred to as a "jogging simulator." This being because there's very little to do, but miles of ground in between those patches of nothing. So you spend most of your time just going from place to place, with basically nothing to do once you arrive there. With that in mind, Stranded Deep could best be described as a "rafting simulator." This is my major grip with the game, beyond any other. There are countless (possibly infinite, randomly generated) islands in the game. Don't get excited though; they are all the same, only with different random ship wrecks around them (that are the same as the shipwrecks at the other islands, just situated differently) and a different assortment of sticks and rocks. All the islands are very barren. A few sticks, rocks, and coconut trees, like it was a dessert island in a Far Side cartoon.
But the WORST thing is that all of those identical little islands are like, I don't know, a million miles apart? You have to row your raft from one island to the next (and later in the game, you might be able to craft a crude raft with a boat engine to do this about 15% faster), and every trip between islands takes about 5 minutes of real time. You have to hold down the left mouse button to row, so my index finger starts to get tired after playing this game for a little while. I'd say that 50% of the game is holding down the left mouse button and slowly, slowly, achingly slowly inching your way toward another island that offers the promise of more NOTHING. And sometimes a shark will bump your raft and knock you off. You might get lost when this happens, because until you're quite close to that next island, it continues to look like it's on the distant horizon. But don't worry; I promise you there was nothing interesting at the island you were aiming for. Sticks, rocks, and disappointment.
As I said above, I know the game is "early access" so it might take a little while to work out where exactly it's going. But after it's been available for purchase for more than a year, the changes I've seen are like...now you can skin sharks instead of just killing and eating them. There's still no point, there's still no faster way between islands, and still no real REASON to do all that exploring. Ironically, the only reason you usually need to travel in this game is to find supplies like medicine to cure the ailments you picked up while travelling between islands. The best strategy in this game is, generally, to sit there and do nothing. You can pay $15 to do it here, or do it for free on your couch.
This game has potential, but I do not recommend it until commercial release (if indeed that ever happens).

When I first bought this game over a year ago, I was very excited to see how it would develop over time, and I was looking forward to a more polished survival game that didn't rely on zombies or zombie-like creatures to create tension. However, it's been over a year, and this game, as other reviews have stated, still struggles with some of the same issues it had when it first entered Early Access. Don't get me wrong, the game hasn't been abandoned (far from it), but the focus seems to be mainly on new content and not on fixing the current content as it is. (You can still get stuck on/in things, or get flung into the air to your death.) The mechanics have changed, sometimes for the better and sometimes very much not (it used to be a lot easier to break rocks and coconuts, for example). New content is great, especially in a game that is admittedly plagued by a lack of anything to really do after you get the basics down, but there has to be a balance between fixing the old stuff and adding something extra.
All that said, I haven't given up on this game. I do still occasionally fire it up just to see how it's been developing, and some of the things I've seen have been promising. As it is right now, however, I can't say I would recommend it. Save your money until the game has had a chance to mature a little more. Maybe after they've fixed the glitch that allows you to chop trees at four times the normal speed.

While I'm not overly fond of making this a real-world gritty story in a departure from the fully established world of the resst of the Ace Combat series, I stil think this is one of the most fun gaming experiences you can have.  It's Project Gotham for airplanes, just enough realism and detail for those with an appreciative eye for military hardware but arcade simplicity and bombastic presentation that keep it well clear of inaccessable, monolithic sims like Falcon 4.0 and its ilk.
Dogfight and Airstrike modes are a mixed bag, and may prove more enjoyable against human opposition than AI (where it can just be a blurry frustration), but there's still no flight game that I've played that conveys the adrenaline and speed of sitting in half a billion dollars of cutting edge hardware going past the speed of sound while absolutely everything else in the sky wants you dead.

Fun fact, my review of Warlock MoA was actually one of the earlier reviews I did. Where is it, you might ask? It was lost to the void of the internet when a page got accidentally refreshed.
Many months later and I’m still butthurt about losing it, I worked really hard on it because I felt the game deserved it. So here is my very very abridged version:
Warlock: Master of the Arcane is a Civ knockoff. It’s not bad but it has some key flaws. The most glaring is how cumbersome the UI is. Coming from Civ is also annoying because basic shorthand like right clicking to move a unit is a completely different function. The verdict is that if you’re hard up for some Civ-like gameplay, Warlock is alright, but I personally would rather just play more Civ. The theme change doesn’t justify the feeling of having to relearn the genre.

The game is a TBS similar to Fantasy Wars and Elven Legacy.
Good things:
Bad things:
The game is fun, but has too many downfalls to enjoy for long. My biggest concern is that the enemy player AI is really easy to beat. They don't have a strategy, they don't match attack types to defence types, and they randomly proclaim peace or war. Even on the hardest difficulty they're easily beaten.
To compensate for the lack of difficulty, the game introduces random mob spawnings. The strength of these mobs seem to be random, so it's very possible that you get wiped out early in the game by a mob spawn. They can spawn anywhere and at any time, which makes it hard to create a strategy to defeat an opponent. Even worse are the Dremer, who also spawn with gates and contimate the lands. This gets really tedious after a while since there's nothing you can do about the spawning, and they just serve to increase the game difficulty in an obnoxious way.
Another thing are the spells. You can resurrect any unit, but not always a hero. You can lower the land and put tough enemy units in the water, making them easy to defeat. You can cast mana drains on your enemies or erupt vulcanoes on their lands. This severely debilitates them, but they never apply these tactics to you. So after some time, the gameplay becomes the same. Slowly advance towards the enemy while dealing with the random spawns until you kill all. It gets tedious after a while, which is a shame as I really wanted to like this game.

State of Decay is a single player zombie survival game between the 78-85% range (depending on how much you love killing zombies).  State is a combination of several factors that makes it really enjoyable to play.  There is loot collection, leveling, exploration, base management, quests, killing zombies (but the game doesn't give you a kill counter), and faction/reputation influence with other survivors.  You might think the game might stretch itself too far, but each trait isn't very deep but still deep enough that it's enjoyable to work with and won't become overwhelming.  Characters level quickly, really good loot isn't rare but there is some variety so exploring is still fun and you want to find supplies for your base, and characters have different traits so leveling different characters can create new experiences of play.
Combat is simple, not quite as fun or complex as Dead Rising, but you can be overwhelmed and there is a slight learning curve so you'll get much better at killing zombies quickly.  Stealth is really unsatisfying though and not really worth the effort.  Like Dead Rising, cars are crazy overpowered and will become your main source of murdering zombies quickly.
Sadly, the game is buggy and short.  I've made cars blow up or get stuck routinely, seen zombies go through walls, escorted survivors who refuse to work on quest objectives so the quest never ends, and so on.  The worst part is, the game doesn't seem to release updates to polish the game, but still releases DLC.  Which is simply insulting.
The game can be beaten in two afternoons and the storyline is simple and unskippable in most parts so if you play the game twice you'll get stuck listening to dialogue you've already heard a lot.  The ending and final showdown is a letdown so being forced to experience it again sucks.
Finally, the game doesn't tell you how to do everything.  I have no idea how to trade with other survivors, but it's possible as you'll get a message saying you can some games.  Selecting special skills isn't clear and is really easy to miss.  When you do notice them, you may not actually select them because you have to hold Q first and the game isn't clear about the fact that you don't actually have the skills.  The game also warns you about overstocking supplies but I see no reason not to and one isn't given.
Overall, the game is fun and easy to get pulled into.  But it is hardly a masterpiece.

I'm going to write this review in stages as I feel this game is a slow burner. I've played for just over 10 hours so I'm going to update this review over course of the next few weeks. Please note that I genuinely want to love this game and will probably spend at least 100 hours playing it. For the record I bought the game on sale for about £6.
So far I've found the game confusing and fragmented. the tutorial is a little brief and fundamentally the game isn't very intuitive. I have played several games, often realizing my errors and starting again as a recursive learning process. The game focuses on road and rail transport; so far I've found that creating a rail link between two cities is very profitable but introducing a third city creates a lot of problems due to difficulties managing which trains manage which lines.
I haven't been able to make a profit on inter-city bus lines as people simply won't use the bus service despite using conventional wisdom when plotting the bus route between the various city regions.
Natural resources seem to move at random between starting games. Sometimes lots of natural resources are produced and can be moved between locations and you can make a mint, and sometimes absolutely nothing is produced meaning there is no reason to even bother with them.
Train lines are confusing and creating more complex train routes is convoluted to the point of not being fun. Creating simple A-to-B routes is more profitable and is easier to manage.
So far I've enjoyed the game, in principle, but still feel like there's a huge amount of room for improvement. The basics are there but a lot of time needs to be spent on balancing and tweaking how the game works.

UPDATE on 5/29/15 - I highly recommend reading through the guides.  After reading how to set up the train and road network for passengers, I was able to make money and even pay off the $3M loan.  I now understand how to expand the railroad and road networks before running out of money. Next up is to learn how to do cargo.

Ever since Transport Tycoon Deluxe, which I played for hundreds and hundreds of hours back in the day, I've been looking for a worthy successor. After all, it's been 20 years since its release. So when I saw the pre-release screenshots of Train Fever, I was really excited. Unfortunately, this game comes nowhere near to filling Transport Tycoon's shoes.
If I've built a rail line and it starts to bring in the cash, I still don't feel that I've accomplished anything. When I've paid off my initial loan and have millions to spend, I just can't be bothered to spend it on anything. In Transport Tycoon I could spend hours perfecting a train line, just to make it better and more efficient. In Train Fever I just don't care. Why? For one because building rail or roads is just too tedious and clunky. Mainly however because the game just isn't very fun.  Almost everything is clunky: the menus, the interface, building things.
One thing I do like though, the very thing that made me buy the game: the graphics. The vehicles in particular look amazing. The towns and landscapes look okay, but are lacking in variation.
I really wanted to like this game, and I've tried several times, but I just can't. If I knew then what I know now, I would never have bought it.

So this is a very, very, very late review, but I felt like I needed to say it after so long.
I'm NEVER going to play Night in The Woods again because it is just that perfect to me. It's everything I ever wanted from a game; a beautiful, yet simplistic artstyle, a charming and gripping atmosphere with wonderful music and visuals to back it up, interesting characters with interesting designs (I love the eyes) and just... GAH. The story is just so perfectly tailored to what I want from a game that's supposed to get me attached to the characters. Literally everything about Bea is pretty much my state of life. Bea was the most relatable character, with almost everything she went through being something that I was or had been going through at the time, she's such an amazing character to me and that's why I sided with her during my first, and only playthrough.
I don't want to play the game again because I'm worried that coming back to it will ruin that charm it had on me, seeing the same stuff all over again with a few minor changes will only spoil the mystique and beauty the game has. I want to look back at what I remember, and remember everything I loved about the game, I don't want to come back to it only to get bored with everything I've already seen and start nitpicking at all of it's flaws and taint the once beloved game for me. I just can't. The fact that I don't have every achievement in the game, and I haven't touched it again since I last beat it, is a sign that I truely love and appreciate a game. It wasn't a life changer, but it was definitely a pleasant experience and one I don't think I'll ever forget thanks to the Internet.
I genuinely love NITW to bits but I just can't bring myself to stick with it.

I was originally just going to punch in 5 minutes so I could make this review just about the Deleted Scenes, but I decided to be fair and try out the base game too.
Condition Zero's Tour of Duty mode is a series of levels that one could describe as a campaign without a plot. In each level, you have to complete a set of tasks, or "challenges", while stopping the terrorists from doing their thing enough times to satisfy the level's non-challenge requirements. You can create your own squad by buying teammates from a roster of 36 counter-terrorists, each with different levels of skill and weapon preferences, with points earned by completing levels.
The Tour of Duty is very simplistic, but it managed to make me like it a bit and I normally hate playing multiplayer-oriented game matches with only bots, which it essentially is. And in my opinion, it on the Easy difficulty feels like a tutorial; One lacking explanations of the game's controls, but also one that trains the player by putting them up against targets that move and shoot back, which is not present in the tutorials featured in the Deleted Scenes and CS:GO. Update: Currently at frustrating point where the Terrorist AI is almost cheating and the Counter-Terrorist AI is braindead.
Then I tried out the multiplayer for a bit. Not long enough for me to actually say anything about it, but from my limited experience it felt like CS:S but different.
It's basically CS:S but deader, has worse level design, and you have to remember to buy ammo. Not my thing.
Finally, the ultimate purpose of this review: The Deleted Scenes. It's a set of 18 different missions, each having a different scenario (and are not connected in a grand scheme or anything like a campaign in say, Call of Duty). I don't have much more to say about it in terms of description, so here's where I begin the "opinion" part (I think there's a much better word for it but I'm tired):
It of course suffers from dated graphics and some weaker level design here and there, but it is
. I've done all of the missions 3 times over 25~ hours and dear god I think I might do it
even after finding all of the secrets within. It makes me furious that CS:GO's campaigns were limited time because I'd replay a Counter-Strike campaign with CS:GO's gameplay and graphics more times than I think I will replay Deleted Scenes. Update: Forgot to say this when I first published this review but the music's great too. Especially the music in Secret War, that level's awesome in almost every aspect.
Overall:
buy this game just for the Deleted Scenes. Unless you like CS:S but want a more retro feel and can put up with poorly-balanced AI in the Tour of Duty, that's like the main selling point.

There are two types of games, those that seek to take you away from reality, and those that make you face it.
This game is the latter.
As a work robot I needed something to bring me back to reality, to remind me of my human roots, and clarify what really matters.
Night in the Woods is about life's truths, sometimes nice, and sometimes ugly. Perhaps both.
You play as a character who is back from college early, rediscovering her hometown and rekindling friendships. The characters are regular people, flawed and with unique personalities. Perhaps you'll recognize yourself or others you know in them, as time progresses. I became emotionally invested in the characters, they reminded me of myself or people in my life. This was due to the excellent writing, which makes characters feel like real people, who have quirks and issues. At the end of the day, Night in the Woods tells what I call The Human Story. It's nice to experience something, and be grounded once in a while.
The music is so good. It adds atmosphere to each chapter and punches emotionally when it needs to.
I reccomend a controller when playing this game, although it is not absolutely needed. Also I am sooo bad at the band practice minigame, luckily it doesn't really matter.
The best games nowadays invest you in the characters, like a good novel. Night in the Woods did it for me.

I got a copy of this game from a dear friend of mine who is a writer, he spoke very highly of the story telling in this game and insisted that I needed to play it ASAP. So I did, and I kind of regret not playing it sooner. The story gives a real feeling of nostalgia that cannot be truly explained, only experienced. The varying color pallet is a big feature, and one that caught my eye straight away, and the accompanying music seemed to match the pallet. Warmer colors always came with a gentle, soothing almost nostalgic backing track, while the cooler colored scene music always felt more appropriate. I may not be the best at describing this, but I implore you, if you grew up in a small town and left for a while, only returning after living away for a good few years to see how things had changed, this WILL hit you right in the feels.
There's a Guitar Hero style minigame that is REQUIRED for the story to advance a few times. Not really bad, but you only get one chance at the various songs. On the plus side, you don't really NEED to do well at the songs, but a second chance to get a better grade would have been nice.
On a final note, if you haven't had the game spoiled for you, there are two main characters you can spend each day with. For your first time playing, spend every day you can with Bea. Her story arc is the most noteworthy in my mind, and what I would easily recommend for maximum crying and feels.
TLDR: This interactive story game is well worth it's price on may aspects. If you have the money, get it. You won't be disappointed.

+-A pro player that knows all the loot spots can often get geared under 1 minute after entering a large city.
- It is hard to find loot at start before you learn where to look for it and therefore an insane number of buyers refund the game under their first two hours.
- Due to the weight limits of the inventory and weight of base parts, in order to build a base, you will have to empty yourself in the two storage boxes first, then build. It is extremely tedious to build in this game and if you want perfectly straight parts badluck, you will never achieve it because there is only a freeform build system without any snapping. Imagine building a big floating platform out of smaller platforms.. when you finish one line of platforms vertically and start another next to it from the top platform, the next you place already won't fit straight and you have to spend 10 minutes placing each.
- Virtually every player uses floating bases to protect his two chests of loot - that is when you build up as high as you can and then remove the lower parts of your base, making the upper ones float. You can still get raided if you do this wrong and very often you will, but for the professional pvpers, it's the only way how to protect their two boxes. If you build on the ground, nothing in the universe will help you to protect it.
- You can only have one tiny and one medium storage box per a base, THAT'S IT, NO MORE. Half of the devs blame it on their own incompetence to write a better netcode, the other half of the devs says it is not about code but an intended design decision. This is a huge source of controversy as it is obviously wrong and a huge source of the fact that while the game sold around 750 000 copies, only 1000 players keep playing it regularly.
- If you want more storage you have to find a tent in the woods or steal one from another base, but the tents can only be placed on natural ground not on player made platforms, and the ground has to be perfectly flat. Tents disappear after 48 hours if you dont open their inventory in this time period. Another option for more storage is finding car shells in cities and filling them with parts, then driving them to your base. Problem is, if they get spotted through a crack in the wall or overwall third person camera, an enemy player can shoot through the wooden walls and make the cars blow. Cars disappear after 48 hours if you dont open their inventory in this time period.
- There are currently absolutely no survival elements in the game whatsoever. There is only hunger and thirst, which can be solved by visiting the first house you stumble upon and filling up your belly. You can even drink from rivers and puddles with no consequence. There is a chance to get 1 out of 100% irradiated when drinking from toilets, but 1% won't cause you any visible effect. As of right now, hunger and thirst are only an annoyance when building a base. In all other times and situations, you WILL be well fed.
- There is almost no personal progression in the game. You can only build a base with two storage boxes, and if you are a pro, it will be a floating base high in the skies hiding cars in it. In order to make it harder for people to shoot through the floating foundation of your base and make the cars blow, you have to make the floating foundation at least a tripple layer of platforms.
- You cannot use a dedicated server of your own, you have to rent one from id3net - that is the company chosen by the devs and nobody else can rent you a server.
- The game is basicaly a very sterile oversized battle royale PVP arena with a beautifully crafted map.
- Instead of fixing major issues like floating bases and lack of storage, the devs are pushing for content like 20 color variations of sneakers or leather jackets.. it is not a proper way to boost the number of active players and despite all the rational criticism they remain numb and dumb about it.
- There is a number of very suspicious individuals on the official forums that will defend the game in every thread no matter what rationa argument/topic/tone you use to confront them. I have a strong suspicion those are the devs themselvs and/or their relatives.
- The devs have heightened the spawn ratio of powerful rifles by at least 5 times, apparently as a desperate attempt to boost the active player count. I find it disgusting, you can now literally meet noobs with AK's and full magazines standing atop of cars being confused what to do about several zombies following them. Before, a powerful rifle was something very rare.

Wow...so I started playing this game pretty much the day it came to early access.  I love survival games that AREN'T HORROR SURVIVAL GAMES.  When I first played this game at it's start, it was fantastic, it had a unique crafting system, unique way of getting from island to island, and it felt nearly complete.  So I started it up after many many months of not playing it, to find that the game is completely different...and not in a good way.  In order to explain this, I'm going to compare the old and new ways of doing things in the game.
-Steering the raft and paddling
Old Way: You walk onto the raft, equip the paddle from your inventory (pick if up if you didn't have room) and left click to paddle.  Make sure you stay near the center of the raft or else you might get thrown off with a big wave.
New Way: You walk onto the raft, Interact with it, and hold W to go where you want to.  You can't alter the speed of which you're going, you can't move on the raft, you're glued to it.
-Crafting tools and shelter
Old Way: You spend the time to gather the various items you need, some sticks of wood, a few rocks, and some rope made from plant fibers.  Drop all the items in front of you and interact with them to make the item you want.
New Way: You spend the time to gather the items you need.  Press C...craft item
So from these examples, you can see how they took two interesting and unique ways of doing things and dumbing it down to the standard survival game crafting.  While this isn't enough to ruin the game, it certainly doesn't make me excited for future updates
That said, still an interesting game, so I'd say go for it

Starbound is a terraria-like, open-world, sandbox-adventure game, that takes place in the vast, emptiness of space. Possibly my favorite thing about Starbound is the races. There are seven of them:
The plant-like Florans,
The fish-like, japanese-like Hylotl
The strangley familair Humans,
the Primate-like Apex (GLORY TO BIG APE),
the bird-like avians,
the robotic glitch,
and the gas-like Novakids.

Really solid game.  It's essentially GTA with zombies and a new layer of strategy.  You can move the survivors' home base around different homesteads and establish a limited number of supply/defense outposts.  You can play as different characters as you find more survivors, usually while you are out scouting for more supplies to sustain your group.  You also level up skills as you kill more zombies and accomplish more missions. It is a fast paced, tower defense game which requires you to be crafty and resourceful from the beginning until the end. But unlike most common defense tower games you actively participate in the battle, you are main defense, your towers, or rather traps, will hinder, soften or thin out the horde, but you'll still have a lot of heavy lifting to do by yourself.
Orcs Must Die! 2 is more refined than its predecessor, it fixes little tweaks that were very annoying in the first game and balances weapons that back then felt a little too powerful and buffs weapons that were otherwise almost useless or felt too weak to be of proper use.
There's a lot of variation in your towers, or rather, traps. You can out them on the ground, walls and ceiling and some traps requires certain strategies to work well. Obviously there are traps that works better with others, but nothing is truly impossible to combine, you create your own set of traps to watch enemies get brutally pierced/crushed/burnt/frozen/stripped to the bones.
The game makes sure to bring new foes and tricks to ensure that you will always try something new, something you hadn't thought before or to show that your old tactics will eventually stop working.
Orcs Must Die! 2 fixes a lot of little things that were annoying in the first game some are noticeable such as clunky physics with Wind Belt, other are more subtle like not being able to place Boom Barrels too close to enemies and removing fall damage which was completely needless.
Another big change was the improvements over control customization and options overall which was seriously lacking in the first Orcs Must Die!
All in all once you play the first game you'll realize how the differences can affect in your game style.
Orcs Must Die! 2 can be difficult, a bit overwhelming at first, but you will rarely feel that the game was unfair, that it did something ridiculous that you couldn't counter before it happened. It is a rewarding experience and you will feel great whenever you pull a maximum rank victory, especially on Nightmare (I'll talk about it in a moment).
The game was tailored for co-op action and after the first stage you'll be facing two enemy spawn points to defend and it can feel unfair, especially in the beginning when you barely have anything to deal with them, it can be difficult but it's still manageable.
While not something I truly appreciate, you'll have to go back to certain levels when you have better equipment to ace it (5 skull). Sure, you can start playing from the get go with a friend, but damn if it doesn't make you feel like a complete pro player when you get that maximum rank victory in a difficult map all by yourself.
The Nightmare difficulty, unlocked by finishing the game once, is far from being a numerical difficulty where the game merely ups enemies health or their numbers (something that plagues the games ever since they were made), it ramps up the difficulty to above the roof showing even tougher enemies and giving you puny three seconds to sell traps/units. You'll be forced to rethink your strategies and sometimes change to things you never ever thought before.
The co-op is just plain fun. Even more enemies to kill with a friend is never enough and being able to share strategies and putting up your traps into synergy is pure glee. If you don't have friends to play with you can always ask for others in the multiplayer groups.
There are two complaints about this great game I have: grinding and character selection.
Grinding is bad enough (maximizing traps, accessories and weapons is expensive), but having to do twice because you have to create two separate game files for each character is just increasing the longevity of the game in a bad way, especially since it can take a while to notice the differences between both characters aside from the obvious.
Changing characters requires you to return to the main menu screen, which wouldn't be such a hassle if you didn't have to leave the Party you made for multiplayer which can be very annoying.
There's also the fact Orcs Must Die! 2 is MUCH shorter than it's predecessor. While the first game has whooping 24 maps in the main campaign, the second game has only 15. Of course with the Classic levels DLC (earned by having the first game) the second game is longer, but I'm was never a big fan of having to rely on DLC to have a game with good length.
Orcs Must Die! 2 is an excellent game. It has tons of replay value and is balanced decently for both co-op and solo play. It does feel like it's an "Orcs Must Die! 1 v2.0" but with so many new traps, a new character and a good amount of changes, fixes here and there, it's worth every penny.
Let us only hope Robot Entertainment will some day make the Orcs Must Die! 3 after they finish up Unchained and let more characters, more traps and, of course, more orcs appear to amp the fun. Maybe even boss battles?

There are two types of games, those that seek to take you away from reality, and those that make you face it.
This game is the latter.
As a work robot I needed something to bring me back to reality, to remind me of my human roots, and clarify what really matters.
Night in the Woods is about life's truths, sometimes nice, and sometimes ugly. Perhaps both.
You play as a character who is back from college early, rediscovering her hometown and rekindling friendships. The characters are regular people, flawed and with unique personalities. Perhaps you'll recognize yourself or others you know in them, as time progresses. I became emotionally invested in the characters, they reminded me of myself or people in my life. This was due to the excellent writing, which makes characters feel like real people, who have quirks and issues. At the end of the day, Night in the Woods tells what I call The Human Story. It's nice to experience something, and be grounded once in a while.
The music is so good. It adds atmosphere to each chapter and punches emotionally when it needs to.
I reccomend a controller when playing this game, although it is not absolutely needed. Also I am sooo bad at the band practice minigame, luckily it doesn't really matter.
The best games nowadays invest you in the characters, like a good novel. Night in the Woods did it for me.
You know the game's good if it leaves you in a funk when it's over.

I got a copy of this game from a dear friend of mine who is a writer, he spoke very highly of the story telling in this game and insisted that I needed to play it ASAP. So I did, and I kind of regret not playing it sooner. The story gives a real feeling of nostalgia that cannot be truly explained, only experienced. The varying color pallet is a big feature, and one that caught my eye straight away, and the accompanying music seemed to match the pallet. Warmer colors always came with a gentle, soothing almost nostalgic backing track, while the cooler colored scene music always felt more appropriate. I may not be the best at describing this, but I implore you, if you grew up in a small town and left for a while, only returning after living away for a good few years to see how things had changed, this WILL hit you right in the feels.
There's a Guitar Hero style minigame that is REQUIRED for the story to advance a few times. Not really bad, but you only get one chance at the various songs. On the plus side, you don't really NEED to do well at the songs, but a second chance to get a better grade would have been nice.
On a final note, if you haven't had the game spoiled for you, there are two main characters you can spend each day with. For your first time playing, spend every day you can with Bea. Her story arc is the most noteworthy in my mind, and what I would easily recommend for maximum crying and feels.
TLDR: This interactive story game is well worth it's price on may aspects. If you have the money, get it. You won't be disappointed.

Basically your plane crashes into the ocean and you end up stranded in a life boat, You find other islands to some what explore to find new resources that help you survive. The problems with Stranded Deep isn't the concept of the game but the lack of depth and content along with many other features it lacks but desperately needs.  New players will find themselves fustrated as they try to figure out how to collect resources which will lead you to outdated Wiki pages and Youtube videos that promise to tell you how to do it but are 20 mins in length of some guy just playing the game. Once you figure out how to collect the resources it becomes another challenge to use the water stills ect that you made, For a developer it must be simple but for a new player it can be difficult to learn so you'll find yourself drinking coconut milk over water because trying to figure out that water still while dien of thirst just doesn't seem worth it. Moving on once you get out in the ocean you may find yourself having a bit of motion sickness as the first person perspective with a boucing around boat can be a bit nauseating and this is something you will have to do quite a bit if you want to explore the world or search for items in ship wrecks. I can say that the game can be a bit scary as you explore ship wrecks in dark water while sharks lurk around every coral reef and even during the day this can be intense as a bright sunny day with clear waters can turn to night as a thunder storm rolls in while your under water which seems like great whites love to prey on you in these most intensive moments. Beyond that Stranded Deep seems to seriously be lacking content because once you build a home/farm and get pass the need to travel with a nicely built base the game just drops off into " Well this is boring... Let's go play something else" For that I can't really recommend stranded deep as you don't have any story pushing you forward with no real end goal other then to end up bored and quiting, Even castaway had an ending, a story for struggle. I think this game would of been great if you had a time limit of say an F5 Hurricane that will kill you if you don't get rescue before it shows up and this could of really driven the game forward as you frantically trying to build up so you can make the long journey to the main land as you watch the dark clouds come ever so closer. I think this would of made Stranded Deep a true fight for survival in a race against the clock then a boring lack luster game that it currently is.

Like others have mention, the first few hours are trial and error. It takes some patience to see which choices are most beneficial. This game showed how challenging living as a Queen was. Every choice and stat that I chose for the Queen would determine how long the Queen would survive. Sadly, it is VERY challenging to keep the Queen alive. The first five tries cause my princess to met her end really quickly. One example would be chocolates. The Queen did not have a high enough skill like Court Manners so the game automatically chose for the Queen to eat the chocolates. The kicker was that the chocolates were poison! Astonishingly great game, especially considering I grabbed it for 3,99€ on sale. Somehow I've never been interested in it, due to being told that it just copies Batman and Assassin's Creed. Oh lord, was I wrong.
Alright, the story was boring. I skipped half of the cutscenes and got annoyed by the main missions, they were so much worse than the rest of the game.
The combat is fun. It never gets boring. Do you like the battles in the Batman: Arkham Series? Here you go. Do you like the stealth mechanics in Assassin's Creed? They are a lot better here. Do you enjoy sniping? You can do that here as well.
The game often gets criticised for the "pointless" Nemesis system. It's not pointless. On the contrary, it makes Mordor feel alive. It's fun outplaying orcs against each other. It's fun assassinating bodyguards of a warchief before killing him.
I've never seen such nice stealth mechanics in an open world game. (except maybe MGS V)
I've never seen such a nice combat in an open world game.
The game is too easy? Go straight to the warchief instead of hunting warchiefs.
The game is too hard? Get skill, get intel, get rid of bodyguards.
Sure, the game is quite easy. I actually listened to music while playing it because you don't have to concentrate much on it. But that doesn't mean that it's not fun or that it can't be challenging sometimes.
Took me 17 hours to beat (100%) and 4 more hours for the two big DLC (Lord of the Hunt and The Bright Lord).
Totally worth the 19,99€ it usually costs.

19 minutes in, already gave up.
- The interface is terrible. No zoom to cursor. Can't scroll on the screen edges that have menus. This includes all corners, so you can't scoll diagonally.
- The cargo system is unrealistic. For example, you have to build truck depots near industries. One of the main advantages of trucks in real life is that they don't require depots or yards - trucks just go from industry dock to industry dock.
- There is no good way to visualize the cargo economy. In railroad tycoon, you could switch to a cargo view, which would show you where a good was produced and demanded. In this game, you just have to hunt around until you happen upon two industries that will create a supply chain.
- Optimization is abysmal or non-existent. This game is incredibly sluggish, and I have a fairly powerful rig.
Looks like it's back to Railroad Tycoon 3 for me.

Having owned Train Fever since before Xmas, and played it long enough to earn a reasonable about of money, I have to say I'm finally disappointed. Firstly the time cycles are outrageously swift - it can take days, weeks, decades and months for vehicles to move around the map, and eons to increase product demand of the various services. But what has really broken the camel's back is the road and rail building mechanics.
I've played many similar games, as I'm sure most people interested in the genre have, but laying a roads, rail and especially bridges or tunnels is way too fussy and time consuming. Add that to how quickly the time elapses, many years will have passed whilst you try to understand why portions of a bridge turn red when there's nothing noticeably obstructing it.  Finally, the costs to demolish buildings and road to make way for redevelopment are ridiculously priced. Hundreds of thousands to remove a small building is unrealistic and punishing if you're struggle to make money. All in all, the transport/city building genre is making serious comeback - Paradox seem to be leading the way with the likes of Cities In Motion, and I cannot wait to play their new title Cities: Skylines.
Having watch footage of the latter, when it comes to the simplicity of building and redeveloping, it should be the least tasking portion of a game, and I'm afraid Train Fever has really understood this. I was really looking for to the game and the replayability factor. Since it's been a couple of months since I last tried TF, I had hoped my concerns would have been noticed and perhaps updates to improve the building mechanics - unfortunately the issues remain. I do hope this can be improved upon after this published my review. As things stands, there are better options than Train Fever.

A gorgeous, colorfully stylized world married with a lush, expressive soundtrack and a story that rends your heartstrings, Night In The Woods lives up to the buzz.
Mae, a college dropout, and her "loser" friends all have problems, but they're there for each other. At least, they learn to be. But in the end, as the tagline says, "at the end of everything, just hold on - to anything." Or anyone. Proximity is all we have sometimes, but it might just be enough.

Night in the Woods centers around Mae and her return to her childhood home, Possum Springs. It’s a quiet little place with not a lot to do, but that’s where its strength lies. Infinite Fall nails this atmosphere down to a science. Just outside her house, Mae can jump from trash cans to trees to telephone pole wires, balancing high above apartments and small businesses.
A lot of optional content lives in Possum Springs. Multiple NPCs share little parts of them, like poetry and star-gazing, with Mae, in bite-sized mini-games that sprout organically from the game’s feedback loop. Night in the Woods shares the day-by-day socializing found in RPGs like Persona; whenever Mae hangs out with her friends, you might start a minigame where you have to throw perogies in your friends mouth or jam out in some rhythm minigames (which are fairly complex and only appear once per song. They’d be nice to replay.)
There’s a childlike sense of exploration in Night in the Woods, and as rich the world can feel, it ends up being mere story padding. Mae’s friends are, like her, cartoon animal caricatures, but with bona fide personalities and hard-hitting dialogue. How the player interacts with these characters and how the story plays out is more akin to a visual novel, and it can get muddled in an adventure platformer.
With how little world traversal and interaction come into play, the world is there for the characters more than vice versa, and finding what to do to start the next story beat can get pretty confusing. Possum Springs’ idiosyncratic style and the linearity of the game’s storytelling just don’t mix.
That being said, the tone of Night in the Woods is masterfully controlled. Sometimes it feels like an episode of Tales of the Crypt, but it can go right back to “mini therapy session” any time it wants. The game constantly changes focus from Mae’s personal troubles with adapting outside of Possum Springs to the threatening underbelly of her beloved home; it starts swirling them together, teasing the player with peeks into Mae’s cryptic nightmares and growing anxiety, and it all ends with…something very weird.
I was disappointed in where the story ended up leading. I was left underwhelmed by a twist I considered too silly for it’s own good, so I took the time to look up what other people felt about it. Among some agreeing with me, I saw passionate responses to it. “What a perfect ending!” “This game gets me so much.” It was a reaction more intense and personal than many other games I’ve seen this year, and I’m counting the drearily thoughtful NieR: Automata.
Night in the Woods is deeply rooted in a place I didn’t grow up in, politics I couldn’t relate to. But games that exist to share moments and memories with other players, that channel such raw emotion from a specific audience, are a rarity to respect. I can’t recommend Night in the Woods from a personal place, but if something in this game speaks to you, reply to it. You’ll start up a nice conversation.

So, as it seems, CS:CZ is suppose to be a singleplayer game, along with traditional multiplayer mode almost identical to one found in the previous CS instalment, the infamous 1.6.
As a player who actually likes playing against bots in online games, such as Counter-Strike (any), Team Fortress 2, FoF, Quake Live, Quake 3 and Quake 3: Team Arena, the whole "singleplayer element" found in CS:CZ is really, really bad in my humble opinion.
The gameplay is just like your traditional Counter-Strike but with predifined number of bots and "tasks" instead. The player is given several tasks which MUST be accomplished in order to pass the mission. Unfortunately, majority of these tasks are absolutely what the player SHOULDN'T be doing in a regular CS match. Here are some examples:
1. Kill x players
2. Kill x players with a specific gun
3. Kill x players with a specific gun and survive the round
4. Win below x seconds
5. Rescue x/all hostages
So, here's my explanation to the following points respectively:
1. Barely any progresss will be made if player's playstyle won't be shifted from cooperative towards tryhardish, with the former being much more welcome in online games. That means, in CS:CZ campaign the player must play aggressively, lone-wolfing, making him prone to dying. Of course, the player may remain cooperative but it will very likely result in a rather unwelcome prolonging of the mission.
2. In order to perform well, players should always use weapons they feel comfortable with/high tier weapons, however in this case the player MUST use a specific weapon (usually a fitting one for the map though). Sure, game forces us to try out different guns but in reality the players usually stick to Deagles, AWPs and M4/AK47 for the most of the time anyways. Perhaps that's the task, but still a crappy one, considering players have their most favorite and hated guns, which will never be chosen in an online game anyway.
3. Same as above but this time with an opportunity to actually fail the task, forcing the player to be stuck with whatever gun he/she has to stick with for even longer until he/she finally manages to score required amount of frags and also survive the round.
4. Another tryhard gameplay promotion. Frag opponents in shortest time possible, meaning, the player must rush B like a♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ in order to pass the mission. At least it is somewhat challenging at times but again highly discouraged in traditional CS matches.
5. The absolute worst of all tasks, since AI controlled hostages can easily get stuck, yet the task will be only ticked off when all of the hostages are rescued. Here's a number of things that can easily prevent player from accomplishing this task:
a. Hostage gets stuck and it is no longer reachable (like jumping from a balcony/roof but the hostage doesn't follow). Even if reachable, it's extremely tedious to go back and it also increases chances of encountering an opponent, which can make player's ordeal completely null and void.
b. Player manages to get to the hostages, takes them with him/her but bots suddenly frag the very last terro, triggering the win-by-elimination victory.
c. hostages get in the way during gunfight, potentially making player stuck, giving terro an opportunity to score a frag and obviously preventing player from finishing this task in this very round. The loss might have an impact on the next round, reducing the chance of accomplishing the task even further.
Summary:
CS:CZ is a lazy attempt at CS singleplayer mode, full of solutions that are plain wrong and boring. Better stick to a regular game with bots and play as you wish. It could have been much better if it would have taken Half-Life's approach. Instead we have a game. barely different from any of the other CS games but instead with bots and boring, forced tasks. Tedious. That's all that can be said about the campaign. As a singleplayer game I do not recommend it. As a multiplayer game, you better off stick to CS 1.6 instead.
