Astonishingly great game, especially considering I grabbed it for 3,99€ on sale. Somehow I've never been interested in it, due to being told that it just copies Batman and Assassin's Creed. Oh lord, was I wrong.
Alright, the story was boring. I skipped half of the cutscenes and got annoyed by the main missions, they were so much worse than the rest of the game.
The combat is fun. It never gets boring. Do you like the battles in the Batman: Arkham Series? Here you go. Do you like the stealth mechanics in Assassin's Creed? They are a lot better here. Do you enjoy sniping? You can do that here as well.
The game often gets criticised for the "pointless" Nemesis system. It's not pointless. On the contrary, it makes Mordor feel alive. It's fun outplaying orcs against each other. It's fun assassinating bodyguards of a warchief before killing him.
I've never seen such nice stealth mechanics in an open world game. (except maybe MGS V)
I've never seen such a nice combat in an open world game.
The game is too easy? Go straight to the warchief instead of hunting warchiefs.
The game is too hard? Get skill, get intel, get rid of bodyguards.
Sure, the game is quite easy. I actually listened to music while playing it because you don't have to concentrate much on it. But that doesn't mean that it's not fun or that it can't be challenging sometimes.
Took me 17 hours to beat (100%) and 4 more hours for the two big DLC (Lord of the Hunt and The Bright Lord).
Totally worth the 19,99€ it usually costs.

This game has the potential to be great. I have played it on and off along with plenty of other similar survival games only to be dissappointed everytime my friends and I visit. Having bought 5 copies, we like to use it from time to time and would stick with it if it weren't so broke. This last go around, my bud fell through the map north of Brightmor just standing still, wasn;t so funny once we realized we have to go forage to replace all that gear. Once regeared, we spent a couple of days collecting food and items from Brightmor and Hayward, cramming and jamming, stacking anything we could into the cars and inventory, as we feel accomplished and decide head back we get in a small zombie fight, put the zombie down and start to head back. Two minutes later we both start to bleed and 4 bandages does nothing, dead. Spawned so far away with no means to get our gear. F that!
So here is what you get if you buy this game, F'd over and over. You get every bit of Alpha problems they describe: bugs everywhere, map glitches, glitched zombie fights, character wipes via glitched deaths, crazy vehicle deaths (you can die just putting a tire on your overturned ATV), stuck vehicles, completely lagged out when a new environment sound activates, crazy patches of darkness and random full bright nights. In a group of five guys like ours, someone is experiencing something crazy everytime we play and having to regear their items from scratch, granted we are active and use all parts of the map and all elements of the game, but that's just way too much wasted time on lost gear, lost bases and lost vehicles. Get your vehicle stuck merely running over a zombie and it could catch fire and blow you up.
This game is a serious rollercoaster of frustration, worth five bucks for some fun testing but not twenty. Be very careful with your decision, it can be such a cool game, but none of our other survival Alpha/Beta testing titles screw us anyone near as hard as this one.

-	The sounds (Audio) are another amazing touch to the game to put the player right into the game so to speak. The startup music is also brilliant. It’s got a sad tone but upbeat at the same time.
-	(GamePlay) I only have a few hours like 75+ hours or so into the game but it did not take me that long to see that the games game play is awesome. Sure there are a few things here and there that could be better, but hey it’s not damaging to the game as it currently is.  The combat in the game both with firearms, explosives etc are outstanding. The new updates with the scopes and other attachements are on point and again are awesome.
-	(Base Building) The base building aspect is great. It takes some time getting used to it however once you get the plans for building new items in game other than those that you start with it gets better.  I like there is no set way things have to be placed… within reason.
-	(Game Play Style) I am guessing that the game was indented for PVP; however there are PVE settings on servers not controlled by the developers. I love being able to play this in PVE to learn the game without having to worry about being shot in the♥♥♥♥♥by some KOS person that is out trolling spawn spots.
Cons of the Game
-	(Storage Boxes) The first storage box that you are able to create is a 10 slot box. Now this is ok for starting out. You can learn the next stage of storage by getting the 20 slot box too, however even then for a base that may have a lot of team members that is not enough.  I know that you can get tents as well as vehicles and use them to store things in and that is great so I guess it kind of balances out in a way, but I would still look into allowing more than one of a storage box type on a base Ex.  (Allowing 2 10 slot boxes as to the 1 only.)
-	(Back Packs) The bags that we carry are awesome and I like that they can be exchanged for others found in world however if your friends are looking for a bag and you find one, you cannot bring it to them if you currently have a bag.  Vests, hats, boots ect. Can be picked up and given, but not bags.  I see room for improvement there.
-	(Item Stacking) Some items that could be stacked a bit higher in storage would be awesome, as it stands now mostly everything has a small stacking number which takes up space. If you are alone I can see this would be good, but with a large team it is nearly impossible.  It would be awesome to increase some stacked items just a few more, nothing crazy or anything.
-	(Changing items) If you find a larger backpack than the one you are currently wearing, you cannot simply grab the new bag and everything moves over to the new bag. You must empty everything out of the old bag first sometimes dropping them to the ground.  This is the same with every worn item that has a storage slot.  I understand if the new bag is smaller than the current bag or clothing etc.. but  not if the new one is larger.
Overall
I have to say that this is a beautifully done game, the play, the graphics, the audio and everything else in between is a just awesome!  I would highly recommend this game to others, however please make sure that your system can handle the game read that into folks.  Don’t come complaining to the devs that something is not working and you are using your grandmother’s first toaster as a PC.  If you do not meet the min requirements I would strongly suggest waiting to buy the game.
Also please keep in mind that the game is Early Access, there will be bugs, there will be changes made by the devs and not everyone will like it. Things change..  Keep that in mind too.
Have an awesome day!

THERE IS NO CAMPAIGN! - for those who may be buying to play through some Epic 4x story mode.
This game is all skirmish all the time.
Pick a pre-gen'd mage or make your own with a selection of portraits, name change,  spells/traits/start bonuses and the choice of commanding 1 of 4 different races (each with their own benefits of course) as your main "civ"
5 difficulties to accompany all players and to increase as you become better.
4 different map types (based on Water : Land ratio), and 4 map sizes. And the option of cylindrical or flat (so you can either exit one side and appear on the other, or have to run right to the other side all across the map in "flat")
Able to face 8 Rival Mages (so 9 players inc you), and this wonderful feature called "additional worlds". Portals in game that lead to magical worlds riddled with dangerous enemies and loots! With the possibility of 6 of these!
So at max you may have 9 players, on the biggest map, with 6 additional worlds to roam to. And that's not to mention all the monsters in the game that spawn with you, the ones that spawn via random events (which can inc loot drops n such) AND Neutral Cities which act like lesser ai and are at multiple levels, so capturing isn't always easy.
Other stuff in the game includes  random quests, Religious Alignment, Powerful Hero units, Spells and Spell Research and Diplomacy. Along with a multitude of different buildings for each race and appealing graphics. I feel the game runs really smooth as well, atleast on my rig.
I HAVE NOT PLAYED MULTIPLAYER so i can't comment, though im sure the same settings apply, exept with other humans of course.
Games can be quite long as well, even on small settings.
For example im playing on the second difficulty "casual" (though i could play higher, still trying to learn the game more), on a small world, 1 enemy mage, 1 additional world and it still takes me 2 hours to win. Though you can win in probably half that, im the type of guy who likes to explore the lands and kill all the monsters and get loots and build heaps of cities and stuff, always more than i really need.
I just recommend this game to anyone into Turn Based/Fantasy/RPG/4X/Strategy and even probably City Builders.
I believe it has something to appeal to all and once you've gotten through your first 1 or 2 games (with very helpful tutorial tooltips which you can enable on and off, so if you forget, you can just play a normal game again and have em pop up without having to do an actual tutorial mission) you will finally start enjoying it atleast twice as much and start thinking of strats and combos and cool ways to play!
I got this for free, but do i think it's worth $25? Hell. Yes. Even without a Story Mode. The amount of content and options is worth, let alone the value for multiplayer. And remember it's for the complete addition which includes the base game and 5 other content packs.
So if it sounds very appealing to you, $25 would be a good investment I feel, and if you score it on any kind of sale even 25% off, bonus!

I bought Dark Souls back during one of the Steam summer sales because everyone was talking about the third installment in the series and I decided to give the Dark Souls games a shot. Lately I was having a bit of a game burnout and could not decide what to play, so I downloaded Dark Souls to see if it was as tough as everyone hyped it up to be. After finishing the game I can say that it is not the hardest game you will play, however it is  a very challenging game and will test you in ways some games today never really do. That does not mean the game isnt fair, it gives you plenty of opportunities to grind if need be or if you need help you can always summon a friend to assist in a difficult boss fight or get through an area you have been struggling with. Dark Souls was the first game I played in a while that really kept me hooked from start to finish. I liked it so much I even played through a bit of the new game plus segment. The best part for me was the gameplay, I really enjoyed how hack and slash it was while at the same time punishing if you are too greedy with your attacks. There are strategies involving dodging, using your shield, parrying, and backstabbing that make combat against enemies and players really addictive. The online aspect of the game is fun as you never know if another player is going to invade your world making it tense sometimes when you see the invasion message pop up. It is also fun to team up with a friend and take on a tough boss together. The bosses in this game are so much fun to go against using different strategies and attacks to make you learn after each death how to better fight them. I would recommend an xbox controller or equivalent when playing this but I will say it is not impossible to play with a mouse and keyboard. My controller broke in the beginning of my playthrough so I mapped out the controls on the keyboard and actually enjoyed it more than my old controller. There are a few different playstyles you can go through as well ranging from the tanky knight, the wizard, the fast moving rogue, or you can make up something silly to use too. The DLC included in the game of the year edition was really fun and had one of my favorite boss fights in it. It adds a few extra hours of playtime along with new items, enemies and lore to soak up. To summarize I would say Dark Souls is a fantastic game with unique and fun gameplay that challenges you at every turn while still being fair enough that it doesnt lose its enjoyment.

Lack of polish showed with its infrequent gitches in zombie clipping with objects or ground, brief & occasional movement issues after exiting a menu, and exit game crashes (not mid-game).
Six hours into the game, I felt like I got into a groove or routine for managing home base & exploration, but I started to realize how repetative some of the side missions start to get as well as the shallow variety in character dialog or personality. My motivation for exploration was finding resources and survivors. Thinking with Time Machine is a twist on the original mechanics of the first two portal games, adding a time travel/clone making gameplay to the portal gun.
TWTM has a lot of great ideas and a lot of creativity but, it unfortunately completely misses the point of a "Portal" game. From my point of view, Portal does what it does so greatly because of two main points:
- The comedy between a character and a silent protagonist right from the first moments of the game that quickly establishes what the game is going to be, making you want to get to the end to get every single moment of comedy out of it;
- How simple the controls are and how they make the game simple but still challenging enough.
Unfortunately, TWTM fails in both things. If the controls were simple enough, then the game would just be fine, it's always fun playing with Portal and the aesthetics sure are amazing. But when you're in a room with absolutely no music, no characters talking to you, only the background hum to keep you company and you need to figure out the time travel mechanics from a silent video that doesn't even tell you the buttons you need to use, then it becomes really tedious.
I'm obviously not saying that I want Ellen Mclain or Stephen Merchant doing voices for this, but someone with enough charisma even on an unprofessional level could pull off a good performance as another A.I./glados-like character.
But, as I said, TWTM has a great amount of potential, and I'm sure that with some tweaking the game could actually become pretty grood. The Time travel works well and the testing chambers have that classic portal look with enough new stuff to make them new and interesting.
I would recommend this game just to check out the idea behind it. As of now it's a 50%-50% between good and bad, the negative vote is just because I know the team could make a lot more with it and Iìm ready to change my rating if any of the problems are fixed.

While at first this seems very complicated, think of it as recording a macro. You hit "R" to start the recording. You hit "Q" when you want to stop. Then, when ready you can press "F" to start it. Be warned that it matches EVERYTHING you do, including delays, so don't stand on a button for a second and jump off and stop recording, thinking it will last forever.
Yes, it is confusing at first. But those screens aren't for nothing. Watch them, as it shows you how to play.
However, there are a couple of things that have annoyed me about these screens.
On the level where you need your twin to assist you on a great height, I couldn't get it to work. I may have been doing something wrong, but it just didn't look right.
Also, on the next level, the answer is different from the actual puzzle.
One thing I will say, DO NOT SEPARATE THE GAME AND THE MOD. You can't install the game on one drive, and the mod on the other. It will fail to launch.
I haven't heard of the audio bugs yet, and I have had all sound, so I don't know what's up with the others'.

The in-game help is horrible, disconnected, and basically doesn't get you up and "running". When you're building a track, to scroll the landscape you have to continue holding down the left mouse button to lay track while at the same time holding down the right mouse button and moving the mouse in the opposite direction to scroll the screen. Really? Did anyone teach these developers how to write software? When laying track it automatically curves when you want to go straight...and then you get another error messages that have more meaning in a C++ compiler than in a train simulation game. It seems like the designers got into a room and decided on the following tenets:
1. Make the help as useless as possible.
2. Make the error messages even more useless than the help.
3. Make the controls for the UI as useless as the error messages.
4. Make the graphics look as close as possible to Pac Man.
5. Make the game extremely unintuitive to chase potential customers away so that we can go bankrupt.
6. Charge a lot of money so we came make as much as possible before declaring baankruptcy.
This wasn't worth the money it cost me, and I would HIGHLY STRESS that if you're thinking about buying this game, invest in a tree stump instead...it'll provide less aggrevation and more entertainment that this game.

Do not let any preconceptions about this game steer you away from it. I thought it was just going to be another interactive story and I'd get bored with it after a couple of runs. I was wrong.
You take on the role of Elodie, a Queen to be after the death of her mother. Her 15th birthday (and coronation) is round the corner but before she can get there, she has to deal with the day to day life of being the leader of a nation. Now I don't know if you're aware of this, but it's not easy to be a figurehead when you're only 14. You have classes to attend after all.
Each week, you choose two classes you want to study. One in the mornings and one in the evenings. These classes give you skills you use to progress in the story and determine what path it follows. In addition, the increase to your skills is determined by your mood, which you can modify each weekend by choosing a certain activity. Eight different moods all affect various classes in either a positive or negative way. So choose your classes carefully to maximise your boosts. Alternatively you can choose to focus on certain classes despite the negative impact (since the more you study a class, the more points you gain in it).
While this may sound like it gets boring after a while, bear in mind that the number of paths you can follow in this game is HUGE! You can have multiple different outcomes for a single event in the story and each outcome can influence further outcomes far down the line that you don't even know about yet. Especially since it's not just the classes that determine how the story progresses, but also the choices you make outside of class.
Oh and here's another incentive. Getting to the end of the game is hard. The goal is to make it to Elodie's coronation but here's the problem. A lot of things are out there to kill her before she makes it there. You will find it hard to avoid every single death scene and in order to make it to the end, you will need to go through several runs to prepare for what will be thrown at you. Instinct alone cannot help you beat this game.
Long Live Queen Elodie!

Miscreated was yet another title founded as an answer to Dayz.  If I was to say that the game doesnt play roughly identical it would be a lie, however thats not a bad thing. While I do love Dayz, Miscreated takes the formula and to some extents....perfects it. Miscreated has the best world design I have seen in a game in this genre.
This however does not mean the game is perfect. Even though it has superior graphics and gunplay, amongst other things that make it stand out this game does have some major optimization issues. I cant even play it at 60fps without drops on even the lowest settings. The map is vastly smaller than Chenarus from Dayz which in turn almost makes the game feel too easy. Since the map is smaller the price of death is less meaningful due to the fact you can get to endgame consistantly and easily in under an hour provided you know the map.
Combine that with what seems to be a more lenghty wait between updates and you unfortunately have a game that will become quite stale if you play it daily.  If your looking to take a break from Dayz but still remain in the same genre this should be your go to game. If you are looking for a replacement then I would hold out.
I give this game a 7/10. Only so low because the map is tiny and I feel that its poorly optimized. My recomendation is to wait it out and see if it is ever finished.

My adoration for State of Decay‘s open-world leadership simulation contrasts with my dislike for how much it tempts me away from real responsibilities. But it also draws out why I like leadership simulations where survival is on the line: I love people and want to help them however I can. This also reminds me that if I want to truly be a great leader, I have to be sure to keep my priorities where they truly matter most: on my wife, my work, and my real-world friendships.

Sometimes a game comes along with obvious flaws, quirks that mar an experience which should have been easily fixable, but because it fills a gap in a library or perhaps a genre we put up with and maybe grow to like it anyway.  This is one of those.
State of Decay is essentially a half-hearted attempt at merging Grand Theft Auto with the zombie genre.  It merges scavenging and mission-based gameplay with some base-building and PERMANENT DEATH in a third-person action setting.
The original game starts off with two survivors who were camping, and upon returning to civilization find everything has gone FUBAR.  You make your way down from the mountains to a small redneck town where the survivors are holed up in a church.  This is when you discover that although your characters are given dialogue, they're not actually the main characters.  There aren't any...   Which is, and will remain weird for the rest of the game.  Rather, you switch between survivors on the fly, and whoever you're playing BECOMES the main character with the appropriate dialogue.  This sort of hive-mind utility isn't something you'll get used to, it's just something you come to accept, along with the other assorted quirky aspects of the game.
The base itself has its own needs.  Food, medicine, ammunition, building materials, and fuel.  There's a depletion from stocks every day-night cycle.  Part of your job is to hunt down these supplies and cart them back to base, or call runners to pick them up.  This isn't such a great idea, as runners are merely competent at best, and because of the zombie spawning mechanism are likely to run into trouble if you are nearby.
You can improve this base with various structures, and each home-site has different slots or inborn facilities.  It sounds intriguing, but is vaguely unsatisfactory for anyone who enjoys base-building.  You only get so many slots, and switching them out for a different structure means sacrificing the old one.  Still, it remains a major factor of the game.  If there aren't enough beds, people will sleep in shifts and be tired with a semi-permanent  hit to their stamina.  If they stay tired too long, they become sick with an even bigger decrease.  Same goes for food sanitation or restrooms (Lifeline).  If they get chewed on by zed, injuries will take a long time to heal without an infirmary.
Other mechanics come into play as every character has their own traits, both innate along with functional improvable traits.  That second set, like fighting, shooting and cardio, you'll want to build up through training, because if a character dies - that's it.  They're gone, along with whatever effort you put into them.
It sounds like quite a challenge, and it is.  The game requires a bit of finesse, otherwise you'll ragequit and come back to it a year later like I did.  At the time, it was the buggy AI.  Zombies would wallhack through doors, characters would stand there stupidly watching you die (which cost me my best character).  These problems have mostly been fixed - mostly.
Missions are varied, but they ARE repetitive.  If you're not baby-sitting or trying to find one of your vaguely moronic fellow survivors, you might be hunting down a special zed - which isn't so special when they're crawling all over the map - or doing a story mission.  The fact is you'll be doing most missions that pop up simply to make sure you don't lose a character.  There are only so many of them in story mode, and after that there aren't any more.  This unfortunately turns well over half the missions in the game into a kind of busywork.  It rarely lets up, and if so not for long.
As you complete missions and gather supplies you gain influence.  Removing gear from the supply locker requires it, as well as building and some other special features that open up from the story.  You'll meet Ray Santos, for instance, who will deliver a random car to your location for 100 influence.  If you're doing all the missions that are popping up, I guarantee you will never come close to running out of influence.
Now here's the kicker to all this: when you turn the game off, it technically keeps going.  When you load the game the next time, it calculates how long you've been gone according to your computer's clock, and runs some formula.  If you've been gone longer than a few days in the real world, I believe it stops there.  This used to be quite a bit more intrusive, but it's probably been patched.  Your morale and supplies will take a bit of a hit if you merely log in a bit over a day later.  I personally have never had any characters die while I was gone, but some of the survivor enclaves usually collapse.
Being that the game is mostly busywork, people gave feedback which led to the creation of the first DLC: Breakdown.  It basically removes all story-type missions from the game, and recycles the survivors if they all happen to die, along with some other changes.  You can theoretically play the game forever.
The second DLC, Lifeline introduces some different mechanics as you play an army base on a different map.  Enough of the mechanics were different to be a refreshing change.
So that's about it.  If you're a zombie fan, and you want something that's finally different, this will probably do it for you.  There is a certain finesse that is needed to not lose any characters.  The way you play has to be "just so."  Everything from strategy to what equipment you should be taking to somewhat stressful time management.  Once you figure it out, you'll enjoy the game quite a bit more.

One of the few gathering games that manages to be fun.
The game includes a diverse amount of biomes and worlds to explore, equipment to find and loot to pillage. Everything is randomized and the experience of travelling through space while returning plunder back to your ship as you gradually build onto it is very satisfying. The game features minor survival elements but is still rather forgiving, and has a simple but fun combat system which gives the player a good feeling of control and precision. Players are even allowed to colonize planets for themselves, and recruit characters to live as tenants or become crew on their ship.
The story mode unfortunately is a rather repetitious chore which rewards players with interesting unique dungeons to raid in turn, and there are imbalances with the loot system which lead to the game rewarding players too much and too easily for plundering neutral settlements instead of spelunking and dungeoneering. Furthermore, if you play the game enough you will begin to see a lack of diversity in the randomization of the worlds, but it is not too noticeable.
Overall, it is one of the only gathering games out there that makes an effort to actually entertain the player instead of just keeping them busy with repetition and pointless baubles.

Here is the fix. (It worked for me!)
1) Go to: ...\Steam\SteamApps\common\Portal 2\portal2\maps
2) Copy the ''Soundcache'' folder.
3) Go to: ...\Steam\SteamApps\common\Thinking with Time Machine\TWTM\maps
4) Replace the ''Soundchache'' folder with the one you copied.
5) Enjoy the game!

If you like building things, watching trains move around a landscape like a virtual model railway then you will probably enjoy this game. Good graphics, gameplay, and ever changing cities keeps the game fresh and if you don't like the world you have created, then go get yourself another randomly created map.
There are some aspects that can be tiresome, such as what has become for me the dreaded terrain collision when trying to build across existing items, and the 'must build bypass first' before deleting town connecting roads. There are some things that could be tweaked from an ease of use point of view, but they do not detract from the overall game.

As of now, this is the most-played game in my Steam Library.  I played this obsessively for a few weeks, giving up entire weekends to it.  When you start one of these games, be prepared to give up the next 20 hours of your life, because that's how long some of these games can take, depending on the game setup (difficulty, world size, victory conditions, etc.)
The graphics, music, sounds effects, and gameplay all perfectly complement each other, and they don't get old even after hours of gameplay.  Because you don't want to leave a game unfinished, you end up saying, "Just one more turn, then I'll take a break."  Three hours later, you're still playing, literally starving because you can't leave the game to cook some food.  The game takes so long because it takes time to build up your force enough to overcome an enemy.  There are also neutral monsters which pose a threat.  Not to mention, you have to wait for the AI to finish their turns.  The wait is totally worth it, because the feeling of slowly overcoming your opponents is addicting.
The AI isn't super smart, which is good or bad, depending on your perspective.  Personally, I liked taking advantage of the flawed AI strategies, like sending their entire army to me by boat, which I destroyed before they could even land.  Diplomacy with the AI is somewhat of a joke.  They might make a truce with you, but they'll break it on a whim.  I tried to be honorable with truces, but after you've played awhile, you start to understand the motivations of the AI when they make a truce, and you can tell when they are about to break it.
Another great aspect of this game is the random world generation and fog of war.  From the initial setup, you have an idea of what the world is like, but not the details.  Curiosity and fear of the unknown helps to maintain your interest as you explore the map.
After playing this, I tried Civilization 5, and personally, I hated it.  I'd rather take a history class.  Personally, I don't like playing games that remind me of reality.  Warlock is a fantasy escape into another world, and it really absorbs you.  I can't recommend it highly enough.

I rarely write reviews (I think I've written one), but this one deserved the praise. Amidst the actual reviewing I'll talk a bit about my own personal experiences whilst playing the game. Therefore for those that balk at reading more than a paragraph about a game, I'll submit my TLDR first up.
TLDR : Stranded Deep, for an early access game, is amazingly addictive. Surprisingly, game mechanics are quite solid, despite the obviously expected bugs and glitches, of which there aren't many at all which would cripple gameplay.
As far as survival games go, I give this a solid 8/10 and cannot wait to see what full release brings. Buy it. Trust me, you've spent more on worse...you know you have ;)
So, I first bought this a year ago I believe, amidst the multitude of survival games storming the early access front. At over 300 games in my library and probably about 50 more outside of steam, I'd say I'm a moderate to excessive gamer with experience in majority of genres. That said, this game shocked me at how pleasing it was to play, considering others in the same vein make me want to gouge my eyes out.
- Graphically, this game is gorgeous. I've tried my hand at game design and fell in love with water mechanics, this game made my best efforts look like absolute garbage, and I made some pretty decent garbage. It's bright, fluid and dynamic, exactly what a game centered around being stranded in the big blue should be. It has it's odd impurities, but it hardly takes away from the glory of it all as a whole. Clean and crisp environment, elements involving fire, water, animals etc all very well executed.
- Gameplay wise, the game relies heavily on physics for a lot of the nittty gritty, and I rarely encountered anything to make me throw my hands up and alt+F4. The ability to use boats to ferry half finished boats and/or equipment from one island to the next is brilliant, you can even make a barge train to ferry over felled trees for lumber supplies. The core of it all of course is to survive, and I highly recommend doing so without looking online how to achieve certain tasks (Oh and beware of snakes - scared the living bajeezus outta me). That feeling of achievement when you successfully implement a sustained source of food and water is second to none. Hunt (Hella fun chasing a wild pig with a spear), spear fish (Animation is perfect), nock an arrow and bring down some seagulls, and when you're ready and suficiently confident enough in your survival, head out to explore.
- Exploration is possibly one of the only gripes I have (At this stage in development), but that could just be me and my passion for finding something new around each corner. Still, there are plenty of islands with resources washed ashore for the savvy survivor to collect and RTB for use in building his or her island mansion. There are shipwrecks and buildings with items for building and then enhancing faster water craft, and is quite enjoyable to advance to a point where you feel you can subsist out there forever.
There is a limit to exploration currently though, marked by yellow buoys to define your borders. Once you reach them and map out your area, have constructed and set up to maximum effect, the world can feel quite small. Hopefully there are plans for implementing full procedural and maybe pirate coves, cave systems and mining? I dunno, maybe even have the protaganist go stuff it, I like it better here, and set up trade routes with passing vessels haha.
-Sound is a bit of a null area for me, I didn't take much notice, although the ambient ocean sounds ands wildlife are very soothing. If I had to pro and con it I'd say PRO - Microwave ding effect when food is cooked (Hilarious) CON - Damn bats... -_-
- Overall this game gave me about 8 hours of fun, I survived for over a month and was completely self suffficient in terms of 'surviving' so I guess you could say...I won the game? The few things I'd like to see fixed before anything else so they do not persist though further updates are as follows.
- Driftwood piles launching into the stratosphere after cutting them down for materials
- Wall/floor placement on second story doesn't work with corner pieces. (Breaks into untextured model blocks straight out of 3DS Max)
- Dismantling of built stuctures such as distiller and fire pit for retrieval of resources.
Anyway, that's probably all at the moment, cannot wait for future updates and will be fimly glued to upcoming news for this game. Well worth the purchase, kudos to the dev team and don't let us all down OK guys ;)

This one positively surprised me. Got this for free during the Humble Bundle thing and had a great time with it ever since. Warlock - Master of the Arcane is a turn based strategy game about a warlock (surprise, surprise!) battling his colleagues in an epic battle for a world filled with Gods, parallel worlds, and more monsters than you can count. The game itself shows a clear influence from the Age of Wonders series. Research spells and unleash them to grant your troops new abilities, weaken and damage your enemies, or change the face of the world around you. Water blocking your way? Raise the land and create a passage for your troops that doesn't put them at the mercy of naval monsters! Mountains slowing down your troops? Flatten them. The mountains, not the troops. Just make sure you have the mana to sustain all your permanent spells. There is little as terrifying as a flying ogre with a vampiric regeneration and an area attack.
Mana, as well as gold and food (your main resources) are generated by city buildings. You can found or capture cities, although make sure they have enough room to grow. Place them near strategic resources for some special buildings, depending on the faction that lives in your city - the undead will utilise a pumkin patch different than humans would. Depending on which buildings you have, you can purchase powerful upgrades for your troops, ranging from a slight defense bonus to health regeneration each turn. They will also gain experience from battles, and you may choose an improvement with every levelup as well.
Battles are fairly simple. Move your troops on the hex of the enemy you wish to attack, and they automatically fight. Damage is determined by the health of your troops (full health = max strength), as well as their damage type and the enemy defense. Heroes on either side, like the aforementioned flying ogre, might turn the tide of a battle, and placing your troops in cities or on mountains might give you the edge you need. Randomly given quests by Gods, guilds or an advisor will offer you some short to middle term objectives and keep you busy for a bit, as you wouldn't want to anger a God. Especially the Divine missions often offer a great reward as well, be it a spell or a troop tied to that particular deity. You wouldn't want to miss out on those now, would you?
All in all a great game with a lot of unit variety, customiseability and a weird sense of humour. One minor issue, though... please don't use Google Translator for in game text. I originally installed the german version, and promptly found some rather glaring issues with that (Close was basically translated to 'near city view' as opposed to 'close that window', for example). Luckily, Steam allowed me to easily switch to english.

State of Decay is a third-person, survival game that was originally a xbox live exclusive. It then got ported over to PC via Steam Early Access. During this time there was alot of bugs as well as lack of keyboard/mouse controls. KB/M support eventually got added in shortly after along with some major optimizations for the PC and is a decent port.
The game throws you into the deep end, you have to survive by scavenging for resources as well as build up a community of survivors that go and help do stuff. Your community is extremely important due to the gameplay mechanics. Survivors have a stamina bar which is used up when you take certain actions like melee, jumping, etc. However overtime your max stamina will go down to simulate tiredness. You can switch to another survivor in your community to let the tired survivor rest up. This is simulated really well to simulate spreading the work out between survivors but it does feel alittle clunky from a gameplay perspective at times (and often you may end up in a situation where you can't switch to another survivor, meaning that you'll eventually lose to fatigue).
Your community base can be upgraded depending on the location and amount of slots that a base has. An infirmary (for example) will help heal survivors that are sick or that have sustained major damage. You can also establish outposts which not only provide protection in a certain area via means of traps, but can also provide resources to your community.
You will get missions very often that will usually get you to either save a survivor, escort them, take out infestations, etc. While there are quite a bit of variety I feel that you are given missions too often in a short amount of time. Most if not all missions are failable if you don't do them in time.
Overall this is a solid game, as long as you can ignore some of the bugs that regularly crop up. Also I recommend picking up Breakdown DLC as I feel this is where the game is at it's best. It's really rewarding to be able to get that RV fixed and advance in terms of difficulty, something that isn't in the stock game sadly.

After recently catching up on basketball since the 90s when the Chicago Bulls were still on top, I wanted to try out a basketball sim.  This is still in the trialling phase and was far from complete (no search recall, could not complete trades) but I still had fun.  The simulation side meant I didn’t have to worry about managing play-by-play or the finance unless I wanted to.  My experience was with the NBA, and the best part was the draft system, which I think is such fun.  I also like how you can decide how many minutes each player should play.  So the game is as light or detailed as you want it to be.

What the first book did with world building, this installment ratchets up to eleven.  We get to learn a lot more about other cultures, societies, and how things operate on Versus.  We also get further development on characters that were only touched on in the Last Ones, as well as incredible new ones that you meet along your journey.
I think it should be noted that most of your time IS spent with new characters instead of the old ones (with a few exceptions).  If that bothers you then you might not like this game.
The mysteries Zack set up in the first book also get explored more here in a very satisfying way.  You find answers to some things, but they often create even more questions.  It doesn't feel jumbled or overly confusing though.  It only serves to heighten the tension.
The last thing I think is worth mentioning is the overall tone of the game.  In The Lost Ones, I could create great relationships with all the people I liked and have a more or less "happy ending."  But things get very political in this game.  A lot of people that I really liked had VERY different views and opinions.  Eventually you have to make a choice on where you stand, and no matter what you decide someone will get hurt.  It's just a matter of who.  In this manner, it reminds me a bit of Heroes Rise: The Hero Project.  This is the kind of game that really makes you think about your ideologies and why you choose them.  Even more amazingly, it doesn't make a judgment on your actions or push you towards a certain way of thinking *cough* Hero Project Redemption *cough*.
Overall this game builds on the complexities of the last one in every way without becoming confusing or preachy.  Versus is an increasingly fascinating world, and your character has the opportunity to become even more unique and customized to your liking.
But the cuss words still suck.

The second book in the Versus collection, this story is rich, engaging, and beautiful.  Even as a short story on its own, the Versus tale would be worth the read, but watching as your choices shape the world in your mind's eye makes it something that each person should experience several times over.  It was a big bonus, for me, to see the ideas and themes from the first book transition to the second.  My biggest disappointment is that book 3 is not released as of yet.  I eagerly await the conclusions!
Pros:
Engaging, descriptive storytelling
Good transfer of stats
Excellently crafted characters
Balanced and satisfying branches
Cons:
Some grammatical/spelling errors
Feels somewhat incomplete (given the episodic nature, it's expected, but it's still a con)
I would definitely play Versus: The Lost Ones before playing this.  You don't absolutely have to, but it definitely helps with world immersion, and to understand the background of these characters and many of the ideas and themes used throughout the story.

I'm a huge fan of basketball and I love management sims like Football Manager so this was an easy buy for me. I have played it for about 10 hours now and I've reached the conclusion that though it is imperfect, it is an excellent sim. This is a game that should attract a fanatical following and the community (like in FM) should improve it by adding content such as new tactics.
Well done stuff:
Unbelievably they have all the exemptions (except the injured player exception) correct.
You can balance out the play time and get advice from the coach. You will want to intervene here or the coach will try to play an older guy that is a star for 40+ minutes against even bad teams.
You can add plays and call them. This works really well if you have a bad defending but fantastic 3 pt specialist. You can make sure he is on the perimiter, drive a player to the paint and toss the ball to one side of the court to draw off guards, and then funnel it to your player on the 3 point line. It works really well.
You'll want to change your database to the uploaded ones with real player names in them. It is uploaded by users to the forums.
Rough edges:
There are a few small player management issues such as number of players in the off-season. I get the impression that teams don't have strategies for tanking if they are already eliminated which helps rebuilding.
I'd like to be able to scout upcoming draft classes.
There are some calendar issues with the game (for when a trade can be made).
What it's not:
It's not NBA jam. You don't have an immersive gametime experience (when they are on the court). The graphics - even in 3d mode - do not compare to playstation etc. The focus of this game is what happens off the court (though you also have a part of the game for calling plays which you need to beat strong teams.)
Conclusion:
All in all it's a great game. I'm super-satisfied with my purchase. Right now it's 40% off so if you love the NBA and sims you should grab it.

Update: Most bugs now appear to be fixed, and if you have any, make sure that first of all you aren't in the beta for Portal 2, since if you are it will CTD as soon as you get past the Valve intro video, if you have sound issues, rebuild the sound cache or do a clean uninstall and reinstall it for the fixed cache direct, make sure you have Portal 2 installed on the same HDD, and if all else fails, verify the integrity of the game cache on both TWTM and Portal 2.
Anyhow, onto the review of the actual game/mod now that I've had time to play it after fixing the bugs;
First of all, if this was a workshop submitted mod (not possible due to the extent of the gameplay and asset changes in some areas, therefore the store mod) it would most definitely be one of the highest rated community campaigns along with 12 Angry Tests and Designed for Danger. It may not be the strongest in terms of pure level design and perfection of the core Portal formula, but it certainly makes up for it through having the most significant gameplay changes to come out of the Portal community yet. If you're a fan of the Portal series, this is definitely a must play, especially considering it's free, you'd struggle to not got any sort of enjoyment out of TWTM, even if you didn't complete it or care for the TM mechanic much.
It doesn't have the strength of a proper retail game which is as to be expected due to the fact it's a community created mod by a couple of guys in their spare time. Most of the downsides amount to length of the mod and levels of polish. If this had been picked up by Valve for instance and given another few months of development time to polish it up and add to it, it could have no doubt been sold as a single player expansion to Portal 2 and have been worth paying money for.
In summary, if you're a fan of the Portal games, play it. It's free, you've got nothing to lose, and there's a very strong possibility you'll like it. Interested in seeing what the developers of the mod go on to do, since this shows a lot of promise from them in getting a job in the industry or creating their own games.

Rust Belt Gothic literature at its finest. I say literature because this game is more of a story played out from a theatrical perspective. It's a heavy story that is ambigous and may often leave you scratching your head wondering what on Earth is going on. Throw in the young adult humor clashing with the thick of real life situations and morals. Think of this game a lot like "Fall of the House of Usher" by Edgar Allen Poe or "The Lottery" by Shirley Jackson with respect to climax and hazed cues throughout the story. The way the story muddies leaves me frustrated at times but always wanting more out of it.
The soundtrack fits the color of the game: rustic and gray with a touch of bright autumn. The emphasis on bass and keyboard reflect a more somber feeling from an old rust belt town yet give a homey-time feeling for those that have experienced small town life with more upbeat melodies. The xylophone, tuba, bassoon, ensemble, and keyboard usage resembles a community lost in its former time: hard-hitting on heritage and nostalgia.
The characters themselves are lively and feel normal when carrying out decisions with gameplay. A great amount of dedication went into the dialog and persona's of each character. It's very easy to give each character their own voice in your head accompanied by any inflections or attenuation caused as the game carries on. It also adds in more of a replay value as you get to learn more about certain characters as you interact with them more.
I will not go too granular into game mechanics based on the popular reviews for this game have covered this topic. This is one of those games where I can spend an hour or two in the evening with a glass of bourbon and play out a chapter- like how I would read a book and pick it up the next night. It just grows on you.

There is so much I loved about this game -- the setting is unique, the characters are all so good, and when I first saw the trailer I knew it was going to hit home in a very relateable way for me, given where I had been in my life at the time. I love the tiny details of the town, and the approriate black speech bubbles that everyone uses. It is without question a *good* game. But it's far from perfect. For one, the gameplay itself is not very fun; the game plays out as a series of days through the course of fall, and each day something different happens. But it's always the same set pieces, and there's just enough reward for exploration that I felt I had to hit every interaction each day. It got pretty repetitive, feeling like I was just completing a checklist so I could move on to the day's event and proceed the story. I wanted to make sure I didn't miss anything, but too often I would visit an area and nothing would be there, only for there to be something cool there the next day. That inconsistency was pretty annoying. It doesn't help that Mae doesn't move very quickly, so I would just sit there holding "left" while she moved through the level. I have no problem with walking simulators, and usually really like them; but having to hit the same spots each day got tiring.
I could set aside gameplay troubles if the story itself makes up for it; this is a story-driven game for sure, and that is where the game does have its moments. I really liked the setting, which was very unique, and the ever-present looming feeling of dread that underscored the town. As others have said, it's very Twin Peaks-like. The characters are awesome and relateable, although I occasionally found myself strongly disagreeing with something Mae did. But the pacing is not great, and there are several days where nothing really advances; the dream sequences were strange, and repetitive, and didn't really add much other than some platforming sections. The climax seems to come up out of nowhere, and slips away without a word. It has an element of deus ex machina, and felt a bit out of place. In the end, I was left with a strange feeling like I had missed something. It wasn't bad per se, but I felt it could have been much better too.
The game has good characters, and a lot of great moments. It captures that feeling of returning home from college to small town really well. If the game had come out a few years ago, it would definitely have really resonanted strongly with me emotionally, but I'm further past those days now so I didn't quite connect as much as I thought I would. The story is not strong enough to balance out the repetitive gameplay. and so while for some people it would be worth playing this, for most I would probably not recommend it.

However it's not without its small issues :
-some performance issues (I7-2600k + 16GB RAM + GTX760 2GB) when zoomed out in large populated bases. particularly if it's also raining. -no keybind for teleportation
-need workshop.... "but dude the game has it ?"  yes it does have it, I mean it NEEDS workshop
-it needs workshop for many quality of life/gaming improvements:
* it's behind terraria in chest/storage management, however a mod fixes that
* most windows are really small: crafting for example shows a handful of items with a lot of screen real estate unused. Again fixable through mods.
* Speaking of windows, those are movable and remembers the position you last put them in, except a bug actually resets those positions every game restart.
-the game has workshop but some stuff is locked from modding specifically new keybinds can't be added for example.

- Killing a mutant during an attack animation results in an invisible assailant that can tear through the player despite thinking they are safe (Had it happen twice, though usually kills at range so the only melee kills I have are these).

- Teleporting. Massive lag spikes do happen.
- Invisible walls... They will mess you up.
- Gravity. You thought the walls were bad? This is so much worse.

I bought Dark Souls back during one of the Steam summer sales because everyone was talking about the third installment in the series and I decided to give the Dark Souls games a shot. Lately I was having a bit of a game burnout and could not decide what to play, so I downloaded Dark Souls to see if it was as tough as everyone hyped it up to be. After finishing the game I can say that it is not the hardest game you will play, however it is  a very challenging game and will test you in ways some games today never really do. That does not mean the game isnt fair, it gives you plenty of opportunities to grind if need be or if you need help you can always summon a friend to assist in a difficult boss fight or get through an area you have been struggling with. Dark Souls was the first game I played in a while that really kept me hooked from start to finish. I liked it so much I even played through a bit of the new game plus segment. The best part for me was the gameplay, I really enjoyed how hack and slash it was while at the same time punishing if you are too greedy with your attacks. There are strategies involving dodging, using your shield, parrying, and backstabbing that make combat against enemies and players really addictive. The online aspect of the game is fun as you never know if another player is going to invade your world making it tense sometimes when you see the invasion message pop up. It is also fun to team up with a friend and take on a tough boss together. The bosses in this game are so much fun to go against using different strategies and attacks to make you learn after each death how to better fight them. I would recommend an xbox controller or equivalent when playing this but I will say it is not impossible to play with a mouse and keyboard. My controller broke in the beginning of my playthrough so I mapped out the controls on the keyboard and actually enjoyed it more than my old controller. There are a few different playstyles you can go through as well ranging from the tanky knight, the wizard, the fast moving rogue, or you can make up something silly to use too. The DLC included in the game of the year edition was really fun and had one of my favorite boss fights in it. It adds a few extra hours of playtime along with new items, enemies and lore to soak up. To summarize I would say Dark Souls is a fantastic game with unique and fun gameplay that challenges you at every turn while still being fair enough that it doesnt lose its enjoyment.

With an adorable and well realised anime style to its visuals and the allure of its fatalistic life sim sensibilities, it's hard not to be charmed by Long Live The Queen at first glance. But play through it a while and you'll quickly come to realise that it's not quite as hard to put down as you might expect.
The problems start right away with the first set of menus. Nowhere is the modifier/mood relationship made fully aware to the player; it is up to them to write down or remember which moods affect which skills and how. This wouldn't be so bad if skill checks didn't start popping up in some very early weeks, and don't let up much, if at all, throughout the game. Given that a new player will have no knowledge of which skills he will need at the end of any given week or indeed which moods will improve the rate at which he acquires these often essential skills, he is bound to get stuck in some pretty bad, dead-end scenarios early on. At least the game offers plenty of save slots for restarting...
Some may find this early discovery process more enjoyable than others, but they certainly could have made it less frustrating. As it is, the game gives you no reason not to forgo the tedium and consult online wikis or guides to ease the process.
Perhaps a more rewarding story may have helped offset this also. Long Live The Queen offers many choices and several endings, but here also the game falls short. It is hard to escape the feeling throughout the game that many, if not most, of the descions were made not made with the intentions of creating a proper, branching storyline, but instead as alternative skill checks  that (usually) offer only minor differences in outcome that are necessary to mask how poorly the game makes player's aware of what skills to prepare.
The story is helped no more by how detached Elodie and the castle where she stays for the vast majority of the game feel compared to interal and external threats around them. There is no change in the scenary to reflect the changing seasons, let alone civil unrest, panic, or conversely celebration. Only the sparce cutscenes which ocassionally occur allow for a change of scenary, but even here the game reuses many of its backgrounds and music. The result is that, for all the lore, history, and noble relations the game might throw at the player, no more than a flimsy idea of the world ever congeals. There isn't even a map the player can regularly look at in game, meaning plenty of the dialouge, fed with little to no context, is bound to be confusing.
Long Live The Queen may be a good looking game, but it is a very hollow gameplay experience. Its simplistic leveling system would work fine proped against fair and strategic decision-making, but instead the only strategy players need to employ is save-scumming. Simply save every week and go back 1, 2, or 5 everytime you failed a crucial check because the game gave you no way of anticipating it beforehand. Even completeing a playthrough isn't very rewarding, as the unlockable windows players recieve along with a customised epilogue do little to fill a world full of facts, but devoid of any realism or investment for the player.
If you want to play a princess life sim with anime stylings that offers about the same level of world-building, but offers a richer and more rewarding leveling system, pick up a Princess Maker game. Some, though not all, have English fan-translations.
As it stands, Long Live The Queen offers nothing that a game released in 1991 (Princess Maker 2) doesn't, but costs ten dollars more.

After playing the first Versus game, I can definitely say the second keeps the tension going. I'm most certainly biased here, but I'm a lover of text-based games, especially when I feel like my choices really matter and change the way events happen. How do I approach this.
I liked The Elite Trials. I loved The Lost Ones, and Elite Trials expanded on the world I already enjoyed. The characters are interesting, the writing is solid, the plot handles itself well, and the author is capable of pulling some interesting twists, though at times it was slightly stretching my willing suspension of disbelief. But only slightly.
The game itself feels… Shorter, but that might be because some parts of it are locked away depending on the choices made in the prequel. Still, there are only two plotlines through the entire game, the MemoryTravel and the Trial, and the trial takes the back seat. I honestly expected more. BUT - I like what I got, and I don’t feel like I overpaid for it. The replayability value is quite high - The game teases many secrets, and I know I’ll be playing it again in the future to try and uncover them.
You will find some very negative reviews concerning the… Preachy nature of the game. They’re not wrong. Zachary (the author), seems to feel very strongly about social issues, something that was fairly obvious in the first book, with the inclusion of a transgender character.
Elite trials is less about the trials themselves, and more about… Politics. There is a segment that concerns society building – and the game comments on the decisions you make and the potential impact they might have. If you find yourself displeased with the hypothetical results, you don’t get to argue. I have yet to experience the full range of possibilities here, so I can’t yet judge how fair it is – but it’s entirely possible your vision and the authors vision differ. So take the result with a grain of salt, and don’t take it personal. As the great Ilya Bryzagalov once said:

That’s more or less the gist of it. I’ve found myself drawn into Zachary’s style of writing, and I find his social commentary both fair and interesting, and not all that intruding. I love the characters, and can’t wait to see more of them in the future. If you liked the first book, then book two is money well spent.

In general, if you enjoyed VERSUS: The Lost Ones, you are bound to enjoy this one even further. The continuation develops on itself quite neatly and the author's gain in experience is shown in the game's more intricate nature - gameplay and story wise.
That being said, VERSUS: The Elite Trails is an amazing story, still one of the best from the Choice of Games platform, and it explores the universe imagined by Zachary Sergi quite well, deepening on its lore and creating new relationships with new characters. However, it can be lackluster, depending on what you are looking for.
Following the trend on most Choice of Games titles (as opposed to some of the greatest Hosted Games titles), this game still attempts, and expands on, putting players in labeled boxes, trying to fit them on criterias instead of allowing their personality to flow. Taking further steps in the Mastery and Growth concepts utilized in the first book, you now have more stat variants and more goals to focus on, which, while they give you plenty of
, they also complicate your freedom of choice, since if you want to actually succeed and thrive in the game's world and score systems, you need to follow a role, an idea, a specific path which the author believes most closely matches with a personality type.
Instead of giving you choices with consequences, the game gives you specific paths to follow, and while it allows you to diverge on those paths at any point in time, it also doesn't let you thrive if you do so. Most times, those paths are not even clear enough to the player, as even your choice of food may affect your stats, your character's personality and power, and this may generate apprehension as the player must wonder whether his choice falls in lign with whatever path he was forced to choose or not, or even fight against his intuition and desire to choose an option he
is right for his character, but the game disagrees.
It is disappointing to see a CoG game at this stage still being so limited in this matter, especially taking into account how experient Zachary is, having released more than 5 books in the platform already.
Combat, while we are still on the matter of gameplay, is short, predefined, and generally speaking, weak. If you like to engage on combat as much as possible, you'll not only be disappointed with the lack of variety, you'll also be disappointed by how weak your character seems, being so near of ever-powerful beings. Though that might just be the circunstances you find yourself at in this story.
As to the story itself, without bringing any margin for spoilers to the table, it expands on the VERSUS universe, ties some loose ends, creates more loose ends, the main story unfurls wonderfully and continuously, and leaves you wanting more. Exactly what you'd expect from one of Zachary's games. If I have any critiques about the game's story, they are those:
First, if you are a heterosexual male, your romance options fall short. As in, they fall into an abyss. The game seems to give a lot more attention, detail and focus to homosexual, agendered and non-binary players and characters. If you are a heterosexual player, your options pale in comparison, giving the sensation that they were rushed and undeveloped. To keep it short, romance is not a strong suit in this VERSUS book, as it where in the Heroes Rise original trilogy.
Secondly, this game - as in others written by Zachary - tries and introduces his imagination of societal concepts to the reader, and these new concepts are often well introduced, being part of the game's world and provoking emotional responses within the player through events. In this game, the author attempts to do the same with even more concepts in a much grander scale, and the experience may cause the player to feel disconnected by how abstract the descriptions are, how unconnected to the main story they seem, and especially, by how the emotional responses are provoked (more like forced) into the player's character, instead of the human reading the story. Breaking the main story to introduce politics many times over actually detracts from the experience.
Finally, the game leaves a lot more room for the development of the story. So much so that I can't really feel it will be over in the next book in the series... Hopefully that's an indication that more than one will come, and that we will have plenty more of the planet Versus to explore.
Ultimately, VERSUS: The Elite Trials feels like an experiment. First and foremost, the continuation to the story presented in book one, but an experiment into something new nonetheless. Some features worked well, others, not as much, and we can only hope that the next title will have thoroughly learned with its predecessor so we'll all have an even grander experience in the next to come.
If you are already a fan of Zachary's games, or the Choice of Games platform, this is one of the gems worth taking. If you are looking for a feature not commonly found in a CoG title, or which goes against what I described in this review, then you are probably better off looking for a Hosted Games title instead.

Just a disclaimer at the start that I didn't like the first part to this series since it failed with its focus because the first game felt more like a setup; a base to build to this one.
Also this is a choice-of-games game, so it will have many of the problems that the other games have - alas many of your choices seemingly won't matter.
So, do you need to have to played the first game? You don't need to actually since the story of the first game is summarized in the beginning which makes you realize not much at all has happened in the first one. It still helps to have read the first one since you need to pick up on the vocabulary that was introduced back then. The sequel does offer a glossary but it doesn't explain every word. Going through the first one was still more of an exercise of pain since it used its bloated vocabulary a little bit too liberally.
The last thing actually got changed in this game. Vocabulary for certain things (like the name for a race or such) are used a lot less and only when it actually needs to be talked about. I still don't understand why the word "♥♥♥♥" is censored since this is not a game for kids. Far from it in fact.
It's not for kids not because this game is gory (there is actually at least one gory scene which is also described in a detailed way) or that it has sex scenes. It's because this game is hard to understand in some chapters. It opens up lots of questions about difficult topics and there are a lot of abstract topics which are also talked about in sentences that a teenager would just skim over.
So, how is the story? You are basically a human space alien that is able to temporarily copy other people's abilites and dive into their memories by touching them. You hunted a monster that threatened to kill your kind but both of you get teleported to another planet. You then need to appease to people in politics.
The problem that this game still has is that it tries to be more than it needs to be. This game builds the expectation that you are going to use your awesome powers, fight people and get into romancing. All of these things rather take a back seat. In fact there is a rather large sub-plot where you build your own planet. It is well written and would serve well as its own short game - I actually did like the experience it provided. The experience just feels empty if it isn't being built upon later on. You cannot visit the planet you've created and that sub-plot is just dropped and could've easily been cut.
This is what the game is: a collection of sub-plots that only have remotely something to do with your main goal: Find out the identity of the champion of the player character's home planet and kill the monster that threatened to kill your people.
The writing itself is actually pretty good, but the not so subtle commentaries about society are things that also didn't really need to be there. The preachiness is something common to this particular author (Zachary Sergi) which again was worse in the first game. It has become better in this sequel but it's still a bit annoying when it does pop up. An example is capitalism vs. communism which just mentions things you will already know. That one at least only pops up once unlike the commentary about religion/customs.
As much as I am criticizing this game, I still liked it after I finished the one path that I did. It did not fulfill the expectations that I had. In fact I was left rather cold on the romance department, since the pay-off was just 2 short paragraphs. I still liked the experience it provided with intrigue and the divine beings that appeared in this game.
So ... do I recommend this game? If you're new to this series and your expecation is to romance people, or have thrilling fights in text form, no. There are better options for that if you didn't already check the other choice-of-games games.
I recommend this game to people who have already read the first part since this actually does something with all the world building the author has done in the first part. I also recommend this to people who want to read something different which you have to spend some time with to think about.
Other than that I still recommend a good choose-your-own-adventure book over this game if you are looking for interactivity in text form.

The exploration and conquest are mostly open-ended, you are fighting generic fantasy enemies without any specific goals or personalities, just for the sake of conquering them, just like in any Civ game. Unfortunately the AI lags behind the rest of the game quality-wise. It is rather predictable and tends to make stupid decisions. There are also bugs that should have long been corrected, especially the interface becoming unusable because of a pop-up window that can't be closed properly. Right, there is an easy workaround, but this is no excuse for not fixing a bug. Otherwise the user interface is exactly what you would expect in a Civ game, very functional and comfortable. The graphics are excellent as well. I wouldn't recommend buying it at its full price, but it has been included in many bundles and even given away for free on various occasions. I think it's definitely worth picking up for a few dollars when given the chance.

Train Fever is a railroad-focused business simulation game. In other words, it's a modern-day Transport Tycoon with procedural content and a sophisticated city simulation.
"It’s the year 1850, and there are great times ahead! Establish a transport company and be its manager. Build infrastructure such as railways and stations, purchase transportation vehicles and manage lines. Fulfill the people’s needs and watch cities evolve dynamically.
Train Fever runs on an engine specifically developed for this game. The engine has a great innovative scope and is specialized in procedural content and urban simulation. A key point is the fact that there is no grid that game objects have to be aligned to, allowing for a great degree of freedom. - Recommended!

You will find a lot of other reviews that pretty well describe the content of the game.
Instead, let me recommend you this game or not depending on what kind of gamer you are. Because I believe it really depends on that.
Basically, if you love to play with trains, trams, trucks and busses and to throw in some tycoon-like gameplay, this will probably be a game for you.
If on the other hand you are looking for a strategy game, a business simulator or an advanced train simulator, this could disappoint you.
Train Fever is a middle-of-the-road game when it comes to the balance between an eye-candy, fun transportation game and a hard-core ressource management game.
Train Fever does have its addicting side though. Is the next train stop profitable? Did the passengers from the tram transfer to the train? How much faster did the track become after the rebuild you made? Oh is that the time? I should go to bed now.....I will....in a minute.....I just need to.....
Lastly a warning to you if your patience with imbalanced games is short. Once you dig into the game you will (at the time of this review) find quite a few lose ends in how the game works. It is not something that is going to ruin the party for a casual gamer. But parts of the games' economic simulation is broken to be honest. TIme will show if that is adressed by patches or not. But it should.
I'll give TF 4 out of 5 stars for the many addicting hours of play it offers. It would get 5 of 5 if they would fix the broken parts  and include either a multiplayer option or some AI. Sadly there is presently neither,

This game has a heck of a reputation for being difficult.  Seems like any list of hardest games ever includes Dark Souls. I half expected to rage quit this game inside of a few hours, mainly because my gaming skills have never been that great.
So I dove in expecting to get whupped.  Whupped I got.  Regularly.  I also found one of the best games I've ever played.  It is instantly engaging and I'm transported into the world of Lordran.  The world design is beautiful and clever, areas interconnect in surprising ways, and you'll spot places you've visited while enjoying a scenic vista from a high point.  The world really comes alive for me with a bleakness and sadness that isn't accidental.
The game does not hold your hand like many modern games do.  I'm often left wondering where to go next, or faced with multiple choices and only the difficulty of the denizens are clue to my next path.
The game IS difficult, however it's not the type of difficult that requires lightning reflexes (although they'd help).  Analyzing your failures leads to improvement.  The penalty for death isn't too harsh.  You return to the last bonfire (checkpoint).  You lose any souls  (experience & currency) you hadn't spent.  All the monsters you've killed respawn.  You can recover your souls if you make it back and pick them up without dying again, which usually isn't a problem.
If you stick with it, you'll reach a point where something clicks, and the mechanics of the game make sense.  It doesn't get easy, but it gets much easier.
Bosses are another matter.  They are supremely challenging and incredibly varied.  They don't feel cheezy in difficulty.  There always seems to be a way to figure them out and put the hurt on them.  Adapt and conquer.
Multiplayer can be your focus, or it can be almost completely ignored, and it does it with grace.  You can try to summon help or offer yourself to help others.  You can also invade other players, or be invaded.  Being informed that you've been invaded while working your way to a boss is guaranteed to get your blood pumping.
All in all I'm loving Dark Souls, and can't wait to get back to it.
