State of Decay boasts decent graphics, a nice sandbox mode and free reign to do whatever you want. Sounds like zombie game heaven, right? Unfortunately the gameplay is just drab. If State of Decay pushed for survival-focused gameplay, all of this would be fine. But no: survival boils down to breaking and entering into nearby houses that magically restock food, medicine, "materials" and ammo after enough time has passed. There's absouletely no challenge in surviving. In fact, I always had more♥♥♥♥♥♥than my base could hold! The only interesting part of this game is how your characters can die, but I'm not even sure what kind of scenario you would have to be in to finally kick the bucket. In my fours hours of play, there was no amount of zombie hordes or special infected combined that I couldn't mash X through or shoot from afar. As an avid fan of Tolkien's work, I was worried that
, with its flashy screenshots, would introduce flashy magic or similar stuff too much apart from the lore.
I was happy to find that concern nil: while they have certainly taken many artistic liberties and little inaccuracies abound, the overall lore is adeptly executed.
Here I will cover both the main game and briefly its expansions.
You play as Talion, a ranger and a great warrior. He and his family get murdered by orcs, but a vengeful wraith brings him back, effectively rendering him immortal. Together they start a reign of terror in Mordor to murder all the orcs.
You have several objectives:
Conveniently, the curse of the wraith keeps you from leaving Mordor giving an in-universe reason for the boundary. Otherwise, a large region of Mordor is up for exploration. Everything is accessible from the beginning, though you get more skills and upgrade weapons along the way.
Wraith grants you The Sight, that's basically an X-ray vision with Terminator-grade recognition powers to identify mission objects and special enemies from afar, hidden stashes from up close.
Missions, while usually occurring within the same open-world region, are found around the map launching a separate mission phase, whereupon you must focus on the mission lest it get cancelled or utterly failed (with endless re-dos) by useless wandering or loitering.
Missions are reasonably varied, though aside from the few rescue missions, they very often involve massacring or assassinating countless orcs. It's cool that many quests can be completed either through direct combat or by more tactical stealth strikes.
I played exclusively with keyboard+mouse combo but gamepad should work alright.
Moving Talion works well and expectedly: mouse moves camera, WASD moves Talion. Aside from running, you can stalk, climb almost any surface and use ropelines to swing long distances.
Combat is of the safe formula: attacks, combos and parries work with a couple of buttons. However, the controls soon get much more complex: there's a separate key for each special combat ability to a total of some ten different keys. That's huge for a mere action-adventure.
Granted, not all of them are needed all the time but it makes it hard to return to the game after a long break.
Completing quests and generally wreaking havoc awards exp that yields various skills and upgrades to make your un-life easier. These range from e.g. pinning orcs with arrows to tele-strikes to insta-kills (many involving those extra buttons), among others.
It's particularly fun to get to tame and ride the crazy monster animals of Mordor, like warg-like caragors and troll-like graugs. Especially graugs are super-fun as they both barf and munch on the silly Uruks.
All regular enemies are orcs of different kinds: warriors, archers, berserkers etc. and have their special skills. Any of them can be promoted to captains, receiving a name, quotes and special abilities (and/or weaknesses).
Because of special abilities, captains are usually harder to kill than normal orcs: you might even need to beat a short QTE to finish them.
Captains hang around doing orc-things: organizing hunting parties, hosting drinking feasts, trying to assassinate each other, you know, the normal stuff that bigwigs-in-chief do. The thing is, you can infiltrate any of these and ruin their day. The reward for captain skin is a shiny rune to upgrade your weapons, the worse the enemy the better the rune.
If they still manage to slay you, they become your Nemesis, which is infuriating so of course you try to kill them again. A kind of multiplayer feature, you may encounter the Nemesis of your friends and avenge them too.
As a late-game feature, it's possible or even necessary to build an army of your own by converting the orcs and their dear leaders to your cause by mind tricks.
I completed the main game to 100% in 28 hours. But it got two big expansions, both of which introduced their own maps with new game mechanics.
brings a new biome to bring some color to the greyscale of Mordor. It introduces new creatures (similar to previous caragors and graugs), along with a new friendly face involving a story to hunt those creatures.
has you play the wraith. He works a bit differently to Talion and has some awesome special powers but the story felt more lackluster, probably because it has so little to do with Tolkien's original lore.
The rest of the DLCs are mainly cosmetic. The Test challenges introduce leaderboards with specific challenges that really test your skills with the game mechanics. You have to play at least a couple of them for all achievements.
Very stable and awesome graphics. Not even the few QTEs in combat bring too much shame to it. I had fully completed it achievement-wise after 54 hours, so I dare claim it has plenty of content too.
Combined with lots of (in Tolkien-terms) fitting lore, I think
is a must-play action-adventure for any avid gamer.

HeartZ Co-Hope Puzzles is a quirky puzzle platformer, played using 3 different characters with unique abilities. Punch, dash, bite, or teleport your way through multiple stages of electrifyingly good fun. Although HeartZ has a great solo campaign, support for local coop with up to 3 total players raises the experience to a new level.
Escaped with the help of a mysterious artefact, HeartZ employs the use of 3 unique test subjects with special artefact-empowered abilities and color representations. In order to survive, the test subjects must fight their way through maniacally produced levels of trap-filled danger and mayhem. Throughout the game, the player has the option to change characters at any point in time, and in fact, must do so often for many puzzles (if playing solo). Due to the artefact’s bestowed power, the subjects can only utilize their abilities when the orb is in proximity. This will often times force the player to use traditional platforming skills to get from one place to another, without relying on the sole power of the subjects’ abilities.
HeartZ is comprised of several Acts, each with multiple levels within. Throughout a level, copious amounts of checkpoints are provided for respawn locations and character progression. The numerous amount of these checkpoints make this game really friendly for casual or younger audiences. Regarding that last point, every death in HeartZ is presented in a really comedic or cute manner. For example, falling into a fire will cook the test subject and turn it into a hot dog.
After the completion of each Act, a summarized report of the player’s actions is presented. This report includes the number of times the player died/jumped, challenges achieved, and treasures discovered. Collecting all treasures of specific acts will unlock costumes.
Traditional platforming elements are utilized in HeartZ, including: moving platforms, crushing machines, rising floor sequences, switches, levers and numerous obstacles requiring specific abilities to bypass. This game’s highlighted feature is puzzle solving, and HeartZ does a great job ensuring that these puzzles are fun, challenging, and varied.
Although most puzzles involve maneuvering all 3 characters to a specific set of switches or levers, many other unique puzzle mechanics are implemented to break up any monotony. Some of these include: color specific platforms that only the respective subjects can stand on, size specific pathways and Teslas (field generators) that attract and trap the artefact if it gets near.
To aid in solving some of the more difficult puzzles, the game provides hints in the form of ghostly apparitions of a character at specific locations near an obstacle. Also, if something is amiss, the player can choose to restart the level. Again, due to the plethora of checkpoints provided, dying is never a problem. There are also fewer platforming challenges than puzzles.
Stated as having full controller support, HeartZ incorporates gamepads fairly well; however, one minor annoyance is that that it is not possible to rebind the buttons on a controller. For many platformer fans that utilize the controller, it is preferable to move the character using the D-pad. Movement is, by default, mapped to the left analog stick.
It is imperative for any eccentric platformer to have precise maneuverability and handling of the character, otherwise, deaths will start to manifest from poor design instead of a player’s skill. Fortunately, HeartZ has a sufficient controls system, ensuring that most deaths stem from the player’s faults. There was one minor problem observed throughout the game that caused a few undeserving deaths, regrettably. It was an issue with character and hazard hit/hurtboxes, especially Spittle’s. Due to its disproportionate head, any vertically moving platform can easily crush Spittle if positioned poorly. There are also times where it seems that a character shouldn’t be on a rising platform, but is carried upwards anyways; or instances when the character should have run off the rising platform but hasn’t.
The developers seem to show active interest in supporting the game, as seen by the developer responses in each thread of the Discussions board. HeartZ was only released last week, so until a little time passes and players report suggestions or uncover bugs, it will be difficult to observe how frequent the updates will be.
There are a few suggestions that may improve gameplay; these are listed below.
HeartZ is an extremely cute and fun puzzle game, despite the plethora of entertaining deaths that the player will experience. The game’s aesthetics and puzzle mechanics earn it a recommendation for any fan of puzzle platformers. Unfortunately, I didn’t manage to experience this vibrant game with other couch buddies, but I will say that the solo playthrough is still a worthwhile experience.

This is my first review ever for a steam game, so forgive me if its a bit amateur.
So one word for this game, well two words. RISING TENSION.
The first time you boot up the game you will experience tension, not fear, but tension. It slowly creeps up as you wander the country side scavenging for weapons to fight off the zombie/mutants, every so often hearing a growl or groan or howl in the distance. Maybe seeing what looks like a person walk onto a road.  Maybe you decide to kill the creature or maybe go the other way. Either way you have to make a decision. So you survived that encounter but then you realize you need food and water and you have none.
Behind you is a forest, in front of you a small house. A ways down the road you can see a water tower and the rooves of more homes. But you are hungry now. The small house is closer. As you walk to the small house the sun starts dipping. It gets dark. You pull out your flashlight and right before you turn it on, through the window of the small house someone else turns theirs on.
You freeze.
Out in the dark no, weapons, starving, what do you do? Should you head inside and risk it? or go to Town?
You take the safe route. Go to town. Your hustling in the dark not turning on your flashlight. Smart move.
As you get closer to the town you see one, no two, no four flashlights.
What do you do? Hide?
So you hide in the bushes and you hear them through the proximity chat, talking about the light in the small house, as they walk by your bush towards the house. Its pitch black and you are still starving.
The players meet half way between the town and small house. You hear gun shots. Two of the flashlights wink out. The rest keep moving.
Finally you are able to move. Down to the town.
That was my first encounter with this game and it was intense. This game as it stands is fantastic. The realism with the scavenging makes sense. The load out also makes sense. You arent playing as a typical video game hero who can carry an armies worth of equipment. Your decisons as to what to carry matter to your play style and to your survival.   Every encounter is full of tension. Since names do not pop up you will never know if the person you encountered is one you killed before or killed you.  One who helped you or held you up.
The balance in the game is wonderful. Knives are a little over powered. Otherwise I never felt anyone player was superior to me. Equipment does matter, but a few stabs or lucky head shot will equalize everything.
Its a good looking game to.
It reminds me of a long form version of the main gameplay in PUBG. Scavenge, survive, trust, kill?
I highly recommend it.  Cant wait to see where the developers go with MISCREATED. but i hope they do not change the realism or add levels or boosts.
I give this game 5 stars and im happy to support it.

Well I had to think long and hard about this review, well what to write. I only ever read negative reviews to see what the problems with a game are.
Yes there are a few glitches that I have experienced, nothing game braking, especially for early access.
I'd suggest changing the 'drop item' key from 'J' to - by the Numpad perhaps. Get it away from where the weapn light and laser keys are. Or like I did twice before realising what I had done you'll drop your AT15 with a Halo, light and laser while going down stairs and it will disappear, one glitch... Not to worry you'll find something again.
Negatives are very subjective for a alpha game so when you read things like; "The map is to small, DayZ is heaps bigger." Yes that is correct yet DayZ is kinda empty with perhaps 4 main player areas. Or "The zombies are on paths and there isn't enough of them." Yet you can out run them, sneak past them, and out think them. "Base building is a waste of time, objects don't snap together." Yep hopefully that will be toogle-able. "There is no storage" Storage is limited so there is no item whoring. Albeit there isn't enough which leads to other problems... Vehcile whoring..
First of the game looks like there has been no human maintenance for years. Grass is overgrown, bushes are unkept. Vines work their way in houses. Walls are rotten, rubbish everywhere. Distroyed cars and broken fences. It looks great and runs really well. You shouldn't have a problem with your FPS.
So the map. It is opening up. There is a great sewer system to explore. A lot of the buildings in the north city Hayward Valley are enterable. If they open up even more of the larger building that would be great. Say with 20 floors to explore....wow! So all houses are open, most buildings in Hayward and there is a lot of roof access. There are caves and plenty of places to explore that all feel apocalyptic. I can't wait to see the next map update.
The mutants, I like. They are not over powering, they don't have esp and there isn't hundreds of them making it impossible to move around. I hope the Entrada devs don't change this to much as it stands it feels like a good balance. Sure there will be tweeks that will happen.
Base building will get better. It works and pretty well. If you could toggle a snap to feature it would be easier at times. Item storage is limited, which has it's own pros & cons. I would like more yet who wouldn't.. Depending on the size of the base, the number of parts it does despawn after time if you don't go there. You can't build within 200m of another base or town. I understand the reasons yet it would be damn cool to fortify a smaller 3 story building... Which leeds me to tthe game The Dead Linger. In that failure you could nail boards over windows, that would add to this game..
Crafting works and opens up with recipes found around the map. This can only grow is scale.
There are things that you can't do yet can in other similar games. Going prone, unless I havn't figured that out. Clearing trees for base building.
With updates and more added to the game it will hopefully only get better, they may make a change that everyone hates sooo... hopefully not..
Now a few issues I have seen. The forums have no Dev input that I have seen. Players and fans asking, suggesting and looking for info and for the most part they are dead. Aparently there are cheaters. I havn't seen any yet I'm in australasia not near those doggy European players... ;) The server rental is high and very controlled They won't release server files which is a shame when I have server machines hosting other titles. I gather the control is done to keep hacking down..? yet the price is up there. For me the $60 to $80 NZD price per month depending on payment period is f*cken ridiculous.
From a game hosting perspective I could just about give a negative review for the game hosting policies alone and forget the pros mentioned above.
I will update this review the more I play and discover.

"Long Live the Queen" is quite the interesting turn-based RPG. You play the the young crown princess of a fictional kingdom as she trys to navigate a political, military and even supernatural minefield. Every decision is an excruiscating trade-off with potentially deadly consequences. Level the wrong skill, approach the wrong suitor, trust the wrong people, eat the wrong chocolate and you're dead. Yet, in choosing to level one skill you're possibly falling behind in something that can save your life later on. The more you play this, the more that become apparent.
The game is deeply story based, which is a bit of double-edged sword. The political world of Nova and it's surroundings is lovingly detailed, even if you only get narrow view of any part of it at a time. But, there are no random events to shake things up. Big parts of the story will reoccure no matter what you will do. That said, there are enough choices to keep you from having the exact same play-throught twice (unless you're trying to do exactly that). Yes, this does mean ultimately potentially limited re-play value, but the story and it's world is good enough to justify it in my mind. Indeed, knowing what's coming down the pipe might be your only way to have a fighting chance at this game. Even with theis foreknoledge, it's a tough game.
Ultimately, the combination of story, setting and gameplay shine through. Even with the gift of the player's foreknoledge, there is no truly clear right answers, just some that are less wrong. Ultimately I think that's a sign of well designed gameplay that is definately worth experiencing.

Long Live the Queen is an odd title, but very in its own niche. If you can get passed the "anime" aesthetic (which is more "moe" than anything else), you find yourself in a heavily political fantasy game. Every class you take to build your skill tree is important to your survival as well as the relationships you build in your own kingdom and on. What may seem daunting and a little frustrating at first, you'll come to find that some deaths are avoidable, even without having the proper skills (such as choosing not to follow the shady figure in the woods). Events are also not random, so the more you play, the lower the difficulty gauge.
Overall, I find this little gemstone to be alright for what it is. It's not a horrible time-waster, and it's pleasing enough on the eye. However I would reccommend only getting this game while it's on sale ($5 or less), as it's short and does not have as much replay value as one would hope.

This is the best LOTR game since EA's series back when the movies were still new, and I'd go so far as to say that it's better than those games. Technically SoM isn't connected to the Jackson movies, hence why it's branded as Middle Earth instead of LotR. But that is actually a positive thing, as it allows the game to be more bloody and violent than it would have been otherwise.
Gameplay is basically Ubisoft: The Game, but with an added nemesis/leadership caste on the enemy side. Fighting consists of sneaking about and stealth killing, or melee combat ala Batman: Arkham Asylum. Both work pretty well, but unfortunately the level design in the second map is rougher than the first, making stealth harder than it should be. Some walls in the towns aren't climable unless the player is angled just right, and I got stuck on objects sitting on the floor multiple times. The main story missions are strangely easy, as are the boss fights. The real difficulty lies in the side missions to complete your weapon's legends, which are totally optional.
Graphics are fine, not much to say. Music is decent but completely forgettable. That's one area where the game suffers from not being an actual LotR property.
The story is nothing special - the game excells more as a means of expanding the back story of Middle Earth. Seeing what Mordor looks like and how Ork/Uruk society works is much more interesting than the MC's revenge plot. BTW, the plot massively jumps the shark in the last 5 seconds before the credits roll. If you at all care about Tolkien's canon, the ending is downright horrible.
Overall I recommend this game to any LotR fan who enjoyed the earlier Assassin's Creed games or Far Cry 3/4.

I suppose how much someone might enjoy OMD2 really depends on if they have a co-op partner.  This game was designed with the idea that you'd be playing co-op.  That doesn't mean you can't play it single player (and the game gives you more inventory slots for traps, weapons and trinkets if you do), but it's a lonely experience.  Even the campaign assumes you'll play co-op, as both characters -- the War Mage and the Sorceress -- converse during the game.
That said, if you do have a co-op partner (my wife is mine), then this game is an absolutel blast!  OMD2 successfully mixes strategy (tower defense), action and some wacky humor, so the game never gets dull or takes itself too seriously.
How you play depends on you.  You could rely more on traps or weapons or even trinkets, although the latter do more to augment gameplay than anything else.  Some weapons and traps are better than others on some maps, so you have to be able to adapt to your surroundings.
If you own the original OMD you get ten maps from the original game to play in OMD2.  Although this is a cool idea, thanking those who've supported the developer, some of the levels aren't new to OMD2 and others don't work extremely well with some of the newer traps.

Ok I must admit after playing Innercube, Cubot was a little bit too easy for me. Innercube has six  different colored sided cubes, but Cubot cubes are just one colored. Well but let's now discuss Cubot.
Cubots is the currency you can earn in this game after completing each level. You can buy solutions for that (it starts with 8 cubots) but who seriously does? There's apparently no other purpose of Cubots. Like in Hexcells where you need the points to unlock next levels. In Cubot every level is automatically unlocked after beating stage 6 - evertyime. Each level has 8 stages a 10 levels that makes 80 levels altogether - That's OK.
The levels can be distinguished by new cube types (different colors: red does double steps, green has reversed movement, and so on ... ) or new puzzle elements (like colorchangers, portals, elevators or stoppers).
The aim is to bring all cubes to the same colored fields in the end. Very positive is that the level design has different layers where you also can fall down from a higher level. I also liked much the level select menu with a miniature picture of the whole map. They even lately added a level editor.
Now comes the moan. This game makes fun for sure. But it's not as high as expected. It seems sterile that after every solved stage 7 you'll get as reward a hardcoded wise quote of Erno Rubik, Eric Schmidt or Albert Einstein. It isn't random and/or surprising. Also the puzzle elements are well mixedup in higher levels, but there's no higher value to progress at all.
I missed some basic game elements like the "undo" button which I'm used to. Some menus do not respond on the first click. It also seems after once changing the camera view or use the mouse roll gesture the WASD controls get temporarly deactivated. That's annoying because these are just little fixable bugs. But my first impression got spoiled due to that.
Cubot is not a bad game. I wouldn't say that and I recommend it. But sometimes you have to bite your teeth together to playthrough a certainly well meant great game with little nerving mistakes.

I was excited for Train Fever and when I got to play it, I came to understand that I just don't like it.  I want to like it, it's not a /bad/ game, it's just severely lacking in... everything.
- There's no artificial intelligence, so don't expect competition.  You're on your own to play at your own pace; not a bad thing, but not very exciting either.
- The game is excruciatingly slow.  Even on the x3 speed setting, you will mindlessly stare at your monitor, waiting for money to roll in, to continue your expansion.  Even when it does roll in, there's not much to spend it on, because...
- There's no content.  Train Fever presents you with new vehicles, rarely, and when they arrive, it will always better than the last one.  You're never given multiple vehicles where "one might be better than the other depending on play style/situation."  No, the latest vehicle is always the best, both in capacity and speed.
- There's a severe lack of content.  Yeah I said it about the vehicles, now I'll say it about the industry.  There's wood, iron, coal, oil... goods... uhm... people... oh that's it.
- Upgrading vehicles is a chore.  The game, thankfully, gives you a replacement option when it reaches end-of-life to be replaced with the same or better vehicle.  However, if you want to manually upgrade your vehicles to a new one, you have to send it to a depot, wait for it to arrive, sell it, buy a new one and add the new one to the line.  Why can't we use the vehicle replacement option for "immediate" upgrades?  (Yes, you can choose 25% life to replace, but then you run the risk of replacing new vehicles that don't need it - a waste of money)
- The game has severe balance issues, still, outside of early access.  You can make more money from a bus or tram route in a city than a rail.  The bus or tram route cost you ~$300-400k to start up or less.  The train will run you millions on track alone, only to turn around and have citizens rarely use the trains.  (Edit 03/03/2015: I later determined that rail, is in fact, a money maker - my apologies.  One superb strategy is to set up your inner-city transportation network with a large stop near your rail depot; citizens will "transfer," effectively netting you income from them twice.  So balance in this respect is no longer an issue.)
- Don't bother, ever, trying to put road over rail.  Don't bother, ever, trying to put two rail near each other.  The build tools are so ****ed up that no matter how many hours you waste, you can never get things to work out.  Road too steep!  Rail obstruction!  Chaos!  The build tools puts a MAJOR hamper on the ability to construct your routes efficiently; prepare for headaches.
- The game runs choppy as hell.  Optimization this, improvement that, it's all for naught.  I can't understand why a game with so little going on runs so poorly.
At the end of the day, I feel no sense of accomplishment and no motivation to keep playing.  It's just not *fun*.
I would love to see new game mechanics to spice Train Fever up.  More resources, more vehicles, competition...

Terraria Fan here:
Having completed both Terraria and Starbound, I have a good grasp on these games. They are NOT the same game and you will get a great experience from both games.
Building: The building in these games is the (obviously) most similar aspect. Side scrolling block by block mining and placing. Pretty clear this was gonna be the same. Starbound does feature more detailed and diverse block types however.
Combat: The combat in SB is is based on weapons that are procedurally generated and recieved in drops, unlike TR where you create a lot of your weapons and they have modifiers. I found myself finding a better weapon and ditching my current weapon only to find a new better version 30 seconds later.
Other comparisons: The crafting is similar (get X amount of this material to make this, create this craft station to make this the next tier). The story of SB is an actual scripted story where TR has basically no story. The NPC system of SB is more diverse but more of a chore to get what you want. Personally, I like TR's NPCs because they are set in stone what you get and how you get them and its not a chore to think about them.
The biggest thing is the planets. In TR, you have one world. Even if you make 34 worlds, they are gonna be the same format (which isnt a terrible thing in a way). The SB worlds (all 4832344839 of them) are all different. They have recurring themes, but they will always be layed out different.
In conclusion, this review seems to champion SB as the superior game, but they both have their bright spots. I definitely recommend both games and I reiterate: This is NOT a Terraria clone. Bravo to the company for taking a concept created by one game and making it their own creature.

This is a fun game, no doubt about that. But it's also glitchy and repetetive. I'd give it a 4/10.
I'd give it this score because it really didn't do anything else for me besides being mindless fun. And while it was plenty of fun, it has no reply value and I'll forget about the entire story within a month.
Despite that though, this game did a lot of thngs right. The missions, while repetetive, were fun and varied. There was plenty of weapons to choose from, and I absolutely loved the Reputation currency.
Combat was fun albiet a bit glitchy. You could swing your weapon towards a zombie 3 meters away and it would register the hit. Melee combat is pretty awkward at times, agility is non-existent so dodging around and being a fast attacker isn't a possibility. You're kind of forced into fighting like a berserker. If a crowd surrounds you, all you can really do is spam left click and Z. Running is an option, but if you've already swung your weapon a few times, chances are that you won't have the stamina to get very far. That being said, even though you're pigeonholed into doing the same thing in every fight, smashing heads in was fun throughout the entire game.
Guns were mostly fine. Except, when enemies got too close you lost the ability to aim. Which is probably more due to your viewpoint being different from the point of fire, but it's still a pain if you're trying to line up a shot and the bullet flies off at a 45 degree angle. I mostly played with melee weapons as guns brought a lot of undead, a feature I liked a lot. Made you think twice before unloading a clip.
I felt that the upgrades you could make to your home base was lacking. This was something I was looking forward to having more control over. Ideally, one would be able to raise the height of the walls surrounding the house, bar the windows, and make sturdier gates. Unfortunately, there was absolutely no fortification besides the flimsy window boarding which was a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ If you boarded the windows during seige missions, you couldn't clear the wave of zombies, and the mission wouldn't progress.
If the issues with the fortification and base upgrades were resolved, this game would be a hell of a lot more fun.

Night in the Woods is a game for the ages. One of the best games to drop in the past five years, let alone this year. And boy oh boy is it an absolute treat to play.
I’ll skip the plot synopsis as every other review states it already and instead get right into the good stuff: the writing and the characters. These are the meat on Night in the Woods bones.
The writing is nothing short of phenomenal. It has a perfect mix of ironic wit and hopeful sincerity that makes all these anthropomorphic animals seem nothing short of human. None of it falls flat or on deaf ears, with every scene having stellar conclusions be it through an enormous emotional punch straight to the gut, a quick laugh, or a hopeful glimpse into the future to think that just maybe everything will one day be okay.
The characters are by far the best part of the game, as I’m sure everyone will point out. The cast tackles all sorts of issues and developments that plague the human condition. From simple teenage angst all the way to the struggles of adulthood, trying to balance money to provide for a family, paying off bills, and barely scraping by in the process. While I think the main demographic of the game is 16-24 year olds I can clearly see people in their 30s and up enjoying this game due to the sheer relatability of the adult side characters.
The setting is another pivotal part of the game, but I feel like it’s something that should be experienced for yourself as the town is practically a character in itself and evolves right alongside the plot and character development.
Gameplay wise the game is nothing special if you’re on the prowl for the next Devil May Cry in regards to games feeling “gamey.” Instead, Night in the Woods gameplay falls more into the category of a soft platformer with some seldom, but greatly enjoyable rhythm sections when Mae’s friend Gregg suggests you rejoin the band you and your friends started in High School. It’s all quite simple, but loads of fun.
If you at all enjoy books like Catcher in the Rye, or any film directed by Wes Anderson, or games like Persona; you will without a doubt love Night in the Woods. I truthfully can’t recommend or praise it enough to do it the justice it deserves. Just do yourself a colossal favor and play it.

I've played this game for a few days now. It's actually a pretty good game.
The down side is the loot system. You will not get loot for more than a few matches in a row. After that you have to wait a few hours or play without the prospect of loot for your fights. Not quite there yet though.
On the plus side, if you can get over the mental hurdle that is the loot system... the fights have a strong tendency to be fun and well balanced. Almost every fight I have had has been close and could have gone either way. There are counters, so there is some strategy involved... Oh, and one other thing. The devs seem to be hard at work and responsive here, at least for now. So I believe things are and will continue to improve.
Overall, a fun game for what it is, if you can live with the loot system. I do think they need to work on the loot system though, as it is annoying too many players. Hard to build a large enough community for PvP if too many leave on the first day.

Lemme tell you something, partner, this here game is a half-done, graphically-good-looking but gameplay wise a complete♥♥♥♥♥♥game.

The map is big considering that you have nothing and have to run everywhere 24/7 and that sucks because you feel like you're not getting anywhere anytime soon. Now let's talk guns... One of the 3 problems I have with this game is guns. They sound like mouse squeaks. GUNS DON'T SOUND LIKE THAT IN REAL LIFE OR OTHER GAMES AT ALL. In other games gun shots are at least loud and recognisable but this game just did a full revolution and made it completely opposite. Is that really bad? YES, IT IS BECAUSE YOU DON'T KNOW IF IT'S A SOUND COMING FROM THE ATTIC IRL OR IF SOMEONE IS KILLING YOU!!! Now that that's out of the way...
Finding items in this game is like a chore. You run for 20 minutes (another overpriced running simulator survival game) to only find SOME food and maybe an empty clip for a makarov pistol considering that the place is huge and items could be scattered everywhere but they just aren't! In the end of your 20~40 minute running simulation you get killed by those SOUNDLESS GUNS and lose all your♥♥♥♥♥♥and respawn in another place where you have no idea where you are.
And my last problem with the game.... The community. No one will hesitate to shoot you even if you say you're friendly and you just respawned and only have 1 can of dog food. If you wanna skip the reading, scroll down for a basic exxplanatino of what the game has to offer.
Has the potential to be the best survival game I ever played or watched.
Ok that said, this is a very well achieved PvP game. When you start to get into the game you can really feel what the devs intend to do with it and it is absolutely thrilling.
The goal is simple: Explore, gather weapons and supplies and move tactically to obtain an advantage over other players.
You are going to have your heart rate raise and your senses sharpen while you cruise the towns for supplies as a there can be a player hiding in every room of every building, every bush, behind every tree, etc.
There are also a few vehicles you can restore if you find the right components.
So far I have only complimented the game, so why do I not recommend it?
Same as in basically every other survival/early access game:
Bugs, mechanics and cheating are not being addressed with the importance they should be.
The bullet mechanics are just plain weird. Realistic? No. Weird. I am a fairly good shot, I can't kill people in this game.
Just last night I was crouching, holding my breath and raising my sights on an enemy 5m away from me, I shot 4 rifle bullets into him before he even acknowledged me and shot the single bullet that killed me. This is happening to me all the freaking time from all ranges, it's just not possible.
I've won gungame matches in counter-strike for god's sake!!! I went on to a battlefield rust server just to check if I'm really such a big loser or going mad or something and turns out in rust I got some kills while being killed some other times. Rust also has realistic bullet mechanics as you have to compensate for the distance and recoil, etc.
The hitboxes in miscreated aren't well optimized and there's something very off about shooting in this game, which is a really really bad thing in a game that focuses around just that.
Besides the problems with shooting there's this thing where you can shoot fuel cans and make them explode when someone is right next to them, guess what: It doesn't kill a person. Imagine that: a fuel can explodes next to you and you go about running on fire and you don't die or lose a limb but a molotov cocktail kills you right away.
This is not all, I have died hopping on and off vehicles without even starting them, I have had stuff disappear on me in different situations, I have had my car blown up with 6 shots.
I have seen players using speedhacks, there are well known ESP cheats that players are using, I have seen a ghost of a player for a second with his arms extended to the sides sliding just before I got shot in the back inside a building I had just checked, the list goes on.
Another issue that bothers me but I kind of understand is that you always spawn in a random location, now, I understand that it makes the game more balanced, but having to run for 15 minutes before you get anywhere just so you can get there and be insta-killed in a weird way that makes you feel like a worthless loser is not my idea of having fun.
There is also the issue where you are never gonna find a vehicle in a populated server because 2 big clans are hoarding all of the 25 vehicles that spawn in the map. If you don't play on a high population server (at least 30/50) you will never use a gun on anything other than clonky laggy weird zom...Mutants!
I won't even mention base building because it's as if there is no base building. You can't respawn there which makes it faster for you to go search for loot instead of going home to get the gear you have stored in the 2 boxes you can have there. It is also very very easy to break into bases unless they ARE FLOATING! (seriously? in a game that uses physics to this extent, the devs went ahead and make structures float when you demolish the supports?)
Also cars disappear after a day if you don't hop on them, and sometimes even if you do so there's no point in storing them.
I cannot recommend this game in the state it is in and I urge the devs to do something about the essential gameplay factors surrouding this game before giving in to the temptation of adding more content to get more people playing a broken game.
At the moment what this game offers is:
- Running
- Beatiful graphics and landscape
- Searching empty trashcans, empty boxes, empty lockers, empty couches, empty washing machines and empty toolboxes
- Running
- Very well achieved sense of suspense
- Vehicles
- Tactical combat
- Running
- Weapons and overall technology from the past in the future (it's supposed to be 2089 and you're driving/seeing gas fueled quad bikes and rusty pickup trucks and sedans, sedans everywhere and shooting 9mm guns and pump-action shotguns aswell as revolvers.)
- Very well achieved weather effects and overall sounds and atmosphere
- Some more running
- Looting for guns aswell as crafting them (in the near future i guess?)
- Did I mention running?
That's my view on the game. I strongly advise the devs to take a deep look into what you are doing because you want to  be different and create a unique game and you're just committing the same mistakes as every other EA game out there: Not fixing the essentials. By following this path you will have a player base that doesn't care about the game or the experience, they just go and take advantage of the basic flaws in the game. People like me who want a genuine fair and realistic experience will not play this game until it is solid and consistent. At the moment you have the same player base as any other crappy survival game out there: Big groups of people who grief/exploit/cheat.

I really like this game. I see a lot of people write it off as "Terraria in space" but thats not really fair in my opinion. It would be like if you wrote off Fallout as just a "post apocalyptic Elderscrolls game" there are simularities in mechanics, but they are both very different games and I actually like this way better than Terraria. (I got Terraria first & really liked it but still only have around 20 hours in that)
One of the best differences is the ability to explore the other planets in your solar system, and then in later game, other solar systems throughout the galaxy. The planets are procedurally generated so you might know its going to be a jungle planet or ice planet or whatever, but all the layout and what you find down on the planet  is always different.
You can build colonies on planets you discover and eventually you can recruit certain colonists to travel with you on your ship as a crew member. Some crew members can be  brought along as hired guns while others act as cooks or mechanics or other non combat roles.
The game is mostly a sandbox but there is a main quest that is about discovering artifacts of the different alien races available to you as a player, and when you have colonists set up they will also give you the option to do little quests for them. Even though I have 100 some hours in it so far, I have yet to beat the main questline. I am around halfway. These kind of games are easy for me to get distracted digging down deep into the planet exploring and harvesting  for hours at a time.
The last minor thing I want to comment on is that I really like that you only need a single tool to collect resources and you can also use it to place items or blocks beyond the square right next to you. For someone whos every inventory slot in valuable, its nice not to have to have a tool to dig, a tool to chop wood and a tool to mine. Maybe you can argue for "realism" but you are carrying 1k blocks of dirt and stone in your pocket already so that rational goes out the window.
Anyway I think its a great game, if you like to explore huge sandbox worlds I would say give it a shot.

This game took me 90 hours to get into.
It was mostly false starts before my brain got distracted, which it often does. That said; started replaying this a few weeks ago, and something just clicked. All the prior trial and error attempts had sunk much of the gameplay into my brain; where early items were, what to do in general. It all was ingrained somewhere along the way and this time around, I found myself able to dive in.
There is a great deal to take in for this game, and honestly without a lot of help from a good friend and some very detailed wikis (which I only look up after roughly...5 failed attempts at a spot), not sure I'd get as far as I have.  Much of the legendary difficulty of this game is learning about...well, everything. What makes pyromancy different from sorcery, what it means to "fat roll", what damage type is good against which enemy, ect. These are things that have to be beaten into you. And once that all settles, or you know how to figure it out; it just becomes being able to make it through the other side of the battle. The only thing that will stop you, it seems, is you.
The online scene at this point seems to have simmered down to a mostly good natured lot; from my experiances anyways. I got invaded at one point, the person and I bowed and then they threw lightening spears in my face. Good fight. And then I ended up summoning them to help with Orenstien and Smough. One of those experiences that I can't say I'd get from any other game.
So if you've been on the fence about this franchise, please at least give it a try if you see it on sale. It may take time for it to click, it may frustrate the hell out of you for a while. But when it does click, when you begin to see how it works, you'll be rewarded with one of the richest and fulfilling gaming experiances in recent memory.

DARK SOULS™, famous for it's challenging gameplay, is a very good game at it's core.
It features immersive lore and scenery with an easy-to-learn yet hard-to-master combat system which, alltough wonky at times, is more than enough to beat the game which is desinged with trial, error and self-improvement in mind, making just the defeat of a challenging foe or area a reason for celebration before failing miserably on the next challenge..
The Game plays very well and is well paced for the first half of the game, rewarding the player for every milestone.
Considering that the game is about 5 years old now, it's still rather pretty but one of it's stronger points is it's powerfull soundtrack which adds to the theme of the game perfectly.
Unfortunately some parts of the game feel very improvised and too frustrating at times.
Not to mention the poor quality of the port requiring additional files to even play the game properly and limited frame rate. It makes up for it with a variety of interesting characters which tell their own story inside the game through, not only dialoge -which by the way is nicely written- but their actions and appearances in various places, giving a break from the usual hostility and adding to the immersion.

The hours i have on this game for pc are not even close to how many hours ive put in this game back on the xbox 360.
This game is: Unforgiving, Difficult, and occasionally broken. But It's amazing and by far the best dark souls experience out of all the games. Its mechanics are not the best by a long shot, dark souls 3 mastered that but this game is the true experience of dark souls. It is by far the most open world dark souls out there, at the start the only hint you have is from a guy saying "go ring bells". From then on your on your own, exploring the world, facing difficult enemies, and overcoming challenges.
The combat is this game is perfect. Swords, Shields, Magic, Miracles. All of these things are in the game, and all of them are viable. I never once thought one of them to be useless.
The level design is the best in any game i've ever played, Everything that you see was planned out, each item placement seems to have a story of its own and the movement from are to are is so immersive. Look out the distance and say "i wanna go their" 90% of the time you can go there. Enemy placement may seem unfair at times, ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t, etc... (damn arrows) but its never impossible, plan your movements and execute it right and you can make it through any place.
Leveling is simple, but pretty balanced. You'll never be like "i need to grind" in this game (unless you somehow lose your souls nearly every time)
Bosses, are awesome, and probably what defines this series (not to say level design is bad but bosses make up for it cause that is not the case at all) Each boss provides a challenge of its own, it most of the time will take you a few tries to beat a boss (or like 50). All bosses are fun and satisfying to beat (with the exception of one)
Enemies are very well made, placments and all. You very rarely when first encountering a new enemy will think "wow this guy is just stupidly useless"
Pvp is Pvp... Thats all i can describe it as
Co-op is a pain, but when it actually works its pretty fun, i suggest using mods to make it easier.
In short This game is awesome, if your new to the series play it blind, dont look up ANYTHING. You'll definitely get mad at this game but that satisfaction of beating an area is so worth the trouble.

Wow.  Just... wow.  It's hard to say more about this game.  Simply put, this is one of the best Metroidvania games out there.  It really had the same feeling as the first time playing Symphony of the Night.  Good boss fights, good challenge, I loved the exploring to find areas.  The map is phenomenally well designed, with lots of areas that you can see one from place and work your way to later.  And it is bloody massive!  I love the way the game plays with some conventions, such as one of the first bosses where I climbed up a tower assuming I'd be safe, and he just jumped up and crushed me. Night in the Woods is a game for the ages. One of the best games to drop in the past five years, let alone this year. And boy oh boy is it an absolute treat to play.
I’ll skip the plot synopsis as every other review states it already and instead get right into the good stuff: the writing and the characters. These are the meat on Night in the Woods bones.
The writing is nothing short of phenomenal. It has a perfect mix of ironic wit and hopeful sincerity that makes all these anthropomorphic animals seem nothing short of human. None of it falls flat or on deaf ears, with every scene having stellar conclusions be it through an enormous emotional punch straight to the gut, a quick laugh, or a hopeful glimpse into the future to think that just maybe everything will one day be okay.
The characters are by far the best part of the game, as I’m sure everyone will point out. The cast tackles all sorts of issues and developments that plague the human condition. From simple teenage angst all the way to the struggles of adulthood, trying to balance money to provide for a family, paying off bills, and barely scraping by in the process. While I think the main demographic of the game is 16-24 year olds I can clearly see people in their 30s and up enjoying this game due to the sheer relatability of the adult side characters.
The setting is another pivotal part of the game, but I feel like it’s something that should be experienced for yourself as the town is practically a character in itself and evolves right alongside the plot and character development.
Gameplay wise the game is nothing special if you’re on the prowl for the next Devil May Cry in regards to games feeling “gamey.” Instead, Night in the Woods gameplay falls more into the category of a soft platformer with some seldom, but greatly enjoyable rhythm sections when Mae’s friend Gregg suggests you rejoin the band you and your friends started in High School. It’s all quite simple, but loads of fun.
If you at all enjoy books like Catcher in the Rye, or any film directed by Wes Anderson, or games like Persona; you will without a doubt love Night in the Woods. I truthfully can’t recommend or praise it enough to do it the justice it deserves. Just do yourself a colossal favor and play it.

Its a really good game, very simmilar to Sid Mayer's Locomotion Tycoon. The only thing I wish it had was a way to invest in cities to make them grow bigger/faster and more locomotives. Other than that, it is an absolutly fabulus game with a great engine.

The transport tycoon genre isn't the most popular genre, and in the last years we've not seen many new ones pop out. There's been some, but most of them haven't cut it. The last still good transport tycoon is OpenTTD, which is well over 15 years old, so that says a lot. Is Train Fever the true next succedor or just another failed attempt to recreate the true glory of the classic transport tycoon?
First of all, Train Fever looks gorgeous. It is by far the best looking transport tycoon that exists. Every part of the graphics is very well done, and the world looks beautiful (albeit a bit empty at times). Everything from the rail tracks to trains and buses to cities, they are all carefully crafted and you can truly enjoy the result. The game is almost hypnotizing, and I find myself spending a lot of time just following the small trains around, moving through the landscape and the result of my hard work as a rail entrepenour.
Now, graphics is only one thing, more importantly is the gameplay. To coorelate to the graphic part, the game is very dynamic. Cities will over time grow and change visual appearance. Building style will change to fit the current era, and the pedestrians in the streets. Vehicles get new replacements, and the stations and bus stops change appearance as well. Cities will grow when you supply it with passenger services and goods, or simply create a local bus route in the city. When the city grows it's also an indicator of you most likely earning money as well. The cities grow dynamically, adjusting to the terrain, so no two cities grow in the same way, resulting in relatively diverse cities spreading across the map.
A key thing in the game is that every person is a simulated entity, with a home, workplace and destination. Unlike older games, simply attaching a station to a city won't do anything in itself, you need to connect the cities people actually want to travel to. This means that a station with for example a 100 passengers, a train approaching won't necessarily take all of them despite having space. You can luckily easily see where they're heading by simply clicking the station, and it gives you an overview over what lines the passengers are waiting for. Of those 100 passengers, 50 of them could be for one train line, 40 for another, and 10 for the local bus.
Passengers are despite this relatively easy to manage. It's recommended to start with internal bus/tram routes, then connect cities with buses. After time, the demand will be high enough for you to use trains, effectively being able to connect several cities in one route. Now, cargo is something else however. Cargo in Train Fever is very tricky to wrap your head around. It's heavily based around demand. If a city has demand for goods, the factories will produce exactly as much as is demanded, if they have the resources supplied for it. It never produces more. A single factory can have a production up to 400 (which is quite a lot), supplied with only one of each sub resource source (a steel mill for example requires iron ore and coal, but only one factory of each), as production scales with it. The most efficient way to deal with cargo is by using trucks, as they are frequent and cost efficient, easily allowing you to see if a route is profitable or not.
Now, a key element in Train Fever is the upkeep. Unlike other transport tycoons, laying roads and tracks is cheap. Very cheap. Trucks and buses have moderate upkeep (it's pretty reasonable, and will usually end up in profit), while trains have HUGE upkeep. The upkeep scales over time, an old train has signficiantly higher upkeep, forcing you to replace engines often. This however is quite easy, as you can allocate automatic replacement of a line in your route planner.
As time passes, new, more powerful engines will be able, but they will also be more expensive. This approach forces you to have efficient and profitable train routes. A train route can either have million losses or million profits, depending on how well managed it is. I've found that a good approach is to have double track passenger lines with 3-5 stops, with two running trains. As long as you don't overextend your passenger trains, they will be fine (you don't need too many wagons or the fanciest engines).
Cargo trains are a whole different story, and something I struggle with heavily. If I start early on building one, I can get a line with 3 stops to profit, with roughly 150-200 cargo being transported. Establishing a new route in modern times turns out to be harder. If you can managge it right, it will give a decent profit, but in the end it just isn't worth the hazzle. With passenger trains you can easily set up a route with 5+ million in profit, and you can make several of them.
Another thing in Train Fever is transport time. A person or cargo will in total time spend no more than 20 in-game minutes, including walking to the station and switching lines. This means that long cargo lines have limited efficiency, and that passenger routes cannot be too long. Roughly 10 minutes for trains is decent, and a minute for buses. Trucks can go down to 10 seconds on busy routes. This system works hand in hand with the passenger entity system. If a route takes longer than 20 minutes in total, the person will use their car or simply not go (as far as I know).
I believe that's most of the game's elements that's worth mentioning.
The game has a good modding community, and I recommend picking up some mods as it can extend the fun of the game heavily.
Verdict!
Pros:
- Gorgeous looking
- Realistic and satisfying simulation
- Fun to play
- Easy to manage with a good UI
- Challenging
- Easy to mod
Cons:
- Cargo system is simply annoying
- The economy isn't satisfactory for some
- No planes or ships
- Steep learning curve (this can be seen as both good and bad, but I feel many will feel it's on the bad side)
- Can feel repetitive after a while
To conclude:
Train Fever is definitely worth playing if you like transport tycoons. It looks beautiful, and it feels a bit like managing a model railway. It's fun, and gives for many, many hours of gameplay. It takes time to learn, but as you eventually get to know your ways around it you'll feel a sense of achievement. It's challenging, but in a fun way. The stock selection is a bit sparse, but a few mods will change that. The cargo system is ridiculously hard to manage.
In overall, a very good game, but I'm usure as to whether people will accept it as a "true" succedor to previous installments. Personally I won't ever touch any of the old games again.

I really like this game. I see a lot of people write it off as "Terraria in space" but thats not really fair in my opinion. It would be like if you wrote off Fallout as just a "post apocalyptic Elderscrolls game" there are simularities in mechanics, but they are both very different games and I actually like this way better than Terraria. (I got Terraria first & really liked it but still only have around 20 hours in that)
One of the best differences is the ability to explore the other planets in your solar system, and then in later game, other solar systems throughout the galaxy. The planets are procedurally generated so you might know its going to be a jungle planet or ice planet or whatever, but all the layout and what you find down on the planet  is always different.
You can build colonies on planets you discover and eventually you can recruit certain colonists to travel with you on your ship as a crew member. Some crew members can be  brought along as hired guns while others act as cooks or mechanics or other non combat roles.
The game is mostly a sandbox but there is a main quest that is about discovering artifacts of the different alien races available to you as a player, and when you have colonists set up they will also give you the option to do little quests for them. Even though I have 100 some hours in it so far, I have yet to beat the main questline. I am around halfway. These kind of games are easy for me to get distracted digging down deep into the planet exploring and harvesting  for hours at a time.
The last minor thing I want to comment on is that I really like that you only need a single tool to collect resources and you can also use it to place items or blocks beyond the square right next to you. For someone whos every inventory slot in valuable, its nice not to have to have a tool to dig, a tool to chop wood and a tool to mine. Maybe you can argue for "realism" but you are carrying 1k blocks of dirt and stone in your pocket already so that rational goes out the window.
Anyway I think its a great game, if you like to explore huge sandbox worlds I would say give it a shot.

At first glance, this game is like Civ 5. A fantasy version of Civ 5. A half-done fantasy version of Civ 5. I was wrong and right at the same time.
This game - as I just said - is pretty much a Civ 5 clone at first glance, however later on you learn that this game is not quite. With game mechanics that parallel them, this game still has plenty of other ideas, concepts and such which are completely different. The first that springs to mind are the spells.
Spells are either the worst thing you in the history of ever or the best thing ever. Depends purely on which side you're on. These are an interesting - though unsurprising - element added to the game. Their near unlimited number and their wide range of effects can basically make you god-like, however these spells require mana and time to cast and if they are ongoing spells, mana for upkeep. However if you have tonnes of mana and little gold, fortunately you can just have the mass of your army be summed creatures that simply require mana for upkeep rather than gold (Some require both. Awesome...)
An unusual set of elements are artefacts and lords. They randomly come about throughout the game and can be purchased/hired so long as you have enough gold to afford their upfront cost. Although you can find them in the map at various locations, I seem to find them a lot more of them to purchase at the start of the turn. The lords are a lot like their common unit counterparts, however with unique perks and abilities with the ability to equip artefacts to them to change or add more abilities. One lord got my attention and stood out from all the rest. It is - and I'm not making this up - the infamous rabbit in Monty Python and the Holy Grail. I have screencaps of it if you don't believe me. The funny thing is about this creature is that it is one of the most OP units in the game Arm the rabbit with a broomstick and it can fly, crossing all terrain with no movement penalty and the ability to take on any creature. However there are stronger lords beyond this one so [OP intensifies].
The game also has pocket dimensions and they are randomly scattered through the map (supposing you have enabled them) and are infinitely useful once you managed to capture one, drive out all the late-game monsters and in general wrestle them under your control. However once one is under your control, you essentially increased the power of your empire without the further need to war with other Great Mage (players or if you don't have friends like me, the CPU). Even then, if the wars do happen, the other Great Wizards are going to go through hell to reclaim any pocket dimension.
The communication and interaction with the Great Mage is fairly limited compared to those in Civ 5, with no request there being something that can have a minor result if you decline. If someone either demands resources from you or has a request, declining it can either result in outright war with the other Great Mage or destroying your alliance if it's a request. It would be great if declining wouldn't be so extreme and would simply just decrease the Great Mage's attitude towards you rather than... this. Another thing that bugs me is that either there's no option to request a war with another Great Mage or I've missed it entirely.
The same applies with quests. These are also unusual game mechanics that at some times can be VERY ANNOYING! Why? Failing to complete a quest can result in a punishment. Usually they don't amount in much e.g. some gold/mana lost, but some can be kinda... dumb. For example, one god losing favour with you simply because you couldn't build a church in time. For that to happen, you need to get yourself some holy ground and if that's in anothers' land, you have to go forcibly take it from them. Something like that isn't usually done in a small space of time. Taking a city can take many turns, even with a decent, strong army. Fortunately, some quests seem to last forever so you have plenty of time to do that quest. Unless you forget the quest and do other more presssing matters at hand.
Overall, Warlock is a pretty good stratergy game but could do with a bit more effort towards the interaction with other Great Mages and a bit of rebalancing with their lords.

I won't bother explaining the gameplay basics of this game, thats what the tutorial is for HOWEVER I will get this out of the way right now.
Dark Souls requires you to use your brain, pay attention and plan things ahead. Going #YOLO#SWAG#SuchANerd here will only get you the
screen over and over again. You won't believe how many times I've been called a masochist or being asked why I hate myself by people every time I launch the game, which always leaves me scratching my head. I then proceed get completely disregarded when I try to explain why the game isn't balls hard like some memers make it out to be or end up hurting someone's fee fees when I tell them they are just♥♥♥♥♥♥
Now I'm not saying this game is perfect, there are things I like and things I don't like just like every single game in existence.
What I like the most is how the game absolutely lets you tailor your own playstyle, because many of the weapons have their own unique movesets which makes them handle differently. You want to swing a massive greatsword like Guts: you can. Want to be a rapier thrusting♥♥♥♥♥ you can. Want to fight from a distance with a spear: you can. Become the ultimate edgelord with katana and fedora: you can. Go ranged with bow/crossbow or become the ultimate nerd (Mage): you can do it. The starting class you pick really isn't all that important as you can become something completely different by the time you reach the end.
Another thing I really like is how the game handles its multiplayer component. While you're alone for the majority of the game you'll sometimes see the ghosts of other players as well as bloodstains (which indicate they died there, touching one of those lets you get an idea of what happened to that player which in turn might give you some knowledge in advance). Once you restore your humanity at a bonfire you automatically go online. While human you can be invaded by or summon other players for either Co-op or PVP, you can also invade or leave a summon sign yourself (note that co-op and PVP work only in areas where the boss hasn't been defeated yet, so for example you can't summon people or get invaded in an area where you've already slain the boss, but you can invade or be summoned by people who haven't killed him yet).
There are several covenants (think something like a guild) you can join if desired. Some are focused on Co-op, some on PVP and others have PVE uses. Leveling up your rank in whichever covenant you belong to will also gives you neat rewards, so it's definitely something worthwhile. My personal favorite is the Forest Hunters aka gank everyone who dares to set foot in the forest.
I also love the world you get to explore. I went in completely blind for my very first playthrough and ended up having to draw a map on paper just to keep up with all the interconnected areas. I haven't done something like this since the 90s.
For things I dislike: There are a couple of moments in the game that are just cheap and while the majority of the bosses are fun to fight there are several of them that are just reskins and some (like the Bed of Chaos) that are just badly designed and are not enjoyable to fight at all. Some areas of the game can also get on your nerves: Blighttown is the most famous example of that. The zone itself isn't THAT bad but the massive framerate drops is what kills it. I really wouldn't mind if the zone was optional but sadly you have to pass through it to progress through the game. Multiplayer wise on PC you're bound to run into cheaters and sadly the PVP watchdog can't get rid of every single one of them. However 14 year olds with no skill who have to resort to cheating isn't exclusive to this game (it always makes me smile when I beat them at their own game though).
Overall though, these cases are few and far between and don't detract from the overall enjoyment of the game.
Dark Souls is a game that takes me back to the good old days when both eastern and western video games were good, when games required you to work for your satisfaction instead of spoon-feeding you constantly in order to avoid hurting your fee fees and I love it for that. It's far from the perfect game but the few shortcomings it has I can overlook simply because it does everything else so well. It is in no way, shape or form a game for masochists, nor is it the hardest game ever made and to all those who keep spouting this crap, please stop playing video games and go back to facebook or whatever, you'll be making the rest of us a massive favor.

Greetings Everyone!  Today I will be reviewing The Red Solstice; I bought this game way back when it was in early access because I liked the idea of a hardcore tactical shooter with RPG mechanics.  The Early Access was very promising, bugs and all and now I’m back to see what they’ve done with it upon completion!
Let’s just tack this on:  One of the additions since I last played was the singleplayer campaign.  I was very excited as I love squad based tactical rpgs (Aarklash is my highest recommendation) but was almost immediately disappointed how they implemented it.  You can only directly control the squad leader without using the tactical view which is nice as it slows the game down by 90% but what if I want to directly control the medic or don’t want to but made my commander the medic because I needed one.  This added to the fact that the AI squadmates will do nothing but autofire (which was very annoying during the mission where monsters that couldn’t be auto targeted attacked).  I’m harping on this a lot but the single player feels tacked on, the voice acting is shoddy, half the time turrets don’t work (final mission was annoying as turrets couldn’t be attacked because they were perpetually turning off and on).
We’re going to a bug planet:  So many little bugs, I’m not going to say they could be easily fixed but there were programming errors looking up tool tips, I mean really?  The AI squadmates would only half follow you, one time my sniper died because he was stuck on a corner.  When I highlight an ability its range should be displayed (I’m talking to you Heal).  I understand that I could micro better but the games difficulty should be intended, I should be fighting STROL not the game itself.  In addition the game doesn’t seem to remember loadouts mission to mission; yes my medic is going to take life drone…as she always does.  Speaking of healing, medical station bugs out if you die and counts previous uses that you can’t destroy because they aren’t there any more…fun fact.  That was a rage moment of mine.  There are subtitles so that’s good…especially when the music is doing its super stage diving rock out (throw up those horns) right over that stupid story voice acting no one wanted to hear anyway.
No one can hear you scream:  The game’s multiplayer is dead…yup, sorry but it is.  This is a great shame as the main bulk of the game is developed around multiplayer.  I spent a few days looking for some life on the multiplayer but no matter what time I tried I didn’t see anyone.  Mars must have been wiped out (to be fair I did find a straggler or two).  I played with some bots (which is a nice attempt but for the previous reasons it leaves a lot to be desired) that they give you that can level and unlock everything for them the same way you would unlock for your own character.  Oh…I forgot to mention, you level, unlock classes and abilities; for the type of gamer I am this multiplayer would have been amazing.  I remember playing the unfinished version of this game in early access and thoroughly enjoying it.  But with the multiplayer dead and the single player beaten (with no interest of going back into that bug pit) I'm forced so uninstall with sad thoughts of what could have been.  I've thought about buying a copy for some friends but a lot of my friends don't really play 'indie' games and would immediately quit a the sight of bad tooltips.
Ultimately, if you have 3 friends and all want to get into this game together…hmm, was about to say to buy it but with the bugs and unfinished nature…not sure.  The game left me with a large amount of frustration, not just because it was buggy and incomplete but because there is an amazing game behind all that grit.  I love that they continue the story in multiplayer, love the concept of real time squad combat that has a soul’s genre difficulty.  But this game is infected and it is time to find a new planet to call home.

This game feels like an early access game even though it is stated not to be one.
It is definitely NOT worth the 25 euro's they are asking for it. It is an unfinished at best and unplayable at worst game. It has some gamebreaking bugs that make this game a chore rather than a pleasure to play.
For starters, I had troubles even getting the game to work. The store page states that I need a GFX card with half the power my system has to run this game. Even so I had frequent stutters and a LOT of crashes. I spent hours trying to fix this game. The forums are littered with complaints about crashes, many of which have not had any answer whatsoever by the devs.
Eventually I seem to have found some sort of half-arsed solution (since apparently in all cases it's the systems fault NOT the game, when it crashes) which causes my game to only sometimes crash.
Now that I have got my game running (kinda) I face all the other issues:
1. Laying train tracks and stations is tedious beyond comprehension. If you can even find a way to place a track, don't think about removing it and placing it again, because it changes the landscape permanently. Yes you can fix this with the landscape tool, but why would I need to?
2. Placing lines seems to work fine at first but is then met with many complications. Oftentimes resulting in trains not moving at all. There are workarounds for this, but they require manual interference rather than the AI just being clever enough to figure things out themselves. This should be something that works intuitively, but rather than that, it require hours of finetuning just to get 1 train track to run half-decent.
3. The game has massive framerate issues. As stated before I ran this game on a card with more than enough power. I set all the settings to the lowest possible. I lowered the resolution and STILL I had frequent drops in framerate. Once again I went to the forums to check if there was a solution and once again I was met with "You need to update your system" rather than "Our game is not optimised properly".
Overall this game just feels very sub-optimal. The way you would expect an early access game to feel. If I were to play this, not knowing in what stage this game is, I would say late-alpha, early beta.
All that said, the developers ARE updating this game regularly, including performance updates, but I don't get my hopes up too high, since this game has been out for a while and has had many updates and still doesn't run well at all.

It's not terrible. But would I recommend it? No.
Some spoilers ahead.
The gameplay is not that bad, although fighting is a bit like Guitar Hero, pressing the right buttons at the right time. The storyline is disappointing and finishing the game feels empty. There is no reward. All bosses (except The Hammer and a Graug) are a joke, and the Nemesis system didn't work for me.
All these captains have no story and as a result it isn't interesting. The only time I actually felt like one of those guys was some sort of rival was when he had killed me twice. It felt satisfying to take that one out. But then the game spits you in the face by just respawning him a minute later - and that actually happened twice in a row.
The worst about this game, however, is how repetitive it is. You keep doing the same things over and over again. I just tried to finish the Bright Lord campaign, but I simply couldn't do it. I branded all 5 warchiefs (my face had already contorted in pain when I saw that objective pop up, since that is the exact same thing you had to do in the main campaign) and faced off against Sauron, who simply snaps his fingers to turn them all against you and you can start all over again (but then you face them all at the same time as well as normal Uruks all around you). And if you managed to win that (I had to ragequit before that though), Sauron starts to revive them one by one. It's terrible.
Fighting in stongholds is terrible anyway, since you will find yourself surrounded by 30 Uruks in no time. Killing or branding captains or warchiefs (a mission that is probably the most common in this game) is a total pain this way. It isn't fun, it is frustrating. You want to get it over with so you can continue the story. I have yet to try some game modes, but I'm not expecting too much.
