Lets start this off by saying this game is one of those surprises, My first time playing it I will be honest I hated it. The gameplay was just not for me, but the more time I have spent with this game the more I am loving it.
Its like that annoying friend that you love yet want to strangle at the same time, What I mean by that is the survial aspect of this game is wonderful. And the gameplay ended up opening up past what I saw in my first play through. While other zombie games focus more on the killing or maybe the looting this game focuses on a group dynamic. It will make you consider putting your character in danger in order to bring back supplies for a sick group member, or maybe searching a market for more food to feed the group, buy doing so putting yourself at risk to being torn apart and having your character being gone for good. Yes there is perma death meaning if you level up a character and make one mistake they are gone forever all that time you invested in them gone in a blink of an eye. It really changes your mentality on how you go about day to day things in this game, Not only are you wanting to put yourself at risk to better your group but by doing so you risk your own character and these struggles really start getting to you.
You can of course ease the struggle buy leveling your character, traveling with a partner which will cost influnce or calling in favors like back up from a swat team or you can set up outpost to protect them more allowing them a better chance at survial on supply runs they will make.
This game does have some glitches and bugs let me be clear I am by no means gonna say it doesnt this is not a perfect game by the hardware standpoint but for me none of them are game breaking or really upset me annoying yes and that is what I ment by that friend you want to strangle, but by no means are they bad enough for me to rage out and want to never play again. Not once did a bug hinder my ability to play the game or did it effect a mission for me up to this point.
This game is a wonderful refreshing take on zombie survial and at the end of the day that is what this game is and survial game where you try your best to hold out as long as possible with what you can scavenge or with the people you meet its not all that spectacular in the terms of story but at the heart of it you have a real to earth hardcore zombie survial game and that is all it claims to be and it delivers with great gameplay and new take on the genre that I really enjoyed.

This game took me 90 hours to get into.
It was mostly false starts before my brain got distracted, which it often does. That said; started replaying this a few weeks ago, and something just clicked. All the prior trial and error attempts had sunk much of the gameplay into my brain; where early items were, what to do in general. It all was ingrained somewhere along the way and this time around, I found myself able to dive in.
There is a great deal to take in for this game, and honestly without a lot of help from a good friend and some very detailed wikis (which I only look up after roughly...5 failed attempts at a spot), not sure I'd get as far as I have.  Much of the legendary difficulty of this game is learning about...well, everything. What makes pyromancy different from sorcery, what it means to "fat roll", what damage type is good against which enemy, ect. These are things that have to be beaten into you. And once that all settles, or you know how to figure it out; it just becomes being able to make it through the other side of the battle. The only thing that will stop you, it seems, is you.
The online scene at this point seems to have simmered down to a mostly good natured lot; from my experiances anyways. I got invaded at one point, the person and I bowed and then they threw lightening spears in my face. Good fight. And then I ended up summoning them to help with Orenstien and Smough. One of those experiences that I can't say I'd get from any other game.
So if you've been on the fence about this franchise, please at least give it a try if you see it on sale. It may take time for it to click, it may frustrate the hell out of you for a while. But when it does click, when you begin to see how it works, you'll be rewarded with one of the richest and fulfilling gaming experiances in recent memory.

The hours i have on this game for pc are not even close to how many hours ive put in this game back on the xbox 360.
This game is: Unforgiving, Difficult, and occasionally broken. But It's amazing and by far the best dark souls experience out of all the games. Its mechanics are not the best by a long shot, dark souls 3 mastered that but this game is the true experience of dark souls. It is by far the most open world dark souls out there, at the start the only hint you have is from a guy saying "go ring bells". From then on your on your own, exploring the world, facing difficult enemies, and overcoming challenges.
The combat is this game is perfect. Swords, Shields, Magic, Miracles. All of these things are in the game, and all of them are viable. I never once thought one of them to be useless.
The level design is the best in any game i've ever played, Everything that you see was planned out, each item placement seems to have a story of its own and the movement from are to are is so immersive. Look out the distance and say "i wanna go their" 90% of the time you can go there. Enemy placement may seem unfair at times, ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t, etc... (damn arrows) but its never impossible, plan your movements and execute it right and you can make it through any place.
Leveling is simple, but pretty balanced. You'll never be like "i need to grind" in this game (unless you somehow lose your souls nearly every time)
Bosses, are awesome, and probably what defines this series (not to say level design is bad but bosses make up for it cause that is not the case at all) Each boss provides a challenge of its own, it most of the time will take you a few tries to beat a boss (or like 50). All bosses are fun and satisfying to beat (with the exception of one)
Enemies are very well made, placments and all. You very rarely when first encountering a new enemy will think "wow this guy is just stupidly useless"
Pvp is Pvp... Thats all i can describe it as
Co-op is a pain, but when it actually works its pretty fun, i suggest using mods to make it easier.
In short This game is awesome, if your new to the series play it blind, dont look up ANYTHING. You'll definitely get mad at this game but that satisfaction of beating an area is so worth the trouble.

On one hand, you could call this game fantasy Civ V and leave it at that. And you'd be pretty accurate.
On the other, you could call it a surprisingly deep and funny hex-based grand strategy game with clever tongue-in-cheek flavor text and voicing to back up a fast-paced, engaging, and interesting gameplay that will always leave you with plenty on your plate to work on and plenty to look forward to until the moment you win.
You will probably never run out of world to explore, even after searching most of the primary map, since the best resources are off in the distance, hiding, and the alternate worlds have even better loot to find, and you will probably never be able to dedicate as much of your resources as you'd like to exploring, because there are always monsters or angy neighbors on your doorstep just waiting to punch you in the face when you aren't looking.
While it puts just a little much value in the city-spam, Warlock is a fiendishly fun and interesting game that is yes, like Civ, but also independent of it in character and style. And is extremely fun.

Night in the Woods is a game that tells a rather vague, but thought-provoking story centered around College drop-out Mae and her adventures in her dreary little hometown of Possum Springs. Right off the bat I found the game to have a lot of personality and even some of the more minor characters had interesting quirks that stuck in the mind effectively. It's a peaceful, and oddly nostalgic environment with a compelling narrative that really makes you think. It's engaging, and I was very curious to see how the entire experience would turn out.
This is another one of those story-heavy games that plays more like an interactive visual novel rather than a traditional game. There's very little "gameplay" other than the typical platformer controls used to explore your surroundings. There are a few distractions here and there in the form of what I guess you could call mini-games, but those are simply there to break apart the exploration and story progress; most are completely optional, and it's not the main focus of the game.
One small issue I've had with the game is that sometimes it's hard to read the mood of what is currently happening. This is mostly because of how little the characters emote visually; there's hardly any changes in facial expressions to match how they're currently feeling, so when you think it's just some silly, sarcastic conversation and then suddenly one of the characters screams and runs out of the room that can send some mixed messages to the player.
One other thing that bothers me is that there aren't multiple save slots, which would be super helpful if you're attempting to get all of the achievements, but instead if there are some you missed you have to back to the beginning every single time. Though in retrospect it's not too bad because the story as a whole is great, but it would have been nice to have that convenience.
Otherwise I enjoyed this game a solid amount. It's not one of my favorite games of this genre but it has its own charm and it held my interest all the way to the end credits.

Master of Magic meets Civilization 5 and the result is pretty good. There is some problems with details, but overall it works. I'm going to make a lot of references to Master of Magic (MoM) because I love that 20 years old game and this one reminds me of it in a good way. For example:
This game also adds to the mix a parthenon of deities, which is a pretty standard thing in fantasy literature, but usually missing in these games. There are divine spells, which are mostly slightly powerful or a bit easier to cast versions of regular spells, that you can only research and cast if you are in favor of that deity. You can gain favor by doing quests and building temples on the holy ground. While you bow down to one god, you show your backside the opposite god. One way to win the game is to get one god so angry that it manifests on the map and then destroy it. Religion also affects the relationships between the wizards. It's a nice system.
Speaking of quests, they kind of suck. You just get some random build this building/found a city/kill these random enemies that popped up here/capture this city/defeat this player that just pops up. Same with random events being just monster lairs popping up on your lands. Definitely the weakest part of this game. MoM's events had much more style. Some might argue that the AI not being able to handle the complexities could be a bigger problem. I didn't play enough to be sure, but it seemed to be struggling with it. Not worse than Civ 5, but in this game it has to handle with the parallel worlds, terrain changing by spells and stuff like that too.
All in all a very nice concept that could use some tweaking and filling out the content to be really great. I'm glad I got this free from Humble Bundle. Made me put Warlock II high on my wishlist.

Night in the Woods is a mystery adventure game with some platformer elements in which you play as Mae, a recent college dropout who has returned to her hometown only to find that things are not as she had left them. Most of the gameplay involves exploring the town, jumping around on buildings, completing various minigames, and interacting with other characters. But nothing is quite as it seems, and you will find yourself doubting who and what can be trusted.
The art style is simple but beautiful, with all the characters being made up of anthropomorphic animals. But don't let the cute animals fool you, this game cuts extremely deep. There is a philosophical tone to the game, with characters outright questioning the very world around them and sometimes leaving you doing the same.  If you are a fan of the Netflix series "Bojack Horseman", this is pretty much the best comparison I draw as to what the overall feel of this game is like. Although these characters are not human in appearance, they are surprisingly human in every other way, with flaws and struggles that are extremely relatable. You will connect with them and feel a wide range of emotions as you journey throughout the game. Simply put: if you're a fan of sad nihilistic animals facing existential crises then this is a game for you.
This game is an intensely personal experience as it doesn't simply tell a story but rather connects to you on a more emotional level. For this reason my review for Night in the Woods is one of my shorter ones, not because there isn't much I can say about it, but rather because it's such a beautiful and personal experience that no words can do it justice. It must be played to be understood. I can honestly say that this is one of the best and most unexpected gaming experiences I have had all year, and that this game now ranks as one of my most favorite games ever.

Night in the Woods is really well written. Not even by videogame standards - it's well written art by any account. Not only is the dialog good (though a touch samey even when coming from different characters) without sounding overtly cutesy and "hip", but the characters and themes are aptly sketched. The game even has something to say, and says it with confidence and competence.
Definitely a worthy purchase at full price.
That said, even though this is a good-looking, good-sounding and well written "walking simulator", I feel like there could be more relevant gameplay to this game. There are no fail coniditions, and very little you do (besides deciding which friend you should hang out with) actually influences the gameplay or text. I feel like the game could lean a bit more into the visual novel aspect, and have your conversations actually change the way others perceive and interact with Mae (even if some conversations would naturally have no successful outcomes).
I'd recommend playing with a controller (both for platforming and because the game aptly punctuates certain moments when you're using a controller), exploring the rooftops whenever you can, and keeping in mind that you can hang out with anyone except Gregg / Bea without ending the day.

Earlier this year I had bought this game on sale, i believe in June or July. I was pumped, I was hyped. I've never played this type of game before. I heard bad things about older popular games like this being bad. I heard they flocked too this game. WOOOH! Let's play this sucka!
For a while, during my first weeks with the game and playing it from time to time, it was a joy to play even by myself as I made time for it after school. Nighttime is scary and actually dark, meeting people is scary. The first people I met were nice to me, we didnt interact though. We only waved to each other and went our separate ways. Then comes bloodshed. My blood. I get shot once. I turn to the shooter. He's holed up in a house entranceway. "F*** you, F*** your wife, F*** your kids-" and I don't hear the rest as my head is pumped full of lead. Exhilerating experience. Once I died, I knew this game isn't to be messeda round with. Immediately after spawning on another guy, I get arrested for no reason. hooray. I killed myself after that.
After these encounters, hearing others makes me frightened. Footsteps are heard and my heart thumps hard. It still happens to this day ( I'm easily immersed in my games ). But.... That's all that happens nowadays. Most people you will meet... or won't even see will just not be friends. There's always gonna be a sniper scouting every town. As of right now, food and hydration aren't a threat even though I think that should be a major threat in this game. The 'zombies' aren't a threat right now either. They don't come at you in large numbers. The only real big threat from what i heard besides being players is a buff variant ( think of the tank in left 4 dead ).
-Bad community. Everyone just wants to kill each other. This could be fixed in the future by having more 'zombies' around, making the food and hydration more of a fear factor, and maybe adding a little more variant of 'zombies'.
-The game is unforgiving for ungeared lone wolves. You're gonna have a hell of a time tryna suit up and carry everything to be beefed up to survive the zom.... I mean the other players.
-There is just no motivation to work together unless you're in a PvE server. I understand thatmif you don't like getting killed all the time people will say "Just join a PvE serv", but banding together and fighting would make for cooler times too. Wouldn't it be cool to have two factions slowly grow, then as supplies dwindle one attacks the other in an all scale war? Two major groups fighting with small unaffiliated groups and loners in the middle too, as victims or opportunists?
................. That's it really. In this type of multiplayer game, the community is what makes or breaks the game. ESPECIALLY if you're a lone wolf like me. I HAVE bought a friend a copy of the game in hopes that it can be more fun.
I will still support this game as long as we get some good updates soon. But as of now, Only really get this game if you have friends to play with, or dont mind struggling by yourself in an uphill battle.

For a game called "Train Fever", the execution of the namesake is just not very good. Simple cargo-truck, bus, and even tram lines are plenty workable. However, when you start trying to build railways, you run into lots of intractable problems:
1. The handling of elevation in rail tracks/stations is not good. Stations seem to be elevated off the surface of the map (and the terrain raised), or recessed into the ground, for no obvious reason. It's hard to build tracks between relatively near stations, because the system wants to build them at a high slope.
2. Trains often have trouble finding their way on really straightforward rail routes, even when you're using things like waypoints. Conflicts between trains are far too common, and the use of signals is complex and fraught with peril. Basically, forget about having more than one train per track, and expect persistent headaches at terminus stations.
3. It's possible to end up in a state, especially on multi-train lines, where your trains are PERMANENTLY stuck and you simply must revert. That's unacceptable.
4. Train Fever doesn't let you do anything with elevation, except in the form of the afterthought hacks in the path-finding phase during build. No elevated or subway trains, making it hard to do much better than streetcar/tram light rail in the cities.
5. The cities grow so slowly that they never really arrive at the sort of scale that makes a transit system a fun challenge. On easy, you build a few cargo lines, cash in and watch the money stream in. On the harder difficulties, it's a challenge to make headway at all.

This game took me 90 hours to get into.
It was mostly false starts before my brain got distracted, which it often does. That said; started replaying this a few weeks ago, and something just clicked. All the prior trial and error attempts had sunk much of the gameplay into my brain; where early items were, what to do in general. It all was ingrained somewhere along the way and this time around, I found myself able to dive in.
There is a great deal to take in for this game, and honestly without a lot of help from a good friend and some very detailed wikis (which I only look up after roughly...5 failed attempts at a spot), not sure I'd get as far as I have.  Much of the legendary difficulty of this game is learning about...well, everything. What makes pyromancy different from sorcery, what it means to "fat roll", what damage type is good against which enemy, ect. These are things that have to be beaten into you. And once that all settles, or you know how to figure it out; it just becomes being able to make it through the other side of the battle. The only thing that will stop you, it seems, is you.
The online scene at this point seems to have simmered down to a mostly good natured lot; from my experiances anyways. I got invaded at one point, the person and I bowed and then they threw lightening spears in my face. Good fight. And then I ended up summoning them to help with Orenstien and Smough. One of those experiences that I can't say I'd get from any other game.
So if you've been on the fence about this franchise, please at least give it a try if you see it on sale. It may take time for it to click, it may frustrate the hell out of you for a while. But when it does click, when you begin to see how it works, you'll be rewarded with one of the richest and fulfilling gaming experiances in recent memory.

It features immersive lore and scenery with an easy-to-learn yet hard-to-master combat system which, alltough wonky at times, is more than enough to beat the game which is desinged with trial, error and self-improvement in mind, making just the defeat of a challenging foe or area a reason for celebration before failing miserably on the next challenge..

Considering that the game is about 5 years old now, it's still rather pretty but one of it's stronger points is it's powerfull soundtrack which adds to the theme of the game perfectly.
Unfortunately some parts of the game feel very improvised and too frustrating at times.
Not to mention the poor quality of the port requiring additional files to even play the game properly and limited frame rate. It makes up for it with a variety of interesting characters which tell their own story inside the game through, not only dialoge -which by the way is nicely written- but their actions and appearances in various places, giving a break from the usual hostility and adding to the immersion.

The hours i have on this game for pc are not even close to how many hours ive put in this game back on the xbox 360.
This game is: Unforgiving, Difficult, and occasionally broken. But It's amazing and by far the best dark souls experience out of all the games. Its mechanics are not the best by a long shot, dark souls 3 mastered that but this game is the true experience of dark souls. It is by far the most open world dark souls out there, at the start the only hint you have is from a guy saying "go ring bells". From then on your on your own, exploring the world, facing difficult enemies, and overcoming challenges.
The combat is this game is perfect. Swords, Shields, Magic, Miracles. All of these things are in the game, and all of them are viable. I never once thought one of them to be useless.
The level design is the best in any game i've ever played, Everything that you see was planned out, each item placement seems to have a story of its own and the movement from are to are is so immersive. Look out the distance and say "i wanna go their" 90% of the time you can go there. Enemy placement may seem unfair at times, ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t, etc... (damn arrows) but its never impossible, plan your movements and execute it right and you can make it through any place.
Leveling is simple, but pretty balanced. You'll never be like "i need to grind" in this game (unless you somehow lose your souls nearly every time)
Bosses, are awesome, and probably what defines this series (not to say level design is bad but bosses make up for it cause that is not the case at all) Each boss provides a challenge of its own, it most of the time will take you a few tries to beat a boss (or like 50). All bosses are fun and satisfying to beat (with the exception of one)
Enemies are very well made, placments and all. You very rarely when first encountering a new enemy will think "wow this guy is just stupidly useless"
Pvp is Pvp... Thats all i can describe it as
Co-op is a pain, but when it actually works its pretty fun, i suggest using mods to make it easier.
In short This game is awesome, if your new to the series play it blind, dont look up ANYTHING. You'll definitely get mad at this game but that satisfaction of beating an area is so worth the trouble.

Cutish, casual, liquid puzzle game.  Playing with a keyboard and mouse works ok.  Fairly easy to complete levels if you go slow, but fairly difficult to complete levels with the best scores.   Not one I'd play a lot more of, but I got my money's worth.

The good parts: Interesting and clever puzzle mechanics. Charming artwork (if you like the style, which I do).
Neither good nor bad: Using WASD/arrow keys to "tilt" a board to move droplets around goes from "simple fun" to "amazingly difficult" very quickly. If you like challenging physics-based puzzles, that part's great. If you like games with lots of easy puzzles so you can enjoy the sense of progress, you're not likely to enjoy this.
Tip: After the first few levels - GO SLOW. Tiny little taps move the droplets around; too many too fast will shatter them against walls or objects and you'll never get them to move where you need them. (There's a "reset level" button; you can keep trying. But it's going to be frustrating for many players. Action-reflex players will be frustrated at how slow it is; kids--the apparent target demographic--will be frustrated because it's unforgiving of mistakes.)
The bad parts: I can't get it to run windowed; I've tried several methods. (Lack of ability to run windowed really is what convinced me not to bother playing even when I was in the mood for it.) As others have mentioned, it seems incomplete. There's no story at all, no explanation of why you're doing this "alchemy" for the wizard. No sound at all. (Someone else said there's a single music track; apparently it doesn't play on my system.) After a few puzzles to get used to the setting, there's a strong sense of "why bother?"... the best thing about it is that ctrl+esc lets it sit in my taskbar and collect cards.
"No story" is fine for some physics puzzles... but this one sure looks like it was intended to have some context.
Conclusion: I paid 49 cents for this on sale, and don't feel I was cheated - but even at that price, I wouldn't recommend it unless the buyer loved physics-based puzzles AND had time to burn on a slow-paced game AND didn't care that it's just an endless set of tasks with no rewards attached AND doesn't mind the game being full-screen.

A cross between Puddle and marble tilt games.
You tilt the playfield to move bits of liquid through color changing symbols, through static and moving pieces, and into color coded vial symbols, while avoiding falling into hole symbols or off of the playfield.
This may seem awfully mundane and straightforward, but it's actually quite challenging, varied, and at times clever - although at times it can feel pointlessly frustrating too.
The fluid physics simulation works quite nicely (as in gameplay, not realism), and the controls (using an analog stick, at least) feel, uh, fluid...
It held my attention for an hour and a half until I got tired of the game's last few levels, which are very hard. Then there's also an achievement for finishing 50 of the 60 levels under the lowest par time, which is also very, very hard.
Overall, this simple but challenging physics puzzle is worth at least an hour of your time.

If you like turn based 4X and fantasy this is a pretty fun game to dump some time into.  It shares some elements with Civ5, Heroes of Might and Magic and of course Majesty.  Diplomacy is a little lacking and schizophrenic so it's really war heavy, I've found it necessary to constantly sign and resign non-aggression pacts in order to stay at peace when my army's busy clearing another realm for expansion.   The spellcasting is a really neat element though and a lot of fun to play with especially the terraforming spells.  Need a land bridge between continents?  Raise one.  Farms not producing in your frozen tundra?  Make the land fertile.  Don't be afraid to enchant away either, the upkeep really isn't bad considering how much mana you eventually bring in.  The difficulty is a little on the weak side though and once you get the hang of the mechanics  it's not really challenging in the long run, then again that's a problem most 4X games have so I wouldn't let that influence things much.

Every now and then the game randomly fails to load certain interface screens, victory screens, and other UI parts.  You end up having to close the client and restart.  On the positive side, it seems to save your progress from the games where these issues happen.  If they could fix these kinds of bugs which sadly happen far too often, the game would be a great contender for competitive play and streaming.  As it stands now though, the game is fun to play but frustrating to have to relaunch the game after every couple battles or when you get disconnected from a multiplayer match 2 or 3 times.

Early access review (will edit if anything here is fixed): Not too bad of a game. Of course, since it's early access, it's not a complete game and is full of bugs and isn't fully optimized. I'm not going to go into bugs since this is an early-access game, and anyone who decides whether an early-access game is good or not based on bugs is stupid and lacks an understanding of early-access.
Pros:
-Vast, danger-filled, explorable environment that will terrify you, especially if you're alone
-Lots of weapons and gear to collect to make your experience a *tad* bit easier, but you can still easily be killed by mutants
-There is no weapon or gear that will make the game super-easy for you: the fear of death is there all the time
-Crafting system
-Base-building
-It's just scary. The atmosphere is perfect and gives off the intended apocalyptic feel.
Cons:
-No system to see where your friends are. This is a huge downfall, and my friends need to get on skype/discord calls to speak about where we are and where to meet up, and depending on where we spawn this can take hours.
-It's nearly impossible to find a car/boat that you can actually drive and that isn't a "map" car (i.e a car that is part of the map and is not dynamic), and distinguishing the differences between the two is quite difficult. It's also difficult to collect all necessary parts for the cars unless you have a group, because you'll find at most 3 parts you'll need for a car in one area, and the rest will be scatted throughout the map. The only problem here is that the parts *will* weigh you down significantly, and the car will probably be despawned or stolen by the time you make your way back to it. Bicycles are a thing, however, but even these are difficult to find, but they don't need any parts to ride them.
Simple fix: Just raise the spawn rate of cars and put more car parts near car spawns. You could add garages to some gas stations and put car spawns there- that'd rock.
I get this is the apocalypse and all, but it makes no logical sense that there are tons of cars that are broken down and laying on the street (cosmetic, part of the map cars), and you can only fix up like 1 out of 100 of them. How did that 1 car outside get lucky and somehow not completely get wrecked by the nuclear bombs that hit earth, but the rest did?
-Your character will put his gun away automatically and you will need to left click to bring it back up, then left-click again to shoot. This is EXTREMELY irritating, as you can easily be butchered by a zombie because of this. Even right-clicking with a weapon equipped wont bring the gun back up if it auto-holstered it. Out of all the irritating things in this game in its current state, this is the worst. It makes combat not fluid at all.
Is this game worth a purchase? If you like games like DayZ, yes. I believe the developers will make this into a great game, and they have drastically improved the look, feel, and optimization of it within a short timespan. Yes- the devs actually care about this. DayZ is absolute trash compared to this game- give Miscreated your time and money, not DayZ!

State of Decay is a lot of fun, but not without it's shortcomings. It plays a bit like GTA, but in a zombie apocalypse based world.
It totally nails the feeling of holding back a never ending tide of undead, and slow looming desperation. The gameplay is simple, yet fun. Managing your base and survivors is cool, and you end up becoming attached to your favorites. (I actually restarted once because my "main" character got overrun by zombies.) Building up your base, and upgrading facilities was rewarding while not being overly in depth to the point it was annoying.
The combat is easy to pick up, the weapons have variety, and the enemies have a decent amount of difference between them. I like how sound attracted enemies while scavenging for survival tools, and made it seem threatening to be out there, especially when alone. Gunshots attract anything in range of the noise as well (until you get a supressor), which made gunplay a double edged sword.
The cons are: Random bugs with Zombie placement/walking through walls. Lack of quest variety, and being unable to do multiple quests at the same time.
Overall, I was very pleased. While the game does get bogged down a bit in the late game due to lack of mission variety, it's a very enjoyable experience overall. It's the most realized apocalyptic world I've played in a game. No rails, you can go anywhere, and it's fascinating to see the world they've created. I'd totally recommend this to any Zombie game fan, or anyone wanting a solid gaming experience. Great bang for the buck!

Counter Strike Condition Zero is an odd one. Caught in between CS 1.6 and Source, it came very close to CS: Source's release, and was brushed aside. At the time, it graphics were outdated, and its single player content was lacking. Today, the single player content is just as lackluster. The regular campaign is literally offline bots with some slight customization. It's bland, boring, and the AI is pretty terrible. There's also the "Deleted Scenes", which is actually an entirely other game. It's a single player CS Campaign that plays nothing like Counter Strike. It feels more like a fast-paced Arcade shooter. It's plagued with poor map design, cheesey plot that desperately wanted to blend with games like Halo at the time, and gimmicky spy gadgets that while intriguing at first, are poorly executed.
Where Condition Zero does shine is its multiplayer. It's graphics are dated but timeless. It feels like an updated CS 1.6 in visuals, and plays in a way thats really unique to Condition Zero. Ammunition is expensive and money is tight, so you really have to watch your shots in this game. It still has a very large playerbase, and holds up much better than the classic 1.6
While Condition Zero failed to capture a single player Counter Strike expirience, it did create a pretty fun Multiplayer that's still fun to hop on today. It's by no means a masterpiece, but it isn't a bad game. If the CS Anthology pack ever goes on sale, I'd say pick it up and try it out. But on its own, I'd say it's a pass.

Overall, it's a good game. Got the GOTY edition for 4€. I'd say up to around 15€ is a fair price for it, depending on how urgently you want to play it, I'd probably wait until it's <10€ again.
The foundation of the story seemed really lackluster at first, but after the Bright Lord DLC, it made sense. The story overall is decent (I'm not that familiar with LotR lore) with bits of small "random" lore scattered, which is nice for fans (probably).
After getting familiar with the mechanics it was really fun but very soon some problems became apparent.
I played with keyboard and mouse. There is (seemingly) random mouse acceleration which can't be disabled, making it really hard to aim with the bow sometimes. I got kinda used to it but wow can it be annoying.
Climbing walls feels super wonky and I hated it throughout all of the game.
Those things weren't that big problems, because the game was rather easy overall. And even though I usually don't enjoy cakewalks, this game was pretty fun for the first ~10h. Afterwards it was still ok, but it gets repetitive and not really challenging.
Speaking of repetitive: Every orc says an opening taunt/line when you engage combat with them (few exceptions, like stealthing on them) and you can't skip it. In the beginning it's nice, gives them a more "personal" feeling but it gets so annoying being locked in this "mini cutscene" for 3-7 seconds every time. But props for the amount of different voice lines and the interactivity (if the orc killed you before, they will reference it).
Towards the end of the story, I didn't feel challenged at all, not even by Warchiefs. Not even the end of the game/final boss were a challenge.
The collectibles are marked on the map, can be "tracked" and will just show the exact location in the world, so there is no real hunting for that, it just takes the time to get there, make of that what you will. I 100%ed the base game with ease. (I'm only referring to in-game collectibles, quests and such. I didn't bother to get all of the achievements)
The first DLC (Lord of the Hunt) was also not really that interesting or challenging. It added some new variations of existing enemies, but was overall not really worth noting in my opinion. Took me around 4-5h.
The second DLC (The Bright Lord) was a decent bit harder, which I appreciated, but it's also not that long (also around 4-5h). And here I got really annoyed with the "I must introduce myself" mechanic of Orcs, because it often screws you over.
You try to backstab an Orc Captain and instead his introduction triggers and afterwards he's aware of you and you can't backstab him... or sometimes I try to use a finisher on them, they introduce and my hitstreak got reset (which mean I can't use the finisher anymore). That got
frustrating as I felt mostly challenged by the game's annoying mechanic's side effects.
I also ended up attacking the wrong target way too many times due to the subpar controls...
In this DLC some of the runes (they're kind of swappable upgrades, that boost some stats) had no effect/use but still dropped, which I really don't understand (note that this DLC has separate runes/equipment from the base game/hunt DLC).
The ending/final boss here is worth noting, because it was actually not such a cakewalk (still
easy, but compared to the rest of the game/DLC, it was good challenge).
The Trial DLCs... I started one for like 5 minutes and when I realized what they are, I stopped. They don't interest me at all, but maybe some others might enjoy them.
I'd say it's a great game for up to 15€, because it has some really interesting, unique and/or fun mechanics, but it gets boring towards the end in my opinion because of its repetitiveness and the lack of challenge.

Having logged now 30+ hours in this game, I can speak a little bit to its greatness and some nitpicky things that are drawbacks. The game mechanics themselves are straight up great; from micromanaging your individual unit perks to keeping an eye on your macroeconomy, the process is intuitive, and once you've got the mechanics down you can optimize.
Partially because of this, the game feels a little bit like "what if Civ didn't have empire size balancing." Economic advantages snowball to the point that endgames can sometimes feel like a chore. But crushing your enemies into a fine powder isn't so bad of a chore. It's considerably more of a challenge to limit yourself to a certain number of cities.
Also, if you ever played the game Majesty, you'll notice many of the same gods showing up, as well as certain catchphrases. Very nice tickle of the nostalgia bone.

Visual novels are curious things, and yet here's one that really puts in the effort to make you think that you are actually making a difference in the story.
While the story of a 14-year-old princess suddenly needing to take the throne in one year isn't particularly new, what makes this game interesting is how you have to manage that road to ascension.  You're given this wide spread of different skills, and they define what your (unfortunate) princess does well in.  For example, there's the standard court behavior, athleticism, and animal handling, but then there's things like military strategy, divination, and if you manage to trigger the right things, magic.  Even the princess' mood triggers differences in classes.  And it makes sense; in real life, would you like to study proper behavior when you're depressed?
Does it matter?  Oh yes it does.  The game can be exceedingly brutal to your protagonist should you decide to do something unusual.  Spent all of your time sending the princess to combat practice?  Watch her consume a tasty treat and end up dying.  Decided to make her into the finest court royal in the land?  Watch as she falls in a duel or lands on her head.  There's a huge consequence system in place within the game, and while it doesn't hold your hand and tell you exactly what could happen, it does give you enough information to see what you could do to change it.
That made the game much more interesting in terms of replayability.  There are sometimes little messages (optional) that tell you something might happened differently with a given stat raised higher (not unlike flags in dating sims, but not decision based).  This makes the game a little more interesting to continue delving through, as you get to see all sorts of reactions from characters.  And since the dialogue isn't insufferable most of the time, it is enjoyable, to a degree.
Stylistically, it may be that people are not as interested in the anime-esque art style or the storylines themselves, but it is a common thread, and I wouldn't hold it against anyone if the visual aspects weren't appealing.  It's not called a "visual novel" for no reason, after all.
tl;dr, Long Live the Queen is a fresh visual novel, with a well-thought-out gameplay mechanic, and a system to draw your attention in and increase replayability.  Though its visual style may put off some members of the community, I would definitely recommend this game to those who are interested in this genre.

At its core, this is a really good puzzle game with some great ideas. You eventually have to track many things at once that behave in different ways, while figuring out how to make them work together.

The biggest issue by far is lack of any kind of 'undo'. When you've got a level that takes 20+ moves at minimum, and you're going for that minimum score, you don't want to make a mistake 20 moves in! All that said, its worth playing and the price is more than fair.

There is alot to like about this game, but I'm not sure the bad outweigh the good.  Some of the biggest problems are the controls, game difficulty, and the beta state of the game.
The controls are an absolute pain.  You will constantly default to the team leader when you change control modes.  Autofire will turn on when you select another team member.  Sometimes your team will follow you, sometimes the game will toggle off autofollow.  Sometimes you will put out a squad in tactical mode, then the team will assemble on the leader immediatly on leaving the mode.  All these things feel intentional, however and only make the game feel clunky by design.  Other games might get away with it but as frantic as the later levels can get, you will see your team wipe due to this.
I laughed when I saw a note at the start of one level, saying the waves of enemies are NOT endless.  They did feel endless at many points, and that indicates the difficulty.  Too much is not explained, or poorly explained in the game.  Some levels are purely trial and error.  Save points are fairly far between.  At first the game comes across as a frantic, tactical game.  After a few levels it feels like a forced rush to finsh quickly.  Some levels you can slow down and think it out, others you have a set path to victory that is explained in no way, except dont die.
So much is odd about this game.  The skill discriptions that say "Discription Not Found".  The story explained in a text block in the options.  No idea how to gain experience.  I found a few guides that said you gained experience from looting lockers (???).  Alot of this feels like new ideas, and if it was explained in some way I'd give the devs the benefit of the doubt, but it feels lazy and half finished.  Also, I will mention the hoops you need to jump through to get it to run is staggering.  I spent a few days trying to get it to run, just to give up in frustration.  6 months later I tried on a new PC, and it started up without a hitch.
The game has some really cool moments and is addictive to a point.  That point is when you realize its nearly broken in difficulty at certain points.  I'm not really sure the game is worth the purchase price, whatever it is, considering its a dice roll to get it to run.  If you enjoy zombie games, and tactical shooters, it might be worth a look.

The Red Solstice starts as a pretty typical "lone squad must defeat hordes of horrific creatures overrunning the colony" plot, but manages to throw in several twists both in the game and in the plot to make things interesting. While the game can be played as a regular RTS, where you guide the squad and let them shoot anything in sight, by mission 4 or 5 you get curveballs, such as enemies that doesn't appear on sensors (so auto-aim doesn't work) but manual aimming does. Then you get into HUGE enemies (7500 hp!) that basically forces you to utilize each soldier's specialty power, such as gunship strafing, artillery beacon, grenade launcher, HE shells, so you can survive the fight. Gunship strafings can take out a large group of enemies, while artillery beacon can be placed then enemy lead over it so the barrage clean them out. Explosives can be placed, mines can be set, and so on. On the other hand, your soldiers can be seriously hit including poison, broken bones, septic wound, and more. Each soldier can only carry 6 items (some of which can have QTY > 1) so item management can be important as no one can carry everything. In RTS mode, movement controls are limited, but once you enter tactical mode, you can move soldiers about and give more individualized orders. Time also slows down tremendously, giving you time to give precise orders, like go here and kill that (and stay there).
My main gripe with the game is difficulty in accessing all four members of the team, as usually you can only access the team leader. Only in tactical mode can you access all four members. This makes for a very awkward interface when you're the kind of guy that goes after every locker, where you could find inventory from bandages to explosvies.  These are the "crates" in this universe. But the increased reaction time makes entire mess actually doable. All in all, the tactical mode needs a bit polishing, otherwise it's one fun game.

Two key features missing from the original game were Multiplayer and Endless Mode. Orcs Must Die! 2 fixes both of those problems as well as adding many new traps, maps and weapons! New Trolls, Ogre types and dangerous Kobolds take the charge again too over through the human world and stem the flow of magic. Only the Defenders of the Rift and the twisted hallways of their fortress, laced with traps, can stop them.

Quite the fun, fast paced, orc killing game. A bit of a mix of strategy, action and tower defense, this game has something everyone will enjoy. Gameplay is similar to the first Orcs Must Die! but with a few changes that enhance the already fantastic experience. An additional character with new traps, abilities and weapons as well as the classic "bro-mage" of course. Many new levels with countless possible ways slaughter thousands of orcs gives the game incredible replayability. New game modes including endless give hours of potential fun to expand on the already extensive level system. The upgrade system has been expanded as well, customizing traps to suit your needs.
Graphics are identical to the first with a few minor updates, they suit the game very well and look great. The soundtrack is actually quite good as well, suits the game and is not overly dramatic and keeps the mood fun.
Perhaps the biggest addition to this game is the co-op system. Orcs Must Die! with a friend? Yes please!
Overall a must play for everyone, this game has something to offer any type of gamer from a casual "few hours a week" person to a hardcore gamer looking to get hooked on something new. If you haven't played the first Orcs Must Die! I suggest completing it before playing this for story purposes, it is not a requirement to enjoy the game however.

There is actually so much to like about this game -
- Line set up is very easy and the way other games should implement it
- Time progression is great - you get to play through various eras
- Town growth simulation seem pretty decent to me - I have no problem with it!
- You get trains, trams, buses, trucks - not just trains!
- Building rail lines are generally easy.
What I don't like about the game:
- There are very few vehicles available.  There's never really a choice to make - there is usually only one tram, one train, one truck or one train to choose (at some points trains give you maybe another option).  It would be great to have more vehicles without mods.
- It's sometimes difficult to bridge or tunnel over or under tracks - it needs to be simpler.
- This is temporary only maybe, but the issue that others reported where the game freezes on the 1st of each month started plaguing me since the update on 30 January.  That's made it almost unplayable for me.
- More in-game tutorials or help is needed or just some easy to understand documentation.  I thought trains were useless until I did some extensive reading and watching loads of Youtube videos to fully understand how industry works.  At least all my trains are profitable now!
- There should be something else to play for - I've pretty much got most of the achievements now - so not too much incentive to play a game.  Missions maybe or scenarios?
Overall though, this game has kept me entertained far longer than most.

Train Fever offers some great gameplay and trasportation simulation that made me think, "Just one more delivery" then it's one hour later and the sun is about to come up. I was very hesitant at first when I was reading the reviews, then I watched a playthrough on YouTube and the urge to buy it was eating me up on every video I clicked, so I finally musterd up and bought it. I certainly don't regret it and the reviews that people are nagging about are relatable, but definitely tolerable. Of course it has it's flaws, and yes, it is lacking on other key features... Such as a world editor or even scenarios. This game has none! All you do is just build routes for trains, trucks, trams, and buses. Don't get me wrong, it is a fun game. The level of simulation and detail is very stunning when you get down to street level. The way the game tracks every citizen in every city, then those citizens have their own destinations such as, work, leisure, shopping, and home. You can either follow your tains, or follow someone's life. This is what really gives me a rich gaming experience is just how detailed it is.

Although this game offers much playtime, after a while, you run into some obsatcles... After you unlock every vehicle, you run into a "what now" situation.. especially if you already connected every town and industry. You do have achievements to unlock, but those aren't exactly 'scenarios' per say. I really wish this game had some kind of opposing AI or scenario/campaign option and a world editor as well so you can make your own scenarios.

Some people call it a "tycoon" game, but it's honestly not. You don't "own" a company, and you don't "own" any industries. You literally just build lines for your vehicles and make/lose money. There is an economic model in the game, but it's basic. It's not like the Railroad Tycoon series kind of economy where it was rather advanced.

One of the most annoying things that take away from the experience is when you need to upgrade your bus stations/train stations. When your cities grow, more people will use your lines and time advances so you get really nice and new stations, but you first have to destroy the old ones. Oh, and if you have buildings really close, you'll have to destroy those too before you build your new one!, which can be very costly! The game gets real finicky when you try to make/change: bridges, stations, crossings, and tunnels so beware! The game engine is not fully optimized since it's custom made for this game. So, be aware of that after many in-game years your cities will become large. And as they grow, your game will start to suffer in FPS. It doesn't matter how beefy your PC is, it will struggle to keep your FPS above 30 if you have a city with 1,000 people.

The devs need to implement an upgrade system for your stations where you click once and hit 'upgrade' instead of making it harder to bulldoze and stuff, but that was just me from playing Railroad Tycoon 3.

1. Performance is exceptionally poor. By the time you get to 1950, expect your computer to stutter badly even on small maps. This has been only somewhat fixed in subsequent patches but the overall performance still is lackluster.
2. Game mechanics either don't work correctly or are so poorly explained as to be frustratingly obtuse. Some things - like resource production or auto-replacing vehicles - only work sporadically. Others like city growth and even how to set up signals are so obtuse they're not fun. They could have done a much better job of either providing more information on screen or perhaps a better tutorial. There are some quite un-fun mechanics in here that could and should have been much more elegant.
3. Gameplay is fairly limited. There are precious few industries, a static map (there's never a new resource node or challenge you have to react to), limited supply chains, etc. All of thise makes for a less-than-ideal experience. Transport Tycoon this isn't, even if it says it would like to be. There are no ships, no planes either. In short, nothing dynamic happens even though the time period encompasses the Industrial Revolution, 2 World Wars, etc. Cities grow slowly and vehicles change but the lack of industry growth is a massive flaw.
4. Probably the biggest killer is a lack of feedback to the player. There is very limited information. Want to know how many people use a bus stop? Sorry. Want to know why someone decided to walk or drive to work? Sorry. Want to know where that passenger is headed? You could be delivering plenty of coal and iron to a plant and production won't rise but the game won't give you an inkling why. You simply don't know what's happening or how to optimize. In other transport games you can get a sense of where the problems are and how to rectify them. This is a fatal flaw in the game and is the reason for the thumbs down.
This was so close to being good. But I think what may have happened is that they ran into such a roadblock with performance issues they never got around to really polishing the gameplay or creating the reporting tools needed by players to make good decisions. Then they went on to Transport Fever and did basically the same thing. It's quite a shame to say it but this one is more frustration than fun.

Sandbox RPG that stands above the crowd. It does everything that every other game in the genre does competently including:
Combo based combat- get your combo high enough to use special moves. "Play it your way" style gameplay system. The "Batman" protagonist shared by all of these games (IE "dark" and grim sounding with a gruff voice, motivated by avenging his family, and has high mobility). ETC
It also has some huge advantages that put it above the competition. Namely:
Combat is a bit more involved with 2 block and 2 attack buttons needed depending on the enemies you are fighting. Plus the ability to pull out your bow at any time is a huge plus.
The amazing "Nemesis System" which- in combination with the ability to control orcs (or whatever they are called) - provides over 5-10 hours of engaging procedural gameplay. This combined with orcs gaining ranks when they kill you makes the system exciting, and gives you an incentive to stay alive.
The sandbox is small, but also as big as it needs to be. Even without fast-travel, you can get anywhere you need to be in a few minutes maximum. And every area feels unique. No boring walks through samey terrain
Of course it's not without its flaws, the largest of which (that isn't just a result of its genre) is:
The way keys are bound. Every button does 4 things depending on context and I have failed about 6-8 times in missions because my guy stealth mind-controlled an enemy instead of dropping down a ledge. There's no way to separate these functions into different buttons even on keyboard (and you probably should play on keyboard and mouse even though the bow has aim assist).
Overall I would recommend it. It does the AAA experience better than many other games in the genre for a fraction of their price. It's also been ported to every system, even Linux and Mac, so when it inevitably goes on sale for 5 dollars it's worth checking out.

Tank Force is an easy way to waste a few hours if you're not into hardcore simulation games, but enjoy a bit of tank on tank action.  It is a PAY TO WIN game essentially, the more you want to spend, the more success you'll have.
It's got an arcade feel to it, it's easy to play, doesn't require any deep strategy and is enjoyable for a basic tank on tank game.  Imagine a less involved version of the tank combat in War Thunder, it's like that but very basic.  A little too basic IMO.
You enter, wait 30 seconds for other players, and then you scramble to get into the action, which involves locating and destroying other tanks.   The flag of the country other players are from is a cool feature, but the hud tends to be a little crowded.   Once a tank is spotted, it appears on the mini map and the screen as a red indicator, which removes any challenge when it comes to identifying an enemy.
Upgrades are the key; the better stuff you have, the more success you will have.   Rewards are generous and the menu system is easy to use and looks great, but again, it's pay to win and a WoT rip off.
Good Stuff
- easy to play
- enjoyable until you get sick of it, which won't take long
- can sometimes be a challenge when you are getting ganged up on
- The ranking system will keep you engaged for a while.
- There seems to be a mission/campaign type thing in the works which could be good fun
- You can create a team for you and your mates
Not so good stuff
- Graphics make the game look like a 2009 release
- Rounds are too short
- The game is TOO easy, there is little challenge in it
- The hud is too crowded
- The maps are too small, and repetitive
- The more silver and gold you have, the more you'll win - can make the game very unbalanced
- A LOT of server disconnections and other errors which crash the game back to the hangar - common and very annoying, but the game is still in development.
- PAY TO WIN - This is a World of Tanks rip off, and not done particularly well.
Overall it's arcade fun, not for the sim fan.  Currently it's free to play, but there will be in game purchases to get shiny new things, which will disadvantage players that don't want to spend the money, or don't have it to spend.
It's free to play, grab it and give it a go and decide for yourself.

I bought the game during a sale and got a loooot more enjoyment out of it than I initially expected. It's great fun to spend the first while playing the full game through, trying to figure out how to reach coronation without falling prey to unfortunate events (they usually result in your death, but there are other fates that are unsatisfying enough to make you want to try again, too!). Once you've gotten to coronation once or twice, the list of deaths-I mean!-endings is an interesting checklist to complete (I only have one left!), and some of the achievements sound pretty interesting and fun to unlock as well. I'm saving heavily now to be able to tweak my skills without having to restart from scratch, but at this point even if I don't manage to get them all I'm pretty happy with my purchase and looking forward to trying out other games from the developer.
Edited to add: Playing other VNs is helping me better understand why this one is so good. What you choose to study every week has a clear, visible impact on what may happen during the following week(s), because you see what skills are being checked. You can play a very different game depending on what skills you choose to focus on (e.g., I had a go at being nice the first time around and after the humiliating ending it led me to, I ended up putting all my points in military and executing everyone given half a chance in the next run-through ;) Which opened up new storylines I'd had no visibility in until then). You can have spies and send them out to do your bidding. There is no romance as a central plot point and choosing to marry someone (or not) is a more tactical decision. The "default" plot also makes it obvious that there are other storylines you might be interested in unlocking (e.g. the birthday party, Briony) to explore the game/world/deaths even further. Basically playing other games is making me like this one even more :-)

It pains me to say not to get this game, it really does. So okay, if you like visual novels it's decent but falls short on a lot of things.
Firstly, I'm holding it up to Magial Diary standards which was, I believe written by the same person. So if you've played that game you get some scale to it.
Basically there are a few dimensions I'd rate a visual novel on, story, characters, romance, replay value and gameplay.
Story 4/10
Now in the game your mother has just passed away and you're the princess being trained for a year until you can be coronated Queen. There are a lot of sub plots in the sotyr line between family and you'll end up fighting very different wars depending on how you build your character, you might use magic to duel a guy or head out to sea to fight a war. Now while this whole, training to become the Queen sounds good, that's really the main thing to the plot. There isn't much depth to it. Sure, there's some lore of the country thrown around a bit and internal and foreign affairs but... That's it... While Magical Diary had a one dimension of it with just being a school student, you had many different story lines where you either experienced being a treasurer or spent your weekends with the teachers. So each line felt unique and different comparative to just one or two subtle differences being a war on land or a war at sea.
Characters 3/10
With Magical Diary you got the grumpy wumpy teacher who is actually super caring for his students, a demon who is the biggest sweet talker ever and a cute guy who just pulls pranks to get people to notice him. What do you get with Long Live The Queen? A princess. Erhm... Something great about Magical Diary was the character development and progression. You learn the face of the character and then you learn why they are the way they are. In LLTQ you meet a person and say a few lines to them and usually never see them again. Aside from your father the king who you talk to almost weekly but... At one point in the game you can betray his trust and the text says "he will never trust you the same way again." This never plays a part in the game as far as I know. He still talks to you the same way and you just get this feeling that the characters never develop. Even Elodie the main character (princess) is depressed at first due to her mothers death and then she has mood swings every week depending on what weekend activity you give her. So while at first you feel bad for her being sad and depressed you eventually get over it and see it as a way to boost certain attributes. She has little depth to explain how her and her mother use to be nor does she grow and mature. In Magical Diary your own character (default name Mary Sue) progresses from being a human who just found out she's a witch to learning about the world around her and all the magic in it. While she doesn't have that much character growth, it's better than Elodie.
Romance 0/10
Okay, really? A 0 rating? Maybe it's because I'm a girl but visual novels always lure me in with the many romantic options. It's like that feeling you had in jr high when the cute guy walks up to you and you have once shot to say the right thing or he'll think you're weird and never talk to you again. But really, in LLTQ you can just agree to marry someone you just hear about in passing. "Hey this guy is in a nearby kingdom... Wanna get hitched?" At the end of the game you literally click a name from a list to decide who you marry. Most of the guys you never see an image of nor do you learn anything about them as characters. Magical Diary had this magical (lol) feel when it came to romance. You could even woo a character of the same gender. You then went on dates and your actions would decide if you'd stay together or not.  I expected from LLTQ that Elodie would be met by suiters who all wish her hand in marriage and you'd get the typical poor guy from the street who is actually really nice, the guy who just wants to marry to become king, etc, etc. But now, you get a name and a splash screen telling you about how many kids you had. I expected carriage rides on the weekend and roses and flowers. It'd certainly make the death by chocolate a little more shocking if it came from a suiter who you had been seeing.
Replay Value 7/10
Hey! An above 5 rating! But really, no matter how you decide to build Elodie, animal care taker, war master or perfect princess, little changes between each choice and little in the game reflects thus. Sure you get a different event here and there maybe small dialogue changes here and there but that's really it. While there are multiple endings you can get based on multiple decisions, you really learn the main events and know what to answer to get your desired result. Week after week you can just skip text and not really feel any different between playthroughs. While the different endings do entice and warrent a few playthroughs extra, unlike Magical Diary where the other romance options and options on school positions almost became an addicting factor to replay the game, LLTQ endings just seem better to google since there isn't an alluring experience attatched to your path. Magical Diary, you fall in love with a teacher? You have a whole arc where you get married and need to stay on his good side. You fall in love with the sweet talking demon? You're treated to romance and then a choice to go to the dark side or find a way to tame him. LLTQ fails to provide a unique experience with each play through.
Gameplay 6/10
So each week you pick a morning and afternoon class and based on your mood you get either + or - bonus points to that trait. Very similar system to Magical Diary except MD just used stress instead of multiple emotions. So you'd think LLTQ would win here but no... While MD let you pick between green, red, black, etc magic and learn different spells, LLTQ's different skill sets just lead to a new outfit and small dialogue changes with a few plot points being different. Again you either fight a guy with magic or fight a war at sea. While there are multiple paths you can take, after one good playthrough it become easy to know what to do. Just maxing out one section usually gets you to the end to be coronated queen. A thing LLTQ did to be cute was the different deaths you can have, it felt like it could have done more with it. It just seems like there could have been more downfalls to your character. Obviously if a well roudned character was needed then clearly you'd never replay the game because it'd be the same stats you'd level up but being able to get by as long as one area of attributes is fully leveled up seems weak almost. While you'll always have around two attribute areas fully maxed out, it doesn't add much, like you don't get a special ending or events because you mixed animals and magic. Given, MD didn't do that either save for a few minor plot points based on stats but MD more than made up for that.
Verdict 3/10
While you could argue MD is more of a dating sim and LLTQ is a... uh... becoming a queen sim, LLTQ falls short on even none romance related things. Sure the artwork is super cute and adorable but aside from Elodie, the characters don't have much artwork to express emotions like in MD and there arn't that many background images for different areas unlike MD which had tons. Overall, while the game might be worth it when on sale since the cards pay for about $.50-$1 of the cost bringing it down to around $1-2 when on sale (sale price Summer 2014 $2.49) getting it for the full price isn't really worth it. I really love the company who produces these games and the writer who writes it, but having a cute cover artist cover poor plots, lacking elements and overall gameplay just doesn't sit right. 11.2 hours on Magical Diary, 2.4 hours in Long Live the Queen, it's quite obvious which one I kept going back to. For those reasons, I cannot reccomend this

It's both simple and complex at the same time. Simple in that the micromanaging of your character is pretty easy ; complex in that it's more than just clicking a skill and progressing. You have to really think about what you need/want to do.
I would recommend this for anyone who enjoys visual novels and/or enjoys the "choose your own adventure" genre.
If neither of those describes you, it's likely you will not enjoy it.

This is a very fun and challenging Turn-Based-Strategy game. It is just a shame there is no campaign mode.
You basically play just one map and one group of adversaries. Once you finish off your adversaries the game is over. However, you get to pick the difficulty level, and map size (Islands, Continents, Supercontinents, or Great Land),  Depending on the size of your map you then get to choose how many adversaries you face. So this one and done combat mode can be quite long if you choose a big map and six adversaries.
Resource management is easy, which I like. You just build structures based on what you need most for your characters to succeed and then you never have to monitor them. You have spells, characters you create through your facilities, and also characters that come along and offer their services for a price. Take care of these out-sourced characters as they become quite powerful as they level up, and once they are dead their gone. Other than that, research lots of spells and kick some mage butt.
pros: combat, ease of resource management, good graphics and sound, plenty of cool spells to research, plenty of unique characters.
Cons: no campaign, may not be complex enough for hard core RTS gamers.
Worth $20 but probably best to pick it up at one of Steams many holiday sales.

When I first heard about this game I didn't think much of it. I might have even started watching the first episode of a lets play and clicked off because it didn't immediately interest me.
Then it showed back up in my life at the perfect time to ♥♥♥♥ me up good. It made me cry and it made me laugh and it made me think.
It's honestly not the easiest game to play. Most of the time you walk from place to place talking to people throughout the town of Possum Springs. The dialogue is entirely text based, so you do a lot of reading, but I ultimately think this decision is good because some of the lines in this game can definitely come off wrong (maybe even cringey) if they were to be voiced by someone who didn't fit the role perfectly.
But it's all worth it. The game creates really believable and likable characters that makes you WANT to read everything everyone in the town has to say. You don't relate with a single character so much as connect with and understand individual parts of each character's persona. In saying that, there is something in this game's characters for anybody. It covers dissassociation, depression, self-worth, friendships, coming of age, queerness, rebelliousness, and more in ways that don't undermine, simplify, or demonise these things. It's scarily human.
That's not to say the whole game is a walking simulator where you read people's dialogue. The game has some interesting gameplay moments which are a bit gimmicky but still fun none the less (and act as a way to get closer to the characters still) and the actual plot, while mostly hidden for the first quarter to half of the game, is actually pretty unique and engaging without really coming off as pretencious. The ending might be a bit disappointing for some (read: sudden), but that doesn't detract from the journey itself. And chances are, you'll want to go back and replay the things you missed the first time around, which if you're like me, is a lot.
If you aren't into story games, still give this one a look. Check my hours, I sink most of my time into first person shooters, yet this game still stands out as one of the best experiences I've had with a video game.
Also music is 10 out of ♥♥♥♥ing 10. Soundtrack is beautifully done and goes to show Alex Holowka's diversity and expertise as a musician (he also composed music for Towerfall Ascension. talented guy!)

I'm ridiculously addicted to this game.   I played an early build, left the game for awhile, then returned to the latest build, and I can't stop playing.
Looking at some of the negative reviews, it's important to know what you're getting.  I think people are expecting an intense survival game.  Maybe it will be as they continue to flesh it out.
In its current state, though, Stranded Deep is a relaxing game with some intense survival elements (i.e. entering the water for any length of time, which can cause drowing, poisoning, shark attacks, etc).
What the game gives you is a large tropical sandbox to do anything you want for as long as you want.  The caveat is that you are completely alone, save for the creatures in the ocean and two or three forms of wildlife on some of the islands.
If you like doing whatever you want at your own pace, can set your own objectives and goals, like playing open-ended games in the first person perspective, and want to have a mostly relaxing experience where you create your own danger, then this game is for you.
If you want co-op, constant struggle for survival, pre-defined missions or objectives, or an endgame scenario other than death, you probably need to wait for a future build or find something else to play for now.
What I love most about the game is the zen-like experience of being totally alone in the game world (not counting the aforementioned dangers).   It's just you, serene tropical environments, finite natural resources on the islands, and a dangerous ocean that offers infinite food sources, exploration, and potential death.
For those having trouble with framerates or jerky movements, just tweak the settings.  Turn off the volumetric clouds, reduce the ocean settings to low, and tweak the mouse smoothness and sensitivity.   The game still looks fantastic even after making these tweaks.   Eventually, the developers will make the higher end settings more optimized for the average gaming rig.
For those who struggle when games don't tell you what to do constantly or how to "win," try immersing yourself in the situation and doing what you would do next, or even better, come up with a backstory for your survivor and try to play the game through their eyes.  Bottom line, you have to use your imagination to get the most out of this experience.
Overall, I give this game a 9/10, and I heartily recommend it for people looking for a relaxing, entrancing experience with survival elements.

I bought this game a while back and was satified with the infinte world and neat features. Now, the developers have decided that infinite world generation is no longer needed in a game like this. This was the main thing that Stranded Deep had going for it, in my opinion. The expansive world was limited to a 5x5 grid for "testing purposes" but, after the switch to dx11, I fear that this situation of finite worlds will not improve. Many games feature infinite or nearly infinite worlds (e.g. Minecraft, Space Engineers, Starbound, etc. ), so why the step backward for this game?
The devs need to open up past builds in the beta tab and need to start separating the unstable from the stable releases. Pushing unfinished or buggy releases on people, and not putting it under the beta tab for people to try, was not a good idea. I bet the recent ratings would not have dropped so low had they done such a thing.
Maybe there will be a change in direction for this game later on. Until then, don't waste your money.

Wonderful game! Its fine as vanilla, and even better with mods. It's like having your own living model railroad, without spending a fortune. As the game goes on, the towns grow toward your stations, buildings, cars, and even the pedestrian's clothing styles change. You can spend hours just getting your lines set perfectly; the learning curve is not too steep, yet the gameplay is pretty complex, with each individual citizen having their own schedule, home, and workplace.
All that complexity has a bit of a price though; I don't recommend playing a map size larger than "small" if you have a 32 bit system. Even with 64 bits, the game will start to lag toward endgame (there are now mods to help with that though.)
The graphics are a bit cartoonish, which I think was the point, its like a model railroad, not intended for hardcore realism. The sounds are fine, but the music soundtrack leaves a bit to be desired IMO, it doesn't fit the mood of the game at all.
Overall, I HIGHLY recommend this game if you are interested in trains, model railroads, or transit systems at all.
