My review is different from many of the other recent reviews.  I don't mind the single-player campaign.  It gets tough but I enjoy micro-managing the 4 units and upgrading each one.  You go into tactical mode and move each one, use their abilities etc.
I have no crashes on my Nvidia 780 with latest drivers.
As for multiplayer, I've only tried a few times to get into games because I want to finish the campaign first.  I'm about half way through campaign with 8.5 hours played.  When I did join multiplayer, there were 2 games going and I had no issue getting into them.  From what I see, there is a diehard core group of players from Europe and US that play.  I can't really speak to much more of it than that.
There is a tutorial level, and once you 'unlock' tactical mode, you realize that you can control each trooper and really set up some tactical advantages.  There's lots of places to look for crates/loot to help with your mission.  I usually have tons left over.  The spawns aren't endless, but watch your ammo.  There are devices that seal up some of the 'creature' holes so you can start taking back some of the maps and assist your missions.
It's a game like Alien Swarm, if you could slow down alien swarm and micro manage each trooper.  Also kind of like Breach and Clear but with a lot more granularity.
It's $8 on sale right now, which I feel is a REALLY good price.  At $20, I'd say try it, get through the first mission where you learn everything, and wait for the tactical mode lesson because that's the real mechanic to this game for singleplayer.  If you get through it, you should still be under your 2 hours, refund it.
It is still under active development, the devs just released a new game mode last week (2/1/17).

Game mechanics are completely incoherent. The entire combat is designed very well, to fight up about 3-4 enemies at once. When do you find yourself fighting 3-4 enemies at once? Almost never. You're almost always just warmed with 50+ orcs at the same time like it's Dynasty f*cking Warriors. So almost the entire game you are fighting 50+ enemies with a combat skillset specifically designed for 3-4 enemies at a time. What?
The second biggest problem is that during your quest to do something else, including resolving a power struggle, other random orc captains can f*cking randomly just be around the general area or be on the way to the next quest objective, which means now you have to do the actual objective AND fight the new officer.
What is worse, the difficulty of the new captain is completely random. This can derail your side mission and waste a lot of time. What makes this problem even worse is that it takes a whole lot of time to actually pick up powerups dropped from dead defeated captains, during which you are NOT invulnerable.
I have had fights going on for 45+ minutes that started as a simple power struggle, then some orc captain shows up and I have to fight them. Then in the middle of fighitng THAT orc captain ANOTHER one shows up, and so on and so on. It went on for a LONG LONG time before I could FINALLY actually go and pick up the 20 or so powerups from my huge line of defeated captains, or I die from something and then miss the powerups. Needless to say, this is completely dumb.
I think with this game such a randomised experience can mean some players get a set of warlocks that arent too hard to deal with, and some people just get impossible ones until they're level 999999999 with max unlocks everything, the shallow design not helping the cause here. I got some pretty super easy randomized orcs, and I've gotten some bloody impossible ones. For some people it was too easy and I can definitely see that. For me it was mostly too easy, until you get unlucky and get some impossible combination warchief with bodyguard who are also impossible combinations that killed it for me. I feel like the randomisation here is so depended upon yet so underdeveloped. Whoever coded this hasn't actually put in the playtesting effort to actually make it work consistently. It is hit or miss and when it misses it REALLY misses.
I would suggest:
- When I'm on a quest (side / main), like I pressed an ACTUAL BLOODY QUEST START BUTTON TO START A BLOODY QUEST, remove ALL possibility of random orc captain / officer encounters. Despawn them. I want to be focused on the quest experience without being derailed by having to fight 8 other random bloody captains that just stumbled in.
- Make upgrade pickup animation invulnerable, and stun all surrounding orcs when it happens.
- Implement a director AI logic in order to pace out random captain walk-in engagements when the player is focused trying to do something else. Maybe 1 or 2 occasional is good, but when you get a long bloody chain of 20 officers that drag every fight out to 45+ minutes the game is broken.
- Spawn less but more powerful normal guard enemies, or buff AOE attacks. either focus on the 4-5 enemies experience or go Dynasty Warriors route and give me a moveset that can actually deal with 50+ enemies. A moveset designed for 4-5 enemies then throw 50+ guards at me is like giving someone tweezers and telling them to use that to build a tank. Wrong tool for the job.
- If you are going to rely your entire main story missions on randomly generated enemies, make sure the random generation is consistent and actually playtest this random generation. Don't have a boss immune to everything with bodyguards immune to everything except 1 achiles heel. Have at least 2 weaknesses, and rather than hard immunity I think soft immunity works better where instead of just saying no you can't do it, just make it less effective.
For anyone that actually thinks the fighting mechanics this game is remotely good, I have a few suggestions to improve your life:
Step 1: Install Devil May Cry 3
Step 2: Play that for 80 hours straight
Step 3: Go back to Shadow of Mordor
Step 4: Now try to tell me with a straight face that Shadow of Mordor has good fighting LOL don't crack me up.

There are two parts to this review:
1. Was the title well crafted, and stylistically coherent
2. Are you going to enjoy playing it?
Well Crafted?
1. Short answer: yes.  This is the highest quality game that's come out in years.
The art, the physics, the fonts, the sound effects--the distances that you walk to get places--all work to tell the story of a very specific thing which is rarely put into words.  This game does what it set out to do, and does it better, than maybe any other game.  The real question is: do you feel okay about what they set out to do?
Are you going to like playing it?
2. Short answer: maybe
This game is one of the most incisive culture commentaries I've ever seen.  It's fallen straight out of the twilight zone, to give us a peak at what we, as society, look like from the outside.
Noteworthy:
- If you are being critiqued by this game, you may not enjoy it
- If you don't relate to anyone in the game, you may not realize other people feel this separated from game characters already, here in the IRL.
- The story is made from your reactions to the things you see in the game, and it takes place in your head.  If you don't resonante with anything that happens in the game, you won't resonate with the story you make for it
Platformer mechanics:
These are platformer light mechanics.  If you want to master a system, then you won't be able to have that experience, because there's no platforming system to master.  You just use it for transportation, and it's not a lot more exciting than transportation.
Action and pacing:
There is a shocking amount of action in this game, but only if you expect there to be no action at all.  If you're looking for a game which requires you to respond quickly to being in danger, you won't have that experience either.  It's basically not present.
Completion/Collection:
If you're looking for things to collect and complete, you won't find much of it in this game.  While this is an RPG, it's only the story from an RPG, and everything else has been removed.  If you don't like RPGs, because you don't like seeing the world from someone else's perspective, then you'll probably have a difficult time getting into this game.
Skill Mastery:
If you want to master skills, you will have either a good time or a bad time, depending on whether or not you can understand what the game is trying to do.  As you play the game, you're supposed to see some crazy inter-personal dynamics that don't really seem okay.  Now that you've seen them in the game, try to see them back outside, in the IRL.  You will find these social dynamics repeated quite often.  If you feel like you should object to it in the game, think about whether or not you should object to it, just in general, or if there's something more specific you're objecting to.
Summary:
Anyone who says it's a "bad game" actually means they didn't have a good time.  Anyone who says it's not well crafted, doesn't actually understand what it means when a game is well crafted.  If you can't find well crafted things you don't like, then it's probably because the-fact-that-you-like-it-yourself is part of your definition of well crafted.  If that's true, then you think nothing can really be good, while excluding you.  I leave it to you to decide if that's good or bad.
If you want a new experience, play this game.  If you want a new take on your favorite experience, don't look for it here.  This is a new experience, you still might like it.  For me, I probably give the mechanics a 92/100, but I give the guts of trying something like this: three drops of blood, mixed into a glass of rose.

GUIDE TO GETTING STARTED (with review below)
Launch Krosmaster Arena from your steam Library and you should see a pop-up window. Now before you click the big play button there are some things you should know that you will want to do first to get it set-up properly!
First off Krosmaster Arena is actually made in France with an English translation so occasionally some of the menu's can be misinterpretated. THAT BEING SAID:
!!!!! -- BEFORE YOU CLICK PLAY -- !!!!! (from the pop-up's bottom right corner) You will want to click the icon that looks like 2 little gears in the top right corner of the pop-up window (that appears after you launch Krosmaster Arena from Steam) and that should bring up an OPTIONS window that should ask (ONLY the FIRST time) if you've previously created an Ankama account for Krosmaster Arena. If you do NOT already have an Ankama account then please select use my steam account. IT SHOULD THEN SAY CONNECTION SUCCESFUL!!! Now try clicking play for the first time. Chances are that upon the first time attemping to play you will get an error and the game won't launch succesfully, if that happens just close Krosmaster and re-launch it a second time from Steam.
v v v THIS IS IMPORTANT!!!!! v v v
-----------------------------------------------------------------
NOW EVERY TIME YOU LAUNCH Krosmaster Arena from steam you need to click the icon of the 2 gears in the top right corner of the pop-up window and it should bring up a window with the header "OPTIONS" at the top; make sure you are in the tab labeled "my account" with the single button labeled "Sign-in with Ankama Account" click that and it should come up with the message "Connection Successful". Now you can close the Options window and click play and Krosmaster Arena should run successfully.
-----------------------------------------------------------------
^ ^ ^ IMPORTANT ^ ^ ^
Upon playing Krosmaster Arena for the first time you will be prompted with a tutorial that will teach you how to play. After you finish the tutorial's 5 stages you will want the hit your escape key on your keyboard to open your in game options menu and you will want to click on "SAVE MY ACCOUNT" this will make it so that your Steam account is a fully fledged Ankama account so that you can use your same account on mobile devices and so that if you already have the table top version or figure expanions then you can have those Krosmasters to play using key codes. Now when you are filling out this window with your e-mail, password, and username, The category titled "username" is actually your "nickname" it's a translation error. Later on if you've been playing for a couple hours you'll probably get a pop-up in between one of the game menu's that asks you to re-verify your account by asking you FILL IN YOUR >>USERNAME AND PASSWORD<<, but again it's a translation error because what it really wants is your >>>>E-MAIL AND PASSWORD<<<<... Be sure also verify your account by taking care of the verification e-mail that you'll be sent.
=============================================
v v v PROBLEMS CHALLENGING A FRIEND!!!??? v v v
In game when you are not in a battle you SHOULD have a little golden colored bell in the bottom right corner of your screen that you use to accept challenges from friends... How ever if it's not there it's because your screen resolution might not work properly at first and so it's cutting off a sliver of the bottom portion of the game. To fix this all you have to do is go into your options by hitting your escape key and going into the video tab and uncheck full screen and change your screen resolution to be lower. If you want to play the game in fullscreen and still have the bottom portion of the game visible then all you need to do is  (after doing the previous of unchecking fullscreen) exit the game, then re-launch it from steam (Don't forget to click the icon of the 2 gears and connect your account before clicking play) and then enter the in game options by hitting your escape key and then re-enable full screen. From now on your game should no longer have this issue of cutting off the bottom of the screen. =)
You can challenge a friend by entering the arena, and going to the challenge tab at the bottom there should be a button labeled "Challenge a Friend" and then just type in there username. =D
=============================================
TUTORIAL + TIPS UNSPECIFIED:
A few nice tips not specified in the tutorial is that you can left click and hold on the green squares to draw a line for your characters movement and that you can right click to cancel things. Also if you left click and hold on the map you can move the camera while right clicking and holding on the map will allow you to rotate the camera. And one last tip is that in the upper right corner durring a battle there is a button that looks like a brown book with the letter 'K' on it that when clicked will open a timeline so you can see what you and your opponent's dice rolls are.
When you roll a crit it gives +1 to damage given, a shield gives -1 to damage recieved, a flee (shoe) gives +1 for you to flee/escape, a lock (magnet) gives -1 to the opponent trying to flee/escape to avoid being locked, and a Dofus (dragon egg) automatically gives you the roll wanted per given situation. AT THE BEGINNING OF EACH TURN you get the ability to give some of your characters a second/extra dice for certain rolls; Ex.: Like a giving a character the crit die so they can roll 2 dice to attempt to get +1 damage per roll... The dice are six sided with 1 face of each of the 4 main icons, crit, shield, flee, lock, but the dice also have a face with the Dofus icon which can count as any 1 of the 4 main icons, along with the sixth face being a crit + flee icon where you choose either crit or flee.
When one of your Krosmasters dies you lose (and your opponent) gains Gallons of Glory equal to the dead Krosmaster's level, but it should also be noted there is 1 Wild Gallon of Glory in reserve that gets taken before you or your opponents Gallons of Glory get taken. The 1 Wild Gallon of Glory can not be removed from the "Intensity Rises" effect caused by rolling 2 of the same icons at the beggining of each players turn SO LONG as it is still in the reserve. However if someone purchases a Gallon Glory by using one of the shops or when the FIRST Krosmaster dies then the first Gallon of Glory purchased/taken will be the 1 Wild Gallon of Glory (removing it from the reserve) with the rest then coming from the players themselves.
=============================================
REVIEW:
If you want a strategy game that is flexible, diverse, and fluid but is easier and quicker to play than 40,000K or Warmachine, but still able to be competative, then this is the game for you! =D Grid based game play, teams assembled based on point value, Initiative turn order and character activation order, melee attacks, ranged attacks, and summon abilties, along with characters having 1 use abilties per turn, per target, or per game. Stats of movement points, action points, and health points. Per game shops to purchase items for use per game from currency collected from that game only. The ability to purchase the table top version and unlock characters in game using key codes so you don't have to buy the DLC Character packs if you've already got the table top version / expansions. It's a good game, If what I just listed sounds like it might be worth giving a try then I would definately recomend it. =)

I cannot recommend this game to most people. My issue with The Red Solstice is that it feels flawed and incomplete, it is plauged by questionable design decisions and poor balancing combined with a steep learning curve. All that being said the game can be quite fun when playing with a few friends of similar experience level and if you have a group of four or more to play and learn this game with you may find something enjoyable here, but for everyone else I would advise staying away.
The single player campaign is serviceable but quickly gets rote, and the multiplayer component is dissapointing due to many questionable design choices and poor balancing that is made worse by the experience gap new players will face when joining a lobby with veteran players. You'll find yourself confused and more or less useless for a number of hours before being able to contribute to the team, and once you learn how to properly play the game you'll likely find the experience is not at all what you wanted in the first place. The game works against itself in a number of ways that inhibit strategy and interdependence of the classes. The demolitions class for instance will be made almost entirely useless due to the abundance of lootable explosives IF the team even decides to rely on these devices, but more importantly you can beat the game without ever placing a single explosive or launching a single rocket. Indeed most players merely circle the map with auto-fire on while the faster classes loot ammo. There is never really a need to set up static defense, and on the higher difficulties where it would potentially be viable, the cooldown on such abilities makes it impossible anyway. On top of this few teams will think about their location in relation to enemy units and often times are in the line of fire of heavy ordinance which makes it impossible to use without killing a friendly. The depth of the class system is diminished by the nature of the game.
The other big problem The Red Solstice has is it's pacing. It encourages players to never stop moving. The looting, securing objectives, activating power nodes, etc all happen while on the run. Setting up a static defense is simply not supported, there is no way to lockdown doors, and even items like barricades are useless... not as in poorly implimented, as in the developers never bothered to apply collision detection to them so enemies walk right through these barricades. All slower, and defense oriented classes fail to play as one would expect as a result of this, and indeed the game becomes about patroling the map rather than each class utilizing it's niche focus to support the team. The game really only feels like it has 3 classes, the Medic, and then the rest being a DPS varient, with one acting as a fast looter. This game would be far better if it allowed for setting up actual fortifcations to secure areas and encouraged players to balance offense and defense tactics by establishing a zone of control and having mobile members fetch and secure objectives and luring hordes and large enemies into the heavy fire of your static defense. It would be far better if large enemies required explossive damage to make them vulnerable to small arms fire, it would be far better if it encouraged thinking and planning over running and gunning, especially because the game does not control like a run and gun game. It controls like an RTS, but other than presenting the facade of a strategy game, there is litle strategy to be found.
I would have liked to have seen the game rely less on bullet sponge enemies and more on forcing players to manage proper firing arcs or face the deadly consequences. Instead the marine behaves in typical rts faction and spins and shoots incoming enemies automatically. The game does provide a manual aim, but it is poorly communicated to the player and the ui for it is terrible. There is no tactical advance in this game, there is no managing firing arcs, there is no establishing a base of operations, there is no flexibility. Like an rts, you group up and blob the enemy and that is a damn shame.
This sort of gameplay was acceptable when it was a modifcation for a 2003 strategy game, it is not acceptable as a stand alone title, and rather than evolve the concept they ripped it almost unchanged from the mod which inspired it. I am hopeful that with the next game in this franchise they are able to get things right, but from the looks of it so far it appears to be a less interesting alien swarm.
I would advise the developers to look at titles like full spectrum warrior which required establishing firing arcs and moving the squad tactically. Translated to the rts perspective something like that could work well and better define the pace and balance of gameplay.
As a stand alone genre this type of game is still new, and with that comes some hiccups. I applaud these developers for trying to establish this genre, unfortunately the title is too bogged down by the mods that inspired it.

Such potential lost....
Pros:
+ Emphasis on survival in the zombie apocalypse. Few zombie games out now have such a dire need for survival. You need to collect medicine, food, ammo, fuel, building materials, guns, melee weapons and survivors to make things easier to survive.
+ Multiple ways of dealing with zombies. You can shoot them, run them over, let traps kill them, rely on allies, engaging in melee, hiding and outrunning.
+ Game is lengthy. Many, many hours to complete the main story of State of Decay. You go at your own pace, for the most part, so you could balance between completing missions and gathering supplies for your survival. All missions have a time limit but the limit is long enough to do several things before hand.
+ There are plenty of side missions. Along with the main story, there are a ton of side missions to complete. Completing these side missions will gain you trust, alliances, influence, supplies, other bases and cleared areas of zombies.
Cons:
- Animations are horrible. You, allies, and enemies clip through objects, buildings, walls, the ground, other characters. Not only that, but the animations are very fast, jerky and repetitive. Shooting is difficult if in the duration of half a second a zombie goes from standing still to a crouch to a full on sprint. There is also a problem of reach. Some animations show a zombie lunging for a player and attacks that should have missed animation wise actually hit.
- Few zombie models. Just in the beginning of the game you can go through all the models the zombies have save for special zombies. You can count the number on two hands. For a game this long it gets seriously dull seeing the same clothed zombie over 200 times.
- AI is absolutely horrendous. Your fellow survivors will go out on suicide runs. That is a fact. They will autonomously go out on their own and run into hordes of zombies and then as a last resort blow themselves up with valuable resources such as grenades or Molotov cocktails. They also go out on missions that, if you let the time expire, gets them killed. You will find that this side mission happens A LOT. Their pathing is also subpar. They cannot easily get into a car or a building you enter. It takes them a good minute until they finally follow you. Certain special zombies in the game are too difficult to handle solo so it would behoove you to bring an ally, but you have to constantly battle with their AI. These kind of issues should not happen in any modern game. It shows laziness on the side of the developer.
- Lack of good multiplayer features. Only thing you got is leaderboards. That's it. They said right after the game was released that they will not include any coop into the game. Months in, they said that the second State of Decay will have a mutliplayer feature. So expect a very lonely experience surviving the apocalypse with survivors that have horrible AI.

Game mechanics are completely incoherent. The entire combat is designed very well, to fight up about 3-4 enemies at once. When do you find yourself fighting 3-4 enemies at once? Almost never. So almost the entire game you are fighting 50+ enemies with a combat skillset specifically designed for 3-4 enemies at a time. What?
The second biggest problem is that during your quest to do something else, including resolving a power struggle, other random orc captains can f*cking randomly just be around the general area or be on the way to the next quest objective, which means now you have to do the actual objective AND fight the new officer.
What is worse, the difficulty of the new captain is completely random. This can derail your side mission and waste a lot of time. What makes this problem even worse is that it takes a whole lot of time to actually pick up powerups dropped from dead defeated captains, during which you are NOT invulnerable.
I have had fights going on for 45+ minutes that started as a simple power struggle, then some orc captain shows up and I have to fight them. Then in the middle of fighitng THAT orc captain ANOTHER one shows up, and so on and so on. Needless to say, this is completely dumb.
I think with this game such a randomised experience can mean some players get a set of warlocks that arent too hard to deal with, and some people just get impossible ones until they're level 999999999 with max unlocks everything, the shallow design not helping the cause here. For me it was mostly too easy, until you get unlucky and get some impossible combination warchief with bodyguard who are also impossible combinations that killed it for me. I feel like the randomisation here is so depended upon yet so underdeveloped. Whoever coded this hasn't actually put in the playtesting effort to actually make it work consistently. It is hit or miss and when it misses it REALLY misses.
I would suggest:
- When I'm on a quest (side / main), like I pressed an ACTUAL BLOODY QUEST START BUTTON TO START A BLOODY QUEST, remove ALL possibility of random orc captain / officer encounters. Despawn them. I want to be focused on the quest experience without being derailed by having to fight 8 other random bloody captains that just stumbled in.
- Make upgrade pickup animation invulnerable, and stun all surrounding orcs when it happens.
- Implement a director AI logic in order to pace out random captain walk-in engagements when the player is focused trying to do something else. Maybe 1 or 2 occasional is good, but when you get a long bloody chain of 20 officers that drag every fight out to 45+ minutes the game is broken.
- Spawn less but more powerful normal guard enemies, or buff AOE attacks. either focus on the 4-5 enemies experience or go Dynasty Warriors route and give me a moveset that can actually deal with 50+ enemies. Cubot is a very simple game. Move blocks to their correct color. I was like "This is going to be any easy game". Well I was wrong. The first 3 chapters are hard but not too hard, but chapter 4 will destroy your brain! The game looks nice and simple. The game is also really cheap and it's not a bad cheap game.\
I do recommend this game.

+ The graphics are very simplistic, looks like something that a lot of people can design, but that is what the developers seems to be going for, making everything look simplistic, it tricks the brain into thinking it has a deeper meaning, over complicating it. The game is also colourful, even if it uses around 5 colours (black, white, red, blue, green), they are used well and simply to differentiate the cubes.
+ Gameplay is frustrating at a good level, it really teaches us how annoying the human brain can, you will play a level so hard but when you finally look past the complications and realise how simple it is, you have a laugh and possibly call yourself an idiot, then experience the same thing the next level. Although the game is really short and easy controls as if it were a mobile game, so I wouldn’t be surprised if this indie game was ported to mobile devices like
. The fact it allows the use of Xbox 360 Controllers and PS3 Controllers, allows for more consoles to play it, so it could possibly find itself on the Xbox Store or the PSN.
+ The controls are extremely simple, the arrow keys to change angle, and the WASD keys to move the keys, that is absolutely it. Nothing else is needed to play the game. So Cubot continues to keep it simple.
+ The length of the game is short, that is not bad but some people who love puzzles love lots of puzzles, so since this game looks young, they could possibly introduce a Steam Workshop for the community to create puzzles as well, or give a weekly puzzle, so the game can last longer than just play, finish and leave it in storage forever.
+ Simplicity is the strongest feature of the game, it is focused sorely on making the game so simple to the level where it looks complex, but it isn’t. That is what makes the game so great. We love challenges but they give us something so easy its challenging.
Truthfully, I was scrolling through the Store page, just looking around and I find this $2 game on steam, the pictures and description looked intriguing and I enjoy puzzle games, so I figures why not. And it is one hell of a good way to spend two dollars I'll give ya that.
Cubot achieved a level of simplicity whereas it is very complex. The beginning levels of the game is simple but gradually they make it seem harder, but once you see past the complexity and use simplicity, the game will seem so much easier and you will feel like an idiot. They repeatedly shove in your face that this is simple, so treat it simply. But the human brain isn't hardwired to look at things simply, it is hardwired to over complicate things and look too deeply into something when the answer is literally in your face.
I recommend this game if you like having a more than decent puzzle game at a very affordable and cheap price.

It's basically something like a cheaply made version of "elemental" series. The game seems interesting at beginning, welcoming you with nice graphics and interesting introduction, but it  quickly shows it true colors.
The Diplomacy is tragically primitive. You make your offer , other reject it unless you give him really sweet deal. This doesn't lead to anything. This is based on some really silyl calculation, as for example when AI that was loosing badly wanted to make peace with me, it gave me MUCH better offer for peace (peace+ gold + some spell) a turn after it declined my offer (peace for peace)
Enemy can "demand" something from you and you have choices then "Agree" and "War" .
And that is basically it diplomacy-wise.
The "requests" for aid are just some random kill this build this stuff events, that do not bring anythiing to the gameplay.
The spell system is practically broken by the design. You can basically cast a single spell each turn, and that's it. There is no possibility to really "improve" your casting abilities (you can develop a spell that can help you tiny tiny bit).
The portal to other worlds - because it's quite rare you find it usually a bit in the game, so when you enter the portal you usually find yourself with your single unit surrounded by horde of monsters, that dispatch even your advanced units really fast.
The units progress/upgrades has not been give apparently much though, as the cost/upkeep of units rises out of proportion to the units real power. At some point it would simply be insane to produce best units instead of making more of the average ones. This is especilly visible with the ranged units.
The cities seem to grow ower time and this is somewhat related to food available, but unlike in similar productions it's really hard to see/predict when the city will grow and enlarge it's zone.
The worst part is the ending/ pushing towards the win. At the point when you reach the clear domination over your rivals, you will need at least the same time to finally finish them of.
Combat - combat is pretty standard, although one really really irritating design decision is that if you kill enemy or make him retreat by meele unit, your unit automatically moves in the defeated enemy spot. You have no choice in that matter. So basically if there are more enemy units your "winning" unit practically walks in the middle and get's dispatched at enemy turn.

A most wonderful and intriguing game with a deceptively simple gameplay which in truth hids an ingenious and subtle strategic challenge. The player is required to prepare the main character so as to have her, the princess, survive through all the dangers lying between her and the day of her coronation. The challenge lies in the fact that such dangers are various, hidden or sudden and even the most scrupolous and rigid princess trainer can meet failure by the hands of dirty underhanded traps.
This is to add to a scripted plot which will have you face a great variety of situations which will spell doom for those who will simple and single mindedly specialise too much only in certain education branches.
Every situation, every trap that lies ahead, requires planning to get through and one must be ready to make sacrifices or to be flexibile along the way so as not to perish.
The first run of the game is the most fun and bloody and frustrating of course, with the player discovering the scripted plot and its dangers little by little, but it is the most satisfaying too, due to the sheer joy one feels when (though it would be better to say IF) beating the game and finally reaching the coronation ceremony - it doesn't matter how, if by civil war bloodshed or by enforcing your royal divine right through magic or both, you will just feel relieved and super badass for playing it right.
Subsequent runs of the game keep being entertaining due to the amazing number of combinations of choices to explore so as to unblock all achievements and unveil all the hidden subplots of the game, which I found really well crafted and enjoyable.
In conclusion, the pretty girly graphic is but a cover for a truly magnificent and genial gloomy, grim plot worth of the best fantasy books. The setting itself is pretty solid too and one cannot but marvel at such a precious gem this unfortunately pretty unknown game turns to be.
Last but not least, a note of caution and a piece of advice for new players: beware whom you trust.

This is a game I've come to really enjoy. Although singleplayer experiences are normally my thing, I couldn't bring myself to stick with this game's singleplayer campaign past completion of the first mission. However, the cooperative online mode is quite great. It's a bit tough, which is normally a turn-off for me, but the players in the online community are generally quite helpful and give lots of wonderful tips to success. I wouldn't call myself "good" at the game yet by any stretch of the word, but I know enough to be able to have fun and have a better idea of what's going on than I did when I started and was pretty clueless. The other players were really great despite my idiocy in this game.
Long story short, you all drop down on a planet with funky zombie and xeno monsters, you have simple objectives without much going on plot-wise, and while you're running around completing objectives, the types of enemies are getting tougher and tougher. At first, you have time to get a lot done and try to gather up healing supplies and ammo, but later on, everything will be so hectic that you'll be trying to conserve ammo even more and things just keep getting more intense. Finally, if you live long enough, you can escape on a drop ship, and it feels pretty darn rewarding to survive when you're pretty new to the game. After each mission, you're awarded experience points which unlock skills and new classes, which is fun, though each mission often takes 45 minutes to an hour, so you do need a bit of time to play.
Now comes the big downside to this game. It can be difficult to find people to play with. I've been online before in spurts of 5-10 minutes without a single game available to join, or a lobby trying to fill up desperately. It's quite sad because the game is fun, but it's not always reliable that you'll be able to play when you want to. I came very close to not recommending this game for this reason, but there are people who do play online, and I've had more times that people were online than weren't. With that in mind, I do recommend this game. I wish more folks played it, because it's different than many online cooperative games, and is a nice diamond in the rough.

I can't in good conscious recommend this game.
It was moderately fun and expansive as they built it up from it's humble beginnings. Presently, it is widely expansive, appeals to many game genre preferences (like Platformers/Build-Crafters/Adventure), and has lots of replay value. This is before taking into account the amount and quality of the mods available just through the Steam Workshop. The "Frackin Universe" mod alone is like an expansion and more than doubles the amount of game you have.
That said, this game will suck days of your life away. If you are prone to spending hours and hours building and crafting things from gathered resources like one would do in Minecraft or Terraria, then give your pets away: they won't have a parent anymore. Starbound is the 2D dream that Minecraft dreams, and Terraria is Starbound's ugly little brother that doesn't have internet and never leaves the house.
All that time will be gone. If you have fond memorys of playing through Megaman and Megaman X games and got excited at the dashes and jumps and weapon variety...I am so sorry: Starbound is about to take you from your friends and family. If you took the variety of dashes, jumps, enemies, and weapons found in all the Megaman games and gave them a haircut, a hot shower and helped them put together a resume', Starbound is the job they would apply for.
Speaking of jobs, I hope you don't have one. If you have taken time off from work to game...you have set a horrible precedent. You'll soon be on the streets, huddled under a lean-to behind whatever outlet and wi-fi you can steal to power your laptop and feed your dispicable addiction. No Man's Sky had a lot of hype about being able to explore the universe and adventure on procedurally generated planets, encountering procedurally generated creatures, and interacting with three others races... I hope you didn't get into that hype. I hope you didn't get excited about that stuff, because Starbound beats that. To be precise, though, Starbound's vanilla universe is finite. The star map has coordinates ranging from X-0 Y-0 to X-999999999 Y-999999999, (so just, like, a million times a million or something) with a variety of stars clustered in a variety of ways. Each star type supports a specified variety of planet and biome types, which in turn house a specified variety of creatures, resources and races (six in vanilla). These coordinates mean you can travel to exact planets that you have found previously or that your friends have found. Oh yeah, you can play with friends. Several friends. Assuming you have lost all of your friends to horrible addiction, you can start a new character and travel to the same coordinates of your previous characters and find what they built and left behind.
Like your life. Like the work you put into building your life and then you leave it behind for this game. Do you like Pokemon? You can capture creatures and monsters in Starbound. You can bioengineer them to make them unique and special, good at specific things. Release them on enemies and junk. You can capture a space bear, then augment it to super jump and sprint, throw a ghost collar on it, and have an ethereal Ursa Major that follows you around like the spectre of your social life. Do you like farming games? Starbound let's you farm. Starbound let's you pick whatever planet type you want and setup whatever farming setup you want with whatever crops you want. There is a universe's worth of stuff to grow, and that includes livestock. It's a fun little way to build money up to upgrade your ship that is customizable. You can put a bar in your ship, you can house tenants in your ship, heck, you can build a musuem if you want. You know, because you can friggin find and excavate fossils via mini-game and then reassemble them and display them. You can put anything in your ship. Unlike your life. Your life now only has room for Starbound and cold pizza rolls that you forgot for two hours.
I can't stop you. I can't hold you back from ruining your life. Go ahead and buy this game you poor, sick, trash. Play the vanilla version of this game until you feel like you've done it. And you have a silent moment of peace and serenity, and you start thinking about going outside. Then load up a bunch of mods and expand your game by five times and get sucked back in. This game is your life now. Your real home is the one you built on the asteroid in zero-G that you use grappling hooks to traverse about. You have no anchor to "real" life anymore.

Fun, easy to learn and nice graphics! I can absolutely recommend this transport-(mamagement-) simulator!
Short description: Quite like Transport Tycoon, but better graphics and better gameplay. For guys who know Simutrans, Train Fever is the a little less complicated, but easier and graphically more enjoyable alternative.
It's basically a complex 3D transport simulation game, where you can build and expand (reinvesting your revenue) your own transport network across about 100 Years in a random generated map.
Positive:
+ Easy to learn, so it's also easy to build your own transport-worlds full of marvelous train lines, for goods or passengers.
+ Best graphics for a Transport Tycoon I've seen so far.. Really great for rail-fans, thanks!
+ Enjoyable from the 1 hour to the 200 hour of gameplay (and further, if the developers continue imporving the game).
+ You can and have to really build everything along the railway line, so stations, slopes, bridges, tunnels, everything has to be done by you. You can build everything exactly as you want it (if you earned the money). Still (especially compared to other such simulations) it's easy to learn and sooo much fun!
+ The train and tram models (mostly swiss) you can choose from are gorgeous!
Negative:
- Some bugs are still in the game (eg. occasionally building tools do weird stuff), but most of the severe bugs have been repaired quickly. The developers are quite active.
- The user interface is not very nicely designed, but you'll get used to that after 10 mins.
- Only trains, trams and buses so far (no ships, planes, underground trains, cable cars)..
- Not many train models to choose from yet, but the ones they have are very well modeled!
- No DLCs yet, but the still small community is quite alive.
- You can not drive the trains in your world. But the graphics from looking at them should already warm the heart of any train-fan.
- Passenger behaviour is not yet as complex as in Simutrans Experimental, so sometimes it's not 100% realistic... But for most purposes it works even better than most other transport simulations.
- Only stations with up to 5 tracks and no underground stations or big city infrastructures available yet. So in its current form it's more like a transport simulator for rural railway networks, not megacities yet.
Conclusion: It's great fun for railway fans! With Train Fever I can finally my own beautiful alpine railway landscapes - and gampeplay is really fun... I love it. Buy it..

I love the Arkham series, and in many ways this game can be seen as the same game wearing a different skin. Where I think Shadow of Mordor improves upon this gameplay is the the overall feeling. Sure in Arkham you get to be batman, but that also comes with Batmans limitations and reservations. As a ranger and a wraith, Talion is able to progress into an uruk killing machine, capable of crazy combos, insane skills, and satisfyingly brutal slow motion combat finishers. Towards the end I became the expert of my dance; chaining stealth kills until dropping in to a mob of enemies and grinning the whole time.
I recommend this game to anyone who is a fan of Arkham style combat; if only so you can become a dancing master yourself

I'm a huge fan of games that are inexpensive, minimalistic, indie, and puzzle, so I bought this game as soon as I saw it.
The basic mechanic of the game is that you move colorful cubes (each color having specific atributes) to lead them to their goal. The difficulty comes from the fact that there are multiple levels (extending the game into three dimensions) to deal with, and all cubes move simulaneously; when a cube is moved left, every cube will move to the left. This leads to very interesting and unique gameplay, and as the levels progress, the game grows increasingly challenging. For the perfectionist, at the end of each level, the perfect score for that level is revealed, and you can then retry the level to lower your score the one or two (or five or ten) moves. However, completing the game and earning the achievements do not require this, making the game fun for serious and casual gamers.
The only downside I found to the game is that the sound played when you hover over a button, something required in-between every level, is harsh and out of place with the music. This meant that after about ten levels I muted the sounds, but this fixed the problem, and the ambient sound now fit the game excellently.
I highly recommend this game for the puzzles it provides, and doubly because of the cheap price.

Cubot is, as it states, a very simplistic game.
It's worth the cheap price as it is very similar to some mobile games in terms of length and gameplay.
Simple Controls:
The game offers 3 different ways to control the cubes, two of them being the WASD/Mouse and Xbox360 Controller. The controls consist of (if using the WASD/Mouse) using the WASD to move the cubes Up/Down/Left/Right and using the mouse to move the angle of the camera so you can see the puzzle from different angles. The cubes move square by square and that is pretty much it.
Simple Gameplay:
The objective of each level is to get the colored cubes to the matching colored tile at the same time.
The game introduces the player to different mechanics in the puzzle as the player progresses through each level. Using WASD keys (or whatever control scheme you desire), players move the cubes one tile by one tile, two tile by two tile, etc. (depending on the color of the cube). However the puzzles get harder as the player realizes that cubes of the same color both move simultaneously with each press and introduce more things such as buttons.
Simple Graphics:
Cubot offers a very clean and simple visuals. As the screenshots show, it's cubes with various colors and white tiles with colors painted into some of them.
* Audio Simplicity:
After spending a tiny bit more time on the game, I personally thought that the audio was extremely soothing and compliments the pace and style of Cubot. Although if you are very conscious of the audio, it may become too repetitive or get annoying. Cubot's soundtrack is very, as stated before, soothing and quite atmospheric, somewhat similar to Antichamber for those who have played it. However, some sounds are generated from, for example, hovering the mouse over a menu button (as some reviews have stated) may be "out of place," it's just like Antichamber when you pick up a cube or interact with an object, nothing too awkward.
9/10 Simply Complex.

***This review is intended for people who are newer or unfamiliar with fighters. If you're an experienced fighting game player you probably already know why you love or hate this game!***
This is the gold standard for fighting games. No fighter out there is more balanced, rewards fundamentals and guesses/reads more intelligently, or has the staying power of USF4.
The balance is so impressive. So often, fighting games eventually mature to the point where people have found the 2-3 most powerful characters and the rest of the cast is ignored. In USF4 there are definitely characters considered better than others, but the "top tier" consists of almost a dozen characters, and every single character of the 40+ in the game, even the "low tier" is extremely viable.
This game will force you to play more solidly than a lot of other fighters. Button mashers beware - you may take a few rounds now and then but this game is designed to punish you HARD. In fact, if you're new at this, THIS GAME AND EVERYONE WHO PLAYS IT WILL KICK YOUR♥♥♥♥♥ It will stay that way for probably at least 100 hours in. And even then, the skill ceiling is practically infinite. When I bought Street Fighter 4: AE I knew nothing about fighting games. 1400 hours later I'm finally at a level where I'd consder myself "decent". On the way, I've discovered everything about what makes fighters an intelligent, deep, addicting, and all around amazing genre, way beyond what I had ever imagined. It's a genre that can make you feel the raw sting of defeat (where unlike in MOBAs, you only have yourself to blame) and the consequent high of a hard-won victory.
There is a definite lack of in-game resources for learning, so you'll start off stuck in a trench of sorts. You'll have to spend a long time reading up online and practicing to get acclamated to the game systems, which to some may seem archaic at times (1 frame links are a common source of frustration). But if you can fight through this and make it out of this phase you'll be on a journey to discover what makes fighting games truly amazing.
Prefer arcade stick and this game runs smoothly on GTX 970 would recommend people to play :)

Cubot takes great pride in its minimalist presentation. A cynic may suspect that this “minimalism” is a carelessly-crafted excuse for a lazy or empty game. Such skepticism could not be more misplaced.
Cubot is puzzle-solving game comparable to sliding puzzles, or perhaps to Rush Hour. Cubot adds to these games what could only be feasible in a three- dimensional game: three dimensions. The objective of the game is to land each block—puzzles quickly include more than one block, onto its respective target location. Each action, however, moves all blocks in accordance with the game’s rules as well as with each block’s own distinctive properties. There are, as far as I can tell, ten different kinds of blocks. One moves one space per turn, another moves two. One presents or removes obstacles, another moves in the opposite direction of all other blocks. There are 80 levels and, while this isn’t the most difficult game ever presented, it is satisfying to solve (particularly in the fewest number of turns possible).
On top of these mechanics, the game manages to have a personality despite its minimalist form. The music is calm and the UI is very clean. The developers even threw in some famous quotes, and they’re about—you guessed it—solving puzzles. For the low starting price of $2 and the presumption that it will get even cheaper, this game is certainly worth it if you like puzzles (I’m enjoying this game the same way that I enjoy the Portal games, even without the witty dialogue) or if you’re looking for a game that isn’t too difficult to 100%. I am enjoying this game and I am glad to see it on Steam.

Miscreated is absolutely hands down the best post-apocalyptic survival MMO I've played in my life. Games like DayZ and Rust don't come close to how well designed this game is.
Pros:

-The PvP is great with how different each outcome can be per fight. Just because you get the first shot off doesn't mean you'll win. It's all about how well you keep your cool in a fight and how good your situational awareness is. You can surprise foes with molotov cocktails, pipe bombs and you can even explode jerry cans in their faces with a well-placed shot. I also really appreciate the one shot headshot kill in this game because if you're accurate enough, (which let's face it, unless youre 2 feet in front of the person you're trying to kill, you aren't that accurate) you can down an enemy without risking your own life (and more importantly, your gear).
-Cars are pretty simple to get going. Running around a little bit you'll come across most of the parts once or twice before you even know you're looking for them, but that doesn't mean the parts are everywhere. It's a fun little challenge to get all the parts you need to get a vehicle going. Because of the weight system, you can't carry every part on you at all times. Therefore, you'll need to risk putting some parts in the vehicle. However, this means any survivors that come across the car while you're away looking for parts, already have those parts in the vehicle. Now they just need to find what you're looking for. But once you get it going, cars are a super fun way to get around the map at a pretty quick pace.
-The map itself is perfect. It's not too big, like SOME maps in OTHER games (I'm looking at you DayZ), but it's also not too small to where you run into other survivors every 10 seconds. The easy-to-follow road signs with directional arrows make it easy for friends who are new to the game to navigate to you and vice versa. I also like how when you spawn after a death or perhaps it's just your first time on the server, you spawn in the southern part of the map. The farther up north you travel, the more mutants - and players - you'll come accross. However this high risk comes with high rewards, because up north there are 3 (maybe 4?) military tents that spawn military-grade gear and there's the biggest town in the game, Hayward Valley. I also love all the detail and backstory put into the game with graffiti from previous survivors who try to warn you of the plague and give you helpful tips on who you can trust, that being yourself. I also love the caves and how mysterious they are. Just explore the map for 10 minutes and you'll realize its the most well thought out and detailed post-apocalyptic world any MMO has built thusfar.
Now I can sing this game's praises all day, because 99% of everything in the game is actually perfect and I wouldn't change it for the world. All except...
Cons:
-The god-forsaken base building! It's kind of a nightmare... Of course if you love the game as much as I do you'll put up with it, but the base building just needs an entire revamp. Base parts don't snap to one-another, meaning walls can be misplaced easily and floors may not fit together correctly. You actually have to leave a hole in your wall to put a door, which ALSO doesn't snap to anything. There's no doorways either, so there isn't a custom-made wall to fit the door. The door isn't even the same HEIGHT as the walls, so if you put the door next to a wall (which let's face it, where else would we put a door?) it will peak over it which just looks plain ugly. And if you want to double up on your walls so survivors can't just jump inside of your base, the door poses a MAJOR issue.
Honestly I'd love to rate this game 10/10, which I would have before. But out of 90 hours (as of the time I'm writing this), the two hours I spent building a BASIC base, not even anything extravagant, caused me to give this game an 8/10. Other than the base building - which I hope the devs change soon - this game is downright flawless. It's definitely worth the $20.

I can't in good conscious recommend this game.
It was moderately fun and expansive as they built it up from it's humble beginnings. Presently, it is widely expansive, appeals to many game genre preferences (like Platformers/Build-Crafters/Adventure), and has lots of replay value. This is before taking into account the amount and quality of the mods available just through the Steam Workshop. The "Frackin Universe" mod alone is like an expansion and more than doubles the amount of game you have.
That said, this game will suck days of your life away. If you are prone to spending hours and hours building and crafting things from gathered resources like one would do in Minecraft or Terraria, then give your pets away: they won't have a parent anymore. Starbound is the 2D dream that Minecraft dreams, and Terraria is Starbound's ugly little brother that doesn't have internet and never leaves the house.
All that time will be gone. If you have fond memorys of playing through Megaman and Megaman X games and got excited at the dashes and jumps and weapon variety...I am so sorry: Starbound is about to take you from your friends and family. If you took the variety of dashes, jumps, enemies, and weapons found in all the Megaman games and gave them a haircut, a hot shower and helped them put together a resume', Starbound is the job they would apply for.
Speaking of jobs, I hope you don't have one. If you have taken time off from work to game...you have set a horrible precedent. You'll soon be on the streets, huddled under a lean-to behind whatever outlet and wi-fi you can steal to power your laptop and feed your dispicable addiction. No Man's Sky had a lot of hype about being able to explore the universe and adventure on procedurally generated planets, encountering procedurally generated creatures, and interacting with three others races... I hope you didn't get into that hype. I hope you didn't get excited about that stuff, because Starbound beats that. To be precise, though, Starbound's vanilla universe is finite. The star map has coordinates ranging from X-0 Y-0 to X-999999999 Y-999999999, (so just, like, a million times a million or something) with a variety of stars clustered in a variety of ways. Each star type supports a specified variety of planet and biome types, which in turn house a specified variety of creatures, resources and races (six in vanilla). These coordinates mean you can travel to exact planets that you have found previously or that your friends have found. Oh yeah, you can play with friends. Several friends. Assuming you have lost all of your friends to horrible addiction, you can start a new character and travel to the same coordinates of your previous characters and find what they built and left behind.
Like your life. Like the work you put into building your life and then you leave it behind for this game. Do you like Pokemon? You can capture creatures and monsters in Starbound. You can bioengineer them to make them unique and special, good at specific things. Release them on enemies and junk. You can capture a space bear, then augment it to super jump and sprint, throw a ghost collar on it, and have an ethereal Ursa Major that follows you around like the spectre of your social life. Do you like farming games? Starbound let's you farm. Starbound let's you pick whatever planet type you want and setup whatever farming setup you want with whatever crops you want. There is a universe's worth of stuff to grow, and that includes livestock. It's a fun little way to build money up to upgrade your ship that is customizable. You can put a bar in your ship, you can house tenants in your ship, heck, you can build a musuem if you want. You know, because you can friggin find and excavate fossils via mini-game and then reassemble them and display them. You can put anything in your ship. Unlike your life. Your life now only has room for Starbound and cold pizza rolls that you forgot for two hours.
I can't stop you. I can't hold you back from ruining your life. Go ahead and buy this game you poor, sick, trash. Play the vanilla version of this game until you feel like you've done it. And you have a silent moment of peace and serenity, and you start thinking about going outside. Then load up a bunch of mods and expand your game by five times and get sucked back in. This game is your life now. Your real home is the one you built on the asteroid in zero-G that you use grappling hooks to traverse about. You have no anchor to "real" life anymore.

Sadly this was one of the titles I was excited over coming out, but for its price it is beaten by the old dogs in the railroad / transport tycoon games.
In fact, Railroad Tycoon 2 with its shortcomings will actually excite you more, and is more intutive than this game.
That is the game's first downfall, lack of tutorials, or rather a cheapskate way of doing it.
The tutorials in game are JUST a sloppy redirect link to the Steam guides for this game, the public directory of Steam guides at that with lackluster content.
It works, but the instability of the Steam system will easily give you headaches on some days, and leaving you with ZERO tutorials, or forced to watch a 10 minute video to find out how to rotate a building or station.
Which leads us into another problem, zero keybinds, you dislike the rotation of buildings on the N and M key? Tough luck, that is set in stone and CAN'T be changed in the options.
Another problem I have noticed is that the audio tends to go wonky and skips during gameplay, this especially evident with the gameplay music if you are opening menu's or the like, and it isn't a lack of performance / FPS, as the game runs nicely elsewhere when scrolling and zooming, but opening and closing menu's triggers it, and may be a symptom of much bigger problems underneath the surface.
In short, do I recommend you buy this game? Well it is a refreshing breath into the transport genre, but their competitors who only had the problem of being old, with poor 2D or DirectX 6 or DirectX 7 graphics, will  kick this game hard when it comes gameplay.
OpenTTD is a serious contender to this game, and is also under constant evolution, and while it is hard to beat, the devs better shape up and get their act together.
EDIT: As a quick update to the latest set of updates rolled out at 22nd of May 2015, the issues STILL stand, except now you can hear the music problem even just idling in the main menu.
Steam guides are still used, and Steam is STILL unreliable with frequent downtimes, and the keybinds still cannot be changed.

Here comes the most annoying aspect: Building tracks:
Building tracks is similar to RR2 but it does not work out. There are constantly farms. buildings or really small roads in the way. Sometimes it says not enough space. The tool permanently builds cuts or embankments. The whole track looks juist ugly with those. Worst of all you have to build your track in small segments. And don't get me started on double tracks.
The problem ist that sometimes you realize that the planned route will not work out (gradients are not well shown on the map) and you need to plan an alternative route. Well, your money is gone...you CAN NOT PLAN your route. How could they not add a route planner for this game. I wasted so much money trying to build track (and buying this game).
Stick with OpenTTD. It looks dated but the mechanics are solid.

While this game isn't for everyone, I still would highly recommend it if you're okay with playing adventure games.
I got this game a bit late, a few months after release. I didn't want to buy into the hype that everyone made around this game (I haven't even gotten undertale yet), but then I finally got it one day. I do not regret it at all.
This is an adventure game, but without the pointing and clicking, everything is done via the keyboard (or controller if you use one). This can  get a little while to get used, especially at the start of the game (where you have to learn to press spacebar instead of enter or whatever in order to select a menu option); but once you're inside, there's really no going back.
You play as Mae, an anthropomorphic cat who just recently dropped out of college for various reasons. The first few days in game might be a little slow, but it introduces all of the main characters and much of the interactions pretty well, as well as some background. I never ever felt lost in this game, though at some points, I didn't understand what was going on or why, but after reading into the game and doing a second playthrough, you do learn why certian sequences and such were included and what they represent. This is one of the few games that I've ever played that has actually made me feel emotions and joy for doing things. You can build up attachments to the characters and depending on who you spend time with in the playthrough, those characters open up more to you, giving you insights into the way they act, how they feel, and what they feel about you, the character. The main characters all have flaws and quirks, and they make them extremely relatable if you haven't lived through a perfect life. Whether those flaws are related to trauma, situation, or health, they all impact the character of the person you're talking to.  The story ramps up over time, but depending on how you play, it can take a while to get to if you're one of those 'do everything, see everything' kind of people, don't get discouraged by this though. Persistance is well rewarded, either through dialogue, minigames, sequences, or even in some cases, music. There is definitely enough to reward the player for a second playthrough (or even third, etc.) and there are a lot of memorable sequences in the game that you will want to experience again. Saving is done through autosaves after the end of certain sequences and whenever you choose 'save and exit' from the menu dropdown in the notebook. There are several minigames that are presented throughout the main game, one being a rogue-lite dungeon crawler, another a rythm game in the vein of guitar hero, a theivery minigame, and some more. Most if not all of those minigames have a story related impact and can affect dialog and other things in the game depending on your performance. The soundtrack is superb, and is also available to purchase/download as well. I highly recommend getting it as it's way too good for its own right.
Overall, I'd have to say that this is my favorite adventure game that I've ever played. I hope you enjoy it as much as I did.

The goal of Long Live The Queen (or "Dark Souls: The Visual Novel") is to survive until your coronation, guiding your country through invasions, coups, revolts and marauding monsters by training your character, Elodie, in everything from speaking in public to wielding lightning bolts. It is not an easy goal.

The gameplay itself is odd at first, as you are expected to choose which subject stats are important to level at any given time (and which mood you should be in when you intend to learn it) without having any knowledge of the world, current events or the state of your country. After the first death however, ( and you will almost certainly die) you'll have at least some information about what's going to happen and how you should avoid running neck first into that sword next time - At which point you'll notice your new choices have changed events and have found an entirely different sword for you to familiarize yourself with.

The variety of these choices create lots of great branches on the story (which feed into various endings), most of which are hidden from you if you lack the appropriate skills. This CAN lead to it being difficult to improve upon a playthrough as you don't know why an event happened or what else you could have done but this kind of rogue-lite storytelling works well for games as short as these; In longer games with more time invested in each playthrough you might expect more information on far reaching choices but the game's short length allows the potential outcomes to diverge and keeps event occurrences diverse throughout the game. Summary:
+ wide branching story
+ good world building
+ good replayability

- failure states based on near unforeseeable circumstances
- very limited sound/music
- very limited graphics

I cannot recommend Pillars of Eternity. It's a throwback to games like Baldur's Gate. If you like those games, you'll like Pillars. In other words: your mileage may vary.
If you've never played Baldur's Gate or the other late 1990s/early 2000s isometric RPGs, here's what you're getting with Pillars (and why I cannot recommend it):
The Good:
It's big. There's lots of content.
The writing. Obsidian has a pretty good track record when it comes to writing. Pillars doesn't really change that.
The True Neutral:
It's an isometric camera angle. Some people may prefer the World of Warcraft/Dragon Age-style rear camera, but I found the isometric angle fine.
The Bad:
The story (distinct from writing) is lacking early-game hooks. Hours in, you may be wondering where the plot's gone.
The Ugly:
The interface is small and poorly suited to high-resolution monitors. To make matters worse, the interface is also a mess of drop-down menus and indistinguishable icons, a la 1990s cRPGs.
The combat is a mess. This is a game that wants to be Dungeons & Dragons, but in real time. There are a litany of spells, abilities, and items to make use of, but the game doesn't stop and let you think about what you're doing. Combined with the nearly unusable interface, combat is not fun. You can pause the game, however, to queue up actions for your party. And you'll need to pause, or you'll lose most encounters.
The difficulty is deceptive. The path you follow is relatively linear, so you expect encounters to be managable at your level, but there is no guarantee of that. You will receive no warning, either. There is no dungeon master to say dissuade you from getting in over your head.
There is a total disregard for quality of life considerations. If you're used to Dragon Age, for example, you may expect to be able to select a party member by clicking on the character. You cannot. You must click on the colored circle at the character's feet. This is not the only quality of life issue, but it is the one that struck me as the most galling.
All in all, Pillars of Eternity demands you put on your rose-tinted shades for a nostalgia-laced trip down memory lane, ignoring all the progress that has been made in game design since 1998. If you want to relive the feeling of your first Baldur's Gate playthrough, Pillars will suit you well. If you want a game that lives in the 21st century, best to look elsewhere.

I am a semi-veteran of World of Tanks and Armored Warfare and this is what I have to say comparing this game to the two
Tank Force:
-Simplistic armor thickness. Every tank follows the same thickness scheme (from what I can tell which could save on server cost). No such thing as effective armor so the direction your facing only reduces the damage you take which means that you no longer have to worry about spending all your ammo and doing 0 damage to tanks far higher in tier than you
-Shots don't seem to have much travel time or fall off
-No outlining of tanks. In World of Tanks, the enemy model is highlighted if you are hiding behind a bush which is the most ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ thing ever. In Tank Force, if you hide behind a bush, you are only given a cursor indicator and don't actually see the outline of the tank.
-Fictional tanks (we all know that licensing cost money)
-No deflection mechanics (saves server resources)
-There doesn't seem to be a tank repair cost but there is a ammo cost. Repairing your tank in World of Tanks was hell because that alone ate up 70-100% of your income earned and it was very common to go into a match, win(damage+kills+assist+etc), and still come out with a net loss.
-Tanks aren't as unique as they are in World of Tanks but the trade off is that you have to worry less about the pros and cons certian tanks and can just enjoy shooting which could be appealing
-XP is global so you don't have to play the same tank over and over and don't have to do WoT premium+convert xp which cost a ton of gold
-God-tier ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥-level physics. You can do a 1000 degree roll down a hill and still land upright. Sometimes you spawn on top of a tank and do 20 Olympic winning front flips with 10000 degrees of rotation and still land upright. There is also no ram or fall damage. On the other hand, you won't have troll team mates that flip your tank over and cost you tons of money. We all know that the report player has never worked and the guy who flipped you can't be detected by the game engine so he/she can't be penalized
-Collision with other tanks seems to be edgy, you spaz all over the place which allows the enemy tank to easily take the spaz advantage to rotate unless you are at a perfect 90 degree angle.
-The grind is equally extremly sadistic as World of Tanks especially when the next tier tank outputs the same dps as it's previous tier and to be honest, some of these tiers don't even seem to have that much of an increase in performance despite the raging exp/credit cost. It's like the T25/2 which has like 1 small sliver of damage over the Hellcat.
-Purchasing camo is deceptive. You think your buying perm camo but it's really just 12 hour camo with no notification before purchase.
-Game uses AI bots to substitue players. You can tell they are AI and not player made bots, although it could be possible, because they do not show up on the leaderboard if they play 24/7. The AI pathing is quite lame on some maps. The map with bridge and river for example has 3-5 bots on one side huddle doing circles while the other side has like 1-2 bots go into river and do circles
-Detection mechanics seem very cheaply done. Seems like as long as someone on your team sees an enemy team, that tank is permanetly seen until it dies. It is very easy to spot someone even without the auto-spotting mechanics
-Gun elevation/depression seems to be the same for all tanks. Only the hardstats you see on screen really matter
All three are very much pay-to-play-end-game stuff. Sure you feel like you are farming tons of exp and money but the system is set up so you can't play end game tanks without premium because you simply can't afford the maintenance and spending cost without premium status unless you thinking farming 10+ games on weaker tanks to play 1 top-tier game is fun. Using premium gold certianly does give you tons of advantages vs free players. The upgrade mechanic is extremly lackng and limited and tanks don't seen to break as much. Currently no crew mechanic so as of now, it could be considered that gameplay is much fairer than someone brining in a crew of 50% vs a crew of 3 skills+100% in WoT which is literally the definiton of suicide. When you start entering mid-levels, people just start suiciding, there is no penalty and the game is pretty boring, which really hurts your team and hurts your Win/Loss ratio if you really care about that. On the other hand, you no longer have to be penalized by being matched in games were your tank has no hope of scoring because the WoT match maker just Fs you over hardcore.

The range of guns and melee weapons is quite a lot.
Guns = Pistols, rifles, shotguns, grenade launchers.
Melee = Swords, katanas, sledge hammers, crowbars, wrenches, paddles, spiked bats, table legs, etc.
Distraction tools = Talking dolls, alarm clocks, fire crackers etc. Those are used to distract zombies, an example, let's say you're being chased by a ton of zombies and you throw a talking doll down. The zombies will run to the talking doll and you can get away. So they come in handy when you just want to run away or make a horde of them move to a different location.
Side Missions = Gathering supplies, doing trades with other survivors, helping people to kill feral zombies, help wipe infestations, scouting, escort missions etc. They randomly pop up through out the game and it's up to you to do them, you don't have to do it. If you don't it usually results in something bad as in less influence, less trust, stuff like that.
But nothing game breaking that makes you stressed out.
The game continues without you, meaning if you log off, the game will still keep running. So when you come on there is always something that has happend or has changed and you can never come back to the same thing, which in some cases is annoying. I logged off and I came back the next day, and all my neighbours were dead, a member from my base shot another member, 4 people got sick, a bunch of people were tired and i'm sitting there saying "What the ♥♥♥♥ happened?!? I'm gone for 1 day and all this stuff is going to hell and I have to redo all this♥♥♥♥♥♥all over again"
The pros and cons of the game.
Cons = Not being able to heal your partners at all.
Your partners cannot help you carry supplies, they are only useful for killing zombies and that's it.
The zombie spawn rate is ridiculous. Even if you have killed all the zombies in the area, they will keep spawning no matter what, making most things difficult to do by yourself.
Everything you search through makes noise, it even makes the same noise distance as a gunshot sometimes, so zombies from miles around can hear it and will come over to you.
Not being able to hit more than one zombie with one swing of your melee weapon. So fighting a horde by yourself is impossible if you plan on never being bitten.

Babysitting all of your survivors. Most of them need a talking to, resulting in you having to take them outside to kill some zombies, telling them that they are being a butt hole, then take them back to base. Rinse and repeat.
Not having most things in the game explained to you, and not having a short tutorial for it. So most of the time you'll be online looking for solutions or tips, because the game explains it in very little detail, sometimes not even explaining it.
Pros = Tons of different weapons to choose from

Being able to put an outpost anywhere in any building or home.
Choose where you want to settle your new base by exploring and finding potential home sites.
Being able to call in military air strikes that bomb the hell out of hordes of zombies.
Being able to put loot in the back of your vehicle. Makes loot runs a little more fun.
Choosing who can stay and who has to leave your group.
No barriers or invisible walls holding you back, you can literally go where ever you want at the start of the game. Except for 1 area that unlocks towards the end.
Different zombies, you got normal zombies, zombies that can run faster than you, then special zombies as in Juggernaughts, bloaters, feral zombies, screamers, and swat zombies.
Stealing supplies from your neighbours. You'll have different groups settle in random places, you can either give them supplies or take everything they have, which is awesome. They usually have a lot of ammo and food, so steal all that stuff for yourself haha.
All in all, i would say this game is a 8/10 in my opinion. It's fun and worth giving it a try.
