Short Version Review:
"Crashed a pickup truck into a guard rail, got stuck, got beset my 20 zombies pouring out of the nearest house and lived !  Thank you, sledge hammer!  Then rammed a junky little sports car into the truck over and over until it was off the rail.  Got the truck back, left the burning car .... Thumbs Up !!!"
Slightly Lengthier Review:
So far, so good !  To start, I'll begin with the disclaimer of "I've never played a zombie apocalypse game before this one."  Unless you count some of the Fallout Games ( mmmm ... a lot of those mutants were pretty similar to zombies ).  Anyways, after a couple of crash n' burns both figurative and literal, I'm on my 3rd run of this game and it's a pretty fun romp.  There's a whole steamin' pile of paranoia to be had exploring in the towns, trying to keep one eye on the stuff you're trying to scavenge, and another eye out the window for things that might be jumping through it, trying to eat you.  An ear to the ground also helps.  Screamers are no picnic.  And it also might help to drive a little better than me, b/c when I see a mass of zombies coming down the street at me, my gas pedal foot gets a mind of its own.  I've dented enough hoods, lost enough car doors, and blown up enough vehicles to fill a modest junkyard already.  Hmmm, and I'm still just barely into the storyline itself, b/c the act of survival from day to day is a story all on its own.
Of course, no game's complete without at least a few gripes.  I wish some of the NPCs weren't so petty or inherently stupid.  Nothing says " HEY, WE'RE OVER HERE !!! " quite like the sentry on the tower wielding a shotgun instead of a high powered rifle and shooting multiple times at zombies on the fringe of shotgun range.  There used to be an ornery guy with a hat on the tower - he was a jerk, but at least he had a rifle - can't figure out how to get the girl with the shotgun to come down and put the sniper guy back up there .... or convince her to swap weapons ...
The other gripes are fairly mild in comparison.  It's been a bit of a trick for me trying to figure out where the main storyline wandered off to after my original party stumbled half-chewed into this church compound.  We've been fighting to keep our sanity and our skins ever since.  Having a whole lotta fun, though - $5 well spent.

Best Zombie game hands down. It's a survival simulation. Defend and upgrade your camp, Scout for survivors, and keep them happy, full of morale, and disease free though your actions. Save them from danger and scout for supplies. All decisions have weight, Grabbing much needed ammo might mean you are unable to save another in your group. Only zombies respawn, supplies and vehicles do not which means once you have looted an area you need to move your base. Reckless movement, driving, and searching can attract zombies, and it is easy to get overwhelmed and fatigued, with permanent death for your character. Unsuppressed gunshots are a deathwish - especially at night. Progress is saved constantly so no reloads if you screw up. Just continue as another survivor. Deal with limited inventory space, varied encumbrance levels, Damage and fatigue.
Highly recommended.

When they first announced there was going to be a Street Fighter 4, lo those many years ago, I was ecstatic. I'd given up on there ever being another after 3rd Strike, which was my all time facvorite fighting game at the time (and really, it still is). My excitement lasted until the exact moment I saw the first screenshot for SF4. 3-D graphics. I knew right then the game was in trouble, and sadly I was right.
Every version of SF4, compared to 3rd Strike or any of the Alpha/Zero series, feels sluggish and slow. Achingly so. Characters move as if they're underwater. Animations are fluid, but take too long. This is part of the problem of moving from sprites to 3-D models, is that the 3-D models try to mimic the movement of the sprites from the older games, but they can't. They move oddly, and nothing feels right. Then the art style of the game assaults the eyes with puffy, bloated faces for everyone, and they all seem to have some sort of horrifying type of psoriasis.
And then the gameplay. Ugh. The Ultra Combo system is fundamentally broken on multiple levels, not the least of which that it's basically a reward for playing the game poorly. Doing bad, getting your♥♥♥♥♥handed to you? Have a free super move! The only way to build the Ultra meter should be via blocking attacks with Focus or doing damage like the normal super meter.
Throws are done with both light buttons rather than both fierce buttons, which is wonky and odd. No sir, I don't like it. Also, there's no post-KO inputs allowed, meaning you can't do any neat post-KO hits and earn extra points.
I can't speak for the online play because I never cared enough about this game to bother playing it online.
Audio-wise the game is adequate. The punches and kicks are okay sounding. The music...exists, eliciting neither positive nor negative emotional responses. It simply is there. The announcer is ALMOST as annoying as SFZ 3's, but at least that one had the bonus of being in a much, much better game than this. The character voices, once you put them in their proper language (Ryu and Ken speaking Japanese, Dudly speaking English, etc.) are serviceable, though Makoto's voice in 3rd Strike was vastly superior. As was Dudnley's. Basically everything about 3rd Strike is superior to this game, except maybe the roster (though I have to deduct stupid amounts of points from the rostor for characters like Rufus or that red oil covered...thing. Seriously Capcom, WTF?).
Honestly, I've tried several times over the years to play SF4, in most of it's revisions, hoping to see the game that other people talk about when they sing it's praises. However, I cannot. It's terrible failure-rewarding game mechanics, sluggish controls, forgettable music and weird oddities (Saving icon popping up in the center of the screen after every match, needing to hit alt+Enter to fullscreen the game since it's not in the option menu, etc.) all combine to form a game that seems tailor made to make me not enjoy playing it. 3rd Strike is faster, more technical, more skill-rewarding, and has more life and fluidity in it's 16 year old sprites than this game's clunky 3-D models. I'll go back to playing that, instead.
Final score: 3/10

Don't get discouraged by reviews of people who get frustrated by dying early. This is a game that doesn't hold your hand, has a complex system and has quite a learning curve. it is advised for new squads to do easy difficulty first to familiarize. It shines on multiplayer but you have to do your due diligence (i.e. Go through single player, familiarize with items etc.) This game is not about grinding through the ranks. A team of 8 who knows the game  can create new accounts and beat the game while they're all at rank 1. It's about teamwork, respecting the enemies (why most new players die is they don't respect the swarm), achieving goals as a team, and playing your role (as medic, tank, dps/carry, utility, scout, forward observer etc.).  If you are a fan of the old top down squad games like Night of the Dead, Undead Assault and its ilk, this game is for you. If you want a challenging/complex game that requires teamwork and has hero-based system, you'll like this game.
CONS:
- Single player can only give you 10 to 20 hours of fun. Most of the fun is in multiplayer.
- Only a few maps to go through. I believe the devs can create a random map generator. There is a tactical advantage though of knowing the map.
- high difficulty. This is a team game. If the healer doesn't know what to do, or the tank, then the squad will most likely fall. There is a need for a good leader at higher difficulties.
- medium to steep learning curve, depending on how good you want to be.
- if you die early, you will be automatically revived if you are new to the game. However, after a few ranks, there will no longer be an automatic revive. A medic or a mission can revive you, but you will have to wait.
PROS
- Team game. I've played with Europeans, Chinese, Canadians and Americans. A good world we are in. At higher difficulties, you need to talk, so teamspeak would be necessary. There's a different sense of achievement when you defeat a game as a team.
- Hero-based system. You control one character, customize it and change its load out. There are 8 classes that each have a role to play. Mastery of a class is a journey and there are different ways to build a single class.
- Squadron tactics. You have an enemy sniper shooting at 124m away while a swarm is constantly flowing to your team, what do you do? 3 big fatties chasing you? Fast dogs gnawing at one of your team? Some military squad tactics apply, like leapfrog movements, defensive positions, buddy system etc. The squad leaer has a large impact and responsibility.
- Random missions and enemies. Every game is different depending on the mission, the boss spawn etc.

While this game isn't for everyone, I still would highly recommend it if you're okay with playing adventure games.
I got this game a bit late, a few months after release. I didn't want to buy into the hype that everyone made around this game (I haven't even gotten undertale yet), but then I finally got it one day. I do not regret it at all.
This is an adventure game, but without the pointing and clicking, everything is done via the keyboard (or controller if you use one). This can  get a little while to get used, especially at the start of the game (where you have to learn to press spacebar instead of enter or whatever in order to select a menu option); but once you're inside, there's really no going back.
You play as Mae, an anthropomorphic cat who just recently dropped out of college for various reasons. The first few days in game might be a little slow, but it introduces all of the main characters and much of the interactions pretty well, as well as some background. I never ever felt lost in this game, though at some points, I didn't understand what was going on or why, but after reading into the game and doing a second playthrough, you do learn why certian sequences and such were included and what they represent. This is one of the few games that I've ever played that has actually made me feel emotions and joy for doing things. You can build up attachments to the characters and depending on who you spend time with in the playthrough, those characters open up more to you, giving you insights into the way they act, how they feel, and what they feel about you, the character. The main characters all have flaws and quirks, and they make them extremely relatable if you haven't lived through a perfect life. Whether those flaws are related to trauma, situation, or health, they all impact the character of the person you're talking to.  The story ramps up over time, but depending on how you play, it can take a while to get to if you're one of those 'do everything, see everything' kind of people, don't get discouraged by this though. Persistance is well rewarded, either through dialogue, minigames, sequences, or even in some cases, music. There is definitely enough to reward the player for a second playthrough (or even third, etc.) and there are a lot of memorable sequences in the game that you will want to experience again. Saving is done through autosaves after the end of certain sequences and whenever you choose 'save and exit' from the menu dropdown in the notebook. There are several minigames that are presented throughout the main game, one being a rogue-lite dungeon crawler, another a rythm game in the vein of guitar hero, a theivery minigame, and some more. Most if not all of those minigames have a story related impact and can affect dialog and other things in the game depending on your performance. The soundtrack is superb, and is also available to purchase/download as well. I highly recommend getting it as it's way too good for its own right.
Overall, I'd have to say that this is my favorite adventure game that I've ever played. I hope you enjoy it as much as I did.

A very fun game that is helped immensely by the Nemesis System mixing things up and keeping them somewhat fresh.  The story is nothing to write home about but the game essentially develops its own story with the wide variety of enemies, faces and even (shallow) personalities of the various orcs you run up against.  Full of numerous Lord of the Rings references, the visual cues for the game clearly come from the films but there are also a lot of nods to both the LOTR books as well as the wider universe Tolkien created.
With enjoyable combat (think a less developed but more lethal version of the Batman combat from the Arkham games), a neat gimmick, two large maps to explore and a skeletal framework of missions that mostly just exist as an excuse for orc killing mayhem, it's a game that you'll probably get dozens of hours of fun from, if not more.

A word of warning:

I bough this game with the expectation just to play a difficult rpg with great bossfights.

Here is a list what makes darksouls (one of the) best rpg ive ever played.

This game is fun for maybe an hour. Death for a character is permanent, which is usually something I love in a game, except State of Decay will kill your favorite character with one of its enormous amount of glitches. I gave this game many chances, and was let down furiously every time. There is no reverting back to a previous save. If a character dies and you want them back, you have to start the game COMPLETELY from the beginning and lose ALL of your progress. Yes, all of it. Also, you gain "Influence" in the game by completing missions, usually 5-25 per mission, and it costs 100 Influence to bring a companion along with you for help. What they don't tell you is that you can't bring them for help ON ANY MISSION. You'll waste the 100 Influence asking them to come with you, drive all the way to the location, just to have the companion disappear when you get there (no refunds either). I wasted 200 Influence bringing a companion along, the first time because I simply drove past a mission location that I wasn't going to, which prompted the mission to start automatically, effectively disappearing my companion. Then I had to do that tedious and unrewarding mission, drive back home and spend another 100 influence to ask him to come with me again, just to have the same thing happen AGAIN. Also, you can't set a button for "open door" or "barricade window" or anything; it's just one button for everything called "Interact." So on my second time starting the game completely over from the beginning, I lost my favorite character AGAIN because I pressed E to barricade the window and instead she opened the door, letting all the zombies in and killing her. So I started the game over AGAIN, being very careful to avoid this happening, and sure enough it happened YET AGAIN. I play tons of Alpha-access games with less glitches and problems than this one. Get 7D2D or DayZ instead and save yourself the frustration.

State of Decay is a very good sandbox/open world zombie title. As a complete package I definitely recommend the game, especially for those interested in the survival/zombie apocalypse genre.
The level of freedom is, for the most part, excellent. The map is large, varying, and the world is populated by plenty of survivors and even more zombies to keep things interesting. There are an impressive amount of customisable "home sites" where you can set up base, raise defences, and build other useful facilities to help you and your (AI) friends survive the zombie threat. It has a neat day/night cycle and some very nice touches to the vehicle combat. The game does have quite a few annoying glitches at times but they are sporadic and do not fundamentally detract from the enjoyment of the game. The most annoying feature of the game that I found was the fact that there were too many things to do all at once. You will receive 4-5 missions at a time which can be aggravating and at times overwhelming considering many are time sensitive. And for the first time ever, I will complain that this game could have benefitted immensely from an online co-op mode. Enjoying State of Decay with friends and trying to survive would be a lot of fun. It's a real shame there is no such feature.
In all, it is a good game and definitely worth checking out for those interested in a game with quite a lot of freedom and those just generally into the survival/zombie apocalypse genre. 8/10.

I have played this game for hours and hours and hours on Xbox 360, and absolutely loved it. It is to be expected that Indie titles are never going to be of AAA quality, but this game has great replay value.
The premise is a simple one, it's a Zombie Apocolypse, find a base, fill it with people. weapons, ammo, food, medicine and building materials scavenged from the impressively large map. Almost every building can be entered, looted, turned into protective outposts, and there are quite a number of vehicles to choose from, although more variety wouldn't go amiss...
Where this game stands out is the surprising depth once you have learned the ropes, (which unfortunately will take time as the game is certainly not forthcoming with tutorial-based advice!) But the character building system, traits, weapon variety, 'Special' zombies, likeable characters, and multple bases will keep you amused for some time.
Breakdown is my personal favourite game type, as it allows you more freedom and an inclined difficulty level, although if you have played the game as much I have, you will fall into a routine as the difficulty increases and will not find it too challenging.
Lifeline, the second DLC on the other hand is rather tough, again with little tutorial advise for new players.
However this game does deserve your time as it really is very fun, very rewarding, looks great, and it is easy to see a lot of TLC has been put into it by it's development team. Another plus-point in my opinion; Undeadlabs are very active on Twitter, Twitch, they have fantastic forums and have made game update decisions based on customer feedback.
A great game worth playing, especially the Breakdown DLC.

Wow man... Initially I was really put off my the graphics (which looked dated) and horrible colour/gamma display, so much so that I almost didn't bother playing it past the first few minutes... But, the day after installing it and virtually writing it off, I decided to give it a whirll...
What I found was this game is actually incredibly rich, with really nice realistic details, details like like vehicle boots/trunks, why haven't games allowed us to use vehicles to store stuff in in the past? fill the boot, drive it around to various places, then unload when you're home.. (It's a small detail but just one of several that are pretty innovative).
This is the story, just the intro, which seems to be the only thing that's consistent... You're fishing with a friend, and the town gets attacked by zombies, then you meet a chick, and your friend gets hurt and you shack up with other survivors in another nearby town... that's the intro pretty much, the rest of it is up to you, but there are missions that seem to follow a story line... And you can pretty much ignore them until you're in the mood to do them, or in many cases, simply forced to do them because as your band of survivors grow, you find yourself needing say a doctor, or a new place to stay etc...
Now the convo's are pretty great between the survivors, and you build up friendships and or lose them by let's say NEARLY RUNNING THEM OVER, (this game actually takes that into consideration). Or ignoring their obvious pains, like depression, or fear... (I'm sure there's plenty, but I've only been playing for about 10 hours...) So you can work on them, and yourself and build up skills, like brute strength, shooting skills, diplomacy, etc etc (I'm surprised by the number of options)
So as you can imagine, with good conversations, and highly individualistic members, you can actually grow quite attached to the individuals... Here's the absolute ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ though... When they die... they really die... there's no reloading, all saves are auto saves, and once you've made your character a tough nut who's great at everything, like cardio, and hitting stuff, all you need to do is mess up, keep using them when they're tired, and find yourself in a♥♥♥♥♥♥ton of trouble as you're car is pulled to pieces by a swarm of zombies, and he can't fight for♥♥♥♥♥♥cos he hasn't slept for 2 days or his bat has just snapped in half over the last zombies head, cos you forgot to put it in for repairs last night...
But... the game just goes on... You end up taking control of another random character from your group, who might have god awful people skills and couldn't fight his way out of a wet paper bag, but has excellent tv trivia knowledge..!!!
That... although an absolute ♥♥♥♥♥! Is awesome!!! cos it's the sort of mechanic that really keeps you on your toes... And makes you genuinely concerned for the group's safety... To top it off, you're pretty rushed off your feet, there are often several (more than just a couple) of missions that you can do, or you can just go roaming rround towns door to door kicking zombies in the nuts and looking for resources to use in the construction of new parts of your safehouse, which is attacked by hordes of zombies btw, intuitively also by the looks of it... The most frustrating is that it happens whilst you're away also, and without your help, I'm sure you'd lose some good friends, maybe even all of them in the process...
So anyway... in a nutshell, the game is awesome, well worth investing in, and I'll definitely be buying the other 2 parts once i've got through this part... 8.9/10

This IS the zombie survival game you've been looking for.
Let me start by saying, the single player aspect of this game was at first an issue for me.  I thought there was no way to really recreate a good zombie survival environment without having other players in the world.
This game proved that to not be true.
This game FEELS like an mmo, it FEELs like a living world.  It's dynamic, it changes, it feels alive and unsafe everywhere.
Sure there is no multiplayer, but lets face it, zombie survival and multiplayer as most developers are building it currently, is nothing more than shooters with zombies wandering around and food that regens health.
Until players who REALLY want zombie survival, NOT just another FPS, playing single player is going to be the ONLY way to really get the feel of zombie survival.
This game has so many interesting aspects wrapped into one game.  Survival, personnel management, equipment management, fort management just to name a few.  Not to mention some squad tactics since you don't have to 'go it alone', along with fighting, shooting and driving.
This game has so many things to do, plus it has a fairly easy UI to get used to after playing for awhile, that managing all of the tasks/aspects is really easy to do on the fly.
You can play ANY of your survivers once you earn their trust making the game virtually unending since you may gain/lose survivers over time.
Missions are randomly generated and can have all sorts of objectives, all of which fit, and make sense within the game itself.
The map and landscape of the game is absolutely overwhemling in the detail, the accessible places, the destroyable objects, and the dynamic way it changes.
Zombie respawns are seemless since zombies can be 'cleared' to a certain extent but will re-populate areas by wandering, so you never feel safe ANYWHERE.
Fort building, safe house building ( outposts ), placing traps, repairing valuable items, gathering resources, etc etc etc
I WILL absolutely be buying State of Decay 2, and ALL of its DLCs, this game is that good.
I have all of the DLCs for State of Decay currently, but the base game is so good, I havent even started playing the DLCs.
If you want a game that's focused on SURVIVAL, and is set within a zombie apocalypse, this IS the game for you.

Having played it from beginning to end, Pillars is a refreshing mix of dynamic story and charismatic characters, of which keep you tethered to a realm that is reminiscent of Baldur's Gate and as unusual as Planescape: Torment.
Although the combat can be a little tricky, it never became dull or a chore to go through the (huge) number of side-quests and tasks, some of which add to your reputation with a town or city that in turn, make you trustworthy to the best (or worst) NPCs there.
I haven't played the White March DLCs yet, but an RPG like this is difficult to stray from once you get into the heart of the story, which admittedly, does take some time. What it lacks in 'beautiful' character sprites (which, let's face it, are hard to see in an isometric game anyway), it makes up for with wonderful landscapes and backdrops. What it lacks in levels (I believe you can only go up to level 12?) it makes up for with customisable armour and weapons, provided you have the materials and money.
The narrative is unfussy and straightforward, with multiple choices to get to where you need to go. Depending on your character's personality (e.g. Kind, Cruel, Passionate, Rational, etc), characters will react accordingly, which fleshes out your personal plotlines, as well as your companions'. This isn't to say that the plot itself is dull or boring - far from it, in fact - but it's very character-driven and deeply dependent on your choices, sometimes in the most unexpected way. Whilst a lot of RPGs tend to pander this trait excessively, Pillars does something different: they actually mean it.
Long story short: As long as you have the patience, the game rewards you with rich plotlines, intriguing characters and an exquisite soundtrack that captures the essence of this weird and wonderful world. Pillars has a story worth telling - they're just waiting for your character to tell it.

A solid turn-based RPG with deep rules as in old D&D games. Many classes, many spells, lots of customization make for fun and challenging combat system. The story is interesting, pretty chatty but you largely can choose how much you want to hear about it (companions will give you lots of information about events linked to them and the story but it is entirely optional to read it or not). I enjoyed that part though there are more interesting games story-wise around. Despite all this background the companions themselves are pretty disapointing in that they do have a quest but it has no impact on the story and no real reward. They don't impact much on the game either, besides a few occasions where they unlock an extra option in quests.
That's the only real downside to the game to me, companions are only really different to NPC with no backgrounds that can be recruited and created at will by the fact that you can talk to them and have a story to tell. The good part though is that you can replace them by your own NPC if you wish so without losing out much.
Overall it's a really good game, especially in reguards to combats, with well-written quests in an immersive world (no black and white morale here!), the best of turn-based RPG in the past few years.

It is brilliant in almost every capacity, except, and that is a huge problem for me, the magic system in its overall depth and presentation is rather weak, specially if compared to that of baldurs gate 2 / Icewind Dale etc.

If you picked the sorcerer in BG2 you started out pretty weak but you could eventually become the most powerful being wandering the swordcoast. The presentation, in particular the animation and the voiceacting that accompanied every spell and the potential battle-turning impact of a huge number of spells made the experience in regards to the magic system one of the best that exists in all video game history.
I know PoE is no successor of BG2, but the magic system here nevertheless fails to present the "might" that should resonate with every spell. In detail, the voices often brake mid-spell, the animations have an awful harry-potter-styled vibe and the overall pace is much too fast both for the casting and the duration of spell effects. This is true not just for wizards but also for priests and druids, even when it is a bit less akward for the latter.
PoE is still an oustanding game and one of the best RPGs in the last years. I just hope they reconsider their approach to magic in PoE2.

This game gets a 10/10 from me. It's basically Civilization V... but with MAGIC... dragons, gods, mythology, wizards, and monsters. Need I say more? Well here's more:
-The graphics... holy cow the fidelity! So vivid, lush and vibrant! Some of the most beautiful environments I have ever seen. Care was even placed into animating city borders. Everything comes together to seriously make you feels that the world you're playing in is filled with magic.
-The combat in this game completely blows the Civ5 combat system out of the water. Your units can continue leveling indefinitely and gain permanent buffs from the spells you cast upon them. As a result you end up caring about your units and start to grow with them through the ages. They each become quite formidable in their own right. That archer you started out with on turn 1? Well guess what, he's fighting an immortal god now on turn 80 because you kept investing in him.
-There are randomly generating events happening all over the world that affects all players, which is absolutely awesome. You're fighting not just on land and sea but in other dimensions and planetary planes. There is also huge replay ability through the randomly generated maps, and the versatility in which you can play your wizard. Do you want to create the most powerful cities the world has ever seen? Or do you want your units to take on gods? Or would you rather amass the greatest army or navy? Or just burn everyone with your magic!
-The units you can build are based upon your environment... that's right... you can potentially get different types of armies every game! You are no longer tied down to your race or class but can scour the world seeking elves, werewolf, or dragon turtles.
-The interface looks absolutely breath taking. Someone put a lot of love and care into designing an extremely immersive interface.
Cons:
-Unit controls and deselection sometimes executes commands you did not intend.
-There is no visible tech tree for spells, which I'd imagine is quite extensive, you end up praying for the spell you want.

The story is nothing to write home about but the game essentially develops its own story with the wide variety of enemies, faces and even (shallow) personalities of the various orcs you run up against.  Full of numerous Lord of the Rings references, the visual cues for the game clearly come from the films but there are also a lot of nods to both the LOTR books as well as the wider universe Tolkien created.

Strengths:
- Impressively smooth combat mechanics despite large quantities of enemies and a large variety of moves/commands
- Fairly expansive universe to explore, though terrain is limited
- Great storyline, voice acting, and cinematics
- Leveling feels rewarding and continually challenging without cheap AI tactics. You actually feel more powerful as you progress
Weaknesses:
- Missions become a little repetitive over time and get a little boring (especially if you attempt to complete side missions)
- Captain/Warchief missions can get pretty frustrating as there's a confusing lack of instruction for many of them (during a Betrayal, what are you supposed to do exactly if they're invulnerable to arrows and then just retreat from your Dominated bodyguards?)
- There are occasional glitches where you can get stuck between walls, which is also obviously frustrating

A total surprise. I played for hours the first time I launched it. Really fantastic, fun train simulation -- with buses and trams to get goods around cities & to stations. Seems to be modeled after the original Railroad Tycoon (which is a good thing), it lets you build tracks and schedule trains, and actually has signalling, something which later RR Tycoon games "optimized" away. The early years have slow trains, and you have to patiently build up your company. Expand too fast and you'll go broke. The graphics are gorgeous, tons of detail, fast.
Some aspects are a little rough, clearly parts of the UX were an afterthought, but these aren't critical to the game.

I got this game during the Holiday Auction for a VERY good price (thank you devs!) and I have really enjoyed it. Pros: Trains! Rewarding and addicting gameplay, beautiful visuals, lots of world options. Can build while paused. Post-release updates.
Cons: The vehicle choices are very front-loaded, by the year 2000 there's only a few train engines and railcars that are at all useful and only one road vehicle each for passenger and cargo. I expect this to improve with mods or DLCs but I don't see Steam Workshop support coming soon so modding will still require some technical knowledge and tinkering in the game files for the foreseeable future.
While the graphics are great, I get better performance in much more detailed games, which leads me to believe that there's still plenty of optimization to be done. I've been playing it mainly on Linux but I remember it suffering unnecessarily on Windows as well. It also stutters occasionally on Linux.
The interface is clunky, sometimes buggy, and lacks inspiration, though some recent updates have improved the first two complaints somewhat. However, I expect to see GUI improvement mods become very popular.
There's not much variance in the geography, it's basically a green grass field deformed by a randomized heightmap. I'd like to see more variance in biomes and maybe seasons if possible. I expect this to appear in mods or DLCs, though I'd prefer to have seen it in the base game or at least a free update.
Based on recent communications, the devs seem to be relying on the modding community to do a lot of their work for them. I hope they keep in mind that a modding community isn't going to flourish without a great game to build on. This has all the makings of a great game, but it's still got some things to iron out. I hope they keep their priorities in line.
TL;DR: It's fun now, but a cautious buyer might want to hold off and see how the game develops, because it still needs quite a bit of work.

One of the few steam reviews I've written, but this game does so much right and does a few major things wrong that just make it really miserable to play. I've played Baldur's Gate and all the classics that this game attempts to follow and I'm about 30 hours in and have not completed it yet. It's a solid game with lots of value, but there will be points that make you just want to rip your hair out.
- Garbage. Your team mates are completely useless and will often get themselves killed if you let the AI control them. You instead have to micro manage EVERY LITTLE ENCOUNTER like crazy to avoid getting screwed. It starts to feel more like baby sitting suicidal dodo's than leading a band of adventurers.
- You can go from breezing through an area to a random fight with no real pretense where you just get embarassingly shut down. Comes out of no where and you just feel cheated. If it was built up or presented as a boss fight or something sure, but the randomness of difficult encounters is frustrating. Fights are either way too easy or way too hard. Very rarely is there an in between. Sometimes there's a trick you need for the fight, but it's not like the game eases you into it or hints that it'll be a special fight so you'll just get spanked by a random group of trash mobs until you catch on and then it'll go back to being a cake walk. It's not exactly awful, but it just leaves you scratching your head and asking where the heck did that come from quite a bit.
- Dumb, confusing, and frustrating. Enemies will just magically stick to some characters based on god knows what. Once something is stuck, it's a headache to unstick. Sometimes there is just a stupid amount of enemies and it's impossible to protect your back line in some fights. Not sure what the developers were thinking when the enemy out numbers you 2 : 1 and you only have probably 2 tanks. This situation combined with the 2 items listed above just make me alt f4 at times and come back later because you just feel so cheated by the game.
This game has some very rabid fans. Any criticisms regardless of how accurate they might be will get torn apart and the community just says git gud. This game is very very good at telling a story, but there is no denying that it has some serious gameplay flaws. I would definitely grab it for $25 or less, but only pay more if you can swallow some frustration and really enjoy an emersive, story telling, old school RPG.

If you really get down to it, Starbound is a 10/10 game.
It has a great art style, with a combination of nostalgic retro pixel art and amazing parrallax backgrounds, Starbound really is a sight to be had. Another thing I must commend Starbound for in it's art is the variety of biomes. Unlike some space-exploration games, *Cough Cough* No Man's Sky *Cough Cough*, Every biome is unique in it's creatures, sound effects, materials, liquids, and even plants! From the beginning to the end, each new planet offers much to behold and I often find myself simply sitting back and watching the birds fly about the sky and the sun cycle go around and around.
Art: 9/10.
The gameplay itself is nothing new, but the diversity of weapons and armor allow for large amounts of customization in the building of your character. Do you want to be a Dual-Wielding Wand-wielder? Then you can! Want to wield a badass sword made of cosmic energy? You can! And even if the base game doesn't have what you want, the ever growing Mod Workshop is almost sure to have what you're looking for. Hell, it's not even that difficult to start making mods for yourself. Just some basic LUA scripting or some messing-about with "StarCheat" and you can basically make WHATEVER you want! The story is slightly repetitive, and with the unskippable cutscenes making your 20th character can be quite annoying, but that is to be had with any game. Marie Antoinette simulator! This game is incredibly cute, and it's fun, but for such a short game, there are some problems with its replayability.
The idea is that you play as Princess Elodie, attending various classes to gain relevant knowledge and skill to be a leader. At the same time, you have four types of moods on a sliding scale: angry vs. afraid, cheerful vs. depressed, and so on. Various things you do in court will raise or lower these moods, and the strongest mood you feel influences what classes you're best at studying in. For instance, if Princess Elodie is feeling lonely, then she won't give her all with reading history books or learning accounting, but she'll be happy to practice her conversational skills. Raising the skills is very fun, as you get flavor text about what exactly it is that she's learning in her studies.
The game mixes up the routine of skill-raising by making the world around Princess Elodie pretty kill-or-be-killed; you have to always think about the political advantage gained by choosing to study one skill over another. For instance, if you're going on a parade, you may need a polearm skill to defend yourself with, because you're all dressed up and holding a royal scepter--archery may sound cool, but is it really what you need to know to survive as the crown princess? The game has a good sense of making you ask yourself, "What skills will I need to survive?" while still throwing you some curveballs.
The downside to this is that the game is short--it takes place over the course of 40 weeks, where each week is one turn of gameplay. This means that you have to be focused and decisive about the skills you're going to study, because while your stats can raise to 100 very quickly, you can only raise so many of them in the limited time you're given.
To me, this is the game's biggest downfall. It takes about 2 hours to reach week 40, but if you hit a dead end it might take a couple retries to beat the game--still, that's 4, 6 hours max to play this game to its ending. Theoretically, the replayability should be high since there are so many skills, plot deviations, and costumes. But in practice, after you play through the game normally, a lot of the skills lose their appeal because of how limited their applications are, and how focused you have to be in training Princess Elodie. Ultimately, after the first time you play, it feels like you're in a rush to raise your stats.
The game is so relaxing and cute, and it has a lot of charm. I really wish that it were two or three times longer than it is, so that you could spend more time exploring the different skills instead of feeling like you have to rush to a specific build. The short length of the game also makes it feel like there aren't really any characters besides Princess Elodie, because you never interact with any one of them long enough to see more than one dimension of their personality.

Long Live The Queen is a simulation role-playing-game that places you in the role of a princess on the road to becoming queen. Placing aside the images usually conjured by well-known fairy tales, being a princess as it turns out is very difficult. To make it to your coronation you will need to better yourself and make important decisions along the way. There is a lot to learn as a princess, everything from etiquette to history to military strategy to athletics and everything in between. Careful selection of what you learn and how well you learn it can open up new opportunities as well as avoid nasty failures on skill checks. How well you learn a subject is also dependent on your mood which can shift depending on what actions you take and how you spend your weekends.
In many ways, Long Live The Queen is similar to Princess Maker which also features a princess with different skills to learn. The key difference being that in Princess Maker you play a king raising a daughter where as Long Live The Queen places you in the role of the princess dealing with political issues of every sort. There is a lot of agency to Long Live The Queen and the story can take radically different turns depending on what actions you take and how well versed you are in certain subjects. So there is much more at stake in Long Live The Queen than in Princess Maker. Who do you trust? Do you take the diplomatic solution or use force? Do you get involved in problems where success is not guaranteed? The first few times playing you will usually meet an untimely demise before ever seeing your coronation.
Overall, Long Live The Queen is a fantastic and refreshing game. With so many decisions to make, there are a number of directions the story can go. And even if you fail, it's still enjoyable to just get back up and try again with something different. So if you've ever wanted to be a princess or just have fun as a ruler, I would highly recommend this game.

Type: Strategy
Similar to: Civilization
This game can't avoid comparisons to Civ, so let's look at the differences.
Warlock:
* Is more focused on magical/fantasy units
* Has hireable champions, after a fashion (Lords)
* Has more varied NPC enemies and cities
* Has enemy player AI that will actually ally up with you (revolutionary, compared to Civ V's broken diplomacy)
* Has quests that feel impactful, opposed to Civ's city-state questing
* Has no focus on city production; buildings and units happen in an orderly queue that's only ever several turns deep
Downsides to Warlock:
* Unit selection feels a little sticky, de-selecting isn't all that fluid (Civ also has this problem)
* The game's a bit of a resource pig (try typing in another window while it's up)
* There is nearly nothing by way of a tutorial, so get ready for reading up on forums to learn about Religions and the like
This game is worth a play through and is probably a good pickup for strategy fans if it's in the sub-$15 range. Replay value is moderately high.

There were a few companions whom I absolutely loved, and most of them I found at least interesting and intriguing. The casual banter between party members reminded me of BG (in a good way), and often evoked literal LOLs. The beauty of the scenery (and the soundtrack) were exceptional.
It's not flawless. I found a few audio-bugs, and I've read valid criticism of the combat mechanics. Since much of the dialogue isn't voice-acted, it'd likely be less enjoyable to someone who dislikes reading. This game is one of the most difficult games I have played so far. It features immense tactical depth and requires constant communication with your teammates (so Teamspeak or anything similar is almost mandatory).
While the above may be harsh and frustrating sometimes it becomes incredibly rewarding, should you manage to finish a mission with zero casualties and all objectives completed.
Would I recommend this game? Absolutely
Are there any downsides? Well, the controls take a while to get used to and the playerbase is not the biggest there is. Nonetheless I always manage to find an open lobby and the community is very friendly towards new players.

An offspring of the original NOTD:AM,SO,SWAT game in Warcraft 3. The Red Solstice is an 8 player tactical, co-op objective based top down shooter. You are one of the black ops unit send in to Mars to investigate and contain a virus outbreak. You'll be pitted against hordes of infected on a desolate planet scouring for ammo, weapons, medical supplies while racing against time to complete your mission objectives and boss fights.
The game features a variety of combat classes to choose from such as assault, heavy support, recon, demolition, medic, terminator, marksman & hellfire. Players are able to level up their classes to gain additional skills & stats as they progress further into the game. If you're a fan of Alien Swarm or NOTD get this game. Word of warning though this game is extremely challenging and requires quite a bit of strategic planning and teamwork if you wish to survive.

Personally I really enjoy this game when playing with a group of serious players on the hardest difficulty.
Is this game for you?
To really enjoy this game, you need to be a team player. When you start playing, you need to listen to more experienced people and learn from them. This is not a game for you to run around trying to be a hero, you will die, and get people killed.
This game does have lots of little tips and tricks you learn that are the difference between clutching a victory on Soldier difficulty (2/4) and breezing a a win on Aetriden difficulty(4/4). The people running around in circles on autofire are the ones doomed to soldier forever, then they get made at the game for requiring they actually learn something to win.
The game is somewhat repetative, there are 6 maps, ranging in difficultly and layout, with more planned as free content expansions, none of this paid dlc stuff. There are two primary storylines that can spawn, and a dozen or so secondary missions that spawn randomly through out each play through, certain secondaries are locked until your are in a group that is higher rank as they are more difficult, such as the Eye of the Storm mission. However the replayability comes from this random element, as well as trying to beat the game's current most difficult map, Military sector on Aetriden difficulty, which has currently only been beaten once!
Some people complain about the 'toxic' community on this game, well I believe I am one of those 'toxic' players apparently, because I require people in my games to be on teamspeak. The reason for this is simple, I play higher difficulty games and there is no time to type everything I need to tell you through out the game. Winning Veteran+ difficulty is extremely unlikely when not on teamspeak because not being able to hear the leaders instructions leads to small mistakes, which lead to deaths. As for the moderation of TS, I've seen 1 ban in the last 2 months, and that was someone trying to be disruptive and harassing the community.
The game has a few problems, desync is an issue sometimes, there are some other glitches too, however the developers are highly active within the community, to the point one is online on teamspeak almost every day listening to feedback, and if anyone is having any issues. Some bugs were creating in recent patches, and fixed almost immediately. Others have been around longer but are much more complicated issues that are hard to fix without breaking everything around it, or are inconsistent and difficult to replicate and pinpoint.
All in all, I'd give TRS an 8/10 as it stands right now, and that's trying to be highly critical of it. Most games I see coming out would be lucky to reach 6+. However, this game is not worth you buying it if you don't want to invest time and effort into learning it and getting good, you'll just end up out of pocket, upset and writing a bad review here or being an actual toxic player within the community. If you are willing to invest into this game however, endless hours of sweat, tears and laughter await you, just beware the levi in the bush!

This is a great descendant of Transport Tycoon. The kinks have been patched out for the largest part. I would give it an 8/10 in it's current state, whereas at release, it would at most have been 7/10.
It features trams and buses, lorries and passenger and freight trains, though currently only European ones. An American-themed DLC is in the works apparently and should be released quite soon, according to the developers (I guess that means within two to three months).

This game always felt like a very expensive Beta.   And it is. It's a 40 dollar beta.  It is unsettling knowing that the devs can essentially take the money and run at any point.   Though, they've stuck with it so far.
So...why shouldn't you get this game?
As stated, it's simply not finished.   This is hearlding to be the next Transport Tycoon/Locomotion.   And it's just not that.   Want to electrify all your rails?   Click every individual section,  miss one and your train wont run.  Don't know what section you missed?  Good luck finding it.
Want to built a road across your rails?  Too bad.  Demolish the rails and build the road first,  then you can fiddle around.
The building system is beyond fickle,  though in honesty,  it has been improving.   It's still awful.   You will spend more time cursing it out and trying to get a simple little bit just to work.  It needs a lot of work
Natrually,  there is no true build mode,   so any minor change that doesn't work will be bulldozed out of your own poked, paid to be laid again, and bulldozed when that doesn't work.  Early on, if you make even a slight error building your track,  you can break the bank.
Likewise,  making a profit is not very difficult...but it's also not very intuitive.
Industry chains are short and pathetic.  They are rarely profitable, unless you manage to hook up differnt industries on one line,  and you're better off using Trucks most the time.
Oddly enough, Intercity busses are perferred later in game over trains as well.   With roads being much easier to manipulate and control,  trains really just become a novelty.
There is water in game,  however it serves no purpose other than to build bridges that don't like being built.   It's a shame because the water actually looks lovely,  and forms into huge lakes, rivers and streams.   It just begs for water transit.  The starting year is 1850,  Paddle driven ships were in full swing,  and hadn't fully replaced sail yet.
Maps are more than large enough. So yes, this is a positive.  They can be downrigt massive.  Archipeligo, and more water based maps would be completely doable.  Along the lines of huge maps,  unlike in Transit Tycoon, or Locomotion,  these are actually big enoug that airplanes would really make sense.    Unfortunatly, there are no airplanes.
Optimization is ok.  It chugs later on as cities grow.  But this too has been improving.  It also still needs work,
Variation is low.      It's a solid start of mechanics...but there needs to be a lot of refinement,  a lot of additional content,  and♥♥♥♥♥ I dont' even care if ships, aircraft, are additional cost DLC,  that's fine. I understand these people need money to make their game,  but 40 USD is simply too much for such an incomplete game.
EDIT
You will have fun with this game.  It is pretty,  trains do run once you -eventually- get the tracks down.  Profits can be had, the whole 9 yards.  You won't,  however,  have 40 dollars worth of fun with it.   It seems that not hours after this review went up,  the devs announced a North American DLC.   So,  variation in theory should be helped,  but the flaws of construction,  limited industry,  water transit, and aircraft still remain.
END EDIT
EDIT 2 - USA DLC released-
Okay so we now have the American DLC.   It was free so if you haven't bought this game yet,   well, still don't buy it.   It doesn't really "Fix" any of the issues. If anything it makes the game much harder in the early era due to how the US stuff is balanced.  You still can't do basic things like buiding a rail road crossing with a road. (you have to built it with a rails overtop of roads),   building tunnels or bridges in a tight space is still a pain,  industry chains are the same,  etc, Nothing was fixed,  just content.  Vehicle content.
I hate being so negative about it,  but come on!  If there's one good thing to say about this,  it's that the DLC was made with help from the modding community.  That in it's own right is a seed of hope.  Hope that they get more and more help from modders and actually fix/add all the things this game needs to be good.
If you see it on sale for cheap,  I'd say pick it up now, but it's still not worth the full price they're charging, so overall recommendation is "no"
-END EDIT 2-
A final note, The modding community is quite nice,  but unless you know german or russian.....well...hard to read.   The potential is there,  but  it needs a bit more realization on the dev's end before getting there.

The first and most important thing you need to know about Krosmaster Arena is that this game is actually a sort of cross-compatible  companion to a board game/miniatures skirmish game. Each figure or set that you can buy comes with a code to redeem on the digial version so you can play online with other people. If the rules seem complicated and hard to follow or it seems like this game is too P2W, it's because this was a collectible miniatures game first and a video game second.
If you're coming into this game now, you're about 3 years late, and that means you've missed 3 'seasons' of characters, add ons, new rules, countless tournaments, meta-strategy development and erata. If it seems like everyone else knows what they are doing better than you do, it's because they probably do, because they've been playing this since it was originally a browser-only application.
All of that said, I think this game is amazing if you're a fan of Ankama's Wakfu and Dofus universes, if you like RPGs, if you like strategic games, and if you like collectible games where you can try all kinds of silly combinations and tactics, mixing and matching your team of units, then you can probably get into this game and have a lot of fun without spending a cent.
Like many other popular free to play games, you can dump in cash and get some of the most powerful characters, but the rules of the game and the random elements mean that having Goultard or Nox or Qilby is not a guaranteed win. In many cases, those characters can be a liability because they are huge targets and they drastically restrict your team composition by taking up most of your points. It all comes down to a careful balance of skill and luck,
If you don't want to spend money, there's a weekly free rotation of characters for you to use without restriction. If you play enough, win enough, do the single player challenges, and sometimes just hang out long enough, you can earn additional figures without spending a cent.  And with the physical game still releasing new sets and new characters, there will are plenty of future updates planned, meaning more maps, more single-player challenges, and if the Krosmaster Quest Add-on is any indication, we may even see a full-blown co-operative campaign mode some day.

I do have to say it is loosely connected by super-long ladders and rather empty underground zones, often forcing butt naked marathons for boss battles that require multiple tries. Fromsoft did resolve those problems in later games, yet the underdeveloped underground zones are one of the fun aspects that are unique to DS1.
+Some REALLY REALLY EPIC BOSS FIGHTS. Beating O&S was one of my best gaming moments.
+NPC interactions and questilnes are much better than DS2. Many memorable characters with just enough depth.
I gave DS2 a 10/10, and some of my first experiences with this game made me think DS1 should be 11/10. But with some old mechanics and framerate issues(even using Dsfix) I was fortunately able to settle on 10/10 for DS1 too. It really does have the charm of that big brother that had significant influence on its younger brothers and just gaming in general.

As a newly young adult getting ready to start college, this was a game that intrigued me from the moment I first heard about it. Unlike other narrative-based games, I wanted to experience this game first-hand, instead of just watching a Let's Play, which I assume many people did. Let me tell you, it was money well spent.
I'll start off by saying, yes, this game isn't for everyone. If you're looking for intense gameplay, you won't find it here. That's because Night in the Woods is a game centered around immersion and story-telling, and if you're perfectly fine with that, then I can almost guarantee it won't disappoint.
All of the characters and scenery are absolutely beautiful, both in writing and art style. The soundtrack is very ear-pleasing, and fits the atmosphere of the game well. What surprised me though was just how real and relatable the characters felt. Being a socially awkward bisexual who's gone through a lot of crap that I'd rather not explain, I see a little bit of myself in each one of the four main characters. Even the side characters are charming and memorable, each with their own personalities and unique dialogue.
I could go on about how much I love Night in the Woods, but I think that would ruin the experience for most people. If you're around my age, I think you'll find a lot you can relate to in this game. You don't need to be as big a gamer as I am to enjoy this emotional rollercoaster of a story about finding peace and purpose in your life among the rest of the world.

This is not a bad game. It is a pretty fun game. But nor is it a good game.
It starts out in a camping resort of some sort. The starting area is of course very easy and helps you out to get the hand on the controls and mechanics. It is much more of a survival zombie game than for example Left 4 Dead or all those other FPS zombie games. It is not as hardcore as DayZ although. But I still liked it and I just finished it after restarting.
From my understanding it is a smaller studio backed by Microsoft behind it and I say they made a good job. I did not notice many bugs or glitches. Graphics are decent and controls not bad -IF- you have a controller. It is also nice that you can avoid zombies and try sneaking (Which I didn't do much). As said the focus is more on survival and gathering resources and survivors for your home base instead of wildly shooting cause that will have you dead if you are ill prepared. And a dead character stays dead.
The characters you gather all have diffrent traits and "personalities". Which is interesting at  first but later on proves to be shallow. Non the less the more you gather the more room you need, the more food you need and so on.  Sadly the game do become a bit of a rince and repeat after a while when every mission is "Oh no we seen a special zombie out here" "Create noise to make the zombies do this while I plunder" or "Oh no scavengers in need of help". Also we got the "Sadness, anger, fear" traits where you just tell your friends that you and him/her are going to smack some zombies the old fashion way. This is one of the more annoying missions since they just about killing zombies and put you at risk just to appease some of the idiots in your crew. There is also missions to save or help other survivor groups. These could be so much more if they deepended the social mechanics and maybe added in more of an RPG mindset to the game.
The map is pretty damn big too and I did not scavenge much outside of any of the  three settlements. The country side is not that appealing since it is mostly wastes of land you drive through to g et to your next objective. But this adds to the atmosphere since it is supposed to be a small county with a large farming community.
This is a clusterf*** of a review but I still think the strong parts is the survival part, the less focus on action. The tiny bit of social interaction and dialogue (even if the voice actors where like 3-4? Least it beats the 2  guys making the voices for Skyrim! Hue hue) The atmosphere can be great at times and some vistas are nice.
BUT. The game is bit to much of a repeat, there could been more interaction with your group and the others. The Wilkerson have some interesting missions but not much more than them being a bit of the Merle of State of Decay and then nothing happens. The game also would be much much much better with co-op or multiplayer where each player runs their own group. The special zombies are also kinda a pain the♥♥♥♥♥ This must be some kind of thing from L4D.
To end it, yes I do recommend it if you want a open world zombie survivor game and zombie movie lovers will see many references. Also! ♥♥♥♥ you Ed for being such a cry baby. God damnit.

This game is so unique, I really wish the developers could have gotten it right. Maybe in the future, but I really hope they will continue expanding on this idea. I'm really sick of zombie games these days, but as an open world survival rpg it's different fun and addictive. My enjoyment though so far is being hindered by quite a few things.
After the introduction the game just thrusts you forward with little to no instruction. Things are subtly added to a journal, but that fills up very fast. The UI isn't the greatest, there are some parts I still don't understand.
Using a keyboard doesn't feel good at all, it can be hard to turn my character. Melee combat is very sluggish and not satisfying, it can often feel pointless. Gunplay is fine, but guns and ammo are scarce. I find this more enjoyable, but because the melee just isn't viable, it's kind of a problem.
The game is open world and the events are in realtime. If you can't pickup all the supplies you find, you can radio in for a scavenger to come and loot at your location. Driving feels pretty good, but vehicles seem to take a lot of damage quickly. You can also use the trunk of any vehicle to store you supplies. There is actually a bit of highway driving, and it would be nice to have a radio or something haha. Survivors will help you based on an influence system, the AI however is really bad, so it can be tricky at times to maintain your trust when they dive in front of your car or walk into range of a molotov cocktail.
Zombies seem to be attracted to light and sound. This can be really fun for strategizing. You can craft and buy silencers or items like talking dolls, alarm clocks, firecrackers and flares to lure zombies. These items work sometimes, but I find they don't keep their attention for long. This mechanic is very enjoyable, interesting a new. Sometimes I would stay in a car and honk the horn the lure the zombies away from a house, or maybe throw down a noise maker to attract there attention in a jam. Unlike any other zombie game, you can think in this one, depending on your supplies or situation you have to decide fight or flight.
I didn't know until several hours in that this game had permadeath. It was pretty brutal, and I was pretty bummed out losing that character. I really like this though because it keeps you careful. All playable characters have status effects, and you have to make sure their ailments are tended to.
Feeling a little overwhelmed at times with quests. If you try to focus on the main storyline, you might hear of a survivor that needs help nearby. Failing to help then can result in negative consequences to your base. If you focus on side quests you'll be barked at a lot about the main quest.
The characters and voice acting could use a lot of improvement. The girl on the outpost radio has by far the worst voice, she sounds completely oblivious of the zombie apocolypse. There isn't really any advanced graphic settings, just preset ones for different specs. They look fine, but it's the effect that makes the game look bad. High contrast and poor lighting leading to graphical glitches, and overall it just isn't very pleasing to the eye. This is probably the first game I've played with the gamma slider in, and it helped a bit.
Originally I had this review set to recommended, but I'm changing that as it's been a week of hopping in and being extremely frustrated because of poor mechanics stopping me from progressing in the game. I highly recommend that people check this game out, maybe play a friends copy or watch some let's plays, but as a paying customer I'm a little bummed that I can't enjoy this with it's problems.

Before we begin, I'm going to say that Starbound IS NOT a bad game. My review is not negative on the grounds that I hate it, I actually used to find it incredibly enjoyable and it sometimes still is in the rare occasions that I play it. BUT... This game changes too frequently for me to keep up with or even bother trying to learn the new mechanics.
I've been playing Starbound since it was brought to my attention via the Yogscast when they played it back in December 2013. I loved every minute that I spent exploring and crafting and mining. Hell I even loved when a giant meteor smashed into my base and destroyed 90% of it. It was new and it was awsome.
Then with Starbound-
Create a new character and get into the game immediately
Use coal to power your ship and fly between planets freely
Tiers of pickaxes similar to Minecraft will different durabilities and mining speeds
Complete freedom. Do whatever you want anywhere.
Cave systems full of loot chests and gear
Structures and villages full of NPCs
Fast forward about 3 years later and 1.0 finally launches. It was my first time back playing it since my laptop died in 2014. So many new features were added in the mean time and hell yeah that sounded fantastic. Then I loaded up the game. It started with an unskippable story for my race (#GlitchForLife) Which wasn't so bad at first to be honest, but it's there everytime you make a new character. I was locked out of the cockpit for my ship, the ship now had an AI unit, and now there were quest objectives on the surface of my planet. In theory it sounds like a great game. That is where it started to lose me. The core gameplay was almost entirely different and I was faced with the choice of story narrative or sandbox.
Starbound now-
Story narrative, different intro depending on your race
Forced questlines
Dungeons and bosses
More gear
If you're a newcomer to the series then PLEASE give it a chance. I was forced to forget everything that I had learned in the time that I had been playing and that pretty much killed the game for me.

I'll try to say things others haven't already said.
This game has been through a lot of different variations of the "sandbox survival" genre. I think the big problem the game had originally was that it began as a very unforgiving survival experience with a more realistic planetary colonization feel, and then suddenly switched into a more upbeat space adventure RPG within a few updates. This caused a shift in the fanbase that left a wave of negative reviews, as the "Legacy Starbound" had attracted Rust and DayZ style fans that didn't like the sudden change of pace. This wasn't a huge concern for me since there are enough of those games already existing for similar price. Now, the full version has an acceptable balance of 'actually fun' and 'survival' mechanics that I'm happy with. Besides that, the game is great for all the other reasons others have listed. My only negatives -- lack of a deep main quest and multidimensional characters -- aren't very fair because the game's center is how it plays, not the story. Fun with friends too.
Oh, and don't forget about mods. Download Frackin' Universe after a good playthrough. I'll let it speak for itself.

Duke 3D is a classic game that still plays great today.  Unfortunately, this port is horrible.
It's a shame because the true 3D rendering, colored lighting, and ambient occlusion go a long ways toward making the game look a bit more modern without sacrificing its classic look.
20th Anniversary World Tour has two absolutely crippling issues.
First, VSYNC is forced on, and there is some kind of mouse acceleration or something in effect.  Disabling VSYNC in Nvidia Control Panel helps a lot, but you are still going to be faced with laggy mouse controls.  When the game plays perfectly through eDuke or even in DOSBOX, there is no reason to put up with input lag.
Second, the ingame music plays back in MONO for some reason.  The music files themselves are stereo, so I have no idea why this is.  This frankly makes the music annoying to listen to, like it is playing through a little radio on your desk.
Another issue (though minor) is that none of the expansions are included, even though they were included with the Megaton edition previously available of Steam.  I don't mind this so much as I never liked any of them, but it's a bad move indeed to release an updated version of a classic game with content removed.

Yes, having a bunch of different clothes variants is amazing but doesn't shadow the fact Street Fighter is a pretty good game.
I first picked this game up with huge anticipation. I've seen the tournaments, I've watched the Pure Pwnage episode on this, and I've played Street Fighter 2 The World Warrior back in 94' like it was Call of Duty to these kids today. To say at first, I was a little disappointed. However, with a bit of practice and exposure to unique combos and moves, I became immersed. Besides the regular arcade/world tour mode, the game also features a challenge option for you to try out and test every characters combos and special moves. This is extremely helpful to new players in learning how the game mechanics work. At first it seems impossible to do anything super or ultra combos, especially with all the joystick or d-pad movement. After hammering it out a few times in this mode, you get used to the movements and mechanics start making sense. Some moves require all three punch buttons to be pressed. I didn't know that it was supposed to be at the same time and tried hammering three quick punches to which no special move would occur. It dawned on me eventually to try pressing all three punch buttons which resulted in a successful special attempt. It can seem extremely difficult, challenging, and even apathetic, but stick with it and keep plugging away and eventually the control schemes all make sense. I felt the combos were a bit more fluent than what Mortal Kombat X's was. Just like in the old Street Fighter games, you can grab and throw your opponents. The basic controls are weak punch and weak kick, then medium punch and medium kick, then there is two variances of hard punch and hard kick. Within the game, the player is able to choose the costume, fight style and taunt of the fighters before entering the stage. There are two bonus stages that are also featured throughout arcade mode. Similar styles and patterns can be noticed between fighters where some feel balanced, some are wrestlers, and some are acrobatic.
Story lines within the game don't tell a lot of story, but do give a bit of insight into the characters of the Street Fighter World. Each character has a short story segment at the beginning and then again at the end tell of their triumph.
The graphics in this game are distinctive. It follows a 3D sort of pattern but it's definitely 2D. I really like the art style they chose and they way they chose to end fights. Upon delivering a final blow, players can see their final actions carried out in slow motion. Sounds are good and do not necessarily mimic the old noise were used to. None the less, some of the old sounds are noticeable while the new ones deliver the impact they are meant to deliver.
Multi player is absolute overkill. I don't think there are many players like myself still stuck in the 90's trying to put two punch combos together. Match making does a decent job trying to pair you up with someone close to your talent but often feels like it misses big time. Either really get to know this game and spend time learning character move sets, or be stuck getting punched and kicked thirty times in a row followed by a special combo.
Overall, it is a pretty good game. I'm not a huge fight fan, but I do like my street fighter.
For future SF games, it would be nice to see them try to new things with the game and maybe even go for a 3D plane. I have no problems with the way things are now, but why not try to add a bit more? To buy the full version of the game it costs about $45... I think for $45 there should be a bit more into the game than small variations on fighting. And maybe for guys like myself have certain move sets for certain characters that fight in different ways?
RATING : 7.4/10

For a text based game, I would firstly suggest using a spell checker on the text.  In character selection screen there was already multiple uses of the word "weild" (rather than wield).
The text in the game is quite basic and didn't give a sense of atmosphere.  In addition in the 1 hour I played I kept seeing the same room descriptions come up again and again.  I would have expected a text based game to have many versions of 'monsters in a room' but they all said the same 'A wave of hostility hits you as xxxx'.
Combat is reasonable for turn-based. Some strategic options about silencing spell casters, focusing attacks on your tanks (since no rows, everyone stands at the front including archers), healing your characters etc.
Skill trees seem quite limited. 4 main abilities in a class that can be unlocked and then upgraded a couple more times, and then points put into passive abilities.  The game is going more for many classes than particular customisation of one class.
Loot is reasonable, but simple. Very often you will find weapons that do double the damage of your previous weapon (although perhaps that changes once you progress more floors down).
I realise this is early access - but comments by dev in September say it is close to full release.
As a suggestion, I would say the Dev needs to spend $50 of hiring a freelance writer from a freelancer platform to write tons of nicely written variations of room text to give a sense of atmosphere and reduce the sense of repetition.

The game needs more room-types and content in general to be good. I quite enjoy it. Picking warriors over mages really matters. I feel positive about the future content. Replayability is high even now.
However, there are two negative aspects of the game. You can simply overrun AI that it can never reach you and kill your squad at all. I did it. Even when I fought the boss, it killed all my fighters including me and then, my warrior Damon took one on one on this boss. Damon won easily. That's a sort of a balance issue, which can be easily repeated if you get experience gain boosting item early in the game or some damn good roulette results. Another problem connected to balance is at the start, where if you fight twice against 3 enemies and after that boss comes, the opposite happens. You don't stand a chance.
Second negative aspect I can not stand by is that you can play this game for free on armorgames with all content included. I believe they should have some sort of limited acess to the game. I don't like to pay for what is free.
All in all, the game is good and developer still works on it. As it is early acess, both negatives can be erased or fixed and I look forward to the future development.

As a newly young adult getting ready to start college, this was a game that intrigued me from the moment I first heard about it. Unlike other narrative-based games, I wanted to experience this game first-hand, instead of just watching a Let's Play, which I assume many people did. Let me tell you, it was money well spent.
I'll start off by saying, yes, this game isn't for everyone. If you're looking for intense gameplay, you won't find it here. That's because Night in the Woods is a game centered around immersion and story-telling, and if you're perfectly fine with that, then I can almost guarantee it won't disappoint.
All of the characters and scenery are absolutely beautiful, both in writing and art style. The soundtrack is very ear-pleasing, and fits the atmosphere of the game well. What surprised me though was just how real and relatable the characters felt. Being a socially awkward bisexual who's gone through a lot of crap that I'd rather not explain, I see a little bit of myself in each one of the four main characters. Even the side characters are charming and memorable, each with their own personalities and unique dialogue.
I could go on about how much I love Night in the Woods, but I think that would ruin the experience for most people. If you're around my age, I think you'll find a lot you can relate to in this game. You don't need to be as big a gamer as I am to enjoy this emotional rollercoaster of a story about finding peace and purpose in your life among the rest of the world.
