TrainFever is a great strategy game which allows a dynamic range of ‘transport tycoon’ style options to the player, it can slightly compared to Railroad Tycoon 3 but it is completely different game in contrast.
Unfortunately it does have some performance issues and annoying limitations which affect the fun of gameplay; the worst of these is the poor compression of the files which cause the game to become extremely laggy with more and more vehicles, stops and buildings on the map as time goes on. Turning down the settings does nothing to counteract this issue.
The second is the building of roads over railways, which is impossible for some stupid reason - you must build the road before the track. Even doing so doesn't guarantee that the game will actually allow you to place the track afterwards. The same goes for building bridges across railway lines and vice versa. It becomes complete headache whenever you need to modify track routes that have roads crossing them.
Another issue is freight and how industries that start with 0-2 production never seem to increase production. They continue to switch between using your line and not using it, making it impossible to profit from the lines you create. On the other hand, industries producing (usually) 10 items seem to work correctly, increasing based on consumer demand.
There’s a few other minor limitations which I really hope they patch in the future, such as vehicle listings, track layouts and city growth which are hard to explain but make the game difficult to play.

First of all, I'm not really an expert on the game yet. I loved Railroad Tycoon so I was really exicted when I saw this in the Steam-Lottery and even won the game. In short: I can't say I wasted my money (partly due to me not spending any money).
The game is easy to get into, given you know how these kinds of games play out. If you ever played Railroad Tycoon or Sid Meier's: Railroads you'll know what to do from the start. All the others currently have to rely on Steam guides or trial-and-error to get the basics down. Given the lack of interesting industries (without mods) it's not a difficult game, though I don't think it is supposed to be since most of the fun comes from watching your little trains make their rounds and queue up at busy stations. It's a great game for everyone who ever wanted some miniature model trains but either doesn't have the space, the money, or loving parents who'd buy it for them during their childhood.
During my playtime I didn't encounter a single bug.
As it is right now, the game's performance isn't all that great. I often get lags and freezes at the end of an ingame month and a general decrease in FPS as the game progresses, it always stays at a playable rate (lowest I got was 26 FPS). I think that might be fixed in the future though! There also seem to be a lot of updates, so I'd bet my money on that.
The game also offers a modding community, which sadly isn't that big. This can and, hopefully, will change as well in the future though.
Overall I see a lot of potential in this game, but I wouldn't spend the full price buying it.
Pro:
Nice if you like watching trains do their rounds
Decent graphics
Mod support
Active devs
Con:
Performance
Long-term motivation (lack of industries)

I don't write reviews for games.  I'm writing this because I bought this on steam sale, and then was blown away by its quality.
First, the preface.  Long Live the Queen is a choose your own adventure novel, where you play as a princess who's mother just died, and you have to "survive" 40 weeks til your corination.  Along the way, there are plenty of things that can stop you from reaching that goal.
Long Live the Queen does exactly what most choose your own adventures do, and more.  The reason why it's so awesome is because there are SO MANY different things that could happen as you play.  The decision trees are so wide, and all the skills do something.  The depth of the game is so vast that certain events drastically change due to small skill checks that happen beforehand.  It's really well done.
One of the best parts about the game is the fact that you're a 14 year old girl.  Sometimes you (the player) know whats going on, but the naive little girl you're playing doesn't quite get it.  It's like why sometimes kids will be abducted by criminals offering candy; you and I know its bad, but to a child living in the moment, unless their parents said "Don't accept candy from strangers", the kid might be tempted to go into the van.  (Super minor spoilers) An example in the game is when you recieve chocolate.  You know that people are trying to kill you, and as a result, you probably shouldn't eat it.  However, if you didn't research the appropriate skills, your princess might dive into the chocolate without giving it a second though.  With the right skills, you can be like "hmm, maybe I shouldn't" and save it for later.
Also, you get to be a princess.  If you get magical abilities, you'll be given a skimpy anime dress costume that makes your magic even better.  Makes sense.
I will probably never survive to coronation but I can't stop playing this game over and over

Imagine a game that is the apotheosis of all games, a brilliant fusion of story and mechanics and art that leads you to new emotional catharsis when you replay it every year.  The game also washes your dishes, files your taxes, and reminds you to call your mother on her birthday.
Sounds like a game worth having, right?  But what if it cost $10,000, along with half your hair, both your index fingers, your favorite toe, and the promise of eternal agony in your least preferred afterlife?  It's probably not worth it then, right?
Long Live The Queen is a game that is not the apotheosis of all games.  As such, I'd judge its non-sale Steam price of $9.99 as too high.  But if you buy it for $1.99 during a sale, then I'd say it was definitely worth it.
At its heart, Long Live The Queen is a choose-your-own-adventure about a princess hoping to survive to queendom.  It has the added twist that each day, you choose two of 14 classes for your princess to take - classes ranging from Royal Demeanor to Climbing to Military Strategy.  Story branches appear and disappear according to your choices, and it is easy to end up impaled by a sword or punctured by arrows or eaten by krakens.
This has reasonable amusement value, one that does eventually wear off; laughter turns to snickers turns to forced grins.  Fortunately, by the time I reached the eyeroll phase, I judged my enjoyment of the game up to that point to be worth roughly $2.61.  Which meant that I did more than break even on this game.  Hooray!

A nice, entry-level touhou-like bullet hell shoot 'em up, despite it's flaws.
Yes if you like danmaku (bullet hell) or would like to give the subgenre a try. No if you don't like the genre, moe-ish art, or games that go straight to gameplay without much lore, exposition, etc.
It has a very interesting way to provide challenge when it comes to patterns: Unlike touhou, which relies heavily on pure dodging/zoning, and on understanding boss-specific mechanics, eXceed 3rd attempts most of the time to scare or impress the player with the illusion of danger, rather than relying on pure execution on the player's part. A lot of patterns will look very tricky at first, but become really smooth to adapt to as they unravel, providing sudden, wide openings.
Less pixel-tight, grazing-heavy gameplay, and more observation and planning in general, compared to touhou.
+ Good soundtrack, not groundbreaking (using chord progressions that are popular in japanese osts and compos, without straying too far) but gives a really enjoyable and fitting ambience to the game
+ Decent and evolutive level design (the difficulty curve is really smooth, unlike touhou which often provides one with bosses that are too difficult or easy for their stage)
+ Really simple to understand and get used to, making it perfect for beginners who would like to get into bullet hell shmups without getting curbstomped by irregular difficulty curves and complex or unclear mechanics
+ Enjoyable feedback (depending on whether one will find the ridiculous amount of bonus pellets dropped by enemies a bothering eyesore, or a constant, positive stimulus)
+ Light fanservice, OK voice-acting
+ Replayability. Sh'mups like this one depend heavily on one's willingness to try higher difficulty levels.
+ Beautiful bullet patterns (which is a thing in many bullet hell shooters), even though they sometimes lack originality and aren't comparable to touhou's breathtaking patterns)
- Soundtrack does not loop smoothly, leaving in audio blanks which completely break the ambience and immersion
- Soundtrack sometimes doesn't even loop at all (looking at you, Celestia!), which is really awkward
- Forced, extremely small resolution
- Capped at 30fps, and poorly optimized (framedrops to ~15fps on 2015 middle-end machines when specific particles appear, for example when a boss dies)
- Seems to be a trend with sh'mups by very small japanese studios: Character artwork quality is bad (Often broken anatomy, perspective and shading/volume). At least it doesn't reach ZUN-levels of bad
- Character design is often quite bland
- Quite short (stages and bosses are in general shorter than what one can find in touhou and the likes), even though the replayability

Fun, but for something that calls itself "Master of the Arcane" there's awfully little arcane, relying on pushing units around the map.
One or two spells per turn on average, versus countless units, I would have prefered it the other way round. Plus, casting a spell is pretty much the only thing it does not remind the player to do.
I do like the unintrusive way it reminds me of other things, so that's a plus on the interface.
A minus is that it doesn't show me what units I can build where in the city list, so I'd have to guess and check all of them. It also isn't very informative on what I need to do to get what. One of my cities won't let me build a Mana Trap, and I have no idea why. Earlier I wanted to research Fertile Lands, but had no idea how to get that either. At some point I could suddenly cast it (I assume I found it).
A few more postives:
- Customizable Win conditions. No need to keep an opponent alive (like I used to in Master of Magic) to cast the Unity spell, simply untick the win option of beating all opponents.
- Go-to orders come AFTER I did my turn (after pressing end of turn), so I can still change their orders before that, and it's still/again my turn when they end up with movement points left after they arrived. (I hated having to wait through all the go-to orders in Civ before I even get to do something.)
And while you can't disable movement animations/showing enemy moves, clicking somewhere cuts that short (the plain info of "Enter ends your turn" under the purple button at the bottom right corner is perfect for that).
- Little gems of humour hidden away, sometimes referencing films and possibly other media. They always make me smile.
A drawback is that the game slows down after a while on my computer (which isn't that old), with a noticable delay when I click on one of the reminders mentioned above, before it gets to the relevant place. So I have to save, quit, and start the game again to get normal response time again. (Edit: Friend told me how to fix or at least delay that: don't use the wide option of the spellbook.)
But that's not the only problem. With graphics on max, even the Steam chat input was delayed, huh!? (The reason I have the graphics all on lowest. Which still has all the animations active. The tiny figures doing stuff is very cute and well done, but it would be nice to disable that.)
Right now I ran into a graphic glitch that keeps turning up when I capture a certain city.
But overall it keeps me entertained for a while.

This is easily my favorite game. Yes, there are quite a few things wrong with it, but the pros definitely outweigh the cons, and most of the cons are fixable anyway.
First off, the level design is incredible. You can see places you've already been, and places you will eventually end up. It's a really cool feeling when you look off into the distance and think "holy♥♥♥♥♥♥ I was just over there!" or "wow, I have to go
" This game will literally have you questioning which cliffs are safe to drop off of. Loot, shortcuts, bonfires (checkpoints), and even completely different areas are hidden behind fake walls, off the sides of buildings (
), through seemingly impossible places you'd never think you can access, and it's the best feeling when you discover them (or find them on the wiki, we've all been there at least once). Lordran is a beautifully crafted world both in aesthetic and in design.
The story and lore, while obscured in item descriptions and in NPC dialogue, is gripping. Nearly every boss, NPC, and item has it's own story. You will even see some of the NPCs throughout the entire game if you follow their plotline, and most will be able to help you through
Meaning you can summon them to help you with boss fights. The multiplayer now isn't nearly as active as it used to be, but you will still see the occasional summon sign and invade/get invaded every once in a while.
The game is said to not have very good replayability, which I agree with in certain respects, but you can still find a way to have fun with it even after you've beaten it. The speedrunning community is still active, every year a "global restart day" (better known as The Return to Lordran) is held where everybody starts a new game and plays through the game again with heavy use of multiplayer, and mods can make the game more, uh...
We all know the game isn't perfect, in fact, this game holds the title of one of the most poorly ported games from console known to man. Straight out of the box, the game is capped at 30FPS with laughable graphical settings and playing with a keyboard and mouse is practically not an option. However, the DSFix mod (google it) fixes the framerate cap and offers tons of graphics settings to toy around with. Mods to help play with KB/M do exist, but I strongly reccommend to swallow your PCMR pride and buy a controller.

Hi, I got Night of the Woods a few months after Christmas 2016, and I'd like to write a review about it.
First of all, let's talk about the gameplay.
The gameplay is smooth, and transitions very nicely. There's also a small "tutorial" at the beginning of the game, although you have to figure out for yourself how the engine runs. While this tutorial is forcing players to play it, it's enjoyable and doesn't feel like much of one at all.
Now, the artstyle. I really enjoy the simplistic artstyle of this game. It allows you to focus on other details in the game, rather than intricate character designs that you would see in other story based games.
So, the story. Mae Borowski just dropped out of college, and came back to her hometown, Possum Springs. At first, it seems as if minor things have changed. The Food Donkey went out of buisness, there's now a Snack-Falcon, and so on. But then, after a band practice and a night in the diner, Mae is told by her friends Bea, Gregg, and Angus that their friend Casey went missing. After walking outside, they see an arm on the ground. The situation from here continues to get spookier and scarier, until Mae and her friends decide to go after what she suspects is causing all this: the ghost of Little Joe.
This is a creepy story, especially in the dream sequences. Although it's really fun to find out who are making these people dissapear, and even more so to find out why.
The characters are actually really... realistic, apart from their physical appearance. They have personalities, problems, and different relationships with you. This is tied for the #1 reason I recommend this game, along with...
The minigames! The minigames aren't simply wastes of your time, like in countlessother titles. In Night in the Woods, every desicion ever so slightly changes the outcome of the story. Not only do they matter, they're actually pretty fun! On my second playthrough, I spent some hours slashing my way through the Demontower game. And the most fun one forr me is band practice. Although you don't do it too often, it's fun as all when you get to! And it gives you different scores on how well you performed. I felt great when I nailed Die Anyhwere Else. And the music is enjoyable as well. I bought the soundtrack to listen to.
All in all, Night in the Woods is, if not one of the most, then the most fun gamee I have ever had time to enjoy playing. I would reccomend it to anyone ages 13 and up, though, because there are some words I wouldn't want a ten year old kid seeing and asking their parents about. If your 13 or older, though, I would place this at the top of your Wishlist, because I want everyone who has the oppurtunity to play it to take the oppurtunity.
Thank me later.

Yes, having a bunch of different clothes variants is amazing but doesn't shadow the fact Street Fighter is a pretty good game.
I first picked this game up with huge anticipation. I've seen the tournaments, I've watched the Pure Pwnage episode on this, and I've played Street Fighter 2 The World Warrior back in 94' like it was Call of Duty to these kids today. To say at first, I was a little disappointed. However, with a bit of practice and exposure to unique combos and moves, I became immersed. Besides the regular arcade/world tour mode, the game also features a challenge option for you to try out and test every characters combos and special moves. This is extremely helpful to new players in learning how the game mechanics work. At first it seems impossible to do anything super or ultra combos, especially with all the joystick or d-pad movement. After hammering it out a few times in this mode, you get used to the movements and mechanics start making sense. Some moves require all three punch buttons to be pressed. I didn't know that it was supposed to be at the same time and tried hammering three quick punches to which no special move would occur. It dawned on me eventually to try pressing all three punch buttons which resulted in a successful special attempt. It can seem extremely difficult, challenging, and even apathetic, but stick with it and keep plugging away and eventually the control schemes all make sense. I felt the combos were a bit more fluent than what Mortal Kombat X's was. Just like in the old Street Fighter games, you can grab and throw your opponents. The basic controls are weak punch and weak kick, then medium punch and medium kick, then there is two variances of hard punch and hard kick. Within the game, the player is able to choose the costume, fight style and taunt of the fighters before entering the stage. There are two bonus stages that are also featured throughout arcade mode. Similar styles and patterns can be noticed between fighters where some feel balanced, some are wrestlers, and some are acrobatic.
Story lines within the game don't tell a lot of story, but do give a bit of insight into the characters of the Street Fighter World. Each character has a short story segment at the beginning and then again at the end tell of their triumph.
The graphics in this game are distinctive. It follows a 3D sort of pattern but it's definitely 2D. I really like the art style they chose and they way they chose to end fights. Upon delivering a final blow, players can see their final actions carried out in slow motion. Sounds are good and do not necessarily mimic the old noise were used to. None the less, some of the old sounds are noticeable while the new ones deliver the impact they are meant to deliver.
Multi player is absolute overkill. I don't think there are many players like myself still stuck in the 90's trying to put two punch combos together. Match making does a decent job trying to pair you up with someone close to your talent but often feels like it misses big time. Either really get to know this game and spend time learning character move sets, or be stuck getting punched and kicked thirty times in a row followed by a special combo.
Overall, it is a pretty good game. I'm not a huge fight fan, but I do like my street fighter.
For future SF games, it would be nice to see them try to new things with the game and maybe even go for a 3D plane. I have no problems with the way things are now, but why not try to add a bit more? To buy the full version of the game it costs about $45... I think for $45 there should be a bit more into the game than small variations on fighting. And maybe for guys like myself have certain move sets for certain characters that fight in different ways?
RATING : 7.4/10

not quite as good as terraria. it's lacking the fun progression of unlocking and finding the new ores in unique ways like terraria did, and instead advances you through the tiers by unlocking new planets once your gear is upgraded enough to go there to mine for materials (which was always too tedious a commitment, consuming too much time to dig down and navigate the underground for ore that's difficult to find), or instead explore the overworld, looting the generated structures and killing monsters for ore, which was the much quicker option. there was nothing that made you attatched to the planets; beaming somewhere new would only mean sweeping the surface for loot and ore, and then beaming back to your ship once you get bored of walking around. other than seeing and exploring the generated structures for the first time, everything in this game falt like a chore. and even when you found a cool new structure or village, you would start seeing it over and over again on other planets, and the interaction with npc's boiled down to fetch quests or the occasional crewmember to recruit. nothing made you want to stay on a planet any longer than after you had explored the surface, as you're continually advancing through the tiers and anything valuable on the planet eventually becomes obsolete, giving you no reason to build a base or otherwise create some sort of home on a planet as you'll be leaving it soon and forgetting about it. this pretty much made 50% of the sandbox elements of the game, building, completely worthless and unrewarding other than on your ship, completely eliminating one of the large mechanics of the game. while terraria does both of these things much better, starbound still has a lot of charm in it's sci-fi universe, which i personally felt was lacking in terraria. while terraria had a more wacky but deadly fantasy world, starbound had a more grounded, though still fantastical, space opera setting that came with a bit of interesting lore and cool aesthetic.

Very nice shmup.  It's a bullet hell, but it's also pretty accessible to people who aren't experienced with the genre.  Nice art and excellent music in the form of an awesome heavy metal soundtrack.  This is actually a remake of eXceed 3rd - Jade Penetrate.  The original had a slightly less snicker-generating title, and largely the same music (both soundtracks can be bought on bandcamp), though it played significantly faster and the gameplay was different other ways as well.
This game is just a straight-up bullet hell, unlike eXceed 2nd which was a polarity-based bullet hell game.  There are four action buttons: shoot, bomb (clears everything on screen and gets you limited invulnerability), special, and slowdown.  (Five if you count the pause button.)  (Auto-)collect tokens from defeated enemies and graze their bullets (you can hear when it happens) to charge your special meter, and when it's full, release it to do a homing attack.  You also collect attack pods that follow you around, and either shoot forward (when you're not using slow) or do a homing focus fire (when you are doing slow).  Hold down the slow button to move more precisely, and also visualize your hitbox as a bright orange circle at the center of your sprite -- grazing means letting bullets come close to but not touch this!  As you first learn the game, there's also an auto-bomb setting that will basically give you more lives to work with.
The storyline is simple but amusing and fitting.  You're Rayne Lindwurm, the younger sister of the Lindwurm dragon clan.  Your school is conducting what's basically the local preliminaries to fill the seat of a Cardinal Lord in Pandemonium.  By preliminaries, we mean a magical combat tournament of course.  Five opponents stand in your way, all of whom are horrible jerks (except the stage four boss, she's cool), the most powerful and biggest jerk of which is your own older sister, who just loves rubbing it in that she's better than you.  But this time, you get to kick her♥♥♥♥♥
The game has five stages, each culminating in a multi-phase boss fight.  Oh, and if you manage to beat the game without using contniues or auto-bomb, there's a bonus boss waiting for you.
(Disclosure: I acquired this game as part of the Indie Gala Summertide bundle.)

It was an issue on Steam's end, and now many problems have been fixed. Reviews before March 2015 lamenting online play might be outdated. Online isn’t perfect but it is definitely playable (and better than Netherrealm fighters at least).
In my opinion this is one of the best fighting games on Steam. If you want a deep and competitive game or just want to jump into the genre, this is a great title to pick up, especially with EVO right around the corner.
+Diverse roster of 44 playable characters
+All classic SF2 world warriors (Guile, Sagat, Cammy, Akuma, etc.)
+Good mix of SF Alpha and SFIII characters (No Alex or Q though)
+Wide range of controller support
+Very balanced. Every character is viable in the right hands.
+Good soundtrack (Character themes aren't nearly as good as in SFIII: 3rd Strike though)
+Useful training mode with attack data, input display, dummy recording, and even 2 player online training
+Matches can get pretty hype
+Runs well on PC (80 fps on an AMD 7770)
+Solid netcode. Again, not perfect (unless you live in Japan) but most matches are smooth.
+Lots of colors and costumes (everyone has at least 3-4 costumes and ~12 colors)
+New unique Focus Attack system.
+Extensive Trial mode gives a fun way to burn time if you want a challenge
+Interesting Japanese ink brush art style with great 3D visuals (sort of prefer the old 2D sprites though). Fireballs look beautiful.
+Online community is still active
-V-Sync causes input lag
-New Revenge Meter is built up by taking damage. At 50% you can do an Ultra combo. This feels like it rewards bad play and makes comebacks more common and less exciting.
-Ubiquitous 1 frame link combos. These are much more punishable on a missed link due to the large reversal window, allowing players to mash out a dragon punch if you mistime your inputs
-Typical cheap arcade fighting game A.I. with psychic reaction time. Final boss in arcade mode is cheap as hell
-3 joke characters. Dan is funny, but Rufus was unnecessary, and El Fuerte should be removed entirely.
-Character Select starts 1P at Juri and 2P at Hakan. Why not Ryu and Ken?
-Did I mention El Fuerte?
With USF4 what you get is a well polished, balanced, and deep fighter. What makes this game enjoyable to me is the high skill ceiling; every time I play I have the opportunity to improve my ability. Heck, even with the amount of hours I've put in I still kinda suck. Much of my playtime consists of playing in private lobbies with friends, which is always a blast. While Street Fighter may seem technically daunting, I definitely recommend it to those looking to get into the fighting game genre. A learning curve is definitely present, but the fundamentals you pick up from playing this will carry on to other fighters. This is also currently the most played fighting game in the tournament  scene, so those with a competitive drive should be satisfied. Whether you’re familiar with fighters or are a total newcomer, I recommend picking up Ultra Street Fighter IV on PC.

Many people bash Duke Nukem 20th Anniversary World Tour as being inferior to the earlier re-release of the Megaton Edition that was pulled from Steam and is no longer available.  I've played them both and I feel that the 20th Anniversary World Tour is the better of the two and here's why.
1.  The World Tour version doesn't come with the Duke it out in DC, Life's a Beach and Nuclear WInter expansions or map packs or whatever they are.  I've played those three map packs and didn't like any of them as they didn't seem to fit with the Original Duke Nukem 3D.  The new maps are sort of interesting when looked at thematically as a whole, but overall they are boring.  The individual maps are huge. which sounds great, but it sucks because it takes freaking forever to cross them even at a run and there is nothing really interesting to see.  So they are  long, boring and tedious.  I was happy not to see them in the World Tour version and especially liked that I didn't have to play them for achievements.
2.  The World Tour version comes with creator commentary that you can turn on in the options.  When turned on, you get floating icons throughout many of the maps that you can activate.  When activated you get audio recordings from a couple of the original creators of Duke Nukem.  It was super cool to hear their thoughts and such concerning the making of Duke Nukem 3D.  Their commentary ranged from in-game jokes and pop culture references used in the game to reasons or thoughts as to certain creative decisions to coding or visual techniques that they used in the map making process that were actually quite difficult but look so simple and could easily be taken for granted nowadays.  I found the technical commentary to be very insightful.  Hell, I found almost every piece of audio commentary very interesting.
The commentary in the game easily made the purchase of this version of Duke Nukem worth the price I paid.
3.  The third and final thing that made this a superior version was the new episode built by the original creators who did the commentary for this edition.  It was easily one of the better episodes and "expansion."  The maps easily looked like something made by the Duke creators.  The new episode had the same feel as the original Duke Episodes even though they were able to use newer lighting techniques and improved visual assets, most of the Maps were super creative.  The first and final maps especially stood out to me, but all of the maps in the new episode are great.
The World Tour version of Duke didn't appear to have OpenGL rendering.  While many people may have liked that in the Megaton Edition, I was fine with it not being in the 20th Anniversary World Tour Edition.  There was a setting for improved graphics and I thought it was quite good.  It keeps the pixelated style graphics, but used smaller boxes/polygons so that it looked close to OpenGL rendering, but wasn't and I actually preferred it as it felt more like the original Duke than the OpenGL rendering did.
Probably the best feature was the "rewind" ability.  While you could make save files during a level just like you always could, which is useful if you are going to exit the game midlevel, the rewind ability was great assuming you started the level without leaving the game in the middle of the level.  The game records the player's progression through the level so that if at any point you were to die, a rewind function appears on the screen that allows the player to back up to any point in the level or something before the death and allows the player to try a different strategy,  The player can backup even to the beginning of the level.
The rewind function was pretty awesome since there were swaths of time where I would forget to save the game and end up dead.  The rewind ability just allowed me to backup 10 or 20 seconds (or more) and redo the section without dying.  There was even a couple of times I actually ran into an Easter Egg where Duke would say something, but I couldn't hear it because I was listening to one of the creator commentary tracks, so I would pull out my rocket launcher and kill myself.
The rewind ability popped and I would back up a bit and continue.  The game recordng would also note I was listening to audo track so the track would continue playing where I backed up to; I'd let the commentary finish and then walk up to the Easter Egg so I could hear Duke's Joke.  Super Cool!
The only annoying thing about the 20th Anniversary World Tour was when I was playing the game in Full Screen, if I Alt-Tabbed out of the game, the game would automatically disable Full Screen mode go into windowed mode.  Once I was done with whatever I was doing outside Duke Nukem, the only way to get back to full screen was that I had to go back into VIdeo Options inside the game and turn full screen back on.  Once Fullscreen mode was back I had to wait 5 seconds or so because a few of the buttons (e.g. Action e key) wouldn't work.  After the 5 seconds everything was back to normal.
Not too bad, but could get annoying.  But don't Alt-Tab out and you never run into an issue.
Duke Nukem 3D: 20th Anniversary World Tour was a lot a fun and worth the price, in my opinion.

Duke Nukem 3D: The Name Of This Game Is Too Long is a replacement for the excellent Duke Nukem 3D: Megaton Edition which was removed from digital distribution.
Duke Nukem 3D: The Name Of This Game Is Too Long (aka Duke Nukem 3D: 20th Anniversary World Tour) isn’t a bad game. If you like Duke Nukem 3D you should like World Tour.
The thing is some parts of the world are missing from ‘World Tour’. It doesn’t include the expansions: Duke Caribbean: Life's a Beach, Duke it Out of D.C or Nuclear Winter.
I doubt these will ever be added (officially). And if so it would likely be as paid dlc.
The game does include one extra episode Alien World Order.
Which takes you to Amsterdam, Mosow, London, Egypt, Paris, the Golden Gate Bridge San Francisco and then the Hollywood sign.
These new levels look nice with a lot of details. But the enemy placements arent so good. There are a bunch of mini-bosses for no reason. Exploration in these levels aren’t so good either.
There is a new weapon the Incinerator. It can be very satisfying when you’re able to hit an enemy with it.
There are new enemies Firefly Trooper. They are able to shrink themselves which make them annoying to hit. They are armed with incinerators.
Lastly you have the boss Cycloid Incinerator. A red reskin of the Cycloid Emperor. But instead of a rocket launcher he has a flamethrower.
Problem is he has the same AI as the Cycloid Emperor. So he uses this short range flamethrower thinking he can hit me from a distance which he cant. Makes him very easy to kill.
There is also Steam Workshop.
There is a rewind feature which is good, so when you die you can just rewind a bit. It does help with the frustration of accidentally dying and losing progress if you had forgotten to save.
But the game still has a manual save/reload feature.
There are graphical improvements such as “true 3D”. But you already had free mods such as EDuke32 that greatly improved the graphical rendering of Duke Nukem 3D.
And sometimes true 3D makes the game look worse in some areas.
The Megaton Edition looked/sounded better. And had more content.  World Tour has a lot of aliasing (jaggies). The new recorded lines for Duke sound awful at times. Thankfully you have the option to use his classic lines.
So World Tour is really nothing impressive.
It’s a low effort replacement for the Megaton Edition.
I made sure to only get this game on sale, at a heavy discount.
Im giving this a Positive review, not for World Tour, but more for Duke Nukem 3D which is just a great game. Id give World Tour a Mixed review if I had the option.

What can I really say about Duke Nukem that hasn't been said before? 20 years of extraterrestrial butt-kicking, curvaceous babes and cheesy one-liners from a 'roided out protagonist who is the very definition of machismo. Seems like it all flew by in an instant, eh? I've loved DN3D since I downloaded the shareware version when I was still a precocious lad who was probably too young to be playing a game with such mature themes. I would whole-heartedly recommend it to anyone who enjoys prime 90's first person shooters. Great controls, innovative level design, big powerful guns that feel great to use against the numerous foes you encounter. Everything you want in an action game is here.
If you don't already own it, stop reading right now and buy the damn thing. You won't regret it!
For those of us who've been playing for the last couple decades? This particular rerelease, while very good in its own right, isn't completely essential if you already own the game multiple times on multiple systems. There is so much that this latest iteration does right, yet there are certain cons offsetting the pros that make me hesitate to say that it's the definitive version, Despite the minor nitpicks, if you're a hardcore fan of the series, there is enough new content to make it worth your time if you can get it at a good price.
The main draw and reason to purchase this version even if already own the game in another format is the brand new 5th episode, "Alien World Order". This provides 8 new levels set in various locales around the world, designed by Allen Blum III and Richard 'Levelord' Gray, who both worked on the original game. I found all but one of these levels to be very fun and a great compliment to the existing 4 episodes. While they are technically more advanced from a design perspective in some ways, they still have that great old school 3D Realms feel and blend in nicely.
Besides simply getting new levels, this new episode includes additional dialogue for Duke Nukem. Jon St. John returns as the voice of The Duke, with plenty of fresh and funny one-liners. He also did retakes of all his classic lines in a higher sound quality than was possible in a `96 MS-DOS game, so it matches seamlessly between the old and new. I was glad to also see an option included that reverts to his original lo-fi performance if you're a purist. I tend to favour the rerecording for the improved sample rate and consistency, but it's worth pointing out that Jon St. John's inflection and emphasis on words is slightly different in places. Try both versions and see which you prefer.
The last of the new content comes in the form of the "Firefly" enemy and it's associated flamethrower weapon. Some of you will recognise both of these from early screenshots taken during the development process, yet neither made it into the original retail game or the Plutonium Pak. Their inclusion for the 20th Anniversary was a great way to honour the history of the series, while simultaneously giving us something we had not previously experienced in-game before. While I think it would've been interesting to reintroduce even more cut content from the beta versions, this new 5th episode already delivers a great "never before seen" Duke experience just the way it is.
While the new episode is definitely worth playing; there are a couple gripes I have about the overall presentation of the old content. The menu system is streamlined and works well, yet I miss seeing the logo exploding onto the iconic box art when the program starts. I also felt that the gamma correction could've been a little more flexible. I play most of my games using a projector and even with "brightness" set to highest level, certain areas are still too dark. The in-game text also now uses a stencil font instead of the classic fonts from either v1.3d or the Atomic Edition.
The most glaring issue lies with the audio. Certain sound effects like the chaingun cannon firing are very harsh and have too much treble. Others, like the ambient sound of the alien spaceship in E1L5 "The Abyss", were entirely too bass heavy and were abusing my subwoofer. Music has been mastered at a very inconsistent volume with some tracks being so low that they are almost inaudible and others being overpowering at times. Fortunately, the renderings of the classic MIDI songs themselves are quite good, sounding similar to how they would on a Roland SC-55. For someone with decent audio software and a knowledge of modifying Duke 3D; these issues can be corrected and I have done this to my installation, but most people are not that hands-on.
My final point of contention is that while the new episode is indeed enjoyable, there is a bunch of content and levels from previous releases that were not included in this 20th Anniversary package. Unfortunately it does not include the levels from officially sanctioned add-ons such as "Duke it Out in D.C.", "Life's a Beach" and "Nuclear Winter". We also do not get the episode "Plug 'N' Pray" from the PlayStation 1 release, but that is obviously much less of an issue since that was never originally released to PC.
Overall, it's still Duke and it's still great. Despite already owning the game many times over on various computers and consoles, this is the version I probably play the most. Hopefully my review has given players who are familiar with past releases of the game some insight into whether it’s worth an upgrade, or if it would actually be a slight downgrade from the version they’re already happy with. Despite the few issues that I detailed in this port; Duke 3D is a true classic that has stood the test of time better than most. See you all in another 20 years for the 40th Anniversary Holoduke Edition!

So I have logged a measly six hours in Miscreated, and thought I'd sum up my adventures so far. They're not exactly riveting, but since I played on one of the quieter servers, I had a few interesting moments I can talk about.
Day One:
-First enter a server, link up with a group of about four friendly survivors heading for Woodhaven, which at that point I know nothing about.
-Find a crossbow and some bolts, get abandoned by three survivors, leaving myself with one dude, whose name I remember starting with a D. (If you're out there, friend req me fam)
-Come up on an apartment building with a storage lot next to it. Spot a player, and quietly search around while avoiding the person.
-Bump into them anyway, discover they encountered our group heading through Woodhaven. Give them a water bottle and tuna as thanks, and loot apartment building.
-Companion has to log off, so we part ways.
-Loot Woodhaven, find an M1911. Get acquainted with the weapon reloading system, after firing at a mutant and discovering there is only one shot in the pistol.
-As night falls, spot a flashlight inside a bus, a roaring mutant outside. Briefly observe and realize the flashlight is a player hiding from said mutant, and dispatch the mutant.
-Person inside the bus begs me not to kill them, I promise I am friendly. Give them some food and drink, and send them on their way.
-Begin heading south towards the Military Base in the hopes of picking up some good gear. Acquire a pair of bolt action rifles.
-Loot the Military Base for all its worth, get kitted out, lose pants to glitch, run around like a madman trying to find some. Find some. Keep stealthing around and looting(place is swarming with mutants.) When spotted, rely on hatchet to kill muties(three hits to kill, great for saving ammunition, which is scarce.)
-Hear gunshots and continue looting after a quick perimeter sweep. Climb one of the watchtowers and spot a person with an assault rifle creeping around with a buddy.
-Quietly descend and skirt the outside of the base, until finding a hole in the fence and successfully escaping.
-Log off, make this review.
Day Two:
-Do some scavving around, get pretty kitted out. Go check out Hayward and wow, is that place gorgeous. A jungle of overgrown skyscrapers.
-Hear gunshots, gtfo. Head south, towards the airfield to loot it again.
-Along the way, pick up a shotgun and drop one of two rifles for it. Further along the way, craft a flashlight attachment and be sad when it won't fit on either gun.
-Reach military base, find an AT-15. Despite lack of ammo, take it anyway and put flashlight on it. Scav around like a madman, find no magazines.
-Get jumped by three mutants, kill them with shotgun. Take refuge to heal heavy wounds in a watchtower.
-Freak out when a player walks in. After we both recover from the initial shock and over-repitition of "Friendly, friendly!" we have an exchange of words, and I decide he's a good guy. I direct him towards my old hunting rifle, give him some food and a canteen, and we go on our seperate ways.
-Side note: This guy informs me that I am playing on a Dutch server. Go figure.
-Continue on, meet another player looking for the first guy I met. Direct him to the good gent.
-Bump into the two gentlemen again, decide to group up with them as you can never have too many friends.
-Look around for a place to build a base, see a cool cave. Also see a large base by it. Decide to find another place.
-Game starts messing up, so we friend one another on steam and I log off.
So all in all, for me the game was very quiet. I like where it is going, and it reminds me of Unturned if it weren't a blocky game. The gameplay itself, I have not fully delved into, because for me I've enjoyed the adventure(quiet as it has been) over any kind of crafting or base building. I also feel that playing on the barely populated server I am on makes player interactions much more interesting and special.
Perhaps I will update this review later as I delve into crafting and base-building, but as it stands, Miscreated is a solid game and I greatly enjoy it. Pick it up, and give it a try.

Having fixed my issue (related it seems to nVidia Optimus -- turned off, and now I can more reliably get into the game), I would recommend this game, though still with some reservations, as it is pretty buggy.
The game, when running properly, is enjoyable, has a good skill tree, good balance of planning, strategy, and tactics.
The game is also very challenging.  Playing Survival or Multiplayer maps, you can expect to lose, over and over again.  Team play is very important, and it takes a while to get the hang of proper tactics and skill usage.
(As of August 2016)  The community is pretty tolerant, so when starting out in Multiplayer, just listen to the leader, follow the lines drawn, and (try to) fill your role, and you'll eventually get the hang of it.
There do remain a number of detriments to the game, however.  In Survival (and in Multiplayer, if not filling a team with real people), you control one character, and can swap between characters.  For some reason, the key mapping for swapping and issuing commands is different between the single player storyline (where it starts with a basic tutorial of how to manage this) than it is from Survival/Multi.  Also, you can issue commands to multiple characters to carry out concurrently, just don't be surprised when the character you aren't currently swapped into decides to just wander off or stop halfway through his queued command.
In addition, there are quite a few latency/sync bugs in multiplayer.  Be prepared to encounter unkillable enemies when what you're firing at isn't in sync with the server (though, of course, they can still damage you).  Also, skills sometimes just don't take effect.  (This bug I've noticed most with the Medic, which is pretty sucky, when you need health or to remove an ailment, and you simply can't.)
So, if you can bear the (more than) occasional frustrations, or just plan to play through the single player campaign (which is good), then I would recommend this game.

I moved on from DS2 Sotfs to DS1, because DS3 takes place in the same setting and I didn't want to miss out on context.
-Gameplay-wise, animations are less responsive and clunkier than what I experienced in DS2, but still good. DS2 is a better dark-fantasy melee combat simulator, but DS1 excels in other areas and it still works fine.
-Some unintuitive mechanics like humanity, reinforcement and estus upgrades can sometimes be very mean to newcomers. I had to restart my first playthrough after consuming that fire keeper soul I got in Undead Parish. I really do recommend looking up some online resources, or maybe get some advice from friends to some degree before getting started.
+The intricate map design does deserve its praise. You can see in the far distance other regions you have visited or will definitely visit. I do have to say it is loosely connected by super-long ladders and rather empty underground zones, often forcing butt naked marathons for boss battles that require multiple tries. Fromsoft did resolve those problems in later games, yet the underdeveloped underground zones are one of the fun aspects that are unique to DS1.
+Some REALLY REALLY EPIC BOSS FIGHTS. Beating O&S was one of my best gaming moments.
+NPC interactions and questilnes are much better than DS2. Many memorable characters with just enough depth.
I gave DS2 a 10/10, and some of my first experiences with this game made me think DS1 should be 11/10. But with some old mechanics and framerate issues(even using Dsfix) I was fortunately able to settle on 10/10 for DS1 too. It really does have the charm of that big brother that had significant influence on its younger brothers and just gaming in general.
Simply put, a must for anyone who considers themselves a hardcore gamer.

I had trouble deciding if I should recommend this game or not. In its current state I would probably rate it about 5½ out of 10, just into the positive. Anyone who has played and enjoyed Transport Tycoon Deluxe, Sid Meier’s Railroads, or Railroad Tycoon III will probably enjoy playing Train Fever but there are quite a few things that need fixing about it.
The object of the game is simply to build a road and rail network then use trains, trams buses and trucks to transport people and goods at a profit. There are no competitors and no goal other than the satisfaction of making a success of your transport empire.
The quality of the graphics are a lot better than the games above however even on my PC, which is very high spec, Train fever suffers badly from spikes at the end of each game month and especially at the end of each game year as the in-game finances are calculated.
The road/rail construction takes a lot of getting used to and can be quite frustrating at first. You try to build a line and at the last moment there is an unexpected collision with something or the slope is too high. Bridge/tunnel building are particularly difficult as you have no idea how high or low you need to go and how much run-up is required either side. Get it wrong you either pay to demolish it or go back to your last save. TIP: Save before starting ANY construction in this game.
The world the game map is set in is a weird mixture. The vehicles and buildings are all quite clearly German. The town names are all from the UK rail map and the currency is dollars! There are industries you can connect up to each other and deliver goods to the towns to make them grow but there are only three industry chains:
Forest – Sawmill – Goods
Oil – Refinery – Goods
Coal/Ore – Steel mill – Goods
Even Transport Tycoon, which must be about 20 years old now, had a more complex industry set up than train fever and in TTD you could finance new industries yourself which you cannot in train fever.
Passenger and goods for both road and rail require different stations although they can share road/rails.
My biggest gripe by far about Train Fever is the lack of a decent manual/tutorials. You really are dropped in the deep end with no help whatsoever on most of the complexities of the game. I’ve been playing now for over 130 hours and I still have not fully figured out things like the rail signal system and the behaviour of the people who populate the game and why the do/don’t use the available transport.
A game take ages to play. Despite my 130 hours at it, I am yet to reach the end of the timeline, in fact I am not half way through. I seem to have spent most of the time re-loading/redoing constructions trying to get them to work, but even so, to do the full timeline without going back could take days if not weeks.
TO THE DEVELOPERS
Please put an undo/wind back time function.
More complex industry chains required.
Enable station enlargement without demolition
Fix the end of month/year spikes
Fix a bug where some passengers disappear between stations (perhaps the fall out?)
PRODUCE A DECENT MANUAL!!!
This game is really a virtual train set and overall I have enjoyed playing Train Fever but it could be so much more!

This review is the point of view from someone that already played the boardgame. I really like the boardgame, but this review will focus mainly on the transfer from board- to videogame.
It is a nice way to play the game when nobody is around, or your friends that also play the game, live in a different area.
The animationquality is decent, just don't expect anything to spectacular(then again, something to flashy might actually disrupt the strategyaspects of the game).
You get a free rotation of krosmasters which is helpful if you see a krosmaster you might want to give a shot(I use it to test teamcomps with promotional krosmasters I don't own)
I never had server-issues, but some people that live outside of europe reported problems, but since it is f2p you can just go and see for yourself.
The game does most of the dice roling and stuff like that in the background, and since you don't have to set up the board every time you want to play, it is way faster to play than the actual boardgame is.
Last of the actual gaming aspects is the adventuremode, a singleplayermode they added for the online client. It plays a little like a puzzlegame, where you have to find solutions to problems with given tools. I prefer the actual game but you can earn some Krosz(the stuff you need to buy digital figurines) there.
The one thing I wouldn't recommend doing, is buying the krosmasters in their digital form, since that seems rather expensive to me. I suggest buying the real figurines, since all of those come with an actual code for you to enter, so you can use them in the digital version of the game. That way, the Krosmasters are more expensive, but you can play IRL as well, which in my opinion, is always more fun with boardgames.

Krosmaster Arena is an easy to learn, hard to master Strategy-board game.
In this game you play a strategic game with a team, out of many different collectable figurines called Krosmasters, in an arena against an opponent who did the same.
(I play the game around a year now before it was on steam , that's why I have the low playtime)
Once you get the hang of the game you should be able to win more often than not, even with the starting figurines and the free to play figurines every week.
If you are interested in getting to the game competitively, you can play the board game (the 2nd world championship is coming up soon), where you get online codes for the figurines for the online version.You can also collect the figurines ingame where you can buy booster packs with figurines very often, without spending money and get a bigger collection.
There is also a crafting mechanism, which let you craft the more used Level 1 figurnies very fast by disenchanting other figurines you have too many of.
The main problem with this game is that is not that beginner friendly. The rules of the board game are like 20 pages long and they try to fit all of that into a 30-60 minute Tutorial which is not that easy, since you are playing and not reading the manual all the time. If you really want to understand the deep mechanics of the game completely you have to read the rules to the boardgame at some point, because some things aren`t even explained in the Tutorial. You could also watch this video after playing it a little bit then you should understand it completely:
When you want to get better at this game, you can check out my Youtube channel, where I am uploading Gameplay and Tips & Tricks videos.

This is a hard game to recomend but I am going to anyways. This game (at the time of my writing this) has many problems. But I think what the game does do well makes up for its problems. It might help if you go into the game with little to no expectations so that you are less dismayed by its faults. I will list some of the biggest problems I have with the game and then some of the main things I think make the game worth playing.
Problems:
1. Replacing older vehicles is a real chore. The need to keep up frequency on your lines really compounds this problem. Also there is no way to disable the annoying messages that fill the bottom of the screen notifying of a vehicle that has reached its life span.
2. I find the balancing of the stats on the vehicles along with when they come out and are made obsolete to be very poorly done. As one example the running costs of a locomotive is easily 10-20 times that of a road vehicle making the construction of train lines very risky if you don't know just the right circumstances to make a profitable line. And even if you can manage a profitable train line you are almost guarenteed to be able to make a much more profitable bus/tram or truck line in place of the train.
3. Collision issues while doing road and rail construction is very inflexible. It seems the majority of construction atempts are going to give you a collision message meaning it won't allow it. Often times you either have to make significant compromises to your plans, forget your plans altogether, or invest a lot of money and work into making it work. Such as spending millions of dollars bulldozing buildings along a road just so you can upgrade the road or connect another road to the road, even if there was a large open spot where no buildings were in the way.
Good things:
1. The sounds and visuals of the game are very appealing in my opinion. I spend much of my time just following vehicles around or watching people go whereever they are going. I think the next closest game of this type would be Cities in Motion but sunnier.
2. The randomly generated maps and cities are very impressive. Granted there isn't a lot of variety in the generation catogories for the maps, but even so, the type of landscape it does generate is very well done. As far as I know there is no other game of this type that has comparable map and city generation. Also the way the cities gradually develope is well done and satisfying. The speed at which they grow is largely based on how well connected the town is with itself and with other towns as well as how fully it is being supplied with goods.
3. The realistic supply and demand of the passengers in the game is really nice and gives a lot of incentive to connect to every town you can. Every person has 4 locations they are assigned. A home, a place of work, a place to shop and a place for leisure. They will often re-assign locations based on what new options are available. They have a 20 minute deadline on any travel plans they make. So the faster your transportation becomes the further they can travel within the time limit and so the more opertunities exist for you to make money in transporting them.
These are just some of the more prominant issues, both good and bad, that exist in the game. But it hopefully gives a sense of whether you might enjoy the game or not. The balancing problem I mention can relatively easily be dealt with through mods. Finding the right one for your tastes and installing them is a bit of a hassle though when ideally the game could have just been better balanced by the developers themselves.
I personnally think it is a great game and have had a lot of enjoyment with it. But the lost potential of what this game could be is admittedly frustrating and I can certainly understand why some people might be too put off to continue playing it.

Imagine its the 90s and you're reading one of those sweet choose-your-own-adventure books. We all know you'd hold a page at a decision while you'd skip ahead to see what happened with one particular choice then come back and try the other one. Now imagine instead of having 2 hands with 10 fingers helping you do this, you have 4 hands and for some reason, 25 fingers, helping you manage a constant stream of pass or fail skill checks that will constantly change the course of whether you live or die as you make save files to try and revisit your mistakes.
In Long Live The Queen, you level up skills of a princess soon to be queen by taking classes. How well you absorb a variety of disciplines, from simple accounting to military strategy and beyond, is affected by your princess' mood. Learn swordsmanship twice as fast by channeling your anger but anger doesn't help you learn court manners and etiquette. Hopefully being a masterful swordswoman will help you fend off potential assassins. But swordsmanship won't help you if you don't have the foresight with trade and merchantile to know that chocolate from a suspicious location is poisoned. Experience in one area will pass you in skill checks and let events turn out favorably but oftentimes you'll fail many and just come out looking like a little girl (and you are really).
And that's why I like LLTQ. It's a choose your own adventure game with hundreds of tiny variables.

Game of Thrones with a glam, and a lot of it. This tells it all.
The point is not becoming a queen or raising up skills but the feeling that every person in the world wants to kill a kawaii little girl just because she was unfortunate enough to be a princess. This in the end will probably turn this very kawaii little girl into ruthless, merciless person, who values her life more than anything.

Oh, you thought being a princess would be easy? All looking pretty and drinking tea with your little finger extended? Think again, ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. Being Elodie, 14-year-old heir to the queendom of Nova, is anything but simple. Yeah, she can learn courtly manners and how to dance, but to survive at all she has to also study foreign history, learn how to swordfight, become a naval strategist, be able to identify poison
learn how to wield magic (among other skills), all while avoiding assassins, forest monsters, scheming nobles and all-out civil war. Think Westeros, not Disney.
If that seems like a lot to balance - it is. You will die a lot. You will not get to the coronation at the end on your first try. You may not even get there on your fifth try! But every time you die only bolsters your determination to get there - or, at least, that's how it worked for me. And god
is it addictive.
PROS
+ surprisingly deep gameplay
+ lots of endings, so high replayability factor
+ cute, well-done artwork (look,
liked it, but you may not if you're easily deterred by anime, lack of fanservice in said anime, or the colour pink)
+ previously-mentioned lack of fanservice - aside from maybe two of the ten or so outfits Elodie can wear, there's essentially no gratuitous skin or unbelievable boobs in the entire thing, which I found a refreshing change
+ interesting story-world (matriarchal society! fleshed-out history!)
+ addictive as hell
CONS
- generally requires replaying it a million times and/or looking up walkthroughs to win at all (unless you're really lucky)
- the usual cons associated with anything visual-novel-esque - lots of clicking through already-read text, a bit slower-paced than most other games, etc.
Overall, I'd definitely recommend this to anyone who's into strategy, strong female characters, visual novels or having their character die a lot.

Long Live The Queen (LLTQ) is a game I stumbled upon by complete accident. Let me tell you, that was one of the happiest accidents of my life.
LLTQ is an anime-esque visual novel-esque...thing developed by UK based Hanako Games, and it's quite something. LLTQ is a game where you die. And die. And die again. And then you die some more. Yet, dying is part of the fun. For example: someone wrote a silly letter to you about you doing *something* with a squid. Oh, no! A gust of wind picked it up and it's now hanging just off the balcony. Do you climb out to try to grab it?
>Yes
No
You do? Well then, while climbing, you slip, fall, and break your neck on the ground. Your room is on the top floor of the castle, after all. Why would you try to climb from so high up? Idiot.
Except maybe if you picked yes and you actually trained beforehand to be a really good climber, you didn't fall and survived. See, that's what this game is about. Each week, you pick skills to take classes in. And, every so often, you're tested in certain skills depending on what situation arises in your kingdom which could mean life or death for you. And it's oh-so-fun. True, it's very trial-and-error, but with a game like this, with muliptle paths to victory (and many more to gruesome and painful death), that's just part of the experience.
This game is recommended for anyone who wants to become a pretty pink magical girl. ...I mean Lumen. (Same thing.) (Hey, it's a thing to do.)

Call it either a regency or regicide simulator. The challenge is either to help the princess avoid various gruesome deaths and make it to her coronation, or to get her killed in a variety of ways. George RR Martin would be proud. The game is a simple set of choices, building up survival skills and changing the princess's moods to provide bonuses to her learning ability. It's a choose-your-own-adventure at heart, and the choices are static (ie they don't change if the variables are identical) so the game has a limited shelf life. It's entertaining in spurts though, and each playthrough is short so it's a decent pick-up-and-play when the mood is there.

Cons
-The single-player campaign was horrendous.
-I have to individually left click each enemy to attack when they spawn like crazy? No.
-I have to right click and lift finger to move somewhere. I cant use wsad to move or keep the mouse clicked. No. Think of it in this way, Monster is coming, I have to move back or instantly change direction and also fire. In this game, I left click the monster, then right click a path. The tactical whatever to issue orders is nice but it adds complexity to something that should not be complex in the first place. It has been done properly before (If only I could remember that game's name).  Not worth the effort.
-Cant see which doors are open or even if there is a door where you are facing. Developers must have noticed this as well since they implemented precise pathfinding.

-I turn on the ingame lights but everything is always so dark (Except for a few places). I play every game fine with my current monitor setting so I don't see why I have to change it just for this game.
-An elite commando who has to shoot gas canisters and barrels 4-5 times so they explode...? No.
-Enemies in the first 2 levels are just...*sigh*
-I found a merc armor which lowered my hp. I have no idea what its supposed to add as stats.
Pros

Duke Nukem 3D World Tour contains five episodes.
Regarding the old content, the four "Original Episodes" were all fun to play. "LA Meltdown" and "Lunar Apocalypse" kept me on my toes with engaging map layout, useful weapons and new enemies to blast. "Shrapnel City" was overall fun as well, but I did not feel it offered as much as the previous two episodes. I got the most enjoyment out of "The Birth" . It included some fun level ideas and my personal favorite of the boss monsters.
The game does not include any of the other expansions/level packs which is mildly disappointing.
The New Content included a fifth episode that was decent at best for me. In comparison with the previous four, it felt more like an extra or "dessert". The maps are fun on their own. The fire fly enemy while interesting felt very underwhelming and, in my opinion, unfinished. The "New" Boss Monster (besides being a blatant pallete swap) was pathetic and seemed far less fun to fight than any of the previous four boss monsters. The new weapon works fine but like the other content, felt underwhelming and rushed.
Overall I had fun with this game, but I will not deny it has its fair share of flaws especially with its new content. I recommend you buy it on sale if you are a fan of old 90s first person shooters with a B-Movie vibe.

A lot of people say this is the inferior version to Megaton Edition. Well, I've played Megaton Edition, let's see what we have here with Duke Nukem 3D: 20th Anniversary World Tour.
Let's start with a simple list of pros and cons.
Cons :
- The Absence of 3 unofficial expansion campaigns. (Not entirely, will elaborate);
- Price 19.99;
- You will give money to Gearbox, which does questionable things at best (like pulling Megaton off the digital shelves).
Pros :
- New sound and rerecorded Duke Talk (which procs more often I think, there is Legacy as well though)(some are not sold on the new sound);
- Fifth Episode made by Duke's original developers, along with a new weapon and enemy;
- True3D (Supposedly it makes the game better looking, and it does, but when you look up and down it has this weird zoom and I get a headache, so now I keep it off usually, but it's there.);
- Rewinding death feature, no more quicksaving and reloading! (I gotta say, a thing this simple adds a lot to the fun and immersion).
- Out of the box controller support
- Megaton is unavaible to purchase.
Duke3D is an old game per sé and unless you're a die hard fan, I don't feel the price is justified compared to what you got in the Megaton edition (which was at half price); that said, when at a sale, I highly recommend it to people like me, that got late to the party and want to own a registered version of Duke 3D.
You might or might not consider it inferior, but this is still a good version, I like the new Duke Talk, I like that it supports a controller out of the box, I like the time rewind feature, I'm having more fun with this than the Megaton edition (I wanted to own Megaton, but it was already unavaible when I decided to give Duke3D a try). I heard people saying the new sound is lower quality and the new Duke Talk just doesn't sound like him, but I think they're fine, I actually prefer the new Duke (which of course is always voiced by John St John). The True3D, which is a mode you can toggle even in game, is very neat, at first I liked it a lot, but I realized that it does this weird zoom, especially when you watch up and down near walls, and it gives me a headache, so now I play mostly with it turned off.
You have your workshop, which you had in Megaton as well, your multiplayer, but since this edition can only grow and the other you can't find a legit copy (except grey markets, which are not totally legit and are going to finish stock at some point) I would go with this one.
Speaking of workshop, a guy is releasing the levels of Duke it out in D.C., one of the expansions that was missing from this version, so that's very neat, kudos to you mister! Maybe we'll see the other expansions as well, I surely hope so.
As far as the exclusive fifth episode goes, I haven't played it yet, but the general consensus seems to be that it's nothing to write home about.
All in all, I got it at 66% discount, and you know what? I don't regret buying it, I like it and I'm having fun, so it's a thumbs up for me, come get some!
I even nominated it for the " The “Cry Havoc And Let Slip The Dogs Of War” Award", because I feel like a badass playing as Duke kicking alien butt.

On the surface, Cory In The House looks like your average licensed TV Show handheld shovelware. But underneath that, is one of the biggest revolutions the medium has ever seen. Funny, smart, deep, timeless. Read on to find out why this stands as one of the finest licensed video games of all time, or indeed, one of the finest video games of all time.
You play as Cory, the kid from the TV show who finds himself living in the White House. The gameplay is simple; you need to sneak around the various rooms and do various tasks, which often involve talking to someone or getting to a certain room. It sounds simple, but between the deep stat management systems, varied character patrol routes, and the amazing dialogue options, the gameplay is top-notch, making the likes of Metal Gear Solid pale in comparison (including on storytelling prowess, more on that later). The mini-games like the lock-picking are so deep, they could be sold as full games themselves.
The graphics are life-like, the character portraits are so realistic you will think you are watching the show! I haven't seen such good graphics on a handheld game, ever. The audio is as good as a DS game can sound, it's all in there, from the sound effects to the catchy theme from the TV show.As an audio-visual experience, Cory in the House delivers the best on the DS.
What truly shines however, is the dialogue and the smart humor in the game. The dialogue here is comical to kids, but truly hilarious to adults, which are more likely to get the more subtle jokes. And yet, it's full of life lessons and themes that resonates to all of us, children and adults alike. It's like watching the best Pixar film of your life.
The writing here may live on as a timeless example of comedy. What they have pulled off here may be one day looked back as "the Shakespeare of comedy".
Overall, this game is a hidden masterpiece, one that will change the way video games are made. Just give it time. For now, you can be privileged enough to play this masterpiece while the rest of the world is still unaware of its implications and future impact on the medium. They will catch up, eventually.

I play this game since Beta and it is getting better and better. The developers listen to the community and already implemented a lot of wishes. If you played OTTD you should know, that this game is different in some aspects:
- The industry chains are smaller but production does not increase/decrease at random and it matters where you deliver the goods because cities will only accept a certain amount.
- The scale of the game is different, you won't have a station with 10 tracks in each town in this game unless you are crazy.  It is not like OTTD where you build 20 trains for one line, it focusses more on longer lines between cities. That said, you will most likely have less networks and less complex setups for station entrances and rail crossings because it is not so easy to build such things.
- The terrain in this game really matters. In OTTD you can just terraform everything at some point and tracks can just go up the hill anywhere. Here it matters where you lay your tracks and you have to plan according to the contour lines.
If you can live with that, you get a really good game with:
- Great graphics
- Already great mods (see
- Simulated people and goods
- Simulated town growth
- Great maps
So what issues do I have with the game:
- If you build a lot of stuff, it takes time to autosave and sometimes the simulation slows down
- Balancing of some trains and cars needs some work, TFV for example won't reach 300 km/h on most tracks because of weak acceleration (they changed the TFV but I couldn't test it since the changes)
- Trains sometimes drive one after another because of long boarding times. This affects profit and line frequency (this has now been fixed)
-------------------------
Addition now that the US DLC is out:
Some of my concerns have been adressed:
- Performance of the game is better, still a slight slowdown when autosave (but you can now choose how often the autosave is done)
- Balancing is still not perfect but TFV is fixed
- Boarding times are less of an issue
The US DLC works fine, I didn't see all the models yet. But there even seem to be options to enable all vehicles (Europe and US) and just play on a Europe or US map, which is great. I don't know if the balancing of the US vehicles is good because I am still in 1870.
There are still some old bugs in the game but nothing game-breaking, mostly visual little annoying things like missing tunnel portals.
I tested some mods and there are awesome vehicles available. Unfortunately the old mods are broken but there is already a solution out (the community has a mod manager which will do all the work for you). If you do some research it is easy to find new vehicles or balance mods and add them to the game. With the new ingame tools you should then be able to really customize your experience, which is great!

Orcs Must Die 2 continues right where 1 left off. The much-awaited multiplayer experience is here, but this review will be from a single-player standpoint.
To start with, you get to pick between the Warmage and the Sorceress. Both have their strengths and weaknesses, but the Warmage simply feels easier to play with due to his superior health, superior tar trap, and arguably superior weapon. The Sorceress is better for charming single, large targets though, and her acid trap does more damage than the Warmage's Arrow Trap.
Gameplay is more or less the same. If you played OMD1, this will all be familiar. The Elementalist girls are gone, which is a shame. This change means that you have less options to adjust to your enemies in the middle of a level. Fortunately any upgrades you purchased prior to battle can be reset at no cost. Autoballistae are now considered guardians, which means you can no longer spam them. I was sad about that as well.
Amazingly they made the Gnolls more irritating. They seem to have more HP, run faster (both probably untrue, but it feels like it), and can now slow you upon hitting you, making escape impossible. A whole pack of them, especially in Endless mode (see below), will ruin your day.
I'm rather disappointed that the campaign is so short. The first game took maybe 15-20 hours to complete, and had a good progression. OMD2 instead took me a mere 10 hours on normal difficulty. Granted, I already knew the basics of the game, but this was far shorter than I expected. DLC's extend the game's length a bit, but they contain no story segments, and thus you are basically playing for skulls (the game's peristent currency) and variety. Note that you'll have to play through Campaign again with another character if you want stuff unlocked on both characters.
Endless mode is interesting. Waves come indefinitely and keep getting tougher until you can no longer handle it, much like Survival mode in other types of games. This mode by far is the biggest time-sink, though you are rewarded with plenty of skulls to compensate.
If you like the first game and want a way to play it with friends, then OMD2 is the way to go. Overall it's an acceptable game. I still recommend the first game though.
