is what's known in some circles as a "raising sim;" a sort of life simulation game in the vein of classic franchises like Princess Maker or The Idolmaster.  Basically, you're given charge of a character and go about the process of, well, raising them; selecting the skills (and outfits) for them to take life head-on and see to their success (or failure), witnessing their trials and hardships along the way.
You'll be seeing a lot of hardship, too.  Make no mistake: This game is
.  Elodie will be tested regularly on the skills you decide for her to learn, often at what feels like the most inopportune moment (much like how stuff just seems to pop up out of nowhere on you in real life), and she will fail.  Often.  Fail often and regularly enough, and she will die.  Probably repeatedly.  The challenge of figuring out what combination of skills and activities for your budding would-be Queen to learn in order to navigate the perils of courtly life will have you reloading over and over again, and, if you're anything like me, creating a million different save slots to go back, pore over your selections and try to figure out if
choice at
moment was what made the difference between royal victory and a messy death.
If this sounds frustrating to you, this probably isn't the game for you.
If you instead take that sort of thing as a challenge, though, you're going to eat this stuff up, trust me.  Every success Elodie achieves as she nears her coronation will be a real victory for you, as your strategies gradually, painstakingly bear fruit.  And in the end, you will slouch back in your throne, and you will proclaim:
.

Steam time isn't accurate, I've played a lot of this game away from Steam.
This game is entertaining enough if you're out of other new RPGs but it's not that good. Supposed to be reminiscent of Infinity Engine games but surprise, it's only skin-deep. The biggest departure is also the biggest flaw. The game is way too "balanced" to the point of being completely bland gameplay wise.
Not wanting any dump stats in the game is all well and good in theory but everything being fairly good for everybody just makes everything boring and samey. No way to "ruin" your character makes character building very inconsequential feeling, and one of the best things about playing a party based RPG (having to think to build an optimal party) is just completely not there. Which is stupid considering there's an easy way to respec. Why would you ever need it?
Magic spells are lame and don't offer much standout or difference at all from physical classes, magic should never be this boring.
Same with most unique equipment.
Nothing in combat feels weighty or gamechanging or epic or exciting, there's lots of status effects that technically do different things but just make you go "oh, let's pile on more status effects that just lower stats on the monster (make it a little weaker), yay..."
Character graphics are ugly, but the environments are quite pretty, and the music other than a couple tracks is good if pretty unmemorable.
I actually think a lot of the story and the setting is quite interesting (especially in the expansions), and there are some good design decisions too, like being able to generate characters in the inn for your party if you hate all the prefab companions except the Grieving Mother and Durance.
I don't mind the base combat at all, engagement/attack of opportunity system being so focused on is kind of fun once you get used to it.
Still going to keep playing the game off and on, and I'm still going to get Deadfire when it comes out but I'm not too hopeful if they make character building and progression as boring as this game.

TL;DR: I am very disappointed with this version as Megaton Edition simply provided a better end-user experience.
The first thing that hit me was input lag on my mouse. I saw that the number of frames per second was equal to my monitor's refresh rate so I figured it has to be the fault of v-sync being on. The problem is - no such option is available in the options menu. I forced v-sync off in my video driver's settings and the input lag disappeared. However, my video card instantly became significantly louder as it started rendering the game in several hundred frames per second and again - there is no in-game option to limit the number of rendered frames. So what's so bad about it? Both options (v-sync and FPS limit) were available in the Megaton Edition...
The next thing I saw was a lack of texture filtering. This means we are bound to see the game pixelated, which looks out of place coupled with the enhanced lighting. And again - Megaton Edition had texture filtering options...
Another flaw is the unresponsiveness of the mouse wheel when bound to inventory cycling. Sometimes you have to scroll the wheel a few times just to cycle ONE item. It works a bit better with the v-sync turned on... but then I have the input lag back! And yup, you guessed it, in Megaton Edition it was working fine.
After experiencing the above problems I ran the new episode, and I have to admit it is really good and enjoyable - it was made by experienced people and it clearly shows. It's just that the first impression was so bad I don't want to play it anymore.
The problem is - World Tour is the only officially available edition right now, which is still being sold. If you don't already have Duke Nukem 3D in your collection, then maybe it would be a good idea to buy it. Alternatively, you can look for a key for the Megaton Edition at 3rd party sites, as it is no longer officially available. The Megaton Edition does not contain the new episode (Alien World Order), but instead has three unofficial expansions (Life's a Beach, Duke it Out in D.C. and Nuclear Winter), which in turn are unavailable in World Tour (which is a puzzle to me). As for other, new features in this release - such as rewinding time after death, or developer commentary - I didn't really bother with them. The enhanced lighting is nice, but I saw it before in a fan source port EDuke32... which also has texture filtering (unlike World Tour). Proper 3D is also cool, but its lack never really bothered me in the first place as far as this game is concerned, so it's not a saving quality by any means.
So here is the thing: "Duke Nukem 3D: Megaton Edition" was a much more polished product... offered for a twice lower price. If you decide to release Duke Nukem 3D again for a higher price than it used to be, you had better make sure this version is AT LEAST as polished as previous ones. Sadly, World Tour does not offer such quality.
I'll stick to the Megaton Edition, which I was fortunate enough to buy while it was still available. Duke Nukem 3D: 20th Anniversary World Tour is going to be the second time ever for me when I refund a product on Steam.

So, when I first heard of Night In the Woods, I found a lot of positive things about it, like amazing characters, story, and good pacing. But sadly, it was very underwhelming now that I've finished the game. In NITW, you play as a 20-year-old cat named Mae, who just dropped out of college. With this information introduced early in the game, you wonder how the main character handles that change and why she dropped out. You get an idea of the protagonist’s internal conflict and main plot. Besides Mae, you are also introduced to her friends, Gregg, Bea and Angus, who help her adjust back to town.
Now an important aspect of the game is hanging out with either Bea or Gregg, where you can see how Mae plays off them. I finished the game hanging out with Bea every day, but even though I have no idea what Gregg has to offer, and I do not want to replay NITW again just to see the other route. In the Bea route, I learned that she has her own personal problems, such as dealing with her small business and other spoiler related things. Overall, Bea is a well written character, and I enjoyed being with her. This characterization shows how well NITW can develop its characters, but remember, Mae is the main protagonist.
An essential part of a character's growth is conflict. For example, in the game, Bea argues with Mae over her immaturity, but it was quickly resolved the next day, and Mae continues to wander town distracting herself from her problems. Another argument happens between Mae and her mom over the dropout, yet the conflict is quickly resolved the next day and never brought up again. Which brings me to my next point.
What should make the story engaging is the protagonist. Yet Mae is a very flat character, and the conflicts she faces are resolved too quickly. Don't get me wrong, the game has a lot of potential in its story, but it has many plot holes, incomplete arcs, repetition, and iffy gameplay.
Now onto the PROS and CONS.
PROS:
-The game at least connected the background characters to Mae, which helped me understand more about her past and relationship to the small-town cast.
-Most of the NPCs have an interesting and charming personality, ex. Selmers, Mr. Chazokov, and Pastor Karen.
-Beautiful eye candy art and soothing music.
-Possum Spring’s history was interesting.
-Demon Tower is a fun side game with a lot of challenge, great pixel art, and fun dungeon crawling gameplay.
CONS:
-Mae’s character. She may be 20 years old, but she doesn’t act like one at all and is very random. My main issue with her is how she does not confront her problems or have the willingness to grow up even with the support of her friends and family. She has some spoiler related issues, but throughout the game, it was merely pushed aside. Other times Mae acts very mean spirited. She wasn’t a charming jerk who was easy to sympathize with. I really wanted to root for Mae and see her overcome her problems, but she was just so unlikeable.
-As much as there are interesting NPCs, there is also an equal amount of forgettable characters. They don’t contribute to Mae’s character arc, add personality to the town, or affect the general plot.
-The characters never change their expressions. For example, all Mae does is squint, hold her arms up, and shrink her pupils. I had a tough time sympathizing with her and the forgettable NPCs. Even when she cried, it looked fake. The characters felt less real.
-The game’s dialogue was cringey and annoying. Sometimes the characters say “like” a bit too much for my taste. Other times the game attempts to convey a profound message, but it only comes out as a cliché moral.
-A lot of plotholes, which is the most apparent at the end of the game.
-Illusion of choice. Despite Mae having two or more dialogue options, they are either the same response or do not change the conversation’s direction. The illusion also applies to whether you hang out with Bea or Gregg. Sure exclusively hanging out with one friend nets an achievement, but there are only minor changes to the story.
-The sudden story shift halfway through the game (huge spoiler). There was no foreshadowing, and despite the shift, Mae does the same routine of wandering town.
-The very end of the game felt rushed, and the epilogue seemed incomplete. Even after the game’s climax, the characters return to normalcy and shoehorn a lesson at the end of the day.
-Painfully slow story pace. Most of the game is spent wandering town talking to people and hanging out with Bea or Gregg playing minigames. The game is a slice of life, but has lots of filler and repetitive gameplay.
-Mae’s bizarre dreams do not have much effects on the plot, and the gameplay within them aren’t very engaging.
-The minigames weren’t fun either, both content and controls were meh. Some of them had no bearing on the plot at all.
In conclusion, game tried to tell a coming-of-age story with a video game approach. The story fell flat with its incompleteness, whereas the gameplay was forgettable and not fun. I recommend that you research more about the game before buying, like watching YouTube videos and reading BOTH positive and negative reviews. In my opinion, NITW is not worth buying, but if you do want to play this game, wait for it to go on sale. Maybe you’ll have a better time with it than me, but this game is like a gilded statue. The attractive surface is comprised of good looking art, music, premise, and fan opinion, but it masks the game’s deeper flaws.

Takes some gameplay elements from AC and the Arkham games and makes them into a better game imo. Fans of the combat from previously mentioned games will enjoy the very satisfying and swift yet brutal feel of the combat in this game. The story missions and engaging nemesis system dont get in each other's way and for lotr fans (not scholars) the story is actually pretty well done. If you enjoy the feel of the Jackson films and know little tid bits of lore (but do not study it like a religion) you will actually find it fairly interesting (like me), although not very memorable. I can see why people who dont know much about the lotr universe or, like Ive previously mentioned, study it very carefully, would not enjoy the story, however, even with that said, the nemesis system is engaging enough to still justify giving this game a try. Only major cons for me are the ghuls (enemies that are both annoying and boring to fight) and the game world (althought unlike many I actually like the way it looks, I just think it needed a bit more variety). So to sum things up: this is the best lotr game out there and the combat feels like a much more swift and brutal reiteration of that of AC and Arkham (maybe its just the fantastic animations), the nemesis system will keep youe engaged for a while, and the story is atleast presented very nicely, Definitely recommended.

I got this game when it was being offered by the Humble Bundle store for free, and it has easily been one of the best free games I've received in the year 2014. A lot of reviews mention this game to be "Sid M's Civilization, but with the fantasy theme," and they are actually pretty accurate.
If you like the Civilization series (especially military victories), 4x games, turn-based strategy, fantasy themes, and disregarding diplomacy, then you should enjoy this game.
The aesthetics are great, and there are a lot of different unit types and character models. The detail put into the "world board" is very good. The music and sounds are great, and the feedback is always helpful in showing stats like how much damage is done and taken by units.
Warlock offers a helpful tutorial for people new to this type of game, however, if you are familiar at all with the Civilization series (or other games in this genre), then this part is easily skippable. Compared to Civilization V, Warlock is much simpler, and also heavily combat-based (as there are no cultural or economic victory routes). The learning curve is minimal to moderate, depending on your experience with turn-based strategies.
The gameplay is very fun - you start off by building something in your home city, and the game does a good job (like in Civ) of prompting/reminding you when you still have tasks to do (like building when your queue is empty, or moving idle units). After you building completes, you must wait x number of turns before you can build again, and this is indicated by a number next to your city name, which fills up each turn. I do not believe there is a "pay gold to rush build (instant-finish)" option.
The diplomacy is actually quite comical, as there is no negotiation ability - if the AI sends you a demand, you have to either accept or immediately go to war. You will probably notice that the AI enjoys making demands then randomly offering peace after a few turns, only to repeat this again and again.
Since the game is heavily combat-oriented, you will be focusing on building an army to destroy your opponents. There are also random creeps that will periodically spawn around the map, so it is essential that you invest in home armies in case one pops up close to your cities. The leveling up system for units is similar to Civ V, where you can choose different stats to increase (or perks) every time a unit reaches a new level (from battling). There is a large variety in the units you can create and the buildings you can construct, When you take over a city, you will have access to that particular race's build tree (ex: goblins, humans, etc).
In the pre-game screen, you can select from existing races, or create your own (you can pick from a pool of magic skills and perks like extra gold per turn).
Periodically, hero mercenaries will come, offering their service. They are very important, and boost your army strength considerably. Also, traders will come, offerring items that can be equipped by mercenary heroes. Consider investing in both of these whenever you have sufficient gold reserves.
Magic spells are helpful for winning the game, but not essential if you strengthen your stats in other things, like having a massive army, or a very high-level one. Spells include things like offensive attacks, heals (one merc hero has long range attacks AND heal spells; my personal favorite), summoning different units, and map alterations. Something fun to do to your enemy is to turn all of his city tiles to frozen plains or mountains.
Overall, the game is very, very fun, and it is easy to get into the "one more turn" mentality that results in you playing for 5 more hours when you originally told yourself you would only play for 1. If you like fantasy turn-based games similar to the Civilization series, give this game a try.
Highly recommend!

Context: Single player. Love RPG games and enjoyed Baldur's Gate, Never Winter Nights, etc. Play offline.
This game forgot that it is a game. It is more interested in being a story and an aloof story at that.
You start out creating a character but never develops any attachment to it. Then you collect a team still not really caring much about them. Use them to battle – mostly a fruit salad of participants over which you have limited control, often totally visually obscured by the effects of area spells. Best to just make sure that your group makes it through more or less ok and save. Battles are an unrewarding, boring mess. Often spells do not even cast before the battle is over or a character is charmed/dominated and still attacking the team long after the battle is over and even longer after the charmer is dead. After a battle you just gather the party and move on to the next instructed designation. No reward system for battles and hardly any for completing missions other than receiving experience as a collective. In fact, the game totally lacks any reward system of note. Run back and forth to complete missions while uncovering a story which the developers are much taken with. Weapons and armors again are disappointing. Often enemies will have 100% immunity against the special weapon which a character uses, effectively rendering that character useless. It does not help much to try and cover all eventualities as upgrades and experience are limited and very much controlled by rules. The game is ruined by its very rigid rules which defines everything “playable” until it becomes a joyless grey grind running from one area to the next to try and uncover the story while fighting dull fruit salad mob battles.
There is no sense of adventure, no ego boosting sense of achievement, no tactical planning, no strategic character development, no team cohesion (sum of the parts being greater) and hence the game is not fun in any sense. In the end it fails as a game and it fails as an interactive story. Not recommended even on sale.

sticks to the classic RPG conventions, with their versions of race, class, stats, feats, and abilities. You have basic weapon attacks, a small set of high-concept skills like Survival and Athletics that impact attack speeds and the benefits you get from resting. The similarities to D&D can actually make things pretty frustrating for casters as spells are limited to leveled spell slots per day as opposed to mana or refresh timers.
You have to watch that area of effect spells don’t hit allies. You have to watch that your enemies aren’t resistant to the type of damage you’re dealing. You have to make sure your armor isn’t tanking your damage output. There is so much data flying around with every encounter. Abilities with timers, classes that need to power up, class mechanics that conflict with other class mechanics. This is a game that you have to pay 100% attention to.
rewards that attention with fantastically-written characters and layers of dialog options that drastically change the course of your adventure.
really lets you get into the head of your character and direct their story.
If what you’re looking for is a fresh take on the classic Baldur’s Gate-style isometric RPG, you will adore this game.

Pillars of Eternity is a game I bought on a whim due to a friend's recommendation, and I have to say, this is probably one of my best buys on Steam. This game has a great many things going for it: intriguing plot, in-depth conversation and roleplay opportunities; scalable combat; interesting classes, races and backgrounds that gives this game a high amount of replayability; an ability to customize your party with both well-developed built-in NPCs and player-made party members; and a beautiful landscape and fleshed-out setting.
This is a game that I highly recommend and greatly looking forward to the sequel.

On the store page you'll read "Survive on Mars. Or die trying."
Well, get ready to die. A lot.
The planet Earth has been decimated and part of the human race is trying to survive on Mars.
After a storm called "The Red Solstice", the Tharsis colony has lost communication with the other humanc olonies of Mars. A squad of marines is sent to find out what happened to the colony.
The Red Solstice is a top-down, tactical, squad based survival shooter video game with RPG elements.
There are three game modes: Single-player (Campaing), Survival and Multiplayer.
On Single-player (Campaing) you control a squad of 4 marines through 10 missions. The first two missions serve as a tutorial, teaching you the basic controls and how to play.
There are 4 difficulty levels.
At the beginning of each mission you can choose the class of your marine, his primary and secondary weapon and up to 4 skills. However, you start with the Assault class only. The other classes and weapons will be unlocked as you progress on single-player missions.
The game has a good variety of enemies and weapons.
While playing solo you can use the Tactical Mode, where you press a button and the game runs 90% slower so you can issue orders/change the strategy/change the players position.
In the beginning it's important to focus in one or two skills. Don't try to keep all of the skills at the same level.
Also, it's important to have a balanced squad of various classes.
And get ready to die. It's possible to revive a dead squad member, but if all of them die, you'll have to restart from the last checkpoint.
The Survival mode it's like the multiplayer mode, but you play with bots, just like in single-player.
There are random missions and events, 6 different maps, you can also level up and unlock new classes and abilities.
In the Multiplayer mode you can play co-op with up to 8 players, in random missions and events, 6 different maps, you can also level up and unlock new classes and abilities.
Currently there are few people playing this mode, so it may be hard to find someone to play with.

The red clouds part, the dropship lands at an unknown location; and 8 marines set down on the Tharsis colony. I've been one of those marines a few hundred times, and none of those drops went as planned.
Your team will spend the next hour gathering items and supplies, weathering a constant flow of monsters as they roam the colony. This process begins slow, building to a crescendo as the game progresses. During the last third of the round, the danger's so intense: it requires the entire team working together to survive. This formula produces a unique and often panicked rush back to the dropship as the team tries to evacuate.
There are two kinds of marines: the ones that make it back to the dropship, and the ones left behind. If you're looking for a game with deep mechanics, replayability, and a challenge, look no further.

Duke Nukem 3D is one of my favorite games of all time, Period.
Now Duke3D has had 2 editions in Steam, the Megaton Edition (Which ill be referring to ME) and now the Anniversary World Tour Edition (Which ill be referring to World Tour or WT).
So in this review ill be focusing on the two editions instead of the game itself, because lets be honest, Duke3D doesn't need introduction already.
So, how does it compare with the Megaton Edition, Well the main difference between this one and the ME is the new episode called Alien World Order, which features 8 levels (7 without including the secret level) and to be honest, they are really polished and well made levels, which makes this Edition worth it for that alone.
Now it also brings new things to the table that the ME Didn't have like for example:
New Developer Commentary
A new weapon and enemy
New Duke Talk by the legendary Jon St. John
New music composed by Lee Jackson for the new episode
New Rewind system ripped straight from the Xbox 360 Version of the game
And "True 3D Mode" being that is a new engine that the game is running now
All of these are great stuff and addition to an already excellent game
But here's where the problems start
The ME Has stuff that WT doesn't have like for example:
The Three Expansion packs for Duke 3D, these being: Nuclear Winter, Duke it on D.C And Life's a Beach
They also removed the ME from the Steam Store, so you can't buy it anymore (unless its by keys on the internet)

I was playing Mafia, trying to finish it to play this one, ripping my hair out while I was at it, because that freaking game can sometimes be quite a pain in the bum.
Either way, I've played enough Duke Nukem 3D to offer an opinion about the game, and I've played enough of this version to offer my take on it as well.
For starters, Duke Nukem 3D is simply a masterpiece of a game, one of those games similar to Doom, that won't age in the least, there might be some trouble traversing some levels, but these are games ingenious enough to secure their own replayability through the learning curve they also offer to the player.
Duke Nukem 3D its also a game that masters the craft of what I like to call "the flow of combat" in videogames often times you find yourself in the middle of combat, dodging attacks, switching weapons, using each of your abilities/powers to your advantage, and sometimes, just sometimes, it works as if everything "fits" as if every weapon was made for an specific situation, and yet you never really derive awareness of when you have to use any of them, you simply do, naturally.
Now as for this version, this implements a wonderful system that allows you to, similarlly to a tape recorder, go back to whathever point you where prior to your death, it might not sound as much, but for a game like this, I can assure you it's a game changer, and an incredibly benefitial one, blowing yourself up with your own rpg doesn't present that much of a trouble anymore.
The graphical changes at first seemed subtle, but luckily, and astutely the developers assessed this by giving you the ability to switch from the remastered graphics, to the old graphics.
It's quite a substantial improvement that luckily doesn't sacrifice the essence of the overall aesthetic.
Now for the problems.
They changed for whatever reason the way you change weapons with the mouse wheel, effectively ruining, "the flow of the combat"...
Luckily you can still use the numbers in your keyboard, so there's that.
Sadly v-sync its also, always enabled, and sadly, not implemented very well, the game has some horrendous input lag, and there's no ability to disable it in-game.
This similarly to the last issue, can also luckily, thankfully, be bypassed, by forcing v-sync off in your control panel.
So there you have it, overall for the price I've paid for, which I also did whilst on a sale, I really enjoy the implementations, and the changes, I wish for a v-sync option, that I know, sadly, will never come, I also wish for a way to disable the silly, and tedious mouse scrolling problem.
But I recommend it nonetheless thanks to its new features.

A very poor substitue for the now defunct Megaton Edition. Gearbox, after obtaining complete control of the Duke Nukem liscense, quickly whipped up this inferiour product for the anniversary of the game.
It's awful.
The engine itself has several bugs, not the least of which being it never seems to remember when it's supposed to be full screen. It always starts up windowed, even when full screen is chosen, forcing you to disable and renable it every time, and even then it's a crap shoot that it will actually work and go full screen.
The engine seems to run smoothly enough, which it should given that it's a twenty year old engine that's been very slightly modified. But the controls are a joke. No option to change the quick save/load (saving and loading has no confirmation, and you can't even make custom save names, just the default "SLOT 1", "SLOT 2" etc.) [Edit: One new engine feature, the ability to go back to any earlier point in your playthrough of the level before you died, does mitigate the need for the quicksave/load buttons, and is a nice feature to have], and I can't set anything to the side mouse buttons, 4 and 5. Which is where I prefer to have my Big Foot automatic kick melee attack.
On top of that, the Megaton Edition came with three of the DLC packs available for Duke Nukem 3D, of varying quality. None of those are available here. Instead, we get a brand new 5th chapter. And Steam Workshop support. The latter hosts several maps that are either ripped illegally from other packs, or converted from other games.
Duke Nukem 3D was an amazing game when it came out. Megaton Edition was a fantastic, well modified engine that ran wonderfully on modern systems. This is a pathetic soulless cash grab. The only thing it has going for it is colored lighting, and even that could use some improvement.
That's enough about the engine.  So what about the GAME?  After all, to make up for the mission expansion packs, they added a whole new episode to the game.  Well, a smaller episode.  The theme is decent enough, and the first level shows some great tricks in it.  You're going from location to location across the globe.  The new enemy is somewhat frustrating, since it's pretty versatile, with several ways to hurt you and some ways to avoid damage.  The new weapon is quite fun, a modification of the freeze gun just as the microwave gun was a modification of the shrink ray.  The levels themselves overall aren't bad.  The music is awful though.  It just doesn't sound appropriate for Duke Nukem.  Nor for the levels you find yourself in.  More voice lines were added, and some older ones rerecorded.  I think I prefer the originals, but the new stuff is decent enough.
It's not worth the full price though.  It's barely worth the sale price.  Especially if you were lucky enough to get the Megaton Edition.

IF YOU LOVE TRANSPORT TYCOON OR OPENTTD AS IT IS NOW CALLED, BUY NOW!
For veterans of Transport Tycoon [deluxe]/ TTDPatch, and OPENTTD, this is a game you will have quite a time with, for quite a time!  For 20 years I've been holding out on one of the best Truck/Train shipping/logistics games, Transport Tycoon (also: now OPENTTD)... and now we have a 3d version.  Albeit it does not have all the fancy configurables that OPENTTD does, any fan should pick this up.
The game engine is quite similar to CITIES XL, but without the glitches and other issues of XL, that is where any semblance to XL ends however.  This game is definately right in the same flavour of Transport Tycoon, so if you like that one, I can recommend giving this a try.  You might just become absorbed for the whole evening in it, unable to let go.  Quite challenging to make profitable train routes, though busses are pretty easy to work with in terms of turning a profit, one should start there.  A few bus lines up and running in a few different towns, then link them with trains.  Make sure your bus passengers get dropped off near the trainstations in each town, and you'll have a good train service in a few years time.  Remember, as in real life, people will want to use their cars more and more as an alternative to the logistics services you provide, especially as the years progress.  This coupled with the fact that every year equipment gets older, it costs more and more to maintain.  Keep this in mind if you're thinking about short-cutting your train route with a super-highway.  People will notice this and ridership will fall for your trains drasticly.  There is a mod to change the simulation's car max speed to encourage more folks to use your transportation, use that mod if you can't seem to turn a profit, but only as a last resort.  The challenge keeps this game fun through the years.  There isn't quite the hard falloff that TTD had, once you got to a certain point is was easy cruising without a care in the world.  Here, the challenge stays especially if you overlook things or become complacent.
This game was quite rough when it first was released, but now with the patches, and the FREE USA DLC (via the DLC or STORE page for this game), there is so much more to offer, and a lot less bugs.
This game can run for over 10 hours and not have crashing issues.
Good patches last fall/winter and now the DLC update allowed me to update my review.  Train & Bus lines now working as intended, especially where they were problematic before when upgrading.  Loop routes work excellent, give them (and any train or bus line) a few years to mature fully + the grow with town growth, just like in Transport Tycoon.
Landscaping/terraforming tools leave a bit to be desired, can take some time (this is no Simcity).  I can now build farther and longer than before with a section of rail without it failing to smooth terrain.  Before the patch it was mayhem trying to keep with the grade/slope.  You shouldn't have too many problems.  Building a road across double-railroad track is next to impossible, however, so you should lay roads before laying dual traintrack where and when possible.  It is possible to cross with bridges in most instances or tunnel under if you have the room, but this can be quite a test of patience at times and may prove a waste of time in certain respects.   On the flip side, since the patches the other month, building rail over road is much easier.  You shouldn't have too many instances where you cross roads in a manner that prevents you from laying track.  Try to build over the roads closer to a 90 degree angle to make things easier, even if it means making the track bend a bit.
Remember, running a successful business may be challenging, but it is also rewarding.  Very Very rewarding, mind you.  Staying on top of things, with all the effort it takes, really comes with a good sense of accomplishment.  You might really enjoy this one, it's turned out to be a diamond in the rough after the updates - it really shines brightly!
Would be nice to have bigger map size for those of us without lag issues, could build rail systems like they were meant to be.  I don't think the computer processing power/video processing power is quite there yet to be honest, for bigger maps.  Don't let this stop you.
My only one complaint is being unable to lay road overtop double-raid track without knocking the track out first.  Sometimes also, the game may not let you remove certain roads if it feels the road is necessary to the simulation of people moving on their own.  You may have to fool around a bit building a bypass or two before it will let you remove the offending road if it's the only access between two towns or between a town and industry.  This is realistic, however, so who am I to judge negetively on this matter.
Graphics are plenty good for a modern game, way better than 20 years-old gfx.
The USA DLC is really stunning, and is free, so definately a feather-in-the-cap for the developer, especially considering there are many (purposely) community-source models here (the developers actually enlisted the help of modders to package this all up and purpose it for something totally awesome for everyone to enjoy).  Moves like this are extremely respectable, as they really give the customers value for their money spent buying the original game.
Sound is on par where it should be and music is better than many other city-builders, though it is typically the jazz/muzak kind of thing.  Fairly typical of the simulation genre.  It doesn't seem to get as annoying or bothersome as the music from Simcity 4 however.  If you liked Transport Tycoon's music back in the day, you'll most likely be okay with this.
Sound effects are appropriate and expected, they do not dissapoint.
Really is becoming an awesome game.  I followed this game development via youtube for a few years, and I am glad to see it finally mature into a stable, enjoyable product that without a doubt sucks me in for many hours, sometimes a whole night.  I can't say that about too many games.
Don't let the mention of Cities XL push you away, XL is not near as fun, addicitive, and bug free as this game is.  This game is 64bit, and multi-processor compiled.  This will use every bit of gfx and cpu horsepower you can throw at it.  i5 or i7 strongly recommended to play on the largest maps without any significant lag.  To turn on all the bells and whistles graphically, you'll want atleast a radeon 7700/7800 series graphics card (R 260 or better!).  This will run on intel integrated gfx but again a good Radeon or Geforce video card would be recommended for the largest maps on the higher graphical settings.
Users with only 4gb of ram may wish to bump up their machines to 6gb to 8gb total system memory or more, as this game was using 3.5gb of ram on a large map, to help avoid hitching and lag that having only 4gb or less will give you.  Load times on a solid state drive are plenty fast so also no worries here.  If you use a small or medium map you may not need more than 4gb but see the system requirements for more detailed info.
Plenty of community mods are available, but with the recent update this past week, you'll want to make sure you clean out all your old mods, and update them to the new versions otherwise you'll have a bad time with things.  The game gives you an option to load/unload mods right from the menu screen and there are front-ends for this purpose also that work with the DLC.  Check the Steam Forums for more info on this, as it is posted.
Do enjoy, if you loved TTD, you'll enjoy this quite a bit!  To the developers personally, thanks for finally giving us a game to give us our OPENTTD/TTD fix, as after 20 years +, I think it's time for an update to the old favorite.  Still love TTD though, as always will.

The third game in the series is where they really got it right in my opinion, it retains the simplistic approach of 1 but does away with all the empty screens and frankly boring gameplay to mix it with the enemy density and craziness from 2. From 2 it does away with the polarity system, instead adding a very welcome slow down key that also focuses your shooting, actual bombs (tho it retains the mana bombs) and power ups.
If you were to compare it to anything it'd be to touhou or seihou since the mechanics are very similar where shooting, power ups, grazing and so on are concerned. The difference with those games are in the addition of mana bombs, in stage length, where these ones are generally shorter and more hectic and in the voice acting - not only from the dialogue with bosses but also while playing normally, such as when you use a mana bomb, regular bomb, meet a mini boss and so on. It makes the characters more alive despite not really understanding what they're saying, althought you can guess the intent from the tone.
As far as difficulty is concerned this is probably easier than most touhou games, your hitbox is more forgiving and enemy patterns are generally not terribly arcane with a few exceptions. The comparison breaks down where the extra stage is concerned however, since it's not really a separate mode like in touhou and seihou but instead demands you to pass through the whole game first before attempting it.
The music is top notch, the stages are not as linked to it as in touhou perhaps (where you'd see a huge wave of enemies or the appearance of a midboss coinciding with a crescendo or a beat drop in the music) but it doesn't take away from how brilliant it is. It has rather clear rock/metal vibe as well, which you can tell in the final boss' theme, "Intersect Thunderbolt" if you would like to listen to a track first.
Visually there are no issues, all the enemies are clear, the shots are very distinct from the background (without the usual problem of a bunch of small red shots over a red background we've all suffered in other bullet hells) and your character has a clearly defined hitbox in her center. Item drops do not interfere either, since they are instantly grabbed as soon as they spawn, minimizing the problems of confusing or straight up covering stray bullets.
An issue however is with the power up system, as you grab power ups small dragons appear and follow you around, complementing your shooting. Sometimes you might confuse them with your character, especially in full screen mode.
And finally as far as the plot goes they rebooted the series and turned it into some sort of school war where the top students fight for a chance to compete in a tournament for a chance to become some monster big shot or other. It's not nearly as dramatic as the last two games and in my opinion it's a step down from the pseudo evangelion thing they had going on in the last two games, but the characters are still very distinct and charming at least.
Overall if you want a bullet hell and you don't have this game, you want this game. Simple as that.

I do not recommend this game even on sale (this review is made 2.5 months after initial release). Primarily because the user "interface" is really really poorly designed, despite all the nice looking screenshots and videos, this game is almost unplayable, it is more of a hassle fighting with the interface than it should / needs to be.
This game's user interface is on the level of Sim Tower - i.e. non-existent, boring font and text, surrounded by boxes facts and numbers using standard Arial font. Certainly not acceptable in today's standards.
Don't be fooled by the nice screenshots of the game running. You'll run the other way when you actually see how bad the interface is.
There are many other reasons not to recommend this game.
- Performance issue particularly when moving around the map. I have a AMD 290X, one of the top end graphics card money can buy at the moment and it stutters moving around a medium map on medium graphic settings.
- Gameplay bugs, really basic things like coaches for some reason goes to the 2nd stop in a line instead of starting from the 1st once you start a new line. How can bugs like this still be in the game after how ever many patches it has since release?
- Lack of WASD/Arrow key/edge of map movement consistency - it seems like sometimes it works, sometimes it doesn't. Does it even have key bindings? Who knows.
It simply isn't even worth the $20 sale price given the amount of time I spent in it before I've given up in frustration. Given that this game is considered "complete", has been released for some time and not an early access / alpha stage game, people should not put their hopes up that the developers will make this into a polished game with their gratis patching.
If the developers proof me wrong, I'll gladly update and change this review. But at this moment in time, in my opinion it is a $5 game for effort, which is a big shame as it has so much potential. Will the developers unlock it, well if they were planning to I would've thought they should've released this as an Early Access.
You probably don't want to pay to find out. I'd rather pay $120 for the Japanese version of A-Train 3.0 than any money towards some incomplete garbage. Even Cities in Motion 2, a game that is considered "rough around the edges" but complete, is hundrds of miles better than this "game".

I like Grimm. I tried to like Grimm more. It took me close to a year to get through all 23 episodes because of how dull Grimm was to actually play. The way Grimm speaks, elegant and loquacious, was fun to watch. Same with how his dark aura completely spun around the cutesy garbage that fairy tales have become.
The episodic GameTap gimmick might have worked a decade ago when these were first being released, but now? I honestly wish these were just ten minute animated episodes than the mind-numbing sets of levels mixed into ongoing story corruption.
The gameplay will never change. You always have 6+ stages, all have at least one "Secret" (Grimm-marked coin), and all have extremely punishing speedrun times if you choose to do them. It's far less engaging gameplay, far more "we need player interaction to further drive the story changes". Granted at first I did enjoy the Katamari Damacy-esque "get all the things", but by the time I hit episode 10 or 11 I was ready to be done with all of them.
I would have too, but on a personal note I was determined to finish this for a friend who passed just about a year ago (as of writing this) from sudden onset cancer. Grimm and his stories just barely eek out a positive recommend from me, but this sorely needed better meat to the bones, American McGee.
Here's to you, Samantha.

So, when I first heard of Night In the Woods, I found a lot of positive things about it, like amazing characters, story, and good pacing. But sadly, it was very underwhelming now that I've finished the game. In NITW, you play as a 20-year-old cat named Mae, who just dropped out of college. With this information introduced early in the game, you wonder how the main character handles that change and why she dropped out. You get an idea of the protagonist’s internal conflict and main plot. Besides Mae, you are also introduced to her friends, Gregg, Bea and Angus, who help her adjust back to town.
Now an important aspect of the game is hanging out with either Bea or Gregg, where you can see how Mae plays off them. I finished the game hanging out with Bea every day, but even though I have no idea what Gregg has to offer, and I do not want to replay NITW again just to see the other route. In the Bea route, I learned that she has her own personal problems, such as dealing with her small business and other spoiler related things. Overall, Bea is a well written character, and I enjoyed being with her. This characterization shows how well NITW can develop its characters, but remember, Mae is the main protagonist.
An essential part of a character's growth is conflict. For example, in the game, Bea argues with Mae over her immaturity, but it was quickly resolved the next day, and Mae continues to wander town distracting herself from her problems. Another argument happens between Mae and her mom over the dropout, yet the conflict is quickly resolved the next day and never brought up again. Which brings me to my next point.
What should make the story engaging is the protagonist. Yet Mae is a very flat character, and the conflicts she faces are resolved too quickly. Don't get me wrong, the game has a lot of potential in its story, but it has many plot holes, incomplete arcs, repetition, and iffy gameplay.
Now onto the PROS and CONS.
PROS:
-The game at least connected the background characters to Mae, which helped me understand more about her past and relationship to the small-town cast.
-Most of the NPCs have an interesting and charming personality, ex. Selmers, Mr. Chazokov, and Pastor Karen.
-Beautiful eye candy art and soothing music.
-Possum Spring’s history was interesting.
-Demon Tower is a fun side game with a lot of challenge, great pixel art, and fun dungeon crawling gameplay.
CONS:
-Mae’s character. She may be 20 years old, but she doesn’t act like one at all and is very random. My main issue with her is how she does not confront her problems or have the willingness to grow up even with the support of her friends and family. She has some spoiler related issues, but throughout the game, it was merely pushed aside. Other times Mae acts very mean spirited. She wasn’t a charming jerk who was easy to sympathize with. I really wanted to root for Mae and see her overcome her problems, but she was just so unlikeable.
-As much as there are interesting NPCs, there is also an equal amount of forgettable characters. They don’t contribute to Mae’s character arc, add personality to the town, or affect the general plot.
-The characters never change their expressions. For example, all Mae does is squint, hold her arms up, and shrink her pupils. I had a tough time sympathizing with her and the forgettable NPCs. Even when she cried, it looked fake. The characters felt less real.
-The game’s dialogue was cringey and annoying. Sometimes the characters say “like” a bit too much for my taste. Other times the game attempts to convey a profound message, but it only comes out as a cliché moral.
-A lot of plotholes, which is the most apparent at the end of the game.
-Illusion of choice. Despite Mae having two or more dialogue options, they are either the same response or do not change the conversation’s direction. The illusion also applies to whether you hang out with Bea or Gregg. Sure exclusively hanging out with one friend nets an achievement, but there are only minor changes to the story.
-The sudden story shift halfway through the game (huge spoiler). There was no foreshadowing, and despite the shift, Mae does the same routine of wandering town.
-The very end of the game felt rushed, and the epilogue seemed incomplete. Even after the game’s climax, the characters return to normalcy and shoehorn a lesson at the end of the day.
-Painfully slow story pace. Most of the game is spent wandering town talking to people and hanging out with Bea or Gregg playing minigames. The game is a slice of life, but has lots of filler and repetitive gameplay.
-Mae’s bizarre dreams do not have much effects on the plot, and the gameplay within them aren’t very engaging.
-The minigames weren’t fun either, both content and controls were meh. Some of them had no bearing on the plot at all.
In conclusion, game tried to tell a coming-of-age story with a video game approach. The story fell flat with its incompleteness, whereas the gameplay was forgettable and not fun. I recommend that you research more about the game before buying, like watching YouTube videos and reading BOTH positive and negative reviews. In my opinion, NITW is not worth buying, but if you do want to play this game, wait for it to go on sale. Maybe you’ll have a better time with it than me, but this game is like a gilded statue. The attractive surface is comprised of good looking art, music, premise, and fan opinion, but it masks the game’s deeper flaws.

I hope this review doesn’t come off as overly negative, but I feel like there are some valid criticisms that should be addressed. This game has gotten a lot of praise, but there are some things you should know before you buy it.
This is very much a game about a story, not about gameplay. The truth is that this game is not exactly fun to play. It consists of a lot of wondering around without a real objective, talking to the same people over and over, some pretty restricted and unrewarding exploration, and some rudimentary platforming. The moment to moment gameplay is hardly engaging, but this is more of a storybook than a game. In fact, I’m not exactly sure
this is a game to be honest. It seems like it might have worked better as a film, or a short book. Most of your choices do not matter in the slightest, and the ones that do only give you slight variations to the story. The writing honestly isn’t that great a lot of the time, but some people really like and relate to these characters. I think that’s why this game has gotten so much praise. Those people aren’t wrong in liking it, I just really don’t think this is a game for everyone, or most people even. I found it to be pretty boring most of the time.
The story is pretty far from the best story I’ve experienced in a game, and just wasn’t good enough to weigh out the bad gameplay for me. If you feel like you can get over the boring gameplay and you just really want to meet these characters, then sure, go for it, but to the general population, I’m gonna say you should skip this one.

Train Fever attempts to take the railway and transportation management genre to the next level by including elements from many of the past greats. The strongest influence on Train Fever is Transport Tycoon. The Train Fever website acknowledges this by including a small section devoted to the history of this genre. While Train Fever attempts to resurrect and bring rail and transport management back to modern gaming, it fails at standing out among other recent similar titles.
Train Fever tries to be the Jack of All Trades. It includes city public transport, inter-city travel, and cargo supply line management. By putting all these features into one title, not one of them feels fully fleshed out. It may gather a curious audience who has played a game that simulates one of those features well, but it will not hold their attention for long as gamers will find their favorite feature lacking.
The cities are not as large as cities presented in games like Cities in Motion, and the populations are very small. Most cities will start with a population under 200 in 1850. Unfortunately, by the year 2000, it will be a struggle to get their populations north of 1,000. The cities grow  dynamically, depdending on how far the residents can travel on your networks in the space of 20 minutes and how well supplied a city is with finished goods, but they never feel like a metropolis. Managing travel within a city may be done with 1 or 2 bus lines, easily getting 80% line usage from the population. The population is not divided by class, either, and every person feels the same, with random destinations (one building each) for home, work, shopping, and leisure. Which one a person picks to travel to seems random, and times passes so quickly (1 day per second), that there is no illusion this person is alive with a real schedule to keep. Cities are so small that many players have stated they do not bother with public transportating within the city limits and focus solely on intercity transportation.
Intercity passenger transportation is a bit more interesting. Traveling from one city to another will be the first task undertaken that the passengers cannot fulfill themselves by just walking. Establishing a connection between two cities also jumpstarts the growth in both cities and you will see an immediate benefit in population growth. The newly created residents now have a chance to have one of their destination buildings be in a different city than their home. The player has a choice of using bus lines, tram lines, or rail lines to complete the connections. Rail is the fastest way to travel throughout the game, but it is the most expensive to build infrastructure, maintain it, and run it. The running costs of one train will dwarf the running costs of an entire bus fleet or tram fleet. Due to this, many players opt for focusing on road connections using trams and buses. Trains are the fastest vehicle, but due to their expense, most lines can only afford one or two trains, which makes  for long waiting times at train stations. Trams and buses are slower, but running an entire fleet will shorten the station waiting time dramatically. I actually got passengers farther using light rail trams compared with using trains. Late in the game, the costs for running trains increases dramatically, and passenger rail lines are very difficult to make profitable.
When it comes to cargo transportation, the game feels weakest. There are only three production lines, and each line ends in the same generic cargo type "finished good." The lines are:
Iron Ore + Coal -> Steel Mill -> City
Timber -> Lumber Mill -> City
Oil -> Refinery -> City
Players have an option to ship cargo via trucks or by rail.  Trucks can only carry a few tons at a time. Rails need large amounts of cargo in order to be profitable, but it's easier to make a cargo line profitable via rail than it is a passenger line, keeping in mind that freight trains generally have much high running costs than passenger trains. Unlike passengers, cargo has no set destination and can be hauled to any facility that accepts deliveries. This seems like a step back for the genre. Even Simutrans, an open source project with low resolution sprites that look like they were regurgitated from old DOS games, has more production lines with business contracts that provide destinations for all cargo. The one interesting idea that Train Fever presents is that producers will not manufacture without demand. Unless the entire production line is hooked up, nothing will produce. The only way to make a facility produce more is to increase the demand, and that starts at the end of the chain by providing more outlets for the finish goods and working your way up to transporting more raw materials. Unfortunately, the execution of this idea seems lacking. On a small game map, it is possible to supply every city from one cargo line. It does not matter which line you choose, as they all end in the same type of finished goods. Any delay on your line will kill productivity. Train is old and needs to be replaced? You had better put the new train on the track first before getting rid of the old fella as production immediately starts dropping when the line is not serviced. If you want a supply line challenge, try Railroad Tycoon III. Even Railroads! has a better transportation model, as each city will have a variety of needs to be filled.
Routing in Train Fever is the best part of the game, but it can be frustrating. The auto-recalculations of routes at various points in the game sometimes make the game stutter. Routes can also change based on traffic density, turning your nice straight bus route into a twisted death pretzel over time. Rails present some fun puzzles as you try to figure out how to extend your lines without causing train collisions. You can use signals to help with this, but you are limited to simple switches, tunnels, and overpasses on your rail lines. No double-crossovers or four-way diamonds allowed. Designing the throat to a high-traffic station is a pain as you map out where each simple switch enters and exits the throat, and you end up extending the station throat almost halfway to the next town in order to accomodate each one. Station planning is important as you cannot upgrade your station once it is placed. Need a longer platform? Stop all your trains, tear down the old infrastructure, and build an entirely new station. Need more platforms? Same thing. Unless you already have five, then you're at your limit and need to build an entirely new station elsewhere near the city. While train routing is realistic (no trains passing through other trains on the same track), the actual track constructs are limited in scope. Railways X provides a more satisfying layout modeler with far more tools to build interesting crossings and signal systems.
Train Fever has a laundry list of features that made me want to play the game. Unfortunately, each one of these features on its own is handled better by other (and often older) titles. By trying to do so much, Train Fever feels like it glosses over what makes transportation and rail management games fun to play.

A straightforward bullet hell game. You have bombs to clear the screen and a special meter that seems to build up as you deal damage. The special attack doesn't clear the screen of bullets but it deals pretty good damage to the enemies on screen. You clear waves of enemies and then face a multi-phase boss at the end of the level. Sometimes you get powerup drops (like more bombs and mini-tiamats which serve as automated turrets that attack their own targets while you fire).
As for story, I don't think it relates to the previous games. You just fight challengers in the tournament to represent your region(?) and then it ends teasing that there are harder challenges ahead as representative.
What's nice in this game (and not in 1 or 2) is that there's a dot marker on your character to see exactly what part of your character needs to dodge the bullets. I played on easy and it felt pretty generous with the hurtbox (I'm pretty sure I didn't avoid everything weaving left and right between bullets). Also, your speed is significantly slower while firing. The slow speed is sometimes nice for weaving through some bullets but there are also times you need the speed to cross the screen quickly (like to change targets avoid certain bullet patterns). There is a separate slow button to slow you down without firing but I don't understand when I wouldn't just use the attack button instead.
However, unlike 2, boss fights don't show life meters (with more bars for more phases) so you don't know how long the boss fight will last unless you memorize how many phases they have. Also, it doesn't bring the polarity mechanic from 2 which I thought was pretty fun.
I'm not really into bullet hells, but I played this on easy and had a fun enough time playing through. There are patterns you can memorize and progress further by changing up your tactics. In my opinion, I liked 2 the best, 3 a little less (only because 2 has the polarity mechanic), and 1 leagues behind. It's worth a try if you like bullet hells.

Exceed 3rd- Jade Penetrate Black Package is not a hentai game surprisingly enough, instead it is the third entry in a series of vertical bullet hell games. Who is Jade and who penetrated her black package? That is something we may never know. Moving on from that very weird name, Exceed 3 is a reboot of the series and is set in a different dimension. Only one of the previous characters briefly show up and everyone else are new characters. We play as Rayne Lindwurm who is in a fight to the death tournament with other mages to decide who will become one of the 7 Lords of the realm. It all sounds very exciting but in reality it is a pretty boring story and thankfully we still have the option to turn off dialogue. This has the same issue as the last game in that it has the subtitles broken if you are play in fullscreen, which is kind of unforgivable to make that mistake yet again when one your selling points is a “Cutscene-driven story-telling” experience.
We are given the choice to either play Arcade or Practice mode. Practice mode is supposed to let you choose any level but it is broken and only allows you to choose the first level making the mode utterly useless. One of the first things that you will notice is that the graphics are much improved . They are not impressive by any means but it is a big step forward from the last game. Our character does not have the ability to switch magic types and absorb bullet types which is unfortunate since that was a really cool feature. In it's stead we have a fews bombs per life and the ability to make your character move slower. It's nothing unique and felt like a step down from the previous entry. Bombs let you clear all the projectiles on the screen and has a small zone that can damage enemies while slowing down also allows you to narrow your shots and target a specific enemy. You also have a  special attack which fires homing beams at an enemy and is recharged by avoiding projectiles when they are very close to hitting you.
Powerups are also included into this entry. We have one where you someone a familiar for extra fire power and another that gives you an extra bomb. Your familiars are very handy and is the only way target enemies when you slow down. If you die they revert to their powerup form and bounce around the screen until you collect them again. There are three diffculty modes and if you are finding the game too hard you can enable the auto-bomb setting which will detonate a bomb every time you get hit effectively tripling your lives. Which may be a wise choice for new players since Exceed 3 wastes no time showering you with tons of projectiles. There are still red and blue projectiles but their color doesn't really matter this time as they will both kill you in one shot. Controller support isn't listed but it still works perfectly with a controller and has rebindable keys. It does not feature dpad support sadly. Also the escape key still closes the whole game instead of pausing.
Mini bosses have also been added in between levels but they are the same robot each level so fighting them gets a bit boring. There are 6 bosses in the game and it takes quite a while to defeat them since they have like five forms of fighting that will refill their health five times but change how projectiles are shot at you. In the last game they had three forms but changed appearance or had some kind of flashy animation when they switched but in this they just switch projectile patterns making the fights feel a bit too dragged out. Remember to use the slow down feature when fighting bosses as the narrow shots will defeat them a lot faster than your spread shots. Bombs are also very effective against bosses if you can get in close enough to actually harm them with it and may be a better used as weapons when a boss form is too difficult for you as they will cause massive damage causing them to switch to a different form.
Exceed 3 feels like a straight bullet hell game as it no longer requires any of the strategy of the 2nd and does not reach the heights of the previous game in my opinion. It is by no means a bad game though and is far far better than the first Exceed game. It would actually be one of Steam's best bullet hells if practice mode worked, full screen subtitles worked and if bosses showed some signs of being worn down or angered throughout the fight. As it stands it is an inferior sequel with all the same technical problems of the 2nd that have not been fixed for some reason and introduces some new ones including a whole broken mode. Most of the problems with Exceed 3 are due to technical issues and not the actual game itself. Our character is less fun to play as this time around and Exceed 3 has nothing to do with the previous games but it is still a very fun fast paced bullet hell that will keep any fan of the genre entertained.

This game is extremely repetitive and gets old quickly. There's so many poorly designed game mechanics.
1. Every boss battle comes down to "quick time event button mashing", this is stupid on so many levels. Most game developers stopped using "QTE" a decade ago.
2. Every stronghold you visit, the game throws endless number of enemies at you, It gets quite frustrating and is a cheap way to extend the total play time. You are forced to run away and come back and do the exact same thing all over again.
3. The game gave you powerful abilities and a rich open world to explore. However, all mission and side quest somehow forces you to play in a certain way. It's either forced stealth or forced killing styles or count down timer.
4. Skills and abilities require way too much time and effort to obtain, this is a single player game. No one should waste time with endless grinding in a offline single player game. The progression pacing is completely unbalanced.
5. Main story related missions are poorly designed. They are all follow > escort/rescue > forced stealth. You really don't have any freedom on how to approach a misison.
6. Even the developers know their game is extremely repetitive because one of the paid DLC unlock a "infinite combat finisher move" so you can quickly dispatch a group of enemies to save some time. You have to pay the developer on top of the full game just to save yourself some time and frustration. Holy crap....
To sum this game up, it's basically "Wide as an ocean and deep as a puddle". You're basically doing the exact same thing over and over again just at different locations.

I first picked up the game on my brother's family share, I played for a few hours and got bored by not knowing where to go pretty quickly, didn't help to be answered "git gud" whenever I asked someone to help me with the game, community is really toxic when it comes to critiquing the game, so after my first bad experience with the game I took a break from trying to play it and came back a few years later when a friend offered to join in and guide me through the game without spoiling or playing the game for me while I followed they with my character.
It's one of the most talked about aspects of the game, being "difficult but fair", an expression nowadays thrown about more than miracle users bolts, and for the most part I agree with the statement, it is (for the most part) difficult but fair, with the exception of some death in the game caused by bugs or really weird platforming, not enough of those to really bother me but i can't say those didn't happened, combat is usually presented in three ways:
and the game doesn't do much else than those three types of encounters, that said, it does a great job to show variation in how they're presented, which is great and doesn't feel repetitive.
Your character also influences a lot in combat, there are a few classes to chose from but your part of the fight divides into these categories:
Woo, now that we got that out of the way I'll touch in a subject not many agree with me, Dark souls needs an easy mode and a pause button, and here's why: I would not have been able to beat the game for the first time on my own, and no, I do not need to "git gud",gud", I'm not willing to spend time on a game that I'm not progressing and having fun with, I'd love to play the game on an easier setting and experience the game design and it's lore, and yes, I understand the idea of the game of being hard, but having an easier mode wouldn't take away from your experience, it would take away from those who choose to play on such mode, and even then, maybe an easy mode would still be hard for those who play on an easy mode and I'd get the full experience on the same level as others, it doesn't make the game less "immersive", it makes the game more malleable and welcoming for more players; now for the pause button, this one is simple, if you're being invaded or have summoned a phantom the game would disable it, while you're playing offline or there's no one online playing on the same world as yours you should be able to pause it, it's a game for ♥♥♥♥ sake, if I want to pause and do whatever I should be able to as simple as that.
There's not much to talk about on graphics, they definitely didn't age much but they will in a few year, textures near your character are fine and well made but the rendering distance is really low, that can be fixed with a mod called
, that also unlocks 60fps and a few other things, definitely recommend if you can run the game and it's max, I say that not because it requires much of your PC, it's the port that's really bad.
Now on level design, and to be honest I noticed this when I played DS3, the maps on the first game are really big in scale but there's not much going on, especially places like anor londo, darkroot garden, Blighttown(the lower part), and although I like the feeling of a desolated place that used to have many residents I can't help to feel like I'm constantly running to move around on a slow pace, it definitely won't bug many players the first few times they play the game because the constructions are all well crafted and hide a lot of cool background history to the place, but once you're seeing everything for the 5th or 6th time it get's really stale and moving around doesn't feel as fast as it did when you were looking everywhere.
Here's the real deal that made me like Dark souls a lot, don't get me wrong, the rest of the game is fine, yet the boss battles are so much more exciting, every boss has a pretty easy to learn pattern, and you the easy to medium in difficulty ones you can beat on your first try, they are mostly giant monsters that can crush you with their foot and still feels great go head on against them, and by "head on" I mean run the ♥♥♥♥ away and roll like crazy, and it feels even better when the epic boss theme starts to play, you really feel like everything you went trough to get to the boss was preparing you to fight it, and those fights are great.
The lore of the game is pretty boring to discover by yourself, not going to lie, to have to read text upon text of item description is not a cool way to present to your players the world around you, and don't even lie pretending you read through it all, because you didn't, you went to a beautiful man with a YouTube channel called
, the man does a great job on explaining what's know and what's theory on the game's world, props to that guy for sticking to reading through the amount of descriptions to take away information and presenting to us in a fun manner.
Not going to dwell on this one for long, sound design is pretty okay on the game, it doesn't have many tracks aside from boss themes because of design choices, you can't have a place feel empty and dead with music on the background(unless you're either Kenji Yamamoto and Minako Hamano, the gods the designed Super metroid's soundtrack), well, you sacrifice some things for others I guess, at least weapons and spells have a really satisfying hit and cast sounds.

From the guys that brought you Planescape, Icewind Dale, Neverwinter Nights, Baldur's Gate I and II to the more recent Knights of the Old Republic II, South Park games and Fallout New Vegas comes this game. Lovingly crafted and written, this game was crowdfunded successfully by over 70,000 fans. The combat and general apperance of the game looks and feels similar to Baldur's Gate brought up to date for the modern gamer. It is as complex or as simple as you want it to be. Reasonable difficulty scaling means that new players can jump right into the story and just play without worrying about complex mechanics. Easy access to retraining your party or even creating a new member means that you cannot be stuck in an unwinnable situation. Long time veterans or anyone seeking a challenge can dive into the deep combat mechanics and team compositions to min-max an optimal team composition with combat that rewards proper positioning and micromanagement. The world has a rich history that is fleshed out through conversation and books found throughout the game, and choices made by the player do matter. NPCs can be killed with appropriate repercussions, and quests can be completed peacefully or killing everything. I haven't finished the story yet, but it is interesting and drives the player to continue going. There are loads of side quests to do, and the DLC is amazing as well. Pick up on a sale and you will not regret it.
If you want an old style D and D game this is the one for you, with loads of lore and story expect to invest hours into this. great game worth every penny.

A nice touch is that you can siwtch between the rendering modes by pressing a button. This allows you to see the improvements in the grapics at any time.
The Build endinge is used to great effect here. There are working pool tables, light switches can be toggled, movie projecters can be switched on and off and Duke can even take a look at the security systems. This version of the game contains 5 episodes. Episode 1-3 is great, although episode 2 has too many of the exploding dones. Episode 4 is tough but still great. Episode 5 was made for this version of the game by the guys who made the original episodes. And it is reaaly good. My biggest complaints about episode 5 is the difficulty and the boss fight. The episode is really hard. I spent most of my time with a health bar that was below 45. The last boss is also a big dissapointment.
There was also a few bugs. The game crashed once during my time with it. There is a wierd bug with the weapons selection. I switched to a new weapons and after firing one shot the game equiped the previous weapon. This happend a lot ( about once or twice per level) and evel ended up in me being killed. Speaking of dying, the game used a rewind system when you die. This is something I like, mostly because I am not used to quick saving (even in games like quake, I save manually) and would have lost a lot of progress if I couldn't rewind. It also allows you to get better times in levels. If I got stuck and took a while to find ou where to go next, I would kill myself and rewind to the point I began searching for the way forward. That way I didn't use a guide, didn't have to reapeat a level and still got a good time.
One thing that does hurt this game is that the expansions included in the Megaton edition isn't here. I hope that this will be added as DLC later. The game is great value for money and really fun. I would reccomend it to anyone who likes 90's FPS games (Although they probably have it), who want to check out one of the best 90's FPS games and anyone who like Duke Nukem Forever.

Rip off of Civ?

This game is not a Civ5 clone!!!
With that out of the way, what exactly is Warlock then? The resemblances are so similar it looks like a cheap knock off, but is it? I am happy to say that the answer is no. While there are some similarites between both games, warlock focuses purely on war.
You build military on a seperate queue from regular buildings, you have no workers to manage, no happiness to keep positive and by extension no luxury resources, everything you see and find is for war.
You can win by owning most of the land, or researching the ultimate spell, or capturing all capital cities. Don't these victory conditions sound familiar? The only problem is, you will never have a game that lasts long enough unless you intentionally drag it out to achieve any other victory except a war/domination victory.
This game begs for multiplayer, which thankfully it does have! The netcode is pretty okay too. The downside? No simultanious turns. You cannot take your turn (or seemingly do anything) while your foe takes their own turn which means that games drag on way too long! This is a game about war, I have a large military to move every single turn and so do my foes! This limits multiplayer to 1v1 because large groups are not going to finish a match in a day.
Warlock is fun, the mechanics are engaging, the lore is rich and humourous in places and playing 1v1 with a friend is very stimulating. If I could rank a game as neutral then this one I would. But I can't so I can't recommend this game.
One last thing, enemy AI. They are brain dead. You can win games by simply leaving the AI alone long enough to die to wild monsters. I am not even joking. They have no concept of how to play the game and certainly no idea of how to win it. If you played Civ5 and thought the AI there was bad, then that AI will seem like HAL from a space oddysey after you have seen the bone-headed bizaare AI that this game offers. The wild monsters (barbarians) are more of a threat than the actual opposing leaders.
