Quick Review:
The way this game's character reacts in the trailer to the overly simplified and cutesy Fairy Tales is the same way I reacted to the gameplay. It's bland, basic and fairly boring if you're seeking any kind of challenge. I do not recommend paying money on this.
Full Review:
The game's concept is solid and draws me in. The idea of being a small, ill tempered smelly goblin of a man wanting to darken up cheesey good-natured fairy tales is delightful to me. The character almost makes me think of Wario in comparison given the way they act and regard themselves. He likes being foul, he likes that he's this horrid stink-monger and embraces it. Again, concept is great and the art style matches well to boot. The probem here is...
There's no actual game-play. Ironically the game-play is about as one dimensional as the fairy tales your character seeks to undermine, and that's a real shame. Many reviewers are comparing it to Katamari or perhaps, if you owned a Wii, de Blob. These are apt comparisons but Karamari and de Blob had some things that this game lacks:
1) Challenge.
There's no real way to fail in this game. There's no time limit (though a timer is present for some reason), there's no way to potentailly "die" and lose your progress. The "enemies" don't pose any actual threat as you'll out-stink them faster than they can scrub your darkness away. There's nothing preventing you from succeeding. The only possible "challenge" you could say this game has would be if you set a personal time-limit goal as a speed runner. But again, this wouldn't be something that the game is monitoring, it's something you'd do yourself. Challenge just is not here.
2) Some form of unique control scheme or gimick.
Katamari's mechanic was rolling the ball, de Blob's mechanic was platforming and having to physically touch things you wanted to change. In Grimm...you just walk by them. It's not engaging and more shallow then a kiddie pool with half the water drained out of it. I will say this, for children, the control scheme is fine. But they'd need to be very young. For adults or even children over i'd say 5, the kind of gameplay you get is going to get boring real fast. There also seems to be hidden tokens, but I collected many and received no reward for doing so. They almost seem like an after-thought thrown in for the hell of it. Like the game's Timer, no actual purpose, just there for "reasons."
3) Music.
de Blob was a game where you would relax. It was meant to be a chill out game without high challenge. It's sound track reflected that with jazz mostly. Katamari was also somewhat more mellow but with an almost trippy peppy attitude. It's sound track reflected that with Pop and really jumping beats. Grimm has no sound track. It has it's trailer song, and that's it. The trailer song isn't even in the game. The game has only one continually looping track that sounds like it may have been poached from a free-use website (seriously, the composition of it's one and only level music sounds suspiciously like a "My First Level Music" practice file. It loops in less than 1 minute and never leaves). I could forgive the uncompelling controls and game-play if the creator meant for the game to be laid back, but a complete and utter lack of any mood music of any kind is sadly the final nail in the coffin for Ol' Grimm.
In summation, I think the devs of this game have struck gold with the concept and the art direction. Sadly, that gold is tarnished under the complete and utter lack of compelling game-play and a sound track composed of one continually looping (possibly free-use) track. I do not recommend spending any money on this game (YET). But I am interested to see if this game may get some kind of over-haul if it continues to update. For now, at the end of this review, I am uninstalling it but will be marking it as "Follow" on my Steam list to check up on it occasionally. If things improve, I'd be willing to run through the roses again with Grimm and wilt some bouquets once more.

Ever since playing the indoor missions of the original Starcraft campaign I hoped for a standalone game focussing on this setting. And here it is.
TRS combines the looks and feel of Starcraft, blends in some DOTA-like micro control but has the players act cooperatively against waves of zombies and alien monsters a bit like Left 4 Dead.
However, this blend of threats in waves and mission details makes you realize quickly that you need to know your way around before succeeding. By the setting and enemy waves alone, the game is substantially more difficult to master than many of today's games. The difficulty adds to the addictive character of the game - lots of replayability.
The developers continuously keep on improving the game and gameplay. Additionally, they are always open for your suggestions and eager to receive your crash reports. There is a close connection between game community and  developers.
RTS is multiplayer focussed and purely cooperative so be on the lookout for a decent team / squad. At the moment the RTS community is rather small so at times it might be frustrating not to find enough players for your match. This is the only drawback I see and it might become resolved soon once there is a bigger community.

I hope this review doesn’t come off as overly negative, but I feel like there are some valid criticisms that should be addressed. This game has gotten a lot of praise, but there are some things you should know before you buy it.
This is very much a game about a story, not about gameplay. The truth is that this game is not exactly fun to play. It consists of a lot of wondering around without a real objective, talking to the same people over and over, some pretty restricted and unrewarding exploration, and some rudimentary platforming. The moment to moment gameplay is hardly engaging, but this is more of a storybook than a game. In fact, I’m not exactly sure
this is a game to be honest. It seems like it might have worked better as a film, or a short book. Most of your choices do not matter in the slightest, and the ones that do only give you slight variations to the story. The writing honestly isn’t that great a lot of the time, but some people really like and relate to these characters. I think that’s why this game has gotten so much praise. Those people aren’t wrong in liking it, I just really don’t think this is a game for everyone, or most people even. I found it to be pretty boring most of the time.
The story is pretty far from the best story I’ve experienced in a game, and just wasn’t good enough to weigh out the bad gameplay for me. If you feel like you can get over the boring gameplay and you just really want to meet these characters, then sure, go for it, but to the general population, I’m gonna say you should skip this one.

Ultimately, this game, at conception, had great potential to achieve very interesting things.  In the end, though, the lack of things to do is what kills it.  Heres the thing:  Stranded Deep introduces a unique setting for a game.  'The Castaway' style gameplay is inviting at first.  What people neglect to realize, myself included, is that, once a home is built and once you become self sufficient on the island, there is no motivation to continue on.  After the initial 3 or so hours of a game, where you hastily seek food and water sources, and build your shelter, you become trapped in a predictable cycle.  There is no reason to expand your house, no reason to explore deeper in the ocean, no reason to risk your life for gear that would do next to nothing to help your position.  Among the reasons you get trapped in this cycle is because there is no threat to you besides food and water needs.  Waterbound animals, like sharks, do make your ocean exploration entertaining, but you have no reason to fear them on land.  Additionally, lack of any interesting leveling of gear makes it difficult to want to continue on and level up your equipment.  Unlike similar games, like Minecraft, nothing is compelling you to get better.  Once you have the basic equipment down, you've essentially beat the game.  I think this game could benefit from, first, instituting much larger islands, predators or land dwelling enemies, of some sort, and multiplayer.  For now though, I do believe this game is not worth buying.
Update 3/26/17:  The game has been updated some, and some predators have been added, but they stink.  The animals behave poorly.  They also updated the HUD to something, I must honestly comment, is even ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ than what they previously had.  They seem to be going backwards with this title.  Every update is more and more destructive.

Far more versatile than the predacessor with so many different routes and choices to choose. While I personally didn't click all too well with the narrative this time around, at least with the routes I took, I had an absolutely lovely time with the adventures of myself and my cute thief companion I couldn't find a way to romance. There are tons of charming twists and turns to be had with the story, with areas, items, and experiences you could easily miss; something I wish more modern games took advantage of, but that is for another time.
Since this is mainly a story with choices and some cute old school dice-based fights, is the story any good compared to its predacessor? Yes and no. An Assassin in Orlandes benefits from a much tighter narrative experience, being a shorter story over all but had plenty of optional things and outcomes to make it a charming affair, even though a single playthrough you'd see just about everything.
The prose, like story, is much longer winded, and that can be a bit off putting, especially with the amount of purple prose  found in this one. It's all well written mind you, but there are instances of ten page sections where you have little control at all. Like the romance I mentioned earlier, I found it often the case in the writing that in moments of actual important choice, I was but a reader with no control, as "you" makes all the big choices for you. This does not occur all the time, but there are plenty of moments in which options weren't pursued. It could've been a tighter budget or something of the nature, but outside of choosing your next location or how to go about a fight, I found the story a bit less engaging than the first. This isn't bad at all mind you, and there is still tons of choices and options, but it was a bit off putting.
The guys who do these charming little novels clearly put a lot of heart into the writing and development, and the improvements on all their games are clearly their. Even for my critical deconstruction, I still had a blast with this one and will do with many more to come. It may not be my favorite CYOA, but it's hard to not love the variety and creativity they've put into the series. Absolutely worth the purchase if you have the chance.

If you're one of those weird people who complain Pillars of Eternity or Divinity: Original Sin had too much reading and you needed everything VO-spoonfed to you... this game is not for you. Me, I love it. You're a RPG-fan and like stories, and are not silly that you want full VO, then you shall too. Get the first too though and play it, since the story heavily references upon it.
Basically this game looks and plays like a choose your own adventure. There are 3 difficulty levels, casual (unlimited health, back button), adventure (unlimited saves) and classic (what RPG-vets like me run of course). One suggestion during character creation, make sure your fitness is high. Way more important than hitpoints.
Gameplaywise you read sections of text and then make choices. Choices that matter. Choices that may reference "if you have item X" where you think 'were could that possibly have dropped?' There are branching paths and several ways to lead to the same destination and if you replay you may even skip certain sections you were sure were plotimportant and unskippable. Pretty much all choices have resolution, and yes, that can mean DEATH. In classic, prepare to replay sections, though that goes much faster not reading sections you repeat.
Aside from these choices, there are events where you need to roll dice based on your fitness (hopefully you have it high), where failing can have dire consequences (including, yes, DEATH).
And then there's combat. Have you played Risk? Since about the same principle goes here. Including screaming when your rolls go bad (often). The highest roll is compared to the defender, the higher wins. Equal? Look at the next etc. If you run out dice that way before the opponent they win. So obviously you want armor and weaponry that adds more dice giving you a higher chance at those 6'es. Also all dice for weapons decide damage. Double so good to improve. Aside from better gear you can get a temp boost with fitness (you did roll a high number for it right?) It can give you +1 to a roll (yes, above 6 meaning autmatic win if that happens). Catch? It gets harder the more you do it in a battle, and if you fail the roll you get -1 to your roll. And if you used it defensively, and the opponent rolls a 6, you're screwed yeah.
And that hurts, since HP's are low. Restoring HP is rare and low (unless casual) and enemies can do a lot of damage. All the perfect ingredients for the hardcore RPG-lover to have hours of fun. So what are you waiting for?

Longer and more involved than An Assassin in Orlandes, and better for it. There's still the classic Choose Your Own Adventure format with dice-based combat, but the sections are longer, and combined with the minor changes in the text from, e.g,, having a companion or not, you feel like you're interacting with and advancing a narrative, not just going through a dungeon crawl a few pages at a time.
Polished interface with fun dice-rolling physics and -- most importantly -- the option to change the font and text size.
The main negative is that the frequent combat is largely luck-based, and since there's few opportunities to regain health, a few unlucky dice rolls can make the game basically unwinnable without resorting to cheats. Even just doubling the amount of health restored by resting and using potions would make the game more balanced.
EDIT: The developers seem to have fixed the issue with Steam achievements.

Long Live the Queen has often been described as Princess Maker with all the creepy/disturbing♥♥♥♥♥♥stripped out, which is both accurate and apt. There's not much you can say beyond that to really describe the game: you invest in skills, make decisions and hope that when a skill check comes up you can pass and if you fail, hope it is not a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t fatal check.
Outside of the usual grumbling that it is anime as ♥♥♥♥, a common complaint is that the game is too easy and reaching your coronation is not particularly difficult (there's one obscenely obvious path to winning). The real fun is finding all of the alternative events, conversations and side stories in an attempt to collect all the deaths, epilogues and achievements. Want to win a naval battle? Marry a commoner? Join up with the evil guys? Save the day with singing?! All are possible, but you have to invest in the right skills to set off the correct event flags to just get them in motion.
If you're looking for a game to add to your completion list then you won't get much out of LLTQ except a laugh or two, but if you like exploring weird skill combinations and reloading save after save because you got ♥♥♥♥ed over by a completely random skill check you weren't expecting, you can definitely get a reasonable amount of entertainment and accomplishment out of this game.

The game itself is a Life Sim with turn based 'combat' and a rogue-like leveling system. There is no actual animation in the game however, just stills. Stills painted and drawn by the creators in an attempt to compensate for the lack of animation, but it doesn't totally. The trial and error gameplay is tough, but there is an amazing sense of accomplishment when you survive events. Plus there are so many twists and turns that create many endings. I loved this game and I will recommend it, but it's definitely a niche game.

Let me set the scene, your life is great, you get home in a great mood and you think ''nothing can mess up my day now''. Enter Rugby Challenge 3. SSDG(same S$%^ different game). They have simply reskined Rugby Challenge 2 and the game breaking issues are still there.
I will try to explain the issues in a constructive way as I have played through a couple of games and a few seasons as pro.
Pros:
1.Its a game about rugby
2. Looks nice
3. Its a game about rugby
Cons:
1. You cannot change the controls. Not a major issue at first until you play as a pro as the button for ''stealing'' the ball is the same as kick to touch. So everytime you get a great turnover your teammate proceeds to kick it straight into touch.
2. The game follows no logical rugby philosophy. The AI(on hardest difficulty) has this great move where they go down a 3 m blindside only to throw a 20m pass over the ruck to the outside centre. Players face one way and pass another way. AI decides to kick a up and under with one person to beat, its all just laughable(which I guess is a positive). Another one of my favourites is how the ball always goes over the fullback who then proceeds to try passing the ball in the in goal instead of kicking for touch.
3. Do not underestimate how stop-start this game is. Get ready for endless knock-ons and forward passes. Now I watch a lot of rugby and even at schooboy 6th team level there are not as many handling errors as this. I am not talkin about crap players with bad stats, these are supposed NZ all stars just randomly knocking on and passing forward in the funniest situations.
4. The rules do not apply here. So you kick over the defence and the fullback punts the ball back, everyone in front of him is offisides right? Not if the AI controls them. For some reason that boggles my mind offside in that situation only applies to the Player not the AI. This takes away any counter attacking running plays.
5. The scrums are a bit of a joke. Scrumming will become your life in this game. With the number of handling errors this will become your game, waiting for what seems like a hour of back and forth on a scrum. Want to speed up the game? Make a max of 2 contest on the scrum and done.
6. Injuries. Rugby is a sport of injuries. Luckily the devs care about the players so as soon as someone is injured the game is stopped and a scrum has to happen. No matter what the situation it has to happen.
I really wish I did not have to write this review as we need devs willing to try and make games about smaller sports like Rugby. I have purchased everyone from the original Lomu game which still remains the best and most fluid. Alas I guess we have to accept that we will never have an acceptable rugby game and the enjoyment received will be mostly due to the flaws and not due to the gameplay.

"The definitive game of The Lord of the Rings saga"
The story of "Middle-earth: Mordor's shadow" is the world not "Lord of the Rings," the writer J.R.R. Tolkien, but who appears neither in the film saga nor in books. That is, it is a parallel story but with new and old characters.

During the game, Gollum joins the "heroes" in the same way that he joined Frodo and Sam in the first movie in the movie trilogy. That is, he will instigate Celebrimbor to counteract Talion, going through more dangerous and obscure ways.
An intense, action-packed and killing story that will trap the player on a screen, even they are not big fans of the saga The Lord of the Rings.

First of all, this is not the usual twin-stick top-down shooter you might think it is!
The Red Solstice has (especially in multiplayer) way more depth than you can imagine from a first look at the store page.
The game lore pretty much feels like a threesome between Warhammer 40k, Starcraft and Starship troopers. A comfortable couch zone for the typical sci-fi nerd like me with no big suprises.
It has a solid singleplayer experience where you can get a grasp of the core game mechanics, the different classes, weapons, perks and the inventory managment.
Also only in the singleplayer part you can activate a tactical "bullet time" where you can control all of your 3 squad members in detail.
The game is intended to be pretty hard and unforgiving, so even on the lowest diffuculty you can expect a hard time even as a seasoned gamer.
Where it shines most in my opinion is the multiplayer part though.
The mainly played mission mode ties story wise in the singleplayer campaign with different outcomes and procedual generated objectives and different bossfights.
While playing you are under constant pressure from the enemy and you have to be on the move the whole time while looting and managing different important rescources like ammo, medkits and explosives for roughly 45 minutes if u dont die before that.
That experience (especially while playing with a good group of 8 ppl) is a BLAST.
There are also plenty of other modes to mix up your experience once a while like a defense mode or KotH.
I really recommend the game for people that are looking for a very tactical approach on a top-down shooter that recquires tons of teamplay with a very tough difficulty.
The only two downsides for me are:
It takes plenty of time to "learn the ropes" due to the lack of a good tutorial. You are pretty much required to ask other players for good class setups and fitting playstyles. It took my about a dozen times with some random teammates to see the victory screen the first time.
The second one is no fault of the game and the reason for me to write this review: The Red Solstice has a pretty low player base and you can be sitting in the lobby for 15 minutes untill you find a game. I hope the playerbase grows stronger over time.
The upside of that is a very nice and patient playerbase though.
Simply put: Great game. 10/10.

I consider myself a veteran of many "squad-based run-and-gun shooters" like this one. After all, The Red Solstice is based off of games like
and
which are some notable maps/mods for another game called Warcraft III: The Frozen Throne -- a title I've sunk more than 8 years of my time into.
With such a "veteran's perspective" on the genre, does The Red Solstice live up to the hype? In my opinion, yes, it actually does. The developers have succeeded in making an enjoyable game that stays faithful to the source material that inspired it, while doing plenty to make it stand out from the crowd. Let me just give you a short and sweet rundown on some of the core features that interested me:
-----
A light system. Whether it be due to the titular storm that is the game's namesake, or simply that your mission takes place at night, every playable map in the game is cast in darkness, broken by streetlights, burning flares left by your team, fires from ignited fuel barrels, and interior lights that you have to reactivate by finding their central power stations in different buildings. If you are shooting at a target in dim or no light, you are penalized with a substantial chance for your bullet to miss and be wasted. If firing on enemies in bright light, like the brilliant radiance of a Flare Gun item, you can expect near-100% accuracy
.
And sometimes? Sometimes, by random event or by a failed mission, the lights in your sector will go dark. That makes it a
inconvenient time to have to fight off a wave of mutants threatening to chew your face off, because the lights emitted by your suit only extend a few meters in a circle around you. If the light isn't enough to make out enemies approaching you, all you will see in the shadows is rapidly-moving shapes, accentuated by guttural roars from the beasts who can track you like a lantern in a coal mine. Without adequate light, your ammo efficiency, accuracy, and overall combat effectiveness will drop like a lead brick.
A leader/officer system. At the start of the game, you get to designate a maximum of 2 players (from an 8-player squad) to be Leaders. These players get access to special key commands that let them set waypoints and routes for the team, which show up as bright yellow lines on the minimap that are easily followed. Leaders are also the only ones who can access certain game-changing items and features, like the Safety Zone, which is a beacon that calls down fresh ammo and supplies, as well as a sustained orbital artillery barrage in a circle around the beacon while leaving the beacon itself
untouched. Thus, you won't have to worry about some trolling player activating a full-charge Safety Zone without the rest of their team, or running ahead and turning it on and getting the team killed by artillery.
Throwable explosive barrels. No, I am not kidding. Each player has the ability to right-click fuel or toxic material barrels, have their marine/character pick them up, and then hurl them about twenty meters wherever you left-click the mouse. This is AMAZING for area denial, as chucking a few barrels into a narrow corridor can wipe out hordes of zombies with the damage-over-time fire patches or toxin clouds they leave when they explode. Doing this does cost you 30 armor points (you start with ~100 but can get more), though, so you should make sure your shots count.
NOTE:  There is a flamethrower-using class in this game that gets an ability which lets him use fuel and toxin barrels to provide ammo for his weapon. Not only that, it juices his flamer to where it now leaves the same clouds the exploding barrels do. xD
Dismountable turrets. Sentry turrets exist around the map, which you can either spend time activating one-by-one or, if you're lucky, find a central terminal that'll turn them all on. Once active you can "disarm" them
, turning them into a dismounted turret that you can then place virtually anywhere on the ground you please. So not only do you get to save turrets in a bad spot from certain destruction, you also get to use them to build your own defensive positions! ^^
A nice, streamlined explosives system. A good percentage of the items you'll find throughout a given game will be satchel charges, incendiaries, claymore mines, plasma bombs, and directional primer charges. In case you don't know what the latter is, it's a "leap bomb" that scatters a shotgun-like cone-shaped blast of high explosives in whatever direction it's pointed, which is helpfully indicated by red lines so you don't blow your team up by accident. Very lethal to tight groups charging down a narrow hallway.
Anyway, the system. Many explosives in this game are external-source-only, which means you have to supply an initial explosion
to set them off. Some are radio-detonated, like satchel charges or the aforementioned directional primer charges, and need only a quick double-tap of the "G" key
to set off. You can disarm most explosives at will if you need to move them or just don't want them anymore, as long as you have the right tools or skills available
. Since you really need the firepower of high explosives to have any real hope of surviving the late-game waves of tough enemies
, it's really nice to have a system that demands so little micromanagement. You don't have to click the bomb or anything like you might in some other games.

me to the game even more. The Red Solstice has a pretty respectable soundtrack, too, with solid themes all the way from the main menu to the combat suit selection screen to the final, desperate run for the evacuation dropship while the area is crawling with monsters at the end of the mission.
All in all? Yes, I think The Red Solstice might just be a winner. If you like fast-paced, run-and-gun squad-based gameplay, or want to feel like you're Space Marines from Warhammer 40k fighting off a Tyranid infestation, this will find a welcome home on your shelf.

Train Fever in the mold of Railroad Tycoon and Transport Tycoon. The goal of the game is to build a vast and profitable transport network using road and railroad. The game allows you to transport both resources and passengers. It is a decent game in the genre.
What the game does right is the basic economy with town growth and resource supply and demand. It has neat animations to show how the different resources and people are transported when not transported on your network, making it so that not everyone is solely dependant on your transportation even if that helps. The town grows at a good speed throughout the game making your transportation efforts visible on the map.
The build tool is a bit quirky but does what it is supposed to do and you mostly get used to it after a while. The UI in general is a bit quirky with popup windows popping up anywhere on the screen.
The main drawback of the game is the limited amount of resources (just 5). It is also often hard to know what industries will yield a lot of resources and thus be profitable to transport and if you built a long railroad line just to transport the resources of an industry that happened to not be producing anything, then you wasted a lot of money. The economy could in general do with a lot more information and charts so that it is easy to understand what might be profitable.

Wat do you call a group of Zombies?
Hmm, a pack of Zombies? No no, that is not it. Hmm, a gander of Zombies? Nooo. How about a pride of Zombies? Hell no! Aaaah YES. It is called a HORDE, a Horde of Zombies!
And that is what you will be facing in State of Decay. Hordes and more Hordes of Zombies.
But you are not alone. There is lots and lots of melee weapons to help you deal with the problem and there is lots and lots of fire arms to help you deal with the pest. You also have your characters that level in this RPG game. You can go stealthy, high cardio and run faster and for longer than them Zombies or simply go guns blazing and melee weapons swinging. But you will also need your own group, you need to band together and form a group. Work with other groups around the town/state and help each other out or simply let them join your group and become a bigger group.
Your brothers and sisters in arms will help you with your daily life in the Zombie apocalyptic town.
The larger the group the more mouths you have to feed, the more meds your will need and of course the more weapons/ammo you will need for your established base/group. On the other side the larger the group, the better the man power and better the protection. Your home is where you manage the group’s lives. Build a small infirmary, or upgrade your lookout tower for better protection and area coverage. However pick wisely, space in your walls is limited and you put people’s lives in danger every time you and your group go out for resources. On another note what would a Zombie Apocalyptic game be without the army? The army is also present but it seems they have their own agenda and could care less for the survivors on the street.
But how does it all end? What happens to your band of brothers and sisters? I guess you will have to find out for yourself?
Pros:
-Fun Dialogue RPG Zombie Horde slaying game.
-Story line is fairly good. Entertaining.
-Weapons is fun and diverse, always fun to slay Zombies.
-Your group can repair your decaying vehicles and weapons.
-You don’t need to do the tedious runs over and over again, use your group to scavenge and deliver the goods you have discovered.
-You have your group members at your disposal to help with runs and missions.
-Setup more outposts for protection and ease of accessing the group stash.
-Open world to explore.
Con:
-Graphics slightly out dated, but did not bother me that much.
-Game was designed/created for Xbox 360/consoles and converted for PC.
-Game feels a little too easy (however still challenging enough to be fun)
-no Co-OP play.
Conclusion:
I feel this game is worthy of your precious time. It is worth mine. If you can pick this game up on the Steam sale for $4.99 then it is a no brainer (bargain). I would not feel cheated if I was to pay $19.99 for it ether, game is worth the cash. I noticed majority of the players finished this game (main story) between 16-18 hours. I usually play slower and discover every nook and cranny myself. This game would have scored beter if it had the co-op. I presonally would love to build a base and go slay some zombies with my friend. I bought the two DLC's on Steam sale too, but have not played them yet. My score is based on the main game only. I have played this game for 8hours already and is hooked. Very addictive game. Go ahead give this game a try. I recommend it and would give it a personal score of 8/10.

First Glance (~2h played)
Take the old classic Master of Magic, mix with Civ5-like terrain and UI, throw in a hint of HOMM and add decent if not great AI. What do you get?
- You get racial specific, balanced units which can be buffed or upgraded.
- Lots of fighting between Mage armies, minor cities, monsters. This is the main focus of the game.
- There's lots of units, and you dont depend on one race, only start with one.
- Only three races, but at least they're balanced and there's a boatload of indipendent units.
- Simple spell research in place of tech.
- Ability to unleash said spells to modify units, terrain or cities.
- Simple but honest Truce, Pact or War diplomacy.
- A world to explore and expand upon. Then another world when you find a portal link to it. And another one after that...
- Guarded loot as in MoM, monster spawners, rampaging monsters, and other map features to keep exploration interesting.
- Some spells are fire&forget, others are buffs that require upkeep.
- Simplified economy. Few resources to manage, all directly related to keeping your war machine on the march and growing.
- Slightly convulted way in which buildings unlock other types of buildings or even troops.
- Very little terrain feedback! (Archery bonuses, terrain defense, etc).
- Oceans that are worthless except as passages.
- Pumpkins as a resource on which Shrines of the Rotting Pumpkin can be built. ikr, awesome!
- Resources that grant bonuses or allow for units to be built in the city.
- AI that can fight. (turn up the difficulty)
- AI that ... will occasionally attack Ghosts (weapon immunity) with a common melle unit (uses weapons). Genius, but doesnt really work.
Also:
- Gods, ability to anger gods, and become destroyed by angry gods.
- Multiplayer, so you can throw fireballs at your friends like they were pies!
- A dose of humor, as the game doesn't take itself too seriously. Unit responses and even unit names can be humorous.
Between Master of Magic, Civ V and Heroes of Might and Magic, Warlock mostly resembles MoM, but with tactical combat replaced by Civ's system. Why did i not know of this game before? Granted that it's not one of the best ever made, but it's very good and can favorably be compared to Civ V (IF, and that's a big IF, you want the game simplified and focused on combat). As expected of a title with too long of a history, the game is really solid and basic for a 2D fighting game (with 3D graphics). Netplay was a disaster at first, but it's been long since those issues have been taken care of. It's not the near-perfect netplay you see with rollbacks, but it's still a pretty good delay-based implementation that gets all the jobs done. Biggest asset about USF4 is the community in terms of its activity and content. You'll rarely have problems finding matches online despite the split caused by 3 different platforms, there are tournaments streamed on twitch almost every week or two, and the amount of quality tutorials you can find on the web is probably overwhelming. These qualities are pretty hard to find in other games of this genre, so some people consider these to be enough to warrant getting into this game. Another good thing about the game is the character balance across the roster. It's fairly well-balanced, especially when there's 44 of them to choose from.
Enough with the positives... on to why this game can be terrible. The SF4 engine severely differs from previous big iterations of the title (Third Strike, Super Turbo, etc.), and to other non-Street Fighter titles (Capcom or not Capcom). Compared to the history of the main Street Fighter titles, or possibly even all traditional 2D fighters in general, this game has one of the worst entry-point for beginners. The engine does not accomodate combos, forcing players to learn 1 and 2 frame links almost right off the bat. The game is also terrible because it encourages mashing like no other games do, primarily due to the prevalence of tight link combos, extremely fast system mechanics (3 frame throws, 4 frame landing delays, etc. etc.), and extreme input leniencies (323 DP). This gave birth to the situation where a good chunk of the competition (or "meta") depends on option selects. Also, the roster is way too big. 44 characters essentially mean learning 43 matchups, and unfortunately, USF4 is indeed a heavily-matchup-based fighter. Finally, the majority of people can probably agree that the game doesn't have too many characters that have visual appeal unlike other fighting games these days... but that's just what the franchise is about. On the other hand, there are many high-quality graphical mods though, which is apparently a big plus to certain players.
I'm not saying that this game is a shity fighting game. I just have to point to the pros still playing this game to prove that the depth is there. It's just the entry point that's so grimy and disgusting, despite literally 90% of the related FGC telling newbies to start with SF4. Coincidentally, all those people exclusively play SF4 or started with SF4 too. Before you go on to buy skullgirls, no, that game isn't ideal for entries either- though it'd be infinitely better than this thing.
Shoutouts to Chum for being an online chum as usual.

This is hands down one of the most overrated games I've ever played. It is a shameless clone of Arkham City. Gameplay consists of freeflow combat and 'stealth' sections, like AC. Combat is fine, it's not as polished as AC but it's ok. My problem is they literally copy+paste'd the entire combat system. You even press the same button combinations to execute same special attacks. Also the 'stealth' in this game is a joke. I'm not someone who complains about a game being easy but I will about this game. You can literally sneak+run towards enemies while they are facing you and stealth kill them. I will admit it is very empowering and the kill animations are very nice but it gets very boring very fast. Also the camera in this game is a little weird. I don't understand why they chose to put it at same level as your character, instead of a little higher. This is specially annoying when you are running. Speaking of running, this game has a 'parkour' system similar to Assassin's Creed. Would you be surprised if I told you it's nowhere near as polished? Most baffling part is that you can't climb obstacles if you approach them from certain angles, you just stop and lose all your momentum as well as your motivation to play the game.

Collectibles are ok though because they give you a little bit of lore.

The Red Solstice is a game of three modes, and while the core mechanics are the same, placing the title square in the real-time tactics genre with shooter elements, the way the player approaches each of the three is pretty different.
Gamers take on the role of one of the marines who are sent to investigate the events surrounding the massive storm and the damage it has caused, and they will have to carefully use their weapons, movement, placement, special abilities, and other items found in the level to stay alive either to reach their goals or to get extracted.
The single player created by developer Ironward is made up of ten missions and asks gamers to carefully control main character Tyler Hunt but also his squad mates, moving around the locations and achieving objectives.
The Red Solstice offers a different challenge for each new level, and because the squad companions evolve from one to the next, it's important to develop them carefully and make sure that the entire group is prepared for the task ahead.

If you're looking for a hard, carbon copy original of Duke 3D this is not QUITE it, but very close.
Pros:
- Main game environment is still basically the same -- if not more polished -- as long as you turn off the extra 3D rendering/occlusion and use the "classic" HUD. Everything else was left exactly as it was.
- You can change the control settings if you're like me and once again want to play it how you did in the 90's, since some of the controls have adapted to a new genre of gaming.
- Not that I care for them much, but more levels to explore.
- All cheat codes from the classic have been preserved. So yes, mess around as much as your little heart desires!
Neutral:
- Music has been updated slightly. This won't bother some but I truly loved the grungy, bit-ty music from the original (although I guess it depended on your sound system.) Instead of the creepy, suspenseful music it's now become a little more upbeat.
- Not really a huge issue, but the text that appears in the game (like what you've discovered, etc) is different, I just don't feel like it meshes well with the environment/my old memories.
Con:
- There is an option to load custom maps. But no map maker included... so...
- No spinoffs included.
TLDR: Besides some nitpickery, there are no "real" problems in this release, and would still recommend for anyone that wants to indulge in their nostalgia.

Duke Nukem is back with new promising things. However, while the port is intesting, it's no match to the defunct Megaton Edition, which was wayyyyyy more.... eeer.... complete in terms of adventures you can play.
Duke Nukem 3D was released 20 years ago and was in the pure line of FPS back then. Duke Nukem was also a colorful character, interested in booze and babes, if you allow me to use the term often used in the game. Well, let's just say that some alien civilisation is invading Earth and kidnapping women to use them for breeding. Yeah, just that.
Duke Nukem 3D: 20th Anniversary World Tour has the four original episodes (L.A. Meltdown, Lunar Apocalypse, Shrapnel City and The Birth) and includes a new one: Alien World Order. And this is where the disappointment begins, because the Megaton Edition included other campaigns: one in a tropical paradise island that I really loved and another one in Washington DC, with many known landmarks. Unless the future of the game includes these episodes, I would say that the 20th Anniversary World Tour is already inferior to the Megaton Edition in terms of content.
You're going to say that a new weapon has been included in the last episode and I will counter back to you that while a flamethrower is nice, I didn't expect to have a new enemy that can do the same for you and that I never expected to have a sort of lava when missing my target and hurting because I've stepped in it.
As for the rest, it's still nice to have a mighty foot, to use a simple pistol, a shotgun, a minigun, a rocket launcher, pipebombs, a minimizer/maximizer, a ice gun (which can hurt you too), mine lasers (that I don't use at all), the Devastator. They can be used underwater, which is nice.
And apart the traditional armor, you can also count on
Enemies are still the same: you still have simple troopers, the pig cops, the minigun lizard that is quick to die with shotgun but not with the minigun, the octobrain, sharks (yeah, simple sharks), turrets and many others. The bosses are still hard to defeat (and guess what, the new one is using fire - new weapon, new enemies, everything has to do with fire).
But you know what's caught me a few times? The way to change my weapons. I don't know why it was so hard to do it but I ended up with the wrong one (or I can't press the right button or it's just that the little inventory with them felt slow to jump from a weapon to another).
I didn't really pay to the graphics: for me, they're the same. They didn't really change a bit from Megaton Edition. But well, I'm still in awe in front of the levels: the death row, the space station, the city and with the new episode, I really liked the fact that we were visiting some cities, like London, Paris and Moscow. And it's still a pleasure to discover restaurants, Duke Burgers or even a supermarket. Oh wait, there is also a kind of weird level where the hookah made you really high on drugs (or not). Really, it's still a pleasure to play these levels.
The soundtrack is nice but.... why put the default sound volumn so low that we can't really enjoy it? Is this for Duke to say his famous lines to which I didn't pay attention?
Another thing is the achievement. They're classic but I wish some of them were included. We have easter eggs about Luke Skywalker, Serious Sam (new episode) and the DoomGuy that are worthy of an achievement but Indiana Jones or even the Star Trek bridge aren't? And what about the Kurt Russell one? And why not to have an achievement about finishing some levels with all secrets discovered? And while it's nice to see an achievement about enemies being scrunched or incinerated, why not one about being iced and destroyed by the mighty foot? Or being blown up because of the maximizer? It would have been great to have more achievements.
I didn't try the multiplayer and I don't intend to do so.
If I have to resume my experience with Duke Nukem 3D: 20th Anniversay World Tour? I prefer Megaton Edition. More content. For those who own it, the 20th Anniversary World Tour is only worthy of being in your library for the new episode, only when you have a discount. At 20 bucks, i don't feel like enough has been done - putting developers commentaries, a new episode, a new enemy, a new boss and a new weapon isn't really enough as I didn't see a difference in graphics or in soundtrack. I've still enjoyed the game, though I must say that my first experience with Duke was with Megaton Edition, so, there is no nostalgia trip for me.

Quite fun actually. Orcs Must Die! 2 did not have a "wow-factor" for me in terms of the gameplay. I have played too much Dungeon Defenders to be new to third-person tower defense. What this game does shine in is the variety of traps, I enjoy having different load outs depending on the map and my play style. The pathing of waves are designed to be optimized for certain traps (ceiling, floor or walls). The game also supplies players with a good collection of weapons used on Orcs to company the automatic traps. In the game, there are only two classes to choose from; War Mage and Sorceress. The War Mage is a male character whose quotes are quite lighthearted but unintelligent. He has two "uniques" a trusty Blunderbuss, a shot-gun that also doubles as a grenade launcher, and Tar Trap that slows down enemies. The Sorceress, on the other hand, has a very different style. She is more of a passive character than the War Mage. Her unique trap, Acid Sprayer is able to apply short-term effects on enemies and her Sceptre of Domination can temporarily mind control. Even with the lack of characters, Orcs Must Die! 2 is still very enjoyable to play and, if single player is getting repetitive, online co-op is always available.

Longevity often leads to indifference and makes us take things for granted. Some video game development studios have staying power long after their purple patch has faded, reclining on laurels and trading mostly in goty, not so Obsidian. They have always remained brilliantly restless, plucking gems from the ether, mid wrestle with the muse. With the release of "Pillars of Eternity", their seventh (full) game, it's hard to believe that it's over fourteen years since they charged on to the gaming world like the feral children of Black Isle and Interplay. If isometric style is the base camp, they've wandered far off track by way of role-playning. Searching for new tales to retell our oldest stories. Mythologies must always be renewed and retold. They crave to be re imagined, they are stories that are forever becoming. Obsidian at their best, when charged with what in Portuguese folklore is called "Duende", are primal storytellers. They bring us forward and back again like Gatsby's "boats against the current" to a place we thought we'd nearly forgotten. When we arrive there, washed up up on its shore, it is both familiar and oddly, thrilling new. They blow fresh story plots on ancient cinders and make them blaze. In a remastered and ironic age, Obsidian and Pillars matter because they dare to do the one thing that is so unhip and under threat today, and that is to be Real. They fire, volleys of hope, new-ancient strings in their bows.
How do I even sum up the awesomeness that is this game? :) You know, I expected to like it, but I totally adored it. ;)

Train Fever is a sandbox transport company management game with as many good ideas as flaws, making the experience rather jarring and not entirely recommendable, and certainly not at full price.
The main flaws concern the mechanics and the ergonomics of the game. While people often say that such and such game don’t hold your hand, I never felt it truer than in Train Fever. Although prepared, even before purchase, I still had to look up quite a lot of information elsewhere, but this is fun to me, understanding the inner workings and mechanics at play. Sadly, even now it seems to me that some mechanics are still not understood, or at least not fully, making it rather difficult to reach an optimal play style.
But the flaws become even more apparent on a higher difficulty level. While the game is perhaps too easy on lower settings, on hard mode the lower profit margins and the limitations of the construction tool require a near perfect play style. It is just plain unfair: cargo is profitable, but not passenger transport. You would think that a vehicle full of people would make a profit, no matter what, and I’m not talking just about trains here, where you could argue that you need more wagons to transport more people and thus improve the profit margins (which doesn’t work by the way: there is a limit to how much a locomotive can pull, and that’s even disregarding the artificial transportation time limit of twenty minutes the game forces upon you). It might have something to do with the travel distance, which gives a bonus to the income of each line, but since it is rather difficult to measure distances (only travel time), it’s hard to judge what line will or will not turn up a profit without testing first, which is not an option with the limited resources of a higher difficulty level. And even then, it doesn’t explain why cargo is always profitable, regardless of travel time or distance.
Still, you need both cargo and passenger to improve your cities (and even about that I’m not sure since nothing is explained and there doesn’t seem to be a consensus on the forums about it. Some say its cargo, other passengers, others still argue it is both. I’ve heard it say that’s it’s actually the line usage percentage that is used in city growth but from my experience that wasn’t the case, with cities with lower index actually growing while interconnected ones didn’t budge at all, even over longer periods of time). It would thus seem that people and goods are a must to make a profit later on: as you progress in the game, the running costs of vehicles rise, which means that more passengers or goods are required to make a profit. It is thus my belief that you can screw yourself completely over in this game if you take too slow a start, and don’t develop the cities rapidly.
It feels completely unbalanced, with the effect of the player feeling rather limited or the sensation that it comes down to luck. It’s hard to get involved when your impact on the game world feels so loose sometimes.
What actually makes the whole ordeal truly worse is the interface. Replacing vehicle is horribly unintuitive and slow, with the game opening dozens of tabs at a time, grinding the game (already in need of performance optimisation) to a halt, regardless of the characteristics of your computer.
The construction tool isn’t much better. The way double lanes work isn’t intuitive at all, but it is manageable. Problems arise when trying to get double tracks crossed by other double tracks and so forth, although the difficulty might come from the fidgetiness of the construction tools. It’s not completely broken, and that’s what makes it so aggravating to me. If it was completely broken, I would just stop playing, but since there is always a way to do what I wanted, with a lot of work and patience, I tried.
On a final side note, it should be said that the music is fantastic, I did truly enjoy it. Weirdly enough, it somehow felt like it made perfect sense in this game.
Still, the value of the game is to hold ones attention for long hours without pause. There is always something to do, always something to improve, to update, new routes to plan, etc. That, to me, is fun, and truly addicting. It’s one of those management games where time just flies by, something that I haven’t experience since my time with the Anno series. It’s just a shame it had to come with so many faults. I grew tired of having to put up with them and just stopped playing after that, feeling disappointed.

Not as good as I expected. I've played several versions of Railroad Tycoon, along with SimCity and other transportation and urban simulations, and while this one is pretty and has some enticing features, the overall game play is frustrating.
Some positives: It is nice being able to manage transportation within cities and between them. The ability to use buses and trams and not just trains is fun. Detailed reports of how each line and vehicle is doing are nice. The visuals are good.
Some negatives: Overall game play is just plain frustrating. In a game like this, the main experience is in setting up routes and connecting things. This game basically ruins this experience.
It's not so bad when setting up bus lines, since you are using existing roads, but it totally fails when you start laying railroads. It is almost impossible to get a railroad to cross a road. This appears to be related to grade differences, because typically the tracks are running in a cut or embankment that is above or below the road grade. Why can't the AI just automatically regrade the road so that the two can cross, and add to the railroad cost accordingly. The last thing I want to do is have to fiddle with individually grading road crossings, especially since it is expensive and time consuming and may fail, since even after I'm done, I won't be able to know if the tracks can go there anyway.
Industries are a major pain. You are supposed to build a depot next to the industry, and it may or may not begin to fill with some of the goods that otherwise magically travel down the road by other means. After building expensive depots at two industries that should feed into each other and the tracks to connect them, it typcially happens that you watch the goods totally ignore your nice transportation system and continue marching down the road without your assistance. Maybe there is a reason for this--some parameter that needs to be set, some limit on the placement of the depot. But if there is, it is a complete mystery, since there is no documentation that would help you figure it out.
Speaking of documentation, this game really lacks it. There is a very basic tutorial at the start, but nothing for the more advanced things you typically would like to try.
The game largely feels unfinished and untested, and not worth the rather high price that would be more appropriate for a game that totally works.
I love transportation sims, and I laid down a fairly large chunk of cash to buy this. But I'm not playing it. Life is frustrating enough without having a game make it worse.

I was hoping this game was going to satisfy my desire to replace Simcity 2013 and Railroad Tycoon II...yes, I said RRT2.  The graphics are mediocre, at best.  Sure, you can zoom in and see people walking around, but you can't do anything productive with a view like that.
The train's AI is completely below standard.  For instance: Picking up oil with one train and dropping it off at a refinery makes "goods" which is the generic demand for towns.  If you use a different locomotive to pick up goods to drop off at a town, then they jam up at the refinery and sit there waiting for eachother to get out of the way.  Signals are useless as they only allow trains to travel in one direction, not wait for a train to move out of the way.
Wood is the only way to make a decent amount of cash and that's only because "wood" and "goods" can utilize the same cars.  There isn't a way to change the consist of any other trains so you need 3 oil cars and 3 goods cars on the same locomotive and 1/2 the train is empty during it's route.
In short, the mechanics are garbage compared to an OLD game like RRT2 or even Railroads! which was fun, but wasn't as indepth as RRT2.
As far as the "business" part of the game, it's not even close to Simcity 2013.  The "town" doesn't develop if you pump "goods" to it.  A few buildings pop up, but then they stop after a short while.  I'm assuming it's because the goods aren't getting to the "low value" areas of the town but none of my "cargo" (non-rail) stations are productive as far as money goes.  Yes, they work, but they don't make money because the distance is too far.  In order to rectify this, you can lay rails, but then you're back to square-one with the "not using the same train to transport goods of different types" nonsense.
I don't care about graphics when it comes to business simulations (to a point).  I want complexity yet it needs to be intuitive.  This game has neither.  If you can't change consists at a station, then it's impossible to use the same locomotive transport different types of commodities.  If you must have multiple trains on a single rail, then the programmers need to figure out how to make one train wait for another BEFORE they're 2 feet away from eachother.
In real life, companies have yards and spurs....not enough room in this game to do this so "reality" is NOT an excuse for this.
This is the first game that I would like a refund for.

Date of writing this review: 20/10/14. Some of my criticisms may have been addressed by the time you are reading this.
Firstly, I would like to state that I got this game 2 days ago, and I
have 16 hours. In my opinion, the game is the best tycoon game since Transport Tycoon Deluxe.
However, there are a few negatives that I would like to address, and because of these few negatives, people are not enjoying the game, or buying it.
- Dumb Name. Why didn't they call it Transport Fever!?! Would have made much more sense as the game is not only about building train lines.
- Minimal Tutorial. Despite this game being a very complex game, the tutorial is almost laughable.  However, there are several community made tutorials to which aided me in learning the game, my favourite one being
- Rail Building could do some work. In order to build railway, you must do it in several chunks. This is as the game tries to average out the terrain, so that the rail will not go on a gradient - which can cost an absurd amount of money if the rail goes for too long.
- No Airports, or Boats. The airports I can somewhat understand, however the boats I do not. Each map has a river along it. It is crazy to think that despite this, they didn't put in a chance to add boat lines! I do hope that they add these features into a future update, or even a DLC.
- Only 4 Resources. I understand that with this, they were trying to go for the simplistic approach so that the learning curve isn't to big, however at least give me a chance in a settings menu to have more. The game does have excellent modding support though, and so I am sure that people will make mods in order to address this issue.
Once you look over these issues, it can be seen that the game is amazing. All up I am going to give this game an 8/10, and would still reccomend you to buy it, despite these issues. Also, if they do fix up these key issues, it could easily be a 10/10. Enjoy the game, and should you have any further questions regarding the game, feel free to add me and ask me some questions!

I bought this game for trains. Unfortunately, there is a lot more to it than that. I have (currently) spent fifteen hours micro-managing trams, busses and eventually trains. Just when I am getting to have some fun with the trains, all of the busses in one of the towns become end of life and need replacing. There goes an hour sorting that out, back to the trains. Half an hour later, you guessed it, replace more busses. At the moment I am concentrating on moving people around and haven’t even looked at the raw materials and goods aspect of the game. I just want to play with trains and have to mess about with the other stuff to get the required money.
Setting up the busses and trams is fairly straightforward, or so I thought. Apparently there is a twenty minute rule, if a journey takes longer than twenty minutes then the route will not be used, the passenger disappears or the goods never move. This compounds the micro-management by increasing the number of routes required in order to keep them short enough to not fall foul of the rule.
Building a train line can be a bit of hard work, especially for your hard drive. The golden rule is if the land you are looking to build on deviates from flat by a jot, SAVE. There is little to assist in surveying and planning a route, mistakes are costly as there is no undo button. You either revert to a previous save or pay to demolish your mistake. Save files for the “large” game are over 70MB.  Placing track is far from intuitive.
Things I would like to see; instead of telling me something is too old and needs replacing give me the option to replace it there and then, three digit vehicle numbers with leading zeros, better surveying tools, warnings when a route is too long, AN UNDO BUTTON.
Am I having fun? Just about. Do I recommend this game? Just about. If you like Transport Tycoon type games I think you will enjoy this. If you just want to play trains maybe suffering the learning curve of the Trainz Surveyor maybe more suited.

Sooo... This game is a simplistic, fantasy themed Civ V.
Nah really that's it. There's not much happening here. There are three resources to manage, three different races to play, you can kind of choose different 'civ leaders' to play but you can edit them easily because they're literally a few buffs for resource gathering and a few staring spells, you have a bunch of units whose stats are pretty straight forward and you can improve them but they don't really 'advance' other than leveling up and building improvements, your civ researches are replaced with researching new spells, there are neutral 'city-states' that you can fight and take over because there's no diplomatic options with them, there are monsters you can murder, and there are multiple worlds that function somewhat similar to the one you start on but tend to have more and higher level monsters.
That's everything. That's all the game's features, right there. I might have missed one or two things but there's just not much to 'get' from this game. There isn't even a campaign, it's just skirmish or multiplayer. Having played other turn based strategy games, this one seems like it would be good for someone who's never played one before.
That said, it's not bad. Everything in it is functional. You do have to have graphical options above a certain point or a lot of the game's UI features don't work, at least for me, but really it's not terribly intensive even on the higher settings.
If you like turn based strategy and fantasy, this is okay. It does a lot of macro-level controls very well. If you want very precise control, or even a lot of things to manage in your turn based strategy game or, I dunno, a lot of options for things you'll probably want to find something else.

This game is amazing.
First off if you were lucky you got this game for free, if not it goes on sale for less than $5 everytime.
The first thing you will realize is that it is a civalizations type game.
It starts you off as one of 12 (might be more) different wizard lords bound to their own cause, but free to become your own.
Instead of having pesky villagers you have to worry about dying, you have city extensions that produce resources and other bonus wonders.
You should play this like you play Sid Myers Civ 5, and you will be fine, but in case you need it there is an in depth tutorial that doesn't bother you or drag on forever.
Instead of advancing to the next stage in technology like most strategy games this keeps it cool and stays in the same era of weapondry, which is one thing that bugged me when playing the Civ Games. There is nothing more lorebreaking like seeing the Myans with robots nuking and anchient Chinese Empresses.
The game has a large variety of units and has a large focus on casting badass spells if you have the mana.
The enemy wizard lords AI lacks a large variety of negotiations, but at least you wont have Ghandi yelling at you for being a Warmongrel.
FInally, and at long last, I would say this is a very fun alternative to Civ 5 and is significantly better for the low price.

Not usually one to write reviews for games but this game ABSOLUTELY deserves a review. This is one of those games I stray from, then go back to. It's basically the only game I play anymore aside from a select few here and there. The main game itself is fun, good progression, good weapons, fun missions, great concepts and biomes, star/space travel etc. BUT when you start getting into the mods such as frackin universe, XS Mechs, Statistics, and countless others... when you really start tuning the game to your preferences of intensity and depth it is by far the best game of this format I have ever played ever. So much complexity can be added, or it can be kept simple. I reccomend this to every friend I know who has a computer as the requirements to play is are actually fairly low, it's cheap, and it's simple to pick up and start playing. VERY VERY FUN when you have a group or even just one other friend to play with but really the more the merrier in this case. The development team is incredibly active and updates are rolled out fairly often bringing whole game shifts into effect. I have yet to see a single negative update in my opinion. The mod community is incredibly active as well and creating the mods themselves are pretty simple of what I've heard. Some people say this game is shallow or repetitive but I disagree entirely. Odds are they played the base game un-modded and never strayed from it in which case the replayability definitely would be lower. My reccomendation is to play the base game, familiarize yourself with it, then when you get bored or if you just feel ready install frackin universe and other mods you feel fit. Enjoy!

CONTAINS MINOR SPOILERS BELOW:
Long live the queen is a pretty fun little visual novel game set in a typical fantasy world with an Anime artstyle. You play the role of a 14yo girl tasked with becoming queen by her father after her mother has died. The basic format of the game is that you train skills during the weekdays that allow you to make and know better decisions when they're required while also managing the main characters emotions during the weekend.
Saying that, if you're not intrested in political games(games where a main point is forming alliances, making unenviable decisions that will cause at least one or more parties to hate you, and dealing uprisings and betrayals) this game is not for you. There's no action, there's no shooting, there's just the text, art, and the consequences of your actions.
One of the faults in this game I could find was that some of the skills that you can train seemed worthless and a waste of your time, or a choice game up that required a check in them once that was important to the story and never game up again(time and choosing the right skills to train is paramount in this game). For example, I wanted to become a warrior princess in one playthrough and lead with blood and strengh. I trained mostly in swords, military strategy, spying, and intrigue.  In the middle of the game, you find out you're a wizard and magic is 100x times better than any kind of swordplay. During a tournment, a master fencer jumps on stage and challenges you to a duel. You must have an extremly high skill rank in the sword level to be able to defeat him, but with just a moderate level in your magic skill, you can cause him to spontaneously combust, ending the duel right then and there.
The game is fun, and has a charm with it's artstyle and sense of humor. If you have an intrest in fantasy, decision making, political intrigue then I would suggest picking this game up. Just make sure to train your intrigue skill to atleast 70 once so your character knows not to eat chocolates sent with no return adress by a nation that doesn't exist.

Since there are plenty reviews explain game's mechanic, I'll try to keep this short. Overall, TRS is a solid top down tactical survial shooting game.
Due to the "tactical" element and a steep learning curve, the best gaming experience you get from this game is the fruition of the ability to cooperate, adapt, follow and understand the "order" of the team leader (experienced vet).
TRS is quiet unforgiving for rookies, so the willingness to learn and stick with the game is a necessity. In order to prevent the unfair random-kicking in multiplayer mode and the risk of losing game due to the lack of knowledge on game's mechanic, I wholeheartedly recommend everyone (intent to play---casually playing----intent to be a pro):
-Try the single player mode (for the tutorial mainly). It has a pretty good storyline.
-Read those "Everything" guides by Bonzai101, Valore and Grizzly. (You're gonna be surprised by the amount of knowledge you may learn/miss out). Check out those in-depths about classes and game mechanics (leadership).
-Get TeamSpeak (an app similar to RaidCall). "Why", you asked? Well, the best way to learn a game is by playing it. And it's good to have somebody with experience to explain/help through the preparation and ingame if you decide to skip reading the guides. Mic is not required, vet only need you to listen and understand.
The code to the TRS community server is:
+ Inevitably, there are good and bad players. Some will assist you, some just downright ignore or troll you to oblivion; but the majority of the player base will help you with welcome arms.
-One last thing, invite your friend or introduce it to somebody closed to you. The biggest problem with TRS right now is lack of player. The community is too small at the moment.

Okay I'm going to say I enjoy the game and it deserves a positive rating, for the following:
- It is THE best Rugby game out today
- It is an improvement over RC2 in various subtle ways that were needed
- It is the ONLY online rugby game for PC you can buy,
- The fanhub and the wonderful PC modding community mean that the licencing issues will not be a problem for too long.
There is one negative which is that the launch pricetag for what is essentially an update of RC2 (albeit with some very welcome features and modes and fixes) is unacceptable. Please TruBlu see some sense and discount the game so that the community can recommend new players and the game/online community can thrive.
Do I like the game? Yes definitely.
Can I recommend it at £40 - a pricetag which no other premium Steam titles hold? If you are desperate for a good rugby game/online play, then yes. If you liked RC1 but didn't manage to get RC2 then probably. But players already owning RC2 will feel ripped off at full price if they don't have the money to throw around.
Update - I have yet to have an unplayable online game (I've played against 5 opponents - including UK, Aus and S.America - I am in the UK). All games have been quite smooth. This was not the case with RC1 and RC2 at launch - maybe it is to do with better internet connections in general, or perhaps they have improved the code a little in that area as well. Either way - this is a massive plus point for me. Come and join us online.  :)
I haven't yet spent any real time with the offline gameplay modes, so the above is based on core gameplay and online play only at present.

I'm a self-described rugby fanatic and I've been pining for a good rugby game on PC for a long time.  In the midst of extremely poor sound quality, average modeling and animations, shoddy roster management and sub-par commentary, there is a reasonably well put together game here and I'm sure I'll get my money's worth; the real question is whether there is enough to justify the price for the average punter.  At $USD50.00 I'm sad to say that I could see most people walking away.
Before buying, I'd done my research by reading the reviews and watching gameplay on YouTube so I knew what I was in for.  What's most disappointing is that this is really just Rugby Challenge 2.5.  It has some improvements over its predecessor but no where near enough to justify the price.  The new Rugby Sevens mode is interesting but not my cup of tea.  I'd have much rather seen a more in-depth management mode and players statistics that improve over time.  Team licencing is still an issue but the Fan Hub feature is supposed to deal with that so I'll give the game the benefit of the doubt and wait to see if that makes the experience feel more authentic over time.
Overall, I'll have to side with "recommending" this game but only because I feel there is no worthy alternative for someone wanting to play a modern rugby game on PC.  The production quality is disappointingly low and way behind other sports franchises so unless you are a rugby tragic like me, and desperate to play on PC, Rugby Challenge 3 is your best bet.  That said, if it's an option for you, I expect buying the console version would be a much more affordable solution in the long-run.

I played Transport Tycoon back when i was a kid, loading the game in DOS. I love this genre. I wasn’t bothered with Railroad Tycoon, I could never enjoy it as much. It was less about building an efficient infrastructure that you could tweak and improve to much about finances and a false sense of achievement. This game is certainly in the Transport Tycoon league.
The game is in no way flawed, early access or broken as many like to point to. The game is as finished as when Transport Tycoon under Micro Prose was released. Only today too many people online, many of them new (lvl1) due to more people gaining access to the internet / switching from console to PC expect all games to be as refined and polished as the big boys do when they release (a clone) a game. If this is not so, like then Train Fever people will do nothing but slate it, rather than use (play) it!
Review!
The game offers a good sense of achievement, to have your first passenger line develop into a mixed traffic line with signals keeping trains flowing well is extremely satisfying. You then find yourself extending the line, linking more towns and industry. Increasing profit. Working your factories at maximum production. Just the constant feeling of wanting to start a new project on your map, to develop your game.
Once you get your system working efficiently for that time period you will then start to earn good money. Money to ♥♥♥♥ about with, to build that mountain pass to reach that pointless town. Or flat, straight stretch to hit 300kmph despite it not making any economic sense.
The maps are better than I had expected. Big (if you wish) randomly generated maps, each with realistic placing of major towns as in not in a stupid place. It offers a good level of detail as you can see. Most importantly a long route is a long route, and worthwhile.
The game is actively being updated with real worthwhile updates and so far good communication from the tiny development team. The game doesn’t revolve around Steam, Steam is just the distribution. They and a good community revolve around the Train Fever forums. Very active, very interested in the game and very interested in our discussions.
Its not expensive, its worth the money.
I look forward to the future updates with more features being added. Waypoints being my number one.
So!
If you love Transport Tycoon and would happily play it for weeks, buy this game! Buy it and enjoy it.
If you didn’t mind/wasn’t bothered about Transport Tycoon, and could consider buying this then buy it. But do not blame the game, blame yourself for buying a game you don’t need/want.
