Glad I got this game on sale or I would be upset. I picked up this game for my girlfriend and myself. We like grindy survival games with pvp and pve like rust, ark, and 7d2d. We enjoy looting and building up our base. We got this game with those intentions.
We load in and first thing we do is go to key bindings to figure the game out only to realize there is no button for coords or a map. This is a big deal to us as we would like to play together and now have no way to find each other. We look up how to find each other. We pull up a google map on our 2nd monitors and sett off on the roads to find each other. The only way to do so is to follow road signs posted with city names and arrows. After getting a grasp of the map and general area we find each other after two hours of play. We are both have little loot so we decided to get out of the town and make a small base somewhere to loot. Unfortunatly we died leaving the town as the towns are common pvp grounds. This was upsetting but not enough to delete the game. We look up more information and find out that you cannot set spawn points and that theres is a map but you have to find it. No private servers uiinless you pay $30 a month. Ding ding ding we can no longer play this game.
With the map being a loot item that you will drop on death it is not very useful. Not to mention loot is hard to find outside of cities and you have very limited inventory slots so good look fining one and not loosing it. I understand the intent of the features.
No maps/coords so you can't mark stuff and just go back to where you died or to your base or to your friends. No spawns so you can just go regear and kill what/who killed you. This also improves the abilites to raid since once you kill them you are pretty much good to take your time.
While those features might be nice to some people they are not nice for someone who wants to just casually play with his girlfriend. We don't mind getting killed or raided but we would rather focus on building up and looting rather than trying to find each other all day. We literally loaded in and spent two hours trying to find each other. This game is a game I wouls play by myself so I didn't have to worry about that.
This game offers so much and I would like to see more. Maybe set up 1/10 of your servers to spawn you with a map with coords so players that want to go into as game and find friends can. Maybe set up some pve servers with stronger/more difficult zombies so people that will only play a few hours a week can build nice bases and loot and enjoy the game. Give an option to play local servers like ark and 7d2d do.
With that being said I am glad we got to pick it up on sale for half price. This could shape out to be a very good game but they need to add a little more for me to play more. That being said I am not returning this product because I want to wait it out and see what they do with it. I DO NOT recommend paying full price for this game if you intend on playing with your friends. Half price for half a game sounds like a good deal to me. I will now look deeper into games before buyinmg instead of taking them at face value.

Everyone seems to love Warlock. I'm not sure why. Once you know the ins and outs of the game, there's nothing to it and it becomes very boring and uninteresting. Occasionally the AI opponents will declare war on you for no reason. Occasionally monsters will randomly spawn in your territory for no reason. Often times there's zero threat and even on the harder difficulties, these messes can be cleaned up easily. Its less fun and more annoying than anything else.
Warlock is in desperate need of more variety. For game that comes across as a fantasy version of Civilization, it instead chooses to ape Warcraft 3 making for a weird turn based version of it. Ripping off Civ would have worked more in its favor.
Then there are other things in-game that need clean up. The spell book for instance is disorganized listing the spells in order you learned them vs alphabetically or by spell type. In fact, some of the spell descriptions need to be revised for the simple fact none of them tell you who or what it targets. Then there are also redundant spells that are slightly more powerful versions of what you already have. Would've been great if they kept it to a single spell but added a new power level to it in order to decrease disorganized clutter, but whatever.
I bought this game on sale with all its DLC for $6 and pocket change, and I don't feel it was worth it. Not recommended at all.

This game is great. It seems like this game is more "accessible" than Civilization. A hexagonal, turn-based Strategy game where you build towns and conquer them, as well as expand them or raise an army.
Set in a fantasy world where you, a mage, can cast spells, command troops, and build, as well as, expand your citires. The spells you can cast can be to rain fire upon foes, heal a unit, aid your city, or change the landscape. Troops you command range from hand-to-hand troops, ships, archers, wolves, etc.
The reasorces you need are Coin/money, food, mana, and knowledge. Also, to build a structure, a city must have the needed population for it. You can build unites even though some cities may not have enough food, but still important to have food, as well as coin, to upkeep a unit. IMana is needed to upkeep some buildings, and to cast spells. There is a list of spells that can be researched and a list of buildings that can be built.
You can use several mages, some are human, some are monsters/beast, and finally demons. It is mostly for the type of spells or bonuses you get for using a specific mage. One mage, for instance, aids more with healing units.
You can conquer ciities from other mages, or other cities scattered about. There are random enemies that hold no alliegience to any mage and they are a cool, and sometimes annoying, groupd of enemies.
You can make peace or forge an alliance, and brake the allience or end peace time. There are main worlds within a game single playthrough, and there are side worlds which you can conquer or avoid.
I highly recommend this to the people looking for a Civilization-style game, and to those looking to try something new. Play the Demo and see for yourself.

Starbound is, above all else, a relaxing game. They way you're supposed to play it is with your own music playing in the background, and maybe a beverage or some cheesecake sitting within arms reach.

You'll probably find yourself entertained by the many unique, gimmicky weapons in the game, and the great looking environments. Your creational options are vast, with lots of building options, and places to build. It's a space game, so expect a lot of funky looking monsters, wierd items, sci-fi stuff, etc.
Story wise, it sucks. This game has a useless story, it complements the game the way a sore throat complements a headcold. Characters are bland, the narative uses the tried, tested, and awful chosen one thing, and the quests you have to do in between each boss get really annoying. But that doesn't matter because...

-- addition to review --
We just had the multithreading patch, the game has seen some improvements for sure. But IMHO, the core problems from my initial review still exist. And even though gridlocks have been noticable patched, they havent been fixed. They are still there, just less.
Graphics/Sound is all good. Simulation has its problem and illogical parts, which can become problematic at times.
-- original review --
I would have to say it was worth my money considering how many hours I have spent on it, on the other hand the value of that time was taken down drastically by the problems the game has on a simulation level and with its tools. And considering this game has little to no value for a quick 3h game, but is meant to played for many hours I would have to say it isn't worth it as once you reach a level where it starts to get interesting the nuissances become problems. Graphics/Sound/Music was fine. But the core of the game, its simulation is just bad.
Not to badmouth the game, cuz they could still fix things, but to support my negative review here goes a list of things I have encountered: Laying down roads or rails often results in "collision" without clearly specifying what is colliding leaving the user to guess what to demolish. Using the "Load All" option can actually cause your line to be ignored completely. The amount of traffic that buildings generate can bring the traffic in the city to a grinding halt, so that bus routes become so slow that they arent used, causing probably more cars to spawn. You can only draw rails over roads, but not roads over rails or rails crossing rails. You sometimes can build a ridiculous 45 degree slopes, but most other times a 5 degree slope will give some error that it's too steep. There are also some very unbalanced issues. I've seen situations where building a road on fairly flat land cost more to raise lower ground for road than it was to build a bridge over it. Loading bays can hold equal or less to the trucks you have ( in late game ).  2M to remove a football field with 2 bleachers, but 700k to remove a 14 story building. And more of these weird inbalances. I've seen a (in-game) months worth of cars get priority to cross an intersections, while the busses that were the first in their lane never moved an inch. The UI is really lacking in many ways and there is little feedback to the player. Something as basic as visual feedback on the signal states isn't even in the game. I could probably name a few more.

Why not recommend this game? Because i want to love it but i can't.

Like many comments before, this is a game with great potential.  If you can get past the rather odd and very slow start, it's really quite fun, even in this skelton form and clunck track laying mechanics.  But it's a strange place this Tran Fever Land, not least because of ghostly, empty and too-modern looking and generic towns for 1850 and a landscape desperately lacking in flora and fauna... or life of any sort.  Or anything for that matter.  Indeed, with no 3D texture to the grass or cropfields alike, it's like a tabletop.
But perhaps that's where the character of the game, today at least, comes in.  It's a nice cross between a huge model railway and a 3D animated world.  Any new game is like watching a new sitcom on TV - you have to wait to get and idea of the theme, characters and essense before you can settle in.  And you have to give it a number of hours to do that.  so BE PATIENT.  Don't switch channels to soon, folks.
Once I got into the visual style and the towns grew and new vhicles came online I found myself getting quite excited to see old style cars doing the long drive in and between towns (although again the game years and vehicles some out of alignment).  Enthusiatic to get the new, bigger locomotive, combine the stations and bus stops and see passengers begin to bustle and jossle to get to the bus and train.  I even held the trains up a few times to wait for the busload of commuters whose had just pulled up.  Did I care about them?  Or did I just want their fare?  Both actually.  And that means the game is already OK - but it COULD be great.
I certainly hope the makers finish the game.  With the addition of more life to the worldscape, some greater variation in the people (visually and movements), and simplification or vehicle replacement, this could truly be the next generation of Transport Tycoom Deluxe.
UPDATE 4-14-15:  Well, the updates have stopped, so I guess th develpers have moved on.  A pity because with a few enhancements they could have had a really good game here.  As it is, it's an OK game and I stick with my thumbs up.

I'm 3.7 hours into Red Solstice and the more I play, the more I like it. Not exactly an easy learning curve, and I was very close to going for a refund a couple times during the first mission.  Tutorial wasn't bad, but didn't cover many things that would have been pretty helpful as a newbie, things that I had to discover on my own.  Now, having done that I'm greatly enjoying it and would probably rate it an 8 out of 10 at this point. Still, having been a computer gamer for many years, I've learned that one doesn't really know the true 'staying power' of any game until you've played it for a week or two.
I would encourage anyone who gets frustrated in the early going to keep at it. You absolutely need to use the Tactical Mode a LOT to keep yourself alive.  In Tactical mode you can gain true control over your team, so, for example, you can give direct orders for 3 of your team to cover the one who's deploying satchels or resonators instead of relying on autoaim to protect you.  You can manuever much more effectively, and you also get a more personal feeling about each of your teammates when you're controlling them directly.
One key thing (at least for me) that I didn't figure out until my third attempt at the first mission is that the GDD device not only points you to nearby monster spawn sites, it also points you to nearby resonators, which you must have to destroy the spawn sites. Without a resonator when you need it, the spawn sites will just continually churn out mobs, and the more functioning spawn sites, the more mobs until eventually you die a horrid, screaming death.
So use the GDD to find the resonators and you'll find survival isn't really impossible.
Good luck, and if this has the kind of staying power I think it will, my only complaint may be that there aren't enough single player missions to keep me happy, so I'll hope for some DLC in the not too distant future.

"Real-time X-Com" is an apt description.
Bought it for the mp, but the single-player campaign is extremely well done.  In mp you only control one character while giving simple follow/stay commands to rescued AI marines.
In single-player you utilize bullet-time pause to fully control squads.  You'll decide which characters to bring with you on a mission, outfit them, and level them.  The degree of replayability is high, since each character levels separetely, while belonging to one of eight classes.  You're encouraged to attempt missions with different class combos, which will completely change your tactics and playstyle - this keeps things fresh.
Two characters of the same class can be built differently by altering their stats, powerups, abilities and gear (all of which you find as loot during missions).  I have one assault character built as a speedy, evasive, melee expert, used for hit-run bombing alien spawn tunnels.  I have another specializing in grenade AOE support, and another as a pseudo-sniper marksman who holds the mid-line.
SP feels a lot like Dawn of War 2's campaigns during realtime, but the slo-mo pause gives it a tactical X-com feel. You'll also get overrun and die easily even on normal difficulty, just like classic X-com.
Even though you only control one character in MP, things are even hairier than they are in SP, since there's no pause. The easiest "recruit" difficulty will slaughter many players.  I just finished my first "recruit" difficulty multiplayer mission at 27h (though much of it was spent in single-player).
I'm having a blast with it.

Grimm is a 3d platformer that revisits fairy tales. First in the modern watered down state, then has you change them back to a state that resembled the tales written hundren of years eariler. As in back when they were darker, crueler, and.... dare I say... grimmer? True, it still takes pot shots at the stories and cracks jokes every so often, even during the latter state.
But part of the charm is in the humor, even if it does get a little bit crass, rude, and vulgar. For crying out loud, the targeting reticle is Grimm urinating at the spot where he would jump at.
Each chapter is about a dollar or so. There's coins of Grimm found in the stages. Collect all in a chapter (which is a few stages) and you'll unlock a model viewer. The model viewer has only buildings and breakable things to look at, but it does allow you to see the change between the stuff's Sugary-sweet version and the grim version. The difficulty of collecting the coins isn't that hard, just look aroudn the stage. I didn have a little bit of a problem looking for one coin in the final stage, but it turned out to be on top of a building.
The music does fit the setting, both when in the light version and dark version. I'll admit, the music is simple, short and repeats, but it's not going to ruin anything. The grimm-ified singing skull does have a ear worm-worth song in my mind, though.
I had some difficulty at first, getting used to a keyboard and mouse controls, back when I first played this. Precision jumping is a little difficult to get used to and a tad trying during the 'Run!' moments. but given time and patience, you can get used to it.
Is this worth buying? It's a nice jaunt through stories we've all read, listened to, and watched for dozons of times when either we were younger, or were looking after a child. And let's face it, we've all made those rude nasty jokes about fairy tales at one point or another. I say at least try the first stage. It's free, after all.
Fun fact : The little icon for Jack and the Bean Stalk in the 'choose a story' menu uses an earlier version of the Grimm-ified Jack. The little icon has a straw hat, but the grimm-ified version is designed to look more like a punk or something.

If you want to get the most enjoyment out of State of Decay, buy Breakdown as well.
State of Decay by itself is a semi-open world zombie game, with scavenging, exploring, and a pretty nifty combat system. However, the reason I recommend Breakdown is because the base game by itself is linear.
Not in the Point A to Point B Call of Duty sense, but in the 'Every Mission is the exact same for everyone' sense. If you play the campaign, you start as the same person, with the same stuff, and you meet the other people in the game who have the same stuff.
The Breakdown DLC however is a complete rehaul DLC that turns a semi-open world game into a completely open world Sandbox experience. While the map is the same as that of the campaign, the randomly generated locations of resources and the amped up difficulty with the Permadeath and the more zombies everywhere makes the Breakdown DLC the quinticential zombie game if you're into survival as well as slaying zombies.

So, I never played DN before, so this is a review of the game rather than this specific edition (which has a rather poor level of commentary). It's fun and feels fresh and innovative, compared to a game like Doom. The environments include interesting locations like a submarine and a movie theater. There are hidden doors everywhere so you keep clicking the action button on everything, but also certain secret passages can only be accessed if you blow something up or solve a button puzzle. Something new and interesting happens every now and then.

The problem is that this crazyness lacks context. Like, there is some vague implication of an alien invasion, but that is all you get. So yes, you go though the level and it is fun, but what the hell am I doing? I guess a lot of games were like that back then. There is also not a whole lot of flow or rhythm to the game, as again was the case with many games back then. This lack of flow and lack of story makes it easy to stop playing the game after finishing a level and there is not much insentive to go back, other than to find out what crazy stuff the developers have cooked up for the next level.
The graphics are good. There is something about that type of graphics (like Doom and Road Rash) that does not age and always looks nice. It is only when something blows up that things look rather...edgy and fake. There is no natural transition between the thing being there and the thing getting blown up.
The game is ok, and in many ways holds up after all these years, but there sure are better shooters to play nowadays. I play a level of this game every now and then.

Duke Nukem 3D is a great game, and this re-release holds up...mostly well. With dev commentary, a slightly updated version of the engine with less motion sick inducing 3D as well as the ability to swap between visuals on the fly by pressing C, great level designs in both the new and old levels, and the good old crass humor of old shooters, there's a lot to love, but I can't personally recommend this version of the game, unless you've never played Duke 3D.
The main issue comes with the price tag, $20. This game is an updated version of the Atomic Edition, which contained the first four episodes and was sold on GoG originally for $6 (For reference it ran on DoSbox unless you got the Eduke32 sourceport for better resolution and graphical options). It was re-released as the Megaton Edition with support for modern OS'/resolutions and came bundled with official expansion packs that are rare and expensive to find along, and then both versions were taken off shelves due to legal issues. Though this re-release adds a bit, the dev commentary only appears in a few select levels, and the new episode though great is incredibly short. Duke Nukem's original voice actor also returns which is a positive but some lines sound off and it just doesnt mesh well compared to the rest of the old sound effects. The biggest crime this re-release does is that there isn't enough new content leaving you want more and right now there's 0 news on new patches or support further down the line compared to what Battleborn or Borderlands got, leaving a release meant to celebrate the 20th anniversary of the game feel like a cashgrab with new content being held hostage by Gearbox if you owned any number of prior versions.
If this game does gets a $5 pricetag later down the line or appears in a Humble Bundle then by all means grab it and ignore the negative review, but for now skip it. And if you do own any number of versions you wont miss this at all considering fans are making fixes to get the 20th anniversary content running in EDuke32, along with the fact that its still Duke Nukem 3D but there's barely any new content in it to justify the higher price tag.

Being a fan of turn based strategy - and still trying to find something which recreates the atmosphere of Master of Magic - I really wanted this to work.  The combat aspect does but the problem is there actually seems to be so little else.  There's nothing wrong with combat in an empire building game, of course, but the lack of other gameplay dimensions just leave MoA feeling rather unsatisfactory.  With their being few options to win other than destroying - or at least dominating - the opposition alliances seem rather pointless, rather too obvious examples of marriages of convenience.  Focus is so much on the 'home world', units continuously fed and gobbled up into the unending battle, that diverting resources to the alternative worlds is wasteful.  Any serious attempt to move into such worlds requires such numbers that it inevitably leaves the flank of the home world vulnerable, often ensuring defeat.  Sadly, this leaves the additional worlds feeling irrelevant and gimicky, as oppose to the desperately essential New World fat with resources Myrimor felt like in MoM.  There seem to be rather rudimentary omissions too - after all my hours my victory is greated with a rather underwhelming still; there is no leaderboard to record the same after the disappointing image; there are no steam achievements; the choice of wizards somehow lack personality.  It's seem polished at first, but somehow a bit by-the-numbers and rather unfulfilling.  Shame - really wanted just a bit more, but the search continues...

I feel as if this game is getting a lot of uncalled for hate, especially with the recent key giveaway for the game, so I'm going to give it the positive review it deserves. I used to play this game on mobile, probably two years ago or so before I even had Steam. And, for a mobile game, it was a brilliant masterpiece. I feel like the PC port took all of the mobile version and just polished it up into a prettier looking package. Kind of like putting rims on a car; nothing
was done, but there is a noteable difference.
I'll be honest, I can't fully recall playing the mobile version. But when I jumped into this port of the game, I could definitely feel a difference in gameplay (besides the controls, of course). I felt as if the gameplay was simply better.
So let's go into everything now...
are not bad, but they aren't the greatest thing to be seen. To me, the graphics are really good, considering this was a mobile game and also since the graphics aren't too complex, they can run on lower end PC's, which is good.
is all there, with upgrades that you can unlock as you progress and in turn make the gameplay easier. I feel like weapons, even the gold only ones, are actually underpriced. They are fairly easy to get without any grind. Where the game loses points, though, is
The audio is great, don't get me wrong, but what sucks about it is the lack of balance. The guns and zombies are very dominating over dialouge, and the setting can't really be messed with in a way to balance it better. So in a firefight, I have to read the subtitles as opposed to just listening to the story. The final thing I'll touch on is
I think the game is smooth, with fluid controls and a quick response to user input. If a horde of zombies comes up, they can be taken care of without a frame drop, since the enemy number is much more manageable than say, Dead Rising. I feel like that's where Dead Effect did a very good job, since they can make the player feel overrun, but without needed 100 or so enemies to do it. The achievements were a great addition too. They give two extra challenges per mission, which really makes the player become more immersed into the game and helps increase concentration to get that extra challenge marked as complete. I feel the achievements add a replay value that was virtually non-existent in the original version. My one thing to really pick on with gameplay are grenades. When thrown, they slow down everything, which is good for when being overrun, but is otherwise an annoyance.
That's basically all. If the game was created this year, I'd understand the negativaty. But since it's an older game and was a mobile game, I feel this port deserves a solid 7/10, and once I beat it, I'll definitely try out Dead Effect 2.
Dead Effect really is worth the $5, but if you are hesitant, try out the app first!

I'd recommend this title for shooter, horror & sci-fi fans - but it's a hard sell.
The first thing I'd say about this game is that it's pretty - really, really pretty. The hallways & atriums look suitably metallic & pristine in some areas, while also appearing disconcertingly blood-spattered, burned, electrified & scorched in others. Other scenic items, like crates, cabinets, et cetera, look recognizable at-a-glance, but also practical & futuristic. Some of my favorite things to look at, though, are the reflections & shimmer of light & the virtual displays, from pilot's controls & technician's diagnostics to numerous medical & scientific computers scattered around the game. They're all a real treat for the eyes. Unfortunately, the actual animations & "moving" things are underwhelming, in comparison. They're satisfactory, though I found myself stopping numerous times to just gawk at the setting & found myself disappointed with how stilted the reload animations & janky the enemy movement was.
Another thing I'd like to commend is the atmosphere. Matus Siroky created an amazing soundtrack that is both haunting & beautiful - which I've listened to several times & will continue to do so for years to come (unfortunately, more than I can say about this game). DataPads left by the notes of the crew are, for the most part, informative & believable, covering humdrum topics like receiving new orders & gossiping about crew, to more serious ones like the discovery of The Dead Effect, itself - & the terrifying side effects, thereof. The pacing is nice & slow, which fits the horror vibe the game seems to have, but combat & character interaction conflict. Greatly. The juxtaposition of a seemingly grim, traumatizing experience is marred by how comically dense & gung-ho one of the protagonists is, among other such disconnects.
As the game continues, similar breaks in immersion become more & more prominent, which is where it all starts to come apart. Some of the horror elements do not mesh with the other sequences well, at all. For example, the protagonist creeps at a slow, cautious walk, silently, but can sprint for about 5 steps or so, then gives to heaving & gasping. The game (thus far, at least) seems to be taking itself semi-seriously as far as plot, but seems to ignore its own setting with collectibles, achievements / challenges, an item/upgrade shop between levels &, believe it or not, a "death tax," unless you start the entire level over - forcing you to creep slowly around, kill everything & pick up every collectable again if you don't pay it. Beyond that, there are certain enemies that blend in with all the other zombies I've seen so far - except they toss grenades that can kill you in a hit or two. Those 5 steps of sprint will not get you out of range in time to avoid them. I've died a minute from the end of the level more than I'd like.
One thing, that's both good & bad, are the numerous modes available to the player. Besides story mode, there are survival, "Biohazard" & New Game Plus modes - but these all serve to undermine what good setting the game already has. Why does this game need premium currency? That said, the survival mode seemed decent enough & the credits I earned there supposedly carry over to the story, but the income doesn't justify any potential grinding.
So: how's the game? Some of it's pretty damn good, but it also manages to hold itself back a great amount with odd, misfit design choices. I've also heard some questionable things about the developers, if you're concerned about ethics / supporting indie outfits, but I haven't researched any of it. To close, I'd say that if you want to take a look at the setting & you like horror & atmosphere, this is worth a try, but I'd wait for a price break as the game quality seems to lessen the longer I play. From a strict gameplay standpoint, I'll be playing around with the extra modes a little. On the other hand, the other modes are nice, but not enough to bring you in or keep you here.

I now spent a nice amount of time with the game so I can voice my opinion about it.
In many ways it is exactly what I needed, although it could sure use some improvements down the road.
Good:
- Nice graphics. If you're like me and still play openttd / RT3 etc. occasionally, this is pretty cool. I like the vehicles, it's quite nice work on those. It is not a console like 'detailed but cheesy' kind of Gfx, it is not the genre that requires that imo, it just has enough detail where it's needed, like vehicles and cities.
- Interesting economic model. Once you get to understand it the demand based economy is quite simple. I like to follow people to see where they go sometimes, it helped me understand how things work. It's a good challenge to make cities grow, although this means you'll end up with some local lines going into loss, which is pretty realistic I guess.
- For me it's a big plus that it works on Linux. I have been experimenting with living with a desktop Linux for the past few months and it helped a lot to get some nice games on it once in a while. :)
- The modding possibilities look like it will help with replay value. I didn't try mods yet, didn't quite "finish" with the stock game yet but I am sure I will at some point. The challenge will just be to find the more finished, 'professional' mods.
- The cargo moving model can be a bit confusing at first, but it's a nice all around model with the lines, frequencies, the rule that passengers look to find routes that are within 20 minutes of travel time. It challenges you to build more efficient networks so people can get far by combining the use of different vehicles.
- Dev team seems pretty responsive. In a couple of weeks they released 2 patches that deal with stability issues and help those that have problems running the game in the first place. Although for me it worked out of the box in both Win7 and Ubuntu.
The problems I have:
- Building railroad tracks is very challenging at first, although it does get easier as you get used to it. A lot of 'collision' messages, sometimes feels a bit too restrictive but most of the time you can work them out.
- Bridges - I did have a little problem building overpasses at first, you just have to learn that the game doesn't allow too steep slopes. Prepare to have enough room to raise a track so you can cross another, or a wide road.
- Roads crossing railroad lines - at irst this was impossible until I learned that using M and N shortcuts you can raise or lower the middle of the road section you're building. This way I have succesfully built many roads over tracks which was helpful in extending cities around the railroad stations.
- Terrain tool - it provides little information and I hate it, can't use it efficiently.
- There are optimizations required, towards the year 2000 game becomes quite slow. Perhaps it is because so many people walk around and at that point they start using their cars to go around. Although dev team promised to look into it, it will probably require a few weeks to get the first patch or two that deals with these things.
- For a game called Train Fever trains are very expensive to build and maintain so it always requires careful consideration.
- Traffic jam issues late game. Here it helps to plan ahead and use trains for passanger traffic between cities but it's financially non trivial which was difficult at first and I sort of like it now that you need to think and plan a bit ahead so you don't commit financial suicide.
Overall I think it's a nice game. I am glad someone released a game in the genre, always been a fan of these games. TF is good to go from the start, but a few patches will be welcome to iron out some issues. Mind you it's a very small company with a very low budget - raised 250k euros last year for the game, when you think of it some studios spend hundreds of millions. I think it's good to have these independent companies, with all the hit and miss, they sometimes bring a fresh perspective.
ps. Some people seem to have issues with replacing vehicles - it's one of those tings I never had problems with, you can send and sell all vehicles from a line to depots with 1 button, and normally you do it once every 20-30 years, you buy new vehicles in the depot and then assign them to the line once for the whole batch. It's only a pain with trains which I don't use a lot since they're expensive to maintain.

I see a number of people saying this doesn't work on an iMac. Well I bought it today (Sunday 21 Sep 14) and it installed and worked perfectly. In case anyone missed it, this title requires that permissions be granted via the System Prefs. On Mavericks go to Security & Privacy and then choose Accessability. Click the padlock in the lower left corner of the window and type in your admin password. That should case the options to becaome available. Scroll the list of apps down until you find Steam and activate the check box next to it. Close the window and restart Steam. You should now be able to get Train Fever to work. It does also appear to be a 64bit app if that makes any difference to anyone with issues around getting it to work.
The game itself is pretty good. Ifound the thing a bit jumpy when zooming the map out until I adjusted the Shadows option to low. Having said that I also noted that it was a function of detail that cased the stuttering and that all the time you work at realtively close quarters to the ground you can actually have everything set to high including the Shadows option.
It seems fairly straightforward to operate and I recognised a lot of how it worked from having played Railway Tycoon in my shady past. Would I reccomend it? Yes I think I would.
I can see that anyone looking for a  detailed rail sim with mega amounts of choices on a Mac would probably be happier with Trains, but having said that I still think you would probably find this plenty enjoyable too. All in all a good buy.
Hope this helps some of you having troubles with this title out there in Steam land.

Breti gud gaem. Bought it on the casualbox 420 when it came out, and again on the PC a few months back. If you have performance issues, I suggest you download the Shadow Removal Mod on the Nexus, it makes me able to run this almost flawlessly on a terribad Dell Inspiron from 2008. You scavenge for weapons, ammunition, medicine, food, and even other survivors. Some you can even play as. There's a character swap mechanic, and it's encouraged as your characters will eventually become Exhausted. This lowers their maximum Stamina, which lowers combat effectiveness, how long you can sprint, and if you can even walk and roll away from the zombies chasing you.
The story is about as generic as it gets for zombie stuff. An outbreak happens, you're screwed, and then you find some people for a symbiotic relationship. It becomes just basic survival for the rest of the game. I won't really say anything more, but the military turns out to not be entirely bad after all.
There's a perma-death mechanic in this as well. If one of your characters gets swarmed by zombies and eaten alive, that character is gone for good. You can go out in a blaze of martyr-tier glory by blowing yourself up to take out all those zombies if you have an explosive in your backpack. Do try to keep Marcus alive, he's one of the best characters you can get in the game.
If you don't like a certain character you recruit, you can go send them on a suicide mission by playing as them and jumping off a high ledge or just getting them eaten.
When an allied survivor dies, they drop a green Rucksack you can go recover, which contains everything they had when they were alive.
The gameplay is a bit repetitive, but it's enjoyable enough. Once you complete the main story, there's two more DLC's for you to try, as well as a diverse range of mods on the Mod Nexus to further enhance your experience.
Breakdown takes place in the area the main game did, and it's an infintely repeating cycle you can carry your items and favorite survivors over onto the new playthroughs.
Lifeline involves you playing as a military group searching for information in a completely new area with new vehicles, weapons, structures for your base, and other things. You can also simply call in supplies using Influence, the game's currency. Anyway, buy it, it's like five bucks right now and so are both DLC's.
Yes, yes I do recommend this game.

Got into it quite early in the Beta, when it was still a bit of a buggy mess. You still played it, because it was fun. The learning curve is nothing to laugh about, and it is not exactly the noobfriendliest of communities, especially some of the first players sometimes lack the nerves to deal with new players.
Once you get into it though, you will have an awesome experience. Highly tactical, once you get off "Soldier"-difficulty, relies 100% on each teammate.
By now the game has several different maps, playable on 4 difficulties and a handful of different modes that change up the experience like the "Red Storm" mode where you are weak when outside of buildings, but stronger inside, or swarm and fast modes that increase the pressure on your squad. All with 8 different classes, completely customizable with different weapons and abilities, that have to be utilized harmoniously to win.
Protip: Get a mic. Theres a central TRS teamspeak server, that anyone in the game lobby can give you, and coordinating an 8 man team is just so much easier with voice. Learning the game and getting taught will be 10 times faster if you go on ts with one or two of your squadmates.
The best way to get into it would be to grab a few freinds, put it on easy, and just jump into it. You will die. A LOT. but thats fine, and you will have fun getting to know all the different abilities and weapons before getting on with the pros who might be more interested in winning than teaching.
Sadly, this game has a very small player base, so don't expect to play 8 man games 24/7. There are high times each day, where there are usually 2-4 different games going on, but expect to do some waiting in lobby for members. However, this means that you get to know people very quickly, and if you are somewhat nice and don't harass people, you will be welcomed in the community.

Fractal is a surprisingly enjoyable brain teaser, casual, puzzle like game where you make fractals of one color. A fractal is a diamond of 7 tiles / cubes / gems / whatever. 2 on the left, 2 on the right, 3 in the center. How do you arrange them? You simply click an empty space on the grid or the border of the level. When you click that empty space, the spaces around it push out with whatever color gem you have next in your cue. Let's say green gem in your cue you will push out in all directions shifting all the gems in all directions 1 space over. Like pushing lines in 6 directions. You only get a certain amount of 'pushes' per level. To beat a level you need to get X amount of points. When you make a fractal, other gems appear in the level, which may lead to a chain of fractals or mess you up. Sometimes you need to think 2 or 3 moves ahead and when different colored gems get involved you need to make sure one move doesn't mess up something else you've been planning.
1
The campaign won't take more than a few hours, but I can see there being replay value in the way that Tetris is replayable. While the score isn't a big focus of the game, it still gets your brain going. There's no pressure or time limit, its soothing. The puzzle mode has several continuous puzzles.
Eventually the game throws different kinds of tiles your way. If those special tiles are in your fractals, you will get their bonuses. Things like adding more tiles to your cue, exploding all connected tiles of the same color, pushing tiles apart from the fractal and so on. It adds a needed level of depth.
Luckily there are two other modes, arcade and puzzle. Puzzle mode has you completing objectives such as making a triple fractal in X number of pushes or clearing all of the diamonds. It is a nice diversion, but hardly the meat of the game. The arcade is more of a time attack to get as many fractals in a limited amount of time. There are time tiles that will add to the clock when they're in a fractal.
Fractal feels like its more suited for relaxing with a touch screen and mobile devices rather than for people sitting in a chair at a computer. Its still an engaging and relaxing game for a while.

Duke Nukem 3D remains as one of my all time favorite FPS' if not my absolute.
World Tour revamps the game in a new updated engine and it shows, it keeps its old charm while also looking much much better. There is even a hotkey to swap between new and updated graphics just to let you see the huge improvement. The real benefit is the lighting. The lighting gives the game a whole new depth really bringing out its classic detail.
The new episode 5 is also a blast, the new enemies really being a pain when they need to be (especially the first level of all things). Sadly I found the new weapon to be a bit lacking, Its a really strong and fun weapon however it just doesn't feel right, from the ammo you shoot to the sound effect it gives its just a tad dull. Though saying that having new levels from the original designers as well as all new DukeTalk from Jon himself really hits you with a wave a nostalgia not to mention they actually updated all his old lines too.
There is also developer commentary throughout the game which is a joy to listen to as it ranges from them simply making fun of each other to them talking about the mindset of making certain stages which is great. The only downside to this is that I almost feel there isn't enough of it. They don't have it in every level and in some levels where they do they only have a couple of things to say.
However that being said, this game, unless you don't have the Megaton edition isn't worth the price. If your a hardcore Duke 3D fan like myself that is. The Megaton edition comes with all the levels (except the new episode 5) as well as the 3 expansions the game got, which for some odd reason World Tour doesn't come with. For me personally I don't regret it for a moment as the updated engine and new episode as well as the dev commentary really shows how much heart and soul they put into this. For some I'd say pass until its cheaper however if you really are a big fan then don't hesitate.
I also heard in one of the commentary moments them saying they would love to make the game again in completely next gen graphics/engine if the fans wanted it, so if you really do enjoy duke make sure to voice it!

I can see why Duke Nukem 3D was such a sensation upon release. It had gore! And one-liners! And pop-culture references! And quasi-realism! And sleaze! And macho-ness! And "attitude!" And possibly unintentional irony! And scantily-clad women just scattered around for no reason! It was EDGY! And it was the 90s! And it was an FPS, just to top it off!
Aside from that, it had a lot of cutting-edge technical features. It was the first game to have vertical-enabled mouselook, swimming, and (limited) reloading, for a start. (Unless you count Marathon, but Marathon existed in its own weird little Mac bubble apart from the rest of PC gaming.) Also, it had an inventory, a feature that had been present in previous games (Heretic and HeXen), but its items were a bit more grounded in plausibility than HeXen's, and they were actually useful as well. Finally, they copied Dark Forces's technique for creating multi-layer levels by just putting teleports all over the place. In 1996, Duke Nukem 3D was every PC gamer and teenage boy's dream.
On its own merits, however, Duke Nukem's just fine. It's a competently made shooter, with few distinguishing features. The weapon loadout's nice and varied, although the Shrink Ray and Devastator are stupidly overpowered. You take damage surprisingly quickly; this is no DOOM or Half-Life, where you can take a rocket to the face and basically be alright. If you take a rocket to the face in Duke Nukem 3D, you're either dead or dragging yourself across the ground by the skin of your broken teeth (I guess that's what Duke gets for wearing a tank top instead of power armor). The pixel art's pretty good overall, and the sound is primitive but definitely intelligible. The level design evokes realistic environments without being in any way realistic; it's also about as unintuitive and mazey as FPS levels get at times. Some parts of some levels seem to require the use of expendable items, which is a bit of a poor design choice, but it's not a major issue. The game overall is actually fairly short, requiring only about 5 hours to finish the first three episodes. It's occasionally frustrating, but overall pretty smooth to get through. As I said before, it's fine.
This Steam port is also basically functional. There's a weird glitch where occasionally the game decides that the player has died for no reason, but quicksaves minimize the issue, and other than that I experienced no problems. It's always nice to be able to toggle older and newer graphics and sound.
Overall, I can recommend this game. It's a big piece of gaming history, and it's not unenjoyable to get through. Just watch out for the weird attitudes toward women.

The third in the eXceed series - Jade Penetrate (Black Package) - is a worthwhile and fun bullet-hell shmup. That said, it's pretty easy on the lower difficulties. I comfortably cleared it on easy on my first playthrough, so I would recommend ramping 'er up to at least normal on your first run unless you're completely new to the genre. Unlike the previous game, Vampire, Jade Penetrate uses a more traditional mechanic of either spread fire (with fast movement) or focused fire (with slow movement to avoid projectiles and a homing weapon). You have bombs to avoid dying and you also power up your special weapon by "grazing" enemy bullets. While usually a more advanced technique, in Jade Penetrate this mechanic is used in quite possibly the best way I've ever seen it done - many of the shot patterns include very cool circular walls of bullets that you graze as they spin, quickly powering up your special attack to decimate the opponents you face. The visuals are also outstanding, colorful explosions and huge walls of enemy fire - it's just what you'd want from a game like this. Different colored (yet easily distinguishable) shots, score tokens that are collected automatically, and bullets that you absorb upon an enemy's death to rack up that high score. That said, the frame rate can suffer a little bit with so many sprites on the screen; however, in games like this the lagging frames may turn out to be an answered prayer, as dodging enemy fire is much easier.
Powering up your weapons is this game is also quite neat, instead of making your main attack stronger, as many shmups do, in Jade Penetrate you collect "D" tokens which give you little dragon familiars that attack for you. They're actually your homing attacks too, so as the game advances and you face harder enemies that you have to dodge more against, your weapon that always hits (as long as you're focus firing) gets powered up!
I really enjoyed this game, short as it was. As I said, I beat it on easy right away, but playing it on hard proved a worthy challenge and I can see myself coming back to this game time and time again to get my bullet-hell fix. Easily the best in the series (unless you really love the polarity swapping from Vampire), Jade Penetrate is a fast and fun shooter that will test your skill, coordination, and leave you begging for more.

This game does what it sets out to do very, very well. If it had better controller support, leaderboards, and a few more unlockable options Jade Penetrate would be spectacular. B+

Okay seriously these titles are just insane... Jade Penetrate Black Package? Even in the context of the story in this game, that makes no sense at all... oh well, least the game is fun.
Jade is the third eXceed game, and after ditching the Ikaruga game mechanics from the second game it is back to good old fashioned bullet dodging, in many ways this game has less content then the other two but for what it lacks in content it makes up for in polish.
The gameplay is the same as most Bullet Hell games except you can pick up powerups that summon mini dragons that follow you and attack things, otherwise it is like most others though that is not really a knock to it given that is what people are here for in a Bullet Hell, tight controls, great music, hectic gameplay, and nonsense stories, and this game delivers on all of that.
As I said before the game is lacking in some content, there are only six stages and one character with three difficulty levels, each stage feels shorter then most stages in a Bullet Hell game, however despite that it is very well made and fun, the story is, as always, nonsense and has no real connection to the other two games as far as I can tell, but the artwork and backgrounds are done well.
Overall if you play Bullet Hell shooters then this game will be up your alley, it is fun, fast, and frantic, despite what it lacks it more then makes up for it in polish.

One of the few problems I have with Steam is the lack of good 2D shooters. While there have been some recent additions like Ikaruga and Danmaku Unlimited 2, the selection isn't anywhere near what I'd call satisfactory. Thanks(?) to the lack of releases I find myself spending a little time with Jade....Penetrate...Black...Package....uh..okay then.
The storyline is about what you'd expect from a shmup, absolute swill. You're playing these games to dodge bullets and get high-scores anyway. There are multiple stages with bosses at the end of each. These bosses have several forms and numerous bullet patterns to fling at you. Like most doujin shooters, the bullet patterns are immense in their density but don't move very quickly. You don't have to be a veteran of the genre to get far in this game. The scoring system revolves around medal-chaining and multipliers. It's not quite as deep as an arcade shooter but it does the job.
As far as I'm concerned eXceed 3rd is the only game in the series worth playing. This is because rather than being completely inept & frustrating (eXceed 1) or a poor man's Ikaruga (eXceed 2), this game focuses on what makes doujin bullet-hells work. Pick it up, play it, enjoy it.
While we'd all love to make more jokes about black packages, it should be mentioned that originally this game was just Jade Penetrate. It's an earlier version that's very different, and it is more difficult with faster bullet patterns. The "Black Package" is akin to Cave and their habit of adding "Black Label" to different versions of their games. Unfortunately you'll have to look outside Steam if you want to play the original eXceed 3rd. It's more likely to be an overall better game if you're looking for a challenge. I guess most of Black Package's difficulty comes from the scoring system, I cleared the game on my first attempt(and by cleared I mean without using continues).
Overall though JDBP isn't too bad a game. I've certainly played worse in the genre.

Train Fever is an entertaining game, with a few flaws, but an overall enjoyable expierence.
In Train Fever you run a transprort company from the 19th to the 21st century, using buses, trams, and trains to make a profit shipping people and cargo. I liked how the game started in 1850 as comparable games such as Transport Tycoon, and Cities in Motion start way later, which certainly changes your stradegy in the early game. The simulation is easy to understand yet difficult to master. The Graphics are quite pleasing to the eye, and the soundtrack is pretty catchy compared to other sim games I have played. The game is challenging and there are many stradegies to try to make a profit. The Randomly generated maps are a great addition that diffinatly add replay value. ISometimes it is simply great to watch your trains race around the landscape. Basically this game is what Transport Tycoon could have been if it was made today in 3D.
However the game does have some issues. Track laying is very difficult. Rather than clinging to the landscape like you would expect it to, it is completely independant of it, meaning you will have a lot tracks raised and lowered around the ground. It is also finickey and will often give errors when it is clear there should not be one. The UI is not exactly Intuitive either. However it seems the devoloper is apt to fix these problems.
Overall I would recomend this game to any fan of Railroad Tycoon, Cities in Motion and especially Transport Tycoon, as it is a complex quality expierence.

I've been a huge fan of tycoon games - particularly transportation tycoon games for a really long time. I've been looking forward to Train Fever since I first heard about it. Unfortunately, it has proved to be probably my most disappointing game purchase this year.
I think my big issue with Train Fever is that it is just not quantitatively fun. It feels like you are wrestling with the track editor in order to build anything. The challenge isn't identifying where to lay track in order to maximize a profit, but simply in building the infrastructure. A prospect like building a junction between two pairs of lines is almost nightmarish in complexity and difficulty to execute.
I've concluded that the developers are huge fans of trains, to the expense of actual gameplay. Things like the actual trains are rendered impressively well, with little things like the coupling rods on the wheels working perfectly. Unfortunately, trains won't route to spread load between multiple lines on a station. You can't lay road across railway lines - it has to be the other way around. You can't do something as simple as have an intersection between two lines without them connecting.
The game also lacks anything in the way of charm. The music is not particularly good, and gets repetitive very quickly. The cities and industries feel very lifeless. I compare it to the (admittedly flawed) Railroad Tycoon 4 which used music and graphics to evoke the nostalgia of steam era trains.
Could it still become a good game? Possibly, but I doubt it. It feels like it should be in early access, and it feels unfinished. It feels like effort was put into the game, but that gameplay is secondary to just making cool looking trains.
Should it be at the $30 price point? Not at this stage.

A surprising gem!  I got this as part of a bundle without knowing anything about it at all, and was pleasantly surprised.  It's a hex-based strategy game which is realtively light, and whose mechanics keep it tight the whole way through.  The gameplay is sort of like Civilization 5 minus Civilization 4 - city building and resources are dealt with in a minimalist style, and the hex-based combat has a similar feel to the best of Civ 5, with an expanded system for damage types.  It also has an overland magic system that will remind you of Master of Magic.  Apart from tight mechanics, this game is also very colourful - visually appealing with an entertaining roster of units, and a sense of humour which isn't forced or overlaboured.  The only real downside is that the animations are too long, and you need to skip them to play at any rate - doubly bad as that detracts from the atmosphere and also gives you RSI.  Would still strongly recommend if you're looking for a combat focused turn-based strategy game that's a bit more lightweight than other games in the genre.

This game is very challenging.
I would classify it as a 4X game, so you know that as you play each turn, each successive turn starts to take longer and longer because you've got more and more cities.
Does it scratch the strategy itch? Sort of, but not really. There are a few different strategy elements which are mildly interesting. First, you've got your cities. Each city can have buildings, each of which have different bonuses. You have to manage your mana, food, gold, research, and unit production. The trick is to just build cities and focus them on just one resource (to max out your bonuses).
The second strategy layer is the units and combat. You've got melee units, ranged units, and AoE variants of the two. The general strategy is to have your melee units in front and your ranged units in the back, and try to kill the enemy units faster than they can make them. You also get hero characters, which, with careful management, can become very over powered. In fact, the focus of the game trends towards trying to keep your heros alive as long as possible.
Just to keep you on your toes, the game randomly spawns lots of monsters of a random type every 30 turns or so. It is more of a nuisance than anything else.
The AI and diplomacy is absurdly simplistic though, so that's quite a fault of this game. You pretty much have four possible relationships: War, rivals, peace, allies. In terms of diplomacy, the only purpose is to turn an AI player into your friend to keep them off your back while you fight some other AI player. Inevitably, each AI player will declare war on you, so don't bother trying to build any sort of close relationship.
Is the game fun? Sure, I enjoy it. I can easily lose track of time playing this game.
Is the game *interesting*? Not really. The mechanics are just too simplistic to give the game long term interest. There's just not a lot of versatility, so the replayability suffers quite a bit once you've got it figured out.
Should you get it? If you've played every other 4X fantasy strategy game out there, this one just promises to deliver more of the same with some variations to the flavor.

Seeing as how I'd written reviews for the second and third games in the trilogy but not the first... I should do that.
Dark Souls is the game that kicked off the trilogy, and is the catalyst for what became one of the most popular action RPG IPs out there today. And for good reason, because this game embraces almost all the things that... Makes video games great.
Now, the whole edgy "Prepare To Die" tagline is just... Bad marketing. That's commonly accepted among the community at this point. The Dark Souls games aren't hard. They're not hard any more than your average NES game is hard. They have a difficult but fair curve where the games aren't impossible, but they don't hold your hand either. Dark Souls teaches you the necessary skills in the introductory level, then leaves you to master everything else from there on your own using your own reasoning. If you've ever seen Egoraptor's Sequelitis video on Mega Man/Mega Man X, and how those games teach you using context? Dark Souls does exactly that.
And the level design. Oh man, the level design. In a trilogy that has great level design by modern day standards, DS1 still stands high above all the rest even among its peers, Demon's Souls and Bloodborne included. It's the only Soulsborne game with a very metroidvania style take on it's world design, with everything being truly interconnected in a sort of figure-eight vertically stacked fashion. Much of the game is a trek upwards or downwards yet doesn't feel like it. Let me put this into perspective:
Dark Souls 3 is horribly, horribly linear, with one or two branching pathways in the entire game and only three optional areas in the entire vanilla game, not counting DLC. Dark Souls 2 is slammed for it's linear, disjointed level design, but it at least has a proper hub from where you can choose three or four paths to pick from the start of the game, most of which branch into different areas themselves.
Dark Souls 1 on the other hand? It's level design is stacked on top of itself where the majority of the game is essentially open to you from the first half (provided you pick a starting item called the master key, which I'd only recommend doing if you're an explore-a-holic or you've got prior experience with Souls games). Imagine this: In the first half of the game you have to go to an area called Blighttown, to get to a major story objective. The normal way is, after clearing the first objective, you'd go back to the first major area, Undead Burg, open a side entrance, fight ONE boss, then go down to the sewers, fight ANOTHER boss, and get the key that unlocks Blighttown proper, which in itself is a very long area. Or, if you picked the master key, you can go down from the main hub into a lategame area called New Londo, take a shortcut elevator from there into an optional area, take a short route around, and... You're in Blighttown near the boss, taking a shortcut back up where a normal player would typically use to exit near the end of the area.
Most of the first half of the game works like this, and to this day it's one of the most fascinating examples of interconnected level design that any game (yes, including metroid and castlevania, that I've played anyway) has failed to replicate. The second half of the game is pretty linear, and focuses on gimmicks in each respective area, but they're fun gimmicks, save one that suffers from rushed development. You'll see what I mean.
That said, DS1 is very imperfect, partly due to it's rushed development, and partly due to the nature of the PC port. Said lategame area is horribly broken and is essentially hated by the vast majority of the community due to bad design. (Protip: Give 25 humanities to a certain NPC in a certain covenant and it'll unlock a shortcut that'll let you pass the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. Normally new players shouldn't be told this but... It's really bad down there, guys.)
The controls feel very aged compared to the later games too. Dark Souls 3 brought a TON of people into the series and coming off it or 2, DS1 will feel dated. It's not unplayable, just difficult to acclimate to with a lot of the quality-of-life features from 2 and 3 missing entirely.
The PC port of this game is also one of the most disgusting, failed attempts of all time. Hardlocked at 1024x720 at 30FPS with honestly abysmal optimization and almost nonexistent keyboard controls, the PC port is awful. Thankfully, a mod called DSFix exists that repairs all these issues and makes the game better than the console versions in the way it should be, with proper resolution and 60FPS support, moddable texture files, additional graphical features, and better keyboard support. Optimization is improved too, although the game still runs, for all intents and purposes, worse than its sequels.
The netcode, as the game's biggest sin, is awful. The game was originally a GFWL (Games For Windows Live) title, but when that was patched out and replaced with built-in Steamworks support, the matchmaking somehow just... Broke. Hell, the servers were offline without a statement from the devs for a full week at one point, and even now they're still barely working. Thankfully, this is also fixed with a couple mods called DSCM which automates the matchmaking process, and PVP Watchdog, which flags hackers. (And boy are there a lot of hackers.) These don't fix the awful netcode or the abysmal PVP however, where many of the PVPers use twink builds (the legend never dies, lads), or they teleport all over the place and fish for backstabs and parries, or just flat out break your game with hacks. Just go to DS2 and 3 for better PVP. Especially 2.
The co-op is fine, though.
Short version: DS1 is an imperfect game that still stands above the majority of modern RPGs with godlike level design, classic Souls gameplay, and a very fair difficulty curve, only hampered by one badly designed area, broken netcode and a bad PC port, and a little bit of ♥♥♥♥♥♥ marketing that could scare people that really shouldn't be scared.
Dark Souls is easy guys, come on. Give it a try. You'll like it.
Disclaimer: Though this is my longest Dark Souls review of the three, DS1 is not my favorite. DS2 is the best. DS2 IS THE BEST SHUT UP ANYONE WHO TELLS YOU DIFFERENT IS A BAD PERSON AND WANTS TO MAKE YOU SAD.
DS1 is pretty great though. :>

Fractal: Make Blooms not War (Nth Review)
This game has a few problems: The difficulty curve is rather wavy, going up and down through the levels. Some are ridiculously easy and some are not only pretty hard, but also depend on luck - because your starting field is randomized in campaign mode, you can get everything from a 60 points head start to an unsolvable mess.
The graphical presentation is nice, but doesn't go beyong functional, really. Same goes for the Sound.
The game modes are fairly diverse, though the campaign is rather "puzzle"-y, safe for the previoulsly mentioned randomness - which can be really annoying and warrents constant restarts. The puzzles are pretty good and serve as the only "sort-of" tutorial, because a really detailed introdution is missing. The arcade mode is boiled down to frantic clicking, which becomes a bit more strategic with practice.
All in all this is a nice puzzler, with some rather annoying problems. If you're looking for a small game to play in between other things to do, this fits the bill. But it is no game to sit back and relax, because it will annoy you from time to time.
Rating: Only just recommendable.

Since many have already spoken about what this game is and does.. I'd just like to briefly mention why I love it so much and would wholeheartedly recommend it to any fan of deep RPGs:
-Obsidian have really set out to create not only a single terrific game.. but in a bigger sense a new world/IP that they can continue to build on with subsequent games. The lore, from the quests down to the lengthy and whimsical item descriptions, all give you a sense that the world of Eora is a real place full of many mysteries to be uncovered. I was so enthralled with this aspect that I even purchased the Pillars of Eternity Guidebook Volume One (a hardcover lore book that goes into further detail about the world and its inhabitants) to immerse myself even further into the game.
The high quality of writing and voice acting are the cherry on top in terms of delivering this well thought out content to you. I loved the various companion characters that can tag along with you and how they interact with you and each other to make you feel like you are really on a grand adventure with trusted companions. Additionally I was very much pleasantly surprised at how while some aspects of the story may be conventional fantasy fair, conversely there are elements to the story that are unconventional and break with the norm seen in so many games before it. The intrigue of the story and world's lore kept me wholly invested until the very end.
-The artwork and music is magnificent. The environmental art comes to life with a painterly asthetic that made me feel like I was ordering my characters around a series of beautiful paintings.. a really unique experience as someone who had not played a CRPG before. Additionally the hand-drawn art used during certain dialogue and encounter scenes, and for soulbound weapons, adds a terrific visual representation of the scenes/items to get your imagination firing on all cylinders while you read the lore that accompanies it. On top of all of that the soundtrack by Justin Bell sets all of the right moods, providing ambiance and energy in a way akin to Jeremy Soule of Elder Scrolls fame.
-The RPG and combat systems are extremely rewarding. For those of you that love complex RPG characters full of skills and stats, you might just find yourself in roleplaying heaven as I found myself. I loved the tactical challenge that each battle presented to me, and that the game required me to use my whits and do my proper research before adventuring forth. It was a true joy to look over all of my character's strengths and weaknesses, experiment with different gear and buffs, and attempt new approaches when I was getting schooled by the latest army of badass minions.
-Lastly there is a ton of content available to you for your money. If you include the terrific DLCs, there is well over 200hrs of stellar awesomeness to experience if you like to explore thoroughly and take in all of what is offered. There is also enough depth in the character creation and the many moments where the story can be altered by your decisions for you to easily replay the game a number of times. Of particular note is the fantastic way Obsidian presents the player with choices, and rewards and recognizes those decisions made at various points in the game. There are a number of moments that I can still vividly remember succeeding or failing at that really stuck with me, and I'd love to see if I could forge a different path in a subsequent playthrough.
In closing.. if you've read this far you can surely tell that I adored this game for myriad reasons, and can confidently recommend it to anyone who finds that my aforementioned praise resonates with their ideal of a great RPG. This game is a modern masterpiece, and my hat is off to the team at Obsidian for what they've accomplished.

I've had this game for a while now, pretty much around when it came out, played the mobile version before it hit Steam as well and my biggest gripe then was the controls on mobile so I was a little excited to see it hit PC. It wasn't really what I expected though.
So this game and the devs I think get a lot of bad publicity, some of it I'll agree is deserved to an extent but the rest seems to be unfair. I'll talk about that more later.
Game looks good. Lighting and shadows are well done, a lot of real time shadows and dynamic lights.
Plays well and almost no optimization issues.
It's your average shooty bang, really only meant to shoot stuff, that's about it.
Weapon selection isn't too shabby.
Story is fairly bland BUT this might not be a bad thing if you're like me and just want to kill stuff.
Atmosphere is good for the most part.
While the game looks good there are too many effects and bright lights, I actually have a hard time focusing on the zombies at times because the bright lights and effects are so exagerrated and in your face.
The game plays well for the most part but it's got a lot of questionable choices which helps to ruin some of the enjoyment, these could easily be remedied but the devs never really did any quality of life fixes on their PC release. These are pretty annoying because the main reason to get it on PC over mobile is the controls, at least for me, maybe that and not using my precious internal storage. The game does weird things like letting you dodge left and right but it takes a large chunk of your stamina AND it's more annoying if anything as you'll accidentally be dodging all the time because you need to double tap A or D to do so and almost everyone quick taps the movement keys in FPS games to get more precise movement being digital over analog, this will cause a ton of accidental dodges which to me is one of the most annoying things about this game.
Switching weapons can take a while, reloading takes forever as it seems your character has never used a firearm in their life. You can only sprint for maybe 50ft before your character is out of breath, your regular moving pace is extremely slow and speeds up if you hold your movement at a diagnol one, such as holding W and D. There's a dedicated grenade button but all it does is act like switching weapons, instead of just chucking one it switches to your grenades as if they're a separate weapon and this is annoying because you don't just switch back, instead you have to clumsily switch back to your previous weapon and grenade throws make almost no sense, they can either fly fairly far or lob right out of your hand at your feet, it's not a pleasant experience when you chuck one with your back up against a locked door and it decides to hit the ground dead in front of you. The wrist weapon while kind of cool SHOULD be a melee attack or something instead of being a separate weapon, it's just another thing that adds to the game's already incredibly slow snail pace. They could have made the wrist weapon a melee attack and grenades NOT as an actual weapon, this would have saved people a ton of effort as then you'd only need a switch weapon button, grenade toss button and a melee button, not four weapon switch buttons plus mouse wheel to do simple tasks like using a melee attack or throwing a grenade. I personally think a lot of these choices were designed to make the game feel longer. The store page says: "Over 5 hours of story content!", I beat the game at 4.9 hours and that was WITH taking my sweet time to beat it. I also only ever died to those annoying grenade zombies, they chuck grenades from behind a crowd of zombies and they'll either kill themselves by hitting one of their pals in the back of the head OR throw it right through/over them and at your feet and it doesn't make a noise, no visual indicator on the grenade or your HUD and blows up instantly killing you. Artificial difficulty at it's finest. It's a shame because all of this stuff could be fixed without much effort to make a much more decent game.
Speaking of not making noise, there's a lot of stuff in this game that doesn't make noise, foot steps are something you never hear which makes those little imp enemies kind of annoying unless you hear them growl, grenades and such also make no noise when they hit surfaces.
The second most annoying aspect of this game. By the end of the game I only unlocked two weapons, three technically if you count the starter pistol. I got the revolver and the shotgun, upgrading the shotgun/revolver ruined every chance I had of buying a new weapon as the upgrades often times cost almost as much as a new weapon and you barely get any money per level, you'll think you made a lot until you see the prices of weapons and upgrades. Even up until the end I made like $40,000 on the last level picking up every money collectible possible, still not enough to buy a new decent weapon and I never made enough gold to buy the 25 gold pistol and I really didn't feel like playing it again. It felt like playing a pay 2 win mobile game with how little cash it gave me per level. There are very few games I like to completely replay and this game is definitely not one of them so I won't be.
I think the devs get more♥♥♥♥♥♥than they deserve but at the same time as I mentioned, there's a lot of stuff the devs could have improved on right out of the gate before DE2 came to be. I bought this game when it was $5-$10 and I don't regret it but I hate the fact they could have improved the game and made it much better with just a few simple quality of life fixes but never did. The devs also got in trouble for "Data Mining" which they didn't do, it was in their generic contract that covers the mobile games as well, they collect the same info that Google and Apple collects from it's users, probably much less in fact but people assumed they were some how scanning their PC's for data or stealing it from Steam's secure servers which is ludicrous to say the least. I think the devs are good at their jobs, they did create an interesting game but it didn't quite live up to expectations. This is one of those games where I wish Steam let me choose the middle ground for my rating, doesn't quite deserve a negative but also doesn't deserve a brisk thumbs up. If I had to be brutally honest, the game is a 5.5 or 6 out of 10, it's got some spunk but the questionable choices really weigh it down. I'll be giving the game a recommendation to combat the unfair  "data mining" reviews.

This is a Japanese danmaku or "bullet hell" game. The main gist is that you are thrown ridiculous amounts of bullets, usually supposedly in an aesthetic formation that might take a go or two to learn how to best avoid the bullets. Thankfully, while the character sprite is rather large on the screen, the actual hit box that registers the bullet hits is very small - and shown on the screen.
Other than the movement controls, there are four buttons: "slow" (which makes the trailing helpers aim at a target and make you move much slower - very useful), "shoot" (of course), "bomb" (which clears the screen of bullets and most minor enemies) and "special", a button to launch a special attack that eventually reloads.
This game ditches the Ikaruga-style bullet colour coding from eXceed 2nd. Compared to, say, the Touhou series, this isn't as difficult a game; I'd call it far easier than even Imperishable Night. It has voice acting (in Japanese) and static image cutscenes (subtitled in English) that go with it, but the latter can be set to be skipped altogether and the voice volume set to 0 in the options menu.
To my knowledge, there are no alternate chararacters (with different attacks) like in eXceed - Gun Bullet Children, noticeably limiting the replayability.
There aren't all that many danmaku on Steam, and of the three games in the eXceed trilogy, I'd call this the best. Not a glowing recommendation, but...
