Red Solstice is a game that encourages grinding and memorization of map objectives (and it does this even over teamwork) in order to succeed.
Typical games result in 1k - 2k experience for your selected class, and it takes about 10-20k experience to gain one rank in the suit (1% speed, critical rating, that sort of thing). Considering the number of classes there are and there are like 10 ranks in each suit, that is a lot of grinding.
Victory leads to 5k - 6k experience but if you're a new player that will come to you few and far between. And being that each game typically consumes 40 minutes or more, it will still take a considerable amount of time to max out the suit of your preference.
Red Solstice CAN be fun, but the combat tends to be a little bit less entertaining than I was hoping for. I play with auto-targeting for the most part and that actually takes a lot of the fun out of the genre, but necessary, because manual targeting isn't effective enough to take out the swarming armies the AI decides to throw at you.
Game has a tiny community, average at best. Multiiplayer games can take some time to fill (for a newish game).
Art can be hit or miss (portraits). No major complaints, but there isn't enough emphasis on the "cool" element of manning state-of-the-art space marine body armor running around gunning or torching down alien zombies. I don't "feel" it. Far fetched hope that this will be fixed.

Honestly I think this game is awesome.
However there are some cons that should be worked out...
I'll give a list of Pros and Cons
1. Endless possibilities (lots of randomly generated worlds)
2. Thousands of items to collect (if you like collecting things)
3. Vanity items (This is huge for me if you like customizing your characters)
4. Made to be played over and over
5. Moddable (Frackin Universe is by far one of the coolest mods)
6. Hunger - Some games don't have hunger (Eg. Terraria (but Terraria is still awesome though))
7. Pets - You can capture pets like it's Pokemon and honestly we've all wanted to have a pokemon as a pet in a open world.
1. THE STORY - It's a bit long and tedious and really boring. I like the lore but the missions annoy me alot because I'd much rather explore worlds than do missions. The story is also not very in depth, by the end of the game we're still left with many questions. The ending also just ends abruptly and that's that. You get a thank you card for playing the game.
2. REMOVAL OF SOME ITEMS - Granted I never played Starbound when it was in Early Access but whilist scrolling through Chucklefish Fourms and Starbounder Wiki there are so many cool weapons and items that were removed and I can understand some of the other fans out there that lost their favourite item by the time the official version of Starbound came out.
3. Alot of things could (and should) still be added. In a way it feels unfinished. Like one day they just decided to stop adding anything useful to the game. (Eg. A minimap would be great ;
OVERALL, 8/10 I personally would recommend this game.
BUT, I would highly discourage people who either: Hate learning the lore, Exploring, Grinding or if you just want to finish the game as fast as you can. This game was meant to be played slowly with care. If you do not want to spend time on learning about the game than DON'T buy this game. It is not for you.
HOWEVER, to those that like a bit of a challenge or something to take your mind off of or a game to play with your friends than this game is perfect for you!

I'm not going to lie, I came into this game having heard a lot of awful things about it. But I had heard good things about the graphics and the music, and had enough friends say I should buy it and try it before I truly put my judgement forth.
A single playthough hasn't given me enough to really truly say if it's an awful game in the end. The most I can say is that it's not really everyone's thing. To me, it has the seemingly open (yet painfully linear) nature of an interactive fiction meshed into a lightweight platformer. I personally am fond of this style but if you aren't one for story-heavy gameplay-light games, this probably won't tickle your fancy.
Night in the Woods has an extremely surreal story with echoes of Catcher in the Rye. At least for me and others who don't catch on quick, it can take a few playthroughs to truly figure the whole thing out. The art style fits every mood the game throws out there, and the soundtrack is very well crafted for an indie game. The platforming involved is very rudimentary, which is very good for people like me who suck at platfor-- er, don't want to have to worry about complex gameplay to get to the story...
All-in-all I'd say I've played games that are much "better" as regards gameplay elements, but that doesn't matter. Night in the Woods isn't about intense gameplay as much as it is about absorbing the aesthetic and taking the story in as it's dished out. I'd say it works pretty damn well.

A kind of musical adventure combined with a puzzle of hexagons!
Fractal offers various types of gameplay which people with a sense for puzzle games will love. You get to move coloured hexagons around a playfield by placing new ones right next to them. The more connect, the more will spawn and move the others by a field in the given direction.
Main goal is to get a bloom, a flower-type of shape out of at least seven of these hexagons. Several power-ups such as exploding tiles, electric tiles, bonus tiles or push-backs are there to make that easier to accomplish.
Three given gamemodes are present, the puzzle, the campaign and the arcade mode.
In the campaign you get to play through 30 levels of randomly generated fields with given conditions, like limited turns or several colours. Goal is to get enough tiles cleared in a given amount of turns to proceed.
In the puzzle mode you have a limited amount of turns, where you get to fulfill puzzles or given conditions in order to unlock harder and longer ones. The fields are not randomly generated.
The arcade mode offers you unlimited turns, but a timer that runs out. By playing and clearing time tiles fast you get additional time and you manage to get higher scores and reach higher levels. This mode is totally recommended if you want to have a fast paced type of gameplay.
As you proceed in a level, the music will change, the closer you are to failing a stage the music will get slower in campaign and faster in arcade mode. The more progress you make, the more you will hear instruments and beats added to the current rythym, racking up combo spices up that beat too.
In general you get a great game with eye-candy, interactively changing music, wonderful game-mechanic and  a decent variety of gamemodes that should keep you occupied for a quick game or two, or maybe a long-term sitting for a high-score hunt.

For a single player Duke 3D purchase, this edition is the best I've seen and heard so far.
The new coloured lighting, ambient occlusion, "bump mapping" and other engine improvements look great, and fit the non-filtered lego look really well. It looks like something designed by an actual artist instead of a "let's put in every filter ever and call it a day" guy.
The soundtrack sounds good, too. It's digital audio (unsurprisingly), probably recorded from a good wavetable synth or MT32 or something like that - fits the graphics perfectly. The new songs in the new fifth episode are top notch as well, and occasionally reminiscent of John Carpenter's soundtracks.
The fifth episode in general is extremely well made. Lots of new sprites and voice bytes there, and the whole "world tour" aspect is refreshing.
Other have mentioned mouse lag, but I haven't noticed it. I'm usually very sensitive to mouse acceleration/deceleration/smoothing, but at least with vsync disabled (well, Fast Sync enabled in Nvidia's driver) the controls are as they should be.
I've heard that multiplayer doesn't work, but I haven't tried it myself. As I said, for single playing, this is the shizzle.
Maybe a bit expensive, but especially with the new episode and all the visual candy, I'd say it's worth it if you like Duke 3D.

What is there left to say about Dark Souls?
The game holds up really well. It is not the most technically impressive, but it has a wonderful aesthetic. The scope of the world and it's areas and their design is top notch.

There is a nice weight to the combat that the other games don't have and I still enjoy it despite the newer games availability. I will say, I'm not the biggest fan of PVP in this game. I'll take invasions in stride, but the META is mainly fishing for backstabs. Not my favorite.

Give it a chance and you might find something really special here. I know I did.

This is not a game for the faint of heart.
Underneath the cutesy pixel graphics and adorable protagonist is an experience that’s seemingly motivated by torturing the player. Rebirth is easy enough to pick up: you WASD your way through a series of randomly generated rooms on a quest to kill your mother. The game however, will constantly throw a spanner in the works to prevent you from doing so.
You’ll be beaten, abused, and surprised by the allegorical monstrosities that stand in your way. You will die. A lot. Critically injured, you’ll call out to the game for more health pick-ups. And with the ambivalence of a cruel god, the game will give you more bombs, or tease you with hearts placed precariously on ledges you can’t reach.
Desperate for an edge, you’ll pick up a tarot card that you pray will turn the tide and prevent your mother from killing you at behest of the imaginary voice of God. It will read “High Priestess”. You’ll use it in an empty room, and without a word your mother’s leg will come down from the heavens and crush your skull. Game over.
Even the game’s character design is mean. Isaac fights by shooting his tears, and the power-ups that increase his tear speed are items that will make him cry harder. Like onions, toothpicks, a torn photo of his family, or the head of his dead cat. By increasing Isaac’s emotional pain, you gain an edge in battle. Part of you will wonder if this is too much, and for your health you’ll step away from the game and think of happier things, like puppies or bumblebee butts.
And like the masochist you are, you’ll load up the game for more punishment.

This is a port from a mobile FPS shooter. The "freemium" elements can be seen all over the place, but they are no longer used anywhere in the game.
Graphically it is pretty standard for 3D shooters, except the maps mostly consist of straight corridors and rooms.
But gameplay is where it all falls on its face.
You are controlling a special super-soldier wearing armour.
However this seems to be made of wet toilet paper and lined with glass fragments pointing inwards
because you lose one of your precious few health points just by touching a zombie.
It doesn't seem to matter if it is attacking you or not.
Our super-soldier (male or female available) is a highly trained, experienced elite soldier but somehow he is unable to run for more than 5 meters before getting exhausted and gasping and wheezing like he/she has a heart attack. And even an elderly person using a zimmer frame would be ashamed of the normal "walking" pace.
In addition to shooting zombies you can pick up diaries/tablets and read them to get nire information about completely and utterly forgettable and predictable story which is "heavily inspired" (copied) from classics such as Doom3 and System Shock 1&2 (Buy those instead). You can also shoot at some holographic logos hidden on the level to get an end-of-level bonus if you find them all.
Our "super-soldier"  is also terribly inept at reloading his weapons. It looks like someone who has never held a rifle in their hand sloewly fumbling for the magazine and then slowly inserting it before pulling the slide back. This happens even if you don't fully empty the magazine and have one round still in the chamber. The reloading animations are just so atrociously slow. It "only" takes a few seconds with the assault rifle but if you make the mistake of buying a shotgun it becomes much, much worse. A full reload of a few rounds will take more than 10 seconds. While you are attacked by a horde of enemies in a small closet with nowhere to go. Basically you aren't killed by zombies but your inability to defend yourself as the "super-soldier" slowly and leisurely fiddles with his hands. If you decide to switch the weapon, even during the very last frame of the reload animation it will start from the beginning next time you switch to it.
You also have grenades. Which are completely useless. How? How can an instrument of explosive death be useless, you ask? Well, let me tell you. OUr "super"-soldier (this sounds like a joke at this point) can only throw them for about 2 meters. But that is okay as the grenade explosion has a blast radius of about 25 centimeters. It is as if they were ordered form AliExpress.
What's that, dear reader? "Run away?", you say? Oh, boy. I would love to. Too bad the game doesn't seem to like it and locks the only escape route behind me.
You can't heal yourself either anywhere but one-use health stations scattered in the levels.
This is where the game really shows its true, Pay-2-Play nature. You can buy REGENERATING HEALTH for 20 "gold" which you could buy in the mobile version of the game. Too bad you can't use it in the PC version, even if you wanted to waste your money on the game (I think buying this was wasting enough money already), you can't as there is no way to buy gold. And to add insult to injury the enemies drop gold very occasionally bot nowhere near enough to buy anything.
Verdict?
A decent-looking shooter (by mobile standards), completely ruined by glacial, slow-motion reload animations making the game almost unplayable. Only barely worth the €0.99 asking price (was on a 80% sale when I got this).
5/10.

Turns out “zombies in space” is not much of a revelation unless you’re playing Space Pirates and Zombies. There’s potential for revelations, like zombies with alien powers or zero-g zombies or sci-fi guns to mow down zombies, but Dead Effect realizes none of them. Instead it opts to have you blast the same grotesque hordes with the same assortment of guns as you always have, just in front of shiny spaceship walls instead of alleyways or sewers. If the action was competent I could at least give it a pass, but as we’ll go into it can’t even shamble over that bar.
Go ahead, guess how this space zombie game starts. Close your eyes and form an image of the most generic opening to a sci-fi zombie joint imaginable. Got it? Was it you being awakened from cryosleep to find the ship overrun with the living dead? Of course it was, and of course it is. Once you get your bearings and bullets, a mad scientist contacts you over the intercom and orders you around IF YOU WANT TO LIVE and all that. I assume they explain why the ship is full of green zombie gas eventually but I didn’t get that far, so let’s talk about why.
Each level of Dead Effect is a sequence of corridors connecting small rooms and occasional large ones. A couple of these areas have zombies in them, and you have to blast your way past to make it to the exit. These are Romero zombies for the most part, slow-shambling husks that really take a slug to the brainpan to stop, though they sometimes get excited and lunge at you with a sudden burst of speed. Even taking that into consideration, their animations are canned enough to line up perfect headshot chains with little effort. The only real threat they pose is in numbers, and it turns out that’s enough to not only be deadly, but aggravating.
You have your choice of male or female character going in, which also determines your primary and secondary weapons. Dudeguy has an assault rifle and pistol while Ladyperson has a shotgun and revolver, so of course I went with a feminine touch. She’s got no problems chewing through hordes at first but her reloads are absolutely glacial, spanning several seconds for the shotgun. Literally the only thing that kills me in this game is having to reload that god damned shotgun while cornered (which happens all the time because of the tight levels and locking doors during fights). You can find credits to upgrade your guns but I wasn’t able to get enough to really make a difference in 40 or so minutes of play.
There’s a bit of stuff to find when you’re not spilling corpse juices, like extra ammo and credits. Lockers require a little button-mashing game to open and there are holographic signs you can shoot as a collectible challenge. You’ll also find gold on rare occasions, used to buy new guns or unlock permanent bonuses. Dead Effect would probably be a better game if not for that, because it’s pretty obviously a holdover from a free-to-play model on other platforms. You’ll never find enough gold yourself to get anything worthwhile, and I don’t even think there’s a way to buy it if you DID want to throw money away.
Beyond the generic structure and questionable progression, the game feel just isn’t there with this one. Zombie-mashing needs to be rich and visceral to compete these days but everything in Dead Effect feels stiff and canned. Even one-shotting enemies just makes them slump over with poorly-modeled blood sprays out of their neck stump. The weapons don’t feel powerful and there’s very little feedback to scoring hits. The graphics and sound are all serviceable if generic, which is no way to sell a zombie game in this day and age. You’ve got a wealth of better zombie shooters to take up over this one, ones without boring levels, stiff zombies, and loads of other poor design choices.

I really, really, really like this game. I used to play the mobile version constantly. I'll tell you what I like and don't like.
-Graphics are actually really good for a port of a older indie mobile game.
-Took away the more pay to unlock structure and made weapons cost less than in the mobile version and you earn more in game currency than in the mobile version.
-Really bad and cheesy voice acting = much more fun and enjoyable experience.
-Good controls .
-There are some guns I really like.
-Guns (MOSTLY) feel punchy and weighty enough. The sounds for them are mostly good.
-Pretty good optimization.
-Enjoyable single player thats good and short enough for quick playthroughs but not long enough to distract from the main focus of the game (Survival Modes).
-Good (but mostly generic) zombie designs.
-The blood and gore splatters and effetcs are MUCH better than the mobile versions. Looks a little unclear especially at a distance but overall very good.
What I didn't like:
-Mostly uninspired level design for both the story mode and survival missions (Although good for a mobile game and its not bad).
-No online of any form
-Some weapons have really bad iron sights.
-Not enough weapons or added content for a "upgraded" PC port.
Overall its a VERY good port and a good game with a couple flaws. It's normally $5 so there is absolutely no reason not to get it.

Train Fever is a game I enjoy but needs more work. I followed this game for a while before release and Urban Games seems pretty committed to making this a good game so I have confidence in them.
So let's get the basics out of the way. On the one hand it's a pretty straight forward game. If you've played Cities in Motion or Tranportation Tycoon you won't be lost. The game looks pretty good even on my old computer and considering I'm using Vista it runs pretty smoothly.
One of the first problems and it may seem like a small one is that you can't make tracks that crossover each other. You can make switches or bridges, but if I have two tracks (an up and down line) and I want it to cross over and merge with another set of tracks I can't do that. I have to make an additional set of switches. I imagine that will be implimented eventually but it really annoys me because from how I play in games like OpenTTD I usually have one or two main lines with branch lines feeding it.
Another small thing that gets really annoying fast is that you can't build roads over track (unless you build a bridge). Again this will be a quick fix, but it will really started to make me mad when I was trying to upgrade my old lines to high speed tracks.
One thing is that trains are supposed to dynamically spread themselves out they don't stack up on each other, but it seems it has somes bugs. At first it worked fine, but as I got into the late game the system seems to break down so I'd always have three or more trains at one end of a three station line and the other had nothing. I actually watched this for a little bit to figure out why and I think what happens is that when you get into the late game and have trains with a 100+ passengers that it creates  bottleneck with all those people loading and unloading.
I'm not convinced that cargo is really flushed out. I struggle to make cargo lines to make any kind of profit and really by the 20th century it's better to use trucks.
I think the building of roads and tracks needs work. Sometimes it's a crapshoot on what will work and what doesn't.
Still these all strike me as problems that are easy to fix and probably the devs are on it already. This game is really for people who really love transport tycoon games.

But on a serious note this game is a difficult co-op of up to 8 players with a single player campaign to it also.  The Red Solstice has a steep learning curve for new players, and there is also a bit of a grind when coming to ranking up which essentially is just giving you a bonus to stats each time.  This game rewards good teamwork and punishes mercilessly bad teamwork.  They're plenty of in depth guides for new players and the community is pretty helpful in breaking you into the game.  I would advise having a teamspeak or something similar even if its just to listen due to the fast pace of this game.  You may notice at times desynch and bugs not gona lie it's nothing game breaking but it's defently noticable especially if you join a high ping host.  The player base has been revived so finding a match with others isn't nearly as hard plus it's got a single player now so waiting isn't really much of a problem anymore thankfully. That's not to say the playerbase won't leave in the future but for now it's doing well.
As for gameplay this game features 8 different classes each with their own unique abilities, strengths, and weaknesses. During the gameplay you gain energy which can power these different abilites making them more potent or unlocking new ones.  Six different maps to choose from and a myriad of different monsters and bosses all eagerly awaiting to chew your face off.  They're 4 diifferent main difficulties from Recruit to Aetridan with 8 different sub difficutlies to add with it. The objective of the co-op aspect is to survive 15 waves of hellish creatures all the while doing objectives and scavenging for items to use. At the end of the last wave you are to complete the last objective and then evac to the a certain point of the map, on average a game winning match will last around an hour.
So would i recommend this game... hell yes i would.   I had a great time with it and if you're willing to work with people it's one of the most rewarding experiences beating the game with others

A kind of musical adventure combined with a puzzle of hexagons!
Fractal offers various types of gameplay which people with a sense for puzzle games will love. You get to move coloured hexagons around a playfield by placing new ones right next to them. The more connect, the more will spawn and move the others by a field in the given direction.
Main goal is to get a bloom, a flower-type of shape out of at least seven of these hexagons. Several power-ups such as exploding tiles, electric tiles, bonus tiles or push-backs are there to make that easier to accomplish.
Three given gamemodes are present, the puzzle, the campaign and the arcade mode.
In the campaign you get to play through 30 levels of randomly generated fields with given conditions, like limited turns or several colours. Goal is to get enough tiles cleared in a given amount of turns to proceed.
In the puzzle mode you have a limited amount of turns, where you get to fulfill puzzles or given conditions in order to unlock harder and longer ones. The fields are not randomly generated.
The arcade mode offers you unlimited turns, but a timer that runs out. By playing and clearing time tiles fast you get additional time and you manage to get higher scores and reach higher levels. This mode is totally recommended if you want to have a fast paced type of gameplay.
As you proceed in a level, the music will change, the closer you are to failing a stage the music will get slower in campaign and faster in arcade mode. The more progress you make, the more you will hear instruments and beats added to the current rythym, racking up combo spices up that beat too.
In general you get a great game with eye-candy, interactively changing music, wonderful game-mechanic and  a decent variety of gamemodes that should keep you occupied for a quick game or two, or maybe a long-term sitting for a high-score hunt.

A really nice remastering that adds a few modern touches to the renderer while still retaining the original retro feel of the original Build engine.
The new episode - Alien World Order - is a fantastic addition, with some great original level designs from the original Duke3D alumni, Richard 'Levelord' Gray and Allen H. Blum III. However, the quality isn't super consistent, with levels running the gamut from "Exceeds the quality of the original game" with thoughful, inventive and professional layouts, to "Feels like a fan map from 1996" that have horrific flow, very little focus and just feel amateur in comparison to what else is on offer.
The developer commentary would also have been a very worthwhile addition, if there was more of it. While the first level of each episode generally has a few commentary nodes smattered about which contain some really interesting insights into the development of game, later levels contain few nodes, if any at all. It does feel like a bit of a bait and switch; encouraging fans of the original to play through the game again to find new information only to be left wanting once the first level is completed.
While the framerate is mostly good, as you would expect for a game that's has such a low relative complexity for modern systems, I've also encountered rather frequent framerate issues after the game has been running for 10 minutes or more. Switching out and back in to fullscreen mode with ALT+Enter seems to fix it for a short period, however.
Another new addition (At least to PC versions) is the timeline feature, that after death allows you to return to any point in the level, basically making quicksave-scumming an obselete tactic. However, the longer you take in a level, the more squirrelly the controls for the timeline become, with slow updates making it very difficult to pinpoint the exact point you wish to return to.
One thing to note for older fans of the series is that this is missing content that was available in the previous Megaton Edition of the game, that being the expansion episodes of Duke It Out In D.C., Life's A Beach and Nuclear Winter. Honestly I'm personally not particularly upset about the loss of these episodes as I found them to be bland, uninspired and tawdry affairs, but others have fonder memories of these and as such it's worth pointing out their absence.
All up, it's a decent package and is arguably the most definitive edition of the game for newcomers of the series, and a nice spit-shine for returning players.

Dark Souls might be one of the best game ever made.
In Dark Souls you play as "The chosen undead", a cursed man of unknown origin. After you escape from the jailcell you're trapped in, you go on a long and difficult adventure to restore light to the world.
The beauty of Dark Souls is that all the gameplay mechanics work together in (near) perfect harmony. The difficulty elevates the story and themes in the game to new heights. The story of the playercharacter is in many ways identical to the player's own story. The soundtrack enchances the atmosphere of the game better than in any other game I've played. There are many more exmples of this, and the game is truly masterfully designed.
The gameplay of the game is exellent. Everything in the game is built around combat, and it works really well. You have a light and heavy attack with each weapon, and some special moves to counter and break your opponents blocks. There are also a ton of different weapons with different movesets, so there will be options for any kind of player. In addition to the physical combat, you have the option to use miracles, pyromancy and more. The combat may sound basic, but with the game's exellent level and enemy design, it is fun and intense the whole way through.
The gameworld is the real star of this game. It is fairly big, with many different places to visit. What makes Dark Souls' world exceptional though, is that it is all built as one big entity. What I mean by that is that the world is not cut into different levels, it rather feels like one big level that you explore through the whole game. The different areas of the world are connected togehter by multiple paths and shortcuts you can unlock. It's difficult to explain how amazing this world design is, but if you play the game you'll know what I mean.
The last important thing I want to mention is the story in the game. Or rather, the lore. The story of the player's character is not particularly interesting, but the lore of the world is. It is very deep and philosophical, and not in the "cheesy" way. There are tons of interesting characters and events that are impossible to forget. The lore in Dark Souls is not easy to piece together, but if you do, you'll be rewarded with some of the most interesting stories gaming has to offer.
All things considered, Dark Souls is one of the best games ever made. It is masterfully designed, and will be a rewarding experience to anyone who does not give up because of it's difficulty. I can't recommend this game enough, so please play it if you have not yet.

This game really brought challenge and fun together well. So much exploration, no direction to go. You could go and fight an end-game boss before fighting some of the easier bosses. So many around every corner and with the specific fast travel points, (when you actually unlock fast travel much later) this adds a whole new level of backtracking, but in a good way. Sometimes you'll have to get creative with how you approach enemies and even exploring. The name explains the challenge, Prepare to Die. Fitting, to say the least. There are a few issues though about this game, ones that really hinder the performance. The biggest being the co-op system. A lot of the time it isn't exactly reliable and you could sit for a long time to just find your friend's summon sign, or vice-versa. Other than that maybe a few bugs here and there but the co-op issue is my biggest pain. Still, I highly recommend this for all you who want a challenge. And a little tip for you guys: Some monsters have tails. Target the tails.

HEY. YOU. WITH THE STEAM FUNDS.
Yeah, you, the one scoffing at why you even clicked on the review page for this game you think you'll never end up buying. I get it, I do. It's frilly, it's girly, it's not your tipical action RPG. Well listen up boys, cause this ain't any sort of namby-pamby walk in the park.
Before you punch a wall to regain your manliness that you feel has dropped by even looking into this game, you should know something. If you're into judging a book by it's cover, you might be turned off by Long Live The Queen's anime-esque art style or it's female protaganist - you don't know how wrong you are.
LLTQ is a text based RPG that puts you in the shoes of Elodie, Queen of Nova. Or, should I say, almost queen; tough luck buddy, you've got 40 weeks to survive before you get that far.
Oh, I know what you're thinking. '40 Weeks? Like three months? Ha. I'll finish that, play some Dota, AND punch a wall to get back my manliness card.' YEAH NO. You're dealing with assassins, monsters, rebellions, a set of pissy (read: deadly) relatives, and an entire kingdom looking at you to fix it. Or not, you know. They could always just kill you - I'm sure that'd fix the problem. Somehow.
And here you're saying WOAH, HOLD UP. I've seen this before! You won't get me with your cutesy violence and your lack of guns!
Listen up, son. You can be impaled, exploded, imploded, poisoned, drained, and, in one unfortunate ending, eaten. Trust me, this game is very much not what you think it is. The numerous death senarios coupled with the surprisingly gruesome art makes for just as wild a ride as anything you've got.
And trust me, I haven't played this for nearly 40 hours for nothing. You think you can make it through in one shot? Don't make me laugh. You'll be dead before you even try to eat- never mind.
As for me, I'll be leveling up my mage skills. I have a date with an enemy Lumen, and I don't intend to let him walk away with his limbs intact.

This review is going to be targeted at the negative reviewers. Lately the top negative reviews are coming from people who haven't played the game enough to know how to get ahead and have a good time doing it. Thruth be told that the game is in alpha and there are many many things that may need polished and/or reworked, it doesn't mean its a bad game at all. So time to give a little incite as to what it's like to play AND ENJOY Miscreated.
So from an experienced player in Miscreated i'm going to share what I know and my opinion of the game and address some of the common misconceptions people get from playing the game for a few hours not knowing what they're doing.
+ Loot is not a problem. A lot of people say that loot is super rare and you can never find guns. that is not true. You just have to know where to look. The spawn system in the game spawns loot everywhere (literally), but obviously it's better in certain spots. There's many videos on YouTube if you want to get some tips in where to look for loot in Miscreated, a few tips of my own are to always look in cars (especially police cars), to check the tops of dressers and shelves, and to leave no stone unturned. Look everywhere, once you get a feel of the game you can sweep through houses and towns swiftly and if you're lucky you can get fully geared in less than 20 mins.
+ Combat is difficult. I had a hard time getting used to the combat, it seems unfair and often makes you rage when you get shot once and die, but the other day you shot a guy 4 times with a shotgun and he didn't. It's painful, but that's the way it's meant to be. It's the same way for everyone. I think it needs to be polished up quite a bit, but it's fine where it is at the moment. If you play smart and watch your surroundings you can avoid being attacked in most scenerios; being snuck up on always happens though. It takes a long time to get used to the combat and the aiming (it's more gritty than traditional shooters in my opinion). You will die alot, but if it wasnt this hard then it wouldn't be as rewarding. Luckily, the map is urban asf so you can dissapear faster than your dad 8 years ago. Keep in mind that not everyone has the time for this or has the patience, if this game isn't for you then don't post a negative review just because of that.
+ Play with friends. The game can be easier in a group and more enjoyable (as is in most survival games). If you want Miscreated just to have a laugh with friends and have some survival combat aswell then play with your friends. If you have no friends (lel) then don't worry, not everyone in miscreated is a bandit. Trying to find people to group up with isn't hard, but there will always be people that don't want to and will just kill you :P that's just how it is.
+ - The game also has RP potential (if you're into that); you can hold people up and take their sht then ride off in a
transit bus with your squad. Sit around the campfire and tell stupid stories or some sht. Get on teamspeak or discord
or whatever and try to focus on having a good time more than getting phat loot becuase you'll have more fun.
+ - The map is barren. Not like in a desert wasteland, but as an urban wasteland. There are so many nooks and crannies and hidden places that there's a bit too much. It's not really bad but not really good either. People will complain that the map is small in regards as to where you can actually find people and useful things and that is understandable, but not everyone likes to explore the map just to explore or maybe not enough of a beefy PC that it's cool to do so. The game is BEAUTIFUL. The graphics is a big + to the game; optimization isn't too horible either. I do believe that some more hidden areas could be more rewarding, but some of them already are; people just don't bother to search for them.
+ - IT'S NOT FINNISHED! Combat is not polished and reworked enough yet to be perfect. The map isn't complete yet. Key game systems such as armor and hitboxes were just added. Base building is♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ It is in early access and things are being added and polished constantly; the devs really listen to their playerbase and update the game accordingly. They put in a massive effort to make this game and are still working on it so give them some credit. They can do things in what ever order they please so don't b*tch about one thing or the other while they're working on something else; they'll get to it eventually because they're good devs. Not everyone has the patience for this and posts toxic comments on updates ignoring all the improvements that were just made to the game. Chill out kid ur twelv it's in aplha.
+ The game is worth it's $. Miscreated is only $20 and is on sale on occasionally on weekends and most holidays. Pick the b*tch up for $5 to $10 on a sale and give it a go; it's damn well worth $30-$40 for people that can learn to enjoy it.
+ Servers are not a problem. There are servers for people who like it full to the brim with lads fighting like rats over the guy with the duffle bag. There are servers with moderate population (which i recommend 15-25) so not every town is looted to the last drop and there is enough people to where you encounter them often. Or if you're lame and just want to play alone there's probably an empty server where you can be lame I guess. And atleast for me ping isn't and issue either; I can find my perfect server in less than 2 mins and bookmark it for later.
So to sum it up it's a good game with lots of potential and its getting improved all the time. If you don't have the patience to deal with dying or don't have enough time to have consumed by this game then it might not be for you. Survival games aren't for everyone; that doesnt mean that survival games r bad just because you don't truly like them. This is a damn good game. Some cons in the game would have to be that zombies respawning is more of a hassel than it should be, you can only carry so much on your person (So many slots depending on your pack size and 1 supply type item) so I find myself going back to the closest buildings on foot because it's not worth the noise to take a car only to find that the house I just cleared now has 7 zombies in it again. It'd really be nice if they put at least a moderate delay so you don't end up clearing the same building 3 times just trying to get the supplies from it. Played this game for a bit now, trying out all sorts of difficulties, settings and map varriants. in overall i would say that it most reminds me of the early days of Transport Tycoon(build, setting, trains -etc), with a mixture of Industry Giants(time line), and Cities in motions based line building and interacting system. the playing it self feel fine and good on higher difficulties the game can become quite challanging as well to make the most of your little company and set-up a profitable line system to not run to deep and debt and fail, although the 3mixture seems like a real good combo there are also down sides, such as the line system not being able to work out how switches interact on multible track stations. which severly limits your options in station building and useage of the stations, when you make a loop track with 2 lines going opposite of one another the game will still run both trains in the same direction which will lead to a full stop since the trains will meet and be stuck since non took a side track. The industry is really limited and seems to dislike trains for cargo, as i placed many times tracks + freight station next to a industry which will then refuse to use the station and line, and even when it uses it, it just does not want to increase in production nor upgrade to match the capacity of your trains on its side. that said, it will interact propperly with trucks(tried on mutlible time era's (1850's, 1900's, 1950's and ++)).
that said in overall i would say the game can be very fun if your a true fan of the series like Cities in motion, Indrustry Giant, Transport Tycoon -etc. so far even before the patch the game ran really stable on my system and never resulted in crashed. big maps can take a while to load but are worth the wait in the end. the start no matter how you start(easy, medium or hard). is a challange, setting up wrong will make you fail and quickly run in debt which then leads to a restart of the game. The one thing that was quite annoying is to see that your passengers will just dissapear from the train/bus they sit in as it moves(had a train with 120passengers leaving the station, to arrive at its destination with just 105passengers).
Pro's:
- Big maps.
- good city devolopment.
- Infrastructure build option.
- Line system.
- loads of options in difficulties and optimizations of the lines/tracks/roads.
- Easy interface.(though feels a bit empty).
- Easy train/bus/truck build mode.
- 3-D
- Music
Con's:
- Industry dis-likes trains.
- Very limited Industry options.
- The build system although good working seems to have troubles adjusting to slightly lower tracks then railroads, making it hard to build tunnels and overpasses easy.(eg. it wont suggest to make a tunnel or bridge if it cant make a on level overpass. but just keeps saying "Collision" when you then raise the terain for say a bridge overpass the road will collide with the raised height for the bridge)
- Passengers will just vannish from your trains as they ride.
- Trains/Busses dissapear as purchace options after a X amount of time, sometimes forcing you to buy a to expencive train to keep a line open.
- City's seem to expand away from your station(at least in my games Xd).
- Not easy to upgrade a train/bus/truck. said item needs to first go depot, trucks and busses need to be sold(very easy botton for that though), but upgrading a train, means sending it to station, open the train window + Depot window + Buy train window, Buy a train, remove the locomotive of the said train(sell or move). then place the new locomotive on the excisting train. re-assign its route and send it out again). It in overall is not a dissaster, just time and engery consuming if you get a big network with 50/60 locomotives that need to be replaced since they ran over their livetime span.
In overall though despite the "flaws" that i have encountered i still love this game and will continue playing it with pleasure, some of my con's might just be from still getting used to the building of. for instance, though seeing somethings added(maybe as optional options(like TDD). where you can keep the old steam locomotives/carriages/trucks/busses -etc would be nice to see, as well as more industry, and no Anti-train mentenality on industry would be very nice as well.
all in all i would still rate this gate with 8/10 cause i just love these games, and this games somewhat cleances my thrists after TDD :D

QUALITY OVER CONTENT>

Summary:
Starbound is a well-rounded side scrolling adventure-crafting-survival game that is enjoyable to play alone or with friends.
Graphics:
For a side scrolling RPG the graphic is quite good, in my opinion better than terraria although there is no graphics options such as anti-aliasing, Ambient Occlusion to make the game look even better.
Sound and Voice:
The music is well written, starting from the main menu you will encounter the soothing piano music playing in the background. Throughout the gameplay the background music will perfectly adjust to the biomes or location of your character to provide a seamless gameplay. There is no voice is the game.
Gameplay:
Starbound is unique in its own way, the gameplay is simply new and refreshing for a side scrolling adventure-crafting-survival game. The difficulty of the game is well set, it is challenging enough but not too easy for entry level player such as myself. The story is entertaining and will keep you playing for a good 8 hours. The random generated quests by NPCs are kinda repetetive but they will keep you entertained for a while. Despite the procedural generation of its own planets and biomes, if you play the game long enough you will encounter very similar structures such as dungeons and villages. The algorithm for procedural generation could be improved to provide more depth to the gameplay, keeping things fresh everytime.
However, Starbound  supports MODS and the devs have been working with the community to add new and exciting content in the future.
Conclusion:
I would recommend Starbound to both experienced and new players to its genre. This game is defintely worth trying out, as of patch 1.3 the devs provide enough content and I can see so much potential in future patches as free-content will be added overtime + capabilities of modding.

Dead effect is a PC port of a mobile FPS with much improved graphics. You can still see the remnants of the previous mobile control scheme e.g. the "tap to open" mechanic for breaking open locks and the dodging of attacks by the first miniboss.
I can't recommend this game given the many issues but here are the pros and cons in case you wish to check it out.
Pros:
- Not bad graphics but with a caveat down in the cons section.
- Slightly different take on the whole zombie thing (I won't spoil the surprise)
- An actual explanation of repeated enemy models and why you can respawn which you usually don't see.
- Really easy to get achievements with the exception of the kill 10k zombies which is a grind I am still working for
- Got this for a tiny fraction of a dollar on BundleStars
Cons (or the long list of why I can't recommend the game)
- Odd gun stats, for example:
- The 7.62x39 AR you find does less damage than the 5.56 R you buy later which does much less damage than the 5.56 AR that is more expensive.
- Shotguns have ridiculous range. I was killing two zombies in one shot at about 50 yards.
- The gun are loosely based off of real world equivalent guns AKM, M4, XM8, Franchi SPAS, etc. though they don't follow them well. The XM8 equivalent starts with a 20 round mag and the SPAS equivalent is a pump action shotgun when it is semi-auto.
- The SPAS equivalent is also listed as taking 34 gauge shells but does more damage than the 12 gauge shotgun? 34 gauge is tiny... it is also the BEST gun in the game
- Your character tosses grenades like a pansy
- A lot of textures are bloomed out or darkened too much to hide their poor or lack of textures. Also blood spatters don't look quite right.
- gold being a holdover from the mobile days being separate from money so when you run out of gold items to buy it just sits there for no reason
- Zombies with ranged attacks are insanely accurate. Grenade zombies are the worst.
- Game is super easy, if it weren't for the grenade zombies instakilling you from nowhere, the game would be a breeze
- Some of the achievements aren't clear. For example one is to get through a mission without using a healing terminal. What you don't know is you also can not die and spend money to respawn OR have the auto healing effect that you pay gold for on for the mission.
- The zombie hitboxes are somewhat off. there are zombies that have really high body resistace but die quickly with headshots but at certain angles, their body hitbox extends out a bit and blocks off their head.
- The zombie attack animation compared to registered hit to player is off. Several times I have been hit by a zombie when they were still at the beginning of their swing.
- Spelling and grammar is bad, though they are not native english speakers from what I gather so I don't judge them too harshly. Also, I make many grammar and spelling mistakes so who am I to talk.
So, to recap, I would not recommend buying it for $5. If you happen to get it for a fraction of a dollar from Bundlestars, give it a play it will be a quick time sink with easy achievements. Don't pay too much attention to it while doing so.

I wanted to put a couple hours into the game before I wrote a good review so here it goes. TRS is a different kind of game, that goes unsaid, if you are not into working with a team via a Chat client (Teamspeak, mumble, etc) you may see some real let downs come gameplay time. Like any other stragety game knowing what the game plan is for your team is important and without a solid communication system you will see teams in public lobbies fall before wave 10.
Good news is that there is a teamspeak server dedicated to TRS (ts.game-com.de) and as a new player to the game I can say my experience went from crappy, to excellent the moment I signed on there and began playing with people. Not only do you learn a lot from more experienced players (Veterans) but you get to learn a lot of things you wouldn't find out by playing in random lobbies with random people.
"But Dagnome, there is a in game chat"
True, but like most games with built in VOIP it isn't very good or used at all.
To sum up, if you are looking for a great team game to play with your friends then TRS will hit that sweet tooth, it can be frustrating because on teammate can screw up the whole game, but it can also be very rewarding like the time me (Medic) and an assault survived together after our team was slaughtered and evaced to safety

The Red Solstice is a top down, strategy shooter that plays like a blend of quality custom Starcraft 2 maps and Alien Swarm. It pits you and up to 7 other Human controlled marines against hordes of the monstrosities created by the STROL virus. To survive and complete your objective you must work with your teamates,scavenging materials, making plans for the hectic closing moments of a match, and dispatching the various dangers you will encounter during your stay at Tharsis colony. A Typical match of The Red Solstice can last around an hour, so do not expect the typical drop in drop out style multiplayer that many games today utilize. keep this in mind when you put aside time to play the game.
I would like to mention that this game is hard, and can be incredibly brutal at times. Excpect to die quite often as a new player, so don't feel put off by it, it happens to everyone. Despite the difficulty, failure still nets class and account experience for you rendering even a loss into meaningful progress of both in game XP as well as real life player skill. To help alleviate the difficulty for newcomers, a certain ammount of free automatic respawns are granted to players below a certain rank. Additionally, players seeking assistance can ask both the developers and the community for advice as this game has some of the most active devs and most helpful community members of any game I have ever played. The community has also prepared a variety of guides that cover almost every aspect of the game with an incredible ammount of detail, I highly recommend new players look over these.
In conclusion, The Red Solstice is a very unique, and very fun game. It offers a large ammount of replayabillity in the multiplayer modes and a good ammount of content aimed at those who prefer single player activities. I wholeheartedly recommend this game to anyone willing to give it the modicum of patience required to learn its particular nuances.

NOTE: Since people will see this game and say: "this looks like Civilization 5." I will say it right now that the only similarity between this game and Civilization 5 are the Hexagon Based Grid Map, Leadership Choice and User Interface (UI). Everything else is completely different.
INTRODUCTION:
Warlock: Master of the Arcane, despite sharing the same look as the more popular Civilization series, is definitely NOT the same game. Warlock: Master of the Arcane plays differently with its own mechanic that delivers a lot of fun to strategy and fantasy world players alike.
It is an X4 Strategy game originally released in 2012. It lets the player take the role of one of several 'Great Mages' who vie for control of the world of Ardania (from the Majesty Series of games) using vast armies and mighty spells to aid them in their struggle.
PROS:
+ Fantasy Theme: -This game places you in a fantasy world populated by different mystic and magical creatures. Raise an empire of the Undead, Monsters, Humans or Elves and utilize a wide variety of magical spells to buff your forces or smite your foes.
+ Combat Focused Gameplay: -The Empire building on this game is based primarily on combat, fighting with the other factions and the different monsters that constantly threaten your borders. It delivers a very satisfying gameplay since most Magical Spells will make for some very interesting strategy. (Ex. Having problem crossing that lake? = Waterwalk.)
+ Extensive Upgrades: - Each military unit has so many upgrade choices each time they level-up that once they reach max level, they can be called Hero units in their own right. Add to this your Tech upgrades and Spell buffs, then you will have beast of an army.
+ Epic World: -The game offers your standard Small, Medium, Large and Huge map sizes but it also allows you to add more 'Worlds' that you can invade. Just look for the portal that goes there and fight extremely dangerous monsters inside before reaping the rewards.
CONS:
- No Vsync: -This is inexcusable. The game suffers greatly from Screen Tearing and yet the options menu offers no Vertical Synchronization option to mitigate this. The player will be forced to use manual Vsync provided by the Nvidia Control Panel (or its AMD equivalent).
- Brain-Dead AI: -The AI really needs some more work to be done. I have seen the AI countless of times mobilize for an invasion, only to cancel it the last moment and just have its army run around in circles rather than coordinate a proper attack. The monsters roaming the country side poses more of a threat than the Faction AI. (It might be different on Hard or Impossible)
- Lack of Variety: -There are 16 different Great Mages you can play OR your own Custom Mage, but the bonuses or faction specialty is so negligible that it almost makes no difference. Add to this, there are only THREE, playable starting races in the game.
- Poor Research Tree: -Instead of Tech, you research Spells, which is good, but there is no Research Tree available. as far as I know, the game randomly generates 5 spells and will require the player to choose one of those spells to research.
CONCLUSION:
In its own rights, Warlock: Master of the Arcane is a very refreshing take on the 4X Turn-based Strategy Genre. I definitely feel this game deserve your attention if you are a 4X or Strategy fan in general. It provides a fun and enjoyable experience.

Like Civ 4 and/or 5?  A fan of traditional fantasy settings and overly powerful magic spells?  Want to mix the two?  Warlock is just that.
The setting is based on the Majesty universe: all the typical fantasy tropes (humans, undead, dwarves, elves, dragons, trolls, etc, etc in a medieval time period) with a lighter (less doom and gloom, more tongue-in-cheek) feel.  The gameplay is mostly Civ, but with a few twists.  Build progressions for cities feel like a good mix between Civ and the Majesty world, and the tech tree is replaced by a progressive magic research tree.  Want the best units?  Rather than relying upon long term tech research, powerful units are acquired through hired or captured heroes and specific city building dependencies.  Research is still a big part of the game, but it instead leads to more powerful spells that you cast to effect the world directly: heal, destroy, buff or curse units, terraform land, bless your cities, etc.
While I was never personally a fan of Civ's barbarian AI (frequently capable of screwing players randomly early on, never relevant in later game), Warlock really improves upon the typical "barbarian" elements and adds a more RPG feel with interest and depth to the later game and a better balance early on.  Rather than generic hordes or goodie huts, enemy AI forms into unique AI enemy sets,  complete with quests, unique spawn points, and build-up over time.  Ignore those generic AI spiders over there?  They will grow stonger, more numerous, and vastly more dangerous over time.
Another twist is the addition of alternate worlds accessible through discoverable "gates".  Like the general map, these lands are completely developable, but they tend to contain higher level AI enemies as well.  Conquer one of these worlds and you'll have some great resources at your disposal, as well as a narrow gateway to defend your territory via these secondary worlds... but to do so you may have to fight some tough AI "barbarians" on this second front, all while playing the main map's Civ game against your usual foes.  Let an opponent "dig in" to one of these zones and you've got an even bigger fight on your hands.
Also, since the time-span is limited and not a span of all civilization like Civ, it pays to maintain, improve and defend every unit.  Even docile units gain XP and level up, and the most active units can accumulate quite a pile of buffs and levels.  Dislike losing veteran units in Civ?  You'll really hate losing them in Warlock.
There's some general system steamlining too.  Personally, I find the lower level of city and civilization micromanagement an improvement, but if you prefer city management to unit development, your mileage may vary.  Diplomacy, general civilization alignment, and city development and mass unit buildup is fairly simplified by Civ standards in favor of hero units, conquest and a questing system.  It doesn't feel like an oversight though, since the former, simplified areas aren't really where Warlock concentrates its focus, and the later mechanics are well fleshed out.
Overall, Warlock is a pretty great take on the Civ formula.  If you like fantasy rpgs and 4x style games as well, you'll likely find Warlock at least worth the entry price.

First of all, there's some really bad mouse smoothing or acceleration going on, which took a lot of getting used to and took away much of the enjoyment.
New lighting effects are neat, but make some places feel much darker than they used to be. There are no graphical options so you can't e.g. use 3d rendering without the other visual effects.
Rerecorded lines are very hit and miss, some sound like they should, some sound bored and out of character (especially the "ugh, where is it").
Developer commentary, which is the main reason I was interested in this game, is really bad. Barely any trivia or insight, just them sounding bored and saying how cool the stuff on the level is. And it's only available on 2-3 levels per episode (except for E5 which is fully commentated and possibly the most interesting one).
And finally, the episode 5 itself. It's good, but not worth more than $5 in my opinion. Introduces only 1 new enemy which is more annoying than anything, setting you on fire, and goes for more modern level design, with very little backtracking. The levels themselves are much larger in size, but they feel like they're borrowing from the modern-retro level design of Painkiller and Serious Sam, with loads of ammo, big arenas connected with corridoors and huge hordes of enemies from the start. Which also means almost no pacing, they're throwing Battlelords at you from the first level. Yes, the episode is harder than the previous ones, but it's not because of smart enemy placement or puzzles to figure out, but the number of enemies thrown at you at once.
Overall I can only recommend this version if you haven't played Duke 3D at all since it's the only version available right now, though you can still find Atomic/Megaton on key reselling sites, which is a much better option.

While Fractal it has its pros and cons, its low price point and addictive mechanics make it a must-play for anyone who enjoys casual puzzle games.
One of the most noticable aspects of the game is its beautiful graphics. It runs excellently in full HD resolution on the highest graphics settings despite my machine's very limited processing and graphics memory. In addition to the sheer quality, unique little doodles on each campaign level add a little something extra.
Unfortunately, these doodles tend to be the extent of the in-game instructionals. If you're like me, and prefer to learn to play a game by playing it instead of reading through a manual, it will take you some time to get acquainted with the mechanics. The addition of late-game mechanics hinders game progress, as I tended to die (and be forced to restart the level at a low point value, or replay the campaign from the beginning) several times before grasping the intricacies of utilizing new powerups.
Also disappointing was the soundtrack: the game devs heavily push the soundtrack on the store page, insisting that it's ever-changing depending on how well you play. This simply isn't the case. It's the same soundtrack every single time, with slight changes in tempo if you really start to suck.
However, the addictive gameplay mechanics more than make up for Fratal's failings. It makes for a great time-waster, and is well worth its sale price.

DISCLAIMER: This review mainly focuses on my experience with Miscreated.
When I first played this game I thought it was just another DayZ survival game.
My friend thought otherwise and saw a whole lot of potential.
After many updates later my friend then encouraged me to give the game one more try.
Playing the game for a 2nd time was very different from the first time. There were a lot of different feelings to this game.
In the world of Miscreated you feel scared. Scared for your life because you invested lots of time into finding loot or certain aesthetic gear.
In this game you also feel like everyone is hostile;you will find many people that want to kill and loot your body. If your someone with decency, then you feel sorrow for those hostile players that you have shot and murdered over self defence. It feels absolutely traumatic to experience. I think it's a good thrill that everyone should experience.
As for finding friendly people in this game..people can be trusted but you need to make certain precautions to make sure that they will not kill you. In the game you can find an item that allows you to speak to people but only at certain frequencies (Walkie-talkie). If you are not on the same frequency you can still hear them faintly depending on how far apart your frequencies are. You can adjust these frequencies using pg up and pg down buttons on the keyboard. I found this part about the game being the most coolest part.
When me and my friends were playing this game we met some people that claimed to be friendly. We took these percautions, and to ensure that trust; we ended up adding eachother on steam, and invited these players into our discord. From there on we travled and experienced the world of Miscreated together.
Although playing solo is still fun to play. I strongly recommend playing this game with a group of friends.

I've played this game on and off throughout the development cycle, and while I love all the extras that have been added into the game, ultimately after a few hours, there just isn't much to do.  It's not just a matter of finding your dream island- that's easy enough. Even if sharks are surrounding it, 9 times out of 10 they won't even bother you.
You normally end up with so much food and a measely amount of water, even with the recent addons of the water collector- if you don't have the fortune of finding 2 buckets, you're going to be suffering from lack of water really fast.
Mostly however, it's just the lack of danger that gets to me. Yes there are sharks, and yes I've died to them countless times- but it's usually after I'm bored with the game and actively searching for them as a means of something to do. That's not how a survival game should work- there needs to be a lot more danger present that can appear at any time. I want to know that if I take a chance getting into the water, there's a stronger chance that I won't be able to make it back out if I'm not careful.
I'm just not feeling it currently. I just swam from one island to the next without coming across a single shark. Why even need a raft in the first place?
I love this game, and it has so much promise, but there needs to be more danger to engage with. Otherwise it gets dull after the first few hours.
Would I recommend it? Currently? No. It's got nothing to keep you coming back for more unlike other current survival sims. But it's got promise. I hope it can eventually get to where it needs to be to become a strong title in the genre.

So I decided to take the time to make a full-on review of this game, covering several aspects of the game. I have no real TL;DR, so just read the first and laft segments.
“What is State of Decay?”
State of Decay is an open-world zombie game in which you scavenge for supplies to assist your small community of survivors. As you slay zombies, explore, and loot buildings, you'll discover a variety of weapons and items, along with other survivors you can recruit to your cause of survival. You'll also level up your character's various attributes, such as fighting (reducing stamina cost to swing a melee weapon), shooting (increasing accuracy), and cardio (increasing your maximum stamina, reducing stamina cost of running) among others, giving a definite character progression among your survivors.
“What's the story?”
The story is rather simple, as one would expect; after coming home from a camping trip, Marcus, your main character, and his buddy Ed notice some sick-looking people. After approaching them, they're attacked, and fight them off – only able to survive by destroying the head of their assailants (sound familiar?). They quickly meet up with Maya, an army veteran with a sharp eye and good trigger finger. Following a radio signal to a church in town, they meet up with some more survivors, and... that's about it for meaningful story. The remaining story just gives a reason for the less generic missions. It does its job, but isn't particularly deep or interesting. (6/10)
“How does it look?”
The game actually looks quite good. The semicartoonish art style (think Saints Row) lends to the vague absurdity of a zombie apocalypse, and the models are very nice looking. The only problems lie in the lighting and the leaves. The trees and bushes look quite ugly and static, and are distracting from the otherwise good-looking game. As for the lighting, the game is actually an eyesore at night, opting for a black-and-blue look. It's meant to deter you from exploring at night, but it's rather annoying to boot up the game at night. (7/10)
“How does it sound?”
The audio quality of the game is fine. None of the voice actors really stand out, and if there's any music in the game, it's completely ambient. The sound of cracking zed skulls, of course, is satisfying, and there's a nice “thunk” or “blam” to your melee weapons and guns, respectively. (6/10)
“How does it control?”
The controls on the Xbox 360 pad (the controller I used) are nice and responsive. You move [of course] with the left stick, move the camera with the right stick, jump with A, melee with X, kick with Y, sneak with B, aim with LT, shoot while aiming with RT, use items with RB, sprint with LB, and use the D-Pad for various functions [left and right are to select different usable items, up brings up your character screen, down brings up your radio menu]. There's no delay to the controls, and it plays rather smoothly with this setup. (10/10)
“How does it run?”
The game runs smoothly enough... Except when it saves. Saving, at least on my machine, causes horrible stuttering for about 10 seconds. This is also one of those games where you need to be able to see what's going on at all times, so as soon as it starts chugging, I have to hit the pause button instantly. It may just be my machine, and I'll be editing this when I look it up. (No rating)
“How does it play?”
The game takes place in an open world county, with a small town and a couple of outlying neighborhoods making up a majority of the meaningful map. There's quite a bit of resource management – you have both limited inventory slots (which can be expanded by having a better backpack) and a weight limit, your main bases use up the various resources (fuel, ammo, food, building materials) every day, and vehicles are, while not scarce, quite valuable (and fun to drive). They break down quite easily, and until you get a certain upgrade for a base, are unrepairable. You find plenty, but they're usually damaged out in the field. They're valuable for a few reasons; you can store items you've been scavenging in the trunk, bring along other survivors if you feel the need, and run over zeds in the road to save time and take out Hordes, along with the obvious (faster travel).
Hordes may be making those Left 4 Dead veterans twitch to see the word – and they have the idea. Hordes are organized groups of zeds (all the common variety) that can easily kill an unprepared survivor. Luckily, there are no special zombies (Screamers, Ferals, and the like), so they can easily be dispatched with a vehicle. However, most other special infected are much more difficult to slay. Ferals take several bullets to the head, and Screamers will stun you with their earth shattering, banshee-like yell. If you let too many “boss” zombies accumulate, you'll lose morale in your survivor group and have to go on a mission to kill them to regain trust. The variety of enemies does help combat be more tactical – do you really want to use a bullet on this common zed, or do you want to save it in case you come across a special one?
Combat at first seems like a simple button mash, taking breaks to recover stamina. However, as noted in the intro, the only way to kill your enemies is to destroy the head. While any weapon can do this, certain weapons (blunt and heavy) are better than others (bladed). You can of course, disarm (both literally and figuratively) your foes, by shooting or slashing their limbs off. However, they can still bite you for a little bit of damage. Choosing the right weapons to take with you from your stash is a huge part of your strategy.
Scavenging by yourself isn't the only way to get items, however. The game will automatically send survivors you don't control on missions to collect supplies, but it's not exactly free to take them. By completing missions and bringing back supplies and other items, you gain Influence, which is essentially your money. You can use Influence to take items and ammo, call in favors, or expand your base. Unfortunately, unless your survivor has enough fame, there's an arbitrary cap on how much Influence you get each day.
Arbitrariness doesn't stop there, however. In the name of “realism,” if you take a survivor out for too long, they get tired, reducing their maximum stamina until you take them back to the base and switch to someone else. However, there's no warning as to when your survivor will get tired, causing me to get more than one character killed. Speaking of which, perma-death is in this game. If you die as a character, all those stat gains go down the drain as them. However, you can at least recover the items they've collected, including their ever-valuable backpack, by going to the spot they died, as well as reducing the penalty to morale. And survivors don't only die in your care; unless you have enough mini bases set up around the world, there's a very good chance the computer-sent survivors won't make it back from their mission, causing frustrating losses of resources. (8/10)
“How do you rate the game overall?”
Despite all my griping, I still absolutely love State of Decay. It reminds me a lot of that Flash game, Rebuild, only you get to do the missions yourself. You really do feel the loss of a character (generic as they may be) when you screw up and die. The combat feels nice and solid, if a bit clunky at first. The visuals and audio are nothing to write home about, but do the job. When the game goes on sale (as it's liable to do, as of late), certainly pick it up. It'll last you a while; with the Breakdown DLC, you can play essentially forever, or until you get bored with a group of survivors.

However I have had this game for 2 years, (the amount I've played probably doesn't express that but that's because I was using my older brothers account.) and I have been here when things were more simple. And it's not that all of the changes are bad however more recently I've been been encountering more bugs and glitches. These include that the resolution keeps messing up and that the game is having problems starting. Another thing that has come with this more streamlined update is how it got rid of the sense of adventure had before. If you want a huge ship and to fight bosses you have to do boring search missions of different planets. While yes this is a good way to introduce players to certain types of the planets in your game a player was most likely to stumble upon an ocean planet or a volcano planet. I also dislike this minor thing that is the depersonalization of the S.A.I.L I used to love playing as a NovaKid and coming back to my comfy ship accompanied by my pets and a S.A.I.L with a personality. QUALITY OVER CONTENT>

After 140 hours of gameplay, not recommended.  It is a very boring game.
Do not believe the minimum specs listed - not even close to accurate.
Graphics are poor - dull, drab and lacking crispness.
Railway operations are too simplistic and do not work like a real railway operations. (when I saw steam engines running at speed pumping out black smoke I should have realised then that that the devs probably did not know much about trains)
Many bugs still to be fixed.
Signals are invisible except on max zoom level.
Track laying is a pain even when it decides to behave correctly.
The industry/goods side of things is very weak.
Game maps tend to be repetitive.  Played one map then you've played them all.
And the showstopper - there are too few trains.  One train will usually be enough to service an entire line connecting 5 or 6 towns.  In the 20 or so games I have played the most trains I have had running is 5.  The game becomes one where you watch 1 or 2 trains run back and forward over a featureless landscape, then upgrade them when a new engine becomes available, and then sit there and watch the 2 trains run back and forward over a featureless landscape, ........  It's like a record playing the same song again and again.
There is no incentive to build long lines as exist in the real world because no-one wants to go anywhere far away.  There is a 20 minute rule where the population won't travel at all if the entire trip is longer than 20 minutes (which equates to the next train stop usually).  This is possibly a result of modelling passengers individually.  Each boid chews up cpu and so the game has been dumbed down to minimise the number of boids but maximise the number of boid trips by making maximum trip length quite short.  End result is that the game just doesn't feel like a real railway.

There is a lot of joy in making a working train line and seeing it become profitable.

I wouldn't buy it. Not yet.
The game is a cross between Cities in Motion and OpenTTD. It's built in Unity and is a lot of fun to build train routes with.
There are however a host of problems that need to be addressed before it's really a "final" game. The UI is cheap. Cities do not scale properly based on the decade you start in (1850 / 1900 / 1950) which can create monetary issues ias it lacks balance. Vehicles do not use stations in a smart way (a route will only use the same track, always.) and while pedestrians are very smart with their travel, the game doesn't seem to produce a lot of demand as you'd expect. The industries are not profitable with trains (because of their high operating costs)
The game is also very laggy and processor-intensive because it's using Unity.
Lastly a lot of things that should be easy (scheduling to prevent bunching up trains, upgrading trains and engines over time, etc.) that are in much better-developed, free games like OpenTTD are completely lacking in Train Fever.
The developers really should have invested more into the game in terms of development. And the game could use more fine tuning before it's where it needs to be.
But do I play it? Yes. It's still interesting. I'll probably get bored of it unfortunately like with Cities in Motion due to the simplicity of the game.
