A spiritual successor to Transport Tycoon, this game will be very easy to pick up for any fans of the original. It has a very similar feel, though it incorporates some of the better aspects of games such as Cities in Motion and Railroad Tycoon - this includes from Railroad Tycoon the automatic goods transportation at a slow, but nevertheless present rate, meaning they aren't entirely reliant on your company to transport things - as well as the detailed city sector, supply and demand and "line" system from Cities in Motion.
This means, for example, at a passenger station for trains, you might want to bring in more people from around town via buses and trams that otherwise would not be at the station, and then unlike transport tycoon, it doesn't have a system where "everything at the station boards the first train arriving and then travels to the first stop that train goes to and all unloads". Rather, the game individually simulates everyone in cities, meaning they could have a job in another town, or want to go shop, or leisure purposes - whatever. As a result, they have a specific "line" they want to board, and a specific stop they want to get off at should the line have more than 1 stop. You won't have situations where everyone boards whatever train and travels to wherever as a result, and you will find that new lines that expand to new cities will result in any lines it connects to seeing a boost in passenger usage as some will get off the train and immedietly wait for another line to get to their destination - hence, more money as they pay twice to get there.
This also presents a challenge as time goes on, because starting in the early 1900s, people begin to get cars to drive about. This means fewer people will want to use mass transit systems you've set up, and you'll have to make your systems faster and more efficient to make it preferable to driving as cars become more widespread. It also presents traffic issues for your buses, trucks, and trams, as they now have to deal with traffic on the road which more often than not is slower than they are.
These concepts do not apply only to passengers, however. Cargo runs on a similar system - you can't just hook up, say, any coal mine to any steel mill and expect instant cargo. Raw material producing plants have a specific location they want their goods transported to, possibly more than one depending on the size of the industry. Then, that cargo place where the raw materials are delivered has a specific place IT wants to go - usually. I've found that goods are a bit more lenient in this sense, and will allow you to go a bit further away to a neighboring city or something. This also presents a difficult issue because one of the easiest ways to set yourself up for the remainder of the game and never worry about bankrupcy in transport tycoon was to immedietly make a massive freight line that covered a large distance, giving you a lot of money for the distance and speed delivered with every train. You cannot do that in this game. That makes freight LESS profitable than passengers, and means you have to rely on the heavily variating levels of passengers on trains to provide the most money. Even then, trains get progressively more and more expensive to maintain - they are FAR more expensive to keep running than they were in transport tycoon, especially in later stages. To make it more difficult, every item in the game comes in much shorter supply than it would have been in transport tycoon - you won't find hundreds of passengers or freight lining up at a station within a couple years of service. In fact, you won't find hundreds of items lining up for likely a hundred years or more, if ever.
I have to mention the music of course. It's quite catchy. Comparitavely with the other 2 transport tycoon games, it's actually quite good and does a good job of being background music that isn't too flashy or disturbing to the gameplay while at the same time, not too drab to feel boring or something - and it's coupled with a FANTASTIC tribute song to the original transport tycoon theme.
Now, the downsides. The game is currently littered with things that plainly are bugs or things that I'm not sure if they ARE bugs. An example of a bug is passengers and cargo will disappear off things they are being transported on during longer trips, or that while you can make a railroad cross over a road, you cannot make a road cross a rail...which is frustrating. An example of something that COULD be a bug is the lack of ability to make twin crossover tracks, or any crossover tracks at all. 2 tracks can NEVER cross each other for any purpose, which means to do something as basic as a crossover between 2 rails, you have to do 2 sets of alternating switches next to each other, which causes pathfinding issues likely as another bug, and to have rails cross for a different route or something, you need to have one route switch onto the other, then back off again. It could be a bug, but if not, I find it very irritating regardless.
Another curious thing wrong with the game is it's lack of basic options such as keyboard rebinding, switching units from metric to imperial, or zoom/snap to an object you have selected (making you have to find it yourself using the PIP screen). It also lacks multiplayer or any form of AI opponents - I myself am more a fan of multiplayer in these games than AI, but I know there are people who wish for them or just both in general. The "expansive 256 km squared" maps really aren't that expansive - on large, the maps are 4-6 cities in length...being only 16x16 km in size for the large map. This could explain the lack of multiplayer or AI, because the map would fill up FAR too quickly with other companies.
Overall, I love this game. I have always wanted to see what a transport tycoon game might look like in 3D, and what do you know - here it is. They got the scale and realism right, making it great to look at, and for a team of 3 people I am VERY impressed with their graphics engine they created. This is a difficult game making it hard to recommend to anyone who hasn't played a transportation sim before, but considering the majority of the world has played one, I would HIGHLY recommend it to you fans out there. Enjoy the game!

First of all - This game is not in any way a Civilization V clone/knock-off. This game only uses the same core elements, but all the rest is completely different.
If you're into turn-based strategy games, you're definitely going to like this game. It's brilliant in every way. Though the diplomatics aren't really in-depth, the game is extremely polished. Warlock: Masters of the Arcane also has brilliant lore. Every single unit has a unique description that's written in an informative way to tell you the backstory of W:MotA.
Mind you, if you want to buy this game to mainly play multiplayer, you're going to be in for a bad time. Unless you have a friend, there will most of the time be noone in the lobby.

Basically a fantasy version of Civilization V, but without some of the convenient shortcuts and amenities. Simple and intuitive, but giving a lot of possibilities. Does not include many races, and only one is added with DLC, most of which you can do without. A recommend, but not a must.

You could maybe call it the Warmonger's approach to the Civlisation series, most notably Civilization V, with many familiar mechanics that ensure you can get into the swing of things easily. Then you add fireballs, golems and all sorts of wonderful mythical beasties. With 3 distinct factions (4 if you count the DLC one), each with a different playstyle, as well as a pantheon of several gods, each with mighty spells and minions they can provide, the game is extremely fun to play.
The main problem of the game, in the eyes of some, could be that it is all about war, unless you're playing with other players. The AI is notoriously bad when it comes to diplomatic pacts, usually all too eager to ask insane sums for any request, and prone to backstab you as soon as they see fit.
The necessity of a strong military is further increased due to the large amounts of neutral beasts roaming the lands, all too eager to burn your mighty citadels to the ground. Legends abound about the destructive power of bears.
Nonetheless, if you're a warmonger and you like a spin of fantasy in your strategy game, I'd say Warlock is the perfect choice for you!

I backed PoE and have completed the game three times via its non-Steam version as well as once on PS4. All told, I've probably spent 150 hours or so with the game and its expansions. I'm now playing through the Steam version.
The events within Pillars of Eternity take place within the Eastern Reach, located in the southern hemisphere of Eora. This region contains a number of nations.
Essentially, the player is a foreigner who is the lone survivor of a mysterious storm. After surviving the storm you witness cultists performing a ritual that strips souls from bodies. After experiencing this you learn the ability to read souls which makes you The Watcher.
You must learn the truth behind the cultist’s actions and essentially save the land.
It is within its core gameplay where Obsidian hoped that Pillars of Eternity would be a spiritual successor to those legendary titles. The game is party-based, real time-with pause tactical roleplaying game. It utilizes a fixed isometric user interface for the game-world with two-dimensional pre-rendered backdrops. Furthermore, its reliance on the archetype character classes and gameplay mechanics draw upon the influence of your prototypical Dungeons & Dragons type game.
Before setting off on your adventures the player creates their character. The eleven character classes include your typical archetypes. However, each has distinct differences that can go a long way to altering the manner in which a player would handle challenges and the way in which events play out within the game.
Primarily, the Pillars of Eternity has a main plot with quests that need to be completed for the game to continue. However, as is typically the case, there are a substantial amount of optional side quests that range from mundane to outstanding. Thankfully, in my multiple playthroughs, I can claim that there are very few fetch quests.
The actions of the player play an important role in the game. The player can develop their reputation, both for the best and the worst, and this does change the way events play out. This creates the distinct possibility for multiple playthroughs. It also creates a reliable system for the player to become fully invested in each character within their party and eliciting a carefully chosen behavioral response.
The game’s combat system is well developed albeit it feels standard for the genre. Damage affects both endurance and health. Endurance regenerates after combat while health can only be regenerated through rest. However, if a character loses its entire health the character is permanently deceased. Players need to be mindful of when and where they rest as there are certain places where rest is impossible. Consequently, rest becomes an important strategic component of the game.
Unfortunately, the downside to the game’s party is that the companions are too easy to recruit. There isn’t substantial enough challenge to getting them to join your party. This results in a loss of connection in understanding the significance of their individual motives.
The presentation is never the highlight of these types of games. And so it continues to be in Pillars of Eternity. However, I must advise that I found the artwork and the soundtrack to be of the highest quality.
The artwork adds aesthetic value to the game’s production. The color palette has had a lot of thought put into it. The dungeons are as dark and as gloomy as they should be. The right areas shine within each location.
Likewise, the soundtrack has been very carefully determined and features tracks that are befitting each theme and event within the game. Consequently, this enables the player the opportunity to be immersed in the title.
If you’re an old-school RPG gamer then you’re likely already aware of the game. If you still haven’t purchased this game and given it a thorough playthrough then purchasing the definitive edition is the way to go. It contains the base game, the Deadfire Pack, the Royal Edition Upgrade Pack as well as the two high-quality expansion packs which are the first and second parts of The White March.
Furthermore, coming in 2018 is the sequel to Pillars of Eternity. The sequel has retained the Pillars of Eternity brand name but includes the iconic II as well as its subtitle, Deadfire. The closed backer beta recently launched and early signs from those who have played it insist that the game has the potential to be even better than the original. Therefore, this is the perfect opportunity to get into a continuing franchise.
Overall, Pillars of Eternity is an outstanding role-playing and combat game. The game is superbly written and is generally a delight to play.
Regardless of the outstanding quality of Pillars of Eternity, I argue that it isn’t for everyone.
Unfortunately, if you’re not the type to enjoy reading substantial amounts of text throughout your game then you’ll likely have a bad time. The writing is of high quality but it takes an avid reader to digest it all. However, if you are a reader then you’ll potentially find that the game’s difficulty tends to be at its highest at the beginning and middle portions of the game. It tails off towards the end and there will be times where you feel as though you are overpowered. Unfortunately, something that has been fixed to a significant degree but remains imperfect is the game’s typos and spelling errors.
The voice acting could also do with some improvement. It’s far from the worst that I have heard but given the budget that Obsidian had to work with, I feel that they could have had a much better result.
Pillars of Eternity is my favorite RPG. It is clear that it is a labor of love. That much is clear. It isn’t perfect but the imperfections add character to the presentation of the game. Having played through the game several times now I eagerly await the sequel.
Arbitrary score: 9.3/10

First off, i have no idea how to start this off...so how about we begin with what the game is most famous for : DEATH.
The game is designed to make you struggle (even though the frame rate is your biggest enemie) , but the game doesn't depend on it.
What do i mean with that? Well...I think some just play this game for the challenge and don't even give it a second look, the point i am trying to make is that the game isn't good because its hard it's good, because it's one of the most polished and most thought out games out there.
I didn't die too often in my first playthrough and still felt the bitterness of the world...the atmosphere, the music, the textures, the enemies, the story, the npc's, the level design, everything sucks you into the game.
At least that's what the game could do, but everyone is so busy with surviving and getting gud that they won't experience this masterpiece. I didn't realize♥♥♥♥♥♥on my first playthrough and even on my second one i was blind, but after watching countless lore-videos i developed my own opinion on the "good ending" or the gods and enemies you encounter throughout the game.
If i had to compare it to something, i think my choice would be a book...you have room for your own imagination, can cosplay as someone you want to be, can kill everybody but have to live with the consequences, or trust everybody and get killed for it. You experience that you have to truly work for something to get what you want and even after you succeeded you have a long way in front of you. You see fallen heroes, you see "friends" get devoured by depression, and you will of course die...
Because this is such a monstrosity of a game i would like to recommend how you should play your first playthrough (Attention to the word RECOMMEND ) :
Install DSFIX!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!
Don't get spoilered and don't read any guides for the first playthrough.
Play it your way, if you build a tanky beast that just trades hits with everybody its fine, or if you're rolling around like limb bizkit...
Play it offline, other players can ruin your experience. Some will say it's part of the frustrating nature of the game and a way of making you feel lonely in the cold world of dark souls...at the end of the day it's your choice.
Absorb your surroundings, read item descriptions and listen to npc, you will have a better time like this, trust me.
The loudest thing in the sound settings is the MUSIC.
And after beating the final boss, you can go and watch all the lore and spoiler videos you want...you will want to try the things you didn't get, seak the placed you didn't find,try the mechanics you didn't use,get the items you didn't see, fight the bosses the way they are easier, fight the bosses the way they are harder,get shortcuts, enter new covernants, learn to parry every boss,get deeper into leveling, develop your own fetish for some armors, develop your own strategies for some places, and many more.
I hope my review is somewhat readable, i know i am a few years late, but i still have friends that have never heard of this gem and i highly recommend it.
At the end i just want to say: "Be careful out there, wouldn't want to see you go hollow"

Night in the Woods is a difficult game to describe. It looks like a platformer and while there is some platforming in here, that isn't the focus. This is a story driven game. You play Mae, a broken young woman who has returned to her small home town of Possum Springs after dropping out of college for unkown reasons. She is not a particularly likeable protagonist. She is mean to her friends and her parents . In a weird way that makes her relatable though, she isn't some super heroic being who embodies perfect nobility.  She is flawed and tends to lash out in ways that are ultimately harmful to her. I ended up genuilenly curious as to what made her the way she was and wanted to find out her story.
Most of the game consists of Mae wandering around town and interacting with her friends and the people of the town as she tries to fit back in. While you can bounce about and climb on the rooves on the houses (Do so, there is stuff to find), the game is mostly about conversation. Possum Springs is a dying little community, passed by by the world at large. The mine that provided most of the work has closed and unemployement is high. A lot of businesses in the town are closed and abandoned.  Mae herself is broken, but so is her town. There is a kind of overwhelming sense of melancholy that pervades the experience and anyone who has lived in a small town like this is likely to relate. It's a game of small moments, of chats with friends and family. Sometimes funny, sometimes painful. There is an underlying mystery that you delve into but really, it's the small chats and your friends and family who will stick with you.
The graphic style is fairly simple but has a huge amount of charm. Everything is well animated and the world has a lot of detail that contributes to making it feel like a lived in space. Alec Holowka's music is also excellent and I had it stuck in my head for weeks.
Ugh, this is a weird review because talking about the things I loved about it would mostly be spoiling the plot and the game is all about plot. So yeah, coming of age story in a small town. It's good.

State of Decay.
Now with its two DLCs Breakdown and Lifeline (at the time of this review's writing. Idk if they intend to release more dlcs)
The base game is a fun, gritty experience at a post apocalyptic world where zombies overrun the world and you control survivors and try to tough it out and survive. Your decisions have weight and consequences, whether you choose to handle a situation as soon as you get into it or delay your decision, there are consequences that will affect your game in ways that amaze me. Though i really dislike the fact that the zombies themselves can run, there are mods for that. Sure the unmodded experience is fun too but i feel like mods tend to enhance gameplay. I myself installed several, mostly ones that make the zombie population a lot more dense and force them to shamble and walk towards you.
Adds a lot of tension as you try to mow down zombies with a table leg you just found in a house you were scavenging. Every hit exhausts you, you run and hope they don't catch up. You panic as you keep running to avoid your death at the hands of the zeds.
You get back to your home base, you build more improvements and go over your plans to hit the next few houses for supplies and maybe even radio other survivors. And for a moment, you feel safe and sound. Until a siege comes along.
What i think that this game does best is make the player emotionally invest in the characters.
You grow attached to a certain survivor and you want to see him/her make it out. You grow attached to some survivors and you do everything you can so that they survive. When i had to put down a few survivors because they were infected, that really hit me hard in the feels.
and i was pretty bummed when my chosen survivor got torn in half by a horde during a scavenging mission gone terribly wrong. Good job Undead Labs.
Though after my main survivor died, i kinda didn't touch the game again.
:<

I am quite enjoying State of Decay so far, finding it quite addictive.  There are a few flaws (stamina, stamina loss after exploring for too long etc) but the overall gameplay makes up for these imho.  Well woth the £6 i paid for it whilst it was on sale :)

This game is a really mixed bag. I realise it's a port of a mobile game, and pretty good for a mobile FPS, but there are places where it makes this painfully obvious.
Funnest part of the game: the guns. These run the gamut of "futurized" assault rifles, pistols, shotguns ect. to electrified and explosive compound bows/crossbow, laser energy weapons, and a chainsaw as well as a selection of grenades and mines.
The weapons are decently fun and effective to use, but this is somewhat ruined by the tedious upgrading system. Upgrading weapons can take HOURS as upgrading one weapon means playing the same levels multiple times through just to get enough credits to do so. A smarter game would disperse weapons with varying attributes through out the course of the game (like DOOM), but as I said this is a mobile game meant to simply eat up spare time. And hey, any game with a Super Shotgun can't be all bad, right?
The game also gives you the option to "aim down sights" with your weaponry but this feels purely cosmetic as it doesn't seem to effect the accuracy of your shots.
The designs of the game's weapons seem really uninspired, just taking real world weapon blueprints and adding tons of metallic clutter to make them all "futuristic looking" which can be used to describe most of the game and it's environments. It's all just very post-DOOM 3 sci-fi metallic clutter, really generic and unremarkable.
I haven't touched upon much else outside of the weapons because there's really nothing to talk about. Outside of the campaign there are a couple of survival type game modes but these offer very little outside of achievement farming, the game also offers a harder New Game +.
Also it needs to be said the sprint mechanic in this game is infuriating, you can sprint for maybe 2 seconds before you meter runs out and you start panting like a 300 pound geriatric. The flashlight works on a similar mechanic but is way more forgiving, but this is only undermined by the fact that there is virtually nowhere in the game you even need the flashlight.
I feel as though a saving grace of this game could have been some sort of multiplayer as it looks to have the potential for decently fun PvE and PvP-ish modes. Atleast the second game from what I have seen has addressed some of these issues, so that may be more worth your time and money.

Middle-earth™: Shadow of Mordor™ is an open world, free to run around and slaughter anyone game. Especially once you learn to ride Caragors it is really fun to go on a killing spree.
Pro:
- The orcs are very well designed and differ in their appearance.
- You can listen to them talk (about you) and spread rumors.
- As the story developes, so does Sauron's army. Orcs get promoted or killed, gain power, get into struggles with each other. It feels very dynamic.
- The nemesis system is an interesting concept where you get a chance to manipulate the forthcome of specific orcs or weaken others.
- Riding Caragors. Fun.
- The graphics look nice enough, even Mordor has its beautiful corners.
Contra:
- Once you encounter a Warchief and rub your hands with a thrill of anticipation, grab your trusty mount and fill your arrows, the game throws a handful of other Warchiefs at your location. For example, you have to go and kill Bolg the Defender, find his location and confront him. All of his Uruk Bro's come help him, which is okay since you're a badass Ghost-Ranger. But suddenly Golm the Gruesome, Kâka the Sh!t Vendor and Olgoth the D!ckbutt appear out of freakin' nowhere and ruin your day. And you will begin to hate those orcs, since they act like the school bullies who used to put you into a trashcan at every lunch break.
- The animations for the orcs is well made, but when you decide to play as an elf, you expect to look nice, right? Well, sorry -  you're one ugly elf. The facial expressions look hideous from time to time.
- Most runes are rather poor or utter useless. Like gaining 5% health on a headshot kill. With 5 arrows (Hello? I'm an elf! Shouldn't I be able to fart arrows?) you'll have to kill 5 orcs to gain a reasonable amount of health. Too bad you're surrounded by D!ckbutt and his friends.
- Every time you die, you'll spawn on one of the safe(ish) towers. And everytime you'll get the same dialogue. It is short, but after being mauled to death by your nemesis for the dozenth time you'll not want to hear this again.
For me there's nothing else to add. I recommend the game, it is challenging and at times really frustrating. But it's still in good fun, once you manage to kill those Warchief and his best buddies you'll feel like getting rid of a huge dump, finally flushing it down the toilet and wave goodbye with a superior look on your face.

Strange, exuberant, grimy and fun. Grimm takes the boring and safe modern versions of the Grimm Brothers tales and other wimpified stories and turns them into episodic set pieces for the player to play through, turning them back into the dark, dismal and macabre moral stories they were originally intended to be. Despite many technical limitations and drawbacks, Grimm has keen writing and a fairly unique gameplay style and with great source material and in good old fashioned Spicy Horse Games' style, turns it into something wacky and fun.
Grimm is worth noticing because of its unique gameplay style, strangeness and storytelling. When reduced to simpler terms it's probably best described as a 3D platformer with a collect/complete mechanism similar to that of the Katamari titles, but with a stronger focus on storytelling and writing, and boy does the writing shine. With source material like Grimm it's hard to go wrong, but as this game tries to show, due to modern safety, mass appeal and 'Disneyfication', we often do. Using exuberant writing and matching it with the macabre mix of childish wonder in the characters and an equally childish mucky & disgusting art style in the set pieces, it really brings the Grimm tales and other story pieces to life while still holding enough fun gameplay value to catch the attention of anyone who might not familiar with the stories and tales.
At nearly 8 years old at the time of review, and built in Unreal Engine 3, Grimm is still very enjoyable and due to the catoonish style the graphics haven't aged as poorly as you'd expect. Yet it does still feel like dated artefacts in low budget set pieces. But I think this is a more personal thing and if you like the simplified art style of other Spicy Horse games then you'll have no big issue with the graphics or art style.
The small design flaws and technological failures however are abundant, especially in the earlier episodes, and range across the board from minor things like lack of controller support on the launcher, strange limited resolution options, no launcher resulting in manually having to set the resolution and other settings again and again for each of the 23 episodes, to more obstacle causing problems like crashing every time you Alt-Tab out of the game, gameplay freezing, launch errors and plenty more.
Many of these problems are bluntly addressed in the
as unfixable due to the source code having been lost along with many other company artefacts due to a lightning strike and power loss, and as always the Community has found and posted many relevant fixes and useful information, but it's still reason for pause when considering a purchase if you're on the fence.
Priced at just $9.99/8.99€ for the Complete Pack at the time of review, and STILL unavailable in the UK due to problems with Steam Store integration, it's best to try Episode 1 - A Boy Learns What Fear Is which is available directly from the store page for free (and includes access to the trading cards without imbursement). The first episode is pretty representational of the 22 others, and if you enjoy the gameplay, story or writing enough to try out the other episodes then the Complete Pack is the most sensible option. All episodes can be played for free, but since the Episodes and Seasons are both overpriced when compared to the Complete Pack this option doesn't make much sense, though for those on a budget it's worth noting that the latter seasons are far better and Season Two is probably the best of the three.
Due, presumably, to the limitations of the Steam Store, this title never goes on sale on Steam, but has been included in bundles for as little as $1 for the Complete Pack, so looking around for a better deal may well be a better option, but even at $10 and even with the technical problems and other issues, this is still a strong recommendation for anyone with a grammatical fondness or anyone looking for something a bit out of the norm.
* The First episode is available for free and includes trading card drops. It's a great way to test whether you'll enjoy this title
* Grimm has been made available on Windows phones via GestureWorks
* Collecting all the secrets gives reason to play through another few times and reveals the light and dark versions of several gameplay elements in a gallery

这款确是极好的，Ironward工作室的又一款高逼格作品。
地点：火星。
在一次席卷大洲的腥红风暴后不久，整个火星殖民地的通讯陷入了沉寂。作为特种陆战队中的一员精英，你的小队被指派前往调查。
然而在着陆后不久你们便发现，将要对抗的（又）是潮水般不知疲倦的亡者大军。根据以往的经验，你们尝试计划行进路线，并默契地交叉掩护，时而全开火力，时而奔命街头， 分享利用着有限的物资补给。似乎你们在这场疯狂中生存了下来……
听着很耳熟？没错！如果你钟爱魔兽3的亡者之夜（特别行动/余波）系列，或者星际2的不死突袭3，那无疑这就是你的菜。这款续作在职业可塑性、游戏可玩体验、易操作度、团队沟通便利度，以及该系列故作（死）高（不）大（悔）上（改）的新兵非友善向方面等等等等，都有着诚意十足的良心改进。
如果你还未听说过这个系列或者很不幸的一直操作苦手，那你不应该错过这款续作，"The Red Solstice"。游戏里加入了全新的单人剧情模式，在享受乐趣的同时，你已经成为了半个老鸟。据（无责任）小道消息，仅单人剧情便具有很高的挑战性和可玩性。
好了大兵，准备好了吗？多人大厅随时等待你的加入，来这里我们一起战个痛快。

+ The scale : big map, big stations, long trains, big cities
+ The simulation : cities grow with your changes, each cargo/passenger is simulated, cities got residential, commercial, industrial and leisure buildings.
+ Good building options
+ It's 3D, not particularly pretty but still nice though a bit empty and green.
+ Mod support (hopefully)
- Poor performance
- The UI is appalling
- Lots of options are missing (key bindings, UI scale, mouse speed, etc)
- A line will always use the same path and platform so 2 trains from the same line can't wait in the same station (or it is not as simple as it should be)
- The building tools are annoying. Why use drag and drop when you could just click once to start and click another time to just finish a segment then accept it or move the ending point. Not to mention you have to build segment by segment, can't do multiple points. Really annoying when you're building complex paths.
- Bridges and tunnels are a pain to build and they're way too high/low. Too much collision during building overall.
- Rails can't cross eachothers. You can't control what you wanna bulldoze so you'll end up destroying the 2 segments of a crossing when you only want one.
- No AI
- To replace a vehicle, it needs to go to a depot and you have to change them manually one by one ... REALLY ? After 25 years, I had like 30 vehicles and couldn't bear having to micro manage this part. Stopped playing right away on my first game. Depot aren't really fun to manage, trains don't need to service.
- The cargo chains are limited (but mods seems to fix that)
- The first 50 years are boring to me, not a lot of vehicles available (6 engines maybe ?) and they're extremely slow.
- Can't upgrade a station, have to pause the game, destroy it then build the new one. Stations limited to 5 platform. But since one line seems to use only one platform, you don't need more right now.
- Simplistic : the economy, the train tracks, etc. Did I mention the economy ?
- No map editor (yet)
And I'm probably forgetting some stuff.
Most of those points can be fixed but there are too many problems right now to make it really enjoyable.
I'm optimistic and hope they will sort everything out cause it got good foundations.
And hopefully, mods will make this game really complete.
Now, I don't recommend it, it's not finished and can be really frustrating. We'll see how they patch that game up.

Train Fever is rough around the edges but there’s a solid foundation there that just needs a bit of refinement. This is a game that could have benefited from an Early Access period though not necessarily a very long one.
The foundation of any transport game is the cargo modelling. If you’ve played Transport Tycoon there’ll be an adjustment period as in Train Fever industries “order” goods rather than accept them. In Transport Tycoon you can happily take iron ore to a steel mill all day long and make a tidy profit. In Train Fever that iron ore will only appear if there is a demand for it – the steel mill has to see demand for its end product in order to want to pay for iron ore and coal. No demand means no cargo to transport. Instead of setting up a transport route, you have to set up the entire chain. It’s an interesting mechanic but unfortunately it’s a bit finicky and it can be hard to figure out why an industry is not producing anything after the millions you have invested in a shiny transport network.
Passenger transportation works differently too, as individual people and their journeys are simulated. People will walk from their residences to their destination if no transport route exists. If your service comes to their stop often enough (represented as Frequency in the game) then they may choose to ride your buses and trains. Conversely, if they can get there quicker by walking then they’ll do that. That means that whenever you set up a new route there is a higher expense because you have to supply enough vehicles so that the Frequency on the route is low enough for people to take it – another adjustment for those of us used to building a line with a single train set to full load and then letting it do its thing.
Construction is seamless and mostly intuitive, which is lucky because the tutorial in the game isn’t particularly fleshed out. You can drag out new sections of road or rail, and rail will show you the maximum speed trains will be able to reach on the new section (based on gradient and the radius of the curve). You can tweak the height of the endpoint and drag it around to a new location until you’re happy and then confirm the construction. Unfortunately tracks can only cross each other without a bridge, which makes diverging routes harder to build than they should be once you have double track covering the map. The game will give you a message if you can’t build track in the way you want, but on occasion there’ll be no explanation, just no “confirm” box. This tends to be only a small annoyance, and most of the time building new tracks is enjoyable.
Outside of the construction interface the user interface has a clean look. The highlight is the line manager where you can also manage your vehicles, easily sending all vehicles assigned to a line to their nearest depot and even having them automatically sold when it’s time to replace them. It can get a little unwieldy as you start managing more lines but the devs have thought of this with a “visible only” feature which filters out lines not currently on the screen. Depots make it very easy to buy vehicles and then add them all to the same line. There doesn’t appear to be a way to resize windows and the font can be hard to read sometimes – a UI scaling feature would be nice. A word of warning: the game seemingly has no keyboard shortcuts at all and so relies entirely on the mouse which can be fatiguing.
Line management is intuitive as well – create a line, hit “add station” and click away on the stations in order. The game will calculate a path for vehicles to take, and vehicles will automatically space themselves out along the route. The more vehicles (or the faster the vehicles), the higher the frequency. Pathing works very well for road vehicles, but with trains it’s another matter. Currently train lines choose a specific platform to use at a station, and trains will usually wait until that platform is free before pulling in, even if your station has other empty platforms they could use. I’ve even had a train sit waiting for the specific platform so long that the next train on the line was queued behind it; the second train picked the empty platform instead with seemingly no rhyme or reason. I’ve started building platforms based on the number of lines that will be serving the station as opposed to the number of trains I expect to service the line, which is annoying.
The game’s graphics are great as can be seen in the screenshots and videos and sounds are good throughout. Admiral James T. has done an incredible job with the soundtrack, with tracks which sound like tributes to themes from Transport Tycoon and even one which may be a nod to Theme Hospital. After about 9 hours of play I’m still enjoying the music and smiling when I recognise one of the tribute songs.
Even with the rough edges however I’d recommend this game to anyone who enjoys transport simulations or trains. You’ll have to take some time to figure out the new mechanics and on occasion you will be frustrated by the mostly minor issues. If you can move on from those there is an enjoyable game here.

I use the stable version only. If I am wrong on any point, feel free to message me. I may add more later.
Pros:
+ The building. With commands like /admin, you can spawn furniture and such not normally accessible. You can create towers, dungeons, etc. Underwater building -- this game has it. Oh yes.
+ Penguins you can hire as part of your crew. Crew descriptions can be rather comical.
+ You can traverse space. The sheer number of planets and star types is satisfying enough. The weather conditions matter to an extent. You can visit radioactive planets... They are interesting.
+ Has survival, hardcore and casual modes.
+ Controls are smooth for me.
+ You have pets.
+ You can multiplayer via Steam friends, achievements are supported. You can host a game or join one.
+ You can collect stuff. Bugs (you use a bug net), fish (a fishing rod you can upgrade), action figures, pets (from the wild that you capture with poke-erm, capture pods!), cooking recipies, and fossils!
+ Soooooo many clothes and outfit combinations. Dyes (in the game already) and mods add to it.
+ The modding community has extra races and customization options, if you don't like what is available. (It's easy, you just subscribe on Steam and suddenly you have more hair options and color options than you know what to do with! XD)
+ You build up your ship, you can even take away background blocks and stylize it/color the walls however you desire.
+ You can skip the intro mission.
+ Tons of weapons?? PEWPEW SWORD OF FIIIIREEE! HACKHACK!
+ Codex entries are actually worth reading/collecting.
+ You can colonize and terraform other planets.
+ Does have dungeons.
+ You can steal NPC houses and turn them into a home for a colonist. Smack the deed down, lol.
+ There are collars you can slap onto pets to give them a ghostly appearance. I usually use one on a poptop because of their melodious... calls?
+ Cutting trees down is relaxing. Ckckckh, timbeeer! It really is fun.
+ You can farm. Farm animals, grow crops. Build a barn.
Cons:
- You can't interact much with your pets outside feeding them and giving them a generic dog house to sleep in.
- You can't name your pets or ride larger ones--there isn't much variation among them, either. No marking variations. There are some cute designs, but when you can't pick your pet out of a crowd...
- Dungeons get repetitive.
- Can't change the outside of your ship without mods.
- Can't skip most cutscenes. Admittedly, some DO cover up loading screens, so it's not TOO terrible, but slightly annoying.
- Not much to do endgame except collect, build, look for codex entries (most of which you'll find during the main questline)... Questing is "meh," mostly "go fetch this, defeat these guys! Deliver this to ____," but I think it's meant to be experienced in multiplayer.
- Pet tethers, items that keep captured pets in a certain area, are short ranged, and your captured pet doesn't have any cool animations while it romps about. It just paces, which can get annoying.
- Your vanilla AI ship bot is kind of dull, but there are plenty of mods that fix that.
- Nothing majorly race-specific exists, other than armor, but I've equipped "racial" (using the term loosely) armor on different characters, it's nothing special. Race-specific dialogue isn't that shiny, a Hylotl may say "our races have a history" if you're Floran, but it doesn't prevent you from going anywhere or utilizing the existing merchants.
- No way to change character appearance after creation, other than editing files and risking losing stuff... I think a hair salon or a similiar feature would be nice.
- It would be nice if there was an easier way to preview clothing items, like a store, maybe virtually. I mean, it IS futuristic. You could craft a "catalog" station. It could have a catalog of items you could preview on your character and a small description on where to get them (if a particular shop or something has it-- if it's randomized loot, you can say randomly found on ____." Or maybe you could "order" it, and after a select number of in-game days, it would be delivered to you? Like for a fee, I could order a mercenary or someone else to go out and get it. Idk just... Something.)
- The races are interesting, I wish we could explore them more "personally" (not just with codex blips) with meaningful interactions (either with generated NPC's or chosen NPC's). Maybe a short mission to decide how your character's childhood went? One memory/flashback? No? Merp.
- No friendship system, factions to join (enough to fight against, I guess), family system, or marriage system. I mean, HOW COOL would it be if you could have two characters be brothers or something, one with a family to think of while adventuring, and how amazing would it be if you could show off your little generated family, and/or have another character murder it? XD Extra XP. I dunno, that's a lot all at once. Ignore me, I am impossible. But huh, as a graduate, if you follow the intro... It gets kind of old after awhile, and suddenly you want a different background for one character, something solid to refer back to... Maybe he/she/other is one that didn't get to go to school, a scrappy lil' beast/merc who isn't all about helping everyone out, you know?
- No kids??? Anywhere?? No pets of other characters, 'cept maybe a dog or something here and there. They took out the pet food bowl??? SO MANY QUESTIONS.
- NPC's don't do much except patrol and sleep...

Great spiritual successor to Master of Magic. The concept is very reminiscent to Civilization although it adds a lot of unique features of its own which creates a really great 4X turn based strategy game set in a fantasy setting.
You control an empire as a wizard, where you conduct research and cast spells, wage war, do diplomacy and develop your infrastructure. You can choose between 3 races that are distinct in their own way and require different playstyles. The maps are varied and filled with loot, monsters and tricky terrain. The AI is also really capable and it can be quite challenging.
The graphics are marvelous for such a game and so is the soundtrack. I definitely recommend this game for anyone who is looking for an experience like Master of Magic or who want to play a game similiar to Civilization but with a fantasy twist.
The only downside that I can think of right now is that there aren't that many factions to choose from and that the map generator can sometimes create really silly maps.

Warlock is Civ V fantasy knockoff that ends up being an interesting blend of the elements of RTS into the TBS formula. It is  unfortunatly marred by poor AI. The game attemts to make up for this by spamming monsters to add to the difficulty. Rather than solving the problem, this simply makes late gameplay tedious and  emphasizes the incompetence of the competing mages. Overall, not a horrible game, but there are better games you could spend your time on.
Why you should buy it:
*Civ style fantasy game.
*Strong tactical element.
*Unique city building and unit treatment gives an RTS/TBS hybrid that has potential.
*Competent graphics and polish.
*Steam cards.
Why you should avoid it:
*Little or artificial difficulty.
*Shallow and tedious gameplay.
*Poorly implemented magic system.

Night in the Woods is, to me, not a game but an interactive storybook. The gameplay mechanics are simple, though platforming and the guitar hero segments can be frustrating if you're not good at it, and does add a layer to the story as you wander through the town day after day, and at a point at the end. However, the story and characters are where it really shines. The characters and story stay with you long after you finish the game, and the symbolism and themes present throughout are interesting and worth discussing.
10/10, would recommend to anybody who loves a good story, well-rounded characters, and a great soundtrack to play to.

State of Decay is a game which was created by the people who listens to people, as I believe. Many gamers were complaining about the lack of such games and State of Decay came for our rescue. This game is very well designed and quite fun. However, the came could be an unforgettable game if their flaws were to be less.
Good Sides:
+Open world and zombies. Together.
+Being able to use different characters and their physical states and traits affect your gaming experience with them.
+Our characters are not godlike beings. Can die easily -especially in Breakdown-.
+Limited space that we have on us and even on cars bring a good challenge to the game.
+Fairly good optimization for older gaming systems.
+Atmosphere that it creates on the player is magnificent.
+The music is quite fine and tuneful. Thus they really boost the atmosphere that is created by the game.
+The world keeps on living.
+Door slams.
Bad Sides
-The side missions are a bit dull after a while and it doesn't mean whether you do it or not which I find it quite bad because some are rescue missions and usually the characters who are in trouble come back home safe and sound.
-Interactions in your community or outside of your community are almost none.
-Animations are very limited, especially on executing zombies. Since you're going use that button a lot, it could get a bit boring to see same animations over and over again.

update: Turns out that even though many servers advertise loot multipliers, none are real.   The game does not actually support changing the rates and all those servers are falsely advertising high rates to sucker noobs into joining them.

Old review removed.
tl;dr: Not recommended because of minor bugs, minor issues and general lack of storyline, character development, lack of NPC's, feels like chore simulator with no end. Still keyboard issues (not responding / lag) and/or getting stuck between a rock and a leaf. Still awfull bat sounds that make nights a freaking nightmare simply because of the sound. Otherwise fun game for a few hours, great scenery, great audio, good crafting system. Mission suggestions at the bottom of this review.
New review version (4-4-2017): nice improvements, added instructions, total of 5 objectives (done in less than 30 minutes). Still great scenery, great sounds, great visuals.
- Horrific bat sounds, just plain awful. Bat's don't sound like that.
- keyboard imput lag / being stuck -> can take 3-8 minutes of your precious daytime. unable to move.
- drop key next to W, so if you play in the dark with a regular keyboard, be prepared to search for your hammers, axes you've dropped and what not.
Still feels like 'chore simulator' because there are no other objectives. This game surpasses any other survival game when it comes to possibilities and refinements, but there's just nothing more to do than to survive. Which is completely boring after a while. Once you get down the mechanics, and set up a camp, there's literally nothing left to do apart from building more. But with what goal? There is no goal other than to survive. For a singleplayer game with no NPC's other than a few animals, that becomes pretty boring pretty soon. It feels like you're copying an old bible for the sole reason of having a copy. There is no fun element yet, no objective.
There's no story, no entertainment. If the devs need help, I can spare some time and write some complete storylines down. I have a few suggestions at the end of this review
For now, the game is worth 10-15 bucks. It keeps you entertained for a few hours, but it has a low replay value and no story whatsoever.
Storyline suggestions:
After the first tutorials: mission popup 'collect the message in a bottle'
Find bottle on the beach, there is a note.
'I'm the pilot of flight XXX, located at island XX (drawn silhouette), need help ASAP. Injured. Today's date.'
You can pick up the NPC from the closest island and bring her/him to your shelter.
Objective: Craft a bed
Objective: Nurse him/her back to health with food and water.
"I need some sleep, you should get some too"
Night falls, you sleep.
When you wake up, your raft is gone and so is the pilot.
Objective: Build a raft.
Objective: Look for the pilot (see drag marks on the beach, some buoys in the - oh wait, they don't float - some buoys in the water leave a trail.
You reach another island, pilot drank sea water and died. Take all his stuff. Leave a dead crab on his body to warn the animals not to mess with you.
Suggestion 2:
Find mushrooms, trip balls, eat bats. Kill all the bats minigame. Become the bat. Wake up hungover.
Suggestion 3:
Meet tribal people fleeing from their dictator oppressor. They fish and hunt these islands. Create a village to marry one of their ladies, or men, attack helicopters, whatever.
Suggestion 4: SHARK RIDER
On the pilot, there was an instruction manual on how to make a shark charriot.
Objective: craft the charriot.
Objective: create bait
Objective: lure 2 sharks with bait (one at a time, held by the charriot)
Objective: Surf's up! Ride your live surfboard.
I don't know, but it would add some fun to the game. I could write/work them out further if anybody is interested, but right now, I'll leave it with this.

Anyone who who knows anything about Steam will tell you that game devs who sell their wares on Steam do NOT have access to the personal data of customers. Why do I bring this up? Some EXTREMELY ignorant people misread the companies fairly boring and unexceptional privacy policy and concocted the conspiracy theory that this game was a "datamining" plot to steal credit card information and other personal data.
Seriously? If you buy a can of Coke at Wal Mart, Wal Mart may have your credit card number but Coca Cola does NOT. If you are worried about this, ask anyone who knows ANYTHING about Steam whether Steam gives credit card numbers and other personal data about customers to the game devs. (You might try looking up how Digital Homicide was kicked off Steam for attemtping to use a legal subpoena to get Steam to share personal information about its customers.)
Phew! And now that is out of the way, I can review the game itself. I saw this game and the sequel Dead Effect 2 on a let's play with Jim Sterling and I thought they looked fun so when I saw them on sale on Bundle Stars (seriously check out Bundle Stars sometime people) I bought them both for pocket change. Now I find that I am actually playing Dead Effect in preference to the AAA games in my library... So yeah, Dead Effect is a very decent, well made game though I would say that Dead Effect 2 is better and if you decide to get either, check out Bundle Stars because it's usually much cheaper than buying from the Steam Storefront.
To sum up, great old school, story-based shooter with more than a little in common with Doom 3. It is cheap because it is an inexpensively produced but well made Old School shooter rather than a AAA title with microtransactions and mulimillion dollar facial rigs.
If you buy this on Bundle Stars, you will more than get your money's worth^^

How do Blue Sharks Reproduce?
The mating ritual for blue sharks is very interesting. Some watching it may consider the male to be extremely aggressive. He will be biting hard on the female but it doesn’t hurt her. It is a type of grip so the two don’t separate before the sperm has been placed inside of the female.
A litter of blue shark pups can be from 4 to more than 130. They are viviparous. The pups are immediately left to take care of themselves once they are in the water and out of their mother’s body.

Pillars of Eternity tries to build upon Baldur's Gate series, but forgot to be fun. In fact, it resembles more Icewind Dale, since combat is the pillar of the game, not roleplay.
Divinity Original Sin brought back the classic isometric crpg, and Pillars of Eternity is Obsidian's bet to continue the revivial. It is commendable that the game was possible thanks to the backers.
In Pillars of Eternity your character is a watcher, someone who can read the souls of the dead. There are various races to choose from when creating your character, but nothing mindblowing. Each has its unique bonuses or penalites, which the player has to take into account according to his/her style of play.
The story, pains me to say, is boring. While it is well written, there is really no motivation to follow it, since it revolves around religious conflicts and the part you played in a previous life. Of course, you have to "hunt" down the baddie to uncover the secrets of your past, since this game cannot depart from the "lost memory" cliché. There are plenty of books for the player to read about the lore, but I rather read a legal code.
Perhaps the story would be less tedious if the gameplay was engaging. It is a personal taste, but I find the combat to be a chore, rather than fun, and the game is all about combat. You can go solo or with  up to five companions . None are engaging or evolving throught the game, being Eder the exception. You can set each party memeber's AI to be aggressive, defensive, defender of party or passive, to use per rest skills etc. Morover, you can configure two different sets of formations. Though it sounds interesting, the implementation is rather poor since even with the set AI, many times you will have to fight the AI to be able to pull off a hard battle, micromanagement becomes tedious rather thant tactical. Combat is all about how you perform in a messy brawl.
Speaking of tactical, combats are all about groups of enemy NPC swarming your party, or a big boss with enemy NPC swarming your party. Do you want to approach combat with setalth? Forget it. Do you want to take one enemy with tactics? Forget it. Once you attack one single opponent, the whole bunch of enemies in the area comes to his aid as if they had Whatsapp. Stealth is limited to a radius, meaning that you cannot hope for your rouge to performe as in Baldur's Gate series. It only serves as a means to reduce the radius in which enemies detect you.
This time around, potions play a role, but limited. You cannot drink potions before battle, you have to wait for the sequence to be able to do so, losing important seconds which the enemy AI exploits to deliver the first blow. You can eat food before battle with bonuses to endurance, constitution, resolve etc, but you cannot do so during combat. It is like the game wants it to be hard for the sake of being a chore, pleasing the hardcore gamers who enjoy tough battle after tough battle.
Remember when you could role play in Baldur's Gate or Planescape Torment, or Arcanum? in PoE that illusion is more superficial. Despite the rich dialogues, choices come down to a funnel. Would you like to solver an importat quest without a fight, forget it. Would you like to have alternatives to solve a quest? forget it. All comes down to the damn tedious combat.
My personal experience with leveling up is unsatisfying. I played the base game four times (trying to like the game) and now I playing it all over again with the expansions. I already reached the cap level of 16 and I still have not finished The White March 2, meaning that I still have to solve the main quest of the base game as well. Therefore, there is no incentive to continue playing having reached the level cap, since the story is so boring.
As for the graphics, the backgrounds are nicely done. The animations are good and you can see the two sets of weapons your party members carry ot one given time. Magic effects are colorful and varied, but sometimes they get in the way making difficult seeing what is going on, forcing you to check the combat log.
Music: The best part of Pillars of Eternity.
All in all, I fought to like this game with its expansions, but failed. I like isometric crpgs and appreciate the effort put in PoE. Howver, playing as wizard, fighter, rouge and ragner, I did suffer the combat and found the story unengaging. Nevertheless, I have high hopes that Pillars of Eternity II will actaully find the fun formula of the classic crpgs it tries to emmulate, while feeling refreshing.
I can recommend it only for hardcore gamers who like rpgs for the combat as the main feature, even if it is chore. If you, as a gamer want to role play, better look for it elsewhere.

CRPG's are back baby.
Pros:
Great Story, especially the end and both White Marches DLC
Beautiful visuals, art, and spells
Player Keep that gives bounties, collects taxes, can be built up and houses an awesome large dungeon below
Choices that determine the ending
Almost every ally story is awesome to take part in
Depleting skill bar is a great visual tool to let you know WHEN your people will perform their action
Durance voice actor nailed his character. Raw and unforgiving.
A good amount of quests
Many great and varied classes; I had every single party member in my party at some point throughout the game, and loved each skillset addition they brought to the group.
Cons:
Although the talents awarded from leveling up are great, more work could be done on the skill side (Athletics, Survival, Mechanical, etc.). For most, Mechanical was most important to have on a player, with Athletics and Survival being the base stats to raise in order for all characters to deal with scripted actions. Lore is only useful in using scrolls, which are not necessary unless on much harder difficulty, and stealth  was almost unneccessary save for a few chests near enemies. Hopefully this is further thought out and expanded so that all skills will be in some way desirable as much as others.
Too many "Unique" weapons and armor, with minor stat adjustments, which made them feel much less special. Made the soulbound weapons not feel too much of a better step up without the bonus situational stats.
The idea to level the soulbound weapons is great, however it is possible to acquire them to a point that it will be too late to perform the necessary actions to level them up, as most require killing certain enemies or a large number. I managed to level every item up near the end of the game, but I was using a guide knowing when I would get each soulbound item, giving me the forethought to not kill too many enemies and leave the map without enemies to level up with.
No greater class specific quests, such as in Baldurs Gate 2, that really gave a nice side questline dependent on what class you chose. Very minor con, but would still like to see classes such as wizards, fighters, rogues and paladins given their own short questline.
Judgement:
Pillars of Eternity is a great rebirth of the CRPG genre, but has made minor deviations to the formula (which is well within their right to do so). Some of those deviations are great additions, and some remove what made elements like Legendary weapons and class quests seem that much more special. Art, Sound, Story and Combat Mechanics are solid. Just a few gripes with end game items, some skills not feeling as important, and wishing there were class specific quests.  I did every single quest and explored every nook and cranny, and the game did a good job of keeping me looking for more.  Other than that I'd give Pillars of Eternity a 9.5/10.
Happily awaiting Pillars of Eternity 2

Great game with lots of potential (mods!). However, there are also some very weird, random, and obvious shortcomings (some are really really annoying) in this game, such as:
- No real tutorial available, while the game has a steep learning curve.
- No background sounds available, which is a big shortcoming!
- No clear way to tell where people want to go to/work/leasure, which requires a lot of expensive trial and error. Use the Traffic Giant method by showing through colors where people work. Now only a 'Land Use' map is available, but it doesn't mean people actually work next door (why have a transportation simulator otherwise).
- No minimap in the game, a big shortcoming with the huge maps.
- When you have many lines, it becomes very hard to distinguish where lines are headed on different tracks, especially when you are colorblind. Would be better if you could highlight certain lines more clearly.
- Very few vehicles available in the game, although modders are working to change that
- You can construct railway crossings over roads, but not the other way around, which is SUPER ANNOYING
- Only straight railway stations? Really??
- Upgrading railway stations is incredibly annoying
- Depots are one way only, which is terrible in case you have to replace a train in late game. Drive through depots are more realistic, and much better.
- For some weird reasons,you cannot construct "X" crossovers for rails, only Y mergers, which is very annoying when you merge a lot of rails. "X" crossovers are part of elemental train track design, and leaving it out is completely random and not well thought out.
- They should have made it easier to make flyovers. Making realistic flyovers is very hard due to the way the bridge pillars are implemented. Tunnels should be easier to make, too.
- No way to customize the paint schemes of the trains. Devs say this is for reaslisms sake (while oddly not incorporating any realistic logos), however in real life, trains have been in different color schemes all the time in different decades (e.g. german trains) or special schemes. The trains are also a random collection of german/swiss/austrian trains, which makes the lack of paint schemes even more weird and unrealistic.
It just seems to me that the devs didn't really think it through that much. However, despite these shortcomings, it is still a great game to play. Lets hope that the mods or devs will alleviate these weird shortcomings soon. Some pros:
- It looks great
- Trains are nice (especially steam trains!)
- Runs smoothly for me so far (Retina Macbook Pro, with nVidia card, with Bootcamp), no crashes or bugs to speak of
- Give it a few weeks/months when some mods have arrived, and it will be even more awesome.

When I first bought this game months ago, I will admit that it was in bad shape. Poor graphics optimization made the game nearly unplayable, with frame rates regularly reaching intolerable lows.
Fast forward to today, and things have greatly improved. The game is a satisfying blend of RTS and action, and it really does perfectly capture that sort of panicky scoot-and-shoot flavor of sci-fi horror films in a way that other more visible/mainstream games haven't. Team-work is essential, but not forced.
Currently the game is facing a major problem, though. In order to complete a scenario (that is, not die while frantically holing up in a building/deathtrap as ammo supplies dwindle) and complete objectives, you really do need a team of 6-8 players. And, sadly, the game is dying. Which is a real shame because it's fun and has greatly improved since its early mis-steps.
If this goes on sale for anything 15.00 or lower, consider buying this game. It really is a unique and action-packed romp. It is in need of some more polishing which, if the player base doesn't completely dry up, will no doubt come along.

Better than any Civilization game.
The combat mechanics are explicitly exposed: Units do some amount of damage, which is partially mitigated by various resistances. Targetting the weakest resistance is a big part of being successful in combat. However, you can't just pile on resistances; you get diminishing returns, so you will always take -some- damage from a powerful attack.
Units can't stack, either. There's none of the Civ-style nonsense where 1 low-tech unit can indefinitely fend off mountains of high-tech units (1 pikeman vs 5 tanks, pikeman wins, gg).
And then you have the spells, which are balanced by how rarely you can cast them. Which spells to cast is a major strategical decision.
I highly recommend it if you like 4X games. The DLC adds interesting things, too.

TL;DR: Great game that is difficult but fun to learn the ins and outs of. Be aware of the glaring FPS and crashing issues that exist without DSFix.
If you play this game and don't know about DSFix, get it ASAP. It makes DS so much better.
Be aware that there are some serious issues that you almost are forced to get fixed with DSFix. Also, physics in Dark Souls are tied to framerate. This means that any jumps that you may be performing, or any rolls or what have you
This means that if you are trying to make a jump to a certain area in the main hub area (you know what I mean), it'll be a lot harder to pull off in 60 FPS considering the fact that your distance per jump is decreased. I'm not sure by how much, but I know that it is decrased. If you're having some trouble in a certain area due to platforming or not being able to reach a jump, it might be a good idea to decrease the framerate down to 30 FPS so that it's a little easier.  But if you still experience crashing, one tip I can say is that unplugging any microphones for me somehow made the game work, and I can't really explain why, but it did.
Dark Souls is a great game. It's so fun, it's open ended, invigorating and fair with its infamous "cruelty." It isn't cruel, however; this is how you learn. Each death provides you an opportunity to reflect on your mistakes that you made when you died to that enemy or other ailment, and going back to that point.. It really gives you a sense of accomplishment when you finally overcome your mistakes and you finally beat that boss, or overcome that stupid obstacle. It's all about death in this game. Embrace it, don't get mad at it (unless, well, it's from falling damage when platforming. Then riot.)
The game, once you get it working, is absolutely fantastic. It's a great feeling playing this game for such a small amount of time and being able to say that I'm doing really well with my build. This game is so fun to play, and it's so fun to experience. There's definitely a sense of replay value, too. I had fun making a joke save to kill all of the NPCs and stuff and even fight bosses again. It's fun.
Overall, once you overlook the bad port and get it fixed, Dark Souls is definitely worth the buy.

This is a really great game. It's basically an openworld zombie survival game kinda like GTA V but all the civilians walking around are zombies.
You can play the game as you like and missions pop up for you to complete. It can feel a little frantic sometimes, especially if you don't know what you're doing.
Other survivor groups pop up from time to time and if you don't pay attention to them, they can be wiped out easily. Even some of your mission choices can get them killed (with the reward being some other in-game benefits to your group).
An unusual feature of this game is the ability to switch between most of your survivor group. Your survivors can and will die and so you don't have a main character as such, but you can decide to just play one particular person if you like.
They're going to need to rest eventually though!
You can recruit other survivors to your group, scavenge for resources like Ammo, Medicine, Food, Building Materials and Fuel.
All of the above is self explanatory except fuel. You never need to top your vehicles up, fuel is used to make certain weapon items.
Another feature that I love is the ability to move your survivor group to other homes and set up there.
Not everywhere can be a survivor home and some locations have different benefits than others.
I haven't really experienced any bugs.
The only slight annoyance was my vehicle disappearing after i drove like a maniac and overturned it.
I had left it for a few minutes to help a survivor kill a special zombie and when i came back to retrive the vehicle it was gone!
It was full of ammo, medicine and food that i was going to return to my base so it was a big hit that I took.

..I could go on and on.
After completing the last mission, I felt there were still so many things to try out, and achivements to accomplish. But at the same time I felt like waiting for a sequel which will hopefully have the refinement this game lacked, while retaining all the truly great things it did have.

I am really curious about the design sensibilities of oldschool game designers in the modern world. That is, what if some old map designers made new maps or a new game today. I was already thrilled about Romero's Doom maps, so I was curious what the two Duke 3D map designers would do today. That's why I bought this game, and it's true 20 bucks for additional episode on a dated game is a bit too much. Yet, there are some interesting changes that makes it worth for me. First, it's the audio commentary (which unfortunatelly seems to exist so far only in the first map of every episode but there are plenty of them). Then, new voice overs, which however sound a bit off (I cringe especially with "where is it?" sample when I push the walls). Then the special effects, ambient occlusion, a bit better lighting, a new flamethrower weapon and annoying flame throwing enemy and boss, a lot of new textures and level settings (even though lowres).
I mean, I am kinda mixed, but I personally enjoy replaying the game, listening to the commentaries and playing the new maps. Now, the new maps, so far felt a bit,.. very well detailed, funny new themes and jokes, some of the best scenery in Duke 3D. BUT.. the feel more linear. At least half of the levels I played (I stopped on the egypt level so far). And that's what I was curious of. Will the old creators do oldschool interconnected levels? Will they follow modern design sensibilities of simplifying things? Why? Why everything goes there? The first level is full of scenery but extremely linear, uses however the portal trick somewhere to confuse you so there are few interesting tidbits, but if you put it down you wonder why?
Later levels become bigger, but filled too early with big boss enemies (those huge hitscanners that made build engine games annoying compared to Doom) but it's ok except from a final boss in church level where there is not enough space and I die constantly (where I discovered the interesting rewind function, an interesting feature, yet it made possible to rewind and win, albeit after many tries, kinda making it pointless/casual). Many times you open a door with the red key, to find a small room with the yellow key for example, while it should be open the red door to discover a brand new area, where you had to search for the yellow key. It's very much open the door to hand you plainly the next key. Why? I haven't found a very interconnected level like in the old Duke3D, Blood, Doom and anything, makes me wonder why? It kinda solve my question what would happen if old designers were to make new levels again. Would they succumb into linear holding hands levels (although at least the difficulty and fun remains the same because enemies and shooting and moving is exactly the same)? Now I kinda see it (hopefully it gets better in future level, but I DNKROZed (which became DNGOD, why?) the final holywood level and it ends up being quite small and linear and not enough space with the final boss. I would replay the old classic maps and make some comparisons as I go along.
Yet, I feel like recommending this one, because I had great fun with the shooting and player movement and the enemy responsed I got used to, it just plays like the old one well, the new levels have the scenery and atmosphere but not the complexity of design or size, and the commentaries are very interesting historically even if they do not exist in every level in the classics. Some stuff are good, it's not all that bad, but I still question why we can never get the map complexity of the old classic FPS even when veterans come back (I am really curious what Romero is going to do with the other new FPS, really).
Also, maybe wait for the price to drop. 10$ or less would be a definite Yes from me, now it's a light one.

For anyone old enough (and/or lucky enough) to remember the majgical time of original Baldur's Gate, Baldur's Gate 2, and the other Forgotten Realms ERA RPG's....who MISSES those games.  Pillars of Eternity brings back the love of story driven RPG with the isometric view - back home.  In glorious granduer!
This is a thoroughly engrossing story/game, and will be most appreciated by those who enjoy experiencing the journey of the story vs. rushing to finish.  Superior writing, and fresh approach to a new world/universe provides the best of today's technology and development/design experience with all of what we love(d) about the Baldur's Gate Series.
If you loved those games - you'll love this one.  Stop Reading and Start Playing!
Pillars of Eternity is an excellent single-player RPG with a deep story, amazing world building, and a well-designed game system.

How I see it: a time controlled, top-down isometric, party-based, RPG adventure game. It's also the most visually appealing isometric style game I've ever played.
Highly customizable options to scale difficulty in all forms: from actual gameplay difficulty to interface/hud clues. It's possible to tailor the game for a very immersive and challenging time, if you want it.
Lore, lore, lore. Too much lore for most people to be interested I imagine, but it's there, and even if you don't immerse yourself deeply in the game, it's nice to know that it's thought out and you can dip in whenever you want. This includes optional dialogue options, tons of ingame books, and lots of optional characters to engage.
COMBAT: Real time, but you can control its speed, and pause at any moment. Each attack has a specific cooldown period. Several classes offer a variety of combat options from control to damage output. You control a party of up to 6 members. Each member can be assigned AI or be completely manually controlled.
MY PARTY: My main character is a druid, and I have in my party: Fighter, Paladin, Priest, Ranger, Cipher. We wreck. I would not choose a non-tank character as your first character. Being able to engage enemies and take damage is critical, especially in the early game. My party is 50/50 and the balance feels great.
WARNING: The learning curve is steep. It took me about 10 hours of trying and failing, quite frustratingly so, until it all clicked. Keep at it until it clicks, and the game opens up. During some points of the game you will shred, but then hit a wall. In all cases where I felt like I might be underleveled, all it took was a different tactic.
MY WISHES: I wish the game were more open world. I don't mind the way that the map system works, but I wish each zone was much larger with more to see. I understand that this game is not about grinding, but the current zones make the game feel a little too much on rails. Ultimately, I don't know how this would change the game, but I often found myself wanting more from the map. The optional DLC supposedly expands the map, so I'll give that a shot.
CONS: It's almost inevitable that you'll need to restart at some point, because once you feel like you've learned how to play, you might also feel like you've screwed up or missed content. Combat can also feel incredibly micro-managed and choppy, and I don't personally trust/enjoy using the AI setup. But this feeling is minimized once you really learn what to look for in combat and what is actually dangerous. The more you play the game, the more fluid it becomes.
PROS: Highly strategic combat in the bigger encounters. Your positioning and choice ot party can majorly affect the outcome and longetivity in battle. Good looting feels: I find plenty of currency and items to choose from. Never feeling strapped, and always finding more to spend on. I haven't done more than one playthrough, so it's hard to gauge exactly, but choices do seem to matter quite a lot for smaller events... not sure how strongly they affect the entire storyline. Oh, and it's super good looking.
