Picked it up (plus DLC) for cheap on the steam sale. It's well worth the $4 i paid. (haven't played the DLC yet but will soon)
Pros:
The Animations are excellant (so many cool animations for fighting, climbing, finishing enemies etc)
The combat system
Killing Uruks
The ability unlocks (the wraith powers are especially fun)
The Nemsis System
Side Quests were varied (at first)
The legendary powers/weapons are fun.
Cons:
Although it started in a cliche way, I enjoyed the core idea of the story. BUT it got convoluted, confused and stupid by the end, they should have kept it much simpler.
Talion got annoying (maybe just me but i didnt like his face) I just changed his appearance with one of the DLC characters.
Side quests got repetitive by the end.
I got overpowered quickly, the legendary weapons/powers are especially overpowered.
Final Thought:
A fun game I would recommend at sale price, don't take the story too seriously (you can skip all the cutscenes with escape). Don't get too wrapped up in doing the side quests at first, I suggest playing the main missions and when you see an unlock you want grind out some side quests to afford it. And remember to try and behead the Uruks if you want to kill them permenantly otherwise there is a chance they can come back with battle scars and a grudge against you.
***Spoilers***
It's like the idea for the story was solid but they kept adding in plot twists and extra characters that made it too complex. Talion was basically schizophrenic by the end, one of the final cutscenes had Talion hearing about 5 different characters voices in his head.
At first I went and cleared all of the side missions before moving onto the second map. By that time I had unlocked almost all the abilities and bought most of the weapon upgrades before even being able to command and control (brand) the Uruks. One of the final battles was so easy I used the legendary bow power to spam fire arrows and then used shadow strike to kill all the warchiefs, it was all over in about 1 minute.

This game was on my radar well before release thanks to previews which presented it as a set of tough moral choices. The game turned out to be a time management puzzle, which certainly still has potential. Unfortunately, the execution is poor.
Firstly, it's badly written. I actually wondered at times if it was meant to be a parody, but that just doesn't fit with the themes. Some of the action hero style lines seem like something out of a McBain segment on The Simpsons, and they are nowhere near as bad as the attempts at philosophy - I cracked up at "We aren't so different, you and I", amid turgid lines about the void of space.
Secondly, it's badly designed. The RNG and difficulty are mentioned in other reviews, but how about the sheer ridiculousless of having to click through every bit of dialogue in the chapter if you have to restart (which you likely will due to the aforementioned issues). Mindlessly clicking the mouse 100+ times and waiting for crappy animations to play out only adds to the annoyance of an undeserved failure.
While the time management puzzles themselves have some appeal, they're undermined by the poor structure around them.

Nearly everything I've experienced with this game has been positive.
I first saw this advertised on the Frontpage, as a pre-order. With only 11 hours to go, I went ahead and bought it after watching the trailer and looking at the screenshots - it definetley looked like something I'd enjoy.
Loading the game took a little longer than I was comfortable with, and the menu music felt really dated and out-of-place. That was very quickly rectified by a short stop to the Options menu. Unfortunately, this game seems to suffer with load times - loading any save game (which are >= 250MB each...) takes around three minutes; after loading in, there's some slight lag while the game builds up the environment.
Gameplay was surprisingly enjoyable. You have control of buses, trams and railways and need to connect up two or more towns and build a successful business. It can be hard at first, but once you've swept past the learning curve it all falls into place. Furthermore, the random terrain generation (seeds) makes each replay a unique experience in its own right.
It does have some other shortcomings, though. Terrain is annoying; if you make a mistake, you can't rectify it with the terrain tools if it's too close to a structure or river. I was left with two sheer cliffs after demolishing my railway bridge - I could not remove them.
Overall, I'd rate this game a hearty 8.5/10 - it's still got potential, but enough content to keep me interested until the next patches/DLC.

What's this? A game that can actually claim to be a worthy successor to the Transport Tycoon subgenre of tycoon games? Why yes!
While the game is definitely a bit rough around the edges (as of release date) and the transport mechanics are a bit of an initial uphill struggle, it's definitely worth the sweat and tears. Once you grasp the basics a very robust sandbox "Transport building" game awaits you at the peak.
Living and breathing cities that change as the years go by not only in size but also in style and complexity - Lots of challenges along the way to supply the ever increasing demand for goods and commuters force you rethink old strategies and adapt to the turn of the century. From simple horse carriages and early steam engines to modern Electric trams and trains, you'll be spending far too many hours playing this - if you give it a chance and live with the few annoyances it current has.

Definetely a big recommend!
The game is missing a big tutorial, it just starts with basic tutorials how to set up your first transportation line with automatically moving vehicles. However, it's all about transportation and getting money for it. So there is not much more you have to use, except your human logic.
So your transportation lines have to make sense. At first you have to check WHAT should be transported. For beginners, use trains and check out two companies that are close to each other.
Company 1: Produces oil and sells it on the market
Company 2: Needs oil in order to produce goods
So, as you can imagine, in real life Company 1 would love to sell it's oil to Company 2 who absolutely needs it. BID AND ASK. All right, so just build two railway stations next to these companies, connect them. Create a new line in between these two railway stations, buy a train, tell it to drive according to the line you just created and thats it.
The companies will notice AUTOMATICALLY that there NOW is a possibility to sell/buy oil from each other. The AI in this came is intelligent enough to notice this advantage. So Company 1 now notices, that there is a way to transport and sell it's oil to Company 2 using your railway station. What does Company 1 do now? It starts stacking up the produced oil barrels on your railway station. Your train will arrive, pick up the barrels, drive to Company 2 who automatically buys it. After arriving at Company 2 you instantly get the money. That's pretty simple.
Now, for example, Company 2 takes Oil and produces GOODS. Villages and people living there need the goods. So what you can create a second transportation line between a nearby village and Company 2, in order to transport the produces goods to the village. Similar as in the example above, the companies/villages will notice this advantage and start ordering goods from Company 2 using your second line. Again you're earning money.
Now, as the village gets goods to develop, you can also start building a THIRD line. On the lower right side of the user interface you can open a menu. One of the points allows you to show the houses of villages in colored codes. After enabling this option, you will see blue, yellow and green houses.
Green houses = Houses where people live in
Yellow houses = Stores and places for people to have fun (e.g. after work)
Blue houses = Offices/workplaces for the people that work
If you zoom in you can see that people have to walk a LOT from their homes in order to go to work every morning. So what you can do is simply creating a THIRD line to allow the people to travel from home to work by bus. Again the AI is intelligent enough to notice this advantage, so they will immediately start using your busses and pay money for tickets.
Then, after more and more people work, your city gets more efficient. Companies grow and develop thanks to your lines transportating the workers, so after growing even MORE people can work there. Also the houses where families life in. The better the lines are set up, the more attractive the area in your city gets, leading to a rising population in your city. You really can see the city growing over time.
So a last example, after work the people may be exhausted, so they need to relax, maybe going to yellow houses and playgrounds in the city. so why don't create a fourth line that transports the people in between work/stores/their home? They will use it then again.
All you have to do in this game is thinking logically. The world is amazingly intelligent, it is fun to watch the city growing. Even companies grow if they notice that they can't produce enough products anymore in order to supply other companies. Every single move and line you create, every single bus stop, can change the peoples behavior and influence the way your city grows. This is fantastic.

This is a very nice Transport business simulator.
The developers clearly have an eye for details.
It is a challenging game. Most of the complaints you see about how hard the game is, are simply part of the challenge of the game. It shouldn't be too easy to get your company profitable. You need to think about the best solutions. How are you getting the most profitable lines for the least costs?
If you could just start laying tracks and buy trains, without consideration, in my opinion that would make the game too easy.
The modability of this game is exceptionally good. If you seek a game to start learning to modify games, then this is the game for your. Modding is that easy for this game.
Of course the game has unsolved issues and still needs a lot of polish, but which game doesn't these days at release? The developers have proven they work hard to solve reported issues and I'm sure they will keep doing so.
As a beta tester, I have already a lot of hours put into the game. Not only to test but also to actually play, it's simply fun to play.
I think the game is worth it's full price at this moment and it will only get better.

You run around, collect items, ammo, and weapons, and try to survive the onslaught of monsters while completing missions and helping your team mates. Solid overall premise and good execution here.
The community seems pretty quiet lately, though, and it's hard to get a full game together at times. I think this title would probably work better as F2P with a well thought out microtransaction model and some weekly events, since there would be more people online.

Dead effect Review - Raymond KT
Summary: Fight for your life in the INDIE SCI-FI FPS game fit for both casual and hard-core gamers with a passion for hunting down hordes of zombies. Prepare yourselves for the incoming nightmare
Wherever you turn you see evidence that it’s a mobile game ported to PC – it’s sluggish, not very exciting, the visuals are dated and the interface should have been completely redone to fit mouse instead of touchscreen. You will enjoy Dead Effect as a mediocre and stupid action snack - but it basically is the real charm of this game. We can neither recommend nor reject the game to your attention. The question whether it’s mixed for you or not you has to answer yourself. If you feel the need for some mindless shooting when taking a break from more thought-demanding games, Dead Effect will fit you. Otherwise stay away from it, or it will drive you crazy. With few euros you have an old style shooter with little personality, graphically old, a little repetitive and with some bugs still to fix. But Dead Effect is also fun, has a good sci-fi/horror atmosphere, is cheap and gives the same feeling of a decent b-movie. A corny, simplistic zombie shooter, which also doubles as a collection of all the genre clichés.

Hybrid Civ 5 / Masters of Magic / Majesty. Welcome addition to turn based city building strategy. Some UI issues such as non-centering on selection, and lack of alpha-ordering of spells and buildings, but generally well assembled. Based on the Majesty world with voice acting from some of the original cast (particularly the advisor). Quite addictive, surprisingly deep for a game of this type from a studio that's not done them before. Possesses similar depth of power to MoM, largely due to use of 'temples' as per Majesty.

As far as TBS games go, this one is terribly simple to the point of insulting to those with any experience in the genre, with AI oppenents that are simply laughable even on the hardest difficulty. City growth is pointlessly limited and constricting, not to mention slow, with games being as good as over before getting past your basic warriors. The magic system is an enjoyable power trip once you learn to use it ,then a terrifying fall back to reality when you realise the enemy can too, then back to power trip when you see that no, they really couldn't use magic to save their lives. I would recommend this game to someone new to the genre as a whole, as the game itself is fun with all the mechanics meshing together rather well with alot of room for error, and is a good judge of whether you may like the strategy genre, but for those looking for a deeper experience I would recommend they look elsewhere.

The closest game yet to being a proper successor to Master of Magic.  Tactical battles on an overland map, city building, a variety of units that don't simply follow a rock-paper-scissors paradigm.  Terrain and unit types allow creation of choke points and standoffs and your overland spell casting helps you to overcome them.  Smooth interface, quick gameplay, and a lack of emphasis on creating a superstack and dashing around to protect/steal everything are advantages over MoM, but MoM was superior in terms of encouraging unbalanced experimental gameplay and had those fun late-game global enchantments like Armageddon and Time Stop.  Warlock has excellent options for maps and victory conditions.  The computer map generation here is very well done, essentially equal first with what MoM achieved in the industry.  Each piece of Warlock DLC adds something useful and I don't see anything that breaks the original game balance.

Dark Souls is where the whole sub-genre of "Souls like" games, like Nioh, came to be. And, yes, this review is long overdue, but I needed to play through it a lot. Dark Souls is a difficult, skill-based, fantasy RPG that is one of my damn favourites and has the best bosses in any Souls game, no, any game, that I have ever played.
Dark Souls does have some issues, I won't lie. And most of them are PvP issuses, and damn area issues. The first is PvP. It can take hours to summon in a friend, and if you do finally summon them in,♥♥♥♥♥♥can still go wrong. But thats about it for the PvP. Some of the areas, however, are awful. Blighttown, Lost Izalith, Depths, Tomb of the Giants, and maybe like two more. If you don't know why they're bad, then look them up, and then you'll understand. There are also some bad bosses, such as the Bed of Chaos, Capra Demon, and Demon Firesage are just a few, including maybe like 2 more. But that is all the main issues with the game.
Now, we can get into the good stuff. Dark Souls l has some of the best bosses in gaming. There is Orienstein and Smough, Artorias, Black Dragon Kalameet, Manus, Gywn, etc. They are amazing, and provide an amazing fight and rush at beating the boss. Some of the NPC's are some of the most memorable in gaming, including Solaire of Astora and Havel the Rock. The PvE is pretty good, and gives a fair challenge each time you fight, and even some of the other bosses are amazing. I could go on about the bosses for a long time, since they are the content of these games. But, I'll let you fight them.
The story in Souls games are very convoluted. The basics that they give to you are that you are the chosen undead, and that it is your job to relink the first flame. The rest of the story is hidden, and you must go through item descriptions and dialouge to find the rest of the story. But that's the cool thing about it.
Overall, this game is amazing. I highly recommend it to new comers of the souls series, and I promise you will not be disapointed. I love this game so much, and I know you will too.

After about almost 400 hours, I think it's time that I finally write a review for this game. I have gotten every achievement in this game and I have put quite a few hours into the antibirth mod. Even after all that, I could easily see myself put a 1000 hours into this game.
The replayability of this game is based on the amount of items and synergies that exist in the game. No run has ever really felt the same as the last. If I had to mention something bad about this, it would have to be that if there is a specific synergy that you like, then you might not see it too often.
The bosses and enemies in the game are all really well designed (save for a few, but I will talk about that later). Each boss seems like it has its own personality.
There are plenty of problems in this game like bugs and the such, but as you play most of them will get covered.
I would say 100% purchase Rebirth, however I don't think I could ever recommend Afterbirth and Afterbirth+. If you play Isaac and are itching for more official content, then I think you should pick up the DLC, but for someone who just plays the game casually I don't think the purchase would be worth it. The two main bosses added with the DLCs are too mediocre and the new floors are lackluster as well. The greed gamemode gets pretty boring after a little bit of playing it. If you want more Isaac content and you don't have the money, then I would recommend Antibirth, which is a free mod made by Isaac fans that adds a huge amount of content. This includes many new bosses, floors, and items.
TL;DR:  BUY REBIRTH, buy Afterbirth/Afterbirth+ if you want official content, get Antibirth if you still want more content or don't have much money.

Duke Nukem 3D is back! And it looks better than it ever has before with Gearbox's own special "2.5D" lighting system! Coupled with new high fidelity re-recordings of all the original 'Duke Talk', plus a plethora of new quips from the man himself, Jon St. John, you'll find yourself getting lost in alien butt kicking nostalgia in entirely new ways and places!
Ranging from the smokey 'coffee shops' of Amsterdam to the ancient ruins of Egypt's long lost empire, you'll span the whole globe, ridding it of the alien menace once again. With the brand new Incinerator weapon, you'll be turning up the heat on those alien SoB's in no time, that is, if the new Firefly enemy doesn't return the favor before you can!
For those who prefer a more classic experience, the new "2.5D" engine can be toggled on and off at a moments notice, with no interuption to gameplay. Should the alien menace prove too much for you to handle, you can easily restore yourself back to any previously played point on your current level with the 'Flashback' system, as seen on the Xbox Live version of DN3D. Plus  anybody wanting to go 'behind the scenes' can do so with the new addition of developer commentary scattered across each and every level.
The original crew has out done themselves, with astounding attention to detail and clever mapping tricks, combined with Lee Jackson's new rocking tunes, Duke Nukem: World Tour is a treat for any fan of the classic that is, Duke Nukem 3D!
Hail to the King, baby!

<edit>
The first patch hit and the SFX quality has been fixed, in addition to several other things I failed to mention previously (like the FoV). I'd like to add that the one-liner I mentioned  ("Ooh, that's gotta hurt" being "Oooooh, that's gotta huuuuuuurt") is actually very close to the original and I was mistaken. So far Gearbox seems to be listening to the feedback.
</edit>
Alien World Order (the new episode) overall is fantastic. The level design, music and high difficulty level (though Blum and Levelord seem to like spamming mini bosses here) are amazing.
My main problems were:
SFX quality
Final boss in AWO (The AI is broken - the boss has short range flamethrowers, but does not really try to get close enough to damage you with them, making this fight trivial... On the other hand, if he does get in range, he melts you in seconds)
Technical problems with some of the sounds aside from the quality (like ambient sounds stacking on top of each other creating a loud clusterf uck)
Though all of this should be easily fixable. I hope they will. As for the new recordings of Duke: most of them are fine, some of the sound exactly the same as the originals (but, obviously, with higher technical quality). Unfortunately, some of them are stretched out too much (primary offenders: "Groovy" being "Grooooovyyyy", "Ooh, that's gotta hurt" being "Oooooh, that's gotta huuuuuuurt"), but it isn't that much of a problem. Some are spoken in the same exact tone (though the originals were guilty of this too). However, the worst are the pain sounds etc. - the "gasping for air when getting out of water" one sounds as if Jon wanted to spit out phlegm or was chocking on something that definitely wasn't water.
Overall, was it worth it? Yes, the episode alone is worth it, but that's considering they fix the technical issues. I will edit this review accordingly, if the fixes come.

1  The new episode is amazing, it is very well made and I would say is much higher quality than the 3 episodes megaton had with duke it out in DC being the best, ( I have that expansion still on disk) and the other two being alright, while it is a better quality that still does not change the fact that they had removed duke nukem whatever version you had from steam and GOG from purchase. So you cant buy any other version of duke nukem other than this one. The new episode is the most challenging duke nukem episode even more than the duke nukem forever mod.
2 The game has bots you can play against in multiplayer right now so if you cant get a online match set up because your internet isn't the best or nobody is online when you are you can play some death match but they are very easy sadly. Good for people who need to learn the multiplayer at least.
3  The game has a new graphical feature called 2.5 3D or real 3D. It does make the game look better than megaton sometimes and you can turn it off to make it look more like the original, but unlike megaton you cant play the classic 1998 build port of the game so unless you have the classic already there is no way get the original version.
4 The game also has the rewind feature so that if you die you can rewind back a few seconds to where you don't die. It is a n ice interesting original feature I have not seen anywhere other than on the xbox 360 port of duke nukem but it makes the game much easier, fortunately you can turn if off if you want to play the game the way it was made to be played when you die if you didn't save back to the start of the level pistol start.
Cons
1  The biggest issue here is that they removed the atomic edition, the megaton edition and I have not checked the console ports of duke nukem but it seems that due to license issues nobody can buy duke nukem anymore other than this version of the game. and the issues with that are if you owned say megaton edition and you wanted new players to join and play death match with you they cant buy the game on steam anymore. If you wanted to play the 3 bonus expansions that came with the megaton editon, duke it out in DC, life's a beach, and nuclear winter, you cant buy those anymore. I will call this for what it is very very anti-consumer, they should have dealt with the legal issues so that we can play as many versions of duke nukem as possible not remove a great game from sale.
2  The multiplayer seems to be just like megaton edtions mutiplayer on steam and that means peer to peer networking making it stable but often very lagy empty and dead. I have played the game around launch and I could hardly get a good match going. I feel like megaton had better mutiplayer somehow despite as far as I can tell it is the exact same. They should have improved it better.
3 The game has no Linux, Mac support, I have had technical issues like if I move to fast into a crowded room the game will slow down asif I was playing this on a console. I have played the xbox 360 version of the game and I don't remember it lagging in single player like that, the multipalyer is also laggy as well.
4 The sound. Now john saint john did wonderful voice acting despite his age, and that is not my issue here, the issue is the games sound effects, and music sound worse than the original duke 3D did if you spent time getting it too work well. It also has worse sound than the megaton edition and it sounds very muffled. I think it should have the options between old and new sound effects, music and johns voice of duke.
To conclude, the game is great playing it very very fun, it has some features better than eduke32, megaton, and those other ways of playing the game have advantages over this version. The port of the game itself works perfectly fine if you ask me I played megaton before playing this port and after a bit of configuration I didn't notice any difference in how the game ran controlled and felt but it needs work in a few areas. The game hopefully has a better build engine and might be able to run better more detailed maps than the megaton version could but I have yet to see it. I found this game really really hard to recommend for 21.99 dollars but the game was well marketed, it is duke nukem and it is not something I did not want like duke nukem forever was and I really really like duke nukem it is my favorite game to play in death match so I do have a bit of a nostalgia bias.
Do I recommend you buy this game? If you do not already own the megaton edition  and you have hardly or never played duke nukem before I recommend it 100%. But if you own megaton edition and any other ports of duke nukem and you already got 500 kills in death match, beat 4 or more episodes then I don't recommend it. If you use Mac or Linux you cant seem to run the game,but I see quality here the levels are very well made a man who legally named himself the levellord and other duke devs made levels for the game the humor is still intact and the game is hard and fun. I do overall these many issues recommend it to you. I would say it is worth 21.99 dollars and it is totally worth it on sale.

Writing "if you liked X then you're going to like this" feels a bit stale as reviews go, but in fact - if you liked games such as Neverwinter Nights then you're going to like this. It's a rehash of the classic isometric RPG with gorgeous graphics, a compelling story and a large number of ways to shape your own adventure. Multiple classes, multiple races, multiple backgrounds that actually affect the story and your interactions with NPCs - it's all there as you would expect and well implemented.
On the downside, the voice acting feels random at times - some lines are voiced, others aren't, and dialogues tend to be very (very!) long and wordy. A shame, as other games have shown that you can have a deep story without walls of text. I actually gave up on my first attempt through this because I got bored, and after finishing the main campaign I felt no inclination to get started on the DLC right away. All in all however, I'm going to recommend this as it's a solid game with everything you could expect from a modern iso-RPG.
7/10.

Well...
Pillars of Eternity...
I have already beaten the game and took about a week off before writing this. And that's how I am going to lay out this review.
I recommend the game, but read till the end.
Basically, I was able to progress in the story without being, what I am going to refer to, trolled. What I mean by that, is that sometimes games try hard to get in your way of progress. This time around I was immersed in the game only because of its story. Pillars of Eternity does not shine in terms of gameplay, combat system design, visuals, effects, open world design, yada, yada. It does fairly decent in all of those departments, but it is nothing to write home about. It is solid. Nothing new and nothing to cringe for. Nothing innovative and nothing unfamiliar. Nothing too hard to understand. Every component functions just as expected. One might say that is a bad thing; one might say that is a good thing. I think that Pillars embraces hard, long-established role playing mechanics. And that's that. Neither good nor bad. It's just an RPG with a solid foundation; nothing is exceptional. Conceptually, all nails are hammered. The developer did not have more time to polish the game, and it feels sometimes. But then again the price is reasonable, and the crowd funding campaign was not that large.
Cad Nua is an unnecessary component, yet it has received so much praise. It feels like they've put it over there because it SOUNDS awesome for the player to have their own fortress. And while I did spend money on rebuilding it because I wanted to see where it was going to go, it didn't end up being anything spectacular. I was playing mainly within the confines of the story because it was the only thing that was driving me to participate at all. To me, anything outside of these premises felt unnecessary and uninteresting. There were a few surprises here and there, but very little compelled me to explore more. Too often the side content raised my eyebrows in disbelief. When I see a case of that, I skip it entirely and just plough through the main story, if that holds my interest, that is. And Pillars did. Short case--Pillars has a good main plot and a very decent antagonistic force. I liked Thaos. The expositional 'aha!' info-dump makes an appearance twice, but other than that, progression is fluid and does not obscure your path or its objective. There is plenty of lore and the world is consistent with it. I think it's a clear sign that the writers have taken some extra time doing it. Combat is based on d&d but does not give you the skills like how you'd expect them. It is also balanced and does not troll you with significant difficulty spikes. Basically, you can respond to anything the game throws at you. If something comes across as too hard, you can boost specific stats, either through items or easily-accessible character respec or change your approach by reevaluating the ever changing combat scenario with accessible pause mechanic. Again, nothing significant. Just a solid foundation that lets you play at will, if you like tactical combat, that is.
All in all. A must for rpg fans. Quite skippable if not. Maybe, perhaps, it will even be difficult for players with little to no previous classical rpg experience. But there is something in it for you if you enjoy a good plot. And this one even has got philosophy involved.
Just a solid rpg title.

Picked it up (plus DLC) for cheap on the steam sale. It's well worth the $4 i paid. (haven't played the DLC yet but will soon)
Pros:
The Animations are excellant (so many cool animations for fighting, climbing, finishing enemies etc)
The combat system
Killing Uruks
The ability unlocks (the wraith powers are especially fun)
The Nemsis System
Side Quests were varied (at first)
The legendary powers/weapons are fun.
Cons:
Although it started in a cliche way, I enjoyed the core idea of the story. BUT it got convoluted, confused and stupid by the end, they should have kept it much simpler.
Talion got annoying (maybe just me but i didnt like his face) I just changed his appearance with one of the DLC characters.
Side quests got repetitive by the end.
I got overpowered quickly, the legendary weapons/powers are especially overpowered.
Final Thought:
A fun game I would recommend at sale price, don't take the story too seriously (you can skip all the cutscenes with escape). Don't get too wrapped up in doing the side quests at first, I suggest playing the main missions and when you see an unlock you want grind out some side quests to afford it. And remember to try and behead the Uruks if you want to kill them permenantly otherwise there is a chance they can come back with battle scars and a grudge against you.
***Spoilers***
It's like the idea for the story was solid but they kept adding in plot twists and extra characters that made it too complex. Talion was basically schizophrenic by the end, one of the final cutscenes had Talion hearing about 5 different characters voices in his head.
At first I went and cleared all of the side missions before moving onto the second map. By that time I had unlocked almost all the abilities and bought most of the weapon upgrades before even being able to command and control (brand) the Uruks. One of the final battles was so easy I used the legendary bow power to spam fire arrows and then used shadow strike to kill all the warchiefs, it was all over in about 1 minute.

I had to play through it on a lower difficulty because I wanted to experience the story. I would deffinatley recommned this game. However, I would suggest players reduce the difficulty if they are getting frustrated. It is an extremely difficult game.

I love me some good story, even more when your actions have repercussions in said story, but I can't forgive this game for
inflate its time of gameplay with a boring, RNG dependant ''gameplay''. Having to repeat a scene over and over again because you got unlucky, losing interest, nitpicking on thing that you didn't notice the first 3 times...It is really not worth the effort.

This game is fun. It's also dark, and some people of a certain religious or moral persuasion really won't like it. There's a reason for the darkness and moral ambiguity, though, which I'll expand on later.
You play a character named Grimm, whose mission is to restore the 21st century versions of fairy tales to their original medieval purpose. This involves removing as much pink and shiny “niceness” as possible, and replacing it with darkness and corruption. That said, the whole thing is handled in a fairly humorous manner.
The graphics are not spectacular, and the game play is not demanding. It is, however, very funny, and I'm enjoying it a lot.
If I have a gripe, it's that the game doesn't even attempt to address the censorship of the sexual content of the old fairy stories. On the one hand, given the current moral panic over the effects of computer games, I can understand. But on the other hand, isn't it just that censorship that the game seeks to address?
Anyway, it's an enjoyable game, and very thought provoking.
I apologise for this next section. It started as a review, but became an essay. I'm concerned that some people who have written about this game don't understand the history or purpose behind it.
The stories we now know as “fairy tales” were largely based on folk tales current in 16th and 17th century Europe. The stories, however, are in many cases much older. They captured people's imagination, and were passed down orally from generation to generation, because they performed a valuable teaching function. They warned people of the dangers out there. They were not originally intended for children, and many of them explore extremely violent, sexual and disturbing themes.
For instance, the oldest known version of “Sleeping Beauty” is “Sole, Luna, e Talia” recorded by Giambattista Basile, published in 1634. In this story, the handsome prince does not kiss Beauty to wake her. Instead, he rapes her while she's unconscious, and then departs, apparently without a thought. Leaving her still comatose, but now also pregnant with twins.
In the original version of “Red Riding Hood”, there's no granny, no cottage, and no huntsman. There's just a little girl, alone in the forest, and a wolf. And it kills her, and eats her. She doesn't get rescued, there's no happy ending, she's dead.
19th century writers such as the Brothers Grimm and Hans Christian Andersen recounted many of these stories. But, in keeping with the moral code of their time, completely removed the sexual references, and greatly toned down the violence. Even so, this sanitisation was nowhere near enough for 20th century moralists. Disney is an easy target here, but Disney are far from alone in further Bowdlerising the stories to the point where they're fluffy, happy, and completely inoffensive. The problem is that the modern versions of these stories are also totally meaningless, and devoid of any of the original teaching. “And they all lived happily ever after” is a modern lie. It's not true now, and in 1600 no-one would have been stupid enough to say it.
That's what American McGee is getting at here – these stories were originally extremely nasty, but deliberately so. They were intended to teach lessons about a violent, dangerous and untrustworthy world. In censoring them to suit modern sensibilities, they have been completely stripped of their original power and purpose.

Playing a certain class gives statistical bonus to that class via Specialization rank. There is three diffirent maps you can play, and every game you can choose from 7 diffirent game modes ( popular are "Fast Mode" and "Bunker Mode"). I would give 2 recommendations to this game if I could.

Counter Strike Condition Zero is an interesting game to discuss not because of it's merits as a game but largely for it's history. It had a surprisingly troubled development and changed hands between 4 distinctive developers before finally becoming finished.
The game was originally designed by Rogue, the developers behind Strife and American McGee's Alice. However the developer went out of buisiness so Valve instead gave it to Gearbox, who Valve had previously worked with on Opposing Force and Blue Shift. Much of the game is based around Gearbox's version, which focused on creating more impressive graphics and remaking many of the classic Counter Strike maps in better detail.
However, the project changed hands again and the game was handed off to Ritual entertainment. The guys behind SiN. They remade the game as a pseudo singleplayer title before Valve decided to hand the game off to Turtlerock studios. Who would years later create Left 4 Dead. Who finished the game and completed it based on Gearbox's version. The content Ritual made would be released as the "Deleted scenes".
The final game is very much inspired by Counter Strike 1.6. It plays very similarly albiet with nicer graphics and a very different art style. It was also the very first Counter Strike game to ship with bots by default. The game also contains a singleplayer separate from the Deleted Scenes, however this is just an Unreal Tournament style ladder featuring botmatches.
When Condition Zero came out, it was seen as outdated. It released two years too late, and the very same year as Valve's own Counter Strike Source. As a result it isn't often talked about when compared to the other games. Since you do get it by default when buying 1.6 it's interesting to play for curiosity's sake, but you'll likely find more players for 1.6 or Source.

I beat Dark Souls.
I'm proud to say after years of false starts I finally conquered the game and I'm left with nothing but praise and a new found love for the Soulsborne series. Everything in Dark souls is unfair until it isnt, its a lot like the movie Edge of Tomorrow, that constant restart that leads to leads to success. In that way, if you are attentive you learn something from every death and carry that into the next encounter or boss fight. I can't count the amount of times I called ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t while playing the game only to shortly after realize it was something I did that lead to my death, and while that happens a lot in games for me I can't think of many in the last decade that that is the case nine times out of ten. I went into NG+ approaching SL120 and thinking I was the lord of the land only to get ganged up on by three of the common enemies in undead burg and dying in seconds. The game put me back in my place and I've remained there ever since. Of course areas like blight town pose no real threat to me now and the threat of being poisoned isnt a problem once you realize you can't get poisoned again until the status wears off. I feel like I;m doing some hardcore parkour when I traverse the area now. Same can't be said about the catacombs, still makes me its ♥♥♥♥♥ every time, pinwheel withstanding.
I can't really speak authoritatively on the combat, weapon/armor buffing, or PVP as I'm not as nuanced in all of that but what is there as a system and in practice is very deep and I've enjoyed what I've done with each of them.
The game has really put me in a place as a gamer I havent been in a long time. I'm actually interested in the lore and finding out details about the various bosses and npc I encountered. It's also the first game I've ever turned the soundtrack up louder than the dialogue and sound effects. This made for an epic final boss fight against Gwyn, Lord of Cinder and I think his theme has become my favorite song from any game's soundtrack. The boss fight itself might be my favorite from any game (once I actually learned how to parry him).
Ill continue to work towards getting 100% in Dark Souls, but for now after beating the game twice to get the two seperate endings, I think its time to move on to the next game in the series and see if it can maintain the same sense of wonder and enjoyment I have for Dark souls.
A really fun and engaging game, still holds up and deserves the respect it's gotten from the gaming community.

Dark Souls is by far the most addicting game I have ever played. As someone who never played many video games before I was introduced to Dark Souls, I now find myself holding all games to the Dark Souls standard. FromSoftware, the game company who made Dark Souls, designed the perfect mixture of dark, dungeon-crawling, RPG action that made this game so well designed and so incredible. There are certain criteria that a dark fantasy RPG game needs to hit in order for it to be great, and Dark Souls set the bar very high for all of them. I personally think these criteria are playability, story line, difficulty, and graphics.
Dark Souls has an amazing amount of playability. This game begins in an unfamiliar world filled with strange and original creatures. My first playthrough took over forty hours to complete, and that is when I hadn’t gone through and discovered all of Dark Souls’ hidden content and relatively secret bosses. Forty hours to play through the main content of this game felt like a lot to me, but then the final cut-scene ended and I began right where I started the game. I had not heard of the feature of “New-Game+” where the game just ramps up the difficulty and the game continues on from the beginning. So, Dark Souls definitely had a sufficient amount of playability for any level of gamer.
When it comes to the storyline, it is by far the most interesting concept in the world of Dark Souls. It is vague and hard to detect, all while being incredibly deep and emotional. Many fans of the series have put hours of their own time into describing their interpretations of Dark Souls lore. I found myself lost in the complexity of the stories behind all the games NPC’s and bosses. The game’s director, Hidetaka Miyazaki, read English books that he could not fully understand as a kid, so he had to fill in the blanks with his imagination. This is the root of Dark Souls. It is a game that is reliant on the player’s interpretation. How the player sees the story, is what the story becomes. I find myself thinking about the “Hollows,” or the undead that have lost their minds completely, as being directly connected to the player. The player spends hours getting through sections to find the next bonfire, dying repeatedly, then finally reaches the momentous moment of defeating the final boss, only to restart the game with a difficulty spike. The story, being up to the players deciphering, is both addictive and clear when putting the time in to think about it making it one of the most satisfying storylines I have ever played.
The difficulty in Dark Souls is what this game is most commonly known for. People who have not quite grasped the concept of the game will claim that it is too hard. But the game is fair to the player. It requires strategy and patience but to truly defeat the game, players must overcome the idea that the creators want to make it impossible. Dark Souls does require a heavy trial and error type of gameplay, and because of this, it is easy to become discouraged by the big red letters that all avid players have come to dread, “You Died.” The difficulty in this game is what makes it so great. Players learn from their mistakes, they see new patterns in a particular boss’ fighting style, and then eventually they triumph. It’s a game that creates a deep sense of accomplishment and that is due to its difficult gameplay.
Dark Souls, while incredible in most other aspects, is not perfect. The graphics in this game are not able to hold up compared to more recent games. The game can be choppy and has a couple of minor glitches, but to be fair to the game, it was released in 2011. The game did well for the technology available. While new games may have superior graphics, they will hardly compare to the gameplay and the deepness of the world that is Dark Souls.
Overall, this game is definitely one that everyone should pick up and play. Dark Souls contains many interlocking areas to explore, as well as having an extremely immersive storyline to follow. While the game falls short with graphics, it makes up for it with gameplay. The learning curve is a steep one, however, it is not impossible, and yet Dark Souls appeals to all categories of gamers. The RPG world of Dark Souls is one that takes standard open-world games and makes them look empty.

Pillars of Eternity is a fun isometric game that is similar to Baldur's Gate. I will give a TLDR at the bottom.
To start, the story for the game is interesting, and you play as a Watcher, someone who basically can interact with souls. You journey to take your vengeance and to slay the main antagonist, bringing up to 5 people in your party on your way. Others that agree to join your party but exceed to 6 party limit can stay at your keep once you get it. There is quite a bit of content to the game even without the DLC, and the game really does provide you a great deal of gametime. The base game comes in three acts, with each developing the story a bit more. My personal favorite was act II, and the ending of act II was quite a great one. There are tons of side quests that you can do in this game that make the story longer and more interactive. Some side quests make yield exp, some may yield reputation, and some may yield good gear and weapons. Regardless the case, there is a great deal of content to be explored.
There are also many different classes that you can make a character with, or you can have the other 5 people of your party members be influential characters that each have their own background and history. You can also design the other 5 of your party members yourself from the many different classes to explore the different party compositions. Each class also has different spells/abilities that you can pick to upgrade or increase when you level up. There are passives and actives for every single class, and based off of how you built your character up, the character can fight in a different style than if you built it up another way. For example, you can build your druid to be a healer or an animalistic fighter, and they can both work out well. As for the actual combat, it is basically a real time tactical pause type of combat, similar to Baldur's Gate and Dragon Age Origins if either of those ring a bell. With the real time aspect, you can get some of the actual action, but the tactical pause allows me to micro-manage my combat. My lineup that I went with was 1 human tank, 2 hunters with companions, 1 wizard, 1 druid, and 1 chanter. The party combination served me really well, as the 2 companions of the hunters were able to flank and draw agro rather well.
Aside from the gameplay, the game had great landscape design, great music, and pretty good voice acting. Although the art may look a bit "old" and not like the modern and fancy graphics, it is trying to get that appeal, which I thought worked well. The music really is one of the best parts of the game. There was not a single soundtrack for the game that I did not like. Whether it be combat music, inn music, or environment music, all of it was excellent. The voice acting was pretty good for the most part, although sometimes it would randomly stop if I skipped through dialogue too fast. Additionally, sometimes the little banter between party members and certain lines that party members said got on my nerves. It's interesting hearing it for the first time, but after you hear the same line over 100 times, it really gets old really fast.
TLDR: Excellent quality game that would be great for people to try out especially if you like Baldur's Gate.

I think it's a good game.
You can build passenger and cargo lines (with trains, bus, streetcars, trucks...) and connect the towns and industries to each other, which is fun.  The simulation is very solid. Every inhabitant has a persistent home, work, a recreational area and a preferred shop where he or she likes to go. Cities grow when they are connected to other cities via your transportation network or get goods delivered.
The optical presentation is nice which makes it very satisfying to watch the networks come to life. The cities are very lovely done, except sometimes the surrounding lands feels a little bit monotonous. There aren't any premade maps, instead they are procedural generated.
There are some rough edges at the moment, some are mentioning a bad performance. I had this problem at first, too. But simply lowering the graphic settings helped a lot.
The biggest oversight in my opinion is that the developers somehow missed to provide a user guide and the tutorial is lacking. It doesn't explain all important things. Some people are simply lost and rely on user generated guides or youtube videos at the moment, which understandably frustrates them. So if you plan to play Train Fever I like to advise you to look at some guides and videos first. (
)
For instance there are things that work differently than in other transportation simulations or aren't very obvious: Stops don't have a coverage area, instead people are trying to reach their destination in under 20 minutes. For instance this can mean they are willing to walk 17 minutes to a bus stop, use the bus for 2 minutes and walk another minute (of course it's better the closer stops are). They won't use a transportation network if travel times are longer than 20 minutes or if they can reach it on their own faster (by foot or car).
With freight it's similar. It's not possible to order freight, own can only provide lines and the  "business owner" decides whether to use your trains and trucks, to deliver freight on his own or to not produce at all. It needs to be delivered in under 20 minutes and the frequency and capacity of your vehicles determines how much will be delivered using your transportation network.
What really stands out is the ability to mod the game, which will contribute immensely to the longevity of it. There are already mods available that add more vehicles or more industries and goods.

Some games make you grin when you think about them. Some games make you cringe when you think about them. This game causes me to do both, and for the same reasons.
This is one of those games where you are surrounded by enemies, have limited ammo, and are stuck in a cramped space the whole game. This is part of what makes me cringe when thinking about this game.
Despite that you are stuck in a cramped space, there is no "enter cover" system like you would find in Mass Effect 3 or Gears of War. If you want to hang back around a corner and send rounds into the skulls of the zombies, then you can. You can even position yourself so that you can clip the arm/leg/ammo box of a target without taking fire from them until they move enough to actually hit you. This makes me grin, as I dislike the cover system that's implemented in Gears of War.
You can pick up credits just lying around the map to upgrade your weapons damage, piercing, fire rate, reload speed, and accuracy in between maps. This, too, makes me grin, since I like upgrading weapons to make them more capable.
Speaking of the maps, if you've got 30 minutes to kill, you can run most of the maps in that time. They aren't horribly long, and there really isn't any secrets to find like in DOOM, Hard Reset, or Borderlands.
The games graphics are not going to win any awards, and the whole game is basically a tunnel shooter with flashing warning lights and hissing of pipes letting of putrid green gas to create that creepy vibe, but they aren't horrible and give proper illusion of depth. The zombies look obviously "not real" in way that makes me smile as well and think back to the "Return of the Living Dead" movie. The game easily hits and holds 60 FPS, with vsync on, not even slowing down when there's 10+ enemies in view and I'm unloading buckshot for all I'm worth on my High End system.
Unfortunately, the controls as default seemed to make this unplayable. This is in large part thanks to a setting under "Gameplay options" called "Mouse Acceleration." Normally, when you move your mouse, the cursor on screen follows that movement at a flat ratio. If moving the mouse 1 inch results in the mouse cursor moving 3 inches, then moving the mouse 2 inches should result in the cursor moving 6 inches. Acceleration throws that out the window, and sometimes you'll turn to your left properly and sometimes you will turn all the way around and be looking behind you. Sometimes it's somewhere in between. Just move this slider all the way to the left and that problem goes away.
Overall, this is a fun game experience in my opinion, though nothing you will brag to your friends about.

Disclaimer - I lost patience with this game in chapter 2, after two playthroughs.
I really wanted to like this game.  I love the pixel art, and the setting + writing is good for an adventure game in this price range.  However, the randomization factor (RNG) is so badly implemented that I can't recommend playing it on anything other than puzzle mode (no RNG).  After playing for a while, I think they may have accidentally implemented a flat RNG instead of a bell curve (or something else with too much variance).  When every decision has a high importance of success, don't use a low variance RNG.
Unfortunately, they also dropped some important game elements in puzzle mode which make the game clearly worse.  For example, one of the options in chapter 2 is missing, and it also removes the use of an option when it's not at 100%, even though it may list a very high chance of success.
When playing on puzzle mode, the other issues, such as lack of player feedback, start to show more clearly.  Having to restart a 20+ minute section because a puzzle element had a fail counter that's not clearly expressed to the player is frustrating.  There are also instances of very low percentages of success with no ability for the player to increase them.  If the player cannot affect an outcome, don't make the outcome result in the player losing their time and having to replay it.
I think this game has a lot of potential, and while I wish I had the patience to deal with the poor mechanics, I'd rather just go play something better.  If you're a student of gaming, this is an excellent case study in how badly designed encounter mechanics can ruin an otherwise great game.
Despite the other feedback I've read, I don't think there can be a 'git gud' at a game that relies so heavily on RNG.

I got this for christmas from a good friend of mine and I have to say that I am very grateful he gifted me the Thief series. And although he forgot Thief: Deadly Shadows, I had more than 20 hours fun with Thief Gold to this date.
So. Let's review it, shall we?
I'll split this into two main points, Gameplay and Atmosphere. I won't touch on the story so much, you should play the game yourself to fully appreciate it.
All set? Cool, let's go.
Gameplay
As you would expect from a game released in the late 90s, it's quite dated. If you start it up for the first time, it is downright horrible. You'll need to change the controls accordingly, and you want to install TFix for the game to work in your favor, so that you can properly play it. I set the movement to wasd, looking around originally was on the Arrow keys, if someone knows the Might&Magic series, that was a popular control sceme back then.
You can cycle all your weapons with the Mouse wheel and you inventory with MOUSE4 and MOUSE5 (that's what I used at least). It is actually quite clunky and confusing if you have collected many items in a mission and you try to find your flash bombs while being chased.
Movement is pretty straight-forward, you can run, crouch and toggle walk (which I never used), look around with the mouse, you can even bhop if you have an even stretch of terrain going in one direction, which helps you getting away from danger. I think they fixed it in the second installment of Thief, there you cannot gain speed with bhopping anymore.
If you stay in the dark, you'll be hidden from eyesight perfectly. That is, if no one is searching for you. Otherwise they will spot you, no matter how dark your light gem at the bottom of the screen is.
Concerning the light gem: it's probably the most useful tool in your arsenal. It tells you how well hidden you are. If the light gem is white and a small, red dot is glowing on the side of it, you're visible to everything that should lay an eye upon you. If the gem is dark and the dot is green, you are perfectly hidden.
As explained, this will not always protect you from enemies. If they are alert enough, they will actively search the dark for you, also looking around doorways and scoping out dark corners and crevices.
Another aspect of the gameplay are footsteps. Maybe you know this from Dishonored. If you run, the enemy will hear you, you can purchase special boots to soften your footsteps, that feature is absent in Thief. Different surfaces will make different sounds, some louder, some not audible for the enemy. If you walk on metal, gravel or marble, you make the loudest noises, carpet or grass are silent. Wood and stone are generally pretty nice, if you run on them up to a guard from behind he will most likely go into stage 1 of "detection mode" before you knock him out, not more.
There are some useful tools to help you get around in a mansion spiked with marble floors or in a tower with too many iron walkways. You can purchase Moss Arrows, which make your steps silent. You can shoot it onto the floor and it will spread out in a circle, allowing you to walk on it silently. Enemies won't notice this change.
There's also a rope arrow which can be shot into wooden surfaces, helping you to get to elevated or hard-to-reach places.
Water arrows can douse torches and fires, helping you not getting spotted that easily.
Combat is clunky and hard, encouraging you to sneak. If you meet a guard directly, you're most likely dead.
However, I found that there's a small window of opportunity with knocking out unsuspecting enemies:
Of course you can walk up behind them with your wooden club (called Blackjack, for non-lethal takedowns) and give them a little strike, rendering them unconscious. Or, you can also hide behind a corner, jumping out at the last moment before the enemy rounds it, giving them a whack with the blackjack.
Most of the time they'll go: "Hey! Who are y... OUF!" meaning that you knocked them out before the AI could grasp you're really there and go into stage 2 alert mode.
You also have fire- and gas arrows, which are quite rare, but your best bet against any enemy. Also, you can use Holy Water on your water arrows to deal with some of the more paranormal enemies.
If you fight and seriously injure a guard, spider, etc. they will run away and call for help, alerting everyone around you, and let me tell you, you don't want that.
Especially the later enemies are quick and very tough to fight, so sneaking is generally your best option. You can always distract them by shooting noise arrows or throwing an object in a certain direction.
Atmosphere
If you play the first two hours, you'll notice where Dishonored got its inspiration from. Guards constantly speak to themselves, cough and mutter, whistle or hum a song. Occasionally you can overhear a conversation between two guards, telling you more about a situation or giving you subtle hints where a specific object is located.
Ambient noises are more rare, but they are there, for example dripping water in a cave or running machinery.
The music is gloomy and dark and it changes from area to area, when you walk out of a house into the courtyard, there might be something else playing than two seconds ago. The transition is quite fluent and on-point, immersing you pretty good. Usually, you can hear when you are in an area where you need to go, it is just the subtle change in tone of the tune playing, you'll notice it when you get there.
The game looks dark and moody, with some impressive shadow casting for the time. Also, Thief 1 & 2 still have one of the best sound engines ever made, when you hear sounds from a certain direction, usually, there's also something there that makes these sounds. I found that the engine bugged sometimes, but maybe that's because of the level design.
Speaking of that, the level design is impressive, yet sometimes confusing, with parts branching off and running back towards the main path. it looks very believable and has some special detail for it, although things like debris and small objects lying around are missing. I think the maps are quite innovative and they never get boring, they are nice and rememberable. Also, the lighting is one point most of the time, a cave is rather dark and cold looking, a library is either flooded in warm light or also gloomy, depending on who possesses the house it is built in.
Not all enemies have the same voice lines, and especially the Hammerites impressed me, using old, Shakespearian language to indicate that they are quite sophisticated, yet a bit fanatic. Mages are very calm, but also have a certain majestic undertone. Guards can sound professional or quite dumb.
The voice acting is alse very believeable and shows that the Thief voice team did an outstanding job with recording them.
Special mentions go towards the voice actor of the thief himself: Stephen Russell, who is the perfect fit for master thief Garrett, providing him with just enough character to not be over the top. He often gives remarks (that can be quite snarky) when reaching key locations or targets. Also, before each mission, he tells a bit about the following task, that he has to do. This is combined with some of the most fitting musc for a serious "mission briefing" by the main character himself.
I'd like to mention a very specific thing I looked forward to after each completed mission. There's a segment where the screen shows quotes from books of the Hammerites or other parties, accompanied by music, which is drastically rising in intensity, indicating a climax, which is usually a deep tone switching over to the briefing music. Shortly after the tone, Garrett starts talking, which is the point the intense music was building up to. Absolutely well done and awesome. Click here to see what I mean. It is the briefing of the tutorial to prevent spoilers.

Duke nukem 3d is an absolutely fantastic game and a classic FPS that remains just as enjoyable today as it was 20 years ago (suck it down). This remaster is the best looking version of the game, and doesn't alter the original aside from some new sounds and prettier visuals. This is a good thing, but why do I not give it a "recommended" rating?
1. The options menu is very sparse, and eduke has much more customizability and is FREE!
2, This ties into the first one, and it might be nitpicking but there isn't even an option to turn off the auto-aim! Sure I know that's how most of the 90's fps games are but if I'm paying $20 for a 20 year old game the least you could do is let me turn off auto-aim because IMHO auto-aim is annoying as ♥♥♥♥. It's not an engine issue either, BLOOD runs off the build engine and auto-aim can be disabled by screwing with the config file.
3. There is NO option in the menu to play user maps, and instead we have workshop integration. While workshop is cool and all  but I might want to play a map off the net.
4. The developer commentary feels kind of half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ It's cool to listen to the devs but it isn't present in all levels. And they seem to have even screwed up by putting a commentary track from the new episode 5 into level 1. Might have been intentional but it feels weird when they talk about new content in the first minute.
5. The biggest fault with this version is the absense of the expansion packs. They were included with the Megaton version of the game (that gearbox had removed). So unless you resort to the "under-the-router" method of aquiring them you are out of luck. The expansions are a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥to get physically.
Some people complain about the new re-recorded voice work but I think it's more jarring than anything. I wouldn't say that it's actually terrible but it's bizarre if you are familiar with the old game. John says the same things, but he is trying to differentiate them from the old ones by saying them differently.
So I would tell you to wait and see if they update this in the future before you buy it. It isn't a terrible version, just subpar as of right now.  If you have never played Duke3d before this might be worth it, but it is pretty easy to find the game physically. Just make sure you get the Atomic edition of the game and download Eduke32.  Your only other option is to *COUGH* ARRRRRGH! *COUGH* the game from you-know-where.  Gearbox had the atomic edition removed from GOG's store, so unless you bought the game beforehand you are out of luck if you are planning on legally buying another edition digitally.
EDIT: Someone in the comment section says you can still buy Megaton keys.Some online key vendors are still selling them but I don't know if they will work or not.

Fantastic isometric co-op game, that is anything but a run and gun shooter.
It blends just enough strategy with action, that demands teamwork between your comrads or you will meet certain doom.
Given it's in early access however, this is a review based on the current build of the product.
Content is lacking in some corners, but for it's asking price of $19.99 USD, it makes some other early release titles for the same price pale in comparison in terms of offered content.
The game truly needs some way to tweak a perfect balance of progression and level/player balance within the game, which currently it lacks.
I personally enjoy the ol' "chase the carrot on a stick" progression system, but only when it pairs well with the content in mind, which is certainly tricky.
I'm certain that over time, this game will grow and continue to provide additional content, methods of progression and more, so with that said...if you're a fan of over the top (view) tactical shooters, that provide a deep sense of team work with a slice of lone wolf goodness (as skill does matter) but don't mind the often restrictive nature of "play that class THIS way and none other", then you'll certainly love this game.
It kind of reminds me of the Space Hulk game in a RTS sense (rather than turn base) with a mix of twin stick shooter goodness.
P.S. This game only really works with a keyboard and mouse, a controller really isn't needed for the style of the game (and i'm not sure if it even supports one currently), so keep that in mind if you're thinking you could have twin stick shooter style controls, this is mainly due to the interface.

I found this game by searching for the multi-player co-op tags on steam.  If you're looking for that kind of experience, and like challenging games, then this game is for you.  They are reportedly working on a single player mode, but cooperative-multiplayer is where the heart of this game is.
The game IS challenging.  If you are playing at the correct difficulty for your team, you will lose more often then you will win.
Even though it's early access, the game is very playable.  They've had some buggy patches but they tend to fix them pretty quick.  The devs are on a fast-release cycle and they listen to the community as to what is and isn't working, what's fun and isn't fun, and they participate in the forums.
Now that the game is more stable, the dev's have been focusing on adding more content (maps, bosses, missions, skills, etc) which is keeping the game fresh and challenging.
If you can get this game on sale, or money isn't a big deal,  I'd definitely recommend the early access version.  If you are on a tight budget, you may want to wait for release.  I have ~500hours on record so far for a $20 game.  So I'm very happy with the value I'm getting.

An effective and surprisingly somber story. Mae can be grating at times, the the first half is a little aimless, but it's all worth it in the end.

This game is amazing! The story is in-depth and captivating, and I absolutely love the quirky personalities of the main cast; they remind me a lot of my own friends and I. It's not often I find a "weird" or "awkward" character that isn't presented in a way that seems to be begging to be #relatable to the YA audeince, so it's refreshing to find a story about a group of imperfect misfits that each manage to have individual well-rounded personalities.
The visuals are beautiful, and I LOVE the use of colour and (ha) shape language. The clean, lineless artstyle and the calming background music really contribute to the overall atmosphere of the game.
I also love the way that the narrative makes you question things, and gives you a chance to figure out and decide for yourself what's really happening. Very rarely did I feel like I was being beaten over the head with exposition or being railroaded into specific plot points. It's very immersive in that regard, as very few things happen that you (or rather, Mae) are not directly involved with.
It's got a lot of heavy themes, but it seldom felt like there was a moral being shoved in my face. As I said, the game is very good about letting the player decide how they feel about things instead of telling them how they should.
Definitely worth the purchase, and one of my favourite games to come out in the past few years. Even playing through multiple times doesn't detract from my enjoyment, and I feel like I'm always discovering new secrets.

It's truly a very touching story based game in which any decision you make will alter how the game plays out.
The characters are very appealing/relatable, and I enjoyed learning as much as I could about them throughout the game. And like real life, if you spend the day with one of your friends, you don't have time to hang out with a different one afterwards. And each friend leads to a different 'minigame' and hangout area depending on the day you hang out with them, meaning you have to play the game multiple times to experience it all.
The town is full of life, and not just because of the art style, but the game literally has moving cars, people walking around, leaves on the ground which can be knocked around, animals climbing the buildings and carrying around acorns which can also be knocked around by the player as well. It pays attention to such small detail that it feels realistic.
There are tons of areas to explore for such a small town, especially amongst the roof tops. And there are a lot of secrets which you can't even get to in one playthrough, allowing for much replayability should you really enjoy the game.
The game took me 12 and a half hours to finish my first playthrough, and most of the game had me super invested in the story and wanting to know how it will eventually end. The ending itself was... eh. I'll save the spoilers and just say that it's not the same game by the end.
Overall, Night in the Woods is a great experience. The characters feel real, the town feels alive, there's much to explore, you choose your own adventure, and I had much fun with it.

After about almost 400 hours, I think it's time that I finally write a review for this game. I have gotten every achievement in this game and I have put quite a few hours into the antibirth mod. Even after all that, I could easily see myself put a 1000 hours into this game.
The replayability of this game is based on the amount of items and synergies that exist in the game. No run has ever really felt the same as the last. If I had to mention something bad about this, it would have to be that if there is a specific synergy that you like, then you might not see it too often.
The bosses and enemies in the game are all really well designed (save for a few, but I will talk about that later). Each boss seems like it has its own personality.
There are plenty of problems in this game like bugs and the such, but as you play most of them will get covered.
I would say 100% purchase Rebirth, however I don't think I could ever recommend Afterbirth and Afterbirth+. If you play Isaac and are itching for more official content, then I think you should pick up the DLC, but for someone who just plays the game casually I don't think the purchase would be worth it. The two main bosses added with the DLCs are too mediocre and the new floors are lackluster as well. The greed gamemode gets pretty boring after a little bit of playing it. If you want more Isaac content and you don't have the money, then I would recommend Antibirth, which is a free mod made by Isaac fans that adds a huge amount of content. This includes many new bosses, floors, and items.
TL;DR:  BUY REBIRTH, buy Afterbirth/Afterbirth+ if you want official content, get Antibirth if you still want more content or don't have much money.

I beat Dark Souls.
I'm proud to say after years of false starts I finally conquered the game and I'm left with nothing but praise and a new found love for the Soulsborne series. Everything in Dark souls is unfair until it isnt, its a lot like the movie Edge of Tomorrow, that constant restart that leads to leads to success. In that way, if you are attentive you learn something from every death and carry that into the next encounter or boss fight. I can't count the amount of times I called ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t while playing the game only to shortly after realize it was something I did that lead to my death, and while that happens a lot in games for me I can't think of many in the last decade that that is the case nine times out of ten. I went into NG+ approaching SL120 and thinking I was the lord of the land only to get ganged up on by three of the common enemies in undead burg and dying in seconds. The game put me back in my place and I've remained there ever since. Of course areas like blight town pose no real threat to me now and the threat of being poisoned isnt a problem once you realize you can't get poisoned again until the status wears off. I feel like I;m doing some hardcore parkour when I traverse the area now. Same can't be said about the catacombs, still makes me its ♥♥♥♥♥ every time, pinwheel withstanding.
I can't really speak authoritatively on the combat, weapon/armor buffing, or PVP as I'm not as nuanced in all of that but what is there as a system and in practice is very deep and I've enjoyed what I've done with each of them.
The game has really put me in a place as a gamer I havent been in a long time. I'm actually interested in the lore and finding out details about the various bosses and npc I encountered. It's also the first game I've ever turned the soundtrack up louder than the dialogue and sound effects. This made for an epic final boss fight against Gwyn, Lord of Cinder and I think his theme has become my favorite song from any game's soundtrack. The boss fight itself might be my favorite from any game (once I actually learned how to parry him).
Ill continue to work towards getting 100% in Dark Souls, but for now after beating the game twice to get the two seperate endings, I think its time to move on to the next game in the series and see if it can maintain the same sense of wonder and enjoyment I have for Dark souls.

First CRPG type game I’ve ever played. Love it so much!!
Some of my favorite aspects of the game:
-deep class customization,  each class has a few optimal builds, and SO many viable builds. They give you freedom to do whatever you want, and it’ll still end up being viable on lower difficulties.
-any class can equip any weapon armor set without a need for stat requirements.
-stats are interconnected. For example: the might stat gives a bonus to fortitude defense and increases damage done from ALL sources, and healing done. So all dps classes and healers benefit from might. Intellect gives a bonus to Will defense and increases AoE radius and duration effects. So all classes that have AoE damage, healing, or status effects benefit from intellect!
There are more abilities for each class than you can choose at max level, meaning high replay value! You can also respec you character (and created companions) at any inn. So you’re never stuck with the choices you make.
If you like games like Baldurs Gate,  and Dragon Age Origins, GET THIS GAME NOW.

An absolute blast from beginning to end. This is the best isometric RPG since Baldur's Gate 2.
The setting is well developed and immersive. The story is mysterious and compelling. The NPCs are… fine. I wasn’t really enraptured with any of them but it never really detracted from the experience. The choices you make during the game are impactful but not game altering (sort of like Baldur’s Gate 2). The BBEG has a distinctive personality and ambition, which really draws you into the narrative (also very much like Baldur’s Gate 2).
The combat system is nearly perfect. There's a wide variety of character classes and abilities, each with a particular role to fill and boundless synergies to experiment with. The mechanics hit the sweet spot of being complex without being burdensome; they’re straightforward without being too simplistic. Coming into a fight, dying, reloading and trying a different tactic, and succeeding after four or five attempts is as rewarding as I could ever hope for.
I wanted to play a game that was basically an updated Baldur’s Gate, and this delivered perfectly. They’ve simplified a lot of out of combat mechanics (retraining, easy to follow quest and journal logs, home base building, inventory management, building your own party from scratch, etc.) so that is feels like a modern game with a strong old school inspiration. This is the complete isometric CRPG experience for a new generation.
