I found this game to be very enjoyable.
The basic premise is that you play as a disgutsing littly dude named Grimm who wishes to take away all the neat and tidy and childish out of commonly known fairy tales and replace them with filth, gore and dark undertones.
The game itself was released in an episodic fashion when it was brand new, coming out every week, but now all three seasons are here.
Each episode and gameplay plays out the same. You begin with Grimm telling you the cutesy version of the fairy tale in the episode (ranging from Father Death, Frog Prince and Snow White as a series finale). When that story is finished, you enter each scene as Grimm and begin spreading filth. Grimm has an aura/radius of darkness that turns the light hearted terrain and objects into darkness. Starting off, you can only convert buckets and flowers, but as you convert more you gain more points towards your darkness level (shown at the top of the screen). Higher levels of darkness means a wider aura, faster speed, higher jumping, and, most importantly, the ability to convert larger objects. During the conversion, fairy tale characters and creatures will attempt to clean up the mess, but they don't prove to be much of an issue.
The usual goal in each scene is getting to a certain level of darkness and then "butt-stomping' (jump twice) the plot point to proceed. Once all scenes have been converted, the story is then retold in its raw and dark way and the episode is over.
The art style fits the theme of the game, with really childish creatures that turn into ugly monstrosities. It's just enjoyable to see what one fairy tale object will convert to, such as a regular tree turning into a tree filled with hanging corpses.
The humor within this game ranges from fart jokes to satire to black humor, all of which makes the game much mor enjoyable. Grimm himself is an enjoyable narrator and character. Fun fact: the voice actor for Grimm voices EVERY character in the game, which shows off the guy's incredible voice talent.
The one downside is that once you play one episode you basically have played them all. The gameplay is the same through each episode, though some introduce other gameplay elements.
To defend that point, however, the game is built around the narration of the story and the curiosity of how each story (and every object in it) will look after Grimm has converted it. So, even though the gameplay is the same, it is a different story to muck up. The choices in fairy tales are great, too.
If you don't mind the repetitive gameplay, definitely give this game a go. Sometimes it is good to pass 30 minutes of time by playing an episode, and you got three series of episodes to play, which will keep you occupied.

In a sentence, State of Decay (SoD) is a single-player GTA-style open-world survival RPG that requires micromanagement and has modest elements of base-building. It's nice for a particular kind of patient gamer such as myself, but if you're less tolerant of repetitive resource runs, primitive AI, and standard open-world-game glitches, you might want to rethink this as a purchase. However, do note that as of now, the devs for this game are still making patches, updates, and DLCs for SoD, so keep the date of this review in mind. The game itself is one main campaign (plus side storylines), which you'll generally only want to play through once. If you're also hoping for a more free-form NewGame+ experience, do note that it is a DLC feature which will cost an additional USD$7. SoD also has another DLC campaign for a similar USD$7. SoD begins excitingly. You are inserted in the midst of a traditional zombie apocalypse, and you must learn the ways of combat and survival. After some time, you'll have get both a base and a larger of upgrading that base into more hospitable and effective headquarters. In the beginning, the excitement of scrounging through ruins for resources is exhilarating; scraping together anything you can, desperate to get in and out without alerting too many zeds. This leads into the slower-to-build satisfaction you'll get from successfully surviving and successfully fortifying your base. All this happens in the open-world area of Trumbull Valley, which effectively conveys an overall feeling of post-apocalyptic despair and empty desolation, further enhancing the feeling of surviving in such a place. However, there is a problem if you dawdle. If you don't advance the storyline and just spend a long time exploring and scavenging, eventually that experience is going to get dull. Zombies will get less dangerous as you become more experienced, and when the scavenging process becomes routine for you, the repetitiveness will leech more and more excitement out of it until it becomes akin to a daily chore. Particular kinds of special infected can turn scavenging excitingly dangerous again, but those are an exception rather than a rule. Now, I should mention a feature that may frighten off uncertain players: offline progression. When you exit SoD, its in-game world will continue progressing up to 2 hours (one in-game day). During that time, various projects can be completed, AI survivors may scavenge more resources, and random positive/negative events will occur. And what happens during this offline time depends on the condition of your base when you left. If you're worried, keep in mind that these negative events will *never* result in the outright death of any survivor (though leaving a rescue mission unstarted/unfinished might). Also, you can control this to a degree by changing the time on your computer's clock. A particular frustration for me in SoD was the AI of NPC allies. As you can only control one survivor at a time, the rest that you rescue will be controlled by the AI, who only seems capable of the most basic of combat/actions: only attacking zeds within a short-range radius; only ever fighting with basic melee swipes/finishing moves, even if you've given them guns and unlocked special moves; being unable to help you with anything (carrying resources, closing doors, searching houses) except for outright combat. All this just makes the single in single-player overwhelmingly apparent. Your saved NPC allies aren't fellow living survivors; when you aren't in control of one, they become machines with a single directive "Kill Zeds" and no situational awareness. That's why they'll run directly up to a zed that explodes into poisonous clouds and why they'll shoot grenades at close-range targets. If you do get this game, State of Decay is a game that wanted to be bigger than it had time/resources for. It immerses at the start, but that feeling wanes after a while. Instead, SoD's selling point is conveying the satisfaction of survival against the odds of intentional zombie threats and unintentional tedium. I did enjoy a good part of it, but that was in spite of a host of irritations that may prove game-ruining for less RPG-experienced players, and immersion-breaking for survival-games enthusiasts. Though the devs tried to make this a long-term game, this is really just a game you'll want to play through just once or twice. In fact, I really only recommend this game to those who are familiar with GTA-style games and the glitches and AI typical for such games, as well as those fellow RPG players like me who can become easily accustomed to (and do not mind) the grind of repetitive activities.

While it isn't the cream of the crop for the Zombie Genre this game certaintly has its own quirks.
The base game is a simple story of survival and (albiet hollow) choices but does a good job of introducing you to game mechanics and giving a interesting idea of the Zombie apocolypse.
For the actual gameplay you're helping run a (small) community and have to scavange resources to survive.. does a fairly good job of this! As you progress through the story you'll start to notice resources becoming harder and harder to come by.. particularly when building up the base and specially if you're taking your time, of which you're effectivly limited on.
The main nuisance of an otherwise good game.. is all the fetching you've got to do (unmodded that is), the AI isn't terribly bright and in larger communities you'll find yourself having to pull out various members out of various jams or risk losing them constantly.. in a game where death is "Permanent".
- - - -
Breakdown is a total survival mode, increasing in difficulty (More zombies, less resources, less transportation) as you complete levels. Shares all the nuiances of the main game, but adds in more weapons of various types as well as potential of unlocking "Hero" characters (Special characters with boosted stats and helpful perks) that you can also start with should you decide to start from the beginning again.
Unlike the main game, you only 'Complete' a level through the completion of a specific task and can only transfer up to 8 other characters (including your own) to the next level of difficulty. The main idea is to survive as long as you can and rack up a high score. Simple to do, but difficult to pull off as the levels increase.
- - - -
Lifeline follows a similar idea of Breakdown, except you now have virtually unlimited resources (provided you can continue to earn influence) and you need to survive waves every so often. Like breakdown the waves get progressively harder and while you're not exactly limited on ammo.. people can still die and it is difficult to recover personal to fill in gaps in defense.
There is also a story to uncover in this mode and you're on a timelimit for most (if not all) of the required missions, however they add in backstory to the main game. You also get to hear bits an pieces on how it all started.

Civilization + Age of Wonders mash-up with magicks, mystical beasts and various races!
PRO:
+Surprisingly well done round based strategy game with interesting races and ressources
+ Level up your troops with important skills! Build smithies and supply your troops with weaponry and armor upgrades!
+ Hire heroes, equip them with weapons/armor/wands depending on their class to pimp their combat/spell-capabilities!
+ Research and cast awesome spells reminiscient of Age of Wonders that greatly impact combat and economics!
+ Modify map tiles to change their bonus ressource output, sink islands to drown troops or create hills to give combat benefits!
+ Races all have greatly differing play styles!
+ Pick a Lord(Avatar) and personalize your starting spells and skills!
+ Multiple planes of existence work seamlessly!
+ Finish little quests to boost your finances, defeat "barbarian"-style beasts and loot their lairs for XP and artifacts!
+ Multi-Player has bots!
CON:
- No Single-Player Campaign! Only "Skirmish"-esque maps with default bots for solo play!
- Gameplay will get repetetive after 3 rounds
- Multi-Player is not simultaneous, you have to wait for others to finish their turn before you can act...
- Races are not equally newbeginner-friendly
- Tech trees not available ingame, google for them/ninja them from the game's webpage
- A lot of content splintered over DLC in an attempt to make the Ultimate Edition more attractive
- "Barbarians" spawning in regularly can become a nuisance later...
DLC WORTH THE CASH?
Only if you can get the Ultimate Edition cheap, the items and Elf race are worth it to enhance the experience!
Recommended purchase if at 10-15 bucks, improve replayability with DLC and multi-player!

Cory in the House is a television show, which aired on the Disney Channel from January 12, 2007 to September 12, 2008 and was a spin-off from the Disney show That's So Raven. The show focuses on Cory Baxter, who moves from San Francisco, California to Washington, D.C. with his father, after Victor Baxter gets a new job in the White House as the official head chef. The series marks a Disney Channel first, as it is the channel's first spin-off. This is also the only Disney Channel spin-off series to be broadcast in standard definition for the entire length of the show. Reruns of the series have not been produced on Disney Channel, or on Disney XD; however they continue to air on the Family channel in Canada. Raven-Symoné guest-starred, reprising her role as Raven Baxter in one episode. In 2014 Disney Channel started airing a weekly block called Disney Replay on Wednesdays nights, during which episodes of Cory in the House air alongside That's So Raven and Kim Possible, among others.

I love this game! It was a lot of fun while I played it, but it definitely needs to be fleshed out further for me to continue playing.
Pros:
-Beautiful graphics! I love how realistic and gorgeous everything looks. It all really looks good!
-Minimalist UI! - I love this! It really makes it more immersive.
-Lots of fun! - I love crafting and building and exploring new islands and shipwrecks.
-Stumbling across random new items in shipwrecks--it was always enjoyable discovering something I'd never found before. Each new item was delightful!
-Realism - As mentioned above, I love all the effort put into making the game realistic and immersive! It was a pretty good balance between being realistic and still being fun (because, of course, being too realistic can make things become tedious).
Suggestions:
-Deterioration rate of needs didn't seem terribly balanced/realistic. I only had to sleep every 2-3 days (not at all realistic), and hunger was never a problem for me. All I ate was fruit (which I did mostly as another way to hydrate myself when I didn't have fresh water available and didn't want to waste a coconut). I never fished or cooked potatoes. I cooked one crab in the beginning before I realized I didn't need to cook/eat much. The only thing that seemed pretty accurate was the thirst deterioration, and that was (realistically) a pain to stay on top of. However, it could still be realistic but less bothersome if the passage of time were slowed down.
-The Timescale - The days passed waaaay too quickly! I know a lot of people say that 1 second equalling 1 minute of gametime is pretty standard, but I could barely accomplish anything before the sun set. I know that's part of the challenge of it, but the current timescale is more frustrating than simply "challenging." I was only able to progress to the point that I did because I didn't have to sleep much (which, as I said, is not realistic), so I was able to work through the night many nights (which was a nuisance because I'd much rather work by daylight than headlamp).
-Respawn rates - I tried to refrain from cutting down palm trees because coconuts are such a lifesaver and I wanted them to respawn, but in 22 days of survival they never respawned, so I guess I might as well have cut down the trees I was trying to save. Yukka plants seemed to respawn overly quickly (although maybe real life yukka plants grow really fast--I don't know). I never needed to worry about overdoing it on making lashings. Also I think it would be good if the ficus trees respawned (but slowly... like... 10 days after being cut? Maybe more?)
--The seagulls and bats are a nice touch, but way too loud/noisy!
--I would love the ability to make a map. On the one hand, I like how realistic it is that I have a hard time keeping track of what island is where--the realism is definitely good... but there must be some way to balance it so that it is realistic and challenging, but not overly frustrating. Although you know, I think a lot of my frustration at not remembering which island in the distance was which had to do with the days being so short. Because the days are so short, there's just no room for error in your navigation--you better know where you're heading and be super prepared for anything at all times (I carried around an emergency stash of 4 green coconuts just in case I ended up having to stay the night on an island I didn't mean to, and I wasn't always confident that that would be enough). Having to be prepared is good, but the constant struggle between need deterioration, losing daylight, and not having your bearings on directions and locations made gameplay borderline tedious at times. I would loved to have been able to loosen up a little and not worry so much. Obviously if you're stranded on an island you're going to be constantly preoccupied with survival, but this is a game, so I'd love to be able to lighten up a LITTLE bit more.
On the whole I think it is a wonderful game with loads of potential. Even as it currently is, it's a lot of fun, and I definitely recommend trying it out if you love realism-based exploration/survival games with beautiful graphics.

Although I pre-ordered this the minute I saw it, I was very apprehensive towards it at first. That being said, now that I've played it - I do highly recommend this game if you're a fan of Duke Nukem 3D.
I've been playing Duke Nukem 3D for fifteen years and I've purchased the original, Atomic Edition, Kill-A-Ton Edition, Megaton Edition - pretty much whatever bundle or version has been available to me. I've played using the High Resolution Pack through it's evolution, I've played the famous Roch maps, I've made a terrible set of maps with the original build tool, you name it. I followed the progress of Duke Nukem 3D: Reloaded with great anticipation and was sad when I heard the plug had been pulled. I'd always wanted to see what a remake of Duke Nukem 3D would look like given all the technological advancements that have been made since it's release. When I first heard about the Anniversary World Tour, I assumed the "True 3D" they mentioned would be something like that. When I saw the trailer and realized this was not the case, I was disappointed. I was more disappointed to learn that the Megaton Edition had been pulled from the steam store when it was much cheaper and featured a whole host of extra (fan-made, but highly acclaimed) content, including two additional episodes.
My first instinct was to think "that's a bit of a♥♥♥♥♥♥move", selling something for a significantly higher price with less content, as you'll see is a common complaint in the bad reviews here. I mean, I could justify the price increase if it was actually a remake like Reloaded was supposed to be, but it looked to me like it was just the same old Duke with fancy lighting from the trailer. I preordered the game still, given there would be additional content from some of the original creators (such as the eight new levels and accompanying music tracks). I've always been a sucker for more Duke Nukem 3D content.
Release day has come and I held my breath and gave it a whirl. I played a bit, flicked on some of the old cheat codes to warp between levels and places to sus the entire game out and I have to say: I really regret doubting this release. It's beautiful. The lighting in the new engine is a great addition to the game, making old levels seem a bit more lively and making the new levels look stunning. On top of that, all of Duke's comments and vocal SFX have been re-recorded faithfully to the original with amazing clarity. If you don't like either of these options, you can turn them off and have the game look exactly as you remember.
The new content is well worth the price on it's own. All of the classic music is available in the traditional MIDI format and also in OGG format, recorded with hardware specified by the composer. It's not as clear as the SC-55 pack that was available for eDuke and (I think) included with the Megaton Edition, but it's on par (and I can't help but enjoy hearing tracks the way the composer wanted me to hear them). There are also nine additional tracks, available only in the OGG format. They're all faithful to the original contributions Jackson made to the soundtrack. The new levels are absolutely huge. I remember when I first played the original release, I always wanted large, outdoor levels and this release has finally made that a reality. Their locations are incredibly varied (from Pyramids to the Golden Gate bridge, to an epic return to Hollywood in the finale), and combining the vast, gigantic landscapes with the new soundtrack with the new levels gives them a larger-than-life feel, If you were around to experience the joy of getting the Plutonium Pak and "The Birth" as a new episode for Duke way back in the day - this new episode will give you that same feeling. Without spoiling anything pertinent, there are also a new type of enemy, a new weapon and a new (but somewhat familiar) final boss whose setting really feels like a good climax to the game.
The menu is swift and easy to navigate and you can select any level to begin it (except for secret levels) rather than starting each episode from the first level. Other than that, it's a bit lacking. There's no Anti-Aliasing (which in this day and age is a pretty big thing to leavel out), although you can force a form of post-aa (FXAA, SMAA, MLAA) in your respective AMD or NVIDIA control panel. There's no anisotropic filtering option either, though in this game that's not a very noticable exclusion. You can redefine your controls, but by default they're set to the mouse and keyboard setup most modern first-person-shooters use and there's no quick toggle to the original DOS controls, which is a bit of a shame. I do think the new setup is easier to use and more practical, but something about Duke Nukem 3D makes me want to use the A key to jump, not to move left. It's a minor annoyance, but an annoyance nonetheless. Additionally, the sound effects sound much more muffled on this particular release than any other, and that is particularly noticable with the new high-fidelity recordings of Duke.
Anyway, I've probably missed some points here and there but the game itself is definitely a good investment whether you're new to Duke Nukem 3D or a veteran like myself. It's not the remaster we wanted, but it's definitely an improvement and well worth the money.

Pillars of Eternity is an RPG just like the older Infinity Engine games like Buldur's Gate, or Icewind Dale. The combat is real time but you can pause any time to issue commands. The biggest difference being that this game doesn't use the Dungeon and Dragons rules. Other than that the combat works very similarly
The story in PoE is excellent. The way they let you shape your character is really really good. There is always a wide range of dialog options, everything from plain out wrong, to mr goody two shoes, and straight up jerk. The NPCs will react accordingly making the story as interesting as you want to make it. Your companions will speak up accordingly if they are with you at the right moments. They throw a lot at you, but it will be easy to pick up as you play more.
Your character will 'inherit' a keep with a huge dungeon underneath. You build it up using whatever cash you make in your adventure. Speaking of which, you will have a bottomless bag. Big upgrade from rpgs like this. You no longer have to go back to town all the time to unload your bags. Just pick everything up! It automatically goes to your stash.
If you like RPGs, Infinity Engine games, buy with confidense. I got 22 hrs of playtime beating just the main story, and some of the side quests. There is a ton of optional content I have yet to experience but it's a great value at any price.

Overall this is a great game in my opinion. The combat system is great and relentless on harder diffuculties, so to those of you looking for a challenge then I highly recommend you buy this game. The game is also rich in history and has an astounding amount of lore for those who like to enjoy games and get to know the background of the game world.

NOTE:- This review is based entirely on the base game; I've not played Breakdown or Lifeline.
State of Decay is a great game, but it sometimes seems to go out of its way to make it difficult to love. It started its PC life as a fairly shoddy-sounding port, which is why there's so many negative reviews about it. But those have mostly been patched out, and I didn't encounter any of the issues that early reviewers found so game-destroying. There's still plenty of issues though. Not being able to give someone following you items to carry that you find whilst exploring is annoying, zombies clipping through walls and biting you is annoying, and the constant spamming of repetitive missions and Lily's awful, constant radio chatter will annoy you. The game is annoying.
It's also great, if you can look past the issues. Exploring the large map, on the prowl for resources, is enjoyable. And dangerous. The survivors dotted around are not going to respawn if they die. Some of them can join you, if they trust you enough. If you befriend them, you can play as them, or have them accompany you. If they die, they're gone. The game does a great job of making deaths devastating, which makes up for the thin story and character development. Your group of survivors is unique, and losing some of them genuinely makes you feel bad, especially when your only good chef gets ripped in half by a zed, just because you got gung ho and beeped your car horn instead of sneaking quietly through the bushes. Speaking of which, the game suits playing a fairly stealthy style. But you don't have to. I started off being very open and smashing every zombie I saw with a pipe, or a cricket bat, but it's very easy to die that way. You can be confidently breezing through the game, but you can get sloppy and make one mistake, and suddenly your favourite character is dead. You can zoom around in a variety of vehicles and run over zeds in GTA-style, making a lot of noise, or you creep around and skulk in the shadows. You have to manage your home base, your survivors, and your supplies, and there's plenty of challenges to each, and some trade-offs to be made. Yes I know the game has been released before surge of iPhone games but the mentality still stays.

CONS:

So now I'm a little over 100 hours into this game. I'm still not going to recommend it in general. But if you've read even this far, then read on and decide for yourself whether you should give this game a try.
At this time (9/15) the game hasn't had any improvements aside from a few crash hotfixes. It still feels like an early release game, yet it is purported to be gold. There is talk on the forums - none from official sources - that this game will be improved over time.
So let's keep that in mind - this game was rushed to release, is missing a lot of common features, has awful UI. Many things are non-intuitive.
For a "business simulator" a lot of important business data is not available - prices of any sort, cost of maintenance for rails/stations/etc, capacity of same, plenty of other data is nowhere to be found.
Schedules cannot be set for any vehicle, and only the most rudimentary of waiting orders that are used at your own risk. For a game about logistics, you have little control over the logistics of your vehicles.
Tracklaying is complex and has no undo button or planning mode. This can be very expensive, especially with your first few trains.
Replacing/upgrading vehicles is very tedious and can throw off the productivity of an entire line. It can take more than an hour with an extensive network of vehicles when upgrading to a new model.
This game has very little in common with OTTD, RRT, or even SMR. If you're a long-time transport/rail game fan you'll need to forget all the strategies of the past - Train Fever needs you to play its way.
So if you want to play this game, you'll have to learn how to work around all those things. Once you do that, you'll still notice the problems, but you'll find a surprisingly complex game underneath. Lots of interesting transport planning to do, with interactive routes. Growing your towns is really fun. A lot of this game is really fun. And, for me anyway, super addictive. I can't think of a game that hooked me so bad.
So if you're willing to put in 20 hours or so studying and failing and getting frustrated, and then another 80 thinking you know what you're doing when you really don't, you'll probably enjoy this game. I'm sure I'll need to put in another couple of hundred hours before I really feel like I've got this down. It's just a shame it will be this clunky should-be-alpha-early-release version instead of the $35-value-gold-release I was lead to expect.
Here's my original review verbatim from 9/4 when I first bought it. My complaints from this original review are still valid, by the way!
I'm a long time Transport Tycoon/RRT/etc fan - I love trains and business simulations. The business simulation in this is very shallow so far. The limited industries (4 chains) are inconsistent and unpredictable. The limitations of "full load/any load" are pretty annoying, it's difficult and non-intuitive to set up lines where trucks/trains wait until full but also don't clump up.
Laying track is a mix of awesome and annoying. I love that you can adjust the way it sticks to the ground - grading and curves really make a difference. Because of that it would really be nice if you could plan out more than one segment of track at a time. Not being able to upgrade/replace stations easily is frustrating - not only when moving to multiple tracks but also to just adjust an original placement. Again, a planning mode would really help.
To be fair this is my early impressions, I've only played for a few hours, but honestly playing this pretty much just makes me want to play open TTD. I can't imagine any of the complex logistic chains from OTTD in this game - not only would laying/routing all that track be a nightmare, there's just not the supply/demand available in Train Fever.
It's a shame too because I was pretty excited for this one for the last year.

Train Fever is everything any tycoon fan could want, a game that feels like it was made by a A+ developer, funded by one of the big giants, but it's all made by a small indie studio, which makes it even more incredible than it already is. the tycoon genre has long had games that were good, but not great, and far, far too many games that were bad. Laying tracks is easy, but it can be tricky. However, like other parts of this game, once you learn it, you souldn't have problems.
The game might not have a million features, and at times the wait untill you get a new train is long, but it's enjoyable. That's what is important, i really, really like this game. Dark Souls is a hard game. ♥♥♥♥ing hard. At least when you first play it and know nothing about how it all works but its challenging in a very fair and genuine way the vast majority of the time - enemies hit extremely hard but so do you, the odds are against you but you always have something to help you out. I've been a huge fan of the Souls games since its inception with the fantastic little classic Demon's Souls and while it took me way longer to finally sit down with Dark Souls, I can say it's easily one of my favourite games of all time and having just finished my fourth playthrough, I thought I may as well write a short review because why not right?
Pros:
*Very simple mechanics made deep and engaging with the huge array of enemy types and having to learn their patterns and weaknesses - learn, slash, block, roll and parry your way to success
*Fantastic level design with interconnected areas that help to create a cohesive and well-constructed game world
*Huge choice of weapons, armour, spells, miracles, pyromancies, etc - every character you make will be completely different from the last if you experiment with all the different builds thus offering huge replay value
*Incredible lore (arguably the best in gaming) told in the most minimalistic fashion possible
*Lots of bosses - Artorias and Manus being two of my favourites
*If you're a sap like me then you'll care a lot about the characters and then be heartbroken when you have to kill them without uttering a single word (I'M SO SORRY SIF!!!) - the lore is that good
*The online system blends a singleplayer adventure together with a persistent MMO world of coop play and PVP invasions, making the journey from start to finish incredibly diverse in online mode
*Runs WAY better than the horribly optimised console versions on a good rig
Cons:
*The PC port is still pretty damn pants - it's behaved itself for me as I find 30fps perfectly playable and I only ever had one crash; the only time performance ever drops is during Seath the Scaleless but thankfully he's a very easy boss
*Player connectivity based on soul level is pretty♥♥♥♥♥♥- people can stay at a low level the entire game, get the best, fully upgraded equipment and freely gank players or breeze through early bosses in coop
*The geometry... Good god the geometry is horrible especially when it swings your camera around and blocks your movement with short curbs - The Great Hollow and Lost Izalith are your worst nightmare for this
*The biggest brick wall players will face is the infamous pair in Anor Londo roughly halfway through the game, arguably the hardest fight in the entire game and I wouldn't blame players for giving up then so be wary
*As much as I love parrying, it's pretty overpowered once you get the hang of it - it makes the final boss a bit of a joke
*STAY THE ♥♥♥♥ STILL SEATH AND LET ME CUT YOUR GODDAMN ♥♥♥♥ING TAIL OFF!!!!!
*Bed. Of. Chaos.

This is one of my favorite strategy games.  Relax, build armies, conquer the world.  City management is minimal, army management even less so.  So what's so great?  It's just straight up build and conquer, with random events, heroes popping up to help you, and black market merchants selling you cool items for your heroes.  Combat occurs on the map, stack by stack, very similar to Civ 5's combat.
Easy to grasp, it does require you to think about what you're doing if you want to succeed at higher levels against more enemies.  You've got to manage your gold and mana, heal up your armies, cast spells, do research, and figure out which mage-enemy is going to go nuclear on you next.  As your armies gain levels, they earn helpful perks.  You're able to build buildings in your cities that give your units perks to armor and attack and upgrade armies accordingly.
Many races to play, each with their own native traits.  Choosing your race (mage) definitely impacts the gameplay.
The only downside is the "Majesty" voice announcer, which wears thin after awhile.  Fortunately, he doesn't speak very often, but he can be annoying.
Otherwise, a fun evening of conquest and spell slinging.

Pillars of Eternity is an RPG just like the older Infinity Engine games like Buldur's Gate, or Icewind Dale. The combat is real time but you can pause any time to issue commands. The biggest difference being that this game doesn't use the Dungeon and Dragons rules. Other than that the combat works very similarly
The story in PoE is excellent. The way they let you shape your character is really really good. There is always a wide range of dialog options, everything from plain out wrong, to mr goody two shoes, and straight up jerk. The NPCs will react accordingly making the story as interesting as you want to make it. Your companions will speak up accordingly if they are with you at the right moments. They throw a lot at you, but it will be easy to pick up as you play more.
Your character will 'inherit' a keep with a huge dungeon underneath. You build it up using whatever cash you make in your adventure. Speaking of which, you will have a bottomless bag. Big upgrade from rpgs like this. You no longer have to go back to town all the time to unload your bags. Just pick everything up! It automatically goes to your stash.
If you like RPGs, Infinity Engine games, buy with confidense. I got 22 hrs of playtime beating just the main story, and some of the side quests. There is a ton of optional content I have yet to experience but it's a great value at any price.

Overall this is a great game in my opinion. The combat system is great and relentless on harder diffuculties, so to those of you looking for a challenge then I highly recommend you buy this game. The game is also rich in history and has an astounding amount of lore for those who like to enjoy games and get to know the background of the game world.

Pillars of Eternity is easily one of the best RPGs of the past ten years. While the story is rather typical RPG fare, the setting is rich, the companions are interesting, the lore is deep, the mechanics are fun, and the setting is not your typical generic fantasy. While the generic fantasy races are present (humans, elves, dwarves), there are also three unique races: the wild and furry orlans, the hulking and colorful aumaua, and the godlike (who are actually modifications of the other races, believed to be the blessing of a god). Rather than the High Medieval inspiration of many RPGs (or Late Medieval, in the case of Dragon Age), Pillars of Eternity taps into the less frequented Renaissance. It also draws inspiration from less common sources: the Inuit-inspired Boreal Dwarves, the Polynesian-inspired Rauatai, and the Aztec-inspired Ixamitl, for example. If you enjoy RPGs, you'll enjoy Pillars of Eternity, and it is easily the finest modern example of an isometric RPG.

Truly one of the best value for money games I have ever bought. If you want to go on a zombie killing spree, you'll actually have to plan escape routes, bring supplies and be very mindful of what's going on around you, because if you go ahead and facetank the horde, you're gonna get murdered pretty quick!
It incorporates what I don't see enough of in general zombie survival games, the SURVIVAL factor. You need to gather and store supplies in order to keep everything running correctly. Strength is in numbers, but the more people you recruit, the more supplies you have to dish out to everyone. If you don't meet your daily quota of supplies, then your camp can fall ill, or your defences can be weakened, etc. However, supplies are not in such a high demand that you'll find it a chore to go and find them, they balanced the feature very well.
All in all, this is one of the most perfect zombie games that I've ever seen, and I would definitely recommend it to anyone who's up for a survival game, and not just a mindless hack & slash.

UPDATE: Nov 28 2016
Since the writing of this review, the following issues have been fixed:
Sound Quality has been restored to the original quality present in the DOS and Megaton releases.
Original Review:
Long time fan of Duke, figured I'd give this version a try despite owning the originals and Megaton edition, for the sake of comparing them.
This version is inferior to both the Megaton Edition and the fan-made port eDuke32. The sound effects in this version of compressed to an inexcusable degree. Everything sounds like it's underwater.
The newly recorded voice lines don't really carry the same feeling as the original lines, either. John St. John didn't give it his all in his performance and Duke sounds more bored than anything else. Gearbox were considerate enough to allow us to select the original voice lines, but like the sound effects and music they're compressed beyond belief.
The new graphics are kinda nice looking, but they're no better than eDuke32's "Polymost" graphics. In fact, they're basically identical.
This version of the game also uses the "rewind" system from Megaton edition, which I don't like at all. Basically, when you die, you're given the option to rewind the game to any previous point in your playthrough of the level. This removes a lot of the challenge from the game, removes all consequences for failure, and there's no way to turn it off.
The game has no option to disable VSync as far as I can tell, and the game has mouse acceleration enabled with no way to disable it. There is also no way to adjust the FOV. All of these features were present in the Megaton Edition.
Also, and this is the most damning thing, this version of the game includes none of the game's expansions, with the only reason given being a smarmy "those aren't 20 years old yet :)" from Randy Pitchford. Megaton edition included these expansions and their exclusion here is inexcusable. The only feasible reason that they were excluded was so that could be sold later as DLC.
All in all? Don't buy this version. It's inferior to the Megaton Edition and costs twice as much as Megaton Edition. Chances are, you probably already own Megaton edition since Devolver practically gave it away for free numerous times. If you don't own it, unfortunately there is no other option for you. Thanks to Gearbox's underhanded business practices, Megaton Edition has been removed from all official online retailers and the original versions of the game have been removed from GOG. Legally, this is your only option for playing Duke Nukem 3D, and that's absolutely sad.
Save your money. Don't bet on this Duke.

Well this is the laziest rerelease I've ever seen in my life. The Megaton Edition, which was removed because it provided 5x the content this does for less money, was superior in just about every way. It's hard to wrap my mind around how they actually made this edition WORSE when they already had the Megaton to work with.
The remastered Duke voice is higher fidelity, but the voice acting itself is clearly phoned in and un inspired.  They did no remastering with the original sounds and so the stark contrast with the voice is distracting and grating more than enjoyable. Ignoring the voice issue, I don't even know how, but the sound effects sound worse than in Megaton edition. It sounds like they ported from a Gameboy version. The strangest things have been removed. The intro menus look nicer than Megaton, but all in-game graphics and HUD are pixelated and ugly, they got rid of the reskin and pixel smoothing Megaton allowed you to turn on or off. You can't rename your save games, it's just "Slot 1". Why? Such a trivial change that would require you to actively change code to remove functionality.
They added colored lighting, a feature present in every Build source port for the last, what, 5 years? 10? No updated textures, no 3D models, none of the other functionality offered for free by EDuke and others. Only new weapon added is a variant of the freezethrower that's been lurking as dead code in Duke 3D since day 1, which was never implemented because it didn't add an enjoyable experience to the gameplay. Only one new enemy I've encountered so far, a trooper with a flamethrower. All the expansion packs have been stripped out, presumably so they can sell it to you again as DLC.
I'm not done with the campaign yet, but I will say the new levels are very well done so far and the new music is good. The rewind feature is a nice addition to complement traditional save game system.
Overall though this release could have been so, so much more, and it turned into a petty cash grab. Think about it... 20th anniversary edition. Think how much that means, how much content and functionality they could have given us. Think of what countless fans have been releasing for free, purely out of love for the game, for over a decade. Think of what Bethesda did breathing new life into the Doom remake. Think of how Gearbox could have seized this opportunity to make amends for the travesty of Duke Nukem Forever. Instead, we get this trash. I don't think Gearbox cares about or respects their customers, and I don't think they love the Duke IP.
Don't buy this. Don't support this kind of corporate greed and consumer gouging. I don't condone piracy, but I sure as hell won't be surprised when the new campaign files find their way on the torrent sites just to sidestep this abomination. At least wait for a 75% off sale to get this. I wish I'd paid $5 for it. $20? Get that crap outta here.

There is no way to do justice to this game in a review.
Upon first being announced, Starbound immediately hit me as a "Terraria-killer", AKA a game that would surpass Terraria in the field of 2D-sideways explorer/builder which Terraria had pioneered masterfully.
Especially after the 1.0 release, Starbound has not disappointed me in that way; there are far more things to do in Starbound than one can in its predecessor, and the developers have continued to add content with each new release.
If taking the mods in account, there are so many ways to adapt your Starbound-experience to what you expect of it that you could spend years exploring and building in it, much like the 3D Minecraft from which this type of game branched out.
The learning curve can be a bit high for people, especially since the tutorial basically just teaches you how to mine blocks with your trusty Matter Manipulator and slash at things with your sword and leaves you to figure things out on your own from there on out, but even so you can usually build a rudimentary home-away-from-home on your first planet within the hour.
Exploring from such an outpost will gradually allow you to expand on your crafting knowledge, allowing you to get better equipment and explore farther, and deeper, and your ship's S.A.I.L. offers enough guidance in the form of missions to at least keep you going for a while.
The varied NPCs you come across in your travels are occasionally helpful, even if the missions they offer can be tediously repetitive, and you can even build homes for them to move into at your colony-site of choice, allowing you to gain income from rent and occasional extra missions.
Starbound's lore is rich and delivered through books found on your travels, and each of the base playable-races has their own background story in that respect, and their own legends to learn about. The developers truly built a universe that's rich enough to rival what No Man's Sky promised and never delivered on.
If you like 2D exploration and crafting, Starbound is the game for you. See you in endgame. ;)

Now, about the game. Think tower defence combined with fast paced action 3rd-person-hack-n-slash/shooter. Two available characters that play similar enough and yet different enough to make things interesting both in solo and co-op play. Tons of traps and levels, and even more in reasonably priced DLC. All this leads to lots of fun killing orcs and solving the trap placement puzzles of each level. Well, they aren’t really puzzles, but if you are a perfectionist you will treat them as such. Sure one can “beat” a level, but it’s so much more satisfying when one “masters” it (especially on hardcore, or endless, or endless hardcore!!!). Figuring out awesome trap layouts and combinations that work in each level is good fun. The game is well balanced as well so same cheap trick won’t work everywhere and this will keep you thinking. Most levels strongly encourage co-op because of their layout, however it’s possible to solo them all (if you’re up for the challenge). This game can definitely burn you out if played too much. But you will then dream of killing orcs and be drawn back into it (maybe this trap combo will finally yield that 5-skull rating? Must try!)
In short, really no reason to not play this game.

Night in the Woods, is a game like no other I have very played in my life. Heck Night in the Woods might be one of the most interesting but also relatable piece of media I have ever experienced.  Because of the excellent writing, each character feels incredibly human and real, as if you could pull up a Skype chat and talk to them about life at any moment. The narrative is a deliberate slow burn, that sells the mundanity of life and the sometimes hopeless feeling that one gets knowing that their life is falling apart yet they are unable to do anything to stop it. One of the games major themes is social anxiety and depression. It captures the essence of thoughts like: your life will never change, everyone is better then you and you're complete garbage, or that no matter what you do, no one cares. All of the AAA games in the world with their 80+ hour games, decked with huge expansive world, with probably the closest to realistic graphics as humanity can get; will never hold a candle to how real and emotionally grabbing it felt playing a 8 hour indie game, in a small suburban town, with a cartoon cat and her friends.
This game has better characters, dialouge, and thematic resonance than most books. I've played it twice already and plan to again. Get it.

If you have played CIM the lines are going to be very familar to you +

Current Con's
It has an internal logic, but the developers don't want you to know what that might be.  So you'll end up with trains using what track they feel like or sitting at lights for no reason at all. --
No significant tutorial, coupled with a entirely opaque UI, be prepared to spend time on goggle learning how to play. -
Track laying is both powerful and at the same time utterly dreadful, it forces you towards level tracks, generally good, but it will give you bridges for some drops, tunnels for gentle hills.  You can get around this, but you have to very carefully lay small segments of track, obviously you start to lose sight of the other station. -
Making money is very hard, at least at the begining the maintence costs are simply punishing, trains are a giant money sink, road transport makes money, rail transport costs money, -
Industry model seems broken to me, like the above, I am sure there was a reason my carts were sat waiting for coal, but the game wasn't about to tell me. -
This really isn't ready for prime time, i could have added more issues, but it seems unfair, the framework for a good, possibly great sim is here, but this really isn't it.
I would wait for patches and/or mods before purchasing.

Dark Souls is the infamous action RPG that you've already heard about. You've probably heard about how difficult and punishing it can be, but it can actually be quite easy if you learn how stats and equipment work.
You CAN get through the game by learning enemy attacks, baiting out certain moves and punishing them, all of which can be very fun if you like action games; however, this game is an RPG to it's core with a slew of different damage types and armor resistances, meaning some damage types will work better depending on the enemies' armor.
These basic RPG elements impact the game rather heavily, meaning you can simply change weapons/armor and turn a difficult boss fight into something trivial, even though you still need to know the fighting basics.
Because of this focus on damage types and stats, you might assume that your starting class will determine what bosses you find difficult, but in Dark Souls your equipment changes your gameplay more than other factors. While playing Dark Souls you can often just change equipment, dynamically changing your build as you find out what works against certain enemies.
With all of that said, luckily the foundational RPG elements aren't completely enforced, you can always just learn the boss's patterns and win with a build completely ineffective against the boss. Or you can just use Havel's set, the Black Knight Halberd, and chug like a scrub winning no matter what.
Although Dark Souls is a rather solid gameplay experience, Dark Souls shines best when you can appreciate the art design. I'm happy to say with this game the marketing is pretty much spot on, so if the marketing materials interest you, you won't be dissapointed.
If you like the idea of an action RPG with a focus on RPG elements, you'll enjoy the gameplay. If you like a dark, gritty, atmosphere with lots of dangerous creatures, you will like the art design.
Even if you just think the marketing looks cool, the game is 5 bucks on sale, so might as well pick it up.

Pillars of Eternity is a worthy (spiritual) successor to the classic D&D Infinity Engine games like Baldur's Gate, Icewind Dale and Planescape: Torment. It's a party-based RPG (you control up to 6 characters), isometric, top-down, pausable combat game with all the classic D&D tropes. The maps are beautifully drawn. The story and world are top notch. The combat is fun. The companions are good and entertaining. The voice acting is top notch.
Where Pillars really shines, however, is not so much in what makes it familiar (the game engine, party-based combat, the D&D style classes and spells), but with what makes it
. Freed of a D&D license, Obsidian was able to do more, and they did. This is also a double-edged sword, as what makes Pillars unique can also make it a bit difficult to get into.
Pillars takes place in a new world and as such the associated lands, regions, dieties and lore will be very unfamiliar to those of us who have spent a lifetime playing D&D RPG's. This lack of familiarity can make it difficult to get a foothold on the game and the story early on.
However, there is a huge payoff here. Obsidian entertains us with completely new classes and spells that D&D doesn't offer. I had a particularly enjoyable time with the
and
classes, since they were new and unique to the genre. And while the game sports many of the classic D&D spells (Fireball, Magic Missiles) it also employs a host of new spells that entertaining and useful.
Wizards, in particular, are very fun classes to play due to their ability to switch out spell books before or during combat (with a small, temporary penalty) which makes them a very versatile force to have in your party. Against larger, boss mob style foes, the Wizard might wish to utilize a spellbook full of ranged damage-dealers. But in more intimate encounters it's totally conceivable for the wizard to load up on defensive spells and summon powerful melee weapons to fight up-close and personal with his/her companions. It's a complete joy to play a wizard in this game.
Likewise, Obsidian does several nice things upon level-up for other classes, giving some classes access to specializations that allow the player to shape the class in distinct ways. It's entirely possible to play this game dozens upon dozens of times with the same classes and never have those classes behave exactly the same way. Each class can be tweaked and specialized in a variety of ways so that each play-through they have a slightly different flavor. It really is a testament to the way Obsidian has designed the classes that they are so malleable and yet they retain their unique class-specific qualities at the same time. When it comes to class-based RPG's, Pillars hits a clear home run.
As far as story goes, Pillars is wholly unique and new, fresh and interesting. There's a rich history to explore here and Pillards of Eternity makes it central to your character's progression even if it doesn't seem entirely clear at all times. Part of that is learning the lore of a new world as you go. The writing is solid, of overdone at times, but nothing that most fantasy RPG folks won't forgive.
The game also strives very hard to make your choices matter as you move through the game. I really appreciated this as this seems to be something that other games in the genre lack. If you destroy a powerful dragon, for instance, other characters later in the game may take note of it in converasations. This is a welcome touch.
Conversations are also really well done. Often there are several options for the player to choose and those choices can be influenced by the player's own stats and abilities. If you cannot choose a reply because you lack the Resolve or skill to make that choice, the game still shows you that you would have had that option, and what the minimum requirement would have been to make it available. This sort of thing strongly encourages replay.
Finally, a word about the expansions. I bought both the White March 1 and White March 2 and played those DLC's while doing my first run-through the main campaign. The DLC's are REALLY well done; top notch. They provide their own map, locations and a quality story. It's more than just a raised level-cap. There are also new companions with interesting side-quests worth exploring. The DLC also introduces Soul-Bound weapons, items that can only be bound to one character and get more powerful as the character using them reaches certain milestones (like kill X number of creatures with this weapon to unlock the next ability). They're very well balanced, unique, and fun. I would definitely recommend to anyone buying the game to go ahead and get both DLC's at the same time. You won't be disappointed.
This is clearly the most fun I've had playing an RPG since Neverwinter Nights 2, Baldur's Gate 2 and Temple of Elemental Evil (patched with the Co8 Patch though). It's just a great, great game and I can't wait for a sequel.

There is no way to do justice to this game in a review.
Upon first being announced, Starbound immediately hit me as a "Terraria-killer", AKA a game that would surpass Terraria in the field of 2D-sideways explorer/builder which Terraria had pioneered masterfully.
Especially after the 1.0 release, Starbound has not disappointed me in that way; there are far more things to do in Starbound than one can in its predecessor, and the developers have continued to add content with each new release.
If taking the mods in account, there are so many ways to adapt your Starbound-experience to what you expect of it that you could spend years exploring and building in it, much like the 3D Minecraft from which this type of game branched out.
The learning curve can be a bit high for people, especially since the tutorial basically just teaches you how to mine blocks with your trusty Matter Manipulator and slash at things with your sword and leaves you to figure things out on your own from there on out, but even so you can usually build a rudimentary home-away-from-home on your first planet within the hour.
Exploring from such an outpost will gradually allow you to expand on your crafting knowledge, allowing you to get better equipment and explore farther, and deeper, and your ship's S.A.I.L. offers enough guidance in the form of missions to at least keep you going for a while.
The varied NPCs you come across in your travels are occasionally helpful, even if the missions they offer can be tediously repetitive, and you can even build homes for them to move into at your colony-site of choice, allowing you to gain income from rent and occasional extra missions.
Starbound's lore is rich and delivered through books found on your travels, and each of the base playable-races has their own background story in that respect, and their own legends to learn about. The developers truly built a universe that's rich enough to rival what No Man's Sky promised and never delivered on.
If you like 2D exploration and crafting, Starbound is the game for you. See you in endgame. ;)

In this review I discuss two things: the game itself and the business practices of Gearbox. My negative rating is due to the poor business practices of Gearbox and does not mean in any way that I think what actually is here is bad. I love Duke Nukem and I enjoyed the 5th episode and the cool features this release has. But...
The problem with this release is that it's clearly a cash grab, not-so-subtly confirmed by Randy Pitchford himself (CEO of Gearbox) via various tweets (more on that later). To concisely put it, the new episode is awesome, the additional features and graphics are pretty cool, but this is missing 3 expansions found in the now removed Megaton edition. The missing expansions perhaps aren't a big deal, but a complete edition of DN3D which will include those expansions, the 5th episode, and more, has practically been confirmed by Randy to one day be made. So what does that make this? A cash grab.
The new episode features 7 main levels and a secret level created by the original level designers of DN3D, also the guy who did the original music is back! That's pretty amazing to be honest. Read About their thoughts for each of the levels, including the interesting tidbit that each level took approximately 2 months to make:
The new levels are really well done, and fairly tough too I think. They aren't as compact but are bigger and more spread out because they don't have to deal with hardware limitations like they did 20 years ago. The new incinerator gun is op; ammo is plentiful, it holds 99 shots, and the shots 1 hit kill the regular enemies and do massive damage to the others. It sucks against enemies that can't be set on fire though. The new firefly enemies are annoying (in a good way), but they tend to be glitchy because sometimes when you shoot them the shots don't register. It's nice seeing completely new areas and artwork. I also really like the new music too. Basically it's a worthy addition to Duke Nukem and deserves to be the official 5th episode. My only complaint is that we got just 1 new enemy.
The game has a true 3d render which you can toggle on and off (the original render was 2d sprites which stretched when you looked up and down). The rewind feature from the old DN3D release on consoles is finally on pc. When you die you can rewind all the way to the beginning of the game and any point in between and start over from whatever point you choose. Really cool! I'm a big fan of developer commentary and some of the things they have to say are interesting, I just wish there was a lot more. I'm not a big fan of the re-recorded Duke voice lines, fortunately you can toggle the legacy lines back on.
It's all straight from the horse's mouth, Randy Pitchford. Here are tweets where he mentions a definitive edition:
Here is where he tells you the only reason to buy this game is if you want to play the 5th episode as soon as possible, like I did, and assuming you don't already own DN3D:
The difference is when a company like Bethesda is going to make a complete edition they don't remove expansions for sale, release a new expansion, then tell you if you want the old expansions along with the new expansion in one package with some more goodies then you'll have to wait and buy the complete edition later.
Here he suggests waiting for a sale:
Yes everyone knows almost all games get a sale eventually, but as a developer it's bad business to
your potential customers to wait for one. Plus I already told him I bought it. Reading comprehension deficiency?
Here he confirms there will be no dlc, free or paid:
I guess it's good he won't try to nickel and dime us by making us pay for what should be there, but why can't the missing expansions be free dlc?
If only we knew what you know so we could understand these baffling business decisions.
Duke Nukem is as great as ever. If it weren't for this being an incomplete edition due to a feeble reason then this would get all my thumb ups. If you don't care about the missing expansions or the reasoning why they aren't here and you want brand new Duke then by all means buy this game! I want more Duke so I bought this despite knowing everything here before release.

This release has numerous flaws however that I find both weird and unforgivable. There appears to be no way to turn off auto aim which becomes more of a hindrance when you have played duke 3d as much as I. In its current state I just can't recommend this version of Duke 3d for the price they ask.

So today I finally finished this jewel, this beauty. I haven't been into some game for very long time. I am at this moment finishing all the collectibles (I know, I am surprised too that I am actually doing it but it's great fun) and I will be moving on to DLCs so I will update the review later.
This game for me is straight 10/10. I absolutely loved it. I had great fun and enjoyed every moment in it. Music was great, VO is amazing, story is great, graphic is very nice and playability is great. You can do almost everything you wish you could do and maybe even more. This game was definitely created with love, great ideas and coolness in mind. For me this was one of the best playthrough ever.
Best thing about this game is also the Nemesis system which makes the world actually live around you and react to what happens. That's one of the systems I would from now like to see in every game. For example when you get killed, the orc gets stronger, maybe even promoted and a lot of changes in Sauron's Army, guys gets promoted, killed, riots etc. Awesome thing. When you die you bet your butt that you are going to hunt that orc who killed you. You will drop everything and make that thing target of yours. Great feature is that you actually like in a normal world, you are getting informations for the orcs like weaknesses and strong points. I can't wait to see how they will upgrade the system in new one. Also great touch was that you can actually avenge your friends if they were slain. That was great feel. And of course, they can avenge you and you get a message if they were successful.
That all said, there were some things which bothered me little bit. So you have climbing and sometimes it didn't register I wanna climb it and instead I just jumped. It could be me but I was usually huging the walls. The second thing was that sometimes you had neverending hordes of enemies keeping coming and keeping coming. For some time because I enjoyed the combat especially later when you open many talents it's awesome, but sometimes I just wanted to just continue, so yeah, it's not a bad thing but for me sometimes it was too much too often, but hey it could be just me. Third thing was the last boss. The build up for that was great. Really. But the last last boss was eventhough cool, kinda disappointing. Something like the bold guy from FarCry 3. I might have missed something and maybe it's something in DLC, not sure, but I was mainly surprised how big the build up was for something which ended eventhough very cool, very quick. That was surprise for me.
But still, this was amazing (still is, I am not done) game for me and you can say that I really like it from that I am actually doing all the collectibles, secondary quest and DLCs. I usually don't do that.

I generally don't review things openly. My opinion is generally kept to myself, maybe stated with a few friends but rarely made public. I haven't put many hours compared to some other players, but I feel as though I have a rather good taste of the gameplay, mechanics and whatnot. My opinion is my generalization of the game pending my tastes and style of gameplay. You may not match mine in any way and thus; read other reviews. If you have popcorn and a comfy chair, let's discuss the good, bad and ugly of my favourite Alpha; Miscreated.
Good=
+Stable
+Runs well (Ryzen 1400 OC to 3.9 with Rx 480 4GB and 8GB of DDR4 Ram at 3.2Ghz)
+Weapons feel like treasure, not a common commodity. I have seen about 4-5 Mk18s and I gasp every time
+Survival basics are easy to acquire (Food, drink and clothes)
+Plenty to kill. Hunting is fun in itself, Wolves provide best supply of meat (due to numbers). Mutants can be a challenge.
+Variety of weapons (With a downside)
+Base Building is decent, definitely hoping this isn't a finished design cause it needs work.
+Every type of building is able to be entered. Not every BUILDING ITSELF. (Eg. Some Apartments are blocked off or doors locked, others with the same style are not and can be looted) Id say a good 90% of structures can be entered and looted)
Bad=
-Why, and I mean WHY did you guys design the bullet damage model the way you did? .308 and 7.62x51 are so closely identical but yet the M40 can insta-gib you while the Renegade 700 (.308) does 60Hp. Hunting rifle uses the same round as the Renegade and does even LESS damage? Who the fu-, oh, and .223 vs 5.56X45mm. Why. I mean, why. Come on, I should be able to load .223 into my 5.56x45mm rifle. No drawbacks to it, now 5.56 into a .223, yeah, bad idea but cmon now. 7.62x39mm for the AK (assault Rifle as its called) should also have its own unique damage model, not that of the 5.56. I wont go into more detail, but this bugs the crap outta me.
-Stamina. Ok, I like it but I gotta call it out. Why can I jump about 5 times and run outta stamina (which recharges hella fast) but yet still sprint and use my melee weapons without penalty? Stamina needs a rework.
-Vehicles. Another thing that benefits me, personally but not other players. I can hear you guys in your cars. It's how we hunt you and follow you. We know you load them up when on looting runs and we will let you do the work for us since we can actively listen for you. As much as I love hunting and looting people, maybe make them quieter and/or add a door lock for cars that can be crafted from Electrical parts.
-Base building. Oh my ♥♥♥♥ its so good but soooo bad, granted; my own Bias comes from Arma III when I could clip one object into another to create a seemless edge. In here, no. Either allow clipping of items into each other or a snapping mode for parts to fit together, also, aside from a free rotation, please at static rotations (45, 90, 180 degress etc.)
-The invisible wall. I get it, Trump2k16. Gotta build a wall. Aight, no biggy. WHY THE HELL IS IT INVISIBLE THOUGH. Especially along the side of the road to Clyde Hill where I could have taken cover from a vehicle but instead nah, can't go into the tree line. Become next Roadkill statistic.
Ugly=
--Grass render in distance. 50m away seems to be the load factor for grass, after that its bare hill. Making the only viable place to hide when tailing/being tailed is the trees. Please make grass/vegetation load in a bit farther away as minimum.
--Weapon attachments. I understand, they are still being implemented fully. That said, the scope (which is supposed to be rare) I have found more of than Holo sights, lasers or those lovely suppressors. The Ba70, Hunting Rifle 85, Renegade 700 and hell, even the standard Mk18s/AT-15s and M0d16s should be able to use attachments from each other. Maybe not the scope on the At15/Mk18/Mod16 but it would be nice to use a scope or RDS on the bolt actions.
--Map. Dont pick one up. Shift+Tab and search for 'Miscreated 2017 map' in the browser. Load up the most recent high-res image and use that. Saves weight and storage space and can be used if you're driving a vehicle. Bam, you're welcome.
--Players. Jesus H ♥♥♥♥ you guys are salty as all hell. It's a PvP survival. Some people like to hunt for other players. Get over it. You didn't check your position, your situational awareness was non-existent and loot is fairly easy to get back in 30 minutes. For every player I kill that gets cranky in chat, I will be leaving a salt on your body and a rag.
--Despawn. Ok, so you get killed by some dude who likes to leave salt on your body. I get it. You figure 'hey, I will just run back up to my body and get some or most of my stuff back right?' You were wrong. Your body can despawn within about 5 minutes which, unless you die in the spawn area (South East side of the map) you will never make it there in time.
I still, however, thoroughly enjoy this game with all its broken stuff. It runs well, looks great and when I see a player, it gives me a heart attack worse than thinking of spending another 4 years with my ex.

Be aware of what you are buying before you purchase this.
I think it's rare that a developer has something interesting to say with a video game that could not be said just as well (or better) with a novel or a movie. Gods Will Be Watching is one of those rare cases; unfortunately it's also kind of inaccessible. It's not a bad game, but it's not the game you might assume it is at first glance. It looks like a point-and-click adventure. It's not. GWBW is a game about fate and meaning that can only be won through repeated trial-and-error. This is not an oversight, it's intentional and integral to the game. I'd go so far as to say it's the game's reason for existing. If you play to the end, you get to understand why. Getting there is not always fun though, it can be frustrating and annoying. Again, that's the point.
I know this sounds kind of pretentious, and I guess maybe it is, in the way only real art can sound pretentious until you experience it and it moves you. In its defense, the developers have added several new play modes (including an "easy" mode and a "puzzle" mode) that make the game much less difficult while still preserving the story and soul of the game. WIth this change, I think they have successfully solved the only real problem with the game which was that the heavy amount of RNG really obstructed the enjoyment of the narrative.
Read a couple other reviews and see if this sounds like something you're interested in. If it is, don't pay full price; put it on your wish list and pick it up on sale. If you go in with your expectations set correctly, I think you will be pleased with this well-crafted but conflicted little work of art.

If you're planning to buy this because you saw words "point & click" or interesting pixel art and expected an old school adventure game - stop for a moment, please. Although Gods Will Be Watching is played just with your mouse, and even has a decent story to boot, it's not really an adventure game. This is a time management puzzle game.
Each of the game's chapters is a static screen with a specific task you're required to complete - hack to computer while keeping hostages safe/alive (while preventing the breach of your position) or create a serum while also digging a tunnel and multitasking the hell out of your characters. What underlines this game is a combination of statistics, database and some RNG elements that will not be explained properly to you, nor you'd be able to understand them on your first try. Yes, you'll fail these scenarios, most likely you'll even get stuck on the FIRST SCENE, especially since the gameplay relies so heavily on trial and error.
You will always have to juggle several factors in this turn-based puzzle game, yet none of it is really what can be considered "fun". Words "tedious" and "unfair" are more likely to go through your head while playing Gods Will Be Watching, as your progress may (or may not) get halted just because of the bad luck, especially in the second chapter. Also, you only get a limited number of turns/moves to complete everything that's been asked of you, so it's mostly about optimization instead of experimentation and immersion. This is a game where not even a walkthrough can help you sometimes, and it's highly recommended not to play on normal or original difficulty the first time unless you're a masochist.
Story? It's intriguing, that's for sure, even if slightly on a silly side (what serious organization would call themselves Xenolifer?). Too bad you'll only get the bits of information and world/character building in non-interactive scenes inbetween long puzzle sequences.
I haven't completed the game. I might do one day, when the bitter taste of bad game design vanishes from my memory.

I've been a huge fan of Scott Benson's work as an animator and an illustrator/designer for years now, and I was super hyped when I heard he was working on his own game! Because of school, I didn't have the chance to play it until now, and boy did it exceeded my expectations!
Right off the bat, the art direction is simply beautiful! Simple yet complex. The game is essentially an interactive Benson illustration that tells an autobiographical story of growing up in a lively, small mining town where weird♥♥♥♥♥♥happens.
NITW gets waaay too real for comfort, specifically with interactions with Bea and Mae's mother. The way the cast reacts to everything happening around them is extremely believable. There's definitely no shortage of 3-dimensional characters, aside from maybe a couple random NPCs... That changes after the ending though (no spoilers, but you'll know what I mean).
Speaking of NPCs, I'm one of those people who has to talk to every NPC I come in contact with. Luckily, NITW features a lively town full of a diverse cast of folks who all have interesting, funny, and/or important things to say. Each new in-game day I looked forward to revisiting each of them to see what else they had to say.
My only complaint is that I wish the dialogue options had a bigger impact on the actual plot. They are mostly there for your own enjoyment, and each option still creates different minor story outcomes. And its worth replaying to see all of the different hilarious and dramatic differences you can do. Yet, you have no long lasting affect on the plot itself, which could have been interesting. There are, however, different routes you can take depending on which of the characters you decide to spend more time with, which reveal various things about the characters themselves and their motivations, issues, relationships, etc. Regardless, I still see lots of replay value.
My favorite aspect was the feeling of ambiguity and uncertainty at the end. It made the characters feel even more real then they already did, and like.... damn... its not a perfect game, but boy does it make you think about life n♥♥♥♥♥♥..

Dark Souls is a hard game. ♥♥♥♥ing hard. At least when you first play it and know nothing about how it all works but its challenging in a very fair and genuine way the vast majority of the time - enemies hit extremely hard but so do you, the odds are against you but you always have something to help you out. I've been a huge fan of the Souls games since its inception with the fantastic little classic Demon's Souls and while it took me way longer to finally sit down with Dark Souls, I can say it's easily one of my favourite games of all time and having just finished my fourth playthrough, I thought I may as well write a short review because why not right?
Pros:
*Very simple mechanics made deep and engaging with the huge array of enemy types and having to learn their patterns and weaknesses - learn, slash, block, roll and parry your way to success
*Fantastic level design with interconnected areas that help to create a cohesive and well-constructed game world
*Huge choice of weapons, armour, spells, miracles, pyromancies, etc - every character you make will be completely different from the last if you experiment with all the different builds thus offering huge replay value
*Incredible lore (arguably the best in gaming) told in the most minimalistic fashion possible
*Lots of bosses - Artorias and Manus being two of my favourites
*If you're a sap like me then you'll care a lot about the characters and then be heartbroken when you have to kill them without uttering a single word (I'M SO SORRY SIF!!!) - the lore is that good
*The online system blends a singleplayer adventure together with a persistent MMO world of coop play and PVP invasions, making the journey from start to finish incredibly diverse in online mode
*Runs WAY better than the horribly optimised console versions on a good rig
Cons:
*The PC port is still pretty damn pants - it's behaved itself for me as I find 30fps perfectly playable and I only ever had one crash; the only time performance ever drops is during Seath the Scaleless but thankfully he's a very easy boss
*Player connectivity based on soul level is pretty♥♥♥♥♥♥- people can stay at a low level the entire game, get the best, fully upgraded equipment and freely gank players or breeze through early bosses in coop
*The geometry... Good god the geometry is horrible especially when it swings your camera around and blocks your movement with short curbs - The Great Hollow and Lost Izalith are your worst nightmare for this
*The biggest brick wall players will face is the infamous pair in Anor Londo roughly halfway through the game, arguably the hardest fight in the entire game and I wouldn't blame players for giving up then so be wary
*As much as I love parrying, it's pretty overpowered once you get the hang of it - it makes the final boss a bit of a joke
*STAY THE ♥♥♥♥ STILL SEATH AND LET ME CUT YOUR GODDAMN ♥♥♥♥ING TAIL OFF!!!!!
*Bed. Of. Chaos.
