I will always go back to this game and try out all kinds of new and different builds and I eventually hope to get every achievement but I'm in no rush because whenever I want to play something fun, familiar and satisfying, I will always have Dark Souls to keep me company.

I picked up my rifle and stepped out of the dropship into the dark unknown, my boots caked in red dust and dried blood. The corpses of the team sent here before us were strewn all over the area. I could already tell, this was going to be a long mission.
If it’s not demons plaguing your usual trip to the Red Planet, then it must be aliens. Welcome to The Red Solstice, a Steam Early Access title developed by Ironward and published by Nkidu Games, Inc. The Red Solstice is a tactical top-down action shooter with an emphasis on teamwork and survival. The general story revolves around you and your team of space marines exploring what remains of human civilization on Mars after a massive storm (named the “Red Solstice”) has nearly wiped out all power and communications on the planet. At the same time, a large collection of alien lifeforms have emerged seeking to kill everything they see. Graphically, it seemed okay. The art design depicted a very dark and gritty sci-fi world, which I liked. What annoyed me slightly was just dark some of the levels were, though. At times, it became slightly difficult to see where exactly I was going. On another note, the various types of aliens you fight looked pretty cool. My main concern though, lies once again in the controls, namely, the camera.
In Red Solstice, the camera has a bad habit of not following your player at all, meaning you have to not only constantly direct your character on where to go, but you also need to manage keeping the camera on them at all times. Combine that with the fact that you and your allies will be getting attacked constantly by enemies, and things can get hectic pretty quickly. To make matters worse, the camera isn’t locked to the application’s window. So, if you happen to be playing in windowed mode (like I was), and your cursor happens to drift outside of the game for a second or two by accident, the camera will end up showing you what’s going on about five miles to your left instead of what’s currently gnawing your kneecaps off.
Multiplayer has some interesting class choices, ranging from your standard assault troopers with machine guns, to people who go around wielding flamethrowers, looking to make a quick barbeque dinner out of their enemies. It also seems to contain its own separate campaign missions, which is pretty cool.
At the time of writing, there are seven available game modes. Hardcore Mode spawns boss monsters randomly with each wave, and you gain a bit more XP with each kill. The Primary and Secondary Missions modes are the story missions for multiplayer. Fast Mode makes all of the enemies significantly faster, though slightly weaker. Red Storm mode reduces your armor over time, and you’re noticeably slower when not inside buildings. You also take more damage from bullets while inside buildings. You do get a nice chunk of extra XP for your trouble, though. With Swarm mode, you get a bit of zombie apocalypse thrown in with your alien infestation, as there are a LOT more zombies. Thankfully, they’re also slightly weaker than normal. Finally, there is the currently being worked on “Bunker” mode, where players must protect some sort of object known as the Orbital Beacon. There are two other modes, but they are currently greyed out, so I assume they’re not ready yet. For the sake of trying to explain what they might be, I’m just going to go off of what they’re described as in-game. “Random Waves” mode features “completely randomized waves based on pre-defined types of wave groups,” and “Point Capture” mode involves the players capturing a series of points inside the map by defending the points from oncoming waves of enemies.
There is also a nice levelling system implemented, with there being a maximum of 25 achievable ranks, complete with unlockable weapons and perks. As you gain higher ranks, the stats of your character also increase over time. Weapons are pretty standard as well for a sci-fi game. Machine guns, energy pulse rifles, flamethrowers, shotguns, grenade launchers. Nothing too out of the ordinary. You can also add small, but balanced power-ups to your characters fully customizable load-out, which allow you to do things like reload your weapon faster, make your armor stronger, or do more damage. On top of everything, the game also seems to hold future promises of a singleplayer campaign, which I think could be pretty interesting.
As for the sound, much like the graphics, there isn’t much to say. Guns go bang, aliens screech and growl. It’s all pretty standard stuff. The voice acting was also pretty average. One very minor complaint here, adjusting the volume levels in the settings seemed a little weird. You don’t actually hear any changes you make until AFTER you’ve saved and left the menu.
Personally, I found this game to be a little too run-of-the-mill for me. It’s by no means a bad game, but right now there really isn’t anything to it that makes it stand out from anything else to me. But, if this looks like a game you would be interested in, then by all means check it out. The Red Solstice is currently available for purchase on Steam for $19.99.

Although do I recommend Pillars of Eternity, this will be far from a love letter. It's a project of an enormous scale and this alone has its specifics, that I will make sure are adressed. Also, while Baldur's Gate and Planescape: Torment are quite dear to my heart, I will avoid making too many references to these games as I think it's fair to judge Pillars of Eternity (PoI) as its own game. As of writing this review I have played through it once, but quite extensively doing all the side content and completely exploring all the side characters.
A big point of hype about the game is the fact that the setting is entirely original, crafted by yours truly Obsidian entertainment. I would say they succeed in the creation of a world where the constant feeling and tone are of a sort of melancholy and doom and where you rarely find humor or optimism in the characters you meet.  There is this particular member of your party who has a sort of gallows humor attitude, but even he comes off as a tortured figure, especially after his companion quest is done. The world is extremely well fleshed out there is an abundance of all sorts of ingame books, footnotes, scrolls and even an entire Cyclopedia which lets you read on any creatures you meet inside the world. The strongest point of this game's lore side, however, is the language the characters use and the way they speak to you. I was pleasantly surprised by how little they felt the need to explain things to my player character, but rather acted naturally, which is also a feat of the competent voice acting. For the majority of my playthrough I felt well immersed, but sadly, towards the end this quickly started falling apart. I am not quite sure why the story writers needed to do this, but the developments and the interactions with the main villain pretty much left me disenchanted with the world this game takes place in. More on the story further down the review.
Like other similar story driven PC RPG games, Pillars of Eternity gives you an open world to explore, with a healthy amount of side quests and dungeons to solve. There's also a twist which comes relatively early on with a castle, which comes into your possession for you to renovate develop. This is a pretty fun and flavorful twist, which I feel was unexplored. I was quite disappointed to find out that the garden maze, forum and other parts of the keep were pretty much useless beyond the stats they provided. Also, there was a disappointingly low amount of NPCs to imprison in your dungeon.
However all of these things are minor compared to the combat, which is a pretty central thing in any self respecting CRPG game. Here it's pretty fun and I never got tired of it honestly, despite it being very frequent and largely unavoidable. It's largely got to do with how challenging it feels and how rewarding it was when I 'solved' a strong encounter. Leveling your characters and knowing what your (dozens of) spells do is pretty important and there isn't a single ability, scroll or trap that's worthless and you'll always be rewarded for clever positioning and resource management.
Balance wise, all of the classes I felt were at least “good” with the exception of Ranger. I tried pretty hard to turn Sagani and her little fox, Itumaak into killing machines, with little success, which meant I had to get them relegated to doing side quests, which I guess was useful in its own right. Wizard is one that I felt was extremely well executed - you collect spells, which you learn either from leveling up or the grimoires of the enemies which you defeat. It was really fun to create and manage different spell tomes with spells for different purposes and switch between them in battle.
There are a lot of different in-game artifacts to collect and while I found it interesting that there isn't a linear progression, it was quite laughable how rarely I came across items which were strictly better than the ones I already have for the applicable slot. Some slots like helms and boots are actually pretty rare to come across and rarely give meaningful stats, which I found kinda lame.
What I didn't find lame, though, is the way the game designers handled cutscenes and special encounters. There aren't any, but the way some encounters are solved is with “choose your own story” screens, which was brilliant. Certain events and shortcuts in dungeons are solved this way and have stat checks, companion interactions and all sorts of clever ways to reward you (or punish you) for your build. Great feature.
This is a part which I couldn't help but have legendary expectations towards - after all, this game was made by some of the same people that wrote the story for and designed Planescape: Torment. While Pillars of Eternity has some overlapping themes with Torment and Baldur's Gate, the story itself felt kinda linear and there was a disappointing lack of character development in the companion characters as well as the main characters of the game. The companions sadly aren't much in this game. They take surprisingly little work to recruit (it's almost always “cool, let's travel together”) and at the same time, they show almost no attitude towards the playable character either. There is little emotional connection. It wouldn't be so if the design of said companions wasn't so great in some cases. Some of them like Grieving Mother and Aloth have really interesting premises, but fall short because doing their companion “quests” makes little difference and it almost feels like they were abandoned. Other characters like Durance and Kana just drop heaps of dialogue for you to read through and that's about it (though I have to admit Durance is a badass). The story itself start off promising and keeps you engaged pretty well, but about halfway through the game decides to wander off in a completely different direction and turn it into a “religion vs. science” conflict, or “emotion vs. rationality”, whatever you wanna call it. Similar concepts were in many of the late 90s/early 2000s RPGs but here it's executed straight up poorly. A part of this reason is the main villain's identity and motivation. You never quite learn why he does what he does, because the game just doesn't bother explaining it at all. It explains quite a number of things about him, including his connection to the playable character, but before you know it you're placed with an ultimatum and the game leaves it this way. I know this part of the review seems overwhelmingly negative, but believe me, there's just an annoying contrast between great and horrible in the “story” side of things. Now to move on.
Pillars of Eternity is an excellent game and a masterpiece, which is unfortunately plagued by few, but confusing shortcomings. This shouldn't stop anybody from getting the game as it's nevertheless superb in terms of scale and execution of the brand new setting and combat design. The first 40 or so hours I spent in this game were some of the best I've ever spent playing a game so I can't recommend this game enough, despite the flaws I described above.
I recommend this game.

This game is cheap, and its cheap, but the kinda of cheap we can all like. It does nothing that any other run around on a space ship and gun down monsters game hasnt done already. You go up escalators,and down them, upgrade gear, turn on and off ventilation shafts and charge or ignite reactors, you get duped by weirdo scientists, and help reduce the mass surplus population on the spaceship called Immemorable.
The story is lame but if you notice the subltely of Dead Effects creepy spaceship crew a more pitiful plot arises. These are not zombies, or brain fiending cannibals, they are the weary, dreadful, lonely people you see around the holidays. They crawl, limp, stagger, sway, their ways down a multitude of similar looking cooridors in the hopes of finding someone who will listen, who will embrace....who will give a hug.
The freaks aboard this ship are not after your brains
They are.....HOLIDAY HUGGERZ!
These lethargic egg nog turkey filled stuffing - stuffed fools only want a hug, soloed out by the holiday season and a comfortable lack of social attunement they will be after you, to squeeze out the life you have so that when they look around the scenery is only bleak as their misery allows.
Okay - so you can get the story isnt that great, the action is only so so, the upgrades, level design and overall attempt at an FPS is mediocre. So why get it, because it so basic, so regular, and you can zip zip zippedy zip through the game in about 4-8 hours blazing down hug crazed 30 somethings with a snickerish delite.
You get the all the usual weapons (machine guns, shot guns, 45 acp pistols), but Dead effect brings a few unique ones to the arsenal - nothing ground breaking, just another perspective on already created weapons - the bow, crossbow, EMP pistol and rifle were dubiously fun, and the chain gun - it was probably the most responsive and well made version I have seen in a game.
Some achievements are picky - especially the ones requring no healing, that means no regen abilit either. The slay 5000 and 10000 zombie achievements are easily accomplished through 2 or 3 (about 3000 kills each) playthroughs or grinding in the biohazard and survival modes. These modes can be used to grind out currency and upgrade weapons before taking on the new game plus mode.
There are two characters to chose, the choice you make does not alter the ending story, only thing that is different is the voice and choice of starting weapon which can be changed out, and the opposite weapons purchased and used equally well.
One other thing I like about games like this is....it ends. It doesnt have 200 hours of monotonous game play, its only a small grind for the 5000 and 10000 achievement. Otherwise the developers did a pretty good job informing the player of achievement progress and not making the achievements too absurd to complete.
Overall if this game is on sale, and your a sci-fi/zombie/infected/killing floor/pain killer/Serious sam kind of FPS player this game will be about 24 hours of fun.

State of Decay, in a nutshell, is totally worth buying.  If you have played any of the Left For Dead series, Dead Island, or Dead Rising, you will love this game.  This open world role playing game is packed full of hours and hours of engaging combat, scavenging, and good old zombie killing.  While this game can be played on both Console and PC I recommend that you play it on PC, for both graphics and comfortable playing.  The dialogue is good and the zombie killing is great.  Recommended for just about anyone above the age of 12, but do not, and I repeat.  Do not play before you go to bed!!!

State of Decay is a game that tries to fill a void in the current zombie game market, but kind of mixes and matches multiple mechanics that are not fully realized and do not really integrate with one another. The engine might be kind of overkill for the art style, the game is riddled with bugs, the story is non-existent, and in the end, game ends up heavily repeating itself.
The game is refreshing in the way that it makes you take care of the bigger picture than most other zombie games. You have a base with a group of survivors in it. You control one survivor at a time in third person. You can explore, complete missions, or scavenge for resources which are in constant demand. Survivors get tired when they're out and about, but you can switch between survivors. Survivors can also train to be better: melee fighting makes them better fighters, running improves cardio etc. Characters have different traits that can make your life easier or more difficult as time passes. When you log off the game, the game keeps track of how long you've been logged off, and when you log on again, the game simulates how events have turned out. If you've left the game with survivors dealing with many severe problems, most likely those problems have escalated and caused some kind of harm.
The game does feel a bit like it combines multiple zombie games into one. You have special zombies (Left 4 Dead), melee focused fighting system with some shooting (Dead Island, Dead Rising), managing a base and its resources (Rebuild series), stamina and health that do not replenish automatically and require special attention (DayZ) etc. This is not bad in and of itself, but the game should try to marry all of these elements together. Many games have this problem where mechanics are added without really understanding how they interact with rest of the mechanics. A mechanic might work on its own, but combined with another mechanic could cause frustration or make one mechanic completely obsolete (Saints Row 4 homies vs. superpowers of pretty much all other characters).
There are most likely multiple things to do at any one time and those things can be very far apart on the quite large map the game takes place in. When your survivor gets tired, he/she loses maximum stamina, which effects how much that survivor can sprint, how long and how hard your character can keep swinging a melee weapon etc. Characters with already low maximum stamina are essentially rendered useless from the get go, and being tired can also visibly affect even the high stamina characters. This causes strongest characters being used (and improving) the most with very little incentive or opportunity to improve lower level characters.
The tiredness system ties into another problem. Most of the missions have something to do with your own group having trouble with something: they need to hunt a special zombie, they're surrounded, they need escorting, someone at base needs to be talked to because of anger or fear etc. The entire situation reminds me of Spore's galaxy stage: being diplomatic would mean befriending other civilizations, but as the game went on, these civilizations would send an increasing amount distress calls and ask the player to do laughably trivial tasks or face that civilizations destruction. State of Decay is not so obnoxious with the amount, but those calls get aggravating with the time it can take for one survivor to traverse the map from point A to point B. You cannot send capable survivors to take care of the situation, so the character getting tired quickly causes constant yo-yoing between different locations and the base, which causes major stuttering in the games flow.
State of Decay is not an atrocious game and I've had some fun with it, but I can't escape the feeling that it's not completely thought out. Heavy repetition, very little flexibility in controlling the group, light weight story and very little interaction with survivors of your own group and even with other groups make this game feel very bare. Maybe in the future someone will get this right, but State of Decay gives a peek into what new could be done with the zombie genre.

First things first: The rerecorded lines are terrible. St. John sounds bored, there's no umph or badassery, and the high quality sounds out of place amongst the low quality sound effects and alien noises. Thankfully, you can turn on "Legacy Duke Talk" which disables the rerecorded lines.

I had to turn the brightness way up to see in some of the low-lit areas (and I'm not talking about the pitch black areas like the area before the elevator in E1L2.) Third: The available options are pretty limited and barebones, but they get the job done. You can change keybinds, mouse sensitivity, controller settings, whatever. You can turn the new lightning system (and the rerecorded Duke lines) on and off. That's about it. Not that I'm complaining, really.
I have yet to touch the new episode and will update this review with my thoughts on that once I'm through it.
All in all, if Episode 5 is decent, this is still basically just a slightly watered down version of Megaton. As a huge Duke fan, I don't regret paying the $20, but if you're on the fence about buying this and you already own a previous version of Duke 3D, save your money.

I was priveleged to be able to play Duke Nukem 3D back in the 90's. It was one of the most impactful games of the decade for a number of reasons, from its smooth and highly optimized gameplay, to its level variety. Many focus on its sexual content, but that was really just a backdrop of the game that provided a few chuckles due to how ridiculous it was—assuming its style of humor resonated with you.
Duke Nukem 3D: 20th Anniversary World Tour hasn't tampered with anything that made the original fantastic. In fact, it makes it better.
All four original episodes are included, in addition to a new one. They're just as you remember, except you can use a rewind mechanic to revive yourself quickly upon death. This is a key component of this re-release as Duke Nukem 3D is a very difficult game when compared to most modern titles.
Gameplay feels fantastic with keyboard and mouse, ensuring that quality of life isn't impacted by the original game's age. However, it is worth noting that games from Duke Nukem 3D's era tend to lack the entertainment values of modern titles. Because fo this, it does struggle to hold your attention in the long run.
With all this in mind, Duke Nukem 3D: 20th Anniversary World Tour has arrived with great execution. It's a trip down nostalgia lane that makes no compromises and feels authentic to the original script, albeit with some minor additions to make it feel fresh. It might not entertain newcomers who aren't deeply interested in discovering what extraordinary games from its era were like, but that's okay. There's a sizable audience who simply wants a reason to rewind 20 years and see what made headlines.

Not as good as Terraria.
Yes I know, I shouldn't compare them, they are different games. But let's be honest here, they share so very many similarities.
I will start possitively. If what you like is exploration for exploration sake, (with pretty minimal depth), Starbound is great for that. Starbound is more a 2D exploration/walking simulator mixed with a quest based adventure.  I enjoyed the variance of races, structures, planets, and the universe as a whole.
My first problem, is that depth is surface deep. Sure I love wandering into an unknown civilization and exploring, learning. But here it's just some structure(s) on a planet, occupied by unexplained entities, with minimal canned text lines, no depth of story and lore to speak of, nothing past the surface to explore. Where is the mystery? Variety doesn't mean anything if that variety doesn't exist for a reason outside of "more stuff".
This is where my second and more major issue comes in. All of that lack of world building depth can be forgiven to a degree so long as the gameplay and progression are satisfying and rewarding. Problem is, it's not. It's as though they took everything that made Terraria fun, and threw it all out of the window.  For starters, outside of the stuff on the surface of the planets, there's no reason to ever go digging around.  Underground exploration ius even more pointless and tedious than surface exploration. The combat is boring and unintersting. Your weapon choices are super generic gun/sword/bow choices and any progression is barely noticable. Weapons don't feel unique or fun to use in any real way. Traveling until you get a hover bike (even then it doesn't traverse well) is SLOOOOW and so god damned BORING. You spend 90% of your time walking through uninteresting, boring terrain.
Seriously if I had to sum it up in a couple of words, the game is slow paced and boring. Maybe it would be fun on a large server of people, but i don't know, even that probably couldn't save it.  I wanted to like this game so much,, but really, I just couldn't get into it.
Go play more Terraria instead.

"A video game has never made me truly feel happy; something I can just lose myself in and leave my troubles for a while, and develop an ever-growing desire to learn how to become...a better person. I love this game so much. Thank you, Chucklefish Games. Thank you so much~<3"
This may as well be sole love letter to Starbound, and how I hope you can come to see the majesty—the infinite beauty that is Starbound, and all the things that come together to deliver such an immersive experience.
I haven't been in love with a game as much as this one in SUCH a long time, and, whenever the last time was, I doubt it made me happy like this one does. It literally makes me happy. It's such a beautiful work of art, and I say 'art' because, to me, it's truly 'exploration unending'. I never ever thought I would ever touch a game like this, all with it's building necessities, because I didn't think I could do it; that it was just going to be too much for me. But it turns out... I love it. I can make whatever I want, and I can do whatever I want, and I can play how ever I want to. The entire intergalactic world is mine to explore [eventually, if I ever stop making my home all pretty-like].
The game's beautiful soundtrack accompanies you through a likewise beautiful world—whichever one you visit, wherever you are. It's SO easy to get lost in the world the game built for you, and more-so the world of the game itself. You can do anything you want: from mining out materials for things to build a home with, or any kind of decor you would like, or weapons and armor to fight monsters with. It seems pretty self-explanatory, being another game in the survival-exploration genre, but this one stands out SO much; more than Terraria, more than Minecraft, more than literally any other crafting game out there. The universe is a scary, daunting place to some...unless you're a 'wanderer' like me :p [in which case I'm all for infinite discovery]. Again, I haven't done much in the actual story of the game to iterate on that, so I'll explain how it makes me feel, exactly.
Whenever I've come to be too stressed or angry [because of many things about my work], I always come to Starbound now; it's one of the few methods I use to really relax [which is hard for me to do], and just pour so much time into the game. It makes me feel accomplished with what I keep surprising myself that I can do, and, I know it sounds silly, but it's great for building up my confidence again—to help me become a good person again. The entire universe that's accessible to me always leave me in want, and I can easily obtain the desire I have to explore, accompanied by the amazing soundtrack [everyone loves music, and anyone can appreciate it, I'm sure].
Starbound takes me away from this world and places me in another, one where I can build a family [of friends[[of housemates and neighbors]]], and it stuns me. It leaves me stunned because this is truly everything I want in life, right here. I've been hooked on this game because it is everything I could ever want in life, because it the game and its music soothes my anxious heart and soul, because I can make a name for myself, and make many real friends along the way.
I love everything about Starbound... Our world is a pretty ugly place sometimes, but we have the capacity to make it both beautiful and definitely enjoyable~<3

There are many survival games out there... **but they all play differently**. Stranded Deep fills the niche of single player you vs environment in a tropical setting (Cast Away style). It's probably closest to The Forest (though still quite different), however I found as a solo player, Stranded Deep was less time consuming to construct a base (requires far less resources + you can many wood sticks at a time). Also I love that you can craft with only requiring resources to be around you.
It's a very beautiful game and quite relaxing to play. I'm enjoying it quite a bit - only encountered one bug which I was able to fix by reloading the game (I think it was caused by me alt tabbing). There are a few clunky elements with crafting and the like – but the developers will be improving it.
I recommend this game for people who have patience to wait for a EA game to develop + are happy to provide *suggestions* on ways the game can improve. Also the team is small - so while it's updated monthly (plus hotfixes), the amount of content seems smaller than most other games - so keep this in mind before purchasing. It's not worth the full price at this stage - so better to pick it up on a sale.
If you do decide to pick it up, I recommend creating a new world with the generation seed of 80085 – it has a good starting island with a nearby large one you can start setting up your main base of operations.

(Spoiler free)
Night in the woods follows a similar set up as Life Is Strange, a young adult or teen leaves her home town only to come back and realize things aren't what they used to be. Mae, the main character can come off as charming and lovable but often times you'll find her doing things you may not personally align with. So it can sometimes feel as if your impact on how she acts is very little despite having control over her dialogue choices. This gets frustrating when some key conflicts of the game are influenced entirely by her anger or opinions without little room for you to fix or impact the situation.
Get used to seeing the same places over and over again with little variation, you spend your waking hours in the town and any off limit areas aren't really areas for exploration. Once you visit them you realize how little impact they had.
Into The Woods starts off as a very enjoyable game but overstays it's welcome by being made longer through artifical means. Each area of town is sperated by it's own loading screen, which means that if your computer isn't the fastest you'll have to make the choice between rather you'd prefer potiential new dialogue or to get on with your main goal.
At night Mae will dream about a shadowy city, and the only gameplay will involve running around a very small minimap to cause events to occur and wake you up.
Mid game the dreams will begin to bore and annoy you simply because they serve little purpose.
As for the story? There isn't really a solid foundation to work off of. You learn very early on that someone has gone missing and find an object that gives you a hint of it's plot but only in the last hour or so of the game does any of this come to a conclusion.
The twist is very weak and unappealing and seems to make little sense, but you'll be forced to stick around because of the personal character development, music, art style and hidden lore.
The game is polished but feels unfinished none the less because of how under developed the main story is.
Furthermore it's actually quite hard to call NIght In The Woods a game. It acts a lot more like an interactiven novel the only game elements avaliable are through a grabbing mechanic used a few times and jumping.
Which brings us to the topic of controls, despite Mae's animations being pleasing to the eyes the jumping feature was intentionally made to be more of a challenge then needed. You are required to run and jump two times  before you can "super" Jump.(While retaining your speed)  Which means that many platforms are harder to get to. But since you have to be running and jumping without turning or slowing down it becomes a challenge. This challenge isn't enjoyable or adds to the game, it just seems like a pointless element meant to try and create challenge where there shouldn't be any.
In conclusion Night In the Woods is artistically pleasing and enjoyable at first but quickly overstays it's welcome through artifical means. By forcing players to play the same dream quest over and over again to exploring the same small area for the majority of the game it leaves little surprises and any surprises it does have are shallow.
It's a 10 dollar game trying to be a 20 dollar game by extending it's length. But on a steam sale I'd HIGHLY recommend giving it a chance simply because the animation, characters and music is amazing. But if you aren't interested in an interactive novel more then game then this migh tnot be for you.

Dark Souls is a hard game. ♥♥♥♥ing hard. At least when you first play it and know nothing about how it all works but its challenging in a very fair and genuine way the vast majority of the time - enemies hit extremely hard but so do you, the odds are against you but you always have something to help you out. I've been a huge fan of the Souls games since its inception with the fantastic little classic Demon's Souls and while it took me way longer to finally sit down with Dark Souls, I can say it's easily one of my favourite games of all time and having just finished my fourth playthrough, I thought I may as well write a short review because why not right?
Pros:
*Very simple mechanics made deep and engaging with the huge array of enemy types and having to learn their patterns and weaknesses - learn, slash, block, roll and parry your way to success
*Fantastic level design with interconnected areas that help to create a cohesive and well-constructed game world
*Huge choice of weapons, armour, spells, miracles, pyromancies, etc - every character you make will be completely different from the last if you experiment with all the different builds thus offering huge replay value
*Incredible lore (arguably the best in gaming) told in the most minimalistic fashion possible
*Lots of bosses - Artorias and Manus being two of my favourites
*If you're a sap like me then you'll care a lot about the characters and then be heartbroken when you have to kill them without uttering a single word (I'M SO SORRY SIF!!!) - the lore is that good
*The online system blends a singleplayer adventure together with a persistent MMO world of coop play and PVP invasions, making the journey from start to finish incredibly diverse in online mode
*Runs WAY better than the horribly optimised console versions on a good rig
Cons:
*The PC port is still pretty damn pants - it's behaved itself for me as I find 30fps perfectly playable and I only ever had one crash; the only time performance ever drops is during Seath the Scaleless but thankfully he's a very easy boss
*Player connectivity based on soul level is pretty♥♥♥♥♥♥- people can stay at a low level the entire game, get the best, fully upgraded equipment and freely gank players or breeze through early bosses in coop
*The geometry... Good god the geometry is horrible especially when it swings your camera around and blocks your movement with short curbs - The Great Hollow and Lost Izalith are your worst nightmare for this
*The biggest brick wall players will face is the infamous pair in Anor Londo roughly halfway through the game, arguably the hardest fight in the entire game and I wouldn't blame players for giving up then so be wary
*As much as I love parrying, it's pretty overpowered once you get the hang of it - it makes the final boss a bit of a joke
*STAY THE ♥♥♥♥ STILL SEATH AND LET ME CUT YOUR GODDAMN ♥♥♥♥ING TAIL OFF!!!!!
*Bed. Of. Chaos.

This is a tactical survival game where your (up to) 8 person team must complete missions while surviving waves of zombie like creatures. Also, there is permanent death with only a few chances at revival. If your team survives until the end, then a match can last about 60-70ish minutes, but there is an option to call an early EVAC (if it is not lost or destroyed). There are multiple classes to choose from and each have their own set of abilities. Each class is fun to use, provides something different that is useful to the team, and there are limits on how many of the same type can be in a group, so I would say it's rather balanced in that regard. Also, playing as the medic (healer) is enjoyable, since they are constantly active and are seldom blamed for deaths. In game the abilities can be upgraded and downgraded, so that you can switch between for the task at hand.
The current game is fun and replayable with the developers working to add more features for the final release. By the mid to end point in a game teamwork becomes key and each person gets to add to the effort whatever their class does.
Now I will list some of the cons. Note that I am reviewing this game in it's beta state.
- A lot of info about items and features in the game is not stated. This con is the first con because updating text is an easy fix and they have not.
- There are some random crashes. Usually only a small amount of games crash so it is still quite playable, but after a patch it sometimes crashes much more often.
- The community overall is fun to play with, but there is a bit of an issue with some people being jerks, such as telling you to pick this class with these skills and do exactly what they tell you to do the entire game or you're a ****ing noob.
- At current there not as many players, but I think that stems from the two issues stated above (lack of needed info and people being jerks). This results in a longer time in queue, but not too bad.

Genre - Co-op Squad based survival
On paper this game sounds great to me. You are part of a squad of marines have to complete missions and protect each other from alien hordes. There are different classes with their own perks and unlocks as you play through the game. However, it doesn't quite work at the moment. The objectives are not clear and a lot of players tend to play bunker, which seems to involve staying in one place and killing endless swarms of aliens. When you do get into fighting the inventory is difficult to navigate and it is not clear what the stuff does. The shooting seems to just involve selecting auto aim and reloading when needed. Really wish I had invested in another early access game as think there is too much that needs changing here to make this game enjoyable, although I could be wrong...please prove me wrong developers!

Type of Game:
Third Person Tactical Real-Time Shooter
Version Played:
Early Access PC version through Steam
Similar Games:
Warcraft 3: Night of the Dead mod, XCOM, and to a lesser degree Left 4 Dead
The Good:
One of few games that offers 8 player coop over a non-local environment!
Multiple classes to choose from, with unique abilities and loadouts that run the whole gamut of shooter/MOBA tactics
Assault, Heavy Support, Recon, Marksman, Demolition, Terminator, Hellfire, and Medic
Randomly generated map content helps make every gaming session different and unpredictable
Randomized missions also offer different objectives and locations that add to the replayability
Also adding to the longevity of the game are the handful of different gametypes that place different changes to the setting and difficulty levels
A wide variety of weapons, which feature numerous stats that determined their purpose in varying combat scenarios
The music and sound effects are well done and aptly convey a sense of dread and suspense
The story line and lore is complex and deep, which can assist with the player’s ability to immerse themselves in the game
The game rewards great teamwork which is important to have in a tactical shooter
Very few bugs and glitches for an early access title, especially considering the massive amount of content offered
The plethora of achievements and rank unlocks help encourage game progression
The Bad:
Overall presentation is not very polished and doesn’t help market the immensely deep game underneath. A serious example of making sure not to judge a book (game) by its cover (presentation)
The voice over during the beginning cutscene is atrocious and immediately puts the players expectations low
The complex user interface and menus are also off putting and require putting time into the tutorial to fully understand
While the tactics keep the gameplay varied, the actual gunplay can get repetitive though this can be said of most shooters
That said, if you aren’t a fan of shooters this won’t change your mind or opinion
Can you play it while the children are awake?
There is quite a lot of gun and other weapon-based violence. There, at least in my time with the game, is no profanity. I’d say it would be fine for children 8+, but that of course can vary depending on the child.
Did I make time to complete it?
This is primarily a multiplayer game, so completing it is not an option. I did, however, put numerous hours into it.
Redlight or Greenlight?
This game is currently at a greenlight.
The content that is currently offered is well worth the asking price of $19.99. In fact, the amount of content is beyond most shooters that currently available as completed titles. I will say that I was interested in this game due to the RPG and progression elements, but I am typically not a fan of shooters. The last statement of the cons rings true for me as this game did not change my poor opinion of shooters. If you are a fan of the genre, however, you will find PLENTY to enjoy in The Red Solstice.

While I ultimately agree with a lot of the criticisms people have made against PoE (slow first act, not super user-friendly if you're new to it), I enjoyed the hell out of this game.  It seems like a lot of people here are veterans of the isometric RPG genre, while I barely remember playing Bauldurs Gate years ago, which is probably why I don't understand the harsher reviews here.
I actually put this game down for some time after getting stuck trying to beat the Skaen priest in Dyrford(?), but ultimately picked it up again and actually decided to
.  From that point on, I didn't put it down.  All the numbers, buffs, de-buffs, status effects, etc I brushed off because I thought it was too much data, actually started to make sense.  After this realization, the game mechanics became much less frustrating and I'm pretty excited to start a new campaign.
The story is pretty great, but with the slower first act failing to rake in people's attention, I think a lot of players might've had trouble paying attention/understanding the overall plot in the later acts.  The major plot points aside, I loved the companions!  Every single one of them were fleshed out with their own personal quests (Pallegina's could've been much longer :/ ) and after learning about the sequel, I squealed a bit when I learned of the 3 returning companions.  I will say the "reach out to soul" interactions with random NPC's was cool the first few times, but never did it again after a certain point.  Not very exciting stuff as far as side content goes.
I think one of the better points made against the game is that if you don't have a lot of time to devote, you probably aren't going to have a great time, which is something I hope they fix in the sequel. The 137hrs I have on record isn't a commodity everyone can afford, so if you're not producing content that is encapsulating  players within the first couple hours, it's probably too slow.
This review is probably a mess because this is actually the first review I've written for any game.  But that's how great I think it is, despite the valid criticisms.  If you're looking for a great RPG with the time to invest in the story, learn the game mechanics, grind out for new equipment/skills, then I definitely say give PoE a shot.  It's a slow burn in terms of getting to the satisfying feelings, but it
great when you get there.  8/10!

Spoiler-free review. [TL;DR: This game is probably a magnificent gem once you've heavily invested time in it. But the game fails miserably in its first segment to get the player hooked. Having a busy life and tons of other great games to play, I couldn't push the game to the point where it might get interesting.]
So, you start off with the Character Creation screen, but since you know nothing of the game and it's hard to understand how the million stats work in relation to one another, you're going to spend a solid half-hour to an hour on this screen. Additionally, the dozens of spells and abilities to choose from are overwhelming as well. By the time you're done, you're burnt with information and want to get into the action.
Then the game proceeds to launch you into its prologue, bombarding you with useless expositional dialog with highly forgettable characters... until you finally get into the meat of things. But your character is seemingly untied to the events he/she witnesses: at any point, your character could pack it up and go home or settle somewhere, your character doesn't need this adventure, the plot doesn't relate to him/her... and so, to you.
So, in all, the first few hours are terrible at teaching you the game and making you care for the story, that is, to get the player involved! There's probably some greatness thereafter, but I was already burnt at that point and I probably will never have the patience to push past this point just for the hypothetical chance that it gets better thereafter.
Compare this to the previous game from Obsidian: Fallout: New Vegas. The introductory movie was incredible, you were given an antagonist right away, a mystery to solve, still you had the full possibility to build the character you wanted to roleplay as. The stats are not as confusing, so character creation doesn't feel like a chore.

But if the genre had more actual games, I'd probably skip PoE or at least leave it laying on my wishlist.
Pros
+ Graphics is awesome! everything is 3D, and we have some very beautiful places to see and visit.
+ Camera doesn't move, it doesn't even rotate. At the time that was a limitation because games were 2D, it's good to see a game that revives the style doing the camera right.
+ Up till now, I didn't feel the need to rotate the camera even once. Placement os very good, nothing goes out of sight. When a char goes behind a tree or a house we see their shape.
+ Gameplay is the best! It's very very well done, battles are fun to play, they are very tactical, we must know our chars' abilities and how to play with classes.
+ The best video settings I've seen so far, in ANY game. Srsly, I have 4 displays and my main one is 4K, I ALWAYS have issues of games changing main display's resolution and messing with everything, it's common to have to go to config files to set resolution and windowed mode because games are unable to do it in-game for me. PoE just recognizes display resolution and sets it automatically, and it opened first time without creating any mess! I just set windowed mode in-game and was done. PoE proves it's possible to be done! GREAT JOB!!
+ The stronghold is maybe the best of the lore. Many RPGs allow us to have our own house, but lack stuff to do in them. Oblivion and Skyrim have mods for homes with background stories and even small dungeons. PoE brings it to another level with the stronghold!
Cons
- Too much stuff happening only in texts. The problem is not the amount of text to read. It feels like creators had written the whole game, and then implemented what their budget allowed and left the rest unimplemented, in plain text. For a 2010's RPG I'd expect it to be fully voiced.
And even on voiced talks, char models stay still and there's text describing their expressions, at least some of them required to be cutscened. Voice goes on talking and I don't have time to read what the char was doing or expressing, that's VERY annoying! It feels like the actor on his room reading the text without actually interpreting the char.
- Companions aren't interesting. I don't feel engaged on their quest, I'm unable to care for them. They are as good as hired mercenaries I keep around to fight for me.
- Companions' personalities on idle conversations are different from main talks. In main talks I never see them smile or do anything funny, and then on idle conversations they start doing it. I just don't get depth/familiar with them, and all of a sudden they are so with each other. That's odd, out of place.
- Lore isn't interesting, at all. Take TES or Dragon Age as comparison, they are very very cool, they make me wanna get each and every book in-game and read them to learn more about the lore. In PoE I don't even feel wanting for a sequel, I play on for the gameplay. It's a shame, a game with a so good engine and gameplay, have a wasted lore.
- I don't feel like replaying the game to try different choices. My choices don't seem to make different effects on the game, just create different personalities to my char, but different personalities don't seem to change anything. I know there are factions and I can choose ones and be locked out of others, and I'd need to replay the game to do quests of factions that rejected me. But that's not good enough, it's like choosing to be in the Thieves Guild and because of that not be able to do quests from the Black Hand.
- The story is very confusing. I suppose they didn't wanna hold our hand and explain everything, I'm ok with having hard time understanding what's happening and who is who, if in time it gets understood and we need to replay the game to see the story again after understanding it. I love Escaflowne, that does it nicely.
But the problem here is that we keep reading about people, places and races without any introduction to them. We just don't know what's happening and what people are talking about. And, at least until I've played, there's no proper introduction to anything.
Take the example of the abilities and stats. Every time we read anything regarding Resolve, Lore or Might, we can hover the word and read an explanation of what it is, we don't even need to leave to read about them. It should have been done for places and people too, a little introduction explaining what they are. There are wikis on the Web, but they are larger than I'd want just to get what something is, and wikis have spoilers.

Quick summary: Dead Effect is an indie first person shooter that plays like a less polished, lower budget version of Doom 3 or Rage, but with slightly better visual graphics. There are about 10 missions in the campaign, with no multiplayer. However there are a couple of horde survival type game modes for you to play in order to farm up “gold bars” which can be spent to unlock more powerful weapons.
You play a marine on a space station where a biological experiment has gone awry, killing most of the crew and/or turning them into zombies. There are a few different zombie types to deal with, including a chainsaw wielding fat guy and dudes that chuck grenades at you for horrendous damage (probably the most annoying guy in the game). It’s a good thing one of the perks of surviving the experiment is that you gain bullet time powers, letting you slow down time for a short duration, and put your bullets where they’ll do the most good.
The game is played entirely in First Person Shooter perspective, and you can replay each mission as many times as you want. The reason you’d do this is that each mission has some cash lying around that you can collect, and destroyed zombies occasionally drop a gold bar or weapon upgrade for you.  Between missions you can spend the cash to buy/upgrade weapons, or spend gold bars to unlock new special weapons. There are about a dozen purchasable guns, and only a few of them are purchased with gold bars. You also have the option to buy more ammo in case you run out but it’s generally unnecessary. There are a lot of ammo boxes lying around for you in each level, probably more than you’ll end up using.
Something to note is that the game does not offer saving during a mission. There’s no quick-save or check point saving, so you need to beat each level in one go. If you die, you have a chance to buy back to life, but it’ll cost you some of that precious cash. If you have purchased the “auto-heal” upgrade you can regenerate health over time, otherwise healing can only be done at designated medical stations that are kind of rare in some missions (there are no health kits lying around). A hit from a zombie can take a chunk out of you so this is not a run and gun game. You’ll actually have to be careful for the most part (until you have auto-heal).
You should get Dead Effect if:
+Shiny graphics and ugly zombies are your cup of tea. A lot of the space station is dark and those zombies lurch around in often unpredictable ways, making it a challenge to get that 500 stungun kills achievement (sometimes they fall to the ground and crawl at you in the dark). The stungun is your base weapon that you use when you’ve run out of ammo, and it takes some getting used to.
+You like shooter games where you buy guns instead of finding them lying around. It’s nice to have a choice in what kind of weapon you want, and you can upgrade the stats if you have the cash. Upgrades/unlocked weapons are shared across campaign and survival / biohazard mode, so if you’re having trouble beating a level, you can earn extra money in survival to unlock a few upgrades before progressing.
You should NOT get Dead Effect if:
-You are not a fan of indie games, or games that seem a little “unpolished.” Despite the impressive visuals, the game has an odd “gliding” feel to it. Also, the voice acting is comically weird, possibly translated from another language. Pressing the ESC key pauses the game, but not the audio when someone is speaking (when you unpause, the cutscene continues but the audio is already finished).
-You’re looking for a co-op or competitive zombie shooter. The game has no multi-player and you can’t compare your survival mode stats with other players either. The survival mode isn’t “how long can you last” it’s, “how many zombies can you kill in 3 minutes.” Once you’ve farmed up enough gold bars to buy the mini-gun, you’re pretty much set. That monster can mow through an entire stage without reloading.
Mediocre gameplay, voice acting, visuals, and plot.  There are better things to spend your money and time on.

After more than 146 hours of play, I'm still enjoying this game. And what's more: this game is still being updated and improved by the developers on an almost weekly basis. I'm not just talking about numerous performance updates, but also improvements on the game itself, many of which came from the Train Fever community.
I think that you'll find the game much more playable and responsive than in September. By far most performance issues have been fixed and many smaller and larger additions to the game have made it so it's still fun to play even after 140 hours.
Meanwhile, there is an active mod community that has made it possible to add many dozens of cool new trains and train cars to the game for free and edit it in just about any other way you might want, such as a winter mode, new industries, an updated UI, cool new train stations, and much more. (
)
And finally: this month, a new USA-themed DLC will be released for Train Fever by the developers FOR FREE, which will include 50+ new trains and new American landscapes. I'm going to echo my comment from September here: Seriously, if you like transport sims, GET THIS GAME. You will not regret it.
(I'm a beta tester. A few screenshots of the game are at the end of my review.) (
)
If you even remotely like sim games like Cities in Motion, Railroad Tycoon, Transport Tycoon, or even Sim City, you will absolutely love Train Fever. (And if you loved those games, Train Fever will probably ruin your social life... but that's a good thing, in this case.)
In this game, you get to build a transport empire with buses, trucks, and trains. The maps are huge (even the smallest map size will give you 20+ hours of gameplay) and the graphics are beautiful.
You can build rail lines, bus lines, and cargo lines at will and connect the many towns and industries to each other. If you do it right, the towns will grow into cities and the industries will up their production - which of course leads to more passengers and goods to transport.
There is always something going on; new vehicles are introduced regularly and the needs of towns, cities, and industries change and evolve as time progresses. You start your game in 1850, when only a few steam trains are available, but by 1950 you will have seen a huge selection of trains (including electric and diesel trains), as well as many different cargo trucks, cars, and buses. None of them will last forever, so make sure to replace them with a newer model when they get old!
You can also follow all trains, buses, trucks, and even individual passengers up close if you want, so if you feel like enjoying the scenery (and it is absolutely beautiful to watch), just ride along with your trains. Every person in the game has a set house, a set job, a place they like to shop and a place they work, and you can follow them around if you like. Whether they take your transportation or (from about 1900 on) their own car, depends completely on you.
Seriously, if you like transport sims, GET THIS GAME. You will not regret it.

"“Train Fever”, as a whole, is a pretty fun game that is held back by a number of glaring flaws.  For $35.00 (the retail price as of 10/13/14), I expected some of the above complaints to be addressed by the game’s launch in September, 2014.  Unfortunately, a lot of them weren’t.  I really enjoy plopping down lines and watching my vehicles swarm around the city but am often painfully reminded that keeping up with it all will require more work than it should.  The game has the potential to be something really outstanding once the above issues are addressed.  Until then, it’ll remain as simply an “okay” simulator that could have been so much more."
Full Review:
---
Beta First Impressions:
I'm admittedly a big fan of both the "Railroad Tycoon" series and "Sid Meier's Railroad Tycoon", so it shouldn't be surprising to learn that I was really excited when I received my press key. My experiences thus far are positive overall. It's fairly simple to get into, despite the game not having an in-game tutorial or campaign levels with which to get you acclimated. At the time of writing (three weeks from launch in September), all that is available is a sandbox mode that lets you choose the seed, map size, and difficulty. That alone, I feel, offers a lot in terms of replay value.
The biggest obstacle I faced was laying railroad track as it didn't seem to snap to the landscape. Rather, you can tell the track to go up or down. This resulted in some very ugly valleys and hills being created, though this is a minor complaint. I spent most of my time simply watching the vehicles (yes, you can build wagons and road depots) deliver goods based on the lines I set for them.  There are no AI competitors, which can be a good or bad thing, depending on what kind of experience you want.  I also didn't seem to be able to specify cargo pickup/drop-off ques like I could in "Sid Meier's Railroads"...that is, pick up raw goods at point A and hold them until they got to point C.  I simply had to hope that the game knew what I wanted it to do when creating lines with more than two stops.
"Train Fever" is a little pricey compared to some of the other indie games out on the market, but it scratches that "Railroad Tycoon" itch nicely.  Some more gameplay options and more versatility when laying track and creating lines, I feel, would add to the game's current value.  As it stands, I think the game could be reduced in price based on the content it offers...though I reserve the right to hold judgement on any of the above until the game gets out of the development stage and officially launches.  If forced to simply say "yay" or "nay", I'd lean more toward picking it up as opposed to letting it pass by.  If money is tight at the moment, I'd recommend waiting for a sale and then picking it up.

If your immediate impression of this game based on the title screen is like my own, you'll dismiss it as some sort of creepy he tai grooming simulator thinly disguised as a game. I never would have learned how wrong I was if I hadn't finally started to hesitantly believe the steady chorus of reviewers characterizing it as a strictly PG (for cartoon violence) Choose Your Own Adventure. Thankfully they were right, and much like the CYOA books I remember, seemingly arbitrary death is always one click or page turn away. Unlike CYOAs, there is a parallel spreadsheet game where very limited points are applied towards a wide variety of seemingly random skills. At times, based on "mood", some skills are more costly than others. These skills determine the outcome of many of the choices made for the protagonist. Some checks are visible, while others are hidden, offering entirely new options if certain thresholds are passed. This character development overlay allows for a surprising degree of divergent heroes and outcomes, despite the overall events being essentially fixed from week to week. While there isn't a staggering amount of replay value, players who enjoy trying to find hidden events and multiple endings will find their interests rewarded.

In the words of John Walker for Rock Paper Shotgun, "You know that feeling when you can’t tell if it’s just you? Whether you’re the one staring in confusion, while everyone else is cheering? Gods Will Be Watching puts me in that place. I have not enjoyed playing this game at all. I thought I was going to. I’m wondering if others will."

For a bit of context, I've finished my playthrough on Original (hardest) difficulty while completing all chapters without killing any non-mandatory characters. I think any review for this game needs to have two sections - first impressions, and then a second look after completing.
My initial response was that Gods Will Be Watching is not fun. It is not difficult. It is not challenging, or clever, or engaging. It is a grueling grind against a random number generator with a thin layer of plot plastered over.
However, having completed the game, I can say that every decision the developers made was justified. There's a kind of elegant brilliance to the story, and the characters become really fleshed out both through their actions and how you interact with them. An overarching purpose ties together chapters that initially appear disconnected, and it's rewarding to see all the pieces come together in the final (free) DLC chapter, which is the capstone of the whole game. To put it simply, the epilogue is a masterpiece.
So why the negative recommendation?
The game is it's own greatest enemy. Most of the dialogue is really well-written, but it completely loses it's impact when you've seen it ten or twenty or fifty times. For every chapter that is balanced but difficult, there is one where random chance will punish you again and again. The narrative itself is a unique experience, but demands grueling hours of repetition to discover.
The hardest part about the above is that everything works exactly as the developers intended it, and once you've finished it you can see why they wanted it that way; but the gameplay itself is never really "fun". Gods Will Be Watching would be a great game for the way it integrates its gameplay into a compelling narrative, but it's a missed opportunity because so much of that gameplay is frustrating or rage-inducing.
The experience is too bipolar for me to make a recommendation, although if you have the patience to beat it, it might be worth considering on sale. That said - once you start, I highly recommend you commit to finishing. The tunnel is long, but there's light at the end of it.

Gods Will Be Watching has a wonderful narrative buried beneath its chance-based puzzles. I appreciate it tried to be creative, and the writing is pretty good from what I've seen. That's enough for me to leave a recommendation, but be warned--you may, like me, never finish the game. So just keep that in mind going in. There is no shame in playing on the easiest difficulty, and even if you never see the resolution of the story, the situations this game puts you in are thought-provoking and demonstrate needs-based morality unlike any other game I've played, since in the end you have to acknowledge that your crew members' lives are all forfeit to the horrible calculus that is required to progress through this game.

Night in the woods follows a similar set up as Life Is Strange, a young adult or teen leaves her home town only to come back and realize things aren't what they used to be. Mae, the main character can come off as charming and lovable but often times you'll find her doing things you may not personally align with. So it can sometimes feel as if your impact on how she acts is very little despite having control over her dialogue choices. This gets frustrating when some key conflicts of the game are influenced entirely by her anger or opinions without little room for you to fix or impact the situation.
Get used to seeing the same places over and over again with little variation, you spend your waking hours in the town and any off limit areas aren't really areas for exploration. Once you visit them you realize how little impact they had.
Into The Woods starts off as a very enjoyable game but overstays it's welcome by being made longer through artifical means. Each area of town is sperated by it's own loading screen, which means that if your computer isn't the fastest you'll have to make the choice between rather you'd prefer potiential new dialogue or to get on with your main goal.
At night Mae will dream about a shadowy city, and the only gameplay will involve running around a very small minimap to cause events to occur and wake you up.
Mid game the dreams will begin to bore and annoy you simply because they serve little purpose.
As for the story? There isn't really a solid foundation to work off of. You learn very early on that someone has gone missing and find an object that gives you a hint of it's plot but only in the last hour or so of the game does any of this come to a conclusion.
The twist is very weak and unappealing and seems to make little sense, but you'll be forced to stick around because of the personal character development, music, art style and hidden lore.
The game is polished but feels unfinished none the less because of how under developed the main story is.
Furthermore it's actually quite hard to call NIght In The Woods a game. It acts a lot more like an interactiven novel the only game elements avaliable are through a grabbing mechanic used a few times and jumping.
Which brings us to the topic of controls, despite Mae's animations being pleasing to the eyes the jumping feature was intentionally made to be more of a challenge then needed. You are required to run and jump two times  before you can "super" Jump.(While retaining your speed)  Which means that many platforms are harder to get to. But since you have to be running and jumping without turning or slowing down it becomes a challenge. This challenge isn't enjoyable or adds to the game, it just seems like a pointless element meant to try and create challenge where there shouldn't be any.
In conclusion Night In the Woods is artistically pleasing and enjoyable at first but quickly overstays it's welcome through artifical means. By forcing players to play the same dream quest over and over again to exploring the same small area for the majority of the game it leaves little surprises and any surprises it does have are shallow.
It's a 10 dollar game trying to be a 20 dollar game by extending it's length. But on a steam sale I'd HIGHLY recommend giving it a chance simply because the animation, characters and music is amazing. But if you aren't interested in an interactive novel more then game then this migh tnot be for you.

Night in the Woods is undeniably my favorite game of 2017.
It is an experience that will leave you wanting more.
The story and the characters are simply amazing, and aided by a beautiful soundtrack. They feel alive, they feel human. The topics and problems that they discuss with eachother hit pretty close to home. The main character, Mae Borowski, is a 20 year old College dropout who returns to her small hometown of Possum Springs. In the time she was gone, it had changed. Everything had changed, from the town itself to the people.
Personally one thing that I found especially hit close to home were the various stuff and problems that Mae brought up. As someone currently in highschool, I know that I'm gradually getting more responsibilities thrusted onto me no matter how much I'd love for life to just stay aimless and carefree. That's not possible unfortunately. I personally feel that Mae is a great character whom people can connect with for various reasons. Another thing that I love with the game is the simple fact that you aren't Mae. You aren't truly controlling her. You're just guiding her and her actions.
There were many times that I was going "WHAT ARE YOU DOING?" as I read what Mae was saying. There were many times I found myself loving how snarky Mae is. And even more times I found myself enjoying how Mae can get truly compassionate and supportive with other characters once she gets serious.
Even with the things to do in the game around the story, there are various side things to do around the town. You could converse with her old teacher, listen to poets, or just explore. Even if you have to do the story, there is a large amount of things to do and you won't discover all of it in a single playthrough. If you want every achievement, you'll need to put time into it. At least three playthroughs. Personally I am not going back to obsessively hunt for achievements, this game is amazing and I am leaving it out of my achievement hunts.
Night in the Woods isn't just another bland game of today's industry.
It is an experience.
You will not regret the $20 for this game with its amazing story and characters.

It’s been two years, so I figured I’d take another crack at what there is to say about The Red Solstice…
This kickstarter game, birthed from Starcraft and Warcraft mods, NOTD or Night Of The Dead has come a long way. It's a top down, action based, strategy, horror, survival game, where you control a single soldier, in a group of 1-8 players fighting against waves of monstrous AI controlled enemies. There are options to play with a player controlled team of 3 semi-intelligent marines, but the meat of the game comes from the live co-op play. Over the past few months of playing, I can clearly see that the game has gotten a lot better. I’ve tried to touch on the major categories that I personally feel like need to be addressed in this follow up review of the game, specifically the balance, the community, the controls, and the content. This review is critical and doesn’t cover all of the better points of the game, but addresses many of the issues that were the major detractors of the game upon my first review.
BALANCE
The difficulty rankings have four stages from an easy mode for new players,to the bleeding edge hard mode for those who have sunk in well over 200 hours of gameplay with maxed out suits. The game balancing has been tweaked to make playing the game reasonable at entry level, but maintains a challenge into the harder modes. Regardless, without a solid team, the chance of survival on normal (soldier) difficulty is still pretty low. The learning curve in the game is steep!  Developing 'run away skills' and learning from tactical errors (death), comes with time - more objectives completed, enemies killed and a successfully evac results in appropriate bonuses. There are no dead weight classes once you become proficient, which is nice to see as well. Some vets and more experienced players may try to build specific teams to their meta, but there are no classes that are never worth taking, which brings me to my next topic.
COMMUNITY
This really needs to be addressed based on the very small player base of this game. There are a few great players that are helpful, nice and can make the game great to play. Without naming any names, there was one community member with over a thousand hours who found me when I re-joined the game and was very forward in wanting to provide a positive experience coming back into the game. I have seen a select few work towards raising up new players and helping them with their suit builds and laying out a plan in game to win. They lead by example and remain positive providing a genuinely high quality experience. That being said, some people are cancer. A few veteran players in particular are unchecked malignant growths that have been hanging on for far too long. One example in particular, let’s call him “Lord D-Bag” intentionally fragged a team member without warning because he believed that the team member wasn’t playing to Lord D-Bag’s chosen meta. What followed was a verbal fight and unapologetically run the team into the ground ending in a team loss.This behavior is unacceptable. Veteran players who dictate instead of leading has been a serious problem with the game since the game’s inception. I was happy to see a few friends who I used to play with re-join to have players like Lord D-Bag rudely talk down to them without insight, resulting in a lost player. This mentality of “my house, my rules” has created a small player base, and has limited the game since it's inception. I have to say, fortunately, that these players are now in the minority, but it is something to be aware of and to avoid. If you’ve ever played a game online late in the life cycle, none of this is new, but remember!: Positivity breeds positivity.
CONTROLS
I tell people, whenever I try to explain this game, that TRS is very reminiscent of StarCraft. It’s like taking a Terran Marine and stripping away all of the base building and having a lone marine weather the Zerg. For those who don’t understand the reference, it’s a game of precision. Many slight movements with precise clicks can make all of the difference. A self induced death is just as easy as getting killed by an enemy with a poorly placed explosive, or a missed healing. The skill hotkeys and team movement commands are straightforward. The issues come from the crappy hotkeys for the game items in your character's inventory and trying to control an AI team. When things get heated, you don’t want to accidentally hit the wrong hotkey combination and deploy a tactical nuke instead of a medkit, and it’s startlingly easy to do. This leads to having to click in the inventory to use every item. That’s not the worst thing, but it’s far from convenient. When it comes to controlling AI when you’re playing a solo game, the controls are the same as setting guidelines for a team in multiplayer. You can press the spacebar to go into a “tactical mode” which slows down time and allows you to click on the other character’s banner to directly control them like you would your own character. The problem comes from trying to control the other semi-AI characters when you have another player. The standard controls completely change for whatever reason. Without getting into the details of all of the flaws, let's just say the semi-AI requires a lot of micromanagement, with the memory of a goldfish and no tactical mode to help sort it out. This is exceptionally difficult to manage when you’re in the heat of battle and you need to precision to stay alive. This underlines the requirement playing multiplayer with people ONLY, or singleplayer survival with the AI team ONLY. Difficult.
CONTENT
The amount of content in the game has increased quite a bit in the past few years. Now it has a story driven single-player mode which is focused on plot events leading up to the story of the multiplayer mode. After a single pass on story mode, (which is all you’ll want to do) the game will boil down to its multi-player focus. There are a decent number of maps to play on, which are decently well designed and balanced with their own individual perks and difficulties. There are a lot of customizable multiplayer modes including defending a bunker, killing insurgents, collecting data entries, destroying alien pods and others, with additional modifiers. All of these come  on the back of a waved survival mode. There are also a hand full of different suits your character can wear including a few stand outs like a marksman who has a extremely potent rail gun, a heavily armed demolition class, energy weapon / teleportation specialist terminator and others. They are all unique and have their own perks and uses, though some skills feel underpowered while others are must haves. As stated in the community portion, some players will tell you to change if they find that your build isn't what they want, but in the end, it’s all based on how you like to play, and there are plenty of options to cater to your whim.
CONCLUSION
Though this game has some flaws, I personally enjoy the game. I've put in 360+ hours at the time of this review, over 150 more since my first. At this time I’ve maxed out all of my suits abilities and am able to reach the final wave of survival by myself, but I still haven’t maxed out my maximum proficiency (rank). I still have awards to win and higher goals to conquer. As a new player, online guides are available to help get you started, and there are helpful players who can get you proficient in no time. It’s also nice to see that the developers are still on board, hosting Tournaments and keeping the community live! I am happy to recommend this game to my friends and get them engaged. I think it would be great to bring in new players and breathe some new life into this game.

This is by no means a masterpiece, but I am finding it to be surprisingly fun.
