Everything upgrades, and you can continue for cash. That mechanic is silly, annoying, and another (add it to the list) of painful reminders that this was a phone game. But at least you can continue.
Looks pretty good, like Doom 3 with holiday lighting (Game in general is very derivative of Doom 3, with some Killing Floor in there too). The art assets are solid. The animations and weapons are satisfying. If only they would have spent more care and effort on story, level design, and making the transactions less obvious, this could be decidedly better. That said, it does function as both a fun shooter and as some wonderfully campy kitsch. The actor who voices the German scientist delivers his lines like a bad Ahnald impersonation meets "Und now is dee time un Sprockets ven vee dahnce".  It cuts into the dread that the game does manage to create, and I can't help but laugh. It's like The Tower of Deadly Monsters or Far Cry Blood Dragon, but, you know, with less intent.
The extra modes are good for earning cash for weapons and upgrades and extending the play. If this had been a mod for doom 3 it would probably be considered a classic. A pretty fun shooter that mostly works and looks pretty good, you could do worse. Worth it on sale or in a bundle.
edit:

I have bought
back in 2015, and when I first launched it I think I wasted about an hour trying to complete the first chapter only to be brickwalled by the second one. I haven't launched the game a single time since then. That is, until three days ago.
Now, after about 20 hours of immerse gaming sessions I have beaten it with all achievements. This really is a love/hate kind of relationship I have with Gods Will Be Watching.
The Hate:
This game is
. I am not a fan of punishingly hard games, and that was probably the main reason I abandoned it on the first try. The difficulty is also very inconsistent throughout the chapters - it does not just build up till the end of the game. Even though it is explained later in the story why trial and error is a natural instrument of advancing - I still feel that it is something that will likely put off plenty of people. Gameplay can also be somewhat repetitive, but the constant fear of failure will likely not let you notice that most of the time.
The Love:
Once I managed to find my Zen and enlightenment through frustration, anger and Game Over screens, I actually started to understand how things work. Each chapter is somewhat different and you will have to poke around (and fail, miserably) a couple times before you learn your ropes. It helps that there is a mission-specific tutorial presented in a form of dialogues with some character(s) present.
The story is really great - it is a mix of SK's "The Dark Tower", a touch of "Final Fantasy" trademark 'a bunch of individuals vs. one evil super-conglomerate' theme, a dash of "A Space Odyssey" - all that creates a solid, dark and existential plot. All my questions were answered by the end of the DLC chapter (which is a must, by the way).
Soundtrack is absolutely gorgeous - fingerspit did a stellar job capturing an atmosphere of each chapter.
Artwork is absolutely lovely - that is, if you a fan of a pixel art. If not - I am not really sure what are you doing on this store page at all.
Whom can I recommend it? I can't really say, to be honest. But I can, however, say that you should not play this game if:
If, by chance, things above are not relevant for you - you might actually enjoy Gods Will Be Watching like I did.

From an outsider's perspective, the differences between Street Fighter 4 and its three existing sequels must look marginal at best. The first game made its console debut back in 2009 and helped revitalise the fighting game genre. Super Street Fighter 4 surfaced a year later and added 10 new characters to the roster, but since then, the game-to-game differences have been tailored more towards the dedicated fans. Ultra Street Fighter 4 continues this tradition with five new characters, a trio of fundamental system changes and not so much as a story mode in sight.
If you're not the kind of player who spends hours learning combos in the training room, discusses the finer points of character match-ups on a regular basis and stays up till the crack of dawn watching the Top 8 duke it out at the yearly Evolution Championship Series, then the Street Fighter 4 series' consistent lack of single-player content will be a tough pill to swallow. But for those who view Street Fighter as a competitive fighting game that only truly makes sense when two minds are trying to outsmart each other, then Ultra can be seen as both curtain call from Capcom and the most substantial sequel since Super.
Of the new talent, Poison stands out as the easiest to get to grips with. Her lingering fireball and feet-first dragon punch mean she shares some shoto fundamentals with Ryu and Ken, but when you also consider her Rekka-like whip special and her command grab Ultra, it's clear that Poison isn't as orthodox as she initially seems. The larger than life Hugo, on the other hand, is about as heavy-handed as a grappler gets. His normal attacks have extremely limited combo potential, but if you can close the distance and land his wall-bouncing command grab, you can inflict severe damage.
New girl Decapre can combo into her air throw from her launcher. She can also use the new EX Red Focus to land an Ultra off her Rapid Dagger special.
If the fighting styles of a pink-haired cross-dresser and a gigantic wrestling simpleton don't sound like your thing, then the other new characters offer something a bit more technical. Elena returns from the Street Fighter 3 series with two far-reaching overhead attacks (must be blocked standing) and one frighteningly quick overhead special that can combo into respectable damage. In comparison, Rolento is more of a hit-and-run-style character with excellent mobility and lots of long-range pokes. He can quickly get out of trouble with his EX roll and his Pariot Sweeper Ultra will combo off anything stronger than a sneeze.
The last character on the guest list stands out for two reasons. Firstly, she wasn't previously playable in Street Fighter X Tekken or any other fighting game; secondly, she's the first new charge character to grace Street Fighter in what seems like forever. Indeed, Decapre may look like just another Shadaloo Doll with similar moves to Cammy, but once you actually take her bladed gauntlets out for a spin, you'll realise that she's fundamentally different. Her variable dash can be cancelled into her slide, dive kick, launcher or even one of two baits, and while most characters tend to have one standout Ultra, Decapre benefits from two.
Choosing which Ultra to incorporate into your game plan has been a core feature of Street Fighter 4 since Super, and now with the advent of the Ultra Combo Double system, you have the option to take both at the cost of raw damage output. Other additions to the core mechanics include the Delay Stand and Red Focus. The former prolongs the time it takes for your character to rise after a hard knockdown and is useful for escaping vortex pressure from the likes of Akuma, Cammy and Ibuki, while the latter lets you absorb any amount of hits in addition to giving just about every character a viable way to combo into their Ultra.
Six new stages have made the journey from Street Fighter X Tekken. That should decrease the odds of getting Volcanic Rim on random.
The fact that there's no way to elegantly highlight the impact of these changes without dipping into fighting game terminology just reinforces who Ultra is aimed at. The same is true of the extensive list of frame data tweaks that have been applied to the existing cast of 39. Evil Ryu has more health, Yun's EX lunge punch is (once again) advantageous on block and dragon punches are no longer safe after focus cancelling forwards. This might not mean a lot to casual players, but if you've invested the time with any one of these characters, then the chance to fight with a heavily revised set of rules is an offer that's hard to refuse.
There's no way of knowing where Ultra will take the competitive scene or how much the changes will affect the overall balancing, but if you feel like going back to the series' roots to see how much damage Vanilla Sagat could achieve off a simple Tiger Uppercut FADC into Ultra (it's over 600), then the new Edition Select has you covered. This isn't the first time that Capcom has put all past versions of each character into one game, but its inclusion suggests that this will be the last chapter in the Street Fighter 4 saga. Plus, there's nothing like picking the definitive version of your character when you're trying to prove a point.
Despite boasting a thriving community that streams regular tournaments and keeps the online competition flowing day and night, the Street Fighter 4 series has always been somewhat lacking when it comes to useful features. Ultra helps to remedy this with the option to record your matches while playing offline and change your button configuration while on the character select screen. Better yet, the Training mode has been expanded with a network simulation tool that lets you mimic input latency and a save state feature that makes practising your setups less time-consuming.
Poison's Ultras basically boil down to a kick in the crotch or a whip-assisted assault on the buttocks. Tough choice…
The only feature I couldn't find was a way to reduce Elena's health so I could test out her Healing Ultra, but that's a minor grievance. On the flipside, the new Online Training mode lets you practise against another player without health bar limitations. There's also a revised Team Battle mode that pits two teams of three against each other with a shared health bar that carries over between matches. It feels a bit gimmicky when weighed against the other new features, but at least Capcom has added something that isn't focused purely on the one-on-one experience.
Taken as a package, Ultra is an easy recommendation for players who view Street Fighter as a sport. It offers highly refined gameplay married with a rich art style, and by acknowledging fan feedback in an effort to make a well-rounded game even more polished, Ultra feels like the work of a developer that's content to please its core audience rather than trying to grab everyone else's attention. That's rare, especially from a studio that was responsible for Resident Evil 6.
The only thing that holds this sequel back is the sense that it was made on a fairly tight budget. It's the little things, like the meagre choice of "new" characters and the way that some of the new Ultra animations lack the dramatic flair of their predecessors. But with the development team's passion taking up most of the slack, £11.99 for the digital upgrade feels like a fair price. It's not the Street Fighter 5 that we've all been hankering for, but as the fifth (and reportedly final) version of Street Fighter 4, Ultra is an ultimate end in more ways than one.

State of Decay is a wild The Walking Dead-type game. You can switch characters, and when one dies, the story continues until all of the survivors die. Want the whole review? Here it is:
Story: 10-10
This story is a greatly written Apocalyptic Thriller that has you mostly on edge through every activity. Everything you choose not to do may kill/injure/sicken/etc. a survivor. It may also make people lose trust, friendship or make you lose Influence, a spendable "currency".

Gameplay: 9-10
This used to be a over-the-top game. How it's evolved, It's much different with about the same characteristics of an OTT game. Like I said, Everything you do has repercussions. Whether it be losing Influence, friendship, trust, or a life. All activities are thrilling. Hunting zombies is no biggie unless it's a juggernaut or maybe a feral. The game continues even though someone dies. When you make friends in this game, you will be able to switch to them. If there are no playable survivors alive... well, I haven't gotten to that point.

Graphics: 8-10
The graphics remind me of The Walking Dead. It's not as good, but it's about the same. On high, the graphics are totally performance heavy. Turning it to lowest still looks good. The zombies have a variety of models, making it a more realistic apocalyptic game. The "freaks" look scary, with the exception of Armored Zeds.
Controls: (CONTROLLER SUPPORTED) 10-10
Controls in this game seem awkward at first, but when you get used to it, it gets better. With a controller, it feels better, in my opinion. There are combo-keys you have to press to do a certain action, though.
Sound: 9-10
Could be better. It's atmospheric and all, and the music is spot on, but there could be a better touch to it. It's hard to explain. The emotes fall under here because, well, you can hear them. The emotes are limited. There's not much variety to general emotes, and there's not much variety to what you say when you emote, and there's even less variety for the actions you do when you emote.
Replay Value: 10-10
I haven't reached the end of the campaign, but what I do know is if you have the DLC Breakdown and Lifeline, it's virtually endless. The activities can get (a)boring or (b)risky. There are characters you're gonna want to keep because they're you're "Favorite". Eventually you may want to quit, but still. The Value is large.
Overall Rating Value: 9.25-10
This game is an amazing game if you're into that switch between characters apocalyptic never-ending thriller. I've had so much fun with this game, and I'm still having fun. I'm sure you'll like it too.

I wanted to like this game, I really did, some factors for why are:  A.  This gets rave reviews from most places  B.  A lot of my friends play it  C.  I actually went out and purchased the thing  D.  I've played games that are similar in gameplay and aesthetic to it.  So, with all that in mind, I wanted to find out what the big hullabaloo was, and all I can say is, sadly enough, this game registered as the opposite of fun for me.
Minus mods. taking this game as it is, its character creation is laughably limited; and you're forced between these species with set stories to them.  With a game as open, free and sandbox-y as I've heard this was, I was kinda expecting to be able to create my own story, not be forced into one.
A game being Intuitive is good... except this game is about as unintuitive as I can think, playing the introductory mission feels like your character is walking through goo with how sluggish they pace.  The environments are the typical sci-fi fare, with nothing standing out, and its not all that interesting to look at, same with the characters you can talk to, whom aren't at all memorable and serve as background dressing more than anything.  For something that's meant to excite me for the possibilities of all the adventures I could have with the game, this was a huge let-down, in terms of first impressions, this game is scoring a 0.
Onto the actual gameplay, well, I might explain this by the first mission, where you beam down onto a planet cause your spaceship sucks (or something to that effect).  This is where the player first learns how empty the experience all is, little, to do, I believe you're meant to find something for the ship, but the place is so huge, that task proves kinda fruitless amid the temptation of collecting and exploring.  Normally I love huge open spaces in games, being able to explore every little nook and cranny, but here, everything is just so similar, and repetitive.  And this might have something to do with the game's lack of intuitive-ness, but they seem to have forgotten to issue the hero a weapon, sure, they can mine, but I couldn't for the life of me use my futuristic pickaxe to wound enemies.  And this did get to be an issue where you would lose something (even if you choose the gameplay option where death is doesn't mean anything, it still says "lost 5 per cent pixels", very disheartening) every time you die.  And I get it, if you're going to have deaths in a game, there needs to be consequences that come with it, so as no to make the inclusion of dying meaningless.  However, it gets pretty darn silly when you die, mulitple times, to a single bat or something, not because it's a huge enemy, but just because it follows you around the screen forever or you get trapped.  It's a pathetic way to die, and equally reflective on the quality of game I'm playing.
There really feels as though there is nothing to this game, it's an empty experience, which I suppose does reference the emptiness of space... though nevertheless doesn't cease from it feeling any less empty.

Great game. I could never get into games that didnt have photorealistic graphics, and was always close minded towards them. What a fool I was. After playing This War of Mine, then Rim World, I started to gain respect for cartoony games like these. I am now a believer. Starbound is yet another 2D cartoony sandbox game, similar to Terraria. You run around, collect resources, build houses, craft items, fight enemies, and travel the universe. Kind of like what No Mans Sky would have been if it was actually decent. The thing is, this game, and other like it, are simply profound and very impressive. The scale of it, and the sheer amount of content is amazing. It may seem like a cute game to play for 10 or so hours and be done, but its more than that.
My major complaints is that there is very little context or hand holding in the game. I got stumped MANY times on small little gameplay aspects, things that shouldnt have been confusing or difficult to grasp, but were. No voice overs doesnt help that either, as text walls can be taxing and sometimes you just want to skip through them. I couldnt figure out how to get to any other planet after the first one, which turned out to be ridiculously simple, but due to the intimidating and overwhelming scale of game and clumsy UI, I was stuck on the first for awhile. And the quests have no tracking... Well you can "track" the quest but thats really a lie as it has absolutely no guiding or even a hint as to where you need to go. I also had trouble with armor and outfits, in part due to the terrible UI. So I was getting smashed constantly until I figured out how to make armor. Now Im stuck again trying to find some obscure thing in a quest. I never have problems like this in any other games.
The game is also very difficult. I cant get past some parts because I get stomped instantly. Sad thing is, I cant tell if its supposed to be this hard or if im still missing some major game mechanic that I just havent stumbled on yet. Another wierd thing is that Googling these problems Ive had, provided absolutely no answers. All the wikis and guides arent especially helpful, probably since its all procedurally generated so each play is totally different, which further complicates everything. Again, with any other games I play, even similar 2D terraria like games, I can always find a solution. Either via guides or google searches. My frustration with this is growing, and its a shame because I REALLY enjoy this game. I love making my own little houses. Another complaint is the space ship is so damn small you cant fit hardly anything in it. And theres no home area, you can make a home on a planet but its not mobile, so when you go to the next either you have to make a new one or navigate all the way back to the system, land on the planet, and walk to it.
Overall an excellent game, especially for the price, just be prepared for the steep learning curve. Maybe its just me, but I really hope that this gets updated with some kind of better intro or quest tracking. Would make this SOOO much better to me.

Welcome to dark souls, prepare to die. This will be a review of the full experience including DLCs.
You play by freely walking around in third person with full jumping abilitys, even over low railings and with them often..well death. Enemies will have a certain aggro range and once you reach this they approach you, you hit the enemy by having them be where your attack lands, akin to Skyrim for comparison, only third person.
Dark souls adds a lock-on mechanic on top of this, meaning you then permanently aim at the enemy when using it, allowing you to control where you attacks are directed to, as well as making dodging a lot easyer by being able to focus where "away" is.
In its essence dark souls is like other action RPGs but it doesn't hold your hand or mess around. There is no map, dying makes you lose a decent chunk of progress, "savepoints" are few in between (but you can quit and come back anywhere) and saving brings back all enemies and most importantly all enemies are OP and kill you in barely any time.
This is mostly fair though once you get used to the fact that you dont slay mass amounts of enemies and level up but rather fight for dear life constantly. And pretty much all enemies are just a matter of skill, if you master the controls and learn their moveset you will barely take any hits anymore and thus the fact that you die so easyly will matter less.
Speaking of controls, for the love of god do this with a controller, even on pc, it makes things a lot more managable. Also they are a bit clunky, which gets improved upon with later parts, for example you can only dodge in 4 directions, even though often you would have needed a couple more.
Mastering is easyer said than done though, especially when you choose to fight the enemy close up, you will have to dodge every attack perfectly and in the right direction, know when to attack what to block etc. etc. and the game will punish mistakes by allowing the enemies powerful strikes to get you. This is where all the difficulty comes from, dodged too early twice? Often this means you are dead.
This is actually even part of the charm, so a giant monstrosity successfully smacks you with a club, well you should be dead. And look at that you are. It makes you get to learn how enemies behave and to respect them. Once you are done with this you will probably never forget any of the bosses and most of the enemies will remain with you forever, their moveset, how to fight them. And that's not something most slightly more greyish orcs in other games can claim.
And o boy the enemy design together with the places you find them in is probably the games strongest point, it makes monstrosities look truly twisted and evil, dragons and giants fearsome and the enemies always fit the locations, knights in castles, killershrooms in forrests, and have a reason for being where they are what they are as well as for trying to kill you. Allthough speaking of looks the game looks even older than it is, obviously no modern standard but I'd say still good enough to be very enjoyable.
And once you succeed, once you get into the flow, it feels incredibly rewarding, because all together this means said giant looks like it will just rolfstomp you, and it WILL stomp you so you take all of your skill and roll away right as his giant weapon approaches and attack in the moment of breath his opening leaves for you until you have finally worn him down to death. It just feels like a "realistic" boss fight would and should play out.
Also the game usually hints at danger, even though it is subtle, for example with burnt corpses, animating you to run for your life.
Now a couple of difficulties are unneccesary though. For example as I said there is no map and of course that would break the immersion to a certain degree but you get so damn lost so easyly and until very late in the game you always will have to find your way by foot no fast travel and often not even obvious paths. I believe having a largely reduced map to at least help you out a little would help so much.
The cameraangle can also sometimes be your downfall, luckily though this isnt common.
And the worst part about the game in my opinion is a lack of guidance about what to do. Again obviously there is reasons not to hold hands and give door by door directions, however, let me just give you an example:
right after the tutorial you are at a crossroads. there is many paths to choose and all look like a neat adventure. WRONG all but one of them kill you and there is no real way for you to know except for kind of not being able to beat the enemies and constantly dying. But it is dark souls, perhaps you just need to improve! No, just no, you are running against an impossible wall and dont even know it yet.
This goes further with how ridicoulous the things you need to do to advance get. It is basically talk to NPC A then go back get item B at location C and then and ONLY then you can advance in a place that is nowhere near any of this and seems to have absolutely nothing to do with any of it. This is some hold the red orb and jump in a tornado type of how are you supposed to know that.
Also some of the bosses are just absolutely hard even for Darksouls standards, requiring pitch perfect reactions even more than other enemies and coming at you with incredible ferocity, basically forcing you into a 3 minute cycle of perfection or death. Most of these are optional though. There is actually a lot of extra content, new enemies places bosses etc. both via DLC and just in the game in general for that extra touch of everything that makes Dark souls what it is.
FInally the story: it's complicated. Aside from an absolutely amazing introduction there is no cutscenes to establish anything and while you know your general world and goal kinda, there is such an incredible hidden amount of lore. Like you kill a boss and its eh whatever, though it looked neat, but in reality this was person X responsible for event Y and major player in the history of the world, but you will never know that, because tidbits are hidden in item descriptions of all places, NPC dialogs and most importantly piecing together piece by piece and theorizing.
Oh and the music is pretty neat, subtle, underlining the emotion rather than setting it and just great tracks.
A final key note: multiplayer. At this very moment a revival event is happening and you can actually find people again but thats like once a year and only a few days. At all others times there is a chance you are literally the only person in the game and this kills a lot of gameplay, though not key experiences they are a defining part of what makes this game. For example in certain areas of the game another player could choose to jump into your world to fight you, because things arent already hard enough. Or the fact that there is a certain selection of texts applyable anywhere in the world for all to see. (and this is usually used to write "treasure" at the edge of a cliff) there is "covenants" basically factions in the game with their own items places rewards concepts etc and there is a LOT of them. All pretty much useless without multiplayer. So if you check this game out see when the next revival event is and then see how the entire experience changes.
Tl:DR:
amazing setting and design, brutally complicated, buy if you love piecing together a great story fantasy action RPGs, fast reaction based challenges.

But I must also admit the game is very short, and it gets repetitive very quickly. This is probably the type of game where you finish the story, and never touch it again.
It also becomes a very "skill-less" type of button mashing game. Essentially, you get swarmed by a horde of Orcs, you just keep hitting LMB and when the rare occasion happens they want to help out their friends, you just press RMB, and back to smashing that Orc.
The Vault Stun skill you can earn later in the game also becomes incredibly OP, you essentially spam Space, it stuns them,  you then use Flurry on them and block the occasional attacks, and keep doing that tactic.
Overall, I had a very very fun and unique experience you most likely wont find anywhere else. Plus, the ending is pretty good. :-)

This game is all about choice. Someone described it as a Sansa Stark simulator. That's quite fitting. You're playing as a young princess who ends up in the center of a dangerous political world. Unlike Sansa though, you'll be making most of the decisions.
If you're curious about the gameplay, I recommend that you watch a review or a let's play clip. In short, it's much like a text-based RPG, with manga style art. You'll choose what the main character studies, what she does with her free time, and how she reacts to events. Her education is essential to both her survival and which choices are available.
Recommended to players who enjoy the decision elements in roleplaying games.

The story is mildly interesting, and mildly emotional. The dialogue gives you a good idea of what is going on. You can train Elodie in different skills. In one part of the game (minor spoilers, doesn't affect story) somebody sends you a box of chocolates that is poisoned. If Elodie is proficient in divination she will notice a bad omen and you will have the option of not eating the chocolates. If she has proficient knowledge in poison, medicine, or herbs she will be able to heal after ingesting the poison. If Elodie hasn't been trained in any of these things she will eat the chocolates and die.
I really wish the game would continue past coronation. It is very fun and entertaining, some of the battles and dialogue is really intense and gets you going. It stops short, however. It would also be cool if there was more visual feedback. Instead of:
"A fierce battle rages on. elodie makes lots of explosions with her magic and bodies fly everywhere" it would be cool if there were animations that showed these things happening. Sometimes the battles can be difficult to visualize and it takes you out of the moment.
That being said the game is very fun to play and I definitely recommend it for those who like command line or RPG games. It is very fun and I enjoyed it very much.

I started and the first thing I noticed is that it says press the number 1 for "Ok" and the number "2" for back. This is fine, but it's a bit odd. Enter and escape often have those functions, but no biggie. I then tried to use my xbox one controller. NOPE! Even though there's a controller scheme and a menu option for controller, it won't work. Says that my controller has been disconnected. Tried some trouble shooting and couldn't get it. Ok game, strike one. I'll just use the keyboard. Not too big of a deal. Then I begin playing. The tutorial is walking me through how to play. It's click to move. I can deal with that. It says press 1 for light attack and 2 for heavy,. All right, I give it a try...nothing happens. My hero isn't doing anything when I push those buttons. Hmm. I stop moving and try again. It works! Brilliant! I can't move and punch, you have to stand still and punch. This is a BIG problem. It sounds small on paper, but this is down right obnoxious. This game is a beat em up game with lots of movement, but the devs couldn't get the "punch whilte running" feature to work. I'm 5 mins in and already have several reasons to quit.
Ok, well then I think I can just change the key bindings. Oh boy, here's where it gets really dumb. I go to remap the light melee and heavy melee to my mouse buttons...AND YOU CANT! What a load of crap! Ok FINE! I will play with only keyboard, old school! I start rebinding my keys. Exit back to game...CHANGES DON'T STICK! It went back to default! I go back into the menu and make the changes and notice that exiting the menu returns the keybindings to default. Ok, my patience is about to wear out. I change the bindings again and try to go to an adjacent menu, and then click back. (like, shift over to the graphics options). I get back into game and my bindings have stuck. PHEW! I can now start playing. I think of a few key binding changes I want to make, you know, just to tweak them a bit. I hit esc, which is the menu button...and MY HERO SWINGS A PUNCH! YES, I REBOUND THE MENU KEY AND CANNOT GET BACK IN!
I'm sorry to yell so much, but I've never been so frustrated in the first 10 mins of a game. I'm going to try to return this piece of trash. I'm astounded that it was this problematic.

I never played this game as a kid, only the first, and so I have no nostalgia behind my review for this game. If you really loved the RPG elements of the first one where you could spend hours customising your team and trying to figure out which heroes to put all your money into, don't get your hopes up. They dumbed down the RPG elements so much:
Characters only have four powers - no customising which ones to max out and which to ignore.
Costumes are now purely cosmetic - again restricting your customisation. Heroes have passive abilities to spend points in, the only customising is if you pick pro-reg or anti-reg you'll get two different options. While you can see these before you pick your side, if one hero has anti-reg perks you prefer and the other has pro-reg perks you prefer, then you're going to be at a loss. Money for these points is also now unique to each hero, so if you collect 1000 points and spend 400 on Wolvering, he will now have 600 but the others will still have 1000. So no more lengthy decisions about which heroes you want to specialise in.
Equipment has been replaced by medals - Medals are shared by your entire team, and only three can be equipped at a time. This makes medals with trade offs now useless because instead of you needing to play one hero to the medal, you have to play your entire team to it. So if you want a +melee damage and -power damage medal you have to play all melee heroes which kinda ruins the whole appeal to this game of building an optimal team with different specialists.
Dialogue Options Have Impact? - When talking to characters in hubs you can respond to them "aggressively", "diplomatically", or "defensively". Responding consistently in certain ways earns you medals in line with that behaviour, and otherwise doesn't change the story so just always respond how you want enjoy playing.
The only good change to this game in terms of gameplay was the replacement of Extreme Moves with Teamwork Powers. You gain momentum the same way, but it's shared across the team, and anyone can then initiate a Teamwork Power which will be a special animation where the two heroes you select will do something awesome while combining their powers. This allows for six different super moves, each situational, which does add a layer of thinking and tactics that the first game didn't have. But I must stress that this is the only decent change to the gameplay, as far as I'm concerned.
But if you prefer a simpler game and just want to watch Invisible Woman drag a bunch of dudes into a small area with forcefield for Psylocke to cut them all up in one slash, then this game is definitely for you. The story also has a stronger focus, with heroes not being available to you depending on where you are in the story. It's also a lot better than the last game's. It's basically the Civil War story, complete with the pro-registration army doing some really messed up stuff. Some dialogue options can help engage you in the story, as you get a few nice Easter Eggs/alternative responses depending on who's talking to who (Whenever Invisible Woman talks to Mr Fantastic (which will happen a lot given he's a main character on the pro-reg side), many responses change from the standard given the whole "they're married and the player may not want to follow his side and that's going to have implications for them".
Even though I slammed the gameplay quite hard, and this game is definitely worse than the first game, it is still undeniably fun. Just don't expect the same level of depth in gameplay that you could put into Ultimate Alliance 1.
It is also not worth $40. At all. Get it on sale if at all. Or get your friend to gift it to you. But not as broken a port as UA1.

Welcome to dark souls, prepare to die. This will be a review of the full experience including DLCs.
You play by freely walking around in third person with full jumping abilitys, even over low railings and with them often..well death. Enemies will have a certain aggro range and once you reach this they approach you, you hit the enemy by having them be where your attack lands, akin to Skyrim for comparison, only third person.
Dark souls adds a lock-on mechanic on top of this, meaning you then permanently aim at the enemy when using it, allowing you to control where you attacks are directed to, as well as making dodging a lot easyer by being able to focus where "away" is.
In its essence dark souls is like other action RPGs but it doesn't hold your hand or mess around. There is no map, dying makes you lose a decent chunk of progress, "savepoints" are few in between (but you can quit and come back anywhere) and saving brings back all enemies and most importantly all enemies are OP and kill you in barely any time.
This is mostly fair though once you get used to the fact that you dont slay mass amounts of enemies and level up but rather fight for dear life constantly. And pretty much all enemies are just a matter of skill, if you master the controls and learn their moveset you will barely take any hits anymore and thus the fact that you die so easyly will matter less.
Speaking of controls, for the love of god do this with a controller, even on pc, it makes things a lot more managable. Also they are a bit clunky, which gets improved upon with later parts, for example you can only dodge in 4 directions, even though often you would have needed a couple more.
Mastering is easyer said than done though, especially when you choose to fight the enemy close up, you will have to dodge every attack perfectly and in the right direction, know when to attack what to block etc. etc. and the game will punish mistakes by allowing the enemies powerful strikes to get you. This is where all the difficulty comes from, dodged too early twice? Often this means you are dead.
This is actually even part of the charm, so a giant monstrosity successfully smacks you with a club, well you should be dead. And look at that you are. It makes you get to learn how enemies behave and to respect them. Once you are done with this you will probably never forget any of the bosses and most of the enemies will remain with you forever, their moveset, how to fight them. And that's not something most slightly more greyish orcs in other games can claim.
And o boy the enemy design together with the places you find them in is probably the games strongest point, it makes monstrosities look truly twisted and evil, dragons and giants fearsome and the enemies always fit the locations, knights in castles, killershrooms in forrests, and have a reason for being where they are what they are as well as for trying to kill you. Allthough speaking of looks the game looks even older than it is, obviously no modern standard but I'd say still good enough to be very enjoyable.
And once you succeed, once you get into the flow, it feels incredibly rewarding, because all together this means said giant looks like it will just rolfstomp you, and it WILL stomp you so you take all of your skill and roll away right as his giant weapon approaches and attack in the moment of breath his opening leaves for you until you have finally worn him down to death. It just feels like a "realistic" boss fight would and should play out.
Also the game usually hints at danger, even though it is subtle, for example with burnt corpses, animating you to run for your life.
Now a couple of difficulties are unneccesary though. For example as I said there is no map and of course that would break the immersion to a certain degree but you get so damn lost so easyly and until very late in the game you always will have to find your way by foot no fast travel and often not even obvious paths. I believe having a largely reduced map to at least help you out a little would help so much.
The cameraangle can also sometimes be your downfall, luckily though this isnt common.
And the worst part about the game in my opinion is a lack of guidance about what to do. Again obviously there is reasons not to hold hands and give door by door directions, however, let me just give you an example:
right after the tutorial you are at a crossroads. there is many paths to choose and all look like a neat adventure. WRONG all but one of them kill you and there is no real way for you to know except for kind of not being able to beat the enemies and constantly dying. But it is dark souls, perhaps you just need to improve! No, just no, you are running against an impossible wall and dont even know it yet.
This goes further with how ridicoulous the things you need to do to advance get. It is basically talk to NPC A then go back get item B at location C and then and ONLY then you can advance in a place that is nowhere near any of this and seems to have absolutely nothing to do with any of it. This is some hold the red orb and jump in a tornado type of how are you supposed to know that.
Also some of the bosses are just absolutely hard even for Darksouls standards, requiring pitch perfect reactions even more than other enemies and coming at you with incredible ferocity, basically forcing you into a 3 minute cycle of perfection or death. Most of these are optional though. There is actually a lot of extra content, new enemies places bosses etc. both via DLC and just in the game in general for that extra touch of everything that makes Dark souls what it is.
FInally the story: it's complicated. Aside from an absolutely amazing introduction there is no cutscenes to establish anything and while you know your general world and goal kinda, there is such an incredible hidden amount of lore. Like you kill a boss and its eh whatever, though it looked neat, but in reality this was person X responsible for event Y and major player in the history of the world, but you will never know that, because tidbits are hidden in item descriptions of all places, NPC dialogs and most importantly piecing together piece by piece and theorizing.
Oh and the music is pretty neat, subtle, underlining the emotion rather than setting it and just great tracks.
A final key note: multiplayer. At this very moment a revival event is happening and you can actually find people again but thats like once a year and only a few days. At all others times there is a chance you are literally the only person in the game and this kills a lot of gameplay, though not key experiences they are a defining part of what makes this game. For example in certain areas of the game another player could choose to jump into your world to fight you, because things arent already hard enough. Or the fact that there is a certain selection of texts applyable anywhere in the world for all to see. (and this is usually used to write "treasure" at the edge of a cliff) there is "covenants" basically factions in the game with their own items places rewards concepts etc and there is a LOT of them. All pretty much useless without multiplayer. So if you check this game out see when the next revival event is and then see how the entire experience changes.
Tl:DR:
amazing setting and design, brutally complicated, buy if you love piecing together a great story fantasy action RPGs, fast reaction based challenges.

Let's get the obvious out of the way. Is this game challenging? Yes. Is this game hard for new players? Yes. Is this game impossible? Absolutely not. This game has a reputation for being a very hard game, sometimes being dubbed "The Hardest Game Ever." I will tell you right now that while the game is hard in the beginning, especially for new players, it can easily be learned. It is just another game in which the level designers introduce escalating challenges for the player to face. The game starts off showing you the basic controls (attacking, dodging, healing etc.) but those who pay attention can notice that the game is slowly introducing the player to how certain challenges must be approached (fighting one target, fighting multiple target, fighting ranged targets etc.). The golden rule is to watch your surroundings, and watch your enemies. You will be able to figure things out for yourself, because though the game may not tell you outright, it does show you the ropes before it throws you into the fire. Of course you may get stuck in some parts and there is no shame in looking at a guide. I did as well in the beginning. But before you do, look around the world and look for places you have not seen before. If the area is new, and the enemies are not too hard to fight, then you are going the right way.
This game is very satisfying. If you are new to Dark Souls then you will die, very often. But that is the whole point of the game so do not feel discouraged. This game will be hard in some parts, and you will come across an obstacle that seems impossible to defeat. But when you accomplish the task, and you will, you will feel amazing. You are also given a wide variety of weapons and armor to use. Each weapon has a specific move set that fulfills some task. When you find the armor and weapons that fit your play style, upgrade them and have fun. Weapons are another aspect of this game that are very satisfying. The weapons, ranging from practical to ridiculous, all have a weighted feeling to them. You don't just blindly swing a sword around like Skyrim, there is timing involved. When you get a hit in and you watch the enemies health go down, you will feel like a million dollars.
Along with the difficulty, the story also has a reputation. Much like the gameplay, the story is left up to the player for the most part. You are given an intro cinematic which lays down the history of the world. But once you are in the game proper the story is really only told through NPC dialogue and item descriptions. This makes the story a little bit of a mystery, you being the one who takes in information and clues to piece together the more in depth history of the world. Even when you have finished this game you can spend days watching videos of people explaining what happened in events before the game, and events that are happening in the game. Something as simple as armor next to a bonefire, or a suspicious item in someones treasure chest can open up entire stories.
The entire world is seamlessly connected. Except for a few areas that require special passage, the different areas are interconnected and it is possible to walk from each and every one without having a single loading screen. This helps make the world seem more alive and grand, especially when, in some cases you are able to see one area from another. The visuals are also amazing. Whether it be from the top of a mountain peak or through a lush forest the atmosphere will certainly drag you in. However in some parts of the game, the framerate will go down drastically.
DS Fix is a mod that I highly suggest players to get. One of the biggest problems with Dark Souls for some people is the fact that the game is locked at 30 FPS. This mod unlocks the framerate allowing one to reach 60 fps and solve some of the visual issues that people experience.
Dark Souls is truly a unique experience for any player. I've seen people put off by the difficulty at first and then eventually return to it hooked. If you are a fan of story and lore, this game is rich in it's atmosphere, world building, and unique presentation. Gameplay fluctuates from a fast panicked pace to slow anxious one. There are a variety of weapons that one can pick up and use to fit their play style. Overall this game is an experiment in determination. Every challenge can be completed and every enemy can be defeated. If you have learned the elements of the game, and have adapted to its rules, you will succeed. I highly recommend this game. 1. Is the gameplay in general good?
It wasn't at first, it was very clunky. It now feels really smooth, shooting mechanics are very very good compared to the AAA shooters I play regularly. The game does have good gameplay but the main thing is the theme and aesthetics, they're what make the game so great.
2. is the development efficient?
They seem to fix major bugs quickly and add stuff that are genuinely healthy for the game. No microtransaction or P2W ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t, you paid full price to get the game and you're going to get the full game.
3. how often is the game updated?
Very often and this is why I came back, quit when I first played because of the clunkiness and just general low-quality but it's a completely different game now, it's even stopped me playing Battlefield 4 which I have hundreds, if not over a thousand of hours on.
4. how is the community and game difficulty?
Community: It seems for every person who shoots you on sight, there's someone who will say hello and go their separate way or try and team up. This depends on location of course, if you go to the more hostile areas then get ready to be shot, if you go to the lesser areas then you'll be safe without a gun (most of the time). I've had times where I've encountered groups of bandits fighting while I've had times where 7 friendly people have been running around sharing resources. Overall I'd say the in-game community is great but stay away from Steam Discussions and voicing a negative opinion (constructive or not) on these forums.
Difficulty: Really depends on your skill but I'd say you need to have a good aim if you want to defend yourself from bandits, either that or you need to have great stealth or scouting ability to go around the map safely. The AI enemies are updated constantly so what I say now might be different come next patch. The skill ceiling is not too high, you can kill a player who has 500 hours of experience if you catch them out. I would say the game is not really difficult.
5. base building, weapons, loot. Are those good in the game?
Base-building: Haven't touched it yet and won't until storage arrives (which is a high priority of the Dev team).
Weapons: Tons of different weapons and ammo types considering how Early Access this game is and there's still an attachment system to arrive. Gun physics include bullet drop and bleeding, recoil is realistic and manageable, weapons have their own defined strengths/weaknesses. I'm very happy with the weapon system and this is coming from a guy who has played tons of first person shooters over the years.
Loot: Many different kinds of loot which all have their own uses, would not recommend picking everything up, storage is needed quite badly to be able to take advantage of all of the loot. You can craft all kinds of stuff with what you find but again, storage will make loot and crafting a whole new beast.

Orcs Must Die! 2 takes a fun alternative to the genre of tower defense by including traps and gameplay gimics that stem not from the environmental hazards you put, but by the decisions you yourself make.
Characters are balanced to where they suit the two standards of play: fast yet weak, strong yet slow. It's a simple premise that carries with it a great simplicity to each map that you come across, which blends well together with the complications of the traps needed themselves. The maps, however, do remain static, and the majority of the time, there is not much in the way of mobs to induce panic, other than Kobolds. Complex as they might be, I would think that additions and new variables to the environment over time would go well with the playstyle that they are trying to convey, as the majority of the time, you find yourself at one spot, sitting and shooting blindly. However, that does not mean that the maps are bad, for they do factor in quite a lot of situational advantages for both you and the enemies.
The story is well-driven, and the characters contrast and are obviously played with to such a degree that it's enjoyable to hear the bickering between the two at the beginning of each map. The story itself is driven on implications, and prior knowledge of the prequel to this, which the game actually tells newcomers to the series throughout tid-bits and well-hidden pieces of information that fit within the context of the situation, to where they accumulate beautifully into something that you can structurally understand.
Gameplay is a blast, and it's always fun making the most sadistic things for the Orcs to pile into, one by one, while you blast them into bits. There's no denying that they did this right, as it clearly shows just from picking up the game once, as tight as the controls were. The problem I faced was only with the mouse sensitivity, but I did not get bothered by it too often, for the game does not actively create that as a factor needed to win, which benefited both newcomers and old-timers alike.
Go ahead and grab your barricades and a friend for this game. Orcs have to die, after all, and who better to do it with than a bottle of beer and a laughing buddy by your side?

How do I describe Grimm? It's one of those oddball games that somehow leave an impression on me, but leave me with little to comment. Keep in mind, though, that I've only played the first episode (because it's free, so kudos on you Grimm).
In Grimm you play as Grimm, a nasty little bugger who stinks up the place and pees every half or quarter second without activity (during cutscenes as well, yes). He hates the goodie good and happy endings of fairytales, and thus has made it his plight to stink up the entire library provided by the game. In the first episode, he teaches a boy to fear because the original story didn't (and I have to admit, I'm on Grimm's side on this particular story, because it originally had no element of fear in it). Grimm does his thing (through you), and badabing badaboom, the story is grotesque and violent and disgusting.
I'll say this, the game has an interesting concept, and I can see why people would be drawn to it. There's a clear goal, there's a clear indication of progression, and the controls are easy to learn and master. Now, I'm not going to act like I know how the rest of the game will be like, considering I've only played the one episode. However, from what I played, I felt I had a pretty good idea of how the rest of the game would be.
See, around Grimm is a permanent circle of filth, so to stink♥♥♥♥♥♥up, you run around and perform bum-bashes here and there for greater effect, and that's it (I will admit, it's kind of funny to finally see a game based entirely on the concept of AoE). Sometimes you'll be faced with a platforming section, but the more you have to jump with Grimm, the more you'll realize how awkwardly heavy his jumps are (though considering how heavy he looks, I guess it's... okay?). Additionally, after performing a bum-bash you have a slight moment of "recovery", where you can't input anything and have it registered, and (as I stated earlier) Grimm will start peeing every half or quarter second, meaning you'll be listening to him wetting the ground and seeing yellow dots a lot (if you don't live in constant forward motion, that is). On top of that, the lead-in and lead-out cutscenes last for a long long time (probably like 5 minutes each or something, though when you go in with the mindset that you're about to play a game, it's a little distressing when your hands are on the keyboard, ready to strike into a so far visually pleasing game). It's all nitpicking, I suppose, so take it with a grain of salt for now.
Just looking at the overall look of the game and the concept (and toilet humour), you'd think this would be suitable for children, and I would tell you no. There's blood and gore, Grimm can bum-bash depressed children to death (and watch them explode into a cloud of evaporating blood and chunks of flesh), people are getting hanged and beaten around, so really it's like the GTA of bright and colorful games. But with more death. On the other hand, the contrasts can be really fun to discover, and often inventive, and the voice acting isn't absolutely horrible pigshit, so there's not much to complain about in there (except Grimm's spastic bladder).
So my final verdict is... It's okay. Yeah, I mean, I wouldn't be spending several nights trying to beat each episode the same way I do an insignificant sidequest in Skyrim from 5pm until 4am, for instance. That being said, I can't really say you should avoid it like the plague. Honestly, Grimm is a kind of game you have to try for yourself, and thankfully the first episode is there to give you a taste. I can't say if you'll like the soups the chef puts in front of you, you'll just have to discover that for yourself. If you don't like it, you don't lose anything. So if you have an interest, go try it out.

[Opening]
I'm going to have to revoke my previous review for this game because I just realized I've played every Street Fighter game 'cep' 1 and Alpha 1, including the Street Fighter V beta.  And, in hindsight, I've discovered just how terrible the controls are in this game.
I grew up in the arcades back in the day, playing Samurai Shodown, Street Fighter II Champion Edition, World Heroes and whatever else I could stick my quarters into.  I've always known fighting games to have tight controls, and while I haven't always played them competitively (as much as I would've loved to), this game does not have tight controls.  Lemme tell you what you can expect to see a lot of in this game.
[The Cons]
First off is negative edge.  Negative edge is present in all fighting games.  When you press a normal attack button, then cancel it into a special move, occasionally fighting games will take the previous button press and apply it to your next movement.  This usually happens if you take too long to release the first button you press in this sequence.  In Street Fighter IV, you can expect to see this happen a lot.
The next one is something I honestly don't know if there's a name for yet.  People who play this game will burn meter if for no other reason than to prevent the use of a super move.  They do this because sometimes, when you do a special move with a similar motion to your character's super move, the game will automatically cancel your previous special move into a super move, even if you only pushed the button once.
One frame links (and two frame links, etc.).  Just one frame links.  This is the only fighting game that has them.  For the uninitiated, a one frame link is when you press one normal attack button, then press another one at ONE VERY SPECIFIC frame of animation from the previous attack.  One frame at sixty frames a second.  Doing this is insanely difficult, ESPECIALLY ONLINE, and takes more patience and practice than anything I've ever had to do and I've been playing fighting games for over twenty years.  I just keep my combos simple.
The input leniancy.  This is the game's worst offender.  You will get misinputs for days on account of how the game "guesses" when you do any complex motion.  It even lead to a glitch (or "feature") called priority linking, or plinking, in which you press two buttons of the same type.  Say you want a medium kick to come out at the speed of a light kick.  What you do is press both buttons and the game will always give you the attack of the stronger button, but it gives it the priority of the lesser button pressed.  This makes combos easier, but this input leniancy applies to every button pressed.  When the game handles directional inputs...honestly, I don't know.  I haven't really figured out how it handles those at all.  There's been too many times I just don't know how I got the input I got.
And before any of you scrubs who never played a Street Fighter game before come running to defend it saying "You just can't do these moves/combos 'cuz you suck," remember.  I've been playing fighting games for over 20 years.  I've put way more practice into Street Fighter as a franchise than any of you.  That being said, however, I'll list some pros, now that I've got all the cons out of the way.
[The Pros]
It's got a great cast of characters from all the Street Fighter games and some new ones.
It looks great.
The PC version has easily the best netcode.  You'll still get some lag (and laggers), but netcode doesn't fix people's bad connections, it just makes the game flow a little better.  And it does flow well.  When it wants to.
Being the most popular fighting game currently on the market, you'll never have trouble finding people to fight.  Online is always crowded, no matter which platform you play it on.  It saddens me that I can't blame the netcode for some of the BS that happens in this game.
Ranked mode's scoring and ranking is based off the same as professional chess tournaments.  You get points when you beat somebody, lose 'em when you lose and those points determine your rank.  PP (Player Points) applies to your rank as a player and BP (Battle Points) refers to your rank with your current character.
[Closing]
Play 3rd Strike on home consoles or wait for Street Fighter V.  If you haven't played this game yet, you're not missing anything.

Amazing game. Really interesting concepts that slowly develop into an incredible sci-fi story (and the DLC epilogue is amazing as well). Each level is a different scenario with different mechanics, all focused around making sacrifices to survive a morally horrifying situation, like a hostage situation, prolonged torture, starving to death, etc. The game is turn based, with time only moving forward as you make decisions.
Seems like a lot of negative reviews say stuff that isn't really true about the game, or at least they aren't fully explaining the mechanics they dislike. A lot of people seem to be saying they don't like it because the RNG just kills them. The random elements of the game are fully visible to the player. If there's a 30% chance doing something will kill you, it literally says that on the screen. In most of the situations, you can manipulate the random stuff to give yourself a 100% chance of success, but only if you compromise on other elements of the situation. And that's literally what the entire game concept is about; how much do you compromise in order to survive? Who do you kill to save the group? What moral lines will you cross for the greater good? The Russian Roulette scene gets mentioned a lot... you can literally not have to pull the trigger at all in that scene at will.... but then you will have to be really careful with what you do in the next part of that scenario... The whole game is built on that concept. I mean, it's Russian Roulette, the whole point is that you have a random chance of dying. That's why your enemy is forcing you to play....
Also, each scenario is explained in depth. Negative reviews are saying that they feel like they are just randomly trying to find the magic path the developers want you to take. In reality, there are many ways to win each scenario, and each level follows the rules that it gives you at the beginning of the level. You just need to find a way to make it work, and hope you can still sleep at night after making morally dubious choices to survive.
Also a lot of people are moaning about a certain element of the storytelling. I don't want to give too much away, but those people did not finish the game yet. If you notice what seem like continuity errors in the story... good, you're paying attention. Keep paying attention, because the game ends up telling a really crazy story.
One more thing... many haters say you have to play each scenario over and over and over and they hate that... I'm sure that's true for some people, but I just want to throw in there that I beat many levels in one try, and several others in 2 or 3 tries. Only 1 or 2 levels took me 4+ tries.
Music, graphics, and art design are all awesome too, which really pushes the game from great to top tier.
My only complaint is there is a poster of a pornagraphy magazine cover in one of the backgrounds. I really hate that kind of stuff in games. Otherwise, I think I would give this game a perfect score.

Isometric RPGs are one of my most beloved genres so I had high hopes for something original going in to PoE, having played through games like NWN2 and Shadows of Amn multiple times. I finished the game and enjoyed aspects of PoE, but when asking myself if I would ever play it again or remember much of anything about the story, my answer is "No." For a RPG that is unforgivable, so ultimately it gets a thumbs down.
I have to disagree with the top positive comment for this game: It absolutely suffers from lack of licensing. The story and world are probably the weakest aspects of the game. I don't want to make this review a Shadows of Amn vs. Pillars of Eternity comparison, but it's difficult not to draw parallels because they have such obvious analogs: enemies, lore, factions, quests, major parts of the story: Watcher's Keep vs. Caed Nua, Faction quests: Bodhi / Shadows Thieves vs. House Doemenel / Knights of the Crucible / The Dozens, Plight of the protagonist: Bhaalspawn vs. Watcher, etc...
Positives:
Graphical improvements and ability to zoom in / out
Voice acting is top notch
NPCs are well developed
Weapon enchanting and crafting mechanics are handled well
The story's treatment of souls, Hollowborn, and animancers is the most interesting and original part of the story in my opinion
UI improvements:
-Inventory system is much improved
-Being able to compare multiple items side-by-side
-Command queing in combat makes perfect sense for this genre
Negatives:
Lore is shallow compared to its contemporaries
"Reach out for Soul" interactions are completely pointless. I got to about Gilded Vale until I stopped reading them altogether. Someone spent hours upon hours writing these for whatever reason rather than making the core story and game more interesting.
Quests lack originality and are tedious. For example, most of them in Defiance Bay and Twin Elms are a matter of getting the quest, going to another area and killing someone / making some moral decision, returning to original district to complete.
Pathing is terrible, even moreso because the battles use a disengage mechanic
Battles rely much more heavily on buffs / debuffs and out-casting your enemies. Fights are usually complete curb-stomps one way or another. If you die, you just reload, then cast the necessary invulnerability (domination, stun, confusion, etc...) for that enemy type and it's a cakewalk
There's just a lack of interesting stuff to break the monotony of battles. Examples from Shadows of Amn: Machine of Lum the Mad, Spellhold puzzles, class-specific quests, Planar Sphere quest....basically it just needs more interesting stuff to break the monotony of battles and text.
Ending felt rushed, with little connection to the main character or the antagonist. After finishing the last battle, I said out loud, "Oh, I guess it's over then." and immediately uninstalled the game.
Enemies are almost 1:1 retread of Baldur's Gate series, except with notable exceptions of more interesting ones like Githyanki, Drow, Beholders, etc...
-Kobold = Xaurip
-Nymph = Pwgra
-Vampire = Fampyr
-Mind Flayer = Vithrack
-Ghoul = Gul
-Wyvern = Drake
-Sword Spider = Spear Spider
etc...
TL/DR: Good enough for a single playthrough with improved UI & mechanics over its contemporaries, but ultimately falling short in the areas that matter most: story / world, quests, and lack of originality.

Marvel: Ultimate Alliance 2 streamlines the successful design of its predecessor by locking characters to a single moveset, reducing the number of costumes per character (which now have no bearing on the character's stats), and allowing ability points to be redistributed at any moment. Surprisingly, all of these limitations create a better experience. The Ultimate Alliance formula was built for couch co-op and less complexity makes it easier for players to join in or swap out.
Working against all of that, however, is the way storytelling was streamlined. The first Ultimate Alliance flung our heroes from one corner of the Marvel universe to the next with only the frailest of threads to tie them together. The single united tale this sequel strives to tells - an important one from the comics no less -  is more engaging, but players that join a game in progress will have a harder time finding their bearings.
The wheres and whys of brawling through the requisite sea of mooks now have a greater context and the characters have more to say than another thinly veiled recitation of their backstory. On top of that, the story and maps available are affected by your decisions - well, decision anyway - as you're given the opportunity to chose which side of the superhuman community you'd like to support. This choice also limits which characters are available (at least during the first go-round). Though the game is very clear about the three that are locked to each side, this still means that a player's favorite character might be out of circulation for most of the game, further hindering flexibility.
Despite its own set of glitches - bosses failing to show up to a fight, enemies shooting from beyond the invisible barriers of the map, etc. - nothing that I experienced was painful enough to cause me to put down the game (ample autosaves helped with that). There's enough replayability here for more than the two playthroughs it takes to see every map, so even those in-and-out co-op players will have plenty of chances to piece together the whole story. It's not a straight line of improvement or decline between Ultimate Alliance 1 and 2, more like two different takes on the same formula and you're in for a good time either way.

I will be the first to admit that Starbound spent far, FAR too long in Early Access Hell. Literally multiple years.
But now that it's a complete game and has been "released," it is truly immense. It actually does have all the things open world developers foolishly promise to include in their game, and Starbound did pay for that but now that it's here... oh gosh.
The worlds are ridiculously diverse and the dungeons and biomes and secrets and loot will continue to surprise you and feel new and mysterious for hours and hours and hours. (Maybe not the weapon chests but other than that...) The farming and cooking library is immense, if you're into that sort of thing. The crafting and resource chains are sprawling and rich. The combat is... actually pretty good? It's not Terraria but it's close. There are enough weapons and strategies to feel like you can specialize and choose your niche. There is a "storyline," but it's mostly just a vehicle to encourage you to explore and you'll come back to it every now and then.
And when you're done with that construction and creative play is immensely rewarding. The game itself is more gorgeous than any other block crafter and the assortment of materials is more diverse, and that makes creative mode more robust and gratifying than in minecraft, terraria, DQB, or anything else you want to compare it to.
AAAAAND the workshop has a huge, thriving community with mods that will absolutely improve your experience 1,000% whether you want a survivalist grind or a hundred new block types or overhaul the combat or you're a pervert and you want to be a catgirl in a serafuku or something. It's okay. I'm not judging you.
Just... imagine the game that No Man's Sky SAID it was going to be.
That's Starbound.

Yes, there is enjoyment to be had in this game. The sheer scope of the universe you can explore, build, or destroy is a thing to behold. It certainly helps that future updates will likely iron smaller kinks in the gameplay and a few glitches I've noticed, especially in multiplayer.
No, it's not nearly as good as Terraria. The infamous No Man's Sky offered a massive world with no real planetary or enemy variation, threats, characters, or much of anything to add depth to its ambitious breadth-the procedurally generated worlds, creatures, and standardized resources made exploring your massive world an uninteresting chore. On the other hand, Terraria's game world is far more compact (even the largest worlds you can generate couldn't be more than a few miles in width or depth) yet the ever-changing landscape, small or large pockets of endlessly interesting biomes, loot that feels meaningful, truly challenging bossfights that reward your exploration and risky mining expeditions; all cram unfathomable amounts of real depth to the small but beautiful Terraria world (the excellent score and powerful building and wiring tools certainly don't hurt the experience).
My problems with Starbound ultimately come down to it being somewhere between the two. Although there are challenges, beautiful environments, some solid combat and an interesting cooking/farming system; the nature of the planets and your ship make it feel a bit like no man's sky. All the planets and all the procedurally generated monsters/weapons begin to blur together, so exploring these planets you've essentially seen one hundred times becomes boring startlingly quickly (you'll find yourself upgrading your EPP rapidly so you can try to find something new), and finding a powerful randomized weapon feels meaningless as they're all statistically identical based on the planet's "tier", save one of a few special attacks and elemental damage boosts. Armor upgrades are pretty mucb completely linear "add more damage/energy/defense" boosts, and reskinning the same armor across all supposedly varied races (which, by the way, each play and feel exactly the same).
The main questline is also almost completely bland. In Terraria there are no "quests" other than small fishing tasks; if you feel you're up to fighting a boss you're welcome to try, and certain bosses will unlock new areas or change the world to make it more difficult, its hostile inhabitants more powerful. What's important is that all boss fights, invading armies, any enemy you fight from the smallest slime to 'Skeletron Prime' happens in the same world: you can get right into the action at any time and literally build defenses: fortresses, camps, arenas, bridges; then use them to your advantage against more powerful enemies. In Starbound the boss fights that progress the story feel so disjointed: they happen in a little world you have no power to alter anything, you wander around an enemy- and ocassionally trap-filled maze until you find the boss, get locked in a small room with it, then slog through its telegraphed attacks until you die because your armor is bad or kill it because your armor is good. You have no effect on the pocket world the boss is in, and defeating said boss has no apparent effect on the world around you, so completing the main story feels like a useless chore that isn't really worth bothering with until you (inevitably) get bored of exploring "basically the same jungle planet #46".
On a similar note, your ship feels entirely like a pocket world rather than an actual space ship; you can't move it around except linearly from one planet's orbit to another. The tiresome wait of having to beam up and down from your planet to your ship as the map loads certainly doesn't make it any better that the ship seems so disjointed from the planets you visit. Being able to actually control your ship, i.e. the ability to fly freely around a galaxy amidst planets and asteroids as well as engage in combat or trade with other ships would make this mesh much more nicely, as would being able to physically land one's ship on a planet (it seems they're doing something akin to this in the next patch, I can't wait).
The tech is interesting, however none of them even come close to the interesting variation and combinations of the tens of accessories one can purchase, craft, or murder for in Terraria (although the sphere tech specifically does add something fresh and interesting). The wiring system is well streamlined, and I did enjoy playing with it much more than I did spending all my money to laboriously stretch a wire across my Terraria world. Grappling hooks are also something done very well, instead of a mere "pull you closer to destination" they do have proper rope physics, so with one in each hand you can legitimately spider-man your way around tall buildings, planet canyons, and asteroid fields if you're dexterous enough.
On that note, the two-handed toolbar is also very enjoyable to use: in each of six slots you can equip one or two one-handed items or one two-handed item, then use left and right mouse to operate the object for that hand or, in the case of two-handed weapons, blocks or tools, choose between normal and special attacks or having an effect on the fore- or background tiles. Likewise all building in this game, especially the enormous variation of decorations, blocks, and etc, will likely amaze you so much that you'll travel across the galaxy to find that one beautiful medieval painting in a Medieval Robot Fortress you want to deck out your cruiser with (at least until you get a pixel printer and this all becomes null and void).
As you may be able to tell, my favorite parts of this game are smaller gameplay features that are fun to mess with or bring something new to this "block-based open world crafting sandbox" genre. This brings me to my final conclusion, perhaps a disappointing one: what new things Starbound brings to the table are relatively small "bells and whistles", the "meat" of the more hypothetically engaging aspects of the gameplay that one might expect to spend hours upon hours on in their favorite game range from slightly above average to very underwhelming. Terraria has long been referred to as "2D Minecraft" but it is actually a completely different game, Minecraft has always been about building and some survival in a massive, beautiful, yet hardly varied 3D world, yet Terraria brought something entirely new to the table with a focus on exploration and fast-paced, intuitive, large-scale boss battles. Starbound seems to have taken a step back in this regard; its ambitious space exploration may seem exciting at first, but in the end you find yourself closer to a massively wide yet pathetically shallow puddle, like No Man's Sky, rather than the apparently small but incredibly deep and entertaining ocean of content that is Terraria. Compare the 50 hours I've spent in Starbound, as compared to the 550+ hours I've spent in Terraria, for proof enough of that.
tldr: Starbound isn't perfect but also isn't irredemably flawed. 6/10, buy Terraria instead (it is cheaper), but if you've already wrung that dry (somehow) you might want to give it a try
