I wanted to like this game, I really did, some factors for why are:  A.  This gets rave reviews from most places  B.  A lot of my friends play it  C.  I actually went out and purchased the thing  D.  I've played games that are similar in gameplay and aesthetic to it.  So, with all that in mind, I wanted to find out what the big hullabaloo was, and all I can say is, sadly enough, this game registered as the opposite of fun for me.
Minus mods. taking this game as it is, its character creation is laughably limited; and you're forced between these species with set stories to them.  With a game as open, free and sandbox-y as I've heard this was, I was kinda expecting to be able to create my own story, not be forced into one.
A game being Intuitive is good... except this game is about as unintuitive as I can think, playing the introductory mission feels like your character is walking through goo with how sluggish they pace.  The environments are the typical sci-fi fare, with nothing standing out, and its not all that interesting to look at, same with the characters you can talk to, whom aren't at all memorable and serve as background dressing more than anything.  For something that's meant to excite me for the possibilities of all the adventures I could have with the game, this was a huge let-down, in terms of first impressions, this game is scoring a 0.
Onto the actual gameplay, well, I might explain this by the first mission, where you beam down onto a planet cause your spaceship sucks (or something to that effect).  This is where the player first learns how empty the experience all is, little, to do, I believe you're meant to find something for the ship, but the place is so huge, that task proves kinda fruitless amid the temptation of collecting and exploring.  Normally I love huge open spaces in games, being able to explore every little nook and cranny, but here, everything is just so similar, and repetitive.  And this might have something to do with the game's lack of intuitive-ness, but they seem to have forgotten to issue the hero a weapon, sure, they can mine, but I couldn't for the life of me use my futuristic pickaxe to wound enemies.  And this did get to be an issue where you would lose something (even if you choose the gameplay option where death is doesn't mean anything, it still says "lost 5 per cent pixels", very disheartening) every time you die.  And I get it, if you're going to have deaths in a game, there needs to be consequences that come with it, so as no to make the inclusion of dying meaningless.  However, it gets pretty darn silly when you die, mulitple times, to a single bat or something, not because it's a huge enemy, but just because it follows you around the screen forever or you get trapped.  It's a pathetic way to die, and equally reflective on the quality of game I'm playing.
There really feels as though there is nothing to this game, it's an empty experience, which I suppose does reference the emptiness of space... though nevertheless doesn't cease from it feeling any less empty.

Anybody remember Master of Magic? Warlock isn't an entirely faithful remake but as the subtitle suggests it definitely takes a lot of inspiration from it, marrying Civ-style empire building with fantasy concepts and most importantly magic, right down to spells that can change terrain types, summon powerful units or place permanent enhancements on units.
The game is well-balanced and allows for enough diversity in approach to offer good replay value. It's solidly constructed but maybe a bit too shallow for diehard strategy fans. The GUI can be a bit iffy at times, getting you stuck on screens without discernible exit, but hitting ESC usually solves that problem. Considering the price tag that's not even an issue however.
Beyond the magical elements it squarely falls on the Civ side of strategy games, omitting detailed battles for simple unit vs. unit square-offs on the world map. Anyone who enjoys any kind of Civ game and is looking for something less complex they can finish inside of a few hours should be delighted to have this game. Anyone who likes fantasy themes and is looking for something with a bit of strategical meat to it (where games such as Heroes VI or King's Bounty are mostly governed by tactical rather than strategical choices) should be equally happy.
And lasty there's the humor. The game doesn't take itself or its setting all too seriously which helps keep the experience light. I still chuckle every time an archer hero yells out 'SPROING' when attacking an enemy.

Dark Souls is easily one of the best games I’ve ever played. Although advertised as a game for “masochists only”, I believe anyone can enjoy this game once they gain a good understanding of how the game works.

It doesn’t hold your hand, it doesn’t give you many breaks, and it tries to punish you in every way possible. But pushing through the difficulty is well worth it, trust me. Underneath all the pain is a great and engaging game, that relies on good awareness, and patience above all else.
The fantasy setting is one of a kind, rich with history and characters that made me feel part of the world. From very early on, I wanted to discover everything and travel everywhere. I always had choices of where I went, and what I wanted to do. Whether it be farming for weapons/souls/crafting materials, or continuing with the normal progression.
The multiplayer of Dark Souls is perhaps one of the most interesting parts of the game. Relying on temporarily working with or against other players for short periods of time. Your single player adventure could be interrupted by an invading player, or aided by a friendly player at almost any point. It makes things particularly exciting as you never know what to expect.
With comparison to the sequel games in the Dark Souls series, this first game is much less user friendly in terms of fast travelling, inventory management, and general multiplayer features, but it’s still a solid foundation from which the next games were able to grow from.
Overall there isn’t much I can complain about Dark Souls. It’s a game I will always come back to because it’s just that good. Don’t be put off by the difficulty because once you know how to overcome it, I promise you’ll fall in love with this game.

It's quite obvious most negative reviews are from people who got stuck on the first mission -- which, I will admit, is slightly less forgiving than Chapter 2.. but certainly not anything that should have people rage-quitting and leaving poor reviews on what is an amazing product that obviously had time and real care poured into it's creation.
It's unique (especially in the modern era of gaming where something challening and interesting is viewed as 'weird' and 'too difficult'), intriguing, and presents you with a lot of ethical choices that most other games wouldn't have the courage or storytelling ability to even go near. The graphics are throwback beauty, and the music is well-crafted and suits each scene, as dark and twisted as the game can get... the music is right there the entire time, to set up the appropriate mood of tension and despair.
If you are interested in games that make you think, that challenge you as a gamer, or are just plain bored with the average 'fetch quest simulators' that pass as RPGs and 'enemy wave' FPS games and yearn for a return to the days of Maniac Mansion or I Have No Mouth (though this isn't quite a straightforward point-and-click adventure game -- keep that in mind when going in, this game is hard to draw parallels to).. well, give it a shot on-sale, at least. I picked it up as part of Humble Bundle's current deal (paid $7.00 to get the 2nd tier) and this is by far the best game included in a solid bundle.
Only issue is, it's a bit fast paced... Just under 2 hours in and I'm already finshed Chapter 2 and starting 3. Then again, at sale price it's not an issue - but it's one of those indie games that some people might regret buying at full price. Me, I appreciate a developer who takes chances, and Devolver Digital is one of the most solid publishers out there today.
Editting this review as I just now completed both the main story, as well as the amazingly well-done (far more simplistic in gameplay and lacking the challenge that some of the main game's missions had - but as a storytelling device it brings up all sorts of interesting concepts that will have the philosophical types out there appreciating the thought exercises and the ideas that the DLC, as well as the game at whole, presents) DLC mission, and I must say it is well worth the price I paid (admittedly far less than retail, given I got it in a bundle) and anyone who appreciates a unique game that really does try to be different and manages to, if you take the time to actually read and contemplate the dialogue being played out, actually introduce some very intriguing ideas about existence and reality... well, anyone who enjoys a game that is more than just a series of scenes strung together to justify a set of gameplay mechanics ought to enjoy this.
Games like this are the reason I pay a lot of attention to games on Steam that get 70-79% ratings and the like. A lot of them are just average flak in an ocean of games, but a lot of them are misunderstood gems that sail way above the average gamer's head. This is the latter.

Isometric RPGs are one of my most beloved genres so I had high hopes for something original going in to PoE, having played through games like NWN2 and Shadows of Amn multiple times. I finished the game and enjoyed aspects of PoE, but when asking myself if I would ever play it again or remember much of anything about the story, my answer is "No." For a RPG that is unforgivable, so ultimately it gets a thumbs down.
I have to disagree with the top positive comment for this game: It absolutely suffers from lack of licensing. The story and world are probably the weakest aspects of the game. I don't want to make this review a Shadows of Amn vs. Pillars of Eternity comparison, but it's difficult not to draw parallels because they have such obvious analogs: enemies, lore, factions, quests, major parts of the story: Watcher's Keep vs. Caed Nua, Faction quests: Bodhi / Shadows Thieves vs. House Doemenel / Knights of the Crucible / The Dozens, Plight of the protagonist: Bhaalspawn vs. Watcher, etc...
Positives:
Graphical improvements and ability to zoom in / out
Voice acting is top notch
NPCs are well developed
Weapon enchanting and crafting mechanics are handled well
The story's treatment of souls, Hollowborn, and animancers is the most interesting and original part of the story in my opinion
UI improvements:
-Inventory system is much improved
-Being able to compare multiple items side-by-side
-Command queing in combat makes perfect sense for this genre
Negatives:
Lore is shallow compared to its contemporaries
"Reach out for Soul" interactions are completely pointless. I got to about Gilded Vale until I stopped reading them altogether. Someone spent hours upon hours writing these for whatever reason rather than making the core story and game more interesting.
Quests lack originality and are tedious. For example, most of them in Defiance Bay and Twin Elms are a matter of getting the quest, going to another area and killing someone / making some moral decision, returning to original district to complete.
Pathing is terrible, even moreso because the battles use a disengage mechanic
Battles rely much more heavily on buffs / debuffs and out-casting your enemies. Fights are usually complete curb-stomps one way or another. If you die, you just reload, then cast the necessary invulnerability (domination, stun, confusion, etc...) for that enemy type and it's a cakewalk
There's just a lack of interesting stuff to break the monotony of battles. Examples from Shadows of Amn: Machine of Lum the Mad, Spellhold puzzles, class-specific quests, Planar Sphere quest....basically it just needs more interesting stuff to break the monotony of battles and text.
Ending felt rushed, with little connection to the main character or the antagonist. After finishing the last battle, I said out loud, "Oh, I guess it's over then." and immediately uninstalled the game.
Enemies are almost 1:1 retread of Baldur's Gate series, except with notable exceptions of more interesting ones like Githyanki, Drow, Beholders, etc...
-Kobold = Xaurip
-Nymph = Pwgra
-Vampire = Fampyr
-Mind Flayer = Vithrack
-Ghoul = Gul
-Wyvern = Drake
-Sword Spider = Spear Spider
etc...
TL/DR: Good enough for a single playthrough with improved UI & mechanics over its contemporaries, but ultimately falling short in the areas that matter most: story / world, quests, and lack of originality.

There is also a lot of freedom to play how you want, and make your own version of the story as you go along. The one thing that really stopped me from playing this game more, was that the load times for each map get increasingly longer as you keep playing, until it feels like you are spending more time watching load screens than actually playing the game. I'm still buying the sequel, but it did deter me from replaying the original, and stopped me from doing some sidequests that required running back and forth between a lot of areas.

It may not have as strong a narrative as the games it emulates, but it still provides an overall experiance that sizes up to them. I'd also note that this a great starting point for anyone looking to get into cRPGs.

The definitive fighting game. Now with decent netcode!

OH HELL YES I RECOMMEND THIS!
I've always been a sucker for Street Fighter games since Street Fighter 2 on super nintendo and it's my all-time absolute favourite game franchise alongside Serious Sam and Doom so keep that in mind while reading, I'll strive to be as objective as possible but it can include some bias.
I wasn't such a fan of the first SF4 which I had the occasion to play long time ago and was basically keeping going on Street Fighter 3 third strike (which is an awesome fighting game you gotta try!). But oh boy how things got better with this one!
The learning curve is top notch provided you have the patience to spend some hours on challenges and training room to find out some new tricks and combos. So far, the whole things looks extremely well-balanced and could never complain about a character being too cheap or overpowered (unlike that infamous vanilla-Seth who made me wonder if I was playing Street Fighter or some SNK stuff). The whole gameplay can look pretty SF2esque at first glance but in fact it includes many subtleties I'm discovering hour after hour with pleasure. It's one of those "easy to handle, hard to master" games and even though I'm still basically losing online , the progress I did is extremely gratifying.
Online playing so far went good, I sure can't complain about the lag when defeated wich is a good thing. They included a replay mode which can record your matches if you wish and it's extremely useful to see where you sucked (no, don't tell me "it's boring to watch" DO IT. You can't imagine all the little flaws you can realize when the pressure went down.)
Don't listen to guys on forums who speak about cheaters. I didn't spot any cheater here, just experienced players and it's pretty exciting to have such a challenging crowd!
Training mode is also one of the best if not the best I've seen so far with a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ of useful options.
For solo players, IA is ok, but don't ever think that because you just started to master hardest mode you became the Street Fighter God of Battle. Because it's not enough to stand a serious chance online believe me. It will be challenging enough for not so experienced players and allow you to train a bit against characters you don't know (DO IT.) but that's pretty much it.
One last thing : don't listen to reviews saying online gaming is broken , because this issue has been fixed!
So well, this fighting game delivers for casual players as well as for experts you can't go wrong with this one, just grab it!

After reviewing this game further, I've opted to alter my review and give it a 'positive' review. More of a 'thumbs sideways' review. Here's why:
I like the game. I continue to play it from time to time. As far as games in the survival genre go, it seems to be one of the best. Gameplay is good, as are the premise, layout, and overall mechanics.
Does it have some issues to resolve?  Oh, yes.. a few in my opinion. It is EARLY ACCESS after all. Ranging from annoying to serious. Don't let the overall number of hours played fool you (as it apparently does some of the devs who have seen it and commented with confusion or insulted feelings) - I've had to restart the game from the beginning OR from a manual save many, many, MANY times (at least 15 times). Steam does not take this into account when calculating the total hours played, of course. The hours just keep adding up.
Since update 0.12, I've noticed these issues:
The serious issue:  The rafts disappear. My research has shown me that this happens if the raft is left in the open ocean on occasion. If you have saved your game without knowing this, you cannot get it back and you have a few choices:
1. Start over.
2. Walk, run, or swim everywhere you go. (Sharks/poisonous fish can make this impractical.)
3. Build another raft. (I happen to like mine and it would be a pain to re-create it).
4. Re-start the game from a previous 'manual' save - if you thought ahead to create one, (Also a pain,, and you lose any accumlated gameplay progress since that save was created.)
5. Give up and stop playing.
Early on, I opted for the first option. Then later, opted for the third option. It gets really annoying to save the game, log off, log back on, see if my raft is still here, log back off, create manual save, etc,,,etc,,,etc,,, just to guard against this from happening again.
Moderate-to-serious issue:  You cannot use items from inventory while raft is in motion. This makes no sense to me at all since your 'castaway' character has two hands - steering with one obviously leaves the other free to use items - like a compass. Navigating can be a bit of an unnecessary challenge because of this -  if you cannot see landmarks in the distance. Stop raft, use compass, start raft, travel a bit, stop raft, use compass, start raft, etc... uggghhh.
Annoying issue:  The item drop mechanics have changed since the 0.12 update, and confirmed by other players. The drop item motion now seems to be more of a 'throw-it-to-the-ground' motion. This is not only a bit messy when collecting and stashing items in an organized fashion, but more seriously, it can cause collected/created fresh water buckets to tip quite easily now, wasting time and resources to do it again.
There are other issues, of course.. most are minor bugs/glitches. It is afterall Early Access.
Despite the various issues/glitches/annoyances, it is a fun game to play if you like the survival-type games. I would recommend it - with hesitation. The future co-op option may be interesting. Let's see what the next update brings.

Straight off the bat, I totes agree with the gameplay and its merits. Its availability for added roleplay elements and layers of modding have done wonders and can salve the deeper needs of the more experience players/player group. However, in this one fateful day, where I look in my library and wonder to install it again...

For newcomers, the most enjoyable parts will come when you decide what areas you want to explore, what building you like to build, and finding ways to collect all the niceities for your gaming pleasure. Throw in a like-minded group or server and that is the cream in your coffee of this game. And for the experienced player, thatthe above is Starbound at its core. Combining the luck-and-loot mood of digging and fighting past the night and day. Foraging installations like giant chest with options to build or continue on your nomadic way for personal adventure.
But..
Its where the developers felt the need to make Starbound a "game" - as in some playable arc that the player has to filter their wishes through and wait til the "all important" end to persist. That slaps the player twice: First by not putting them first in the role of the "game" ; and more painfully putting there curiosity and regrettably their endurance in hindsight - all for a one-off story that has as much merit as the one chest of loot in countless numbers.
What was a player suppose to hold off the beauty of the base of the true
for? That question is never answered or rewared deeply and because of that, the "game" has no base. Starbound is player-driven to the core, yet its 1.0 respects that little. Painfully when you notice the grand schemes and options that play out in such a setting. I quote what I said to another gamer: SB doesn't allow you to re-inject experiences in a supportive manner because of its present changes and break the flow to learn what gameplay truly has to offer.
So without breaking off, this is a 2D building and exploration game who want to know its bits and pieces of parts, and then enjoy making that house, running that dungeon, snapping abilities on to your digital alter-ego, and piling up items and experiences like no tomorrow. Hop on your fave server, throw in all your favorite songs, swords, and serene items, and have fun running into the things that give your world flavor.
Chucklefish will keep adding features and more chances to script this fine base to a joy. But remember what makes the gameplay great, 1.0 content is just a playable manual with clues for the fun you can have.

Night in the Woods is a 2017 video game, but to call it one is to use the definition generously. It’s more of an interactive comic book, set in a small town you’re encouraged to explore freely, punctuated by Wario-Ware styled segments. It aims to draw you in with the strength of its narrative and the likeability of its characters. You play as Mae Borowski, a dropout returning to her hometown of Possum Springs after a disastrous term at college. Despite her continuing to assert that this is the best place for her, it isn’t. As the game continually points out, Possum Springs is dying. The factories have all moved out, along with the coal companies that the community was built around, and more disturbingly as the game’s tag line suggests “There is something in the woods.”
When the game says “There’s something in the woods,” what it really is getting at is that there is something in Mae Borowski’s head. This game’s exploration of mental illness, along with the profound disenfranchisement a lot of millennials are facing, is where it really stands out. The game’s plot line surrounding murder, ghosts, and a great, dark, all-devouring hole at the center of the universe are all metaphors for the uncertainty Mae is facing. I’ve read a lot of pieces that have attempted to tackle similar themes, in fact almost every writer will at some point attempt to write a coming home from college story (even Harper Lee wrote one), but Night in the Woods is the first I’ve seen to actually amount to anything extraordinary.
The art and the music are also worth noting. Your milage may vary with the Wario-Ware portions and the sparse amount of platforming, but the art and music really pull through to add a lot of charm to the town of Possums Springs, which makes its slow death all the more tragic. It really goes out of its way to tell a lot of its back story with the environmental design, and does a great job of capturing the lost glory of the town. The character designs stand out as well, and you can tell a lot about the central cast just by looking at them.
All in all, Night in the Woods is a fantastic game, and I’d recommend it to any of my Knox friends, especially those of who have faced some of the disenfranchisement Mae herself is facing. But overall the experience is more like reading a good book than playing through a video game, so if you pick it up expecting something in the vein of Hyper Light Drifter or Fez, you’re going to be disappointed. Like all games that I feel are worth mentioning, it excels at creating an experience, and Night in the Woods is one worth hanging onto.

I would like to say that I respect what the game creators were trying to do here, but I just can't... becasue I don't.  This is merely a poorly done retread.
Let's be honest:  Baldur's Gate 2 set the bar for CRPG's of this style.  Let's talk about what made Baldur's Gate 2 greatt and compare it.
1.  Baldur's Gate 1-3 had a great story.  I'm not going to write a huge paragraph explaining why, but this game does not.  Anyone who has played both (and I expect that's quite a few people considering this is kind of a genre niche gmae) and is HONEST with themseles and others will have to agree it doesn't measure up.
2.  Baldur's Gate 2-3 really came alive due to the great voice acting.  I'm sorry, I know that costs some dough to do, but not as much as you think if you use less well known voice actors.  The age of reading large boxes of conversation and flavor text in boxes is over.  Let's be honest, it's OVER.
3.  The most important thing and the thing that wouldn't be as costly as voice actors is that BG 2 had fully fleshed out NPC's who came alive due to having their own agenda's, pasts, problems, likes, dislikes, and the amazing amout of interactivity that was created from this with your main character AND all the other NPC's.  Heck I had to NPC'S in BG2 bicker for a long time and then throw down and try to kill each other because they were just too different in alignment/ethics!
Bottom line this game falls FAR short of a similar game in the genre that is 10-15 years old.  That's just inexcusable.  I could overlook a lot of this if the game had been say... $19.99 or so, but no, it's the same price as actual top shelf games being put out today, and that is just insulting.  The gameplay is a retread, the story is dull... I'm about 70% through and I just can't muster the will to finish it,  This comeing from a guy who has finished some crappy games and books, just for the sake of completion.
I give this game about 5/10, but that's a crime considering the asking price vs. what you get.

Let's just start off this review by saying that this game is an absolute masterpiece in both it's gameplay and story. I never found any spot in the game where I thought it was boring (or at least no spot that was memorable for being boring). With that said, there are still a few things this game lacks. This will be a spoilers free review.
Pros:
-Story is somewhat intestering and has a villian that poses a unique threat to the world.
-The combat feels refreshing and does justice to it's father RPGs like BG and IWD (only in that the combat has the same tactical aspect as these two games, not the spell system).
-The ability to make your own party from scratch or to use companions is nice.
-The enchanting/crafting system is superb.
-The conversation action that someone can take based off of stats/skill makes the game feel immersive.
-Does an excellent job on taking a new perspective on good vs evil.
Cons
-Lore is thrown at you really fast, but is easy to piece together by the time you are in a second play through.
-Lots of reading from characters who have voice actors, would be nice to have all plot essential characters to always have voice acting. (this doesn't have a really large impact on the experience).
-Some of the companions feel somewhat shallow (not making complex relationships with any of your companions like in Baldur's Gate II)
-Too many NPCs that are made from short-stories from kick-starters. This isn't really a huge deal as some of them hold gear that you can kill them for.
Overall the cons of this game have a minimal effect on the game and I would highly suggest you buy this game if you are a fan of the BG Saga or IWD or are just an RPG fanatic overall.

The review is written the first week of release. This game takes place in the Majesty universe (Ardiana)
A demo is available on steam that gives a good representation if you care to try before you buy.
First thing. Should you buy it? If you are looking at this game because you want to 4X game in a fantasy setting the answer is for $20 or less, YES!
Many people cite Master of Magic as "thee fantasy all others should be measured by." I never played it. My 4X history stared with Civ2, than Age of Wonders Shadow Magic (AoW:SM). AoW:SM was my gem, and I will say Warlock: Master of the Arcane (Warlock) gets close. First there are no separate instanced tactical battles. Fights are pretty much exactly like Civ5. The city building is like Elemental, which means, every building you produce takes up a tile, the space around your city is the limiting factor, every unit/building takes a certain number of turns to produce (there is no varying production). You are limited by area to build (city growth) and for troops your upkeep costs (which can only be balanced by building certain buildings in your cities. That is a unit may cost 3 gold per turn to upkeep, you can build (in one of your limited building squares) a market that will provide you with 3gold. If you produce more troops that you can support you will eventually go broke. In my opinion it works, at least in the early phase of the game. There have been complaints the AI doesn't seem to abide by the same system, and also that players can reach pretty much levels of infinite resources later in the game.
In addition to making units, when they level up you can pick a bonus much like in Civ4/5. Also units can be enchanted (by casting spells onto them at the cost of magic), or be "outfitted" with "equipment" (for a cost of gold). There is no "crafting" or backpack or item inventory. The way it works is once you build a foundry on a map iron resource you will have an option to click on a unit and click on masterwork armor pay 50gold and you're done. It is more a perk than an item. You can't transfer anything, and if the unit dies all your investment is gone. You choice is pretty much spam units, or produce less units but buff them up. Or work somewhere in-between.
There are plenty of special locations on the map. They provide a bonus once you build upon them. For example a silver resource for instance you can build a mine for extra Gold, or a silversmith for the ability to upgrade your troops resistance to melee and ranged damage. I really enjoy the choice of two different buildings most times. In past games it seems you pretty much only get one option of what to build on a resource node. One issue is right now you can not destroy a building, so if you decide you want to change your choice later you can not.
Quests. The games quest system if very similar to AoW:SM. Instead of the spirits of War, Magic, etc, you of the Gods of Ardiana. You get your basic, "Build this", "kill that," "conquer this." Complete quests gives immediate rewards (not completing has a penalty), and in some cases a successful completion will affect your relationship to the corresponding Gods. Favor of a God can unlock extra spells and units, as well as a Victory pathway within the game.
Magic. Magic feels potent. It can keep your troops alive or bring down your enemies. Focusing on Magic research can lead to a Victory pathway.
AI. It does a decent job resisting the player but never really threatens. You can also game the system once you learn the naissances of the AI behavior. For example I let an AI faction that I was at peace with whittle (6 unit army attacking that enemy city for probably 10 turns ) another factions city down to no defense and then just ran in with my rangers and captured it. The AI just slowly walks away, no fuss or complaint.
Overall. Warlock will likely scratch that itch that many gamer have felt since their beloved 4x fantasy game became too outdated. Out of the box it plays much more fluidly and faster than elemental. I've never felt the need to just pound end turn. To me that means the game is fun to play, instead of just parts of the game. For the price of $20 I would buy the game again without second thought. The game is not perfect, there are bugs, but most don't affect gameplay. Also some of the games features to me feel somewhat superficial (diplomacy, getting a quest to build a farm 5 times in a row, having an enemy attack your city every turn retreat->heal->attack again - this doesn't seem effect the output of the city at all) and some promised features that aren't available at all yet (multiplayer). If these features were flushed out just a bit and the bugs taken care of, Warlock could very easily be a satisfying game even at $40. As it is though I think the game is a very good entertainment value for the price of admission. A demo is available on steam that gives a good representation if you care to try before you buy.

So I'm reviewing this in 2017, after playing Dark Souls 3, this likely colors my perception.
This game is amazing, but not at the level of DS3.  There are too many cheap areas, and the slog to the boss after dying is much more annoying than DS3 (there tends to not be paths w/o enemies for the majority of the boss fights).  Blightown and Sens Fortress stand out as super annoying areas to get through.  The hardest thing for me was to get used to being slower, every action has much more weight (and delay) to it than it did in DS3 (and I played a great hammer there).  Once I switched from trying to roll to dodge attacks to shielding (normally) the game became a lot more fun.  The level design on a macro level here is astounding, but as noted at a micro level it can be super-frustrating.  The inability to warp to any bonfire also makes things more tedious (as does the vendors being all over the map instead of clustered at firelink shrine).
All those complaints being said, this game is definitely a blast, and well worth getting through.  It holds up, and opening the shortcuts to firelink will amaze you.  It took me about 50h to get through all the bosses (and the DLC), but that's after having practice in DS3 (which took slightly longer).

It was interesting to me that this game was so simplistic and yet so very complex.
The writing is superb and the story is filled with an unknown mystery, that in my opinion, only serves to make me feel more immersed into the game. Yes, you will hate this game, but I implore you to finish it and then I can guarantee that you will end up loving it. Has re-playability, great soundtrack, brilliant graphic design, fantastic premise and hard yet fair situations to painstakingly manage. If you like anything that resembles a challenge in your games like Dark Souls or Demon Souls then you'll most likely love this game.  The great thing is that it's currently on special in the Humble Bundle deal going on right now, so you're not risking much to give it a go.
The story is compiled into small cut scenes and chapters in which you will play, not necessarily understand straight of the bat, but will certainly enjoy. The thing that drives the story forward above all else is the characters. Each of them feel unique and real, even some of them that may only turn up for small parts of the game are developed more-so than some characters I have seen in triple A games these days.
Music is godly.
It jumps right into the action and in every scenario it will give you several tasks that you must complete in a certain matter of time. It makes for a fast clicking frantic mess that slowly but surely will turn into precise actions and subtle key choices that can make or break your characters. For those who complain about characters always returning in every chapter, even if they were previously killed, then all I can say is that they didn't understand the story so watch out for that one.
Overall this is a great investment of your time and money, if you can overlook little underlying miss-polishes then you will have a horrific blast with Gods Will Be Watching and I can only hope that they make more

Oh boy, where to even begin on a game like this? It is, in a word, brutal. The game drops you in a situation that seems absolutely hopeless, and you're expected to manage that impossible situation and come out ahead. When you get through one chapter, you'll breathe a sigh of relief, and then remember the next chapter will probably be just as difficult and hopeless. It is.
That's not to say it isn't enjoyable. This definitely is NOT a game for everyone, but I happen to love the art and the weird nihilistic tone of the whole thing. It satisfied my need to micro manage, even though in many cases, this game asks you to do too much on purpose. Here's main goal 1 and main goal 2, but don't forget these other 6 things and keep an eye on the moods and stamina because lets throw even more ways to lose in there. Not to mention the RNG is wonderfully cruel in this game. You can play every choice 100 percent perfect and still lose sometimes! That's life. Good play is not always rewarded. Sometimes you'll lose people. You'll learn hard lessons, you'll replay levels, you'll probably get frustrated.
Some chapters are better than others, bad luck on chapter 5 is going to make a lot of people salty. This game is special. It's not what I thought it would be. It's almost intimidating to open it up and play, like you just know it's going to kick your butt. It's dark and difficult and hopeless. I beat it in less than 7 hours (not including DLC chapter) but if someone asked me how long it took, I would have guessed 20 hours. The time spent in this game is dense time.

This game is difficult.
Sure, you will get a few mission objectives.  And yes, you will kill a few dozen monsters.
Around wave 3 the aliens might get lucky and catch your friend alone and/or unaware.
You'll try to save him of course.  No man left behind.  But it was to late, and deep down you knew it.
By wave 5 the aliens step up the challenge, sending giants after you.  It will break a team mate's leg and they will tell you to leave them behind.  He'll hold them off while you run.  You can hear his death cry as you leave him to die.
Then, they will
By wave 7 the stress is getting to you and the remainder of your team.  The aliens come in swarms now, the pack no longer strong enough.  The turrets are helping, but for how much longer?
Wave 9 arrives.  You are low on ammo, medical supplies are scarce, and the objective is on the other side of the city.
What member of your team goes next?  Is it you?  The heavy support?  The hellfire maybe?  Will someone sacrifice themselves to slow down the horde?  Will the horde even slow down as the few overtake and devour its next victim?
Don't die with the weight of your last mistake on your soul.  Everyone makes mistakes.  And even if you do it perfectly, you are just a single part in a chain of events.  Who is to say that it was you directly that caused your entire team will die.
... Do I recommend this game?  Yes.  Yes I do.  For now.  Early access is a far cry from the end product.
The AI could use some fixes.  The monster ability to track you from anyplace to anyplace is a little annoying.  This means that they always know where you are.  You can't hide or lose them.  And they don't have to search for you to start with.
The loot table could use a little fix too, some more ammo would be useful because they always know where you are.  Medical supplies seem ok for now, but I play with people who can drop supplies.
There are still serveral bugs and connection issues, but it is an awesome game with coop, and you can never survive alone!

This is a review of State of Decay without any DLC installed.
In a world saturated with zombie themed games, few stand out from the rest and offer a fun experience.   State of Decay manages to create a terrific open world filled with plenty of action, crafting, looting, and questing.   The quality and quantity of things to do surprised me, considering this was an XboX arcade budget title.
The game starts in a small tutorial section of the map with a few buildings and campsites to explore and learn the mechanics.  This area is part of the open world and not it's own safe place.  Once you get a few things accomplished you'll happen upon your first group of survivors in a safehouse.   This is when the game takes off and things start getting interesting.
Your first task is to scout the area for potential threats and resources by climbing to a high vantage point and spotting landmarks with your binoculars.  This is very useful when adventuring into new areas, as it will mark points of interest for exploring and gathering resources from various types of buildings.
Resources management and gathering is a huge portion of the game.  You'll constantly be looking for supplies in the early stages of the game, but eventually you'll build a self sustained safe house capable of producing the supplies you'll need.  There are five resources to pillage:  Food, medicine, construction material, ammo, fuel.   The more you gather and return to your safe house, the more it rewards you influence points with your group of survivors.
Influence points are like a form of currency within the group.   Everything you take from the group inventory will cost you influence points,  while scavenging and bringing in supplies will yield positive influence points.   These points can also be used to influence people within the group or allied with your group.  If you want a friendly npc to come with you on a scavenging run it'll cost you influence points.  Want to radio in a special request from an allied group of survivors? - Be sure you have enough influence to spend.  You'll be constantly managing influence until the game ends.
The questing missions are what drive the story forward, but the constant crisis of side missions will keep you busy.   You'll be swamped with various tasks radioed to you constantly from your safe house.   Side missions include searching for specific crafting items,  killing zombie infestations, search and rescue of missing group members,  and hunting special types of zombies.  These special zombies will immediately remind you of Left for Dead, with slightly different names and special attacks.
Overall I was very impressed with the amount of time I got from playing.  It's open world, so others may enjoy it more or less depending on how quickly the feel of repetitive side missions sets in.  The map is fairly large, so exploration fans will have fun scavenging new houses for quite awhile.  And like all RPGs, you'll eventually become so powerful the longer you play that the game loses some of its challenge and fearfulness you battle in the beginning.
You can't beat the price of this surprisingly detailed game.   Well worthy of a play, even if you just plow through story quests and want a open world feel.

Night in the Woods is a 2017 video game, but to call it one is to use the definition generously. It’s more of an interactive comic book, set in a small town you’re encouraged to explore freely, punctuated by Wario-Ware styled segments. It aims to draw you in with the strength of its narrative and the likeability of its characters. You play as Mae Borowski, a dropout returning to her hometown of Possum Springs after a disastrous term at college. Despite her continuing to assert that this is the best place for her, it isn’t. As the game continually points out, Possum Springs is dying. The factories have all moved out, along with the coal companies that the community was built around, and more disturbingly as the game’s tag line suggests “There is something in the woods.”
When the game says “There’s something in the woods,” what it really is getting at is that there is something in Mae Borowski’s head. This game’s exploration of mental illness, along with the profound disenfranchisement a lot of millennials are facing, is where it really stands out. The game’s plot line surrounding murder, ghosts, and a great, dark, all-devouring hole at the center of the universe are all metaphors for the uncertainty Mae is facing. I’ve read a lot of pieces that have attempted to tackle similar themes, in fact almost every writer will at some point attempt to write a coming home from college story (even Harper Lee wrote one), but Night in the Woods is the first I’ve seen to actually amount to anything extraordinary.
The art and the music are also worth noting. Your milage may vary with the Wario-Ware portions and the sparse amount of platforming, but the art and music really pull through to add a lot of charm to the town of Possums Springs, which makes its slow death all the more tragic. It really goes out of its way to tell a lot of its back story with the environmental design, and does a great job of capturing the lost glory of the town. The character designs stand out as well, and you can tell a lot about the central cast just by looking at them.
All in all, Night in the Woods is a fantastic game, and I’d recommend it to any of my Knox friends, especially those of who have faced some of the disenfranchisement Mae herself is facing. But overall the experience is more like reading a good book than playing through a video game, so if you pick it up expecting something in the vein of Hyper Light Drifter or Fez, you’re going to be disappointed. Like all games that I feel are worth mentioning, it excels at creating an experience, and Night in the Woods is one worth hanging onto.

The characters are flat and one note for much of the game, there are fleeting moments of edgy backstories and apparent progression but the writing never goes anywhere with it. The plot itself is meandering and unclear from beginning to end, and this is likely on purpose due to the themes explored, but it is not handled in a way that (at least for me) makes for an affecting or effective story. The dialogue is flat out awful, it made me hate many of the characters I was supposed to identify with because it was apparently written by someboy with a very limited vocabulary (like, like, like, UGH!) and an objective to create memes rather than actual character (let's repeat the word 'crimes' until it they plaster it all over Tumblr fan art). I could go on about the rancid writing but I don't want to waste more time talking about this game than playing it.
I played through to the end of this game in the hope that something would happen to recontextualize the rest of the experience and make the game worth the rave reviews it has been getting, but that didn't happen. The ending didn't work at all for me either, it's like the writer(s?) watched No Country For Old Men and thought 'we need to do that'. You're not the Coen Brothers, stop.

Dead Effect is a zombie horde shooter with strong focus on upgrades to your arsenal / abilities and a (deliberately) cliche sense of humour. It's got a bunch of imperfections, but manages to outweight them with a larger bunch of nice features.
There is no map, you cannot jump, the progression is linear and the story line is not to be taken seriously - but it all doesn't matter; what matters is a nice zombie killing spree with a satisfying, well-designed balance between your firepower and the amount of baddies you are able to despatch using one clip.
The assortment of weaponry at your disposal is concise but diversified - shotguns, bow and arrows and even a minigun. Each requires a different approach and technique. Rifles go well with headshots; shotguns mean close combat. I havent tried the bow, but I am assuming it will add the element of stealth, while the minigun will be the very opposite. There are more weapons too.
My main gripe with this game is that it's really short - I managed to finish it in two sittings.
The thing I liked most about it was how well balanced the combat mechanics was - something a lot of games nowadays, the latest installment of Doom included, have problems with.
To sum up, Dead Effect is a pretty cool little FPS. True, it's monotonous at times, but the fun factor of despatching a group of zombies after another while hoarding in-game money to get upgrades more than makes up for the few snags.

While playing Dead Effect, I was frequently reminded of the original Unreal. Not so much because of its gameplay or how Epic's seminal title helped revolutionize FPS games, no. Rather, it was the lens-flare. Lots and lots of lens-flare, and bloom, and colorful lights. Epic used these tricks to advertise its (for the time) awesome new graphics engine. Dead Effect uses them because... they look cool?
Well, I guess they do, although the effect is a bit over the top sometimes. It's not a bad looking game, considering it origins as a mobile-title, although it does suffer from a severe lack of variety and the monster animations are decidedly unimpressive. Still, the sheer number of bad-guys on screen at the same time (10-20 per room) was a welcome change from most other FPS games, where you are lucky to see five or six monster at a time. It's also hard to fault a game that lets you blow away crowds of zombies (space-zombies, no less!) with a gatling gun. But beyond that there is little positive to say about the game; it's short, linear, lacks any sort of novelty, and - beyond its flashy lighting effects - has rather poor production values. It's a C-list game with passable gunplay and a price of less than a dollar. I wasn't expecting much from the game - and didn't get it - but I can't say I left disappointed.
Recommended, with the understanding that you get what you pay for: this is a cheesy, unpolished game that's nowhere nearly as good as most shooters. But if you can forgive its many gaffes and flaws, it has a certain enjoyability to it.

Let's just start off this review by saying that this game is an absolute masterpiece in both it's gameplay and story. I never found any spot in the game where I thought it was boring (or at least no spot that was memorable for being boring). With that said, there are still a few things this game lacks. This will be a spoilers free review.
Pros:
-Story is somewhat intestering and has a villian that poses a unique threat to the world.
-The combat feels refreshing and does justice to it's father RPGs like BG and IWD (only in that the combat has the same tactical aspect as these two games, not the spell system).
-The ability to make your own party from scratch or to use companions is nice.
-The enchanting/crafting system is superb.
-The conversation action that someone can take based off of stats/skill makes the game feel immersive.
-Does an excellent job on taking a new perspective on good vs evil.
Cons
-Lore is thrown at you really fast, but is easy to piece together by the time you are in a second play through.
-Lots of reading from characters who have voice actors, would be nice to have all plot essential characters to always have voice acting. (this doesn't have a really large impact on the experience).
-Some of the companions feel somewhat shallow (not making complex relationships with any of your companions like in Baldur's Gate II)
-Too many NPCs that are made from short-stories from kick-starters. This isn't really a huge deal as some of them hold gear that you can kill them for.
Overall the cons of this game have a minimal effect on the game and I would highly suggest you buy this game if you are a fan of the BG Saga or IWD or are just an RPG fanatic overall.

Pillars of Eternity  is  a Tacitcal RPG by the company Obsidian Entertainment and tries to remind people of the golden age of roleplaying games while reinventing something on their own.
The game itself is set in the world Enroth and to be more Precise most of the time in a place called Dyrwood. The whole lore around the world is very interestening and doesnt have to hide from giants like Dungeons&Dragons. The whole world is usually explained by people or books you read, sometimes trough ghosts even. I liked the setting because its a pretty dark fantasy world.
The story itself is a confusing mess at first, the problem is that everyone talks to you like you know everything, despite being an outsider. It clears up step by step, background of the country and so on will be explained trough dialogue therefore much talk is necessary to understand the story, the game tough got a good balance between fighting and story time.The story is really good and really tricks with the player in some parts. Because most of it is religious telltale it really makes the player interpretate parts of the story, if its true or not, on their own. Cant complain about the story really.
Quests (except main) are mostly basic stuff (kill this bring that to this person), but there is sometimes interestening lore around it. Definetly improvement worthy, but the game doesnt spam you with useless and boring quests either.
The companion is good. One character for each class. They all got a really good background story, but some are more fleshed out than others, very good work on Obsidians part nonetheless.
The fighting system is in some parts really good in others its horrible. While there are many classes and i found for almost of them always a use, there are some races which give you traits, while some races are in my opinion statistically wise complete crap. Same goes with backstory/job your character had. They give you different bonuses, but there are so fiew jobs/backstory to pick from and most of the time even less if you look at the abillity bonuses they give you. Interestening idea, really could have been better.
The equipments are rather strange. Basically there are no real better crafted items than others, there are just enchanted once and some which arent. You could in theory take the first armor you get and enchant it into something godkilling. Kinda strange if you ask me, but a interestening idea. Only annoying is that you need ingredients to enchant items, but its hard to find some of them even for some basic enchantments. Later on i had so much money but couldnt buy anything with it because i already had better gear than the store would sell, but still couldnt buy any ingredients because they are too rare. But the variety of equipment is huge, there are even flintlock pistols which serve as a counter against magical barriers from mages. Really interestening idea, because otherwise bows are better than flintlocks. It got a small downside but still a fresh and unique experience.
But the freedom to create a character in this game is really unique. Other game have dump stats that definetly need to be maxes/picked because you picked a class. As an example if you take a berserker, you usually would dump all points on strength,health and rest on agillity or something? In this game even intelligence is really important for a berserker because it helps with his warcry´s and so on which can stun people or buff yourself. Really good idea, the skilling system is one of the best ive ever seen in videogames.
The skills on the other hand are a double edged sword. One one hand you got a huge amount of skills and abillities to pick from, on the other hand some are so terribly useless. That definetly needs rebalance. Also some classes have not many skills compared to others, but thats just small nitpicking.
I had a couple of bugs in the game, none gamebreaking i couldnt finish one side quests tough that was a real buzzkill but overall its almost bug free, my second playtrough had none.
Overall i definetly had my fun with this game and would give it a 8.5/10. There are many classes and abillites to experiment with, one playtrough will definetly not be the same but the masses amount of junk equipment and skills, some minor flaws with bugs and character creation really kills that 10/10 i would have given it.

I'm really sad that I can't recommend this game. It really sucks you in once you start building the right set of skills to play it. When you hit your stride you just feel so damn good. I'll detail what I found wrong with it below but
TLDR: Game is great until glitchy poorly made bosses ♥♥♥♥ you up.
Edit: I finally did beat them and it felt damn good. Still they're a couple of weenies. Get the game, just be better than me.
Okay Ornstein and Smough, lets talk about why these enemies are terrible to their core.
1- Ornstein can attack through smough. One boss can attack through the body of the other, really from soft? I thought you made this guy a gargantuin giant for a reason. I can understand attacks clipping through scrawny skeletons, but a fat giant that fills half the screen and is wider than the other guys weapon,,, come on.
2- No recharge on attacks. Particularly a problem with Smough, but both enemies in their second stages as well. These two can use their deadliest attacks an unlimited amount of times in a row, up until this point this game did a good job in giving the player a sense that a super attack was a... well a super attack! Particularly Quellag had a large AoE attack that one had to back far away from or take a full health bar of damage. You know what? Good for her, it's a good challenge and a good change of pace, why? Becaue she couldn't use it 5 times in a row.
3- Pillars of course! Pillars in the room should provide cover but both enemies can hit you through them, this desighn ♥♥♥♥ up is fairly simple. Why no make their weapons bounce of the pillars kinda like, oh I don't know, my ♥♥♥♥ing attacks. Seriously something that I really liked about this game was that if the enemy could do some bulshit you could do it to. Kill them with traps, knock them off ledges. But no matter what you do youll never have a broken hit box on your sword :(
4- (Not sure how to phrase this but) Not lore friendly/ Doesn't follow cutscenes/ doesnt make sense. They really sacrificed an awsome vibe just to make this game harder than it needed to be. When you kill one boss and the other absorbs his power in a cool cutscene it feels like a very interesting concept lore wise and gameplay wise. However they really fumble it hard. The boss you didn't kill yet will gain all his health back upon taking the power of the other, but hold on, you smashed his body with a hammer... and electricity went into your hammer... and this gives you health beacause? Okay, okay, fine I guess its cool though, I feel extremely threatend, this character just brutally crushed his only friend to make himself stronger, jeez he must be a power hungry brutal monster! Oh... your friend is back the next time I try the boss. So the whole smashing him to a pulp with a hammer, that was just a little butterfly kiss I guess.
I don't know maybe this isn't a big deal to everyone but the respawning of the killed boss just erased all sense of death and permanence I had with the game, sure the other double boss would respawn (gargoyles) but most things killed by the player respawn. I thought it was a cool bit of lore that these guys where so deadly that they would destroy their only brother in arms just to win a fight, but instead I'm left wondering why they don't start every fight like that if it doesn't hurt them at all.
All in all this boss fight disappointed me immensly. If they really wanted this cool double boss fight that fine! Just be actually able to execute it. If they could have tightend the hit boxes, made the AI not only have a super move response to everything, and made their weapons bounce off terrain then the boss would have been fair. It was a cool idea but they really bit off more than they could chew, it isn't that I couldn't handle this boss From Soft, you couldn't.
I'm sure down the road I'll give this game another chance and come to love it, but for now I'm quitting video games for a while. I think I'll go to a park, maybe write a book, I really just feel like I spent a day giving myself a headache, so tragic after this game was so damn good to!

After playing for about an hour I can say it has a lot of great potential. The atmosphere and enviroment truly give a sense of fear of the unexpected. What awaits you in this game is something truly psychological and a true test of your will as a player.
PROs:
- Incredible sound design
- Well done enviroment
- Great graphics
- Incredible atmoshpere
CONs:
- Can get boring
- KOS (It's a survival game so it's what to expect)
Personal Thoughts:
In my first hour of the game I was welcomed into a very convincing world that shows decay from events that have unfolded. The atmosphere really got my heart pumping since there is this sense of stillness due to the silence and it can really generate some anxiety if you let it set in. There's always a sense of despair while you walk through these abandoned towns and see them inhabited by overgrowth and what remains of less fortunate survivors. I did eventually find some weapons and new threads to accompany me throughout my tread in the world and ran into another survivor whom was armed with a pickaxe and my first response was to tell him not to do anything then fatally shot him in the head leaving him in the woods. Whilst walking through the woods I witnessed some wildlife and my first glimpse of an infected enemy which was some sort of dog but it ran away and didn't engage me. Walking along I found deserted camping grounds and found an unloaded rifle as well as the makings for a camp. I walked along and ran into a slightly more agressive player that ran towards me. I yelled warnings and fired my remaining rounds from my handgun missing once and landing two non-fatal hits. The player began hitting me with their bare hands and landed a few hits but I inevitably won the fight with a hatchet with a swift hit to the side of their head. I then jumped off a bridge into a lake below in order to get to a boat that sadly wasn't functional. I walked down a small road I came upon two players fist fighting. I drew my rifle I yelled a warning for them to stop. They did stop fighting and one player fled the scene as I took aim with my unloaded rifle and made one of the unarmed player get down on his knees and put his hands behind his head. I then proceeded to brain him with my hatchet and pursue the other player. He got the drop on me but when I drew my rifle and he backed off and I procceeded to brain him with my hatchet.
So far this game reall has a grim twist on sense of realism that taps into psycological fears. The game reminds me of the film IT COMES AT NIGHT where it feels like man really is the true monster although in the game there are physical monsters.
I can't wait to see where this game goes in the future since it does feel very well done even in it's current state. Buyers however should be aware that this game is a SURVIVAL game so KOS is going to be a feature that you will run into since people can be literal savages and show very little remorse towards you. I'd recommend playing with friends in order to increase your chances of having an enjoyable experience since playing alone can get boring and probably give you a negative perception of the game since players can and probably will outright murder you without any remorse.
I see a bright future for this very dark and very twisted game. And can't wait to continue being both a survivalist and a monster.

Abstract:
This game, compared to other games of the same gener allows players to have real interactions besides just killing each other on sight ( something that happens quite a lot in other open world games ). Although the game has been in development for quite some time, the developers seem to be hard at work and updates are released just about on time every month or so. here's a list of all the pros and cons that I have noticed so far:
****PROS*****
- If you're a fan of high quality graphics. This is a game for you. This game looks absolutely gorgeous. The game is heavily influenced by The Last of Us which is also about survival in a post-apocalyptic world. So if you’re fan of The Last of Us and ever wondered “I wish there was a open-world game like this” This is a game for you.
- The game runs very smooth for an early access game. I am yet to encounter any character wipes or base/item disappearances. The cars are a bit hard to control at times but with enough practice that won't ever be an issue. Overall the game maintains a steady level of immersion and realism.
- This game forces you to make those split-second decisions and rely not only on your individual skills but to come up with plans and strategies to overcome a situation or face the consequences.
- The AI in this game is one of the best I have seen in any online open-world game of this genre. Except a few exceptions, the majority of the scenarios require your constant awareness of where the mutants are and how you would have to deal with every single one of them. Unlike other game, you can’t just ignore them. They will do major damage to your health if they catch you and might even kill you. These mutants are a major part of the game and you would have find a way to deal with them (especially if you don't have a gun yet). It would be nice if developers increased the number of zombies or added hoard events that would require a team effort to stop.
- Heres something that many people may not notice about this game and I just think that it really is worthy of mentioning and that is the music. The music of this game is absolutely amazing. It really gives you the chaiotic sense of a post apocalyptic world and it is calming at the same time.
****CONS*****
- The base building in the game as of right now might be a bit frustrating at times. Wall placements are on a free roam mode and don't just line up on their own like in other games such as Rust. There really is no real motive behind why players have to take refuge outside of the cities and in wilderness rather than staying in. It would make sense if the main cities were radioactive or dangerous or if there was a lore-related reason behind this
- The map might feel a bit too small for 50 player servers or even the original 32 player servers. This is more noticeable after finding a car for that you are able to drive around the whole island in less than hour but the team is constantly working on adding more to the map. The new sewer system and parking lot expansions added so much to the game.
- The last and final con to this game should be the real incentive of survival which is something that the games of this genre in particular seem to lack and this game is no different in that sense. After obtaining high-end gears and weapons there appears to be no real reason for exploration. Many players would prefer to take shelter and hold onto their loots in the fear of losing it.
Overall I am highly satisfied for how this game is turning out and I hope to see its release as a full game. As of right now it appears that the game's success is heavily overshadowed by other great titles but this game definitely has potentials to be one of the best open-world apocalyptic videogames in the market. I would give this game a solid 8/10.
P.S: This review was posted during the early access release of the game and is subject to change.

Community - 7 / 10

Overall - 7.6

** Check my profile to understand my scoring system**
If you like the Civilization series and the Heroes of Might and Magic series AND competitive multiplayer, this might be the perfect game for you. This title could easily be given to Fallen Enchantress IF it had multiplayer. Since it has not, Warlock is (so far) the best Civ-slash-Heroes mash-up you can get. (Rumour is that Fallen Enchantress will be getting multiplayer soon(tm))
The game plays pretty much like Civilization. In fact it's so identical to Civilization V that I suspect the engine might even be the same (although I couldn't find that info anywhere) so if you're a Civilization V player and likes fantasy, that's probably a must-have. However it's a really limited game. There aren't as many units and nations like you have in Civilization, so variety isn't a plus here. But when it comes to gameplay, Warlock offers several features that are really neat and interesting. Levelling units feel a lot more rewarding than doing so on Civ, since you have many more perks to give them. And the advantages/disadvantages between units are much more clear and functional. City building is fantastic - you really snap buildings into map tiles (hexagons) and there are buildings that have map funcionalities. So if you have a city that's near a mountain pass, you can place a castle on the pass and force invaders to defeat the castle before getting to the city tile. Admitting heroes into your nation feels like the old Master of Orion games and plays like a simplified version of heroes - but it's really enjoyable to see your heroes leading your armies into conquering towns, levelling them and grabbing some shiny gear.
Some gameplay features like different planes and the apocalypse game mode (which spawns hell gates, something pretty much like what happens in TES: Oblivion) give it a charm.
It's not the best strategy game out there - but certainly can be the best choice if you're looking for some grand-strategy with a fantasy setting.

Spicyhorse Games
Spicyhorse Games
January 6th, 2014
Casual, Indie, Episodic
Being a huge fan of American McGee, and subsequently, his company Spicyhorse Games, I'm naturally drawn to games with a macabre twist to them. I was introduced to McGee, as a game maker, back in 2001 with American McGee's Alice, which took a dark retelling of the Lewis Carol story, Alice in Wonderland. The official sequel of the game was released just a few years ago, and can be found here on steam.
Back to what we were originally talking about--- THIS game. Grimm takes that same little twist that you expect with anything made by McGee, but does it in a humorous, yet demented way. He takes the popular childrens tales, and tells them the way they were originally told in, with nothing sugar coated or laced with wool. Let this also be known, that the game features hangings, as well as various other scenes that are not meant for small children, and while the game's graphics could be aesthetically pleasing towards said audience, the game is best suited towards teenagers and adults.
In this game, you play as Grimm, a cranky storyteller, who dislikes the fact that fairy tales have lost their cautionary warnings and dark overtones and means to retell each story the way they were originally told in. He/You do this by spreading filth and darkness throughout each scene and butt stomping everything until nothing is sugar coated. Each episode (there are 30 in total) takes roughly 30 minutes of gameplay, can be played in any order, and currently the first episode is free to play.
The graphics in this game could be considered “cutesy” and childlike but I find them aesthetically pleasing and while they lean on the side of childlike, have that little twist that only American McGee could do. Moreso, I found it pleasing to watch the overall changes within the scenes and areas after you  managed to create enough filth and darkness to “butt stomp away”.
There are some minor issues with clipping in certain areas, but given the price tag for each episode, are a relatively small and minor detail.
The voice acting in this game, especially with the character of Grimm are very well done and fit into the worldstates that each story is told in. The point of this game is a narrative gameplay, and each narration is unique with its own sense of humor.
As I said above in the last section, the game may look like it's targeted towards small children, but its mature tones make the game better suited towards teenagers and adults.
The gameplay is rather simple, easy to learn, but unfortunately gets repetitive. Keep in mind that this game isn't really about the gameplay itself, it's about the narration and the changing of the tones of each story. There are some stories where you will need to occasionally jump onto platforms and avoid things like water and lava, but that is more about timing your jumps from each platform/from platform to land.
Unfortunately, the repetitive gameplay is a real shame for this game because it has decent potential to be better than some of the newer, shinier, 3d platforming titles. Add this to the fact that the game has no way to save your progress, and you get a slightly disappointed feeling... or at least I did.
I recommend this game to anyone who enjoys games with fun little dark twists, who enjoy American McGee games, and who like the idea of short playtime episodes. The first episode is free, and the rest of the episodes occasionally get thrown into bundles, but are cheap as standalone options on steam. While there were some things about the gameplay for me, this should in no way detract people from managing to have a fun playthrough of the game. I also recommend playing the first episode if you are still unsure and don't want to spend $3.99 per “season” of the DLCs.

What drives a man of God to wash away the sins of his past, only to blacken his heart with a multitude more? How far can a freedom fighter be pushed before virtue and righteousness are replaced by a lust for vengeance? What does a privileged society do when the foundation of its prosperity is shaken? Long Live The Queen dares to explore these heady themes and many more, giving you glimpses at just how the seemingly smallest of decisions can forever alter our realities, and our hearts. As a young princess, your actions bring turmoil and strife to an ostensibly idyllic landscape. It's immensely fun to stir up trouble, and even more engaging to see how boldly Long Live The Queen portrays a society torn asunder. You'll be haunted by this thematically devastating adventure, and indeed, its phenomenal final minutes, which are bound to be discussed and dissected for some time to come.

Laughing at the ludicrous nature of the spiky-humpbeast which is making your backside its domain?

Staring in mute amazement, your head ripped clean off and sailing through the air, as that jackass whose been surviving alone the entire game activates the Evac and then gets there first, spawning wave after wave of the gigantic 'hatchlings' which have just de-crowned you?

Chicken Skewers With Grilled Mango Recipe
Ingredients
3/4 cup plain yogurt 2 tablespoons fresh lemon juice 1 large garlic clove, minced 2 teaspoons sugar 1/2 teaspoon turmeric 1 teaspoon kosher salt 1/4 teaspoon black pepper 6 boneless, skinless chicken breasts, sliced into long strips 3 large, ripe mangoes, cut into large pieces
Directions
Place 20 wooden skewers in water to soak. In a large, shallow dish, combine the yogurt, lemon juice, garlic, sugar, turmeric, salt, and pepper.
Add the chicken to the yogurt mixture and toss to coat. Cover with plastic wrap and refrigerate at least 15 minutes (or overnight, if desired).
Heat grill to medium high. Remove the chicken from the marinade, shaking off the excess, and thread onto the skewers.
Grill the chicken, turning, until cooked through, 3 to 5 minutes. Transfer to a platter and cover with foil to keep warm.
Grill the mango until slightly charred and tender, about 2 minutes per side. Serve with the chicken.

have you had bad days? i mean really bad days ... like ... you get hit by a car, go home, your house has been robbed, and your dog died, kinda days. take a few of those days, mesh them together, make a game out of it, and you get this.
that kinda has a 2-fold effect. first of all, it's tough to digest; and i mean really tough, like eating a bucket of nails. secondly tho, it makes a good, compelling story to tell.
that's what gods will be watching is like. a really really tough point and click game. like a lot of tragedies; it just takes a moment to happen, and the same, this game is actually fairly short. but like most tragedies, it has a fairly intriguing tale to be told, to say the least. the question is, can you stomach the pain and suffering to get to the end of it?
personally, i loved the art, and the unique gameplay. the challenge? that's a bit debatable. it's certainly not for casual gamers. no walkthroughs and guides can save you unlike most traditional point and click games. it's all about identifying patterns and figuring out how things work, but over time, you'll get the hang of it (hopefully) ... again, if you can stomach it that far.
if you uh ... believe in the healing powers of hair ripping, spine tingling, frustratingly tough games, this is a must buy! truly made for the masochist in you.

So I'm reviewing this in 2017, after playing Dark Souls 3, this likely colors my perception.
This game is amazing, but not at the level of DS3.  There are too many cheap areas, and the slog to the boss after dying is much more annoying than DS3 (there tends to not be paths w/o enemies for the majority of the boss fights).  Blightown and Sens Fortress stand out as super annoying areas to get through.  The hardest thing for me was to get used to being slower, every action has much more weight (and delay) to it than it did in DS3 (and I played a great hammer there).  Once I switched from trying to roll to dodge attacks to shielding (normally) the game became a lot more fun.  The level design on a macro level here is astounding, but as noted at a micro level it can be super-frustrating.  The inability to warp to any bonfire also makes things more tedious (as does the vendors being all over the map instead of clustered at firelink shrine).
All those complaints being said, this game is definitely a blast, and well worth getting through.  It holds up, and opening the shortcuts to firelink will amaze you.  It took me about 50h to get through all the bosses (and the DLC), but that's after having practice in DS3 (which took slightly longer).

This is far better then reading a book, and there is a lot of reading. The writing is excellant and really draws you into this world. In fact, playing this game is highly stimulating. State of Decay is a sort of hommage to zombie culture wrapped in a game. The sequence of the previous sentence is important because the game takes presidence over the nods to various games, books and movies.
The game itself revolves around the survival of a group of characters that are both scripted and quite a few others you will gather up along the way randomly. You control one character at a time with the option of bringing friends along (at a cost) to help you gather resources, fight special zombies or clear houses of zombies. After the intial tutorial area the game kicks off and you're open to being able to build outposts in buildings or areas of interest, build upgrades and select among the survivors to take control of.
As far as the base game, there is a story that can be completed and the rate at which the game decides to bring on plot points to progress the game seems to be a little randomized. The game will give you time to screw around before it brings on the next plot point, which feels appropriate. There really isn't a need to rush.
The story is a bit of a weak point. I grew attached to the characters even though they were voiced by 4 or 5 people max and repeated lines from other characters. It is evident that there was a budget constraint and while the voice acting isn't well implemented and the story is disjointed with characters' emotions sometimes not amounting to any new events when it seems like it should, the game comes out strong regardless.
My verdict: It's fun. Worth a play.
