I have poured quite a few hours into this game, and I can say that I enjoyed most of it.  It is a 4x hex based game (expand, explore, exterminate, and exploit), akin to Civ 5.  My very limited exposure to Civ 5 leads me to halt any more comparisons there, however I have read there are significant differences between the two games.  I've seen it most compared with Masters of Magic.
The single player can be quite fun due to the interesting characters that exist within the game.  It's also got very solid gameplay and the balance isn't too bad.  The main gripe I've seen about balance is Undead and Favor to Grum-Gog, since it allows the expansion phase to be dominated by the player who chooses it and abuse the fact that Undead don't use food to spam Strong Rats, who use only food as a resource. This can also be abused in multiplayer (which is currently deserted).  Also another gripe I have is the maps are randomly generated, which for the most part is okay, but if I were to take this game super seriously and decide to be competitive, I'd want to be able to make maps to make sure they are well balanced and strategic.
The base game features 3 different races that you can start off with, and each are different enough.  As you take over other towns which belong to a different race than what you start with, you can use their technologies and units to add to your army.  There are dozens of spells that are available that you can use on average once per turn, unless you use a spell that reduces casting time.  The spells range from pure damage to buffs and debuffs to units and global as well as city buffs.  There are also spells you can only get if you worship one of the eight gods, like the Summon Strong Rats I mentioned earlier.
The DLC is decent, one allows you to have hero characters which you can customize with up to three items, one introduces an entire new race, and another allows for a more difficult challenge.  I'd probably get the Armageddon DLC if anything just to make the game a bit more difficult, since the AI's in this game are pretty limited.  The extra race isn't necessary, but it's unique and the hero units are really very strong and can be buffed to ridiculous levels.
Also, before now there was no hope of this game going anywhere.  But there is a new subforum on the official forums for modding.  Before now, Ino-Co or somebody didn't want this to be modded at all, and in turn it pretty much killed the forum community since the game stagnated and there was no more DLC.  Though it looks like that may be reversed soon, which would be way cool.
tl;dr version: 4x game, decent balance, random maps, lots of spells, cool characters, ok DLC, currently no modding, maybe modding later. Good game.

Orcs Must Die! 2 is a solid follow-up to the original Orcs Must Die game.  While they both share the same graphics, and much of the same style, the improvements in OMD2 are really well done.
This is an excellent derivative of the Tower Defense gameplay style, and being able to set traps and play in 1st Person mode during the raids is challenging and engaging.  (There is another game called Sanctum that tries to do the same thing but doesn't make a deep impression - OMD2 pulls it off really well.)
With a new system for refunding your "tech-tree" (via skulls) as you move from level to level, you can try out new traps without having the buyers remorse from the first game.  Along with several new modes and lots of new maps, you can eventually get all of the upgrades - something that would take weeks of play.
The new game includes multiplayer as well, which I haven't tried yet.  I enjoy the single player element enough that I've never bothered to setup the multiplayer side.

A blast of a sequel that improved upon everything from the first game, the most important addition being co-op play! Although some of the maps become frustrating with only 1 player, the sheer number of maps, weekly challenges, frequent additions and updates, upgrade system, and various difficulties can keep you killing orcs forever.

The sequel to the popular Orcs Must Die! is a great addition to the game's unique genre. Orcs Must Die! 2 offers a familiar feel if you've played the original, but it greatly builds upon the first game's mechanics and expands the experience by offering cooperative gameplay, customization and a sense of leveling up by collecting skulls for various improvements. It should be noted that Orcs Must Die! 2 co-op mode is limited to your Steam friends. Regardless, this amazing sequel is worth a play-through for those looking beyond first-person shooters.

Horrendous game. Half of the time you can't even connect to servers despite having low ping; you just get sent back to the menu with no prompt or warning! The worst part is that this problem has been persisting on for 3 YEARS and that a significant portion of the player base still has to deal with this every time they play. Don't let my play time fool you; most of it was spent trying to connect to a server, and once I did the only game play "experience" I received was looting and walking around while avoiding the unresponsive mutants.
The game world is empty and is just full of copy pasted buildings - if you want proof of this, go to the Amalgated Airfield area, find the brown building, then go to any one of the towns and you'll see that same building - WITH THE SAME LOOT SPAWNS, ROOMS, GRAFFITI AND EVEN DECORATIONS - scattered everywhere. Loading times are long and if you think the game has fulled loaded by time you've connected and spawned, guess what? You have to sit down for a minute or so and wait 'til it's actually fully loaded since you're going to be stuttering and freezing if you even move your mouse or your character.
The loot spawn rates are so low and it's set that way whether you're in a dense or scarcely populated server. This makes looting and scavenging an unrewarding and boring experience. Also, your loot doesn't entirely save up the next time you play, even if it's on the same server you're on. I killed two people and looted their corpses and got some pretty good bling, got to a safe spot, waited for the unnecessarily long 30 second timer, and left the server. Guess what happens? My loot didn't save, and my loot was instead reverted back to when I was looting buildings just minutes before I killed those two said people. The inventory system is just so clunky, unimaginative and broken too. Crafting is sparse and most players probably wouldn't bother with it; I know I haven't.
I don't see any unique features in this game. For the hard drive space it takes, the features are too few and the ones that are implemented are awkward and non-user friendly.
If you're thinking of you're going to play a survival simulator; you aren't, expect that you're just going to walk around, occassionally meet people who will shoot you, and collect food and beverages. That's it, that's literally the game. For the price it has; it's simply not worth it, especially when it can't even deliver its scant number of features properly.

Better than Angry Birds!
Does Angry Birds have siege engines that you can upgrade?  No.  Does Angry Birds have mages that cast spells to destroy one or more of your siege engines?  No.
Yes this game has the same basic ideas as Angry Birds:  launch a projectile to hit all the enemies in a set number of turns.  But Angry Birds was not the first game to do that, so why do people disregard games like this just because they are similar?  Who cares which was first, all that matters is if a game is good or not.  Sure there are lots of crappy games that are made to try to get easy money, but dont' assume that this is one of them.
For one thing, this game has no animals.  No birds, no pigs.  The player has siege engines such as catapults and arrow launchers.  The enemies are mages of different types.  If you don't kill them in a turn or two the mages cast a spell and destroy one or more of your siege engines.   And the mages don't laugh and mock you for losing like the pigs in Angry Birds.
There are 4 different types of siege engines you get throughout the game.  You can't choose which to use, they are set in each level.  But you can choose which ones you want to upgrade.   You get upgrade points (I can't remember what they are called in the game) from time to time (I think for beating a level fast or maybe not losing a siege engine or something) and there are occasional orbs in the level that you can get, though they are usually in hard to reach places.
There are also spells you can use.  I've gotten one at the beginning of each world.  Once you use it, it's gone.  But it does help when you're in a tough spot.
Graphics are nice, cartoony, cute.
Sound is ok.
The price is great.  Pretty cheap for the amount of content you get.
Plus there are Achievements and Trading Cards!

The gameplay isn't engaging. You run around trying to make progressively bigger things dirty by touching them, while stopping some very slow cleaners from cleaning up the mess you made. Or in other words: You use the mouse or WASD to move from object to object, now and then you aim and jump for some extra powers, and there's a tiny bit of awkward platforming occasionally for "variety" (during which you get instantly revived from the same spot if you fall). As an idea that sort of gameplay doesn't sound terrible, but it isn't well executed and it ends up being boring and repetitive. It provides no challenge whatsoever, no difficulty progression, no need for any strategy, no need for reflexes or good timing... basically no need for anything more than you staying at your keyboard and/or mouse and running around. I have nothing against casual or arcade-y games, but there has to be *something* captivating about them, and it seems to be missing from here. There are leaderboards trying to entice you to get through a level faster and some hidden coins you can find to improve your score (usually behind big blocky things that confuse the camera and may make you temporarily stuck) but neither feel very tempting, and they are also not rewarded with anything besides bragging rights.
I suppose I can appreciate the art style (even though I didn't really love it) and I suppose there is an attempt here to do something interesting with the storytelling. The concept of turning the original Grimm stories on their head through the gameplay (which has some narrated bits in between and tries to closely follow the changes that you inflict) is not bad.  But I can't really say I personally found the altered stories themselves particulary enjoyable or even funny. There's some dark humor in the cinematics, but the stink and pee jokes aren't my cup of tea and gimmicky trees full of hanging children aren't all that entertaining as far as I'm concerned. Ymmv.
That aside, there are some technical issues that bothered me. The settings (including your chosen resolution) get reset from episode to episode. There are two annoying small cutscenes every time you reach an inbetween "checkpoint" of sorts, and they get old really fast. Yes, you can hit space to skip all cinematics but you have to do that more or less 5-6 times in every single "level" in every one of the 5-6 stages of every episode. The repetitve quips and looping music get old just as fast, and the sound design generally has some issues.
I tried some of the follow-up episodes to see if anything is done differently, but it doesn't look like it. So play the free episode before buying. If you enjoy that one, then you'll enjoy the rest too.

Genre: 2.5D Traditional Fighting Game
Summary:
SFIV is a footsies-based fighting game that emphasizes slow methodical play and meter management between rounds.
Game features the inclusion of 'focus attacks', a universal move that grants a character one hit of armour and the potential to crumple the opponent; the nature of focus attacks allow characters to aggressive advance through attacks without infringing upon the effectiveness of projectile characters.
Pros:
- 39 characters, an additional 5 in Ultra Street Fighter 4.
- The majority of match-ups are balanced (future update to provide further balance).
- Decent netcode if neither player has much traffic.
- Large established player base online and offline.
- Great for players trying to get into fighting games. Will teach fundamentals through play and the abundant tutorials on the internet.
Cons:
- Single-player modes are lacking; arcade mode has terrible A.I. and the challenges aren't fun.
- The game itself does not provide instruction to newer players.
- No theatre mode for the animated clips from Arcade Mode.
Neutral Points:
- There will be a learning curve; it is a fighting game afterall. If you are a new player then you will be terrible for a while.
- Input leniency allows newer players to perform special moves more easily but can become an annoyance at higher level play.
- There is a comeback factor for newer players (Ultra) which becomes a tool at higher level play.
- The plot is barebones, but hey, that's a norm for fighting games.

1.4 hours - here are my quams.
Braking is dodgy. First off, there is no option for front and back brakes which peeves me as a biker generally since the application of different brakes is useful for different types of entry into a corner. Second, there seems to be a delay on brakes, the application of them simply isn't responsible enough - it is as if the controller is slowly applying the brakes but it is slow at all times - which of course means that there is no emergency braking whatsoever. If you're not smoothe, you cannot make any corrections without a short delay to do them which makes being responsive altogether a difficult task. Moreover, the engine behaves as if the clutch is employed almost at all times. There is no real engine braking, which is also annoying for being specific with corner entry.
There is also no track which really requires the use of more than four gears and you'll find yourself in the first two gears entirely save for the straights. Imo, as a 125cc rider, I'd say these tracks are designed really for smaller bikes and thus the power output doesn't really match the tracks in question. It's far too difficult to really feel a good exit because you're constantly applying and un applying the throttle in order to find a good exit due to excessive acceleration.
It's okay, it will probably improve as long as the handling is adjust. For an early model, I'd give it like a 5 or a 6 out of ten.

There is a big Eelphant in The Woodpile for Incline:  The payment model. You get 20 Free Tokens which each last 8 hours, then you pay to play with bought tokens.  Otherwise this would have been a thumbs up.   The developer is working on ways to make the tokens system clearer for everybody, and has taken constructive critiscism on board so respect due for that.
So what's it all about, leaving aside the tokens-to-play matter.
- The physics are actually pretty good. At least as far as lean angles, grip etc go. On the small tracks you rarely get out of second gear, making the choices of a 600RR or an R6 type of bike rather over the top for this type of track.

If you ride IRL and have ever done trackdays or even spectated at many race circuits the flatness of the tracks really stands out.  You'll really notice the lack of cambers and elevations that would make the game more interesting and a more challenging ride.
- engine braking feels nowhere near right,  and the only way I can describe hard braking is as though you are using the rear brake only, with no engine braking to help,  it feels like just 1/3 of what it would be on a 600RR.  Maybe a small bit dive on the front end would give more of an illusion that the brakes were actually as powefrul as they are on sports bikes.  The braking seems more shopping bike than race bike.
-the acceleration, turn-in and handling are actually pretty good at approximating the type of bike in the game. Fairly easy to pick your apex and the bike goes where you want it. Too much power and it'll run wide fairly realistically. The bike will high-side or low-side if you get it wrong, and the front will tuck in if you overbrake in a corner. All the right theory of riding is there.
There are no separate front/rear brakes in the game.

- The tracks, however are all flat. Totally flat. utterly and absolutely spirit-level flat.  But this is early access and there should be plenty more to come.
- Multiplayer is pretty good,  but races can be totally ruined by Kamikaze players. If I had paid for a token  to play an online race I would be mighty disappointed by the kamikaze trolls going the wrong way round the tracks and those who think it is a contact sport simulator.  Hilarious. Not.
-You definitely need a controller.
- The graphics look like an android game,  but you can live with that in racing games, you aren't there to enjoy AAA scenery and most of the time it'll be a blur anyway.

- The "tokens" system sucks, but that's an opinion. This would be a worthwhile stocking-filler indie game for $5 or maybe even $10, but the token idea doesn't work for me.
Dev gets so many things right as well as wrong he deserves a chance to bring this game on. I had some fun races online once I got the hang of it, and I just wish I could have handed over a few quid and simply bought it.  For some people the tokens really are a deal breaker.
It's early access, and more of a Free Trial which gives you 20 play tokens to get started with.  I could see this being a nice go-to casual racing game in due course, I just hope the developer can find some way for players who can't abide the tokens system to just buy the game or play for free and maybe pay for Tracks DLC or something instead.

The sequel to the popular Orcs Must Die! is a great addition to the game's unique genre. Orcs Must Die! 2 offers a familiar feel if you've played the original, but it greatly builds upon the first game's mechanics and expands the experience by offering cooperative gameplay, customization and a sense of leveling up by collecting skulls for various improvements. An excellent follow up to the first great game. I was a little nervous about some of the changes they were making, some of the new enemies, etc, but they did a great job with everything. I love playing as the Sorceress, the wand and other character specific weapons and traps are great.
The one problem I have with the game is that there are a few annoying bugs from time to time. In particular sometimes the monster pathing gets confused and a monster will just randomly break down barricades that they shouldn't. They are supposed to be working on a fix for this BUT there are still situations when this happens because of a "feature". If the path is blocked by a traffic jam of enemies, they will start breaking barricades down, even if those barricades are not near the jam, even if they shouldn't know about the jam because it isn't in their line of sight. I understand them breaking them down at the jam to get through but if the just spawned on the other end of the map and don't know about it they shouldn't break through over there. There are also times when monsters will get caught in the wall and not be reachable, but eventually it will timeout and die, so this isn't a show stopper.
Those minor annoyances aside, OMD2 is an amazing game. Everyone should play it (not to mention OMD1 too!).
The DLC has been coming out a little too frequently for my taste, I wish they would have spent more time figuring out some of these bugs and "features" first, but it is all good and relatively cheap.
There is also free weekly DLC in the form of the Weekly Challenge mode they added after launch.

Think of space marines in any the following flavours: Warhammer/AVP/StarCraft and you'll be close to the kind of trooper feel the game has. You play one character and gain XP in 3 areas. The third is in-game XP - you start at the same basic level each new match and level within that match in a fashion similar to Dota or LoL etc. At the end of the match you lose that progression, but hey it's all good.

Within buildings there are consoles which activate lights and flares which can be fired or dropped to help further. Also there are ad hoc sentry gun positions you can activate and within bunker mode, the option to deploy 'reinforcement' sentry turrets periodically.

A lot of reviews for this game say something along the lines of "no, this is much deeper than the sugary pink teen girl package!!!" but the sugary pink teen girl aspect is exactly why this game works for me. Long Live The Queen is a female power fantasy, which is neither condescending about the kind of fantasy stakes a teen girl might want to face nor the fantasy possibilities she might want to pursue. It has a strong Princess Maker 2 vibe, a game I devoured over and over as a teen girl, except without the weird sexualization of a minor or the paternalistic aspect.
Princess Elodie's agency is front and center here, and the different paths she can pursue through the story are remarkably complex. Beautiful and graceful, able to charm hearts with her artistic talents? Ruthless political negotiator, using her royal relatives as pawns to squash rebellions? Sword-swinging, arrow-dodging military strategist, her kingdom's armies under her command? This barely scratches the surface of the different kinds of stories I pursued in this game.
And oh god, is it challenging. I base this review on my many playthroughs of a beta version of the game before it came to Steam, and I literally lost count of how many times Elodie died. I stacked up 20 save slots per playthrough trying to min-max my points to survive the next succession of challenges. I love this game. I want a whole book of illustrations of the different ways Elodie can bite the dust.

This game wanted to be the successor of Baldur's Gate, and succeeded in doing a lot of things right.
The mechanics are really good and I wouldn't dare going into detail here but I will say a few things about them. Characters have abilities/spells that they can use a limited number of times per rest (when your party heals and gains some specific bonuses) or combat. It might seem a bit weird in the beginning but it adds an extra level of depth and the opportunity to balance the game. There is "sneaking" but it's quite ineffective compared to other RPGs from the same genre, which actually gives the game a good balance and realism but it's not very interesting and it has limited usefulness. The game also has options for a ton of quality of life improvements, like unlimited inventory and you can loot a large area at once, among some of them.
The main story is not told all that great, you're being thrown into it very sudden and you're being told how to feel about it. With time the story and the lore of this world will grow on you and I believe the story gets better; I also liked The White March story line. I would like to say here that The White March not only brings you lots of new locations and stories but it also adds mechanics to the game,  so I strongly recommend that you play with it.
I liked the graphic art style but the sound track was unimpressive. You get to have a stronghold, which I find really cool; I don't think that this is a spoiler because you have a stronghold button on the interface from the start, it just doesn't do anything until you have control over it.

The endless struggle to impact our environment and circumstances measured against the inevitable and ultimate futility of such efforts- that's what Gods Will Be Watching encapsulates beautifully. In life (and in GWBW) we try repeatedly to affect outcomes, despite the fact that results are largely out of our hands. Our actions are always causing change to the total picture, but no one can be sure that the actions we choose to take will result in the changes we seek. It's a lottery and a crapshoot where we play percentages, roll the dice, and hope for the best. That helplessness - that we often deceive ourselves into believing is fallacious - is reinforced in life time and again, yet we continue to believe in our power and control over circumstance. It really is quite amusing in a darkly comedic way. And it's easy to understand why it's more comfortable to believe in our sovereignty. Firstly, to act at all would be rather pointless if we accept the alternative. Additionally, despite all evidence pointing to our near-total insignificance and impotence, we desire, we dream, we want. So we push and we sometimes see outcomes that are in harmony with that pushing, reinforcing our desperately held notion that we are, in fact, making these things happen. This is the flavor imparted by "Gods" for me, and I found it to be quite compelling.
In terms of the actual execution of things mechanically, it really boils down to a game of prioritization. You are continually faced with desired objectives that are often balanced precariously against opposing forces. You are faced with questions about what you can sacrifice, where you can yield versus elements that must not be compromised. And these factors are always dynamically changing, forcing continual reassessment of your circumstances. In this juggling act, balls WILL fall and you will struggle to come to terms with your relative helplessness.
I don't want to get specific in regards to the narrative because I think it is best experienced personally, but suffice it to say that I found it gripping. This was a game that I found grew on me over time and with failure. I was drawn in to the point that my failures weren't a deterrent to my desire to press on, and so it is apparently with us in real life. We act, we fail, and we continue on, sometimes seeing results we desire giving impetus to our continued action.

Ultimate Street Fighter 4: Super DLC Edition
-Plenty of character variety
-Lots of Modes & Unlockables
-NOT for Casuals
-Online Mode(s) are Laggy, Inconsistant & has cheaters
-Huge difficulty curve
-Sore Thumbs & Fingers
-Best Played with an Arcade Controller

-DLC (Disk Locked Content) is Overpriced
-Technical Issues
Remember when you could unlock costumes & characters by simply playing the game?  Well now you have to spend more money cause ♥♥♥♥ YOU that's why!
Even though the DLC upsets me greatly & buying 3 versions of the same game also upsets me (SF4, SF4:AE, USF4)  it's still a great game & worthy of your time.  The DLC is a god awful overpriced cash grab. You might as well just wait for a sale & get all the DLC cheap.  That's what I did.  They don't add anything except costumes anyways.  Some DLC are locked as preorder bonuses & you can't get them anymore which is also just a terrible business practice that I hate very much.
DLC whining aside, the game itself is good excluding the online modes.  The ranked system leaves much to be desired.  Here's how most of my games end up matched when in ranked.  Either the game puts me against an A+ rank (I'm a D rank) & I get destroyed in 10 seconds, the game puts me up against someone who either abuses some kind of lag exploit by downloading in the background or just has a crap ISP & the game is played at 5FPS, or I get put against someone who plays like an infant & I win easily.
Also, there are a ton of fireball spammers (which isn't the games fault but still is an annoyance).  Online ranked is also full of macro users.  What this means is they mod a controller to input specific commands when they just press a single button.  So, sometimes you will find players who are low ranked & somehow always manage to input pitch perfect combos that you'd only see a high ranking player be able to pull off.  AKA, Cheaters.
Also, this game makes my thumbs & fingers hurt.  Like, a lot.  After about an hour or so of playing trying to beat Arcade on Hardest or just playing online trying to rank up my hands will cramp & I can't continue to play anymore afterwards.  Seriously, if you make a game that causes people pain from playing it you've done something wrong.
The real draw here is the local multiplayer & arcade modes since there's no lag & you can set your own rules.  The most annoying part is that this game is designed with an Arcade Stick in mind.  So, unless you're planning on playing this with an expensive & sturdy arcade controller don't bother playing it seriously.  Your thumbs will thank you for this.
The game also doesn't have a tutorial which is a darn shame.  There is a challenge mode which shows you some basics but "some" is the key word here.  It barely shows you how to do anything with zero explanation.  I have plenty of 2D fighting games at my disposal & nearly all of them have some kind of tutorial mode, so why can't a AAA game developer like Capcom hash out some extra funding to make one?  A game like this should have an in-depth tutorial for every indivitual character.  Instead you get a half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥challenge mode that any average player will find impossible to complete 100%.
The game also has issues.  A good example is turning on V-Sync or Anti-Aliasing will cause an input lag effect.  This means there will be a delay on when you press a button to when your character does what you commanded.  If you have both on the effect is very noticable.  You'll have to turn these both off if you want a decent gameplay experience.
Another problem I have frequently is when trying to throw a fireball the character will instead throw an uppercut.  This happens on several occasions & is very frequent.  That's what happens when you make a game that uses such similar button presses to seperate different moves.  This is another problem that seems the only way to fix is to go out & buy an arcade controller or some kind of controller that's better suited for fighting games, which I'm not going to do.
There are also some odd hitboxes, best example of this is Hugo.  He's the biggest character in the game, slow & lumbering grappler, but his hitbox is the same size as Ken's or Cammy's.  Some moves will just go straight through his head while he's ducking.  Not blocking, just ducking.  One of the dumbest things I've ever seen in any game ever.
Combos require too much precision to pull off properly.  You also can't make your own combos in this game.  You have to figure out what combos the game will let you pull off for each character or look them up in a guide.  Also, there are a lot of tricks & such that the game itself will not tell you anything about so a guide is pretty much mandatory to be good at this game.  The biggest tactic being the dash cancel the game tells you nothing about.
Overall, the game itself is good but much of which is meant specifically for E-Sports & serious players only.  Casuals should probably steer clear of online modes otherwise (if you're like me) you'll just get frustrated at how poorly the game controls with a standard controller & how the online modes are just utter garbage that are full of lag spikes & people who take the game way too seriously.
In short, Go Pro or Go Home.

A pretty fun sci-fi zombie shooter. Don't go in expecting a triple A quality game, but what you will find is an entertaining and nicely polished FPS that should occupy you for a few hours.
The game has several game modes, including a short story campaign, as well as survival missions (survive before the time is up), and biohazard missions (survive all enemy waves). The game is not focused on story, so you'll not find any huge plot twists or character development here, but you will get to shoot a tonne of zombies and explore a dark and atmospheric sci-fi spaceship.
The game has a lot of weapons that you get to unlock as you progress, all of which you can improve with various upgrades (damage, accuracy, etc) by using the money that you find throughout the levels. In addition you also get upgrades to your suit and cool things like bullet time and a powerful energy burst attack that pulverizes any enemy in the vicinity.
Most missions are very much alike, so some people might find it repetitive, and the game is mostly fun in short bursts. But the core mechanics are fun and well executed. I've only found the grenade-throwing zombies to be a huge pain as they often hide somewhere in a zombie mob, and before you know one of them is around, you get whacked with a grenade explosion, which can 1-hit kill you if it blows up very close to you. Apart from those, there are no frustrating aspects.
A fun indie game all in all.

It's a♥♥♥♥♥♥game, but it's a lot closer to being decent than people are giving it credit for. If they fixed a few problems, it would have actually been fun.
The first weapon you get is some sort of electrical gauntlet that recharges in a couple seconds. Because of this weapon, I found myself dragging fights out for as long as possible to make the most use of its free ammo. Not the most compelling gameplay mechanic, even though I know I'm more careful with ammo than I need to be.
Ranged enemies can be extremely annoying, especially bomb throwing enemies wich deal 3-4 times as much damage as any other enemy at the point where they start showing up.
The health system itself is simple bar segments, like hearts in old games. You regain all your health every time you use a health station, and the health station is then disabled. This makes certain areas MUCH more difficult than others based on the availability of health stations. Would have been better off going with standard health pickups.
It's very easy to get pinned in by small enemies, at which point you may as well restart. Your character is really quite fast when sprinting, and you have a sidestep move that is actually very nice. However, none of that helps when the corridors are 5 feet wide and you can't jump. I know it was a mobile game, but being able to jump would have made combat MUCH more enjoyable. As it is, you can be standing somewhere and suddenly realize you can't move because 4 or 5 crawling enemies have surrounded you.

To start this off, I'll describe a bit of the game first to help you really know what you're going to be buying. Middle-earth: Shadow of Mordor is a hack and slash game based around the lore of the Lord Of the Rings, with Orcs, formally known as Uruks, running around trying to kill you. It might seem stale but believe me when I say it's not. This game is like Assassin's Creed meets Lord Of the Rings and to me that is one of the best combination out there.
The game's story is interesting I will say, but does have some flaws. If you asked for the main concept of it, I'd reply saying there's a bad guy that's very powerful and seems like he could be unbeatable. Similar kind of format to other campaign's, but either way it was still interesting to me nevertheless.
In summary the gam'es story is not the greatest, but it's still decent.
I've put combat here second because I just can't wait to talk about combat. The combat is the most satisfying combat I've ever played in a game period. The executions just make you feel so badass and like you're a god. You might think it would get repetitive but no, not at all. It feels as fresh as when you first got into the game. There's really not much other to say about it, other than this game's combat is so fluent and satisfying to the player.
In the game, the Uruks have Captains and Warchiefs all around Mordor, and they have followers, which are the standard Uruk you'll see, and the Warchief's followers are some Captains in the branch that are a lot tougher. I feel that if this system wasn't in the game, I wouldn't of liked it as I do. To me the system seems fresh and something you'll rarely ever see, (at least for me anyways) and it just keeps me fresh with content. And then the Uruks rank up when you die, but I'll talk about that in a different section. The way you can work your way to the top of the branch by killing the Uruks is plenty of fun for me and I can guarantee it will be for you as well. All in all, great system for this game.
The punishment in this game for when you die is not very brutal, but definitely something that reminds you that maybe shouldn't die next time. Once you die, the Uruks get promotions, the ones that killed you that is. Not only is it the ones that killed you, but if a captain survived your attack, he will gain power as well from surviving. Letting a standard Uruk kill you will most-likely become captain. Once they kill you all sorts of things happen. Sometimes if they kill you they get different motives to start a feast or feel like their unstoppable and they can defeat anything since they defeated you. That's only just one of the examples of what could happen after you die. Even though it obviously is bad for you to die and have them go up in the ranks, yet it still is pretty interesting to watch it all unfold.

This is one of those games where you wish Steam had a star rating system vice a simple yes or no.  This review is a quick look from a single day playtest.
Background this past week my core group of friends have test 3 games in the same genre and found them all lacking one aspect or another.  H1Z1, Infested and Miscreated  should all get together and have a love child to pull in their best features.
Miscreated although a beautiful world, is lacking.
Antagonists:  Other players are more dangerous than the environment; this is fostered by a distinct lack of mutants.  In over a full day I can count the number of mutants (this games zombies) we encountered on one hand; including spending a full day night cycle in the bowels of one of the larger cities.
Other players are kill on sight (KOS).  There simply is not enough of a mobile adversary in the environment and the reward to risk ratio is much higher than exploration.  Don't come into the game expecting anyone to work together; you will be harvested by other players for your shirt to make into scraps of cloth.
Survival;  Survival games all possess an expected level of difficulty.  However, there is an expectation of reward commiserate to the risk you pursue.  Hours spent within a large city depths ended up in a push; almost every cupboard, box or house ended up with the same "Nothing useful remains" or similar notification.  Your inventory is limited even with some larger packs and with a single can of food taking up a space you are prevented from truly scavenging to lay in supplies; unless you adopt a team based system; Player A is food, Player B is woods/metals, Player C is electronics...etc.
Which while for a group of friends is manageble; makes single player... very meh.
The push for food and water drives exploration but at this point it seems distracting to the point of tedium vice a challenge.  In our entire time in a large city, we left finding next to nothing of value other than some fuel for our car that we stumbled onto within the first 30 minutes of playing; and the only conflict was the poor ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ we ran over on a bridge, as we left the city, as he was typing asking for help in /area chat.
Building; while the building system seems robust (as evidenced by the number of empty, in air, floating bases you would come across. The world was not broad enough where you were not constantly engageing in other players and with the tedium of food and water; base building could not be efficiently explored during the first day of playtesting.  The bigger problem; the work needed just seemed tiresome vice fun and a buddy summed it up best; "it just seems like a game of Playerunknown's Battlegrounds"
Combat: is right where it should be as far as feeling lethal.  Hitting something with a Fireman's axe has the requisite effect.  The biggest issues would be the reloading mechanisms which requires a little too much interaction at this point; open inventory, drag bullets, close inventory, tab to raise weapon again.  The game needs a reload animation whether it's loading single shells or magazines.
My biggest issue again is the lack of things to fight; in a "zombish survival game" I am always leery about popping off rounds lest we draw waves of zed; in Miscreated usually you use the staccato of fire to either find your next target or avoid getting ganked.  It seems you are often hearing people shooting; and usually at each other.
Environment; Beautiful; water effects, rain, the ability to make use of camoflage and terrain, and and lack of player names overhead makes the game immersive.  The interiors are less impressive; and begin to feel very cookie cutter.  The map systems seems artificially difficult but again; tedious vice challenging.
Recommendation:  at this time I think the game needs further development and refinement.  I think it could be one of the better games out there for the genre; but as it exists today.  It's a pass.

My experience with this game so far is mixed. I like the game, but at the same time I do not. I heard the about this game through some friends who warned against purchasing the game. I am however, the type that likes to make my own judgment on games, so I proceeded to purchase the game. The game over all to me had the feel of DayZ, but much more put together and oragnized. My first hour or two went very well, I was finding good loot, slaying some zombies and just over all having a good ol time! Even found a pedal bike to get around. That is until the srever restarted and it completely disappeared and I was back to the running simulator. Everything was great......and then my inventory became full. I told myself it was time to build a base (my experince from most survival games you can build storage to store your belongings) to store my epic loot i was finding....this is where the game took a turn for the worse. It almost completely ruined the game for me, but with the game being in Alpha I am willing to give it more time to see how it progresses. Now I went into this knowing full well it aimed to be more realistc then most survival games, to keep you on edge. However, my actual experience would say yes and no. The game is realistic in the fact when your wondering around you are forced to stay more alert then other survival games, you have to pay attention to the derbi or you can miss really good loot, etc..., but where it fell off from being realistic is how storage, base building, and vehicles work. The issue came with the fact that that your character can only hold 40kg weight limit, close to half of that is already used up with equipped gear, so really useable for me was around 20-25kg. I had the inventory space on my character to store many items thanks to clothing/ backpacks I was finding, but I could never make full use of the intventory space due to the weight limit. To make matters worse you can build small storage chest but is very limited in what you can place in them and only ONE can be built in a base. There are Large chests, but you must first find the guide by randomly looting (I have not found one yet) and even then you are only allowed ONE large chest. Now I understand that this makes you pick and choose what to keep carefully, but the game aims to be realistic. Strictly limiting storage is not realistic imo. In a post-apocalyptic world im sure people would be grabing and hording any supplies they can get ahold of. Now I do not expect there to be unlimited storage, but at least something that gives a resonable amount. Base building can be pain all on its own. The plot sizes are big enough imo, but you have to find perfectly level terrain, I was not able to build on any slopes, and the crafting of base parts can get confusing and can easily become a cluster****. You do not even start off with all the recipes needed to even build the most basic secure base, you must first find one of the three guides by randomly looting (my current base has no roof yet). The weight limit on your toon will limit you to one piece at time for the most parts, which is fine, makes sense. Lastly, vehicles are another beast in their own. You must scavenge all the parts needed: Drive Belt, Spark Plugs, x4 Wheels, Battery, Gas, and Oil. Use them with one of the vehicles laying about that you can and you can drive it around. Alot of people strictly use them for inventory space and enclose them into their bases. On server restarts one of two things happens. Either you loose all gas and oil put into the vehicle (even if it was full before the restart) or the vehicle itself will just disappear all together. I have not messed with vehicles all that much yet, but this has been my experince so far. Also the amount of vehicles allowed on on each server is limit to certain amount. Also another player can easily destory a your vehicle with an assualt rifle and one magazine of ammuntion.
Overall, I love the idea Miscreated has and I really want to see this game at its full potential. As I have said earlier, I am not gonna let the few bad experiences ruin this game for me yet. The Game is in Alpha and I do not know what the Devs have in store for the game, but I do hope it involves these issues and any other issues I have yet to run into. I do reccommend this game, because it is still fun to play and is still actively being worked on. I view the bad experinces I have as incompleted parts of the game and im sure one day they will completed. Until then I will lay and wait to see what the future has in store.

An open-world survival zombie game. I've only played the main game, so I can't comment on the DLCs. There's a huge amount to like here and I greatly enjoyed my time with it. It feels rough around the edges, as open world games often do. I played on relatively low graphics settings and still experienced a few soft-crashes on my Radeon card -this is purely speculative, but I'd wager it works better on machines of similar design to xboxes. Because this is very much a console port in most respects, not that those favouring controllers will notice or mind too much.
What I like:
- Great balancing of melee + gun combat against zeds, neither is punished too heavily
- Scavenging and economy fit together nicely without being excessively time consuming
- Mercenaries style call in menu is great for those "oh crap, how am I going to survive this" moments without being overpowered
- Zombies: not too threatening alone, pain in the♥♥♥♥♥en masse
- Great variety in loot, you're not finding the same tin of beans over and over
- Interesting community mechanics -you're not the only ones out there, even if you sometimes feel like the only person who actually does anything
- Permadeath and multiple characters -I got one of my favourite characters killed by a feral (think L4D hunter) during a routine scavenging mission, the game didn't even break stride
- Good balance of stealth with speed. Sneaking and searching quitely are very worthwhile with weaker characters when a horde or two are shambling past
- The closest thing I can think of to a single player DayZ
What I don't like:
- Dodgy keyboard controls. There's probably a better layout than the default, or else use a controller.
- AI is occasionally idiotic/suicidal/broken, zombies themselves have very basic pathfinding
- Sieges where you board up windows don't really work since 90% of the time you're the only person who'll open fire and melee doesn't work very well through boarded windows. That and the door often stays wedged open letting most zombies in.
- Broken scripting can crop up fairly frequently, including the final mission (slightly anticlimatic, to say the least)
- Most information is hidden away in the game's journal, with plenty of "wait, what was that?" occasions of information overlap/overload
- Little incentive to build up anyone other than two tough characers (probably Marcus + Maya) who you just rotate when one gets tired or injured
- Freak infected are all ripoffs of L4D enemies, (I guess the screamer never technically made it into L4D), but only the juggernaut (tank) is actively unfun to fight (not got a powerful gun and plenty of ammo? Hope you're a bullfighter)
- The game spams time-limited-offer missions at you, many of which can have serious penalties for non-attendance
- Little incentive to acquire the best loot or try more than one or two of the home locations -the final mission is perfectly beatable with common firearms if you bring slightly more ammo than you normally would.
Having said all that, if there were a co-op orientated sequel announced tomorrow, I'd be looking to buy it.

I tried using the camera to zoom in and see if that fixed it but the camera controls were flat out unresponsive. The controls are not intuitive at all even when they do work anyways. It's a LEGO-console Diablo-ish team based action RPG, where you always control a team of 4 heroes (or this time, vallains!) and you practically go forward on linear maps filled with mini sideways leading to the many collectibles that can unlock new characters, art, audiodisc, dossiers about characters and the MARVEL world itself.
The gameplay changed in many ways while feels exactly like MUA1. The same control patterns, grabs, throws, whatever, but characters are much more diverse. Ultimate abilities are gone, however instead you have Fusion abilities that allow a unique super powerful skill-duo of 2 heroes, with not entirely but relatively very, very much unique combinations of 24x23 heroes, such as spreading Iron Man's most powerful laser all over the screen with Wolverine's claws or mirror it back from Captain America's shield for a much stronger single and controllable beam, etc. with 24x23 combinations.
The gameplay's "feel" in general is much more fluid, characters have more unique abilities with less overlapping compared to MUA1, but they also have only 4 abilities instead of 4 choosable out of 7 (but they change if you upgrade them, visually and mechanically too!), and the gameplay design also shifted from less but stronger (more RPG-ish with resistances etc.) enemies to far, far more many that die easier, and I can tell you that slicing through 10-30 enemies with a metallic tornado controlled by Magneto while Human Torch makes the entire whirl burst with flames (or Gambit making each metal piece charged with explosive force) is uncomparable to MUA1's single ultimate abilities.
The combat is much better, there are way, way less empty filler talking (in fact: 0) with a far better Secret War + Civil War storyline that is actually very enjoyable and the new slightly Mass-Effect-ish conversation systems allow for a lot optional talk that isn't written in a tiresome cringeworthy way like before, so definitly huge improvements here. The "gold" you collect is finally automatic and each hero gets it separately so you can upgrade everyone at the same time and never going to feel like "I should have played him/her much sooner, he/she is too weak at this point of the game" like in MUA1.
Having only 4 abilities per hero is I say acceptable in exchange for the Fusion abilities and having more Unique heroes, but sadly everyone has only 1 unlockable alternative costume. At some point in the game you have to pick a side in the Civil War and some heroes naturally belong to your enemy, so they can potentially go locked (templorarly, don't worry just wait for the story to unfold!) and their alternative costumes won't be unlockable until you replay the game again and pick the other side (registration of superheroes or fighting to stay anonym), and this can potentially be frustrating to some. It was for me too for a while, but as much fun as I'm having with MUA2 I'm definitly replaying it in the future if not instantly after finishing it, because your hero progression and unlocks carries over to new game+ on higher difficulties, so I'm not really bothered by this limitation on a few heroes, rather encouraged to play more instead.
MUA2 had an absolutely garbage relase, but it's been fixed up nicely since. Main problems were controller compatibility issues (adressed, though pay attention the store page says PARTIAL controller support, so the layout is not customizable!) and the game was absolutely unenjoyable because of terrible sound issues making everything sound like your neightbour is drilling the wall (this also has been adressed and is perfect now). Regarding performance, you can easily achieve 60fps and play through the entire (very enjoyable) game, however there is some strange fps swinging when the game randomly drops to 40-50 fps from 60 even if you are standing still doing nothing, so there is that miniature drop that happens a few times (like 2-3 times every 5 minutes) but really you won't feel it, because the gameplay and the animation isn't working in a way that would make it annoying like in an FPS, personally I wouldn't even notice it by now if not having fps written in the corner of the screen. Also the game starts in Windowed Mode for some reason, just Alt+TAB away and back and it's fixed!

If you're looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if you're looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.
Eat.

Great game. Difficult and challenging, but fair. Some RNG, but there's enough methods of working with what you're given to turn it from RNG into a well-managed play session each time. This game definitely rewards skillful play, as well as game knowledge - you can only get better as you practice, and you'll feel it.
The art direction of this game is mind-numbingly great as well. Enemy designs are both immediately identifiable and beautifully done - nothing feels out of place, and similar stylistic elements often denote similarities in abilities. The environment is superbly crafted despite the basic room structures - each floor has its own unique personality, and lends to the story-telling of the game in a beautifully subtle way. The soundtrack is flawless - it can be both brooding and heart-racing, while also being calm and soothing enough that it can repeat thousands of times and still sound wonderful, never once being an annoyance but instead a well-established part of the environment.
Overall, this game is more than worth the price tag(s). Playing through it casually gives you an interesting (if horrific) story, told non-verbally almost all the time. Playing it seriously lends a vast amount of replayability and skill-based progression, as well as an extensive list of challenges and goals to complete that lead you ever forward. Playing it competitively is also an option - this game has a healthy speedrunning community as well as the Racing+ mod, which streamlines some portions of the game (such as allowing each character to start with the D6, the primary method of combating the inherent RNG), as well as allowing you to race head-to-head with your friends. The only type of person I wouldn't recommend this to are the people who anger easily - this is by no means an easy game, and will demand patience if you want to fully complete it. The satisfaction will be palpable though, and never once does a death feel like the game cheated you.
Buy this and both DLC. With the latest DLC, the game supports modding through Steam workshop, making the allure of new content easy to sate. Plus the developer routinely adds their favorite mods into the base game, effectively curating the top community content - a wholly welcome gesture, and a heart-warming one at that. Thanks guys, thanks for this wonderful game. The last time I desired to 100% complete a game was likely at least a decade ago, but The Binding of Isaac rekindled that flame in my heart. <3

You can build utilities in your base, and even move bases later on in the game. If your neighbours trust you enough, they might even ask to join your group. You can also ask one of the main characters, Lilly Ritter to radio out to other survivors so they can join you, or ask if any other survivors know where food/weapons/ammo etc. can be found.
Survivors will lose hope in the group's survival, because it's still a zombie apocalyse and they're dead people trying to eat you, so you can talk to them about it and get them to blow off their steam while killing zombies or boost their esteem.
The weaponry in this game comes in different varieties, there's guns and melee weapons, but there's different types of them. for meleee weapons, there's blunt types, edged, and heavy weapons. For guns there's shotguns, snipers, handguns, and assault rifles (which are hard to find.)
Each survivor has their own pros and cons, for example one could be a good shot, but is an alcoholic, which would determine the survivor's stats. In the game, there are six slots for your character's stats. The four stats which every survivor will have is fighting, cardio, shooting, and wits. The other two can be for anything special about the character. For example, the first survivor you start out with, Marcus is a physical powerhouse, meaning you should have him using heavy weapons like sledgehammers, (my personal favourite combo) and he's also a born leader, making him one of the (best survivors in the game hint hint.) Each of those stats can be leveled up to a maximum of seven, but starting at four you can choose a perk that you can also level up seven times. Starting at level four of fighting/shooting, you can specialize in a type of gun or a type of melee weapon then level up that specialization up to seven as well.
The fighting mechanics are pretty straightforward, if you use the rolling mechanic correctly you shouldn't actually have to use guns. There isn't that much of a story, but the game is mainly focused to surviving. The game can get kind of repetitive, but this game isn't actually in a completed state yet. This is one of my favourite games of all time, and I rate this 9/10.

Dead Effect is an extremely fun sci-fi zombie FPS. It has awesome graphics, controls great, decent sound effects and great atmosphere. There is plenty of ammo to be found, several weapons, grenades, gold, and currency that can be used to buy upgrades for your weapons. Its short, kind of generic, but it's the first FPS I've been able to play without getting incredibly nauseated and a horrible headache, so I like it. Is it perfect? No, but I would pick it up on sale.

Yes, it's a mobile port. No, it doesn't look bad. You can compare the graphics to Deus Ex: Human Revolution. And no, the controls don't feel like your playing a former mobile game at all - the developers really put a lot of effort into it.
The gameplay is a bit like Killing Floor in a SciFi-setting, but with more or less linear levels. They aren't very long and the story is average, but it's a really enjoyable FPS if you don't expect an AAA game.
There's also a survival mode, but I have more fun playing the missions. You can collect money, upgrade your weapons and find collectibles which give you background info, there's also a New Game Plus mode. However, I didn't complete my second playthrough because I quickly got bored by the gameplay while playing the lame survival mode for achievements.
For 99 cents this is a really good deal.

Cons:
- There should be a way to close hatches from which zombies come in (at least for some period of time). That would not only add some extra things to do but also could be helpfull in general. -Though the game is good but as a shooter it doesnt really bring anything unique to the table ( as a shooter).

Overall it's a great game and even when it has full price I think it's wort to try. Great game if you want to just log in kill stuff, finish few missions and log out. As well as to read some funny notes that gives you more information about yourself and stuff that is around you.

tl:dr Excellent, but imperfect, RPG with loads of content, balanced gameplay, and good writing.
Pros:
Excellent writing. I am putting the main story in the con section but that doesn't change the fact that there were superior segments of writing throughout the main quest and the many sidequests.
Interesting and well written companions.
Excellent leveling system.
Balanced gameplay.
Challenging but balanced optional fights.
Clever item system that prevents min/maxing, or at least, makes it more difficult.
Tons of content.
Cons:
The main story should have been good but it never really gave you a reason to feel invested. The end reveal had some interesting twists but I couldn't bring myself to care that much. It just did not feel like their was a unifying vision for the story.
Graphically the world didn't feel very consistent either. Basically if you felt like the towns in Elder Scrolls Oblivion were cookie cutter different without a single connecting artistic vision then you will feel the same way about Pilllars.
Sometime it felt like there was too much content, a bit of the Witcher 3 syndrome. I still think Witcher 3 is the best RPG ever made and I still haven't finished the main story. One thing Inqusition did excellently was tie in sidequests to the overall plot. Now the problem with Inqusition is you never got the pay off from those tie ins but I do think Pillars would have benefited from a similiar system.
The castle you get sucks outside the bounty hunter hut and the excellent dungeon underneath it.
Bad graphics. Nature of the game. Didn't bother me because I knew what I was getting into but it might bother some folk.

The story is dark and wonderful. It explores themes like ethics in science, self-determination and religious fanaticism that have been left out of mainstream video games for a long time and asks you to make some very difficult decisions that have a real impact on the world.
The combat is a throwback to the old Infinity Engine games made by the developers who actually worked on those games at Interplay and Black Isle Studios.
They have however modernized or trimmed numerous tedious aspects of those games (I'm looking at you THAC0) and made the end-result feel a lot tighter. Also this game is seriously challenging, if you're completely unfamiliar with isometric CRPGs or if you're in it for the story start playing on easy, there's certainly no shame in it and you'll save yourself a lot of frustration while you're learning the ropes.
The White March expansion (both parts) is absolutely worth the money. You should definitely get it if you find yourself enjoying the game. However, since the expansion's story takes places during the main campaign (between Act 2 and Act 3 IIRC) you shouldn't wait too long after starting.
In conclusion, whether you've been jonesing for that sweet isometric fix for the last fifteen years or you've never even thought about touching the stuff, you should give Pillars of Eternity a shot!

Now that I think about the ordeal it has been a while since I last played this sort of open world game. Well, Middle-earth: Shadow of Mordor happens to be the one which breaks the streak of no-plays. How did it do? Only one way to find out.
Let's get one thing out of the way first – this is a glorified and well-produced fan fiction. I've seen so many people lose their minds over how it insults Tolkien and Lord of the Rings. In my opinion these people are taking their fantasy way too far. Story-wise Shadow of Mordor needs to be looked at as something standalone even if it does draw from familiar imagery and, for book readers at least, character(s) you may not have necessarily imagined as competent warriors. To put matters into perspective game follows one Talian, a ranger of Gondor standing watch over the Black Gate, as some shenanigans involving developer original characters raid the place, put himself and his family to the sword for some weird ritual and call it a day. Or do they? Well, that's obviously not the end of the journey for our ranger as he soon find himself sharing his body with a mysterious Elf wraith and sets out to avenge his family and undo as much of the damage as he can.
Problem here is, well, story is very weak. Not necessarily in the premise alone which is your classical “revenge story, but something happens along the way so things escalate”, but in essence how it's presented. Perhaps due to game format with the way it handles open world, but I think it has more to do with how sparsely the main story is dolled out to you. There's maybe five or six hours of it in a 20+ hour game and that's probably being generous. Just as much is allotted to side missions which I hesitate to call quests because they're really not, few exceptions where you team up with exiled ranger, smug dwarf and warrior princess notwithstanding. Game also embraces “collect X of Y” for side content, but I actually rather liked how these had stories associated with them. Broken dagger is just broken dagger until you find out how a slaved escaped with it, for example.
As far as gameplay goes... well, have you played any of the Batman Arkham games? Then you've played Shadow of Mordor. Not to say game doesn't make use of its license for flavor, but that's pretty much it when you boil it down. You do missions, collect experience and currency called Mirian to further your abilities and upgrades. One twist here is that to unlock further ability tier you need Power aka red points which you procure by dealing directly with Uruks, main enemies of the game. I'll talk more about the Nemesis system itself in a later paragraph because it's the sole highlight of the game, but I wasn't really a fan how some pretty vital abilities are locked from you until story advances far enough. This just doesn't work in an open world game where you can explore the first half pretty much however you want and the second half is a greener version of the first.
It should also be noted there is a stealth system in the game and it synergizes pretty well with the rest. It doesn't feel tacked-on so you will fortunately never have the “forced stealth level” experience. I would say stealth and head-on action are represented in equal parts both in gameplay and abilities you can unlock. There is another advancement route and those are Runes you acquire as you kill Uruks, runes you can implant into your three weapons – sword, bow and dagger – for various status modifiers. This is the main way you can affect how Talion plays seeing as you will [eventually] get your hands on all the upgrades/abilities.
Speaking of the Nemesis I've hinted at earlier now's the time to tackle it. I love the damn thing. Could it be improved? Absolutely, but I think the biggest problem is how game essentially locks the most important aspect, branding Uruks and making them your slaves, until you get to the second half of the game. This feels like a really underhanded move for no real reason because they give you everything else and let you have fun with the system. So what is it? Well, there are regular Uruks running around and then there are Uruk captains with their own hierarchy of power on top of which sit the Warchiefs. These captains/Warchiefs are named and have their own cocktail of strength, immunity, fear, etc combinations which you may prey on or otherwise exploit. So what's the best part then? You can game this system to your pleasure. Until you get the branding ability you don't really have much freedom over “do I kill this cool looking captain or not?”, but once you acquire it the world opens do you. Like that particular captain for his ninja mask? Well, brand him and make him your pet project – he goes on a recruitment drive and you follow, rival is about to execute him and you step in to save him... eventually you make him betray his Warchief and you have an inside man. Sadly, for all the amazing uses and potential the Nemesis system requires you to to be bad at the game to A) actually use it naturally without forcing passage of time if you don't die and B) need it to get things done. Which leads me to another point, that being....
Game is damn too easy. I'm not even such a good player or anything, but had the story not forced my hand in dealing with Warchiefs and if I wasn't interested in the system, I think I would've most likely ignored it all because you are a one-man army. Just play smart and use all the assets as well as check for enemy weaknesses and you'll do fine.
I also played DLC for the game so let's give that a whirl or two.
Miscellaneous DLC is straight up Pay2Win overpowered runes you should forget even exist. Do yourself a favor and don't make an already easy game even easier. First real piece of content we get is Lord of the Hunt in which Talion teams up with Torvin and they hunt even deadlier prey. Really, this is all about riding and creature variants. If you liked monsters in the base game and wanted more, this is it. Torvin's journal entries were a really nice additions. Second piece of story is The Bright Lord which is actually a prequel where we assume the role of [name redacted for spoiler reasons] Elf lord before he became a wraith and see how he got entangled with Sauron. The One Ring is OP as hell, but this story also gimps the protagonist and is probably the most challenging of the bunch. Honestly? Both additional campaigns could use more variety and were pretty short, running maybe under two hours each, but if you liked what you already played they're worthwhile extensions. Trials of War is a collection of challenge maps which weren't really my thing because this is not the kind of game where I care about my score, but you might.
So in closure – would I recommend Shadow of Mordor? Yes, just keep in mind you're not really getting an original experience and if you approach with expectations of LotR fan you might be in for some hurt. This is yet another case where Steam could benefit from some neutral recommendation, but the way things are I give it tentative thumbs up.

Excellent strategy game that's all about conquest, leveling up your units to ridiculous levels of power and supporting them with all kinds of spells. Best dev support ever: since game release they've added Multiplayer, heroes, artifacts, a better UI, terraforming and in DLCs, a new race and the new Armaggeddon game mode.
The demo has not been updated with those features so it won't give you a correct idea of the game.
While people who don't have much of a strategy game culture will compare this to Civ V, developer Ino Co have been masters of hex-based strategy games for a long time, with Fantasy Wars
and the Elven Legacy (not on Steam for the moment as its publishing deal ended) series. They basically took the kind of gameplay they know well how to do and added Age of Wonders-like spell research and city management. There is no tech tree, complex diplomacy, cultural trees, no real research besides random spell picks or any of those Civ trappings, it's mostly about warfare.
My only complaints would be that the AI is not evenly challenging and that endgames can verge on the boring when you know you have the power to crush the enemy but sieging cities takes forever. And don't leave your cities unguarded, as some random events spawn powerful creatures behind your lines.
All in all though, highly recommended. Looking forward to the sequel!

The more polished, better looking cousin of Counter Strike, Condition Zero is the version of Counter Strike to not only play, but for developers to beat.  The addition of the much-required shield has an important balance factor; it counters the usage of the AWP.
The hit detection is once again, superior to CSGO, much like the previous Counter Strike, and the aim for the weapons isn't cartoonishly exaggerated where you have weapons like the M249 and the shotgun being actually viable.
Online play is head-and-heels above CSGO's.  In CSGO you feel like everythings a waste of time unless you're playing in competitive matches, while in CSCZ, and CS, pubs rule the game (like all classic multiplayer games).  I can't say how sweet it was when someone who was clearly a CSGO player who looks like he just started playing CSCZ, killed a team mate to defuse the bomb himself, and then got perma-banned by the moderator.  It was also the moment where I realized that the behaviors of players in CSCZ compared to CSGO are not just different, but the CSGO behavior is just ♥♥♥♥ing awful and counter-intuitive to team work.  You have people competing fo points to get a higher rank quicker so that they can unlock more skins, which they can trade/sell for a hugely over-priced margin (some skins being worth more than CSGO itself).
I guess it just goes to show that if you're someone who actually wants to enjoy playing the game, CSCZ is the game for you.  CSGO is just another "competitive" game with nothing more to it than popularity, driven mostly by the market economy the game has created for itself, suffering the same fate as TF2 and Dota 2.
I would recommend CSCZ over CSGO any day and not because it's what I used to play (since I have none, as I barely ever touched it for more than a few minutes back in the day), but because the balance, design, and overall aesthetic is just so much more satisfying and fun to experience compared to more modern online FPS games.

This game is good, but it comes with a few conditions:
If you have shaky internet, don't expect a good online experience.  It won't even come close to acceptable.
Use forced Vsync via your graphics card (NOT IN-GAME VSYNC).  For whatever crazy and nonsensical reason, this game runs better online with it slammed at 60 fps via Vsync and not just because you have the in-game option set to "fixed".  Also, you'll want to mess around with your Vsync options to test for input lag.  For me, I use adaptive Vsync because the game is generally good at staying at a constant framerate on my setup, so this produces the best in both online environments and in terms of input lag for me.  Regular Vsync and triple buffered Vsync cause a noticable delay on my rig.  For others it is different and it really just depends, but using Vsync in some manner should be aimed for.
The game is standard SFIV fair: easy to understand, hard to master.  This game is both deceptively accessible and not accessible.  Be warned, you will have the urge to practice.  And if you don't, well time to move on I guess.

I have spent almost 60 hours in game and yes that may not be a lot, but I have played other games very very similar to Miscreated. I feel its time to write a review and get the word out on how this game is for those that may be on the fence about picking it up.
First off, the graphics are pretty good. I feel they could be better when maxing out the view distances you still get the blank canvas when looking say at a hillside from distance the grass and trees seem to vanish which allows for the player to be spotted easily, I'm not sure any game of this type has ever really gotten this right, but in a city setting in close quarters the detail is very well put together. I find myself taking extra time just to check out the detail.
Second, the sounds are really good, there are just some situations when the sound could be better....i.e.  Walking in boots compared to sneakers, the sound is the same, very loud boot sounds to give other players an advantage on knowing where you are. Also, when switching out from one weapon to another and droping an object like a can of food on the ground it's absurdly loud and can sound like you just dropped and anvil from the roof, so other players again can pinpoint your location super easy.
The game allows first person as well as third which is always nice in games like this, but with your weapon at the ready bring the weapon up to aim seems to be clunky and takes a second longer than it should.
The base building in the game is nothing special, there is no lower or raise, or tilt to walls, no snap building system to quickly and easily make the walls or floors uniform which really pings my OCD most times. They currently allow for building over road and rivers which is annoying but in reality can be done, but then again I can walk a lot more quiet in my chuck tylors converse than in steel toed boots.
Now the meat of the game, Yes it's in Early Access so I am hoping to see these changes soon....
There is no battle eye system or anti-hack system currently in place and within my first 60 hours I have seem to have run into a teleport type hack from only one player that was actually on an official server. He was in almost every location after I was killed the first time and so called ported close to my location 3 or 4 more times after. Spawning in the game is random and only takes 30 seconds to get back into game after you are killed. Some locations take 5 to 10 minutes to run to depending.
Another exploit I fear is Duping, after hours of nothing but gathering I can only, if I am lucky get 30 to 40 rounds that will fit my gun. I have seen and been a part of gun fights where the groups that are already established in most cases will shoot and continue to shoot as if they have no ammo limit. Upon further investigation, filling your backpack, putting it on and taking it off in a fast pace multiple times then disconnecting, can actually give you a pack on your back and one with exactly the same items you had at your feet.
Hopefully these things are already being looked at and get fixed I would hate for this game to end up being another DayZ Failalone. The game is still fun, and I continue to play it. It has actually come a long way since they first put this out on EA.
