The Red Solstice is a much needed addition to any tactician or squad-based lover's game library. In it, you and up to 7 other Marines battle your way through a rather relentless horde of aliens, moving around a large map to try and complete various objectives before ultimately being overrun and forced to evacuate, or making a courageous last stand.
Though there are a couple performance issues (namely clicks and keypresses not always registering when there is a full roster of players) the game is the only I've seen lately that delivers such an in-depth and tactical approach to multiplayer class-based combat. Every class is vastlly different from the others, but no single role is mandatory to a successful squad. Within certain parameters (Elysium Corp won't let you take 8 medics) the squad design is very adaptable, as is each class based on your playstyle.
Tactically, the game pretty rapidly snuffs out heroes who stay away from the cluster too long, but is not unrewarding to a team that can cowardinate an effective division of tasks. Leaders of the squad can issue orders, and set waypoints for the team to follow. Rather than just relying on good communication, your team can physically see where you want them to move to.
I have yet to see a game that is so rewarding to good communication and planning. It is brutally hard, and the developer holds no punches, but if you can gather a strong group of quick thinkers and loyal marines, you might just save Mars Colony.
The impecable sounds, the unrivaled gameplay, and the immense tactical immersion earn this game a 10 out of 10 from Reaper

All the team was droped from a space ship near a beacon.

All the difficulty was to build the defenses, set up traps, protect sentries and for me, keep the other guys alive until the end of days that came on us.
And we made it !
I was a Medic as usual. After so much failures, i could start to upgrade my character.
The upgrade system is really cool, for each class you have a rank and defines how long you played this class, so the higher the better...
Skills wich increase with levels: at the beginning too few, but with few levels... oh my ! That's so good to place a resurecting beacon during a hellish mission ! You can even call orbital drops to give stuff to your comrades or activate buffs to the whole team.
You have new weapons in two different types: primary and secondary. The primary weapons really changes your way to engage, as a Medic i can choose at high rank a sniper rifle, the basic weapon is a weak assault rifle. The secondary give you some shotguns and explosivs weapons like a rotary grenade launcher,ect..
Weapons are different between each classe. Medic: assault rifles. Demolisher: explosivs. Recon: smg. Heavy: minigun, ect...
Your armor can be upgraded with 4 slots to receive some "perks". A bit complicate to use because each perks increase a statistic of the character but reduce an other one. You want to run faster ?
allright but you will have less damages done... quite nasty :'(
All of that is not too much to prepare yourself for the fire of the action.
And this is really tought !
As i said before you gonna die a lot. But winning is very rewarding. Like some few rares games like Arma or Dark Soul.
Enemies are quite numerous and very violent. Every creature has stats (you can see them when you hover your mouse on them). The special events happens quite often, and a good planning is really rewarding, like using explosivs to make chain reactions and take down a boss or a huge horde of creature in one blow. But when your team is splitting... in general you won't stand a chance.
Every classes needs skills to be mastered.
As a Medic i needed quite some time to understand how to get exp correctly (missions or the most common slaving monsters to get xp). Xp give you the opportunity to increase the level of the skills you have choosen (you can only have 4).  The skill level is lost between each mission.
And like many games, maps needs time to be understood because hunker in a building and defending is really difficult. Especially with the light system that influence the line of sight of the team and the accuracy for shooting enemies.
So...
This game is really good but really hard too with unfriendly players that doesn't give a sh... of what you say in game.
It's a bit messy for now but with few updates... this is gonna be a gem !

Okay, As of July 29th, 2016, the game has been patched. Thus far, it seems that the crackling sound and controller issues have been fixed and the game seems to be fully functional.
This port had a really shakey start, but now that it's been fixed, it's a fantastic game. Having played Marvel: Ultimate Alliance 1 to death on the Wii when it was released, I was elated to hear that its sequel was getting a PC port/remaster. After waiting until the patch fixing the host of issues with the game, I picked it up and thus far I have not been disappointed. One thing that you need to realize before making your purchase is that this game is not a remaster, as many first thought. It has been upscaled to modern resolutions and given a boost to 60 fps, but otherwise, no major changes have been made to the game. If you played the game before and enjoyed it, you'll be getting all of the same. Just don't expect anything new. As such, it's very difficult to justify the price-point, so I'd suggest waiting for a sale to purchase the game, or purchasing the current 2-game package that is being offered. I would not recommend this if you do not have a controller or do not like fiddling with key-bindings because the default keyboard controls are ABYSMAL.
On the topic of controllers, I would like to give Zoe/Activision some serious props as they actually took the time to create an official Steam Controller profile for the game, so it's very much plug-n-play. Not enough developers are supporting the steam controller like this, so it was refreshing to load up my configuration and see that it was already good to go.
I recommend this game very lightly as though it's very enjoyable, the price is very difficult to justify for a seven-year-old game with no modern graphical enhancements. If you haven't played the sequel and don't mind the price, however, the game is an absolute treat.

Finished the game in one sitting. It is genuinely a fun game, and I must have been the lucky few to have gotten no problems  in my playthrough. Chose the Anti-Reg path, and finished the game, no problem. However, to be able to finish the game in one sitting (Like almost 6 hours), I do not recommend the game, as it is a quick playthrough.
Although I would like to have played the game with a controller, unforetunately that doesn't work; however it never really affected me in a negative way. Just mapped the controls to buttons on my mouse (Like attack, special attack, and camera) and the game ran very smoothly.
Gameplay-wise, I loved it. I do feel like there are less characters in the game than the first game, and the game prohibits use of other characters (For an extended period) because you chose one side over the other. I do wish there were more characters, while being able to unlock character through challenges. However, a lot of the characters are accessable from the start, and only a few are left to obtain through the storyline. The characters are still great, and teambuilding is very fun and experimental, because of the fact that you can switch your team in a fight (unlike MUA1), which leads to new ways to play the game and adds to the fun aspect of it.
Graphics are great. It's not The Divison level graphics but it's still good to the point where it doesn't look horrible enough for this present-day game graphics.
Although, I was able to find a bug that prevents you from continuing the game. After finishing the Anti-Reg side, I started up a new game on a higher difficulty on Pro-Reg. Game worked perfectly until you reach the level where I actually got to fight Captain America/Iron Man depending on which side you chose. There is an issue that stops further gameplay, to which I think is a gamebreaking bug. There is a door that requires you to press a button on your keyboard repeatedly to open the door. However, even by mashing the button as fast as you can, or as slow-but-fast-enough, you cannot continue. I was able to pass this in my Anti-Reg playthrough but not the Pro-Reg playthrough. Furthermore, you cannot leave the level until you finish it, but the problem is, you can't finish it. Because of this, you can't return to HQ and replay old missions or challenges, just because the game won't allow it. Until that bug gets fixed, I don't recommend buying the game, because it stops further gameplay, and forces you to not finish the game or continue.

If you had asked me about this game when it first released on Early Access, I would have said "buy it, this game has great promise."
Alas, this is another EA game that had potential, made its money, and has been mostly neglected.  It took over a year for the developer to get a decent hunger/thirst/sleep system in the game.  The game managed to somehow look worse over time, the physics engine is worse and you can expect to be launched all over the place by it, sometimes to your death.  The longevity of the game depends directly on your willingness to "tell your own story" because the game lacks depth...it ain't "deep" at all.
It has some great ideas and the game can still look beautiful, but it is concerning that the developer goes awol and doesn't respond for extended periods of time and the game can go for what seems like months without a single update.  We are always being told by fanboys and developers that we should be thankful to be part of the development process of EA games...problem is, there has to actually be consistent development going on for us to get our fair share of that agreement.  Stranded Deep is being neglected, no question about it and if you think otherwise you either need to look at the infrequent changelogs or you need a time machine to go back to experience the game in its initial EA release and compare it with now.  It was better then, and that is insane considering there was even less to do in the game at that point then there is now.
Subnautica might be more of a sci-fi lean to this "ocean survival" genre, but it is much more worth your money than this.

Not much really needs to be said here. It's a fighting game. THE fighting game, currently, until SF5 comes out. It's definitely a move in a good direction for Street Fighter, as it feels much more approachable to newer players than potentially earlier versions or some other fighting games.
At this point however, you may want to wait to pick this up until it goes on sale, and save some money for SF5.
One thing against this game, however, is that the netcode is pretty terrible. Capcom essentially grabbed the exact netcode for multiplayer online matches from the Games For Windows Live! version, and never really translated it properly to work with steam. In my exoerience, this leads to a lot of lag spikes during matches and even in the lobby system. Even if you have Fight Request turned on during a single player training session, it will lag your game intermittently. It definitely doesn't ruin the multiplayer for this version of the game to where it's impractical to play, but it will be noticeable.

Having beat this game for the first time yesterday, I can give a fresh review.
This has to be one of the most engrossing gaming experiences I have ever had. This game will grab your attention and hold it, for every second of every heart-pounding encounter with a new enemy or an area boss. In fact, many of the 'normal' enemies in this game feel like bosses of other games; the learning curve starts steep and rarely lets up as you play the game. Every new location you visit is exotic, every trip underground filled with suspense. Much of the time, there is more suspense packed into this game than the 'horror' games that are becoming more and more common.
The feeling of overcoming seemingly impossible odds is incredible, and you let out a small cheer for your character and yourself as together you land the killing blow on a formidable foe.
Furthermore, I can finally let my gaming competitiveness subside, knowing I have beaten Dark Souls.
"Yeah that game is nice, but have you played Dark Souls?"
Be Prepared to Die, and be prepared to become 'that guy' in this regard.

A classical hardcore RPG game in the legacy of "Baldur's Gate" and "Baldur's Gate II: Shadows of Amn". Obsidian go to show that they do not need an official license for Dungeons & Dragons to make a great RPG. They have sucessfully created a world and a set of rules of their own including the introduction of some unique races and professions. The game is also very long, mainly if you are a proper dungeon crowler, who wants to explore every corner of the game and complete all quests.
Pros:
* Original RPG world
* Very long, took me 93 hours to complete
* Very interesting companions with their personal tales and quest lines.
* Some of the decisions that you make during the game make a difference at the end of the game.
* Some quests have more than one solution including non-fighting ones.
* You can have your own keep to update, defend and receive quests at.
* Very nice isometric graphics respecting the tradition of the aforementioned "Baldur's Gate" series.
* Very addictive, you get the old urge to look at what is just behind the next corner delaying you from going to bed!
Cons:
* Even though I was reading ever dialogue and kept reading the journal I admit that I did not fully comprehend the story.
* Although there are many endings to choose from as to how to end the story, I did not feel that any of them mattered.
* The companions were not as great as in "Baldur's Gate II: Shadows of Amn" and I did not feel touched by their end game fates like I did at the end of "Baldur's Gate II: Throne of Bhaal". (I admit that I almost shed a tear at the end of "Baldur's Gate II: Throne of Bhaal", when Imoen said her introduction sentence from "Baldur's Gate" "Hey, it's me, Imoen").
Pretty graphics, lovely classical music and gruesome deaths. Fun for the whole family.

Game Summary:
Night in the Woods is about a college dropout named Mae returning to her home town to get away from something that was been tormenting her. However, she soon realises that her home town may not be as safe as she onced believed it to be.
Review:
10/10
Night is the woods sets the bar for storyrich indie games. It's so beautifully well done in all aspects;
- Characters are unique and relatable. I related so hard to Mae it hurt. She's funny, silly, sarcastic and most importantly (my favorite) she makes a lot of mistakes.
. I see myself in Mae so much it freaky.
- The character relationship with one another is so real. Youre introduced to all types of people in this game.
Its a realy cute depiction of the world itself.
- The history of the characters and the town they live in is so breathtaking. The creators really did a good job of creating a world all by itself with so much detail put into it.
- The story is paced so well. There are a lot of thing that the player will not know right off the bat but will learn while playing it. With NITW the player will build a kind of routine of visiting certain places and talking to people in the town. You will actually know this little town inside out by the time youre done. And even though its the same thing each chapter the game does a good job of keeping the story interesting. Some story-rich games lack the aspect of getting its players to come back for more while NITW seems to be doing this effortlessly.
- The ending was just mind blowing. You wont see it coming. Trust me, you wont.
- The loor of this game runs deep. You can pretty much theorize about a bunch of things that happened and go unexplained. Any game (in my opinion) that gets you thinking after the game is done, is a game worth playing.

Night in the Woods is about bonds. It's about anxiety, growing up, building relationships and trying not to tear them down. A charming art style, deep characters, and focus on real human issues really makes you care about this game, and leaves you thinking about it for a long while after you finish it.
The soundtrack in this game gave me goosebumps

I absolutely loved it, but it's hard to explain why without sounding like a masochist.  Every single time that I felt comfortable and started to think that I understood how to play, the game changed the rules and I died.  This sounds awful, I know, but I promise you -- it's not.
Each of the game's seven chapters challenges you to do the same thing -- survive -- but the scenario that you find yourself in (and thus the options available to you) are always different.  Every single choice needs to be considered carefully; a balance of risk-taking and careful planning is often necessary, and some actions will have unforeseen consequences.  The apparent randomness here is a stroke of genius on the part of the developers, as I was every bit as relieved as my characters each time that they survived.

In order to recommend this game, you should wait until heavily discounted. This brings very few new ideas to the FPS genre. That in itself is nothing too bad, but there are probably just as many cons as there are pros.
This has a good selection of weapons, plus you can give them upgrades. To buy either, then you need the $ you find in the game. You will not have all weapons and will likely not have too many fully upgraded weapons by the time you finish this. There are a few different pistols, rifles, shotguns and bows you can get, but it seems that there is 1 of each that is the best. If you die, then you have to also use that same in game $ to revive. You get gold (separate currency) that seems to appear from random fights along the way. You can use that to buy better weapons (most will need a second playthrough to afford). You can also use that gold to buy HP regeneration. If you save for just that, you will get it around 2/3 of the way through. By that point the grenade throwers appear making that regeneration mostly useless since they will usually one-shot you. Since there are aid stations throughout every level the regen is not nearly as useful as you would think.

Also, you can only hold on to one pistol weapon, one 2 hander, one type of grenade, and your default melee attack.

I am really scared that Activision is going to leave us in the dust, but it's only day 1. I haven't heard how the PS4/Xbone versions are, but I just really hope they'll get on patching the PC version immediately, as we deserve better for the price we paid for this game.

The other reviews will completely slam this game, and rightfully so. Both titles are a mess right now, but don't let it discourage you. EDIT:
35 of 40 people found the above helpful. Changing my review will wipe that, but I feel the need to keep this updated. The crackling audio stuff seems to have been patched. The controller issues seem to be fixed, although it's still not compatible with my Afterglow controllers, which made it a pain to use a third party program in order to have my girlfriend join with said controller via an online game in MUA1. Overall, the state of the game now is playable. Not worth the asking price, but if by some miracle it goes on sale, I recommend it. I do applaud Marvel and Bill Rosemann for listening to us and fixing some of these big problems.

I absolutely love this game! Originally I bought this because I loved the design of the main character, Princess Elodie and I had always adored royalty figures. I must admit, I had never expected so much forward thinking and tough choices to come from a game about a pink haired princess. It was a pleasant surprise to see how easy it was to set yourself up for failure in this wonderful game.
The basic goal for Long Live the Queen is to live till you take the throne as crowned queen in one year. During the year you are expected to take classes, attend events and make choices all for the sake of your country. However this is a lot harder than it seems as each choice is vital in ensuring the well-being of your people and yourself. There is no way you will max out most of your skills and there will be events you will not be able to do. I found that it took multiple runs and tons of notes to even survive half way to the day I became queen.
In this game you WILL die. You will be shot, poisoned and even killed by a certain monster. Every time you die you will come back desperate for revenge with strategies that will often lead you to dying again. It is really satisfying when you finally overcome one of the many hurdles the game gives you.
What future queen will you be? An evil warlord, an elegant lady or maybe a magical girl? It’s all up to your choices. Just be careful. You will soon learn it’s not easy being a princess. Even enjoying a simple gift of chocolate will lead to Elodie’s premature death.
Pros: involves a lot of strategy, a great story, adorable protagonist, be the princess you want to be
Cons: you WILL die a lot, I swear is almost impossible to succeed in certain events
I would totally recommend to anyone who enjoys working out strategy, interesting stories and cute anime characters. It is certainly worth the price.

Do you have what it takes to stay alive?
Probably not.
Will it tick you off to no end?
Probably.
Will it be fun?
Only if you're masochistic.
As it turns out, I am apparently masochistic. This game is extremely addictive, with a relatively simple yet alarmingly improbable premise: survive to your fifteenth birthday. You'll face traitorous relatives, violent monsters, unpredictable magic, court room drama, espionage, and murder. There are more ways to die in this game than to survive. You'll get at least four hours play out of it just trying to survive one playthrough.
It's the kind of game that will make you try and try again, and the various outcomes and differences in decision can drastically alter the storyline. Ergo, while certain events over the course of playthrough will stay the same, the end result of differing choices will likely be new to you long into becoming familiar with the game.
All in all, Long Live The Queen is a fun (annoying) little game that will provide hours of entertainment (frustration). It has great art, a quirky storyline, and is perfect for visual novel fans. 8/10.

The game is a mix between Fantasy Wars and Civ 5, where as it has more 4x elements than Fantasy Wars, and a splash of Empire mananagement, but much less than Civ 5. It really does focus on overworld combat. Terrain is important and does influence the performance of the units. It doesn't enter a tactical screen, but plays out on the overworld map, much like Civ5 combat.

The Lords are fully customizable at the start of the game. Every lord starts with 10 ability points (which do not increase during the map) from which a selection of spells and boons can be bought. There are, as said 3 races to pick from for the lord. A 4th race, the Elven, can be obtained via DLC.

In a year that gave me great story-driven game experiences like Dream Daddy, Edith Finch, and The Sexy Brutale, this game somehow managed to top them all. Night in the Woods was very close to being my Game of the Year. 20-year-old Mae Borowski returns to her hometown of Possum Springs, a small mining town that has seen better days and yet still manages to pull her away from college life because... well, that's a good question. At first it seems like she's just burned out and seeking comfort in her friends and family, many of whose lives are starting to move on without her. And I don't blame her because I want to hug each and every one of these people, from her doting mother to her manic best friend Gregg to her goth ex-best friend Bea to... okay, maybe I don't want to hug Germ, but the whole town is loaded with people who are so real, so genuine, that the town itself begins to feel like a character...
But Possum Springs is no ordinary character; it has a lot of skeletons in its closet. Deep within lies a dark, unsettling secret, and the only way for Mae and her friends to unravel it is to delve deep into the mystery and put themselves in serious danger. In the end, this is a game more about the journey than about the destination; so much so that you'll want to play it multiple times to experience everything it has to offer. My advice: don't rush it. Make connections with people, visit the same areas more than once. What you get out of NITW depends on what you put into it. The big theme of this game is capturing moments, making memories, and what it means to want to hold onto the people and places and experiences that made you who you are, even though you know it can't last forever.

One of the hardest things for me while playing Stranded Deep is the fact I am terrified of deep water, AKA the ocean, which just so happens to be the setting of this game. To do good in the game, you must face your fear of what lies beneath the deep( if you are afraid of the ocean )and scavenge resources underwater.
I will simply give a summary of all the aspects of the game and what I find good and bad about each. Lets' begin:
GAMEPLAY: The gameplay is good, it's simple. Survive. You will start out with a lighter and a life raft, and will need to paddle to shore. The map is made up of several islands where you will collect resources like wood and stone to craft shelters and tools. Certain supplies can be found on land, like metals, tarps, and buckets. However, the real treasure is found in shipwrecks under the ocean. Sharks are a constant threat while diving down, so be careful of those little buggers as well.
GRAPHICS: If you have a beast for a computer, and I mean a real beast, than you will absolutely enjoy the graphics of this game. However, if you have a crap computer like me, the graphics are so amazing you will need to turn them down to prevent your computer from exploding. Even on low graphics the game still looks incredible and can be appreciated.
FEATURES: This game has many things to officer, including many gameplay mechanics and features such as:
-A watch that will tell you the time, temperature, date, and your basic needs.
-Several different ocean creatures( crabs, sharks, marlin, small fish ).
-Intense opening scene.
-Buckets.
-Randomly generated map everytime you start a new game.
And many more.
To finish off this review, I just want to list some of the things I personally would like to be added to the game.
-More land-based wildlife on the islands( lizards, insects, birds, etc. ).
-An easier way to get water. It is not easy trying to keep that bucket upright trying to get it over the fire.
-A co-op or multiplayer mode where you can play online or with friends to survive together!
-Larger islands.
-Two different modes: Story, where you must survive until rescued. Or an Endless mode, where you survive as long as possible.
-More sea animals, like more whales( Sperm, Blue, etc. ), octopus/squid, and dolphins/orcas.
So, to end off this review, this game is good. The reason I have little play time on the game is I don't play Steam all that too often anymore, but when I do, I enjoy playing Stranded Deep. I have had no bad experiences with the game so far, and I expect it to stay that way.
PS. As with most early access games, this game includes a lot of glitches and bugs, so be warned!

I never quite understood the appeal of the Dark Souls series on its release, but on giving it a second shot, this game in particular has easily become one of my favorite RPGs of all time.  Starting off as a weak, feeble undead dying to even the most petty of attacks can be frustrating, but I don't think I've ever played a game where watching your character grow in power based on your personal build and weapon/armor choices has felt so satisfying.  However, make no mistake - a strong character will not guarantee you victory.  Skill, patience, and perseverance are essential to success, and overcoming challenges feels very rewarding.
What I feel deserves the most praise, though, is the world and level design of the game.  The lore in the game is very vague and only really relayed through minor character dialogue and item descriptions, but learning about the dying "Age of Fire" and how the kingdoms and lands you explore came to be in such a desolated state was fairly interesting all around.  What's truly immersive about the world's design, though, is how intricately linked together everything is.  Where it be the "a-ha!" moment of finding a new shortcut that takes you back to a previously explored area of the discovery of a path leading to a completely new area you had seen in the distance hours before, the exploration feels top-notch all around.  It feels like a "real" world, as opposed to a series of zones with little in common.
Is this game for everyone?  No, probably not.  There's a very heavy emphasis on learning from your mistakes, and the punishment associated with dying can be frustrating and rage-inducing, especially for those new to the series (losing progress in the form of souls, having to backtrack through previously explored areas, etc...).  If you can get past these, though, you'll be in for a great experience.  I highly recommend this game!

So I started this game by not understanding the lore since the voice sound is by default inaudible, which was in fact rather fine since the lore doesn't make any sense anyway.
This game is basically going from mission to mission, with a rather small variety. Once you've done one steaalth mission and one horde-fighting mission you've kind of done them all.
They tried to bring diversity with a strength-and-weaknesses system, but it ends up being boring more than it is interesting. If the guy is weak to ranged you insta-kill him without a fight, if he's resistant to ranged and melee it's a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ Other s/w don't matter.
Another failed attempt at diversity is the skills tree, you get so many points that you just take them all and end up with every superpower. They could as well have made it automatic.
Also, and this paragraph will be a spoiler, the end of the game is the worst ending I've played so far. The lore still doesn't make any sense, and the game doesn't end in a bossfight. You have to fight the exact same mobs as you've slain the whole game, and just when you thought you reached the boss you do three well-timed clicks, a video goes off and then there are the credits. Now this is said, the combat system is pretty nice, feels satisfying and kind of addictive, so despite the complete lack of depth I still enjoyed playing the game, so if you get it on a discount you can go for it. Paid 20 bucks, played 40h before being bored, totally worth it.

I got the game on sale for really cheap, since it's a 3 years old game. So is it worth the low price of 10 euros with all DLCs? I guess yes... Would have I bought it then, knowing what's in it now? I don't think so. As stated by others, it is an assassin's creed clone with a "Lord of the Rings" flavour.
The gameplay is rough, imprecise, with the character feeling clunky and the design somewhat stupid:
- why did the developpers choose to map the same button to both climb AND dodge, so when near a wall the character would sometimes dodge when I want to climb to escape, and sometimes climb when I want to dodge?
- why would the character stick to a wall or a bush instead of going forward when I try to sneak (and even when I don't)?
- why would the character hit allied units with his dodge and other skills, like subjugating already subjugated units instead of the new one that is at the center of my screen?
- why does my character use his precious finishing moves on nearby grunts instead of the boss I am facing?
It is an ok-ish game for fans of hack and slashing in Middle Earth, in a smallish open world with repetitive tasks/quests. The combat is similar to the Batman: Arkham thingy series, with a complete lack of aiming and obstacles that would block my character (especially on top of walls at intersections or when trying to outrun or catch up bosses). It is a neverending frustration as you plow through the games trying to repeat over and over the same quests.
The nemesis system that randomly build sworn ennemies that chase the hero could have been better tuned, so while on missions I wouldn't get suddenly jumped on by 3 or more bosses that will kill me, become stronger because of my death, and will rinse and repeat every mission until I abandon the game and restart? What kind of completely idiotic gameplay design is this? On the good side, it adds a level of uncertainty in an otherwise bland world.
One positive aspect is the music, that reminded me a lot of Howard Shore's score for the Lord of the Rings movies and contributes to give the game its atmosphere. The visuals are pretty good, and killing orcs never looked more stylish and gorish (and frustrating at times because of innacurate controls).
Get the game if the following conditions are met:
- you're a fan of Legolas in the movies (because you'll get to do everything he does in the movies, except skating on a shield)
- you like the Middle Earth universe but you are not a Tolkien purist
- the game is on sale

I played lifeline, and thoroughly enjoyed it. Here's why. (Spoilers, Kinda?)
Remember how in state of decay you would need to rescue survivors, clear infestations, hunt mutated zombies, and many other things? Lifeline uses those same missions, but with a twist. Instead of saving survivors to stay with you, you're saving doctors and scientists in hopes of researching a cure. Infestations are still existant, and pop up just as frequently, and are dispached the same way as well. Mutated zombies are still existant, and appear to spawn more often, but I'll get to that later.
You'll start off with a base, just like state of decay, you can customize and upgrade. However, they added a generator and a latrine option to build. Then, the seiges come. Zombie sieges come every once and awhile, and to me they're the biggest challenge in the DLC. During the siege, zombies will either come east, west, or north to your base. You can set up traps such as fireworks, landmines, or propane tanks to combat the sieges. The more and more sieges you survive, the more and more challenging the sieges are. Mutations will start to appear, and eventually start to appear in groups.
Now, I would like to talk about the gameplay.
I feel that Lifeline is much more challenging than State of Decay, for many reasons.
Survivors are more likely to die, because of sieges, and when they do, they are much more harder to replace than in State of  Decay. The combat is pretty much the same in Lifeline as State of Decay, aside from multiple new military weapons such as a 6 barrel grenade launcher, SAW, Sniper rifle, and a few assault rifles. Executions are the same, except for a few new melee weapons.
New options:
In your base, like i stated before, there are a few new base "Sections" like the Latrine, Spec Ops,, Landing Pad, and Generator. The latrine has one job, to prevent infection and disease. Spec ops is used to give commands to your soldiers that  have no commands, you can give them orders to search the area for supplies, search for surviviors, or hunt down hordes and thin down the zombies. The generator is used to power your base, and is vital to upgrade some other "Sections". The Landing pad, in my opinion, is the most useful Section of them all. At the Landing pad, you can call in supplise, like construction materials, ammunition, anibiotics and medicine, food, and weapons, or just a package of a bit of everything.
Overall, i feel that Lifeline puts a new twist and options into State of Decay, making it more enjoyable, and making it have great replay value. 9/10

Well....to be honest i wasn't disapointed with the purchase of this game even though I'm not the biggest fan of zombie themed games/movies/books,...but i would recommend it getting it on sale (as most games on Steam).
This game's got a pretty tense single player campaign in which you're trying to survive a zombie apocalypse. You start of with simple tutorial mission that introduces the basics of the game to you. After that...you're on your own.
It's all about survival, gathering supplies, building outposts...all for your small community. What do I mean by small community? Well...if you think you'll be like f-ing rambo and go all out solo in this game you're wrong!
The stamina is drained quickly and it doesn't replenish for quite some time if you're playing with one character for a long time, so you're kinda forced to play with more different characters. Mainly you can play with only one character and have some help in form of switching to other community members, while your main charaters' health or stamina is regenerating (unless you died :P ) .
This is game is, like any other RPG games based on getting lots and lots of quest/mission/assigments (whatever you wanna call it). So you shouldn't be suprised if you get loads and loads missions trown at you wich will lead you running around (more or less) the whole map. And yeah, before you ask...it does get repetitive after a while!
The combat system is really diverse...From fighting, slashing, whacking, shooting, drive thru-ing,...you name it, you got it! You get your adrenaline pumping when melee weapons gets destroyed , the guns gets jammed, the cars get wrecked and will explode after too much of "abuse" from all the zombie killing.
I would defintly recommend this game for players who're seeking a lone wolf survival zombie game. Yeah it does have flaws and some bugs/glitches, but it is enjoyable experience. Also, the missing of CO-OP mode (wich this game should definitly have in my opinion) are the only 2 major things that can make you change your mind from purchase.
The game's got 2 DLC's so far(Breakdown and Lifetime), wich can prolong your playing of this game.
At the end of this review i would like to give a shoutout to Michael Jones from Rooster Teeth/Let's play youtube channel who made couple of let's play videos of this game that made up my mind about buying this game. Also a big shoutout to anybody rating this review

This game is HARD. There is a lot of resource management happening at once, there are enough random elements to make you hold your breath before clicking, and you can easily game over just for missing one action or vague clue.

Now I'm back to it playing light mode and I'm not so busy pulling out my hair that I miss any plot. It's a game I've been coming back to every day because I want to know what happens next and who I can save.
There's a great story here about space war, space spies, and space death, so even if you're not big on micromanagement survival games this would be worth grabbing on a sale to cruise through the narrative mode. If you're an achievement completionist, good freaking luck - you can't get achievements outside of original/light mode. If you prefer action over story, this is not the game for you.
If you're sick of indie pixel art styles, I'm right there with you but it actually does work very well here. The art, music, and designs are great - I've never found myself tired of the soundtrack or having difficulty understanding/finding anything due to art style or game design. It's easy to play and surprisingly powerful.
You're going to love this game, hate this game, or (most likely) hop between the two constantly while playing. I reccomend it.

Decided to finally grab this game on a 75% sale. I want to like this game. There are many aspects that I enjoy about the game. Mainly the storyline and plot. But after a while, reading through the many walls of texts get tedious. Not only that, the font choice (while suitable for the theme), hurts my eyes after a while.
I ended up with more cons as I played the game, and end up not having fun with it. A few issues caused me to give this a "NO". Firstly is that the amount of texts to read can get overwhelming, especially if there are at least five characters, and clicking through it all and reading them for information. There should be an option to skip the entire cutscene, since there is no requirement to pick choices. Then there is the crazy rng and clicking, trying to find the right combination to work and all. While interesting at the beginning, it gets repetitive later.
There are also a few other issues that have me giving up on this game. As I played, there are random flashes across the screen, like those old films you see with static. Not only that, there isn't an option for video setting to change the resolution or whether to have it fullscreen/windowed. Of course, you can press alt+enter as well. But for others who don't know that short-cut, the lack of that option is glaring.
I mentioned that static flash earlier. On my third playthrough, it's gone. Except that now it keeps crashing, especially at Chapter 3. Whenever I click on the "Dig Group", an error note pops up and I've to abort the game. This keeps happening no matter what I did. Uninstall and reinstalled, and the same thing still happens. It's also tedious having to read through the entire WALL OF TEXT again because every time you quit, it starts at the beginning of the level instead of the point of quitting. There are other games who does the same as well, but like I said, clicking through the texts got boring.
All in all, not being able to play past Chapter 3 has me reconsidering the game. There was a lot of hype about this game, but I CANNOT recommend this game. While I did enjoy the game, the cons outweigh the pros.

Honest review from someone who WISHED for this to be re-released on PC for years. I played the originals when they came out, still have my original PS3 copy.
Pre-launch - I was super eager at the announcement of this release, and didn't even care about the $60 tag (Of course I was going to get both.) Tried to do some digging about the DLC content, and nothing was announced at all, so I just assumed they'd release it because why wouldn't they?
Post-launch - Bought the game, and turned them on and dinked around for roughly 10 minutes. I'm not going to give the game itself a breakdown, you can play it for yourself (Most likely you already have). Game looks great considering its age, runs silky smooth, and the controls (Wired 360 controller) work very well. No problems whatsoever. I haven't tried the keyboard, nor do I plan to. A lot of reviews are slamming the controls and I can only assume it's for the keyboard or the Xbone controller. I have no issues. This game DOES come with the DLC characters from the PS3 version, which is very happy news! Game looks great and runs smooth at a constant 60 FPS. While this game lacks the polish that Ultimate Alliance 1 had, it's still a fun game. One of the things that is super weird is the audio. You can probably see in other reviews that this is a common issue. The music and sound effects have this constant weird crackling noise that is sometimes constant, and sometimes comes and goes. I have no idea what's going on, but it is very distracting. As mentioned before, the game lacks the same kind of TLC that the first had. They skimp on voice acting, and instead use written dialogue in a lot of places. The controls are a bit more floaty and don't feel as responsive (This isn't a controller issue, but a game design one.)
Pros
+ Silky smooth 60 FPS
+ Graphics have aged well, look sharper
+ Controls decent
+ Lives up to the hype I remembered in the past
+ DLC characters included!
Cons
- Price
- Audio issues
- Game itself lacks the polish of the first
While I enjoy the game itself, and have fond memories of it, I can't quite recommend others to get it for $40 (Or even $30 if you bundle it...) unless they are just wanting to turn the sound off. While that in and of itself isn't game breaking, the fact that this game was released as wonky as it was is disappointing. The DLC characters are definitely nice (WTF, why aren't they there in the first game!?) this game just isn't quite as great as the first, and the bugs make it harder to enjoy.

I have not finished the game, so my review may be flawed; however, my review is not entirely focused on the story and is in a morally grey area.
The game lends itself to automatically being viewed as a spiritual cousin to the work of Black Isle Studios (Baldur's Gate, Planescape Torment, Icewind Dale, etc.) and uses the nostalgic gameplay to great effect. Where it diverges from their cousin is that combat has become more complex. I played as an Orlen Chanter and found that combat was fun and exciting. The idea of changing my notes and verses in mid battle, a tune changing the magical world around me, was exciting. Pillars of Eternity did not disappoint by making my class a unique experience.
Character creation was well done and, if you wish to write your own story with a lack of all the pre-written characters, you have the opportunity to do so! With the ability to spend a small sum of gold to create a companion of any class or race, creativity for the writers and advantages for the min-maxers is bountiful!
The writing itself is what makes this game and, indeed, the entire studio a divergence from the norm. I was expecting a game that had dark moments, but a lot of humor, mirth, and fun that BI provided in the past. Not so. The story was dark, grim, and serious. Some characters had quirks, but they were realistic rather than fantastical. This made the game an exciting adventure and allowed me to consider more than I had in the past. The story is superb.
Combat is very difficult. The Risk-Reward factor that we had in Baldur's Gate (Rolling the dice and having the chance to kill the boss regardless of all the gear you have) is no longer. Pillars of Eternity will punish you when fighting bosses because they are hard. I went to a castle to fight what I thought would be a low level boss only to get absolutely annihilated no matter what tactics I used.
Great game, great story, and great minds behind this game.
9/10

On paper, at least, I like Obsidian, but between this and Wasteland 2 I've given up on them when it comes to anything but Fallout. The main problem with this game is the game world. This game suffers from a fundamental misunderstanding or confusion about the nature of reality, and humanity.
While games like Fallout 1 and Baldurs Gate had you meeting selfish, brutal, tribal, petty and often racist characters, PoE is devoid of all that annoying "humanity". Instead, you're in a weird, cramped, sterile world where everyone is a sexless meat sack floating through the universe, just waiting for the next piece of loot or some superficial companionship.
If you have any heart, you'll feel a weird emptiness after playing PoE for a few hours. It's as if something is missing. The strings in your heart are not only silent - they're aching for something to move them. Like a mad person locked in a padded cell, behind a screen of dissonance. How could everything be so beautiful, yet have no meaning?
The emptiness you feel, is post-modern nihilism. This game is ripe with it. In a way, it perfectly reflects the lack of meaning and true feelings in modern society. Where is the honorable soldier who sacrifices his reputation, and himself, to uphold the principles of his people? Where is the alpha male slaying the beta in front of your eyes to encircle and ridicule your altruistic, feminine core?
*NO ONE BELONGS. NO ONE SACRIFICES. NO ONE FEELS. PILLARS OF MODERNITY.*

If you are new to cRPGs you might aswell stop reading here, my review is not meant for you nor targeted at you.
If you are a cRPG veteran however, I urge you to keep reading, I only wish someone had told me, what I'm about to tell you, before I had bought the game.
Having played games upon release such as:
Baldurs Gate 1-2+expansions
Icewind Dale 1-2+heart of winter
Plancescape Torment
Neverwinter Night's 1-2+expansions
Fallout 1-2
And most of the "enhanced" editions of all of the above.
I must say in comparison to those, my god was I disappointed.
Introduction:
Game start's off with a textslide introduction reminiscent of Icewind Dale, and yet they manage to fail at the opening, literally not even 20 seconds into the game.
Allow me to quote the part that explains where you are going and why:
"The caravan carries travelers bound for the frontier hamlet of Gilded Vale, you among them, where a local Lord has offered land and wealth to settlers from abroad looking for a fresh start."
So you are an economical migrant, the cringe eh?
You are also deathly ill and won't last the night (doesn't seem too important though), this is why no one but yourself should go and get some berries to cure you, because who the hell needs good story and logic when we can go for massive suspension of disbelief.
I wouldn't mind the fetch quest honestly, but...
In any of the games I mentioned earlier you would be fetching the berries for someone else that was sick, or even temporarily lose a partymember untill you found a cure, because immersion, a word this game has torn out of a dictionary, put on a rocket and shot off into the sun.
But maybe I am wrong and they just want to make sure to let you know that you are strong and can take care of yourself, so you are definetly not expecting welfare checks in Gilded Vale! *facepalm*
So you fetch the berries, get ambushed by some people, go back to the camp and here is finally where the game showcases to you the different paths and ways to do things. Most people are butchered and they are holding a hostage.
You can now through diaglogue achieve different results. Not bad, maybe there is hope for this game.
(No there isn't, you will see why I mentioned this later)
So you either manage to save him or not, the fight ends, lightning storm comes, you run for the cave and here is the second thing that will lift your spirits up.
You enter an interactive textslide where you can make decision based on character stats and moral prefferences. This feels like it really could have been added to the "Enchanced" remakes of the previous titles I mentioned and hit right home. Two thumbs up. It felt new, fresh, and like it belonged in a crpg.
So you chose to try and save the same guy again or let him die, lets move on.
Exit cavern eavesdrop on some shady character with a hood doing a taboo ritual, ritual completes, nuclear blast goes off.
Your companion and the guy you saved are dead but somehow you survived.
Let me spoil it for you right away: It will never be explained in the game as to why or how you survived.
Did you even remember that you were deathly ill at this point? What about the berries?
Needless to say all your choices up untill now have been nullified and this sets up the introduction:
Welcome to Gilded Cliché poor but strong economical migrant, where your choices don't matter and things happen because plot expositions that will never be explained and important details that will completely be forgotten!
I know im being snarky but this trend/theme will follow you throughout the game.
Very important details will be forgotten, choices will be nullified and the cringe levels will keep on rising.
Enviroment: Detailed and beautifully looking areas, which as much as I want to praise it is something that is actually easily achievable due to the claustrophobically small maps/areas.
Honestly in terms of size, this  game would fit into Baldurs Gate 2's city Athkatla
(including the indoor areas such as homes/bars/dungeons/sewers etc)
This game is shockingly small in scope and size, something you will notice straight away after visiting Defiance Bay, the "largest" map available.
And the loading for some of the tiny indoor areas, it will drive you up the walls.
Combat/Classes/Stats:
I don't even know where to begin here.
We could discuss how the stats are butchered and close to pointless.
We could discuss how the skills are underused and close to utterly useless.
We could discuss how shockingly few feats classes have and how little race means both in terms of roleplay but also in terms of class choice.
We could discuss how little spells and abilities classes have, not even simple ones like turn undead for clerics or familliars for wizards. choice of shapeshifting anyone?
We could discuss how neverwinter nights simple fighter has more feats/traits/spells/abilities/skills/toggles than the entirety of this game.
And that sums up the topic, this game has shockingly little of everything in terms of combat.
And that leads us to the next topic.
Items:
Utter disgrace.
Remember when you had interesting items such as shimmering belt? (keeps you perma blurred) boots of haste? (perma haste) how about items that kept you blessed to counter debuffs? Talking swords? Cursed items? How about anything that actually isn't just +1-3 to stats?
Don't worry, items are obsolete:
You will see more interesting items in the first 20 minutes of any of the previously mentioned titles.
Infact the devs knew their items were so bland they let you craft your own ones that have much better AC+Mainstat.
What makes it worse is that +stats don't stack, so you end up crafting weapon armor with whatever extra stat just to puzzle it together with rings/belts.
All the +1 to stats items are useless, especially if they give a plethora of +1 stats because this locks you out of recieving +3 bonuses and is wasting a potential slot.
When I decided to check the wiki after reaching the last part of the game, mostly due to not having found anything interesting, I must say I was not just shocked but also angry.
How lazy can you get? If I hired a team of 100 people they couldn't invent a more bland and downright boring item system.
Story:
I have slogged through utter sh!tshows just to finish a good story.
I have suffered through all nine circles of hell and completed downright sadisticly bad games just because the story kept me hooked.
But pillars...
The story has pacing issue ontop of everything else I pointed out under the "introduction" topic.
There was potential, they could have made you slowly go mad during the game, they could have made better use of speaking with the dead mechanic, they could have made use of the companions better, but alas they went with the bland route.
Conclusion:
I truly tried to like it but it was so inferior to games made close to 20 years ago that my jaw was just dropping further and further down in disbelief as I played through the game
If you are one of the people who actually liked the game than I am happy for you, our tastes differ and I respect that.
I tried my best to put my thoughts into written words and I hope this was a somewhat useful rantview in your decision-making of whether to buy the game or not.
Cheers.

Well, I've got about 25 hours logged, and probably have another 75 in me, and have a 25day game going, and it's going good
Pros
+ Stunning visuals (GTX970, maxed settings)
+ A real sense of accomplishment when you bring yourself back from the brink of death
+ A real sense of relief when you finally find 2 buckets
+ Building your own raft is a real pay-off
+ Due to being randomly generated you may realise you've wasted 15 hours on a game when scuba gear hasn't spawned in places you can find or reach
+ Very few games give you that feeling of the skin on your back crawling, like imagine someone chasing you up a flight of stairs that are never ending, or a hill that is just too steep, and they could be right behind you, or they could be nowhere to be seen, but you know they're out there, somewhere, and today might just be the day you run out of luck
Cons
- Items, when opening loot underwater, and the crate is not on a flat surface, but, on a frame of a rusted old ship for example, disappear under the crates sometimes, and sometimes are just plain empty yet have treasure indicators on them sometimes
- Rafts flipping when disengaging from them, or when just stood on them for a few seconds, and you can only grab and pick up rafts from the top-side when upright, so if they're upside down in the ocean it's very difficult to flip it back (unless people have tips?)
Is it a game that is still developing, with active devs, and a great game all round, for the kind of people who like grind loops in a stranded desert island setting? Yeah, at the moment it's easily 8.5/10

So I started this game by not understanding the lore since the voice sound is by default inaudible, which was in fact rather fine since the lore doesn't make any sense anyway.
This game is basically going from mission to mission, with a rather small variety. Once you've done one steaalth mission and one horde-fighting mission you've kind of done them all.
They tried to bring diversity with a strength-and-weaknesses system, but it ends up being boring more than it is interesting. If the guy is weak to ranged you insta-kill him without a fight, if he's resistant to ranged and melee it's a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ Other s/w don't matter.
Another failed attempt at diversity is the skills tree, you get so many points that you just take them all and end up with every superpower. They could as well have made it automatic.
Also, and this paragraph will be a spoiler, the end of the game is the worst ending I've played so far. The lore still doesn't make any sense, and the game doesn't end in a bossfight. You have to fight the exact same mobs as you've slain the whole game, and just when you thought you reached the boss you do three well-timed clicks, a video goes off and then there are the credits. Incredibly disappointing since you waited the whole game for a worthy opponent and you don't even fight the final "boss".
Now this is said, the combat system is pretty nice, feels satisfying and kind of addictive, so despite the complete lack of depth I still enjoyed playing the game, so if you get it on a discount you can go for it. Paid 20 bucks, played 40h before being bored, totally worth it.
Just do not expect this game to be anything more than your first combats feelings.

I got the game on sale for really cheap, since it's a 3 years old game. So is it worth the low price of 10 euros with all DLCs? I guess yes... Would have I bought it then, knowing what's in it now? I don't think so. As stated by others, it is an assassin's creed clone with a "Lord of the Rings" flavour.
The gameplay is rough, imprecise, with the character feeling clunky and the design somewhat stupid:
- why did the developpers choose to map the same button to both climb AND dodge, so when near a wall the character would sometimes dodge when I want to climb to escape, and sometimes climb when I want to dodge?
- why would the character stick to a wall or a bush instead of going forward when I try to sneak (and even when I don't)?
- why would the character hit allied units with his dodge and other skills, like subjugating already subjugated units instead of the new one that is at the center of my screen?
- why does my character use his precious finishing moves on nearby grunts instead of the boss I am facing?
It is an ok-ish game for fans of hack and slashing in Middle Earth, in a smallish open world with repetitive tasks/quests. The combat is similar to the Batman: Arkham thingy series, with a complete lack of aiming and obstacles that would block my character (especially on top of walls at intersections or when trying to outrun or catch up bosses). It is a neverending frustration as you plow through the games trying to repeat over and over the same quests.
The nemesis system that randomly build sworn ennemies that chase the hero could have been better tuned, so while on missions I wouldn't get suddenly jumped on by 3 or more bosses that will kill me, become stronger because of my death, and will rinse and repeat every mission until I abandon the game and restart? What kind of completely idiotic gameplay design is this? On the good side, it adds a level of uncertainty in an otherwise bland world.
One positive aspect is the music, that reminded me a lot of Howard Shore's score for the Lord of the Rings movies and contributes to give the game its atmosphere. The visuals are pretty good, and killing orcs never looked more stylish and gorish (and frustrating at times because of innacurate controls).
Get the game if the following conditions are met:
- you're a fan of Legolas in the movies (because you'll get to do everything he does in the movies, except skating on a shield)
- you like the Middle Earth universe but you are not a Tolkien purist
- the game is on sale

Most of us could never forget those local arcades even if we wanted to. The smoke, the loud cheesy music, and the nasty Cheetos residue that seemed to be on every joystick.
Street Fighter 4 (in this case Ultra Street Fighter 4, not to be confused with the other 4 iterations) keeps this spirit alive in arguably the most classic fighting franchise in history, with fresh coats of paint and brand new systems. Being a 6 button fighter, I'd imagine you already own a PC compatible arcade stick or a different pad if you so prefer. Unless you want eternal carpal tunnel or feel the need to flex your masochistic man-boobs, avoid using the keyboard at all costs.
Most reviews will say "DON'T EVER BUY THIS GAME EVER EVER CUZ LAAAGGG :((((" and they honestly have somewhat of a point. It's difficult to improve at such a difficult game without fighting others online - one of the most demanding online games to date that requires near perfect execution, which is damn near impossible in some of the servers you get set into during a ranked match. As long as you aren't playing on a toaster, this game will run perfectly fine for all other modes including 2 player local versus. But let's face it, at least 80% of your playtime will be in the training room against an auto-blocking Abel. Let's face it, he has the most consistent hitbox, or maybe you just hate the French.
All in all, USF4 is that arcade experience we've always known and loved, but excluding those guys who don't shower and wear Etnies. What a bonus! Comes packed with great content and all them #alternateskinzzz. If Capcom can get their♥♥♥♥♥♥together with the netcode, there's absolutely no reason for a fighting game enthusiast to not pick this title up on the genetically superior platform.

Great game. Difficult and challenging, but fair. Some RNG, but there's enough methods of working with what you're given to turn it from RNG into a well-managed play session each time. This game definitely rewards skillful play, as well as game knowledge - you can only get better as you practice, and you'll feel it.
The art direction of this game is mind-numbingly great as well. Enemy designs are both immediately identifiable and beautifully done - nothing feels out of place, and similar stylistic elements often denote similarities in abilities. The environment is superbly crafted despite the basic room structures - each floor has its own unique personality, and lends to the story-telling of the game in a beautifully subtle way. The soundtrack is flawless - it can be both brooding and heart-racing, while also being calm and soothing enough that it can repeat thousands of times and still sound wonderful, never once being an annoyance but instead a well-established part of the environment.
Overall, this game is more than worth the price tag(s). Playing through it casually gives you an interesting (if horrific) story, told non-verbally almost all the time. Playing it seriously lends a vast amount of replayability and skill-based progression, as well as an extensive list of challenges and goals to complete that lead you ever forward. Playing it competitively is also an option - this game has a healthy speedrunning community as well as the Racing+ mod, which streamlines some portions of the game (such as allowing each character to start with the D6, the primary method of combating the inherent RNG), as well as allowing you to race head-to-head with your friends. The only type of person I wouldn't recommend this to are the people who anger easily - this is by no means an easy game, and will demand patience if you want to fully complete it. The satisfaction will be palpable though, and never once does a death feel like the game cheated you.
Buy this and both DLC. With the latest DLC, the game supports modding through Steam workshop, making the allure of new content easy to sate. Plus the developer routinely adds their favorite mods into the base game, effectively curating the top community content - a wholly welcome gesture, and a heart-warming one at that. Thanks guys, thanks for this wonderful game. The last time I desired to 100% complete a game was likely at least a decade ago, but The Binding of Isaac rekindled that flame in my heart. <3

Long Live the Queen has you play as a young girl forced to take the mantle of Queen and rule over her kingdom; with varying levels of success.
The game is choice based, allowing you, week by week, to make decisions in your life and ruling which will greatly impact your future and efficiency as Queen of your kingdom. This game is incredibly addictive, in all the right ways. The game is also incredibly deep. I found myself failing the game, replaying, and having an entirely different and new experience. The great thing, though, is that it's very, very, very hard to "see the strings". I couldn't easily deduce a way to "game" the system to ensure a win; the game's mechanics are so deep, convoluted and fantastic that every choice was a mystery.
I had a hell of a lot of fun with this game. I played for 8 hours before managing to complete it, and even then there were sides to the game I didn't experience.
You may look at this game and see a silly game about an anime girl, but it's so much more than that. The characters are deep and interesting, the relationships sprawling and complicated, and the choices varied and important. Everything you do matters. Gamers who enjoy games such as Deus Ex, Alpha Protocol, The Walking Dead, The Wolf Among Us and others will get a real kick out of the freedom of choice your character has, and the reprocussions this can cause.
A fantastic title. Make sure you pick this one up.

As for the release CS CZ game, there is also a campaign mode you can play, the AI in this is much more advance and smarter and not so dumb as the ones from the deleted scenes. However in this version, you get to spend points to recruit members onto your CS team. They also have stats that you may base your picks on. The difficulty ranges from Easy to Expert(when you first start it), so once you finish up on easy(or you can go straight to expert and work your way down to easy?), you get a badge on that and you can start on Normal and finish that and get a badge on that diff and so on.
Once in, the gameplay is similar to that to the multiplayer of the usual CS deathmatch, except that you are given objectives to do and you must carry those out in order to complete the map and then move on to the next until you finish the entire thing on whatever difficulty you chose and the rinse and repeat on a different difficulty if you so choose or if you''re bored from it, you can just start messing around in mutliplayer.
Other than the single player campagin mode, there's also a multiplayer game mode, if you've played CS 1.6, this is what this game mode is pretty much. CS team kill Ts and rescure hostages/defuse bombs whilst Ts kill CSs and plant C4s/hold hostages from CS team. There are many maps, more if you choose to add some custom made ones.
The graphics, well...the non-steam version I used to spend hrs and hrs on as a kid, looks very much more like CS 1.6 but with the usual CZ upgraded stuff and new additions too.
I swear it was last time, just did another sample run and no it looks nothing like the graphics from the deleted scenes Not sure why the different graphics between the non-steam version and the steam version, but I guess this team version would also have bug/glitch fixes that the non-steam version doesn't have. But I'm sure if you google, there would probably be some offline patches you can run to update the non-steam version as well...Also there are a couple or so new things in the steam version vs. the non-steam version I used to play on as well. I must have got the first release of CZ where it looked very much more similar to the CS 1.6 now than the steam version of itself currently.
Also, vs. CS 1.6, this has bots! and not those dumb ones from Half Life! :P But of course that doesn't really add if you're not much of a PVB (Player Vs Bot) kind of person.
Audio is usual, stereo only, not much else to say here...there are other options like change to high quality or low quality sound.
Yeah, not sure what else I should say about it. Oh, they added another class to both CT and Ts which wasn't there in the non-steam version I used to play. And the crosshair mechanics are different too. But I suppose this version, at least the steam version of CS CZ is like a downgraded version of CSS, in my opinion from what I've just experienced and I've played CSS before this steam version of CS CZ and it's significantly different to the non-steam version of CS CZ I used to play.

Pros:
- Overarching story is great, and little snippets along the way makes the world alive
- Great free post-release quests and items
- Your positioning matters, and synergy is very rewarding
- EXP is based on quests, not kills, so noncombat solution is worth it
- Sidekicks has good quests, all of them
Cons:
- White March content is too short
- So many loading times
- Spikes of difficulty here and there
- EXP is based on quests, not kills, so speccing your MC as combatant is more likely counterproductive
- Named sidekicks is mostly generalists - you can spec his skills but will never outmatch minmaxing custom characters
- Most stat checks depends on only your stats, even though many would be logical for your sidekick to take over - and the negative debuff often apply to whole party
Ugly:
- Character models could be better
- Battle mechanics are complex with buffs and debuffs playing major roles
- Paradox Syndrome: this game is so much different than when it was released (discounting White March) you'll essentially playing like three different games each major patch
- If you don't pay attention, your level 10+ party can be stomped ten seconds flat

First off, i just want to say that this is in my top 5 favorite games I have ever played. A lot of people will be surprised by that but we all have our own opinions so just keep that in mind.
Pros:
1. Choices affect the story, some choices even going as far as being able killing off a character from the story entirely
2. You can handle every situation in a multitude of different options
3. Story isn't half bad, and kept me hooked all the way through
4. Each of the main characters are different from one another, and it is pretty easy to get attached to them
5. It has very original gameplay and design, to this day I have not found another game that resembled it (trust me, I have looked a lot)
6. Music is amazing, really gives this game that epic and exciting action feel
7. Free dlc!
8. Once you beat the game, you can replay any chapter you want
9. Has around 10 different difficulty options to really give you the exact expirience you are looking for
10. At the end of each chapter, there are graphs that compare the choices you made in that chapter, to the other players choices (sort of like the telltale games)
Cons:
1. Felt it was a bit short, but then again, it has amazing replay value
2. The trial and error puzzles can get a bit repetive after a while
Conclusion: Overall, I give this game a 9.5/10. I definetly recommend you get this when you can, you will not regret it.

Likeable, realistic characters, beautiful 2D art style, atmospheric music, and an intriguing story with many different side quests... This game has a certain charm to it that is hard to capture or explain. As someone who grew up and is currently living in a small town based on a dying industry, I found this game portrayed the issue of 'comfort of your hometown and its familiarity' vs. 'the desire to leave and venture out of familiar territory' highly relateable, as Mae faces pressure to attend college and make something of herself, while also finding comfort in Possum Springs life, and not knowing what she wants to do with her life. The game is able to have crazy, lucid dream sequences and a wild overarching mystery plot, while still having a 'small town' feel to it. It is great about portraying the issues and dilemmas that many (if not most) people from any walk of life will face, especially the dilemmas that young adults face, when determining whether to begrudgingly take over what past generations of your family have done for a living (like Bea does), or moving out of town and saving up enough cash to leave it all behind (like Angus and Gregg). Mae is unsure of which course of action to take (to leave or stay) making her highly relateable to young adults and teenagers in a similar position. At the end of it all, learning how to find a way to move forward in life and to come to terms with things is a message that is portrayed beautifully and accurately in this game. This game also has replayability, in order to see all it has to offer. The only possible criticism I have for the game is the fact that sometimes I would glitch through telephone wires, but that may be my crappy computer's fault.
Sorry for all the gushing, but in summary: If you like slice of life games, charming characters, and/or games like Paper Mario TTYD and Undertale, this is the perfect game for you. Please, please developers, consider making a sequel, or more games with a similar feel. Also am definitely getting the soundtrack and playing the two prequel games. :)

Pros:
1. Nice graphics, some maps are really atmospheric.
2. Liked the game during the first half. Lots of the side quests were interesting and enjoyable.
Cons:
1. Many unnecessary and uninteresting special skills. I almost never used any of them as a 'Watcher".
2. Game is not balanced, in many cases combat is too easy or too difficult for the same party. Some opponents are ridiculously tough and can mow down your high level party in no time again and again, no matter what you are trying to do. The basic gameplay loop isn't engaging. That's really what you should take away about Grimm. Aesthetically, the game is delightful, and while the direction it goes in storytelling is... bizarre, it's not bad, but the actual gameplay - which is a mix of Katamari Damacy with some extremely basic 3D platforming - bogs it down completely into a mess of repetition and tedium. Essentially they took the basic gameplay of Katamari, completely missed what made it good, and ended up with the mess that we see here.
Admittedly, even some of the later actual Katamari games managed to miss what made Katamari Damacy fun in places, but that hardly makes this excusable. Absent the progression provided by being able to pick up steadily larger objects, the entire game is just running around, watching things turn dark and dirty in your wake, and very occasionally jumping. It's incredibly dull, and it's a shame because everything else about this has potential.
There's been cases where I've stood up rather strongly for games that lack conventional gameplay, such as the excellent The Path, but this is a very different case from that. It's not that Grimm lacks gameplay in a traditional sense, it's that it has it and it's extraordinarily repetitive and unengaging. They could have just actually cloned Katamari in it's entirety and this would have been pretty damn great, but instead we ended up with this half-baked mess of a game. If there was any doubt, not recommended.
Also, while it's not a factor in this review, seriously guys - don't nag someone about the fact that they're playing the free episode when they own some of the paid ones. I have the entire series from a bundle and it's slightly annoying to get little nags in something that I spent money on and own.

Like most people reading this, you most likely just bought Miscreated from the Steam Summer Sale 2017.. or on a cheap discount. However, before I officially start the review for this game, let me just say that this game isn't worth anything more than $10. I will tell you why in just a few short moments...
What I like about Miscreated is that the map isn't too huge. Not a huge time killer to get from one place to another. Which is why I love the game a lot. Unlike DayZ, it won't take you ages to get from one place to another, taking up too much time.
The combat in this game is pretty wonky and unlike any other games. Hitboxes are pretty buggy too. Scavenging system is really nice though, pretty easy to find items too. Not very many challenges in here, wolves aren't anything to really be scared of because they won't even attack you unless you're almost touching them.. same thing with the mutants, they won't be easily triggered to chase you, even if they do chase you, you get literally run away from them in a few seconds and problems solved. Your REAL challenge and fear in this game is mainly the players.

Excellent game. Probably the best zombie/survival game with story based events on steam right now. Simple combat, easy to learn and fun storyline makes this game appealing, and I recommend trying it. Now to reasons why this game is superior to its genre competitors.
State of Decay has randomized traits for each individual survivor, some of which add to the ability of said person.
The developers of the game listen to feedback and criticism, for instance prior to a recent update rubsacks (large resources a character can carry one at a time) or any items at all could not be loaded onto vehicles, but it is now possible.
The game incorporates the needs of humans, food, shelter (building resources), medical supplies to name a few. These items can be collected and brought back to the base that is set up and holding usually 5-10 people in the beginning, and these needs increase as further people are recruited or 'saved' from hordes. Characters when played also increase skill level of a variety of traits, combat, fitness and shooting are just some. Once high enough a greater upgrade is avaliable for that specific trait, such as 50% decrease of stamina used during combat for the fitness trait.
These are just some aspects of this game that stick out, there are many more that make this game a unique work in its genre. 8.5/10
