I mainly am happy with this game because I bought it on sale so like $20 for the dlc and the game I believe. I think it's a fun great open world game regardless though.
Everything I wanted from a free roam survival zombie game. Throws you right in, it's brutal, it's awesome.
PROS/INFO/EXPERIENCE
You build up a community of survivors, they aren't trained too well, just average people. Some have specific traits and background history which is quite interesting. Some may have low cardio and not be able to run as much. Others may have leadership, some may be good with guns/blunt weapons etc. You can train them in weapon specializations which is pretty cool.
When you play a character you play as one of the survivors in your community. One thing I really love about this game - it has permadeath. If the survivor your playing as dies, he/she is gone. You have to search for other survivors, become friendly neighbors, help out in general.
Was on a walk killing zombies casual chat with two random in game characters, make it back. Decide to leave alone to go explore the area, on the way back get torn apart by a feral. 10/10.
Cool guns, silencers, melee, exploration, many buildings, scavening, vehicles, base upgrading, special zombie types, unique survivors, small stories within the game.
Game has some modding support, I use a couple such as allowing the dlc weapons to spawn in the normal game.
Vehicles - The vehicles in this game actually stay where you leave them. There are quite a few vehicles on the map, but it's important to take care of them because they eventually will run out.
CONS/PROBLEMS (for some people)
Alot of people say this game is buggy, and it is in some ways, it has problems. Sometimes the events will mess up, you have to walk outside the building you are defending to kill zombies to progress the mission.
You are constantly warned about hordes of zombies, special zombies, or infestations. May get annoying, but it's a zombie apocalypse, makes sense.
This game is repetetive. I have no problem with that because I like killing zombies, surviving, and open world games, but for alot of people this can most likely get boring after a couple of hours.
CONCLUSION:
If you're wondering how long the game takes to beat, most people beat it in around 15 hours, Im 23 hours in and haven't even completed the main mission. Mainly because I explore and scavenge alot. I also played a bit of breakdown which I played for a couple of hours.
I would reccomend this game easily to alot of people I know, just check it out for yourself and see if you like it! If it goes on sale definetly pick it up!

Almost everything about Warlock is extremely simplistic: from spells to combat to enemy AI to diplomacy, there's very little deep thinking in the game. Diplomacy in particular is a bit daft -- there are few options aside from trade and basic alliance requests, and the only choices when facing an opponent's demands for physical goods are "Accept" or "Declare War". Also, as i s the case with virtually every Civ-like strategy game ever made, the AI will start to cheat once you gain an advantage.
Overall, Warlock is pretty addictive. There are a ton of different units and abilities, and each race has distinctive perks. But as of now, it's way too easy to steamroll the closest AI opponent early on, thereby allowing you complete domination of your region before even setting sights on the next AI player. Hopefully the devs fix the inconsistencies.

As yet another NotD player, my review is obviously biaised. But listen on.
TRS brings to the masses a genre in itself : Tactical Survival.
If you think from the screenshots it looks like Alien Swarm or something, think again.
It's not a game about being a gun-and-kite wizz -- you've got to keep thinking at every second or bad things will happen.
Teamwork is at every corner: unless you know what you're doing, you /will/ die if you even split up the team.
Everything goes down too fast for words: eventually a team of skilled players reach a symbiosis where just moving is enough to communicate.
An armored rushes your team. Whole team spreads out. The flamer moves forward to protect. Move behind him. He's out of ammo and starts moving away. Move on the side and start firing to kite. The demolitions leader orders the team to move away. Sprint off in an arc toward them, Devourer tailing you. The Demo fires off his rocket launcher, missing you by half a meter and killing it. It's fine, he knows what he's doing. Move on.
While not as hardcore as the old NotD maps (i highly recommend the SC2 remake of Spec Ops which is still almost better than TRS... hopefully not for long!), this game is still pretty hard. You will die, and die, and die again. Unless most of the team knows what to do. And even then, one person can screw up : and you'll be that person at some point. Learn. Retry.
And as you get better and better, leveling up and stacking bonuses, you'll find the game itself gets harder. New things appear, sometimes subtle, but enough to make a big difference.
All in all, if you like Zombies, Hardcore, fast-paced games, and Teamwork, i can only recommend this.
The price might be a bit steep, and it takes a while to get used to -- but once you do, it's totally worth it.

Units are also really important to keep alive since they gain feats when they level and keep all the feats when you upgrade them to the next type; you can also buy armor/weapons for them that stay, so they become a long-term investment most of the time.  It lets you skip through opponents' turns quickly so that's a HUGE plus for me, but at the end of the day you go through everything you can make in game pretty quickly, and these types of games usually don't hold my interest too long.
7/10, awesome if it's on sale, but you'll probably find better value/fun elsewhere

This game is
a disappointment.  The maps are dull and uninspired, the gameplay is repetitive to the extreme, and worst of all it features that cardinal sin of game design: Freeflow combat.  This is the same system that ruined Batman Arkham Asylum and Mad Max.  Basically, Shadow of Mordor reduces combat to three buttons, and just in case there is a village idiot somewhere for whom that is too complicated, the game PROMPTS you on screen for when to push them.  This unfortunate bit of excremental design is made worse by the fact that there is A LOT of combat, so unless mindless button-mashing is your thing, you will be bored.
What the game does well is story-telling.  For fans of fantasy and/or LOTR specifically, this is a nice bit of narrative.  The dialogue and voice acting are both good quality.
Overall though, this game isnt strong enough to recommend, unless you get it 80% off like I did during the last sale, or you are just a die-hard Tolkien fan.

Night in the Woods is a story (not so much a
) about Mae, a girl who drops out of college to rekindle her friendships back in what was once her home. The further you play, the more the stories of each character you meet unravel into one. This isn't so much a game as an interactive story, featuring a collection of far-strung mini-games. I haven't played anything quite like this before.
* An engaging story with many dynamic characters and events that will keep you hooked for hours.
* An expansive soundtrack that fits the game perfectly.
* Loads of hidden "notebook drawings" and achievements to be discovered while playing.
* Lighthearted, cartoonish-styled graphics that always impress.
* Two paths for the main story, depending on which character(s) you spend more time with.
* An awesome arcade game unlocked within the game that is remarkable enough to deserve its own review.
* Besides the basic and quickly tiring platforming mechanics and a few "minigames", there really isn't much gameplay. There's a lot of reading, which isn't what most players want in a game.
* A
ambiguous beginning. For the first few in-game days, I found myself wandering around aimlessly, hoping to eventually find someone to progress the time.
* While many characters stand out as lovable, humorous and relatable, others fall flat on their face in that aspect, only having a single defining personality trait that you either love or hate.
* The autosave mechanic makes it almost always impossible to go back to an earlier part of the game without resetting your entire save file. If you miss something, you'll have to play through the entire game to that point again.
* Towards the end of the game (just over two-thirds of the way in), the story begins to spiral out of control, and although this may be intentionally done to represent
or simply to encourage fan-theories to be made of the game, it makes it hard to grasp what the whole point was all along.
* Something-something the fanbase is going to be awful something-something it's going to be like Undertale's all over again unconvincing-cough
* You can buy the soundtrack as add-on content. And it's a pretty awesome soundtrack, so I'd suggest you check it out.
* As of today (May 28th, 2017), there are no trading cards for this game. That might change. I
we get them one day.
* There are a few dozen achievements!... But they're all "secret" achievements. Which makes unlocking them without a guide difficult.
* To put it crudely, this game appears to be unintentionally oriented towards the LGBT non-fascist crowd. Which some of you will hate and others will love.
* Something-something cups on my ears something-something

You play as Mae, a 20-year-old that's just come back to her small town home after dropping out of college and seems to have no idea what's she wants to do with her life. This is very much a story game, where you click your way through the dialogue of different scenes, separated by running from place to place. There is a dungeon crawl game available in game, and the dream sequences are a sort of linear platformer. The characters are hilarious and wonderful, and all of them relatable. The music is beautifully done, and the animation is brilliant.
The game tackles some tough issues. It brings up mental health, the need for getting help when you need it from a qualified professional, which was great. BUT at the same time Mae is kind of a jerk and quite frankly some choices are made by her that left me saying "wtf" out loud. It also tackles the topic of the decline of rural America, the effects of big business on small towns and the reactions of the older generations towards the younger.
I will say there was a moment where I thought "If I have to click my way through the dialogue of characters I don't care about one more time I'm going to pull my hair out." But then Mae said something snarky and I laughed out loud before running off to jump on trash cans and cars on my way to band practice.

You play as Mae Borowski, a young (cat) woman who has recently dropped out of college for unclear reasons to move back with her parents in her hometown of Possum Springs. Along the way you reconnect with her friends, her family and something lurking just beneath the surface of the sleepy town of her childhood...
As a video game, Night in the Woods isn't much to write home about. It features some entertaining but mild platforming, mini-games--some great (like throwing food into Gregg's mouth) and some not-so-great (helping Gregg move the [object] up the stairs)--and very light adventure game trappings that are never imposing. I'm no fan of adventure games, but Night in the Woods did it well enough.
As a story though, hoo boy. If this game isn't taught as literature in college courses RIGHT NOW college has failed. It starts slow but builds up into a deeply relevant narrative to any modern 20-something playing it. The characters, especially Mae's friends Bea, Gregg and Angus, are all likeable and genuinely fun to hang out with. There's the sort of loss that you get once you finish where you still want to hang out with them but the game's over but you don't want to play it again; like Persona 4 but without the 80 hour RPG tacked onto it. As for the game's themes, however, it gets mad props from me for being the first game to openly criticize capitalism and do a deep dive into why the decline of rural America is accellerating so rapidly these days. In this day and age, more games that do this are always welcome.
If you're looking for a quick yet emotionally charged game that will make you analyze the structural flaws in our society, Night in the Woods is the game to choose. If you think that politics shouldn't be in video games, idk dude just play Bejeweled or something. But for the rest of you, get this game and then get the game for your friends so they can play the game ok

Like the previous gems of the RPG genre, Pillars of Eternity takes you to a new world saturated with lore, action, and adventure. I picked up the game in this month’s Humble Monthly game subscription, and was shocked by the high quality, intriguing experience of it. Developed by Obsidian Studios as a spiritual successor to the Baldur’s Gate and Icewind Dale series, Pillars of Eternity uses many themes and mechanics like its predecessors, while remaining a unique experience.
After spending a while designing my character, Pillars of Eternity placed me in an adventurer caravan transporting settler to the low-populated village of Gilded Vale; however, disaster struck on the road when cultists overrun the caravan, killing all but a couple of us. After making our way through the monster-infested ruins of a temple, my companions and I immerged to witness a strange ceremony taking place. Unfortunately, after a mysterious explosion, I found myself the lone survivor lying beside the corpses of my allies. On my own, I traveled through the forest of Valewood till I finally arrived at my destination of Gilded Vale. These intro areas felt very linear, however not in bad way as I never got overwhelmed with where to go or what to do, which ensured I could learn the basics of the game without too much stress or misfortune. Pillars of Eternity really captured the immersive story inside this pseudo-tutorial. It wasn’t until I had options of where to go that I really realized that first story arc, if you will, was simply a tutorial. From learning how the combat system worked, to understanding how certain dialogue and skill choices can affect the outcome of a quest or simply a conversation, I really feel that Oblivion Studios nailed the introduction unlike its predecessors.
Early on, the fighting system seemed relatively easy, just click one of the few skills you had, or simply attack with a sword or bow. Once a wizard joined my party, however; the complexity shot up tremendously. Like how aggro works in MMORPGs, the more DPS you do, the higher chance that enemies will attack you rather than another party member. This created a difficult, but intriguing and strategic fighting system. Mostly I tried to place the weaker characters towards the back of the fight, and the tankier types in the front which, in most cases, worked and provided the best result. Once I learned that enemies could and would flank, the battles became increasingly harder. I’m impressed by the complex, yet relatively simple combat system. It’s not perfect, however; as it quickly became hard to visually see who was friend or foe when multiple people would be standing in the same small area, and the sometimes-vague text on area of effect spells and skills made it difficult to know whether it would hurt or heal just friends, just foes, or both. I think the combat is a little clunky, but as I continued to learn the specialties of the characters better, I began to feel more comfortable with it. Overall, I think the combat feels very strategic and fun, but also a bit confusing and overwhelming in larger battles.
Pillars of Eternity isn’t just a fun game to play, but it’s also ripe with interesting story and lore. Crisp, clean voice acting fills the dialogue options with a sense of life. Books found in various houses, or dungeons detail wars, countries, languages, and more; with some vaguely referring to quests. Occasionally, the player’s companions converse with each other in humorous or character developing ways; from petting a wolf, to questions about one’s home. There’s always something to do in Pillars of Eternity with the sheer amount of quests, some seemingly random, to ones that are downright crazy. There seems to be at least one quest per region, but typically there are a quite a few more.  The mysterious nature of most of them instills curiosity and confusion in the player, but most importantly It keeps them immersed.  Altogether, I think Oblivion Studios created a fantastic narrative, capturing both the immersion of a new world, while keeping the player occupied with interesting, intriguing quests and story lines.
Composed by Justin Bell, the sound director at Oblivion studios, beautiful music fills Pillars of Eternity with emotion. Transitions between regional and combat music enhances the different auras of regions, battles, and cities, some emanating serenity or fear, suspense or action, and mystery or clarity. The combination of the music and environment creates the illusion of an interactive movie. The sweet melody of a violin as you meander down a forest path, or the intense blasting of horns upon meeting a monster, Pillars of Eternity keeps that high level of immersion you’d except out of a Baldur’s Gate sequel. Yet, while the music was a powerful tool it never felt overwhelming, but rather added to overarching mood of the given situation. Their musical direction and vision is really shown in Pillars of Eternity.
Adding to that musical genius, the artists and animators at Oblivion Studios fashioned a beautiful, stylistic world. The semi-realistic art style mixed with the cartoony feel of an RPG kept the original feeling of Baldur’s Gate while improving the overall quality of assets tremendously. The animations having that nostalgic fairly rugged, but fluid motion given an almost life like illusion.  The flickering of lights, and shadow-casting is a wonderful addition as well. I absolutely love the visual design of Pillars of Eternity.
Not everything about this game is great, however. With a steep $45 price, Pillars of Eternity feels rather expensive. Even though the game feels very polished, the price seems rather high. Most games of this genre typically sold for around $20 - $30, back when they were popular which is quite a deal less than today’s Pillars of Eternity’s cost. Is it worth it for the price? After playing, I think the overall amount of game time and polish can justify this costly price.
With an amazing, immersive story, mixed with musical genius and nostalgic artistic feelings; I can say I’m impressed. While not being perfect with flaws in the mechanics, and oversights by the developers, Pillars of Eternity far exceeds my expectations for modern role-playing games. Reviving the isometric turn-based DnD like role playing game, Oblivion Studios created an amazing product that far exceeds the level polish that its predecessors possessed. Overall, I’d highly recommend this game to those who enjoy detailed story, gorgeous art and animation, and especially to those who love the Baldur’s Gate games.

This is really an excellent roleplaying game. If you like RPG's in the likes of Baldur's Gate, you'll be right home in Pillars of Eternity. The story is good and got a lot of depth to it if you engage yourself in it. The NPC's that join you each got their own story that you uncover along the way, giving them much more personality.
The game system works very well too and is open to both casual players and min-maxers alike. Classes feels varied, options are many, combat is fun, and there's just a lot of nice features - getting your own home and the side quests that are related to it are one of my favourite features of the game.
You can influence the ending in multiple ways, though looking back, perhaps the main story line is a bit too linear. I would also have liked that the AI automating you can add to your party members in combat was much more advanced, it's just too simple unfortunately. Lastly, it damages the immersion that in dialogue some parts of the dialogue text switch on and off between being narrated and not, it just seems odd that the NPC you talk to is suddenly silent and then talks aloud in the next paragraph.
Still, these are minor things and I really enjoyed the game.

This game is as close to "The Perfect Zombie Game" as I've played. Base and player management is not something that you always expect to work well within a 3rd Person Shooter, but it definitely adds a level of personal investment into the game.
Overall, the game handles every portion of zombie fighting/survival management right: Sounds attract hordes, team mates can generally hold their own, supplies are low but managable, and death is handled excellently. When your player character dies, your group returns to the base and you automatically assume the role of another playable survivor, if one is living. Death means you lose that person FOREVER, but the game continues on (and saves automatically). It makes dying a SERIOUS deal - most modern games make death feel trivial. It is so impactful in this game, you might find yourself actually making consious decisions not to take risks you might take in other games because you don't want to lose all of the skills/items/time you've invested into developing a character.

You play as Grimm, whose goal it is to make everything around him nasty and turn happy people into rotten ones. You do this by simply walking around. As you do that your stink power will grow and allow you to turn bigger and bigger objects into smelly ones and later even the people. But you have to be careful, the good people are out to clean up your mess.
The game is well animated and the voice-acting fitting. The only problem I encountered was repeatedly getting temporarily stuck on invisible objects and borders.
The creators have repeatedly stated that because they no longer have access to the game source they will not add achievements to this game. This also means that there will be no further episodes added or problems fixed (smoothing out objects edges so as to not get stuck), so don't expect anything on that front.
All in all a really fun and easy game for teenagers and adults looking for a short break.

So... after what it seemed like an eternity, I've finally reached the end of the game. I've seen both endings and, as a matter of fact, I'm not satisfied by the story or the lore. But I am completely happy with the gameplay and the evolution of the level design and overall atmosphere. Waht I will tell in this review is a simple recollection of what I found "good" and what was pretty "bad". Nothing more, nothing less, also because the game itself has reached cult status and it would be pointless making a long review now after 6 years and two sequels.
This is considered by many to be the best in the series. Well, I have to agree on the mere gameplay aspect. What's the gist of it you ask? You're an undead knight, or mage, or cleric, or thief, or whatever you pretty name at the start of the game calls you to be, in a world long gone mad from the lack of the source of life, a flame that the gods of this world tried to keep alive, unsuccessfully, and your objective is, well, getting burned alive to make it last a bit longer, or get rid of it completely and let the world be consumed by darkness. Both are viable options that dont solve anything, and you yourself are a mere mortal in a world that doesnt care about your presence or your actions, just a random knight fighting an endless battle that nobody would ever dare to start to begin with.
The gameplay consists of rolling, stabbing in the back, rolling, more stabbing, retreat to heal \ recover stamina, roll some more if you are not a mage. If you are a mage, the strategy is rolling, rolling, rolling, pause to cast spell, roll till you're out of breath because you have no health remaining, frantically reach bonfire, roll again for the love of God.
Despite how it all sounds, the mechanics are brilliant as any character can become any type of hybrid, in the long run, the class is just a name that defines the initial stats. And that is the fun part of the game, combining elements from spellcasters and knights, forging powerful firemage clerics of the swamp, or battlemages with enchanted axes. The customization of the character and the possibilities offered by multiple equipment slots, combined with the versatility of the weapon change and a great deal of enchantments, is the real strong part of this game, not counting the excellent strategic aspect conferred to it by diverse enemies that all have distinct attributes, capabilities and methods of attacking and defending. It is, simply put, a joy to play.
The structure of each level is superb, as it implies that the player is smart enough to get to any point he desires, while tempting with fair challenges and a number of minimalistic puzzles that provide prompt reward, as well as a quick death, in equal measure, all the while ascending towards a higher goal. The constant vertical layout, both towards the sky and down to the bottom of the earth, makes the player feel uneasy when necessary, and ready to feel better as soon as the sun shines upon the highest peaks. It is all well calculated, each portion of the game is packaged separately and has it's own theme and approach, every area feels unique and with a purpose. It is also important to mention that shortcuts abound as well as bonfires, especially in the latter part of the game, and each level is a self contained set of stairs + rooms always relatively small, once mapped, the areas can be travelled with ease in abou 10 minutes each without feeling boring or repetitive too much. Atmosphere is very satisfactory, too.
But.
As much as I love the game, the "lore" is a jumbled mess of characters saying a bunch of things that dont really make any sense because the very origin of certain concepts are hidden or not explained at all, there is a void between parts of the ggame when it looks like thousands of years have passed while others look like no more than ten years or so there was life there, some bosses may be boring to fight or utterly frustrating to the core (I'm looking at you Bed of Chaos) and the way the game tells you the story is so subtle that is very easy to miss most, if not all, of what is going on.
I like subtle storytelling and "show, dont tell" phylosophy, however this is a little too much. Every character "quest" is optional and at the end of the day everyone dies or gets in terrible situations that you have no choice but to turn around by murdering someone or letting dark forces prevail. The tiniest missing dialogue and a whole quest is lost forever.
Also, the ending is not satisfying as it reduces itself to a 3-seconds long cutscene and that's it. This may be enough for those that simply want to read a good guidebook or lore-frinedly companion book, but if you are playing this for the first time, not only you'll miss much of the story, but almost nothing will be told you directly in any way and you'll more than likely be left in the dark of some major events because of this precise style of storytelling.
If I had to assign a number to my 100+ hours spent on this game, I would gladly remain in the realm of 8+. It may very well be a masterpiece of level design and atmosphere, and a fine example of gameplay on it's own. However, the convoluted story and presentation of it's characters and world, scope and grand scheme of things, is preventing me from giving more, as I felt more of a lack of motivation to play it again rather than getting ready for another try.
For me, it was a grand, unique, beautifully complex, one-time experience.

This review is going to sound bad, but overall I enjoyed this game, despite the problems I had with it.
Let's start with the thing that disappointed me the most: the story. A very lackluster story with a boring nothing ending. The characters weren't compelling nor was the plot itself. The world of Mordor was also bland and boring, with no depth to it. Not satisying at all to explore or look at. I love middle-earth and the world Tolkien has created, but this only really uses it on a surface level. The quests were equally drab and repetitive, featuring mainly the same rotation of objectives you have to complete on repeat. The main story quests were better and more varied, though. Not much reward for completing side quests and objectives either. They mostly end up feeling like busy work after you've done a few.
The combat is Arkham style, so it gets repetitive and boring eventually. It'll depend on your tolerance for it. It can be very satisfying at times to take on hordes of enemies without much trouble or a particularly annoying enemy. It's a very mechanically competent game, if that's your thing.
Again, all that said, I still enjoyed the game and would recommend it for people who are more interested in mechanics/gameplay than story.

A pretty fun game with some nice RPG elements. If this style of game is up your alley in terms of interests then you will most likely enjoy the playthrough. It has a nice blend of stealth and action, basically allowing you to decide how you'd like to complete your mission. You can either crawl about, stealthily slitting the throats of enemies, or you can barge in and cut them all down. There are a variety of missions, from assassination attempts, to rescue missions, to main missions that will have you interacting with fellow protagonists, and a brief but pleasant inclusion of Golem and his obsession with the one true ring.
The combat flows nicely, a bit of a mixture of the Batman:Arkham style combat and Assassins Creed. It's a lot of countering, and combos can bring about executions, stuns, and you can slow time down to rattle off a few kills as well. This game is similar to the Princess Maker series, except the outcomes may be more limited due to the goal of reaching Elodie's coronation - if you die or do not otherwise make it to coronation day, you basically lose.
The gameplay is repetitive, for those not familiar with this type of game. You choose Elodie's classes and an activity each week, and most weeks include an event that lets you make a decision to affect the outcome of the game. The idea is to replay the game (which could be done multiple times a day if you wanted to) to see different endings and outcomes.
I found it to be pretty fun the first few times, but by this point I am just using guides to unlock the remaining endings. Since many require very specific actions, it can be hard to find them on your own unless you want to play it hundreds of times.
- Fun concept that makes you question the intentions of the characters. The first few times I played, I felt very paranoid about the outcomes of my choices.
- A lot of content if you want to see what happens if you pass or fail certain skill checks, or when you make different choices.
- Certain skills/choices are needed to achieve different endings, which limits your choices unless you want to die. If you happen to focus on the wrong skills, there is no real ending since winning always means reaching coronation. However, there are still several different ways to win
- Some skills seem to have been pretty useless. I never found a need for Polearms, but I needed to gain skill levels in it to max other weapon skills.
If you haven't played a game like this before and have a limited gaming budget, I would wait for a sale. But if you like Princess Maker type games, then you'll probably like this.

The game is a 8 player coop mission/objective rts style shooter with marines shooting down enemies that are infected with a virus, The gameplay is very similar to past mods from warcraft/starcraft called night of the dead except it is a very well done and solid carbon copy with a few bugs here and there that will need polishing up of course.
This game is fun with 8 friends if you have them but is challenging and still as much fun with 8 random competent people. Communication is the key to survival in this game using skype or teamspeak whatever you can, or if you have a leader that actually can lead the entire group by giving directions and having the team listen. Hopefully a public voice chat of some kind is included in the future.
The game offers at the moment one map with 2 different mode, the story mode with objectives and missions which are all randomized content where you'll want to complete as much as possible surviving on just one life  before you the timer which is about an hour hits 0 and your group gets overrun, also included is bunker mode where you'll defend a beacon and if it gets destroyed its game over however you can respawn every 30 seconds. The game also has 8 classes at the moment with a leveling system to unlock each one. Also each class has different abilities, skills, and weapons that you will want to use to your advantage. (as a group we've yet to beat the game yet lol but we are working on it)
When starting up, players are introduced with a prologue  tutorial that teaches the player to the nice and clean interface along with how to use your abilities, levleing up, and your bread and butter skills which is flare, running, and autoaim. Very easy to learn if you have any hands on Rts at all.
There are plenty of destructable objects in the environments with plenty of stuff to loot, generators to turn on and enemies to gun down. The game also has friendly fire with certain skills and explosives  so be careful where you call those napalm strikes or blowing up certain things because you might accidently shoot your teamate down. You'll be required to work together with those skills and passives to work on turning on radar, disabling enemy artillery from insurgents, or killing boss infecteds while conserving ammo by looting and exploring  and doing your best to use all items to your advantage from mines to rockets, to even turrets you can turn on or place
Other than that the bugs we discovered so far are not game breaking and the game plays pretty fun and solid for the time being. I found the game very exciting with a group of friends over teamspeak where we were trying to learn it and died to such dumb little things but this game is hard, REAL HARD even with the difficulty at easy so prepare yourself! Writing this review, I'll assume noone has played, "Night of the Dead", the Warcraft III mod this game was based on.
The game in general plays like your average isometric shooter, with a bit of Dota thrown in. You start by choosing one of eight customizable classes, and then their loadout, including their primary and secondary weapon, the ammunition type they fire, up to four active/passive abilities, and 3 perks. As you rank up, the amount of each of these interchangable things you can use increases. Once your set, you can join a match with your customized soldier, and drop with up to 8 squad mates.
The combat is fairly  simple. You move with right mouse click, and select targets and fire with the left. You can also allow your soldier to snap shot at targets automatically(aimbot) at the expense of accuracy. Your weapons use ammunition quickly, and unless you manage it carefully, you'll find yourself unarmed halfway through a match. Due to this, you have to scourage the environment for supplies, which you'll often find inside buildings, or on corpses. Once you find something, you can equip it into one of 6 item slots. The things you can find vary wildly, but they generally consist of explosives, medical supplies, ammunition, passive weapon upgrades, barricades, etc.
Throughout this whole ordeal, you and your entire squad are trying to survive waves upon waves of hideous creatures trying to eat you, all the while trying to complete randomized objectives. At first glance this may seem fairly tame, but the enemy types vary wildly, from zombies, to giant bat demons, and they come from the darkness as the maps take place at night. To make matters worse, most often apply negative status effects to your soldiers. From bleeding wounds, bone fractures, and crippling toxins, you'll soon find yourself ravaged and left to die if you're not careful about patching yourself up and staying togethor with your teamates.
As for game modes, the title currently has a tutorial, and online play with up to 8 player coop.
The game is brutally difficult, even on the easier difficulties, but if you give it a shot, you'll find its highly addicting.

As i played this game i saw several things that i did not approve of, with the realization that this game is in alpha and is subject to change. At first when i had started playing this game i didnt know what i was doing (naturally, because its a new game) but i quickly learned how everything worked. I can say that i enjoyed the actual gameplay of it, the gathering and the survival aspect of it intrigued me. But unfortunatly there were several things that threw me off and the game was a total bummer for me.
1. The fact that you can't build on the same plot of land as your friends makes this game feel like youre meant to be a lone wolf, survival means you need to gather and build, and if you cant do that with friends then it seems like this game would become boring in no time.
2. What is the point in building a base? The purpose of the base is so you can defend your valuables and yourself in case of an attack. But when you log out of the server your body dissapears and no one is about to attack you, thus making a base pointless
3. Your base being spotted from far away. as you are farther from an area the foliage and the shadows dissapear, leaving only the trees, the land mesh, and peoples bases to be seen. The base you built is no longer hidden and anyone can see it from a mile away, so trying to hide your base is pointless, making it an easier target for attacks.
3. You're carrying weight is way too low, and it would take an eternity to get anything done, most of the items are on your actual character which takes up half of the weight, and you are forced to constantly empty your inventory. The weight distribution is also off in this game (for example) you require 2 wood to make 1 lumber, but said 1 lumber weighs more than the 2 wood, which makes no sense to me, where did this extra weight come from?
4. you are only allowed one storage container in your base, the concept of this baffles me. What is the point of collecting items if you have nowhere to store them. It is recommended that you obtain a vehicle for extra storage, but that just seems ridiculous.
5. There are barely any dangers. As I was running around I had maybe come across 2-3 zombies, and a pack of wolves, all who had seemed to be minding their own business. As much as I appreciate not being attacked and having lost all of the items gathered, it was not very challenging and they were easily avoided, especially because they were low in numbers.
all in all this game does seem like fun, but these particular flaws are what made me say no to this game. Hopefully in the future the developers will change some of these stats around but for now i will not be playing it.

-Best played on an arcade stick, but a standard game pad will suffice

The 5th iteration of Street Fighter 4 on PC, and somehow the game has taken gigantic steps backwards.
The game itself, not just the netcode, still needs a major patch and at this point, I don't think we'll ever get it. For example, sometimes the MENUS lag. Yeah.
Widespread frame rate and other assorted graphical issues for almost all users from the get-go, with no clear, definitive way to fix them. There are so many guides and posts for tweaks and workarounds that users can utilize on their end to make the game playable, but there are also so many issues that it becomes pretty confusing. Some fixes work for some users and have no effect for others.

Cursed Castilla is an arcade action game which is based and inspired by the Ghosts and Goblins series and other retro titles. It brings an 16 bit graphics style, a quick action packed gameplay with tight controls and a high level of difficulty.
The story is set in the Middle Ages in the Spanish Kingdom. You play as a knight who is sent on a quest -together with other 3 fellow knights- by the King to cleanse the Kingdom from the evading demonic horde. The story basically is a Spanish mythos and there are several parts of the game where creatures from other European mythologies appear. Since the creators are Spanish the game overall in its music and its design has a Spanish vibe.
The game is colorful and has I think hand drawn graphics, which look awesome. Aesthetically it all fits so well together. It has a retro style but also looks fresh and cheerful since it displays an arcade style. The creatures are well designed and there is a huge variety of enemies to counter. What stands out however are the bosses. There is a huge diversity between them and there was a lot of creativity in their design. For me it was the most interesting part of the game.
The controls are almost identical to the Ghosts n Goblins games, tight as hell and you have to be very precise otherwise the game punishes you like it’s no tomorrow. And since you get the good ending only when you lose a certain amount of continues it will frustrate you a lot when you start losing repetitively. There is also a variety of weapons you can use but I found out that only 2-3 weapons are playable in the later stages so there is not much into it.
The music is decent, not memorable though like other recent platformers I played but most of tracks are kind of catchy and they fit the stages they are played to.
The game overall is very hard. A look at the achievement percentages displays how frustrating the game can be. Some achievements at the earlier stages of the game are only completed by 10-15% of the players, which is insane. In my opinion the game pays tribute to the classics also to that aspect, that of the reward that comes from mastering the controls and being very patient.
Sadly there isn’t much replay ability once you get the good endings, however that could take you forever like it took me 30 hours. Overall Cursed Castilla was a great retro experience despite the high difficulty and I would recommend playing it to anyone who has ever owned a 8-16 bit console and likes these types of games.

This game is wonderful.
While gameplay-wise it is more or less Ghouls 'n' Ghosts, it is clearly made with quite a lot of passion. So much attention was lovingly given to the details in this game - the graphics, sound, and controls all authentically capture the feel of a platforming game from the early 90s. The music and sound effects perfectly capture the aesthetic of the Sega Genesis sound chip, the sprites are all lovingly detailed and well animated, without any of the pixel size discrepancy that you might see in more modern games that attempt to be retro - I bet they even took into account the hardware limitations of 16 bit platformers of the era, and tried to design the sprites around the limited color palette provided by consoles of the early 90s.
The game is quite challenging, but fun in the way that it keeps you coming back. Even though you die, you keep wanting to try again. It truly captures the Capcom feel in that regard, and also rewards you for challenging yourself to complete the game with less credits, or collecting all the key items hidden in each stage. There is even a speedrun mode available for those who are interested. This game is an underrated gem and if you like platformers of the early 90s you owe it to yourself to get this game.

So... after what it seemed like an eternity, I've finally reached the end of the game. I've seen both endings and, as a matter of fact, I'm not satisfied by the story or the lore. But I am completely happy with the gameplay and the evolution of the level design and overall atmosphere. Waht I will tell in this review is a simple recollection of what I found "good" and what was pretty "bad". Nothing more, nothing less, also because the game itself has reached cult status and it would be pointless making a long review now after 6 years and two sequels.
This is considered by many to be the best in the series. Well, I have to agree on the mere gameplay aspect. What's the gist of it you ask? You're an undead knight, or mage, or cleric, or thief, or whatever you pretty name at the start of the game calls you to be, in a world long gone mad from the lack of the source of life, a flame that the gods of this world tried to keep alive, unsuccessfully, and your objective is, well, getting burned alive to make it last a bit longer, or get rid of it completely and let the world be consumed by darkness. Both are viable options that dont solve anything, and you yourself are a mere mortal in a world that doesnt care about your presence or your actions, just a random knight fighting an endless battle that nobody would ever dare to start to begin with.
The gameplay consists of rolling, stabbing in the back, rolling, more stabbing, retreat to heal \ recover stamina, roll some more if you are not a mage. If you are a mage, the strategy is rolling, rolling, rolling, pause to cast spell, roll till you're out of breath because you have no health remaining, frantically reach bonfire, roll again for the love of God.
Despite how it all sounds, the mechanics are brilliant as any character can become any type of hybrid, in the long run, the class is just a name that defines the initial stats. And that is the fun part of the game, combining elements from spellcasters and knights, forging powerful firemage clerics of the swamp, or battlemages with enchanted axes. The customization of the character and the possibilities offered by multiple equipment slots, combined with the versatility of the weapon change and a great deal of enchantments, is the real strong part of this game, not counting the excellent strategic aspect conferred to it by diverse enemies that all have distinct attributes, capabilities and methods of attacking and defending. It is, simply put, a joy to play.
The structure of each level is superb, as it implies that the player is smart enough to get to any point he desires, while tempting with fair challenges and a number of minimalistic puzzles that provide prompt reward, as well as a quick death, in equal measure, all the while ascending towards a higher goal. The constant vertical layout, both towards the sky and down to the bottom of the earth, makes the player feel uneasy when necessary, and ready to feel better as soon as the sun shines upon the highest peaks. It is all well calculated, each portion of the game is packaged separately and has it's own theme and approach, every area feels unique and with a purpose. It is also important to mention that shortcuts abound as well as bonfires, especially in the latter part of the game, and each level is a self contained set of stairs + rooms always relatively small, once mapped, the areas can be travelled with ease in abou 10 minutes each without feeling boring or repetitive too much. Atmosphere is very satisfactory, too.
But.
As much as I love the game, the "lore" is a jumbled mess of characters saying a bunch of things that dont really make any sense because the very origin of certain concepts are hidden or not explained at all, there is a void between parts of the ggame when it looks like thousands of years have passed while others look like no more than ten years or so there was life there, some bosses may be boring to fight or utterly frustrating to the core (I'm looking at you Bed of Chaos) and the way the game tells you the story is so subtle that is very easy to miss most, if not all, of what is going on.
I like subtle storytelling and "show, dont tell" phylosophy, however this is a little too much. Every character "quest" is optional and at the end of the day everyone dies or gets in terrible situations that you have no choice but to turn around by murdering someone or letting dark forces prevail. The tiniest missing dialogue and a whole quest is lost forever.
Also, the ending is not satisfying as it reduces itself to a 3-seconds long cutscene and that's it. This may be enough for those that simply want to read a good guidebook or lore-frinedly companion book, but if you are playing this for the first time, not only you'll miss much of the story, but almost nothing will be told you directly in any way and you'll more than likely be left in the dark of some major events because of this precise style of storytelling.
If I had to assign a number to my 100+ hours spent on this game, I would gladly remain in the realm of 8+. It may very well be a masterpiece of level design and atmosphere, and a fine example of gameplay on it's own. However, the convoluted story and presentation of it's characters and world, scope and grand scheme of things, is preventing me from giving more, as I felt more of a lack of motivation to play it again rather than getting ready for another try.
For me, it was a grand, unique, beautifully complex, one-time experience.

This game caught me off guard. The mechanics of the game put you both in charge of what to study, somewhat like a teacher, and what to do. The results of your actions are not simply based upon which flags (past choices) you have gotten, but also 'points' in various skills, gained by studying, which determine whether or not certain choices are available, and which ones succeed or fail. The point system common in most western games (implemented very well in Cinders), but this is the first time I've seen it applied like this.
It works well once you get used to it, but at times it lead to disconnects between me and the character. Part of the game becomes you trying to teach Elodie (the queen to be) what she needs to get past some event. Fortunately, there are many ways to overcome these events, like learning bad omens from divination ...or sheer knowledge. It lets the game branch out a bit more organically than specific routes, but at the cost of being able to replay it easily.
I wouldn't say the artwork is bad, I mean it gets the job done... but it does nothing for me. It's cute and inoffensive at best, and bland yet inoffensive at worst. You can gain various outfits for Elodie to wear throughout the game, and they all grant bonuses to a group of stats when you use them. The 'magical girl' outfit irks me as unfitting. The concept of magic in the artwork is easily the weakest part of the aesthetics.
Writing is..decent. The story itself is decent but sometimes I question whether I'm playing as an idiot. Elodie has her own personality which is greatly shown in scenes where you don't have a choice. Apparently she's a young go-getter girl with a strong will, but I have trouble understanding how this young 14 year old *sheltered-all-her-life princess*  could say, after witnessing a killing in front eyes, "Clean this up." (With an angry puffed out manga-style expression, at that!) While on another scene she'd think to herself  "I don't know how to deal with handsome older men paying me compliments!". I think my main complaint about the writing is that age-wise it's inconsistent.
I finished this within 4.4 hours, that is to say, I've gotten to a 'good if bittersweet' end after 10 or so bad ends. The replay value, I'm not too sure. That depends on how many possible routes I missed, which I didn't check too thorougly as I was too focused getting through my current route correctly. I
go back to it sometime.

Maybe you like boredom with 1 minute of excitement or actual fun every hour, but to most people I would definitely not recommend this game and would tell you to look elsewhere.

Before you start reading, this review is hilarious and it's coming from someone who loves survival horror and zombie themed games, so read on, I'm pretty critical in this one and for all the right reasons. :P
So at first glance (over a year ago) I assumed this game was utter♥♥♥♥♥♥ however I decided to purchase it on sale and yeah, my worst fears were brought to fruition within the first 5 minutes of game play.
Long story short, it's abysmal in just about every way. It's incredibly frustrating and unfair, LITERALLY it's an unfair game in just about every aspect... I consider the Dark Souls franchise fair... this game, not so much. It's a game that requires a ton of patience and free time so if you have a day job you might want to get your priorities straight before commiting to surviving a zombie apocalypse.
That aside, I'll explain myself as best I can and give an accurate description based on what I've experienced thus far. It's a mixture of Resident Evil meets GTA meets Friday the 13th (NES) meets a bad Sim game. You switch back and forth between survivors with limited storage space, in a decent sized sandbox world, located on a boring map set taken straight out of Friday the 13th on NES... A giant loop with nothing but nonsense in the middle. While all of this is going on, you command your cronies to build medical centers and workshops so you can get a small perk here and there and keep the loafers alive and well, in case you kick the bucket and need a replacement.
I realized this game was junk within the first few moments when I literally found a large backpack in the first place I searched... wow. Surely this couldn't be the highest storage unit in the game, could it? This early? Yup... I went from 8 slots to 10... that wasn't even enough space in Resident Evil! This game is a sandbox world where scavanging items is imperative to your survival and progression... *shaking head* ridiculous.
So needless to say you spend the first, oh I dunno... 15 HOURS rummaging through dilapitated vacant houses scrounging up PEALS (That's Pills in Louis talk) and bags of chips (or crisps). All the while finding rucksacks full of wood, gas, medicine, dill-doe's etc... It's all junk YOU personally don't need to survive but is required for you to keep your "live stock" healthy. Yes, you only have one life to live in State of Decay and are quickly and easily replaced by your "friends" loafing around at your home base. In the off chance you've researched and upgraded a medical facility, there's a chance you'll be resurrected as long as you didn't blow yourself up with a grenade.
So you basically take this game in very, very, VERY, slow baby steps... pretty much a crawl... until you gather enough resources, weapons and survivors to create a small armada of rootin' tootin' zombie killin' mach-ines. You have to level each character individually as well and equip them with crap you find laying around the world... Which is a fairly hard thing to do considering you need to carry around at least two melee weapons of your own, a gun, some ammo, chips, meds, a distraction item like firecrackers, maybe a pipebomb or grenade... so what does that leave you with? TWO maybe THREE slots to work with? Such an amazing design...
I also love the part where my main character is tired from leveling up his level 7 katana skills and needs to rest for 24 straight hours... WHO THE HELL SLEEPS FOR 24 HOURS!? A hibernating bear, that's who, NOT PEOPLE. So now I have to switch to some noob, who's a complete headcase, that has a level 1 star in blunt weapons and need to start smacking zombies in the face with boards that have nails in them all over again... HOLY HELL this game is OB-NOX-IOUS.
So after it takes you a week (of real time) to ransack the surrounding first suburb you'll slowly realize this game is very time strict (and boring)... Meaning every day (in game) that passes, more resources are being used by your room mates and the surrounding area does not replenish resources... ever. But what does continue to respawn are the zombies... so yeah, again, time is of the essence. If you choose to take too much time or are unlucky enough to not find anything worthwhile, the zombies will just bleed you dry and you'll basically be starting the game over on a new profile... Aren't you grateful this game is SO in touch with what a real Zombie Apocalypse would be like? /sarcasm.
Essentially there are only three giant moves in this game (which is pretty bunk for a game with multiple bases and such NON-LINEAR gameplay...pfffffft) Get your home base established and then as soon as possible, MOVE to the south west warehouse and stay there until the finale... Then you can commandeer the fat palatio estate on military grounds and start bombing these undead ♥♥♥♥S with air strikes. It's a good thing I was able to figure this out quickly otherwise I pity the people who wasted their time moving in slow steps from one portion of the map to another trying to syphon resources around them... not worth it, go big or go home.
Alright on to the controls, they blow pretty hard...nuff said.
The story is garbage as well, it's a virtual scavenger hunt game like Fallout but with more zombies and less giant rad scorpions... save yourself, save others, escape and move on to another infested part of America, the end, you win?....riiiight.
Also zombies clip through walls and doors and evidently have become illusionists because they seem to pop out of thin air like magicians assistants... too bad ammo caches don't do the same. :/
Also be prepared for the inevitable back and forth, driving around in circles from the extreme north end to the extreme south end of the map over and over again until your head wants to explode from all the boring landscape... also the cars in this game are made from cardboard and glue... they blow up so easily it's just insanity.
The topography is just a nightmare as well, indestructable wooden fences, mountains, boulders and trees litter every inch of the map that isn't paved road. So if you expect to take a short cut, expect to ram head first in to a wall or get stranded in a ravine looking for conveniently placed, step shaped rocks you can grapple on to. (In other words, don't explore a game where you're meant to explore)
The graphics are abysmal, the animation is stiff and your character feels like you're driving around the Tin Man from Wizard of Oz... if only the dev's had a brain (I'm aware the scarecrow needed the brain but it's just funnier this way, and definitely more fitting with a game dealing with zombies, so shut your CAKE holes)
All in all, it's great if you liked the tripe that was Friday the 13th on NES because it was so impossibly difficult to conquer without a guide of sorts, this game feels pretty much identical... and looks identical to boot... a gaint circle of BULL♥♥♥♥♥♥and NOTHING, aimlessly wandering around looking for the next piece of candy. If you don't have a plan, and prior knowledge of the layout of the game you've already lost both the game and time... both of which cannot be refunded.
If you're like me and like having games spoon feed you a bit at the start and introduce you to the chaos slowly, so you can, YOU KNOW, actually GIT GUD at it, then you're going to hate this game.
It basically throws you in to a STATE OF DISARRY (wink, wink) and softly says, "Okay A-hole, clean up this mess and maybe then you can start to enjoy killing stuff"...
Just another example of a game with an amazingly profound concept and♥♥♥♥♥♥poor execution... If more thought went in to this, it could be an amazing concept for an MMORPG but as a single player game with randomly respawning zombies, awful controls and combat and limited resources, it's not a good mix.
Rating out of 10: Trash / 10.
I'd rather play Resident Evil 6... and that game is only a step above this at a rating of Ballsack / 10.

This is really an excellent roleplaying game. If you like RPG's in the likes of Baldur's Gate, you'll be right home in Pillars of Eternity. The story is good and got a lot of depth to it if you engage yourself in it. The NPC's that join you each got their own story that you uncover along the way, giving them much more personality.
The game system works very well too and is open to both casual players and min-maxers alike. Classes feels varied, options are many, combat is fun, and there's just a lot of nice features - getting your own home and the side quests that are related to it are one of my favourite features of the game.
You can influence the ending in multiple ways, though looking back, perhaps the main story line is a bit too linear. I would also have liked that the AI automating you can add to your party members in combat was much more advanced, it's just too simple unfortunately. Lastly, it damages the immersion that in dialogue some parts of the dialogue text switch on and off between being narrated and not, it just seems odd that the NPC you talk to is suddenly silent and then talks aloud in the next paragraph.
Still, these are minor things and I really enjoyed the game.

If you liked Neverwinter Nights 1 or 2, or wanted to like them but thought the D&D mechanics of it were overly complicated for a video game (I think they were despite understanding 3.5 Edition D&D rules), then Pillars of Eternity might be for you. It feels like playing a NWN game, but with better combat and less character creation nightmares. I literally spent several hours reading the NWN 1&2 instruction manuals when I was younger, trying to make a character that wasn't awful.
One might think this game has been "dumbed down," but I think a lot of people use that term in the wrong situations. If you want to see something genuinely dumbed down, look at the Fallout 4 dialog system. I enjoyed FO4, but its dialog system takes away tons of choices and stat checks that were allowed to let players have far more control over events in FO3 and especially Fallout New Vegas. In Pillars of Eternity, everything feels like playing a NWN game, except you don't have to deal with so much mathematics and such a large number of skills. However, you still get some nice dialog options in Pillars of Eternity, including attribute checks in them, as well as attribute checks during surprise events, etc.
I likely won't ever complete Pillars of Eternity, but it's not due to any fault of the game or any major issues I have with it that I can't stand. Rather, my impatience is getting the better of me since it's a fairly large game, and I'm craving playing other things far to strongly. For folks who like CRPGs, though, this game should be your jam, and I have absolutely no ill will toward it whatsoever. My time with the game has been enjoyable, and I just keep wanting to play other stuff and that's 100% on me and not because of a lack of interesting content and good combat.
Briefly put, Pillars of Eternity is "legit." The story/lore is fairly interesting, the characters are okay so far, the dungeon/area layouts are quite nice and build up my curiosity while I explore them, and it feels pretty good to play. They even do the spells-per-day thing that D&D does, along with spells-per-battle, and ranged weak magic blasts you can infinitely fire with accuracy decreases to compensate. In my opinion, Pillars of Eternity is basically a better Neverwinter Nights game. Different universe, but clearly that sort of game, and with improvements.

"The Last Chapter" (so is the free dlc called) helps uncovers some more story behind the main character Sgt. Burden and I would even compare the depht of the story to other devolver digital title "Hotline Miami", they both have a story that when finished makes you cofused as hell and realised that you did all of what you did, for nothing basically. This game more leans for existential crisis, thinking of how little you mean in the vast universe.
So now to the gameplay and holy $hit this game is hard on the original difficulty. I being a dude that always picks "normal" when it comes to game difficulty, am a stubborn ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and learn to adapt to the game in order to win, but this game has bested me and I had to lower the difficulty of it, just to barely manage beating it. Now if you hate the RNG this game also has a "puzzle" mode that bypasses as much of rng as possible, to provide you with a more of a puzzle rather than strategy feel. But it ain't just a generic point & click, but rather more of a strategy game on original mode having you manage various resources and people, trying to ensure your survival (in this game most of the people are expendable)
So if you enjoy games that are harder than balls of steel, then this game is for you, just pick a mode that suits you and roll. Also if you're a story type of guy (like me) then this game is also for you, since they even have a "narrative" mode that is like COD and let's you skim through the challenges with ease (It took me ~1hr to beat the game on narrative mode after beating it on original light which took me ~5hrs and a wish to kill myself from all the tries.)

Was it an interesting experience?  I suppose so.  Was the story and setting good?  Sure...that's probably one of the biggest redeeming factors for me, but ultimately just wasn't enough to make me want to recommend this game to others.

The main difference (aside from the addition of the Sorceress as a playable character) is a new upgrade/unlock system based on skulls earned by completing levels. It works pretty well and allows you to customize your characters with the traps and weapons you like the best. Other than that, this is pretty much the same game as OMD1, only with new campaign levels and a series of "endless mode" challenges... so, essentially this is more like OMD1.5 than a full on sequel. That said, I am fine with that at the low asking price. I guess the only negative thing I found was that it seemed like levels were designed for co-op. I was able to complete the game solo, so it's not impossibly difficult, but it definitely would have been easier and more fun with a partner. OMD2 provides a solid few hours of fun, plus lots more for high-score hounds.

I absolutely love this game, and have been ever since I bought it during the alpha in 2013. Even since i first saw the 30 second lighting physics-tech demo before that. I love this game.
That said, there are some flaws with it. Did I get what I was hoping for? Well, yeah, but IMO it had a lot of promise that they decided not to go on. For example a huge official server with race wars, an active online community etc would be such an amazing thing and was kinda what I was expecting. But it's fine that I didn't get that, because what I have right now instead is so much worth the money I spent.
The amount of content in the game is astounding; you never run out of stuff to do or strive for, even after completing the main (although very linear, short and kinda dull for the most part IMHO) story, Ancient Vaults are discovered, maybe you want to make a museum for that insanely large underground city you're building with the very much alive and interactive tenants that you've gotten to settle in. Maybe you want to rebuild the protectorate - which you can now, thanks to this game's insanely wide an easy mod-support.
I have played through this game at least 10 times, every now and then, just to enjoy the new and quite large updates and every single time I find myself to fall in love with the game yet again. Due to the many ways to play it you don't ever have to do one single thing all the time (although usually easiest and fastest to get ores by mining, blueprints by exploring, certain items from quests, etc) which makes it just so much fun, at least for me.
For a person who liked Minecraft at its launch, and played a couple of hundred hours of Terraria (although it has become dull as of late and I do not like the recent additions), I can safely say that if you're into extremely deep and secretive universe-lore, character-lore (it is in there if you look closely enough), open-world sanbox games with hundreds upon thousands if not millions of "unique" worlds to explore, a decent (all be it short and linear, and disappointing in some ways for me) story, many bosses, a very much ALIVE world, then I can say you're going to love this game just as much as I did and that this game is easily worth paying $30 or MORE on. All of this and I didn't even talk about the soundtrack.
The soundtrack is one of the best videogame soundtracks of its sort and I love it so ♥♥♥♥ing much. It is an amazing piece of art, and Curtis Schweizer did an exceptionally amazing job.
So to recap:
Game gets a solid 8.5/9 out of 10, it could go for that 10 depending the quality of the upcoming update and where they wish to take the game.
However; it is DEFINATELY worth buying if you like exploration/sandbox games and making up your own goals. I've played this game a lot and I love it to bits.

I played The Red Solstice a lot during the alpha test, and wrote up an alpha hands-on that explains why I like this game.  Here is the link just in case anyone might find it useful since much of it still applies to the early access test:
What was great about the game then is still great now, and things will improve over time during the early access test.  TRS is a challenging co-op game that pulls no punches.  You will die a lot, and it can be frustrating.  But, at the same time, it can extremely satisfying when your team pulls off a successful run.  Not for the faint of heart or easily frustrated, but highly recommended if you like hectic co-op isometric tactical shooters.
In addition, there is a lot of tactical depth to the game that isn't apparent at first glance.  Having eight classes, each with their own skills, means that team composition can vary widely and be tailored to the strategy.  Faster marines for highly mobile teams and scouting, or slow but heavily armed marines for hunkering down.  Each class shares a global XP rank that benefits all classes, but then has its own XP rank for just that class.  This means that specializing can really pay off in the long run.
In game there is a large number of items that can be found and used (mines, turrets, medical supplies, ammo, tac-nukes, and so on), and proper use of these can also greatly affect the tactics.
All in all, a very exciting nail-biting game.  The early access build is not without some glitches, and it is missing a lot of content, SO KEEP THAT IN MIND before purcahsing the game right now.  Nonetheless I am very much enjoying the game just as much as I did during the alpha.

Ok, this game is not horrible, but it is so lacking in polish and necessary features it's amazing it sells the way it does.
Issues:
1 - No multiplayer: For a game that uses blurbs comparing itself to Left 4 Dead, this is a giant glaring omission.  The devs have stated that they see no way to add this in the future.
2 - Rediculous iniventory system: You cannot trade items with other characters standing right next to you.  You have to switch to their character and loot a container, then switch back to regain control of your main.  Which brings me to...
3 - You cannot switch the character you control once the game decides you are in a "mission":  This drives me nuts.  I'm looting a building, one character fills, and I can't switch to a different character with open inventory standing right next to me.  Why?  becuase the game decided I had started a mission.  It does not matter if the mission takes place a ten minute drive away, and I was switching characters in the same building moments before.  Nope, you're in a MISSION now! Game says you're stuck with one character.
4 - Mandatory hard-core mode: I know this is a port from the 360, but can't console developer realize that PC gamers have the ability to store more than a handful of saves on their drives?  Autosaves only, and no loads.  This can be fun, but a player doesn't always want to be playing in hardcore mode.
5 - Consolitius of the keyboard: If you want to play with your keyboard, you're out of luck.  Take crouching for example.  You hold the crouch button on the 360 controller and it TOGGLES crouch.  If you want to use the keyboard, you have to HOLD the crouch button to remain in stealth mode.  Another example of the devs honestly not caring about the PC port.
6 - Massive clipping issues: Seriously, you'll see zombies walking at you bisected by fences, walking knee-deep in fallen logs and head passing through overhaninging branches.  Clipping is a joke.
Mind you, these are just issues I've had shoved in my face after playing a LITTLE OVER AN HOUR.
This game is mediocre at best, and doesn't hold a candle to Left 4 Dead, Dead Island or Walking Dead.  Heck, Project Zomboid is crafted with far more love.
However, it's still better than Infestation: Survivor Stories.

Not a bad game, per se - the story is deep and very well-told. This definitely addresses some very important subject matter in a very down-to-earth way. Most of the major characters in this game are very relateable, especially given what they've been through/are going through. For that matter, the town of Possum Springs is very well crafted - it gives off a real Central PA vibe, speaking as someone from that area. Also, I just have to point out that the music is catchy as ♥♥♥♥. Some of the best music I've heard in a video game (especially an indie game) in a long time. This is something the devs put a lot of thought into, and it shows.
That said, there are quite a few areas in which this game is lacking. I think the idea of the various 'alternative storylines/endings' was a bit overbilled. While the game does offer some options in terms of your actions throughout the story, they don't really have much of an impact on the overall storyline. Also, various scenes are constructed to make it look like you have a choice whether or not to do something that you really don't have a choice. Even worse, there are some scenes where you have dialogue options where you're given the option to say something that clearly *looks* better in the given scenario only to have Mae follow that up with something that drops the situation back to what it was before, if not something worse. I'd say this definitely ruined a lot of the immersion for me.
Also, I'd like to say that for all the characters you get to interact with, you're only really given the option to spend a lot of time with 2 (maybe 3 if you choose to) :/ I really wish more thought had been put into some of the characters other than Mae's immediate family/two closest friends. Finally, I will definitely say one of the game's worst flaws, IMO, is the 'day' structure. Basically, you wake up one day, you have 1-2 specific events that you're supposed to complete, and completing those ends the day, and each day only progresses the story a very small amount. This causes the story to really drag - especially anything happening outside of Mae. For instance, there's a storyline which you get a teaser for very early on (day 2 or so), which is only mentioned in passing until it hits a climax right at the end of the game. Seriously, this could have been built up a lot more IMO.
Overall, good game, love the music, like the story but has some serious pacing issues and 'illusion of choice' scenarios for my taste.

It's like Street Fighter IV but Ultra.

Remember all the great fun you had playing Karate, Swordfight at Midnight, Fighting Road, and Super Black Belt Karate???  Of course you don't.  Why??  Because they all sucked a mile of chicken butt.  There's actually a long list of fighting games that have been put out to the masses over the years but only a choice few actually stand out amongst all the others as great and memorable fighting games.  Ultra Street Fighter IV along with the majority of the Street Fighter franchise is one of those few.  Pop quiz time...... Name all the current Ultra Street Fighter IV characters that also appeared in the original 1987 release of Street Fighter.  I'll give you the answer at the end.
If you've never played a Street Fighter games now is a great time to try your hand at it.  Controls are smooth and easy to grasp with a little work.  Gameplay is realitively easy to grasp but difficult to master, which in my opinion is a mark of a great game.  Online play seems to be smooth and there's plenty to do solo too as no two fights, online or off, will ever be the same.  With all the different characters in USFIV there's bound to be at least one character you side with,  As a matter of fact, there's so many different characters that if there was a downside it's that it's hard to settle in on  just one fighter if you'r new.
If you have played Street Fighter games before then what are you waiting for?  There's a fairly good chance at least one of your favorite characters from a previous version is just waiting for you to use them in a fight.  All your old memorized combos, supers, are still here and most likely use the same movements and button combos to execute.  And if you're looking for something new there's plenty of new and new/old characters too as well as some new moves and ultras.  This has certainly got to be one of the prettiest looking Street Fighters to date.  Colors pop, backgrounds look amazing and have loads of funny/interesting characters in them, and every character has several different DLC costumes you can buy if you so choose.  Other than the cosmetic character costumes though there's no game changing DLC within USFIV so yo don't need to worry about pay to win junk here.
Overall the game looks and plays amazing and is great fun.  Since you can also play two player on the same screen/PC it also makes a great party game and looks amazing on a nice big screen TV or monitor.  If there was one major downside it would be that the game doesn't play well with a keyboard/mouse or a standard Xbox controller.  You can do it sure, but you'll most likely be at a disadvantage when playing against someone who has invested in and trained on a fightpad, fightstick, or one of the newer hitbox controllers.  Owning one of those types of controllers though opens up a world of other interesting gaming on Steam though as all fighting games and many other arcade style games found on Steam just feel better when you use one with it.
So the answer to the question at the top:  Ryu, Ken, Gen, Adon, and Sagat.  There was also another character named Mike who greatly resembles the boxer Balrog so I guess he gets a half point...  Another character from the original Street Fighter named Eagle also appeared in Capcom vs SNK but not in USFIV.  There's your history lesson for today folks...
